Grief, trauma and solidarity as South African running club mourns member killed in wave of femicides
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
04:00:35 UTC
13:00:35 KST

The runners smiled and laughed, congratulating each other on finishing their 5km or 10km Saturday run, their foreheads glistening with sweat in the early morning sun. They helped themselves to water, instant coffee and sugary snacks, provided by waiting volunteers on the lawn outside a gated community of modern apartment blocks, and then stretched out together.
But there were sombre moments too, as they mourned one of their own, who had lit up their Saturday runs around Sandton, an upmarket area of Johannesburg. Elizabeth “Tsontso” Moselakgomo’s body had been found a week earlier, on Saturday 12 September. The 38-year-old went missing three days earlier, after going out for a run alone after work.
South Africa has been overwhelmed with shock, anger and grief at the discovery of nine women’s bodies dumped across Ekurhuleni, the municipality adjoining Johannesburg to the east, since 15 July. Six of the women were found in the last two weeks and two still have not been formally identified. Suspects have been arrested in two of the cases.
South Africa has one of the world’s highest rates of femicide. Women were killed at a rate of 12.2 per 100,000 people in 2022, nearly six times the global rate, according to the UN Office on Drugs and Crime.
Across the country, protesters have marched and running clubs have gathered to demand that police and the national government, which declared gender-based violence a national crisis in November 2025, do more to protect women.
“This has really affected all of us,” Moselakgomo’s friend Sakane Mokoena said to her fellow runners, as they stood in a circle with their arms around each other’s shoulders. “I really want to thank each and every one of you for honouring Tsontso’s name. She really came and ran with us. She was an amazing lady.”
Mokoena then thanked the men who ran with the majority female club, acknowledging that some slowed their pace every week to make sure that no woman was left behind. The group then bowed their heads for a moment’s silence.
“It’s traumatic, scary, confusing,” said Sange, a female runner, who only wanted to share her first name. “Before I joined this group, I was running alone for years in this area … in the mornings, early winter mornings, late winter nights, and with music, earphones in my ears. You know, anything could have happened to me.”
“There’s no scenario where women are prioritised,” she said. “The government doesn’t take us seriously. The men of South Africa don’t take themselves seriously. They don’t take us seriously. It’s just dangerous to be a woman in South Africa and it’s very sad to be a woman in South Africa.”
The club first came back together to run on 15 September, after Moselakgomo’s body was identified by her family.
“I think we all needed that Tuesday run, because we were all sad,” said Nokwanda, who has been running with the group since February last year. “And then we met as a community. And after that, I think we are getting there.”
She called on all men to take responsibility for violence against women: “We as women have been fighting for our safety. I think it would be nice to see men fighting and not men saying ‘some men’, but standing up for women.”
Thabiso, who had volunteered to provide the post-run refreshments instead of running, agreed. “If there’s a message that I can send out to other men is to be better,” he said. “I think as brothers and men, we need to really leave the animalistic ways behind us. There’s much better ways that we can build a society and we need to not be making these women feel like the country’s so bad.”
Meanwhile, the families of the murdered women found across Ekurhuleni are still struggling to come to terms with their loss. Ayanda Nano was admitted to hospital in shock at how her cousin, 38-year-old Dineo Motapane, who she had grown up with, was discovered.
“The state she was in is what put me in this hospital bed,” Nano, who is now raising Motapane’s two-year-old daughter, told the local Sunday World newspaper. “She was decomposed, like she had been dead for days. It pains me that she left us this way.”
At Moselakgomo’s funeral which was broadcast by South Africa’s national TV news channels, her eight-year-old daughter, dressed in a pale pink padded jacket, took the microphone.
“Dearest mother, how heartbreaking that you left me,” she said. “The day feels quiet without your voice. But your love is still here, surrounding me with love … Your beautiful daughter loves you so much. She misses you every day. But I know that I have gained a beautiful angel in you. Love your beautiful princess, Khumo.”

====================================================================================================

A tale of two trap houses: being cuckooed ruined my friend’s life – but did it then help save him?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
04:00:34 UTC
13:00:34 KST

Duncan is a good friend of mine. He looks like a Dickensian rock’n’roller: tall and skinny, long hair, retro clothes. He’s read the Flashman novels three times. We met in secondary school in west London in the early 1980s. We got drunk, smoked Rothmans and banana skin spliffs and played Dungeons & Dragons. At 14, we got into punk together and spent our teens playing music and seeing live bands. As we moved into our 20s, I trained as a journalist and Duncan, a talented songwriter and guitarist, carried on with music.
At the age of 23 he got involved in heroin. He found the lifestyle immediately seductive, his partner at the time, Lucy, told me. He would often befriend his dealers. “I remember more than once waiting in his car as he’d gone up some tower block to score, thinking where on earth is he?” Lucy said. “He’d be hanging out chatting. There were some genuinely fascinating characters with incredible stories to tell.”
We kept in touch. By the 2000s, after a few near fatal overdoses, it became obvious he had a long-term drug problem. But at the end of the decade, when Duncan was in his late 30s, his life changed when his then-partner gave birth to a boy. He was a natural father, becoming a full-time dad when his partner returned to work after maternity leave. Love and dedication to his son reduced Duncan’s drug use, but did not entirely dislodge it.
In 2013, he swapped the west London council flat he had been subletting for a nicer, ground floor studio apartment in a council estate in north-east London, near where his partner and young son now lived. By this time, Duncan was what drug experts call a “functioning” heroin user, managing his addiction with methadone while living a relatively stable life. He was working as a painter and decorator, played in a band that toured the US, and remained a dedicated dad. He got a job as a teaching assistant, helping some of the most troubled kids in the borough, which he loved.
His friends regularly spent time at his flat, which he had turned into his own, homely space. He had repainted his bedroom-lounge, and filled it with his collection of trinkets, retro furniture, artwork, vinyl record collection and a huge plant. His mother visited, his son regularly stayed the night and I crashed on the couch a few times.
By 2015, even while house prices were rocketing in trendy areas a few streets away, Duncan’s estate became neglected and scary at night. Families moved out and were replaced by single tenants leaving prison and care. Eventually, the estate was officially condemned by the council, which planned to decant tenants into a new estate being built a mile away. Duncan had watched as a group of noisy local kids had grown up into a gang of aggressive teenage drug dealers. They were made up of about a dozen boys and young men from the estate and the surrounding area, most aged around 15 to 17, and some as young as 12.
Coming home in the evening, Duncan would find the gang, dressed in black joggers and puffer jackets, hanging around the stairwell selling crack and heroin. “Sometimes, something, or somebody, would get thrown against my window,” said Duncan. “A couple of times I heard someone who got a really bad kicking from them, whimpering outside and I phoned an ambulance. They were horrible cunts.”
Within a year, Duncan’s home would be doubling up as the gang’s drug dealing base.
Over the past 30 years, the British “trap house”, slang for a place used as a drug dealing base, has evolved. Rather than derelict crack houses, drug gangs now prefer to operate from a hidden countrywide network of vulnerable people’s homes that they have taken over in a process known as “cuckooing”.
The origins of this shift go back to the 1990s, when a new wave of professionalised drug dealing crews spread out across the country. Their growth was fuelled by two products that were transforming Britain’s drug trade: crack and mobile phones. Blackberries and Nokias had enabled buyers and sellers to arrange transactions in less visible locations, and dealers now started to expand their operations, using a system of young runners who would call in orders and deliver the drugs.
In Brighton, a gang called the Londoners moved their drug sales teams off the streets and into the homes of local people, where they could more easily operate away from the prying eyes of police and rival gangs. When 10 of the Londoners were jailed in 2000, along with a man whose home they had taken over, a fresh gang from south London arrived to fill the gap. “I was buying crack and heroin from 15- and 16-year-old south London boys on BMXs in 2001,” Pete, a former Brighton street drug user told me in 2018. “I thought, fuck, you’re young. They would come down on the train and set up flats with heroin users.”
Over the 2000s and 2010s, wave after wave of gangs fanned out from Britain’s drug supply hubs – London, Liverpool and Birmingham – to set up shop in smaller towns and cities across the country. They took over the homes of drug users and young women who had been groomed by older male gang members. As early as 2008 Suffolk constabulary reported that more than a third of Class A drug dealers arrested in Suffolk were under 21, and the majority were from London. (Before this period, most crack and heroin dealers in towns and smaller cities were “user-dealers”, addicted heroin users in their 30s or older, who were not as “professionalised” as the big city drug gangs.) Gangs often used sex workers, who targeted male tenants and moved in, bringing the young dealers with them. Community safety teams, who rescued 80 tenants in London in 2005, were the first to call the tactic “cuckooing”.
In 2015, the National Crime Agency published an intelligence assessment that belatedly acknowledged “cuckooing” was part of “an emerging criminal business model”, whereby young people were being sent by drug gangs to sell out of town, which they dubbed “county lines”. By 2018, children who were described as “missing” in their local papers could now sometimes be found on Snapchat waving wads of notes, boasting to their classmates about their out-of-town moneymaking adventures “going country”. Rap lyrics, particularly drill music – where victims of cuckooing were denigrated as “fiends”, “cats” or “nitties” – soundtracked and glamourised the rise of the British trap house.
The reality was far more bleak: children hanging out in dingy flats with ageing drug injectors, earning far less than they had hoped and living in daily fear of being jumped by police, or worse, rival gangs. The whole system was reliant on grooming and exploitation. Over the years, reporting on Britain’s drug trade, I’ve spoken to several young drug dealers and cuckooed tenants about what it was like for them. One boy from Liverpool sold drugs from cuckooed homes in Devon, staying in a middle-aged crack user’s flat when he was 14. There was mould, “a plant growing out the wall” and the place was so dirty he ended up cleaning it himself. He smoked weed “to take the smell of crack away”. Another teenager from London, from a strict religious Nigerian family, worked 15-hour days from cuckooed flats in the east of England for three years. He told his parents he was on football trips or staying with friends; in reality he was holed up with drug users and armed with a machete.
A former sex worker and crack user I spoke to, whose home in Southend was cuckooed, actually felt sorry for the young dealers camped out in her flat. “They used to lie on my settee and sleep with the phone by their head, working 22 hours a day. They were putting on an act, trying to pretend they were the big boys, but they were young kids getting exploited.”
Cuckooing can involve sexual and financial grooming, the targeting of disabled and mentally ill people, people in private rented properties in affluent neighbourhoods, and even relatives and carers of gang members. In one case, said Insp Andrew Cameron of Operation Pantera, which was aimed at tackling the problem in London, a nephew cuckooed his aunt’s house for a south London drug gang. In another, a care worker cuckooed the home of a patient, who was tortured with cigarette burns and beaten by drug dealers. One particularly grim case involved William Algar, a 53-year-old jazz trumpeter from Barnes, south-west London, who had mental health and drug problems. In 2019, his home was cuckooed by a gang of drug dealers. He fell out with one of them over money, and the dealer threatened to kill his cat. After Algar’s sister reported him missing, police found his severed head and torso in the flat, and the rest of his body in a park. He had been stabbed to death with a zombie knife and dismembered in his own bath.
Jack Spicer, a lecturer in criminology at the University of Bath and author of Cuckoo Land, has interviewed many victims of cuckooing. What makes the practice so insidious, he says, is that for many victims there is nowhere to run. Yet Spicer also notes that in some cases, cuckooing can be a more complex scenario than is commonly understood: “From the perspective of an outsider looking in, cuckooing can take on a seductively simplistic appearance: the ‘evil’ drug dealer duping the vulnerable user of drugs, the naive local resident opening their door to the dangerous outsider. At best these tell only a partial story.”
That helps explain why Duncan, a musician, artist and father, ended up opening his doors to drug gangs – not once but twice – and why his two experiences turned out to be so different. The first brought him only misery; the second, in his telling at least, brought him a strange kind of friendship.
Life started unravelling for Duncan in 2016. His girlfriend left him and his close friend, the band’s singer, died of cancer. He was fired from his teaching job after his drug treatment service informed the school that he was in rehab. Losing his job made him particularly bitter. His drug use increased. He stopped returning his friends’ calls and saw less of his son.
Before, he had no reason to interact with the estate’s teenage gang. He bought his drugs – methadone, with a bit of heroin and crack on the side as a treat – from a trusted seller back west. But in January 2017, during a cold snap, Duncan offered shelter in his flat to two heroin users who had been sleeping rough in a tent in a nearby snow-covered graveyard. Patrick, a beggar from Bristol, took the kitchen floor and Josef, an unemployed Polish stonemason, took the living room sofa. “The estate was feeling more and more threatening during that time,” said Duncan. “I felt safer with those two around.” But his two lodgers bought drugs from the gang on Duncan’s estate, and he became a regular buyer, too.
Around this time, Chloe, a school teacher and friend of Duncan’s, began to worry about him. The two of them had been in a relationship for a period, and after they split, they remained friends. To her, he was “the loveliest person in the world – caring, kind and creative”. When they were together, she never saw him taking heroin, but she knew he did. So when he stopped returning her calls, she went round to check on him. The door was answered by a man she recognised as Patrick, the train station beggar, who nervously told her Duncan was out. When she later saw Duncan in the street, he ran off. “I was thinking, what is going on here?” she recalled.
One day, in the summer of 2017, one of the boys from the estate gang knocked and asked if his pregnant girlfriend could use Duncan’s toilet. From then on, said Duncan, the gang’s presence in the flat “escalated”. First it was repeated visits to charge phones or use the toilet. Then, as autumn approached and the weather got worse, the gang made Duncan an offer: £30 worth of crack and heroin a day for the use of his flat as a drug dealing base. He found himself agreeing.
“They had something to offer,” said Duncan, who had developed a debilitating leg wound from years injecting in his groin. “I’d wrecked my health and couldn’t work much so I needed the freebies. Heroin makes you quite fearless. It makes you feel as though you can cope with anything, but it also imbues a certain amount of recklessness. The strangest situations start to seem normal very quickly.”
The gang – a mix of Asian, black and white teenagers – was in and out of his home from about 10.30 in the morning, when one of the senior members would drop off the drugs stash, until late at night. A trio of slightly older gang members, aged about 16 and 17, made him feel particularly uneasy. The younger dealers would all be paid at his flat by a senior gang member in the afternoon. Usually there were only one or two of them there at once, but sometimes his home was packed. They used the flat as a base for dealing crack and heroin, to relax, prepare drugs for sale and to stash their zombie knives.
Duncan said some of the younger dealers were respectful, and that “three or four of the little soldiers were alright to chat to”. He would shoot up while the young gang members were in his flat, trying to find a vein in his groin or his leg. “All that stuff frightened those kids and probably disgusted them, so it kept them at a distance,” he told me. One of the gang would use the bathroom after dropping off the stash in the morning, always leaving the toilet seat covered in carefully laid out layers of tissue.
Without work, and with a constant supply of free crack and heroin, Duncan’s life became dominated by getting high and waiting to get high. And as time passed, the cuckooing turned nastier. “Some of the younger ones were fascinated with knives, they liked to pretend to stab me. They thought it was funny,” he recalled. “Sometimes they poked me with the tips. They didn’t mean it, I don’t think. I got lots of small cuts, it wasn’t too bad. One time they were playing and one of them stabbed me quite deep in the leg. I don’t know why.”
One of the gang’s associates forced Duncan to register a car in his name that was then used to sell drugs. The car accrued a string of fines and was written off in an accident. The debts fell on Duncan.
After a string of complaints from other residents, in early 2018 the police warned Duncan that if he continued to let the gang use his flat he could lose his tenancy. By this time, he was too scared to stop them. According to internal local authority case notes, one housing officer messaged colleagues in February 2018 to say that council staff were themselves scared to visit Duncan’s flat: “Attended flat and went in for short while only … didn’t feel it was very safe. Duncan said he is desperate to move out as soon as possible as drug gang is using his flat whenever they want.” (The council later launched an investigation into its management of Duncan’s tenancy.)
In April, the police emailed the council to say that it was no longer safe for Duncan to stay in the flat because he was being cuckooed. “We are getting inundated with complaints from neighbours. He needs moving urgently in my opinion,” one email reported. “I’ll try and keep an eye on the address although it’s difficult to visit Duncan as he doesn’t like police being seen walking into his property, which I can totally understand. The gang in question seem to have eyes everywhere on that estate.”
That month, Duncan was talking to a housing officer at his front door about how he wanted to move off the estate because he was scared of the gang. Some of the gang were listening from the stairwell and wrongly presumed Duncan was talking to a police officer. They put the word out that they would kill Duncan. Later that week he was cycling near his home when someone jumped out of a car and shouted: “You fucking grass we’re going to kill you.” “I knew I had to get out of that flat,” said Duncan.
A few days later, a place in an emergency homeless hostel was found for him in the east of the borough. Duncan packed what possessions he could into one of his key worker’s cars and left the place he’d made home for six years. His flat, which contained the rest of his belongings, was secured with heavy duty steel panels.
The relief of escaping the gang did not last long. In the dingy, crowded hostel, Duncan’s mental health was already deteriorating, when one day he received a call from the council. They told him that, owing to a communication error, they had accidentally sent all the possessions he had left in his flat for incineration. This was not just furniture, but smaller things of great sentimental value, such as his son’s childhood drawings, his own artwork, treasured LPs and keepsakes. Duncan was heartbroken. He told his housing officer it was one of the worst things that had ever happened to him.
Duncan’s friends had no idea where he had fled to. “This cuckooing thing had obliterated his life, but he totally disengaged with us all during that period,” said Billie, a fellow punk musician who’d known Duncan since the early 1990s. It took her six months to trace him to the hostel. After hearing snippets of information about his perilous health, she left him messages there, but heard nothing. “That was the first time since I’ve known him where I thought: ‘Oh my God, the wheels have completely come off.’ I really think we could have actually lost him then,” she told me.
After 10 months in the hostel, in 2019 he was eventually rehoused in a decent one-bedroom flat in a low-rise estate in a quieter, more suburban part of the borough. But he found it hard to start anew. Debt collectors were chasing him for fines and damage to the cars the gang rented out in his name, and because of the threats to his life, he was scared to go to the part of the borough where his son lived, and where his drug treatment service was.
Worried about him, in March 2019, a friend and I drove to his flat to see how he was. Inside, it was a mess. A bowl filled with stinking, mouldy fruit sat on the table. Duncan seemed to be living on a diet of Shreddies and milk with jam mixed in. He was convinced he had parasites under his skin, in his hair, and in his blood, a feeling that can be triggered by long-term crack use. We took him to hospital for some check-ups, particularly on the large injecting wound on his leg, for which he started to receive treatment.
In between Covid lockdowns he was able to move more freely around the borough, after most of the teenage gang that cuckooed him were arrested. We met a couple of times as he started taking action against the council, with the help of a lawyer, for destroying his possessions. After several months of legal wrangling, he was awarded a good chunk of money, which he mainly spent on an array of beautiful guitars and drugs. He drifted away from his friends again.
Then, in November 2024, I got a call from Duncan. He told me he felt really lonely and he wanted to meet up. He explained that over the past three years, he’d built a close bond with someone, but that person had just been sent to prison. Anyone I know, I asked? No, he replied, it was a drug dealer who had been using his house as a base for his business for the previous three years. I couldn’t believe it. But this time, as Duncan explained over a fry-up in a local cafe, wasn’t like the last one.
Compared with the teenagers on Duncan’s old estate, the second gang, which I’ll call the T-Line, was a more professional outfit. It ran a sizeable chunk of the heroin and crack trade in this part of north-east London. It was led by an experienced dealer in his early 40s. A confident, charming east Londoner, Tony was a well-known figure in the borough’s drug trade. Duncan had bought drugs from him while he was living in the homeless hostel. “He’s a personable kind of bloke,” Duncan told me. “He’s ingratiating. He liked sharing recipes and he liked my artwork. We just clicked, I guess.”
The first time Tony had visited him at home, he noticed portraits Duncan had painted of his own family. Tony said he liked them, and paid Duncan to paint a picture of his own two young sons. There was another thing Tony liked about Duncan’s flat: it would make an ideal trap house. The estate was low key, plus Duncan was one of his calmer, more reliable customers. He could be counted upon to keep quiet. The few times Tony’s crew had been round Duncan’s flat, he had seemed unfazed.
Tony suggested a deal: free daily crack and heroin in return for the flat being used as the gang’s secret weighing and stash house. So in 2021, for the second time in the space of three years, Duncan opened his home to a drug dealing gang. And when Tony asked him if he wanted to help prepare the drugs for sale, in return for more crack. Duncan knew that, legally speaking, doing so would change him from a passive victim to a willing offender. If he was caught he could be kicked out of his council flat and sent to prison. Even so, he said yes.
Duncan’s coffee table was repurposed as a drug processing station. Every day Tony, who now had keys to the flat, arrived at about 11.30am on his scooter with kilo bricks of heroin and crack, usually leaving around midnight. They worked long days together at the flat. It was Duncan’s job to weigh out and line up hundreds of 0.1 gram “shots” of each drug, ready to be wrapped into bags for street sale. Duncan estimates he helped cut and weigh about 5,000 “shots” of heroin and crack every week. Surrounded by enough narcotics to get the whole neighbourhood high, Duncan would have a regular puff on his crack pipe, part of his daily drug wage. “It was therapeutic for me,” he said. “I’d do 100 shots and have a pipe and do another 100 and so on.” As Duncan sorted out the drugs, Tony would be shouting via speakerphone, bossing his underlings.
Members of Tony’s crew came and went throughout the day. The longer the T-Line was camped out at his flat, the more Duncan found himself involved in its day-to-day business. “I did quite a lot of stuff for him like you would do with a friend,” said Duncan. “I tested his gear for him, I opened bank accounts he could use.”
Tony’s world was full of risk and violence, yet amid this dark backdrop, grew a friendship “built through a kind of domesticity”, according to Duncan. Tony brought a packed lunch, usually Jamaican food made by his sister or mother, which he put in the fridge. Sometimes while Tony coordinated drug deals over the phone, and after Duncan had finished dividing up the crack and smack, Duncan painted pictures for Tony.
“I used to tidy the house for him,” recalled Duncan. “I felt privileged to be accepted, and proud he was friends with me. He would make me look after myself. On my own, I couldn’t be bothered, but he got me together.” Even though he provided Duncan with a constant supply of class A drugs, Duncan said Tony “tried to discourage me from using drugs so much”, and “encouraged me to eat better – he was always feeding me his mum’s food”.
As they weighed and bagged drug deals, with Duncan sat at the coffee table and Tony at the small dining table, they talked about everything from conspiracy theories and the causes of poverty in Britain’s black community to their hopes for the future, and their pasts. Tony liked to get involved in every conversation. “He would never shut up, so I went out of the room to make calls.”
Tony told Duncan he grew up in poverty with a “wasteman” dad and had been selling drugs since he was a teenager. His chief motivation was to give his children, who he said were both in private school and the only two black kids in their class, a life different from his own. “He told me he was always going to go a bit further, take more risks, than the police chasing him because he was doing it for his kids, and the cops didn’t have as much to lose as he did.”
But Tony had a plan. By Christmas 2024, he said, he would call time on his drug dealing career. He had prepared the ground by setting up a catering truck and a semi-legitimate transport business. Come the following year, he would start anew.
The problem was that in 2023, things had started to unravel for the T-Line. A rival drug crew started ramming T-Line scooter riders off the road. They responded by squirting their attackers with ammonia. The beef was halted only after Tony contacted a criminal associate who warned the rival gang that there would be lethal consequences unless they backed down. Then Kane, Tony’s lieutenant who distributed the T-Line’s drugs to street dealers, was arrested for running a drug network in Norwich. Tony took on more responsibility, including doing more of the “road work”, moving drugs around the neighbourhood himself by scooter.
“It made him more exposed,” said Duncan. “He was getting more abrasive, more anxious, shouting at people more on the phone. He was very stressed. I told him not to bring bad energy into my place. He said he would try to keep calm, but he couldn’t.” When Duncan discovered that Tony had been hiding bricks of crack and heroin in his flat, he started stealing bits for himself, reasoning it was in his house after all. When Tony found out, they had fierce rows. “I said, if you don’t like it, don’t come back. But he would come back because it was the perfect house.”
Within the space of a few months in mid-2024, both of them came within inches of death. Duncan collapsed at his flat. He had contracted septicaemia after his injection wound became infected, and doctors told him he was lucky to survive. Not long after, Tony confronted a gang of teenagers trying to steal his scooter and was stabbed four times. Lying in the street, bleeding heavily, Tony managed to call a friend, who came to the scene, lifted him into a car and took him to casualty. “When I saw him a few weeks later we hugged. I was really happy to see him,” said Duncan.
Tony was getting increasingly nervous about being caught. He had been in prison three times for dealing. He was getting too old for jail, he told Duncan. He “didn’t have the energy for it” and dreaded being separated from his boys. His retirement date was coming closer.
One day in November 2024, Tony didn’t turn up at his usual time. Later that day Duncan got a phone call from one of the gang to say he’d been arrested after a police helicopter pursuit. Duncan was gutted for him. He was also thinking that, if the police had been keeping Tony under surveillance, his flat would be next. Yet as the days went by, alone at home, it wasn’t fear that he felt, but an intense loneliness.
Before Tony’s arrest, Duncan had ended his “love affair” with crack. It no longer agreed with his body, he felt. He also cut down from two grams of heroin a day to half a gram. “For the first time, it felt like it was holding me back,” he said.
Today, a year and a half later, it seems like Duncan has never been better. He’s eating well and looking after his health. He’s ditched his sometimes curmudgeonly attitude, he has his addiction under control, and he’s seeing his family and friends more than he has done for a decade.
Duncan believes his friendship with Tony helped him turn his life around. “The most obvious way he helped me was by bringing food from home,” he said. “Good home-cooked food. So my diet improved and I got a taste for Caribbean food. Music too. We listened to a lot of music and he turned me on to stuff I’d not heard before. Having a guest come to my home made me look after the place and myself more, and the work, although pretty tedious, was something to try to be good at, so that was positive too. I felt part of something, and part of a team.”
It’s hard to comprehend how Duncan, who had helpful, open-minded friends with money in their bank accounts, would be aided most by someone most people considered his biggest threat. But, in Duncan’s telling, this is exactly what happened. Tony “helped me to pull my socks up, so to speak”, he said. Behind his day job as a drug dealer, according to Duncan, Tony was essentially a businessman, a family man, a nice guy. “Well, it’s an odd person who only has one side to their character, wouldn’t you say?” said Duncan.
There are indeed nice drug dealers, I’ve met many myself. I’ve met some nasty ones too. People do not like to see themselves as being exploited, and Duncan denies he was manipulated. He said the two of them had a genuine friendship, and that if he had wanted Tony to stop using his home, he would have complied. But some of Duncan’s friends have a different take.
Chloe, the teacher, met Tony by accident one day in 2024. After hearing that Duncan had been in hospital and having not seen him in two years, she called round to his flat to check he was OK. As they chatted over tea, the front door opened and Tony let himself in. Chloe was surprised, and so was Tony. She was scared, not because of Tony himself, but because she knew it was drug business. “Duncan really likes Tony,” said Chloe, “but if you’re storing your illegal drugs in someone else’s house, if you’re asking them to do something in return for a thing they cannot resist. There’s a power imbalance; you are definitely the boss”.
Cuckooing is now a specific criminal offence, after the Crime and Policing Act took effect this year. But experts say it will not be stopped so simply. A rise in “deep poverty”, tracked in the Joseph Rowntree Foundation’s 2026 report, has led to more people living highly precarious, marginalised lives in deprived areas. These people are easy targets for cuckooing.
Drug gangs are increasingly targeting people’s homes in cities such as London, Bristol and Leeds. Operation Pantera recorded 1,539 cases of cuckooing in the capital between May 2025 and April 2026. Two years earlier, cuckooing had been flagged by the Met in just 380 investigations. In Leeds, cuckooing is now a major cause of vulnerable people being evicted from their homes.
Tony was sentenced to three years in prison in early 2025, but he and Duncan still chat on the phone, mainly about local gossip. Now and then Duncan buys things online on Tony’s behalf, which a friend of Tony’s will pick up and deliver to him. Sometimes Tony sounds downbeat, says Duncan, but he also talks about his kids, and plans for a future outside the drug business. During a day release in August, Tony paid Duncan a brief visit. “He’d obviously been working out inside, he was huge,” said Duncan. “He told me I looked really skinny and to put on some weight. It was really lovely to see him, he was smiling and we hugged.”
Tony is due to be released in a year or so. I asked Duncan what he would do if Tony wanted to use his home again as a drug dealing base. “I’d say no. I’ve got other things to do in my life now,” he replied. “I couldn’t give him the time he’d need off me.”
Their friendship was partly a matter of timing. “What [Tony] gave me at that time was a purpose,” Duncan said. “There seemed to be more regard for me as an artist and musician within his community than I’d ever felt before and my experience and knowledge of drugs was valued too. It was flattering to be respected like that and to be accepted into that world. And it was exciting.”
Like many of his friends, Billie the guitarist is delighted that Duncan is doing so well. She thinks that his turnaround was more to do with his wound finally healing in 2024 than his friendship with a drug dealer. And she’s scared. “He’s very positive about this person, and they probably saw it as a mutually beneficial relationship, but to me this was complete parasiticism. Hearing that he’s going to come out soon actually worries me a lot. I want to just keep on telling him, think about your son.”
I asked Duncan if he and Tony would still be friends when Tony gets out of prison. He said yes, but only to a point. “As close as we were, there was always a distance he kept between us,” said Duncan. “He never acknowledged his real name, he never told me it or allowed me to call him it. He kept up this pretence that we never actually knew each other well, a bit like people having an affair.”
All names have been changed

Briton due to face Cypriot court after tragic death of two-year-old son
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
04:00:33 UTC
13:00:33 KST

A British father is expected to appear in court in Cyprus accused of “recklessly” causing the death of his two-year-old son, who was fatally injured falling from a fourth-floor window.
The 37-year-old, who has not been named publicly, was on the first day of a family holiday in Paphos on 12 July when the toddler died.
At 9am on Tuesday, 10 weeks after his son’s death, the distraught City executive will appear before the resort town’s district court to answer a charge that until last week he hoped would be suspended.
“My client’s disappointment is obvious,” his lawyer, Alexandros Alexandrou, told reporters after the island’s top legal official rejected an appeal to discontinue the procedure on humanitarian grounds. “He is not in a good way.”
A desperate plea for George Savvides, the attorney general of Cyprus, to intervene was the last hope of a reprieve for a family still reeling from the “unimaginable loss”.
“In these exceptional circumstances, we do not believe a continued criminal process serves the public interest,” said Alexandrou. “The focus now should be on [the family’s] welfare and recovery.”
The toddler’s father was inconsolable when he appeared in the same courtroom to be formally charged in July.
After posting €30,000 (£26,100) in bail to return to the UK to attend the toddler’s funeral in August, the father was forced under threat of extradition to return to Cyprus and surrender his passport by 14 September.
In a move that has stirred further debate over the way Cypriot authorities have handled the case, state prosecutors, addressing Paphos’ district court last week, said while Savvides recognised the father’s grief, it was a matter of “public interest” that the criminal proceedings went ahead.
If convicted, the defendant, described as a banker at one of the big four accountancy firms, faces a maximum sentence of four years in prison.
He now confronts the agonising choice of either pleading not guilty – which will open the way to a trial expected to last months – or entering a guilty plea in the hope that the court will take mitigating circumstances into account at sentencing.
In the event of a criminal trial, there could be weeks of high drama at a time when he was still mourning the loss of his son, his lawyer said, adding: “I will have to sit down, explain the procedure, explain where we stand today and what the pros and cons are.”
On the eve of the plea hearing, it remained unknown how the defendant would contest the charge of causing his son’s demise “through negligent, reckless or dangerous actions”.
The boy, who would have turned three last week, fell from the fourth-floor window at the King Evelthon hotel and resort on the Chlorakas coastline outside Paphos.
The father claims he placed him on the windowsill, – along a corridor leading to a lift that his relatives were about to use – not realising the window was ajar. The toddler then fell backwards, suffering fatal cranial injuries when he hit a veranda 10 metres (33ft) below.
In a nation so dependent on tourism, criticism has mounted as human rights defenders, media pundits and diplomats have questioned the perceived lack of compassion with which officials have approached the case.
While the letter of the law had been adhered to so assiduously by police and court officials, “no one had asked why the window did not have bars”, said a diplomat based in Nicosia, the eastern Mediterranean island’s capital.
“It’s perplexing that there’s all this emphasis on the father being a criminal and so little focus on the circumstances in which the boy died,” he added.
“Why was there even a window there and why was it open? In a country where permits to build hotels are often lax, these are questions that should not be ignored.”
In an editorial last week, the Cyprus Mail echoed that sentiment. “Why are authorities so eager to treat tragic accidents as criminal acts?” it asked, after a similar incident in which the three-year-old son of African immigrants fell to his death from the balcony of his family’s sixth-floor apartment in Nicosia.
Like the Briton, his parents were held in custody for several days although they were eventually released without charge.
With the prospect of prolonged criminal proceedings in store for the Essex-born executive, debate has intensified over the role of Cyprus’ attorney general, long regarded as one of the most controversial legacies of the island’s former status as a British colony.
In his ninth-floor office in the heart of Nicosia, the island’s leading human rights lawyer, Achilleas Demetriades, said the Briton had fallen foul of “an archaic system” that was long overdue an overhaul. Under Cyprus’s post-colonial justice system, such decisions remained entirely at the discretion of the attorney general, he said, and could not be challenged.
“Sadly, this man has fallen victim to an archaic system in which one man, the attorney general, has unfettered power which is finally under review,” said Demetriades, a candidate in the last presidential elections. “This certainly raises human rights issues.”

Investment funds in Spain step up bets on major property deals in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
04:00:09 UTC
13:00:09 KST

The lack of transparency over property ownership makes it hard to track the share held by big landlords and new players, or to get a real-time picture of the market.
Public information on how property ownership is distributed in Spain is still inadequate, especially when it comes to property held by large-scale landlords, defined as owners or companies with more than 10 homes or 1,500 m² of residential floorspace.
The data on the actual share of housing, held by the national land registry, anonymise the identity of owners. In areas such as the rental market, which falls under the remit of the autonomous communities, these figures can be obtained by filing transparency requests to analyse tenants' security deposits. This means many types of housing (owner-occupied homes, empty properties, tourist apartments...) are left out of the analysis. As a result, it is impossible to know exactly who owns these properties in real time.
Tracking property transactions so far in 2026 – those that companies themselves have publicised – does make it possible to see who is most active in the Iberian market. But that does not mean they have overtaken, in number of properties, the traditional players who have shaped the landscape over the past decade: names already familiar in major cities such as Blackstone, CBRE IM, Renta Corporación, Cerberus, Ares Management or Santander and CaixaBank.
New investments (even on public land)
Fidere, a group of SOCIMI real estate investment trusts specialising in buying public and rental housing, has carried out the largest deal so far this year, worth 1.05 billion euros. Canadian group Brookfield bought it from Blackstone, thereby indirectly acquiring its portfolio of 47 buildings and more than 5,000 rental homes, in a transaction completed in March.
In May, Azora agreed to buy from Patrizia 1,200 rental homes in the Barcelona metropolitan area (one of the most overheated housing markets in Spain, with extremely high population density in places such as L'Hospitalet de Llobregat) for more than 350 million euros. Patrizia had itself purchased them from BeCorp in 2022 for around 600 million.
Many other deals have been signed even before the homes are finished: Barings will buy from Aurora Homes 305 affordable homes in Los Cerros (Vicálvaro) for more than 70 million euros, with delivery in 2029, and another 188 in Valdebebas for more than 56 million from Grupo Ferrocarril.
Regional governments and certain town councils are themselves granting concessions on public land to this type of company, in some cases for periods of between 45 and 75 years, in a country where the stock of social rental housing does not exceed 1.72%, well below the European average of around 8-9%. The case of Culmia, the developer controlled by US fund Oaktree, is illustrative. In 2025 it handed over lot 3 of the Comunidad de Madrid's Plan Vive to German asset manager DWS by selling shares in the concession-holding company, in a deal worth 255 million euros.
Indeed, Bavarian firm MEAG bought from Culmia a 50% stake in a portfolio that includes 1,137 homes from Plan Vive II (Comunidad de Madrid), 437 from the City of Madrid's affordable rental programme and 208 under the control of the Generalitat Valenciana.
Is the housing bubble bursting?
Home sales in Spain are starting to slow slightly as a result of the steep rise in housing prices. That is borne out by data from the National Statistics Institute (INE) compiled by Cushman & Wakefield and by studies such as BBVA Research, which forecast a 7.3% drop for this year, followed by a modest recovery of 0.6% in 2027.
In its report for the second quarter of 2026, the property consultancy identified a year-on-year fall of 3.51% in these transactions up to May 2026, to a total of 286,000. Its analysts also note that worsening financing conditions are leading families to move into or remain longer in the rental market, putting additional pressure on rents in this segment.
C&W's report points to "a spectacular 376% increase" year-on-year in investment in rental housing and notes that "in the first half of 2026 the volume of investment is already significantly higher than in the whole of 2025", reaching 2.934 billion euros, in transactions involving large-scale landlords and investment funds.
This figure may seem to contradict the fall in home sales, but the two indicators capture different realities. While sales statistics count the number of transactions, investment volume reflects the money spent on acquiring homes and property portfolios, so a handful of large deals can substantially boost the total. In Spain, purchases of housing by companies and other legal entities represented 10% of transactions in 2025, according to the latest report from the General Council of Notaries.
In any case, these numbers need to be treated with caution: they do not allow the real number of homes in corporate hands in Spain to be verified because of the opacity surrounding total holdings; they only show how buying and selling in the housing market is evolving.
As for other research into the state of the housing market, Oxford Economics notes in its May report that it expects a moderation in house price growth – to 5% in 2027 – after it reached double-digit rates in 2025 (12.89%), with the figure forecast for this year likely to come in at close to 11%. The slowdown, however, could be temporary according to current projections.
The slowdown in job creation, which is reducing incomes among the population, and the recent interest rate rise by the European Central Bank in response to renewed inflationary pressures are among the possible causes of this expected cooling.
Housing has become the main concern for Spaniards. That is the view of 37.5% of those surveyed in the latest CIS barometer in September, who rank it above other economic problems (21.6%) or immigration (19.7%).
This situation is becoming entrenched in the most pressured markets. Spain's six largest urban areas concentrate 36% of households, according to the Bank of Spain's annual report on the matter, and it is there that the gap between housing demand and the supply available to meet it remains widest.

Fuel taxes in Europe: Which country taxes petrol the most?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
03:59:47 UTC
12:59:47 KST

Nearly half of what European drivers pay for petrol goes to governments. Here are the 10 member states with the heaviest petrol taxes.
Filling up a car has never cost more in the European Union.
Euro-super 95 petrol reached a weighted EU average of €2.063 per litre on 14 September, the highest price in the European Commission's series dating back to 2005.
The crisis began at the end of February, when the war with Iran broke out and disrupted energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz.
Brent crude cost about $72 per barrel before the war and was trading at more than $100 for next-month delivery on Monday.
Refineries added their own pressure.
Refining margins measure the gap between what refiners pay for crude and what they earn selling petrol and diesel.
ECB experts estimate that in the third week of September these margins added €0.17 to each litre of petrol in the euro area and €0.41 to each litre of diesel.
Yet, nearly half the money drivers hand over at the pump goes to governments as forms of taxes.
How the tax bill adds up
Petrol is taxed in two main stages. First comes excise duty, a fixed charge per litre that does not automatically rise with the price of oil. Some countries also impose carbon or other levies.
Then comes value added tax (VAT), charged on the fuel’s price after those duties and levies have been added. Drivers therefore pay VAT on excise duty: a tax on tax.
Across the EU, taxes averaged €0.976 per litre, accounting for 47.3% of the pump price. In seven member states, they exceeded €1.
Here are the ten countries with the highest tax bills per litre.
10. Latvia: €0.960 per litre
Latvia raised its excise duty on unleaded petrol in January from €532 to €555 per 1,000 litres, or €0.555 per litre.
A second charge pays for the country's emergency oil stocks, the reserves every EU state must hold in case supplies are cut. It is set at €91.26 per tonne of oil products sold in Latvia, just under 7 cents per litre of petrol.
VAT at 21% adds €0.343.
In total, drivers in Latvia paid €0.96 in tax per litre, according to data filed last week.
9. Estonia: €0.963 per litre
Estonia charges an excise duty of €0.593 per litre, after raising fuel duties in May 2025. When prices surged this spring, Tallinn moved to drop a further rise planned for May 2026.
There is no other fuel levy. VAT at 24% adds €0.370.
That brings the Estonian tax bill to €0.963 on every litre, almost exactly half the €1.914 pump price.
8. Portugal: €0.978 per litre
Portugal's main fuel tax, known as ISP, stood at €0.432 per litre in the week of 14 September. It includes the former road service contribution, which still accounts for 8.7 cents per litre of petrol.
The ISP is reduced by a temporary discount. It applies when prices rise more than 10 cents above early-March levels and hands drivers back the extra VAT the state collects.
A carbon levy adds €0.159 per litre in 2026, and VAT at 23% adds €0.387.
Added together, the three charges came to €0.978 per litre, according to the Commission's latest bulletin.
7. Italy: €1.049 per litre
Italy charges an excise duty of €0.673 per litre. Petrol and diesel have carried the same rate since January, after the government cut petrol by 4.05 cents and raised diesel by the same amount.
Rome has cut the diesel rate several times since late July to cushion the price surge.
Petrol has had no cut.
VAT at 22% adds €0.376.
The Italian state collected €1.049 on every litre sold, just over half of the €2.084 pump price.
6. France: €1.052 per litre
France's excise on petrol, formerly called TICPE, has been €0.690 per litre since 1 March.
VAT at 20% adds €0.362.
French drivers handed over €1.052 in tax for each litre.
5. Greece: €1.133 per litre
Greece charges an excise duty of €0.70 per litre on unleaded petrol.
Two small levies, both calculated as a percentage of the price, add about 1.5 cents: a customs-processing fee and a contribution to a special petroleum account.
VAT at 24% adds €0.418.
The total reached €1.133 per litre, or 52.5% of the pump price, the largest share in the top 10.
4. Germany: €1.179 per litre
Germany's energy tax on petrol is a fixed 65.45 cents per litre. Berlin temporarily cut it by 14.04 cents from 1 May to 30 June because of the war, but the full rate is back.
A carbon price adds about €0.148 per litre. Since January, CO2 certificates for fossil fuels have been auctioned within a corridor of €55 to €65 per tonne.
VAT at 19%, one of the lowest rates in the bloc, adds €0.376.
Energy tax, carbon price and VAT combined came to €1.179 per litre, about half of what German drivers paid at the pump.
3. Finland: €1.193 per litre
Finland's fuel duty of €0.722 per litre has three parts: a tax on the fuel's energy content, a CO2 tax and a small security-of-supply fee.
In January, Helsinki lowered the carbon value used to calculate the CO2 tax from €62 to €56.8 per tonne.
VAT is where Finland stands out. Its 25.5% rate is the second-highest in the EU after Hungary's 27%, and it adds €0.471 per litre.
Taken together, Finnish taxes came to €1.193 per litre, according to the latest Commission data.
2. Denmark: €1.230 per litre
Denmark has the most expensive petrol in the EU, at €2.564 a litre, but it is not the heaviest taxer.
Its fuel duties total 5.36 kroner per litre before VAT, about €0.717.
They are made up of an energy tax, a CO2 tax and a nitrogen oxides levy, with the CO2 part alone at 1.86 kroner.
VAT at 25% applies to a high pre-tax price of €1.334. It adds €0.513 per litre, the largest VAT amount in the EU.
That puts the Danish tax bill at €1.230 per litre, second only to the Netherlands.
1. The Netherlands: €1.270 per litre
No EU country takes more tax from a litre of petrol than the Netherlands.
The Dutch excise duty on petrol is €844.69 per 1,000 litres in 2026, the highest in the bloc. A levy that funds the national oil stockpile adds 0.8 cents.
VAT at 21% adds €0.422.
Every litre of petrol sold in the Netherlands carried €1.270 in tax last week, 52% of a €2.434 pump price.

US strikes on alleged drug boats may be ‘crimes against humanity’, UN says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
03:52:23 UTC
12:52:23 KST

US strikes on alleged drug boats may be ‘crimes against humanity’, UN says
UN expert says US forces have killed 223 people in 68 attacks in the Caribbean and the Pacific in the past year.
A United Nations human rights expert has concluded that US attacks on suspected drug trafficking boats in the Caribbean Sea and the Pacific Ocean violate international law and may amount to crimes against humanity.
In a report published on Monday, Ben Saul, the UN’s special rapporteur on human rights and counterterrorism, said the US has struck 68 vessels in international waters between September 2025 and August this year, killing at least 223 people.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4‘Handcuffed and blindfolded’: Is the US targeting Ecuadorian fishermen?
- list 2 of 4US removes Venezuela from drug list, Trump says
- list 3 of 4Duterte in person at ICC for first time over ‘war on drugs’ killings
- list 4 of 4Mexico rescues eight from clandestine clinic run by violent Jalisco cartel
The US has defended the strikes as acts of self-defence against “narco-terrorists”, and President Donald Trump has told Congress that the operations reflect a state of armed conflict with designated “terrorist” organisations.
The report, however, rejected that framing.
“The United States military attacks are… contrary to international law, violate the human right to life, and plausibly constitute crimes against humanity,” it said.
The findings came two days after the US military announced it had killed four people in a strike on a vessel in the Caribbean Sea. The campaign has also drawn condemnation from human rights groups, which have called the killings extrajudicial. The Pentagon has released videos of the strikes on social media but has disclosed little about who was killed or what evidence tied them to drug trafficking.
Saul’s report said the US has no right to the use of force in self-defence against alleged drug trafficking.
No right to self-defence
It argued that drug trafficking does not meet the legal threshold of an “armed attack” that would trigger a right to self-defence. It noted that international law only permits self-defence against non-state actors sent by a state, but that there “appears to be no factual basis” that some of the groups designated as “terrorists” by the US, such as Tren de Aragua, were acting as armed proxies of the Venezuelan state.
TThe report also noted that less-lethal alternatives were available, including the maritime interception of vessels – a measure that it said has been acknowledged as feasible by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Because of this, the report said the US attacks also violate the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which permits lethal force only as a last resort against an imminent threat – a standard it said was not met.
It went further, arguing that the killings meet the legal definition of murder as a crime against humanity, since they were carried out “systematically” under an organised state policy and are widespread “given the large number of victims”.
It also called on the US to investigate the killings, prosecute those responsible – including political and military leaders who ordered the strikes – and provide reparations to victims’ families.
Beyond examining the legality of the attacks, the report also questioned the effectiveness of the campaign in reducing drug trafficking to the US. It said cocaine seizures at the US border have remained steady, and noted that much of the region’s cocaine moves through container ships that are rarely inspected, and not the small boats being targeted.
It also said the strikes have done nothing to address fentanyl and opioids, which are not typically trafficked by sea from Venezuela and are the leading cause of US overdose deaths.
The report added that by killing low-level suspects, the strikes may be undermining efforts to dismantle cartel networks and prosecute their leaders. “Meanwhile, it has been estimated that the military operations had cost US$4.7 billion by mid-2026 – funds that could have instead been spent on evidence-based law enforcement, public health, and developmental interventions,” it said.

World leaders gather at UN amid wars, AI fears and global divisions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
03:49:53 UTC
12:49:53 KST

World leaders gather at UN amid wars, AI fears and global divisions
World leaders are gathering at the United Nations this week against a backdrop of wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, rising fears over artificial intelligence and mounting economic and climate pressures. The annual General Assembly will test whether the 193-member body can still bring countries together to tackle crises that increasingly transcend borders.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Under a global cloud of wars and bitter divisions, world leaders meet at the United Nations this week facing new fears that runaway artificial intelligence could threaten humanity even as climate shocks and escalating prices are already making life much tougher for hundreds of millions of people.
The annual high-level gathering at the UN General Assembly will also be consumed with major wars in Iran , Gaza , Ukraine, Sudan , Congo and Myanmar and a persisting question: Can the leaders do anything to end them?
And what can they do about the relentless rise of global warming threatening the future of the planet, the growing inequalities within and among nations, and shocks to the global economy as blocked shipping routes and supply chains increase the cost of living and slow growth?
The future of the United Nations will also definitely be on the agenda. At 81, its powers are still the victorious nations from World War II, not the 21st century’s major global players. The UN’s 193 member nations have agreed to a wide-ranging reform package that includes updating key institutions such as the powerful UN Security Council, where the US, Russia, China, Britain and France hold inordinate sway because of their veto power. Reform, however, is easier said than implemented.
Behind the scenes, there will be speculation about who will lead the United Nations next. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres’ second five-year term ends Dec. 31 and no clear successor has emerged.
This meeting is still pivotal
There is still no question that the UN remains THE gathering place for its 193 member nations and their leaders. Some 130 heads of state and government are expected to speak at the General Assembly starting Tuesday along with dozens of ministers.
Among the headliners will be US President Donald Trump and French President Emanuel Macron. Both will speak Tuesday after Guterres’ opening “state of the world” address. Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky and Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian speak Wednesday.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu — whom New York Mayor Zoran Mamdani wanted arrested for his treatment of Palestinians in Gaza until he learned he has no such authority — will address the assembly on Thursday. For a second year, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas won’t be coming to the UN because the U.S. has refused to give him a visa. He will nonetheless address the assembly by video the same day.
The United States, under its agreement with the UN to host the organization, is required to allow diplomats from all member nations to attend meetings.
Equally telling is who else isn’t coming. China’s President Xi Jinping is meeting Trump in Washington on Wednesday, yet he is skipping — some diplomats say snubbing — the UN gathering and sending a vice president instead. Russian President Vladimir Putin isn’t coming either, and Indian President Narendra Modi has backed out.
France's UN ambassador, Jerome Bonnafont, said it is “extremely critical” for world leaders this week to support the UN as the place where the world’s nations meet — especially at a time of such polarization.
“We believe in multilateralism," he said, "and we believe that the high-level week is the occasion for countries in the world to reaffirm that they prefer cooperation and dialogue to confrontation.”
United Nations has not had a great year
There is no doubt it’s been a tough year for the world body. It has been pushed to the sidelines when it comes to its key responsibility of ensuring international peace and security and trying to end major conflicts in the Mideast and Ukraine. The U.S. failure to pay billions of dollars in outstanding arrears has left the organization’s finances in rocky shape.
But veteran UN watcher Richard Gowan, the International Crisis Group’s global issues and institutions program director, says 2025 was even worse.
A year ago, he said, people were contemplating that Trump would use his UN speech to announce that the United States would leave the world organization. Trump didn’t announce a pullout last September and the UN muddled through the past 12 months with financial troubles that forced cutbacks to its peacekeeping operations and humanitarian aid.
In recent days, the U.S. paid $725 million of its dues to the UN’s regular operating budget for this year, enough to keep the Trump administration from losing its vote in the General Assembly. The payment was a strong indication Trump will keep the US in the United Nations.
The UN is no longer “in freefall,” Gowan said, but it “is stuck in an open-ended or permanent crisis.” Put more graphically, he said, “The UN may not be in emergency care like it was last year, but it does seem to be trapped in a trauma center for the foreseeable future.”
Former U.N. deputy secretary-general Mark Malloch-Brown, a United Nations Foundation board member, said, “While the world still trusts the UN, the global public is eager for change."
AI is pushing toward the center of the agenda
The future of artificial intelligence has pushed to the forefront of global concerns, with its speeding advances and the dawning recognition that there are no industry controls, let alone any global guardrails for a technology that has many advantages but also many disadvantages and unknowns.
Days before the global gathering, leaders of three major AI companies warned about the technology getting out of human control and called for a pause, but Trump dismissed their concerns as “a hoax,” and urged continued advances to keep the US ahead of China.
The UN Security Council added a high-level meeting on AI to its agenda on Wednesday afternoon, a sign of the growing apprehension and need to address the issue. It was already slated to hold a high-level meeting on Ukraine with Zelensky on Wednesday morning.
For the UN chief, this will be his last assembly meeting with global leaders. He previewed his speech last week, telling UN reporters that power is shifting in “an era of deep uncertainty."
“At a time when the world faces three existential threats," he said, “international cooperation is more necessary than ever.”
Others will be vying for the spotlight on issues from rising sea levels and funding education to the fight for gender equality. Hundreds of private meetings will also convene in UN cubicles, hotels, diplomatic missions and restaurants.
Esther Brimmer, a senior fellow in global governance at the Council on Foreign Relations and former US assistant secretary of state for international organization affairs in the Obama administration, said in-person meetings can help countries hash out ideas that get implemented months later.
She called the situation in 2026 “much more serious and complex than in decades past."
“With that said, I’m also not without hope as well,” Brimmer said. “Over the past decades we’ve learned a lot about international cooperation.”
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

Brain scans reveal a possible cause of long COVID fatigue and brain fog
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
03:48:58 UTC
12:48:58 KST

Brain scans reveal a possible cause of long COVID fatigue and brain fog
Brain scans show signs that long COVID may injure dopamine releasing neurons.
- Date:
- September 21, 2026
- Source:
- Centre for Addiction and Mental Health
- Summary:
- Researchers have found evidence that long COVID may damage dopamine releasing neurons in the brain, potentially explaining persistent fatigue, low motivation, slowed movement, and memory difficulties. The discovery could lead to new treatments that target the brain's dopamine system.
- Share:
A new brain imaging study led by scientists at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (CAMH) has uncovered what researchers describe as the strongest evidence so far that long COVID is associated with damage to dopamine-releasing neurons in the brain. Published in eBioMedicine, the findings could help explain persistent problems such as fatigue-related loss of motivation, slower movement, and memory difficulties. They may also point toward new treatment strategies.
Long COVID is estimated to affect about five per cent of the global population, including roughly two million people in Canada. The condition can involve a broad range of symptoms that continue for at least three months after the initial COVID-19 infection. Common brain-related symptoms include fatigue, brain fog, memory problems, and low mood. Despite how widespread and disruptive long COVID can be, there are currently no evidence-based treatments, in part because scientists still do not fully understand what is happening in the brain.
Brain Scans Reveal Changes in the Dopamine System
For the new study, researchers used positron emission tomography (PET), an imaging technique that can measure biological activity inside the brain. They examined a well-established marker associated with the health and integrity of dopamine neurons in people with long COVID and compared the results with those from healthy participants.
The researchers found substantially lower levels of this marker in people with long COVID across all major areas of the striatum. The striatum is a group of brain regions that helps regulate motivation, movement, and thinking. Lower marker levels suggest a reduced density of dopamine nerve terminals.
Different patterns of marker loss were also associated with different symptoms. Lower levels in the ventral striatum were linked to greater loss of motivation. Reductions in the dorsal putamen were associated with slower movement, while lower levels in the caudate putamen were connected with memory difficulties.
"Our findings provide compelling evidence that long COVID involves the loss of dopamine-releasing neurons," says Dr. Jeffrey Meyer, Senior Scientist at the Brain Health Imaging Centre, Canada Research Chair, and senior author of the study. "This kind of injury is well known to produce symptoms like lack of motivation and motor slowing, and may contribute to memory difficulties in other neurological conditions. Our results suggest a similar process is occurring in long COVID."
Earlier Research Pointed to Brain Inflammation
The new findings build on previous work by the same research team showing that people with long COVID have unusually high levels of inflammation in the brain. That inflammation appeared to be especially pronounced in regions containing large numbers of dopamine-releasing neurons.
"We know that inflammation can injure dopamine neurons. While our earlier research showed high levels of inflammation in those regions, this study provides direct evidence that the dopamine neuron marker is reduced in the same regions -- and that this loss correlates with patients' symptoms," explains Dr. Meyer.
Taken together, the two studies suggest a possible connection between persistent brain inflammation and damage involving the dopamine system.
A New Direction for Long COVID Treatment
The results could change how researchers approach the biology and treatment of long COVID. Much of the previous research has centered on inflammation in the brain and changes in immune activity. By comparison, very few clinical trials have focused directly on dopamine-releasing neurons.
"These results indicate that long COVID is, at least in part, a disorder of the brain's dopamine system," adds Dr. Meyer. "This suggests that repurposing medications that augment the function of dopamine-releasing neurons, including dopamine precursors and inhibitors of dopamine metabolism, could be a promising approach."
For people living with long COVID, the findings may also provide a biological explanation for symptoms that can be difficult to measure from the outside.
"For five years I have been seeking answers on what happened to me after I contracted COVID in 2021," says Susan Deuville, lived experience research advisor to Dr. Meyer. "It was a crushing loss of the life I had and the person I was before. The research of Dr. Meyer brings hope. It also validates what long COVID sufferers have always known -- long COVID is real and the effects are devastating."
Clinical Trial Planned to Target Dopamine Function
Building on these results, the researchers plan to begin a clinical trial in the upcoming couple of months that will target dopamine function in people with long COVID. The goal will be to determine whether modifying dopamine activity can improve memory, motivation, and fatigue.
The trial will be conducted in collaboration with University Health Network (UHN), as part of a partnership between the hospitals aimed at bridging the gap between mental and physical health care.
The study was supported by the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR).
Story Source:
Materials provided by Centre for Addiction and Mental Health. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:

Meyer. Loss of vesicular monoamine transporter 2 in striatum of long COVID and relationship to neuropsychiatric symptoms. eBioMedicine, 2026; 130: 106339 DOI: 10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106339

Ivan Vazov – eyewitness of Bulgaria’s Liberation, Unification and Independence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
03:45:51 UTC
12:45:51 KST

Author
Yoan Kolev
News
105 years after the death of the Patriarch of Bulgarian Literature
Ivan Vazov – eyewitness of Bulgaria’s Liberation, Unification and Independence
Tuesday 22 September 2026 05:45
Tuesday, 22 September 2026, 05:45
PHOTO archives.government.bg
Font size
On September 22, 1921, the patriarch of Bulgarian literature Ivan Vazov closed his eyes for the last time, bequeathing to the generations some of the most beautiful words dedicated to Bulgaria. His adoration and sincere love of his motherland is felt in each of his numerous short stories, travelogues, novels, plays, poems. Generations of Bulgarians have grown up with his poems, and one of the first things we all learn at school and remember for a lifetime is Vazov’s poem “Az sam balgarche” – “I am a Bulgarian child and I love, cherish and hold dear everything Bulgarian and native”.
PHOTO BGNES
In his works, Vazov touches on many of the topics that agitated Bulgarian society in the second half of the 19th and early 20th centuries. It can serve as a kind of chronicle of the heroic Bulgarian victories in the name of the national goal - the conquest of freedom, the unification of the country after the five-century Ottoman yoke. The proclamation of the Independence of Bulgaria in 1908 so far remains the only event of the period for which there is no specific work written by the author.
"This was a really serious event but let's not take the works of Ivan Vazov so literally," explains Atanas Kapralov, director of the National Literary Museum. “For his 71 years the national poet experienced five wars. But let's not forget that Vazov was not a publicist. His works carry the spirit of freedom and independence to which Bulgaria aspires. Not in vain, no matter how much Pencho Slaveykov wanted his father Petko Slaveykov to receive the title of Patriarch of Bulgarian Literature, the one awarded with it was Vazov.”
PHOTO BGNES
Vazov's works encouraged and still encourage generations of Bulgarians, even those born abroad, to get to know and love their homeland. The numerous works that the author left behind would also make Bulgaria known outside its borders. Evidence of this is the fact that the house museum of Vazov in the heart of Sofia enjoys a large number of visitors:
PHOTO BGNES
"Vazov’s house in Sofia is visited by both Bulgarians and foreigners,” says Kapralov. “Usually foreigners know little about the artist Ivan Vazov. They want to find out from our curators what kind of person he was, because they still understood that this creator bore fundamental features for us as individuals, as a collective image of the Bulgarian spirituality. Getting to know him, they learn more about today's people of Bulgaria. Curiously, after their visit, many of them are looking for his works, most often the novel "Under the Yoke".
PHOTO BGNES
Another interesting fact related to Vazov’s most emblematic work is that in 1894, it was first printed in English. The reason for the delay of the Bulgarian edition was that it contained 24 illustrations, which had to be approved by Vazov, and then recreated with the help of actors. The photographs taken would then be delivered to an artist who repainted them, leaving his mark on them. Often the illustrations looked different from the original photos and had to be reworked, which took time. With its rich language, plot and imagery, "Under the Yoke" occupies a worthy place in the pantheon of Bulgarian literary classics.
However, its presence among its golden pages did not protect the novel from attempts to edit, revise or even shorten it, in order to make it easier for readers to understand and perceive. In this context, the translation of the book in the so-called "shlyokavitsa*", quite expectedly caused sharp disapproval among all segments of society. Although the publication appeared with the mission to remind the public that the Bulgarian language is in danger, the choice of the work seems to have been quite inappropriate.
PHOTO BGNES
"I cannot accept the editing of the work of a classic author“, the director of the National Literary Museum says firmly. “I do not think such a thing has happened elsewhere in the world with the work by an author of such magnitude. It is indisputable that in the novel "Under the Yoke" there are many words borrowed from Turkish but after all, such was the everyday language of the then Bulgarian people. In his work Vazov uses a wealth of words. Probably the publishers of this edition thought that this would make the author more accessible to the modern reader. In this way, however, the connection with the high creativity related to the detail, the introduction of nuances in the work is lost. I am firmly against any updates of classical Bulgarian authors. "
English version: Rositsa Petkova
Note by the author: * Shlyokavitsa - the "alphabet" used by the generation after 2000, which grew up with the Internet. In it the Cyrillic alphabet is replaced phonetically with Latin characters, and the Cyrillic letters “Ш” and “Ч” are written with the numbers 6 and 4.
