Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
02:29:36 UTC
11:29:36 KST

President Volodymyr Zelensky on Sept. 21 arrived in the United States, where he is set to meet U.S. President Donald Trump and discuss efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war.
The two presidents are scheduled to attend the U.N. General Assembly in New York, where hundreds of diplomats and world leaders are gathering to debate global challenges and crises.
In addition to conferring with Trump, Zelensky said that around 20 other meetings with officials and organizations were planned. He also announced that a new deal concerning drones was ready to be signed.
"Of course, Ukraine’s number one priority is bringing peace closer and protecting the lives of our people," Zelensky wrote on X after touching down in New York. "There are concrete security proposals and de-escalation measures that could bring the end of the war closer. We are working to strengthen air defense and ensure sufficient financing for Ukraine."
Zelensky, who held a phone call with Trump on Sept. 20, said their upcoming "meeting could change a lot." The leaders are scheduled to meet on Sept. 22, a Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent.
The Ukrainian leader revealed that he wants to discuss with his U.S. counterpart the possibility of a mutual Ukrainian-Russian pause in strikes against energy infrastructure and targets on the Black Sea.
"There are also ideas on the table for bringing peace closer, starting with strong de-escalation steps. Ukraine's energy sector, critical infrastructure, and our food exports must stop being targets for Russia, and this will lead to matching de-escalation steps on our part," Zelensky said on X ahead of the meeting.
"We are ready to work on this, and we will discuss it with our partners on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York."
Zelensky added that "it will no longer be the case that only the country under attack suffers. The nature of war is now such that the aggressor will suffer as well."
Trump, in turn, commented earlier on Sept. 21 that the war has inflicted heavy damage to the Russian oil refining industry and urged an end to the fighting. The U.S. president has previously linked Ukrainian strikes against Russian refineries to the surging global diesel prices, a claim disputed by experts.
The scheduled meeting comes amid a renewed effort by Washington to broker an end to the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine, ongoing for more than four and a half years.
Trump's envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, traveled to Kyiv and Moscow earlier in September to advance peace talks, which had been stalled for months amid Russia's territorial demands and Washington's shift of focus toward the war with Iran.
The visit also comes shortly after Trump signed a major sanctions bill granting him authority to impose a 100% tariff on leading buyers of Russian oil and gas, and the U.S. State Department greenlit a possible $2.7 billion sale of air defenses to Ukraine.
Despite the renewed diplomatic efforts, the Ukrainian leader has previously said that the active phase of the war is likely to continue into the winter, when Moscow is expected to launch a new wave of attacks against Ukrainian cities and the energy grid.
To secure its skies, Kyiv seeks additional U.S.-made Patriot missile interceptors and is leading talks with the U.S. on licenses to produce them directly in Ukraine.
Zelensky previously met Trump in White House on July 28. During his trip to New York, the Ukrainian president is expected to meet with other top foreign officials, including European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

Yemeni refugees flee across Bab al-Mandab as fighting with Houthis intensifies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
02:25:05 UTC
11:25:05 KST

Thousands of Yemeni people have found refuge in northern Djibouti after fleeing by boat from Yemen's Houthis across the Bab al-Mandab Strait, according to the BBC's Frank Gardner, who interviewed some of the refugees in northern Africa.
Some of the refugees whom Gardner interviewed are from the town of Dhubab, which the BBC noted is on the front lines of the war between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed pro-government Yemeni forces fighting them.
"How could I just sit there when my kids are screaming and shaking in terror?" Ibrahim Issa, a 50-year-old fisherman, told Gardner. "When the sound of the planes starts, and the kids hear the planes, they begin shouting and screaming. As parents, it is our responsibility; what can you do when you see this? That is why we fled, to save them."
Gardner added that several refugees gave him the same message: "We don't care which side it is that's attacking. It's the bombs falling all around us that have caused us to flee."
The refugees' accounts come as the conflict in Yemen continues to escalate, with the US weighing renewed military action against the Houthis.
Trump calls off planned US strikes on Houthis at last minute after Saudi plea
US President Donald Trump came close to ordering a new American military campaign against the Houthis in Yemen this weekend, after Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman personally urged him to intervene, but called off the planned strikes as they were nearing execution, The New York Times reported.
According to the report, Trump had spent roughly two weeks weighing repeated Saudi appeals for US military assistance against the Iran-backed Houthis, whose renewed offensive has expanded the conflict in Yemen and increased pressure on Saudi Arabia.
Trump had told advisers on Wednesday that he did not favor launching strikes. But after speaking with bin Salman on Thursday, he reversed course and instructed the Pentagon to prepare airstrikes against Houthi targets, according to administration officials cited by the NYT.
By midday Sunday, however, Trump had changed his mind again.
The planned US strikes were halted at a late stage, when military commanders had already approved target lists, troops were loading bombs onto aircraft selected for the operation, and the first wave of attacks was close to beginning, according to people briefed on the planning.
Idan Kweller contributed to this report.

EU fails to agree on lifting sanctions on Russian oligarchs

EU fails to agree on lifting sanctions on Russian oligarchs
EU countries failed Monday to reach a final deal that would remove Russian billionaires Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the bloc's sanctions list, with diplomats set to resume talks Tuesday.
EU countries failed Monday to finalise a deal that involved lifting sanctions on Russian oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, with negotiations to continue in Brussels, diplomats said.
Multiple diplomats said earlier that member states had reached a provisional agreement to take the pair off the EU's blacklist as part of a compromise to extend sanctions on almost 3,000 other individuals and entities over the Ukraine war.
But that deal failed to get final approval -- with one diplomat telling AFP that Latvia had lodged a last-gasp objection.
Diplomats said that EU ambassadors would meet again at 0600 GMT on Tuesday to try to hammer out an agreement.
The 27-nation bloc has been scrambling to reach a deal on extending the sanctions regime ahead of a deadline late Tuesday after France and Slovakia pushed for Russian-Uzbek billionaire Usmanov to be removed from the blacklist.
Luxembourg then seized upon the demand by Paris to insist that if sanctions were lifted on Usmanov, then they should be lifted for Fridman as well.
Officials in Paris have cited "national security" concerns for their request on Usmanov, but refused publicly to give details.
The Financial Times reported that the demand may be linked to a potential prisoner release deal involving French nationals held in Azerbaijan.
Luxembourg has pushed for Fridman to be removed. Diplomats said the move comes as he is suing the country for 15 billion euros ($17 billion) for freezing his assets under EU sanctions.
More hawkish EU countries, including Poland and Baltic states, fiercely opposed the easing of the sanctions, arguing that pressure on Russia should be increased.
In return for greenlighting the move as part of the provisional deal, they had got an agreement for the sanctions to remain in place for the next three years -- as opposed to the previous extensions of six months each.
Ukraine had reacted furiously to the prospect of the EU removing sanctions on the two prominent Russian businessmen.
'We need to have this stability'
Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga decried the move, saying it would be "unacceptable and would send the wrong signal to Moscow at a time when pressure needs to increase".
"On the contrary, sanctions need to be tightened," he wrote online.
Multiple EU diplomats insisted that despite the standoff over Usmanov, there was widespread agreement that the EU sanctions should not be allowed to lapse.
EU top diplomat Kaja Kallas urged the bloc's member states Monday to maintain sanctions targeting Russia over the war on Ukraine.
"Sanctions are a core pillar of our response to Russia's war" to deprive Moscow of funding, she told reporters in New York after a meeting of European Union foreign affairs ministers.
She added that officials aim to close talks on the rollover of Russia sanctions soon, and have the extension take place swiftly.
"We need to have this stability," with sanctions remaining in place for a longer time, Kallas added on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly.
The EU's sanctions blacklist includes key figures such as Russian President Vladimir Putin and Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov.
Metals tycoon Usmanov and banking magnate Fridman were among dozens of Russian businessmen suing the EU over the sanctions.
Both were added to the sanctions list shortly after Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 over allegations that their businesses provided significant revenues to the Kremlin.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said Monday that conflicts, wars and crises facing the region and the world require Türkiye and the US to remain in close dialogue, stressing the need for “new momentum” in ties between the two NATO allies.
 
“Conflicts, wars and crises that we face in our region and the world require Türkiye and America to remain in close dialogue,” Erdogan said during his remarks at the “100 Years of Friendship Gala” in New York.
 
“Thanks to the dialogue and coordination we have established with America, we are achieving positive results for our countries on many issues whose global issues we are witnessing, particularly in the Middle East, but also from Africa to Asia,” he said. “We are determined to continue this by redoubling our efforts in the coming period.”
 
Erdogan said Türkiye and the US have made significant progress across their relationship, citing his “sincere and exceptional dialogue” with US President Donald Trump and Trump’s visit to Ankara in July.
 
He said Türkiye is ready to advance cooperation with the US in areas including nuclear energy, liquefied natural gas (LNG), civil aviation and high technology.
 
“Developing the defense industry, traditionally one of the strongest areas of our partnership, both bilaterally and within NATO is essential,” he said.
 
“We want to leave behind the barriers that should never have existed between two allies and gain new momentum.”
 
“Deepening our cooperation with the United States in a multidimensional manner, including opportunities for joint production, will be in our mutual interest,” he said.
 
Erdogan said Turkish companies have reached a level that enables them to invest in the US, expressing confidence that Türkiye will soon rank among the world's top 10 defense exporters.
 
“Twenty years ago, we exported only $248 million worth of defense products annually. Today, we have reached a level of more than $10 billion in defense exports,” he said.
 
He added that Türkiye’s share of global defense equipment exports had increased by more than 120% compared with five years ago.
 
“I hope that the strong ties between Türkiye and the United States and the bonds of alliance will grow even stronger in the second century of our diplomatic relations,” he said.
 
Erdogan also said that Türkiye has maintained and strengthened its position as an “island of stability” despite the crises and conflicts surrounding it.
 
Calls for more US investment
 
Erdogan said foreign direct investment attracted by Türkiye over the past 24 years had approached $300 billion.
 
He also cited reconstruction efforts following the 2023 earthquakes, saying more than 455,000 homes had been completed and handed over to earthquake victims within about three years.
 
Erdogan said the figures demonstrated the resilience of the Turkish economy and called on investors to take advantage of opportunities in the country.
 
“We are now launching a new investment drive on this strong foundation,” he said.
 
He said an investment program announced in April introduced one of the world’s most competitive incentive packages, including reducing the corporate tax rate for investors from 25% to 12.5%.
 
“We tell investors: ‘Come and manage your operations from Türkiye,’” he said.
 
Erdogan called on the US-Türkiye Business Council and the US Chamber of Commerce to continue encouraging American investors to take advantage of opportunities in Türkiye.

SOBO wraps paris listening restaurant in oak, vintage furniture, and acoustic panels
Unknown

11:10:56 KST

Studio Louis Morgan designs SOBO, a dining and listening space
SOBO is an 80-sqm plant-based restaurant and listening space in Paris designed by Studio Louis Morgan and interior architect Louis Aspar. Conceived as a multisensory hospitality experience, the project brings together interior architecture, food, music, materiality and acoustic design. Inspired by the intimate atmosphere of Japanese ryokans and listening cafés, Studio Louis Morgan developed a warm interior defined by mahogany-toned oak panelling, bespoke joinery, vintage furniture and carefully controlled lighting. The material palette creates an atmosphere that is both intimate and contemporary, providing a distinctive setting for dining and listening.
all images by Irvin Heller
Dining, music, materiality, and acoustic design come together
Sound was considered as an architectural material rather than a purely technical element. Custom audio equipment and plant-fibre acoustic ceiling panels contribute to the acoustic comfort of the restaurant while creating an environment dedicated to vinyl listening. Architecture, furniture, lighting, acoustics and circulation were developed as parts of a single narrative. Rather than treating the restaurant as a collection of decorative elements, Studio Louis Morgan designed SOBO around the relationship between space, sound and guest experience. The project reflects the studio’s wider approach to hospitality design, developing restaurants, hotels, bars and other hospitality spaces through the integration of identity, functionality, materiality and experience.

Meloni’s EU lieutenant urges Brussels to work with Le Pen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
02:02:00 UTC
11:02:00 KST

BRUSSELS — The EU must be prepared to work closely with Marine Le Pen if she wins the French election, a top Brussels ally of Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni told POLITICO.
Nicola Procaccini said the EU institutions and the center-right European People’s Party must be “courageous” when it comes to working with the far-right Patriots party in Brussels, the European home of Le Pen’s National Rally, if she wins April’s presidential election, just as they were after Meloni’s victory in Rome in 2022.
“There’s no way to apply the cordon sanitaire to the French Republic,” Procaccini, leader of the right-wing European Conservatives and Reformists group, said in an interview in his office, referring to the informal agreement among mainstream parties to shut far-right forces out of power. He said Le Pen and Jordan Bardella, an MEP who would be likely to become prime minister under a Le Pen presidency, “are reasonable people, pragmatic people, like Meloni.”
Advertisement
Procaccini added that the French duo “will defend the national interest but without crazy things” such as hauling France out of the EU.
A Le Pen victory would turn Europe’s far-right surge into power at the EU leaders’ table, placing one of the largest countries under a euroskeptic force, and forcing the EPP, which largely governs Brussels, to work out how to deal with far-right governments without fracturing the bloc.
The last power shake-up in Brussels occurred when Meloni — whose Brothers of Italy party leads the ECR political family alongside Poland’s Law and Justice — came to power. Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and EPP chief Manfred Weber sought to build bridges with Meloni’s government to bring Rome into the Brussels fold.
Procaccini said he hopes Le Pen will pick the “Meloni way” of dealing with the Commission, which he said means being “pragmatic, frank, open, honest and coherent.”
He added that while “the French right historically is less pro-West than us, less pro-Europe” than Meloni’s Brothers of Italy, he is “optimistic” Le Pen will not be destructive in Brussels.
That’s not how everyone sees it playing out, though. EPP vice chair and Romanian PM candidate Sigfried Mureșan said: “I believe under the leadership of Marine Le Pen, the anti-European party in France will radicalize in the next months.”
Advertisement
Although the National Rally is a member of the Patriots group in the Parliament, the ECR would still gain an ally if Le Pen wins, helping it push a more Euroskeptic agenda.
For example, National Rally’s proposal to halve its EU budget contribution does not concern Procaccini. On the contrary, he welcomed it, saying his group “doesn’t believe in a super-giant budget.”
Right-wing majority
Since the 2024 European election, the EPP has increasingly relied on votes from groupings to its right in Parliament to pass measures such as laws scrapping EU green rules and toughening migration policy.
EPP chief Weber has repeatedly laid out his party’s three red lines for cooperation, which are being pro-European, supporting the rule of law, and backing Ukraine.
Giorgia Meloni reacts during a joint speech with France’s President Emmanuel Macron. | Pool photo by Manon Cruz/AFP via Getty Images
He and his lawmakers say the EPP does not negotiate with far-right groups, but insists that if they can pass their own positions with votes from the far-right, they will do so. In July, the EPP expelled a lawmaker who had organized an event with the far-right Patriots and Europe of Sovereign Nations groups at which they called for the dismantling of the cordon sanitaire.
EPP lawmakers generally view cooperation with the Patriots and National Rally as difficult, if not impossible, given their fundamentally different visions for the EU’s future. In early September, the leader of Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democrats in Parliament, Niclas Herbst, told POLITICO that the EPP should rule out any cooperation with the Patriots and instead build a strong centrist coalition to prevent populist forces from scoring victories in Parliament ahead of the 2029 EU election.
Advertisement
Procaccini said the EPP still wanted to keep its center-left Social Democrat allies onside but argued that the EPP needs to be “courageous” and use the right-wing majority more openly to roll back parts of the Green Deal passed during the previous term.
“They know very well that we need a center-right majority” to cut down the Green Deal legislation, he said, “but the problem is that the EPP doesn’t want to have a relationship with the Patriots.”
Procaccini called the EPP’s refusal to engage formally with the Patriots anti-democratic, arguing that politicians should vote based on substance rather than ideology.
He said ECR lawmakers sometimes negotiate with the Patriots and then with the EPP, acting as informal mediators because the EPP does not want to deal directly with the Patriots, “but there’s not a playbook, it happens sometimes, often, but it’s not a scheme,” Procaccini said.
“I hope there’s no need [for] this role, but if there’s a need to be a sort of bridge, we are able to be the bridge” with the National Rally, he said.
Until the 2029 EU election, the priority should be to continue rolling back parts of the Green Deal and boost competitiveness, Procaccini said.

====================================================================================================

The UK coalition the Lib Dems don’t want to talk about
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

BRIGHTON, England — The Liberal Democrats want to defeat Nigel Farage — just don’t mention working with Labour to do it.
The third-largest party in Westminster has made opposing Reform UK central to its annual conference by the English coast this week. Yet what that actually might entail has been conspicuously absent from the discussion in Brighton.
Neither Andy Burnham’s ruling Labour Party or Farage’s right-wing force — currently a close first and second in opinion polls — is on course to win a majority at the next general election, due by August 2029. It means both could be looking for a coalition partner.
Advertisement
Lib Dem leader Ed Davey — who addresses the party faithful Tuesday — told ITV News on Monday he believes there is likely to be a hung parliament next time around. And he has already talked up the threat of a right-wing pact, warning that Farage and Conservative boss Kemi Badenoch could turn Britain into a “Trump-satellite state” — despite both of their repeated protestations that this isn’t on the cards.
An “orange wall” of Lib Dem MPs “will not let [Farage and Badenoch] pass,” Davey has said.
The subtext is that the Lib Dems will do whatever it takes to keep Reform’s hands off power — and in the U.K.’s first-past-the-post electoral system, that would most likely mean propping up a minority Labour administration.
“Labour is open to working with us,” claimed one Lib Dem MP, citing Burnham and Davey’s collegiate relationship at prime minister’s questions and work on social care, though they were coy about whether that means in a future formal coalition when pushed.
At least five other Lib Dems MPs POLITICO spoke with were also reluctant to discuss the prospect of a coalition with Labour.
And while the Lib Dems are keen to show they would like to be in government again, it seems they would rather leave the realities of how they get there below the radar for now.
Advertisement
Scars on their back
Mention of a coalition often sparks fear into the heart of a Lib Dem because of how the last one ended.
“We got hammered in 2015,” a second Lib Dem MP said, recalling how the party crashed from 57 Westminster seats to just eight after five years as junior partner in the Tory-Lib Dem government.
Though many Lib Dems will defend that government’s record, the 2015 thrashing means MPs would be cautious about jumping into a coalition again.
“I always feel a bit icky when thinking [about coalition deals], because it’s not up to us,” said a third MP. “It’s up to the voters who end up with the numbers for those sorts of things to work.”
Ed Davey talks with Keir Starmer in Westminster Abbey on May 6, 2023. | Pool photo by Richard Pohle via WPA/Getty Images
The last coalition “did us a lot of damage for doing the right thing,” said a fourth MP. The party faced a huge backlash over its U-turn on increasing tuition fees, and its support for massive government spending cuts.
Lib Dems are aware they would have to consider the compromises their activists — as well as voters — would accept as a price for power.
Advertisement
A fifth MP called for the party to have three really clear policies identifiable in their manifesto that would serve as “red lines” going into any negotiations, warning “otherwise we go in with a weak hand.”
One alternative — if Labour fell short of an overall majority — would be for the Lib Dems to enter a confidence and supply arrangement, where they would remain outside government, but influence government policy in return for supporting the government in budgets and votes of confidence.
Clear red water
MPs believe there is peril for the party in being seen to be preparing for Labour tie-up — particularly when many of their voters used to be Conservatives.
In 2024, the Lib Dems made gains in rural constituencies where former Conservative voters wanted to see the back of a Tory government they had once supported — and the party continues to target Conservatives voters disillusioned by Badenoch’s shift to the right.
Davey has been careful not to rule out a future pact with the Tories — keeping his fire closely trained on Farage. But some Lib Dem MPs are beginning to think a more combative approach to Labour is needed.
“The constructive opposition approach went on for far too long [under Keir Starmer],” said a sixth MP in a formerly Tory seat, who thinks the same thing is happening with Burnham who they claim has “no substance.”
Advertisement
That MP suggested the more emollient approach should cut both ways, and “when a Tory frontbencher says something sensible, we should work with them.”
The Tories are leaping on Davey’s stance, branding the Lib Dems “Labour enablers” who are failing to hold the government to account.
A seventh Lib Dem MP said they believe the party shouldn’t rule out working with the Tories — if they return to more moderate roots.
A Liberal Democrat spokesperson said: “The chances of a hung parliament are greater than ever, and in that scenario, experience counts.”
Cut through
Beyond the coalition talk, Davey is facing bigger questions about whether his party is cutting through at a time when U.K. politics is in flux.
“We’re not populist. We’re not going to say things for clicks,” the first MP quoted said, while admitting: “I’m not going to pretend there aren’t frustrations” about the party being heard more loudly and clearly.
Advertisement
The fifth MP quoted above agrees. There’s a frustration around the messaging being “all about who we’re against” rather than “standing up for our values” as the antithesis of Reform, they said.
An eighth MP said they are concerned the repeated references to Reform could work against them because “naming those you want to do down doesn’t work, it does the opposite.” It frames Farage in voters’ minds and risks a self-fulfilling prophecy that fuels his success, they said.
It is against this backdrop that questions have loomed at the Lib Dem gathering about whether Davey really is the right person to take on Farage and Burnham.
Trouble at the top
Julian Brazil, the Lib Dem leader of Devon County Council, told the BBC that “all the evidence” suggests Davey, who has led the party for six years, is no longer the right man for the job.
Most of the MPs Playbook spoke to for this piece did not want to discuss defenestrating their leader — at least not publicly.
Nigel Farage during day two of the Reform UK party conference at the National Exhibition Centre in Birmingham, on Sept. 5, 2026. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images
Yet plenty of delegates are asking fairly existential questions about what the party stands for in the new era of a Burnham led-government in debates on the conference floor.
Advertisement
Research published by More in Common has done little to improve the mood.
Polling by the think tank found fewer people understand what the Lib Dems stand for than Restore — the hard-right party founded only a few months ago by former Reform MP Rupert Lowe. Asked to describe Davey, the two most common responses were “don’t know” and “not sure.”
The fifth MP quoted above warned there is a disconnect between the leadership and the activist base. Those around Davey are “shocked” when confronted with how unpopular he is among some members, they said.
Davey’s told the Sunday Times’ he “shares” his critics’ frustration — but blamed the party’s lack of progress on the “crazy politics we’re in.”
The Lib Dem spokesperson quoted above insists the party is in an “incredibly strong position” and has seen its “best result for a century, and achieved a record breaking streak of remarkable local election results” under Davey’s leadership.
Bobby Dean, the Lib Dems’ shadow commons leader, told POLITICO: “Ed has all the ingredients to be a really powerful messenger.” He points to sections in the More in Common polling that shows among respondents who did know Davey, he was described as “likable” and “competent.”
“Those are like good building blocks to start from,” Dean says.
The problem for Davey is that, six years into the job, plenty in his party are starting to wonder how much longer the building work can go on.

====================================================================================================

Merz’s dilemma: Redraft German economic reforms, or go down defending them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Friedrich Merz speaks at a press conference following a meeting of the CDU leadership the day after state elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin. | Maja Hitij/Getty Images
BERLIN — Friedrich Merz faces a stark choice: Reshape the unpopular reform drive on which he has staked his chancellorship — or risk going down defending it.
The day after his conservatives’ worst election defeat in postwar German history and the far-right Alternative for Germany party’s second win in two weeks in votes in the east of the country, Merz acknowledged that the German public’s rejection of his reform drive was a big part of his party’s problem. But he exhibited no clear plan for what to do about it.
Leaders from Merz’s Christian Democratic Union publicly closed ranks around the chancellor and his reform drive on Monday, despite growing internal concern that his leadership is rapidly driving their party toward demise.
Advertisement
In truth, they have little choice. The alternative — an attempt to replace him — is too divisive and risky at a time when the AfD is leading in polls, and the Kremlin is threatening Europe in increasingly aggressive terms.
Merz suggested he recognized the scale of the alarm inside his party.
“This is a severe blow, and its repercussions will be felt for a long time,” Merz said of the result in the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, where the CDU crashed out of the state parliament with just 4.9% of the vote.
But then the chancellor offered little more than a promise to come up with a plan — saying he had scheduled meetings with CDU leaders and state premiers in the coming days to discuss how they should chart a new course.
“We want to move the reform process forward, but we know that we also owe the people answers to their concerns and fears,” he said. “Many people are worried about their jobs, worried about their families, worried about their retirement income, and worried about health care. It is the historic task of the coalition here in Berlin — and of the political center as a whole — to prepare our country to face all these challenges in the years ahead.”
Economists argue the reforms Merz wants, such as overhauls of the public pension and healthcare schemes to make them more sustainable as the country’s population rapidly ages and costs skyrocket, are essential to reviving Germany’s competitiveness.
Advertisement
Whereas previous governments avoided tackling such reforms due to the political perils of measures like raising the retirement age and trimming health insurance benefits, Merz has embraced the task. He has dubbed himself the “reform chancellor” and argues that he’s tackling a generational task on par with rebuilding Germany after World War II.
But voters view the reform drive — and the way Merz has often taken a lecturing tone when promoting its necessity — in overwhelmingly negative terms.
In late August, a survey by the Hans Böckler Foundation of the German labor union association found that about 81 percent of respondents were concerned about their financial security as a result of the government’s reform push. The same poll found 42 percent were cutting back on their consumer spending as a result of those fears.
This is a problem that CDU leaders now admit.
“Right now, our platform isn’t appealing to many people,” CDU Education Minister Karin Prien told a German public television interviewer Monday even as she argued there was no way around structural reforms.
No better alternative
On Monday, Merz again moved to quell suggestions he would step aside in a so-called Kanzlertausch — or chancellor swap.
Advertisement
“Neither last night nor this morning did anyone raise any personnel-related questions, let alone engage in a debate on personnel matters. Not a single person,” Merz told reporters in Berlin.
Prien was among the CDU leaders who publicly closed ranks — but, notably, her endorsement of the chancellor was not exactly glowing. Prien suggested Merz would stay on because the party could not agree on who would take the helm.
“Our country is in a truly difficult situation, and I’m weighing our options very carefully,” she told German public television Monday. “I don’t see how replacing a leader would actually bring about change, unless there is another candidate available. I don’t see that either. And in that regard, we must now work together with the chancellor — as a government on the one hand and as a party on the other — to discuss how we can regain greater acceptance and credibility among the public.”
Two CDU officials, granted anonymity to discuss the party’s internal mood, said upcoming meetings of party leaders, including on Tuesday, when Merz is to face his parliamentary group in the Bundestag, are expected to become tense. But they said Merz is safe as long as his critics in the party can’t agree on the best candidate to succeed him.
“It’s always easy to voice criticism,” said one conservative lawmaker. “But after that, you also have to be able to say what comes next — and that’s when things tend to quickly get pretty quiet.”
A closed-door meeting of the CDU leaders is also expected to take place next weekend in Berlin.
Advertisement
For many conservatives, attempting a leadership bid at a time of such profound global instability is just too risky. The effort could inadvertently trigger an election or end up strengthening the AfD — now the most popular party in Germany, according to polls — which would certainly render any new chancellor installed without an election democratically illegitimate.
Even if Merz clings to power in the short term, more electoral challenges loom. With five regional elections set for next year across Germany, the chancellor and his party need to turn things around quickly.
Coalition partner demands its price
That makes the question of how Merz will reshape his reform drive all the more important. But the effort to push through reforms isn’t bound to get easier, especially as Merz’s coalition only has a 12-vote majority in the Bundestag — making it vulnerable to even a small defection.
On Monday, Merz’s coalition partners in the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) said they would continue to govern with the chancellor’s conservatives, but suggested they would seek an additional price.
“If the citizens of our country perceive reforms as something that threatens their lives and only leads to deterioration, then it is not only our communication that needs to improve, but also in some areas the substance of the reforms themselves,” SPD Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil said in Berlin on Monday.
At the same time, the AfD is piling on pressure on Merz, using his weakness to attack his agenda as well as his party’s “firewall” policy of refusing to govern with the far right — and depicting themselves as the party of true reform.
Advertisement
“We don’t believe the CDU can continue this way,” AfD national co-leader Alice Weidel said Monday in Berlin. “We’ll see what the next few weeks bring. But Germany urgently needs reforms that aren’t being implemented,” she added. “We stand ready.”
Merz on Monday depicted his efforts as necessary to ward off the rising political extremes in Germany on both sides of the spectrum, saying his success was linked to the survival of ailing mainstream parties.
“It will be a historic task — not only for the current governing coalition here in Berlin, but especially for the party I lead — to ensure that we remain, now and in the future, a united nation and a party that feels firmly anchored in the European Union,” he said. “We must now weather the storms of our time.”

The 17 European Parliament lawmakers you should watch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Not all MEPs are equal.
If you want to know how the European Parliament intends to shape major policy battles on deregulation, climate, tech and the EU budget, as well as prepare for the midterm top-jobs reshuffle and an election year that threatens to reshape the bloc, certain voices are more important than others.
Of the Parliament’s 720 members, only a handful will truly influence what comes next — from heavyweights steering landmark legislation to dynamic duos working hard behind closed doors.
They’ll be doing that work against a backdrop of two years of growing mistrust between Europe’s biggest mainstream political families (the European People’s Party and the Socialists and Democrats), an increasingly powerful far right, a sweeping simplification and competitiveness drive, and a heated migration debate.
Here are the 17 MEPs to watch and the political battles that will define the months ahead.
Power brokers
Roberta Metsola
The boss
EPP, Malta
The Parliament president will sit at the center of the EPP-S&D rift during the midterm top-jobs reshuffle. The EPP is determined that Metsola should remain in her job, but the S&D insists it’s their turn to have someone in the top seat. How that battle turns out will be a key test of whether Europe’s centrist alliance can continue working together after two years of infighting or descend into a nasty standoff. If it’s the latter, Metsola could try to seek a third term as president with support from the broad network of MEPs she has cultivated over the past five years, including on the right and far right of the hemicycle.
François-Xavier Bellamy
Weber’s fixer
EPP, France
If Marine Le Pen becomes French president next year, Bellamy could be the man that EPP chief Manfred Weber gets to conduct damage control in the Parliament. The architect of the EU’s tough new returns regulation, who voted with the far-right Patriots group, Bellamy is a trusted Weber lieutenant, serving as EPP treasurer and group vice chair. Just as the EPP sought to bring Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy into the EU fold, it may try to do the same with Le Pen’s National Rally — and Bellamy, whose Republicans party has moved closer to the National Rally back in France, could be the one calling them.
Advertisement
Camilla Laureti
Schlein’s fixer
S&D, Italy
Italy has the S&D’s second-largest national delegation, behind Spain, and S&D vice chair Camilla Laureti is tasked with making that weight count. Her portfolio puts her inside Parliament’s engine room — covering plenary session preparation, the Conference of Presidents (meetings of top MEPs), and group strategy — making her key to ensuring the Socialists deliver on any deal to rebuild the center and pull the EPP away from far-right majorities. Laureti is also Italian Democratic Party leader Elly Schlein’s eyes and ears in Brussels, an important role ahead of Italy’s 2027 national election. Laureti’s delicate task is to keep potential tensions between the Democratic Party and the Five Star Movement in the Parliament from spilling into Rome and exposing cracks in the country’s anti-Meloni opposition.
Valérie Hayer
Macron’s glue
Renew, France
Hayer chairs the Renew Europe group at a moment when liberals are losing ground across the bloc. She is trying to recruit outcast MEPs and lift Renew from being the fifth-largest group in the parliament. She is also positioning Renew as the bridge between EPP leader Manfred Weber and S&D leader Iratxe García, pushing for steadier cooperation between the traditional centrist allies (and Renew needs stability, as roughly half of its MEPs vote with the right-wing bloc when the EPP joins forces with the far right). Hayer’s position as group leader is secure ahead of the midterms: There is little appetite for change and no clear challenger. But Emmanuel Macron’s eventual departure will cost her a key ally, while she will need to deal with infighting among France’s many liberal factions.
Dolors Montserrat
Spanish campaign antenna
EPP, Spain
If Manfred Weber starts sounding like he’s on the campaign trail in Spain, Dolors Montserrat will be one reason why. The seasoned lawmaker leads Madrid’s center-right delegation in the European Parliament as the People’s Party gears up for a national election due by August 2027, which it is likely to win. Ahead of that vote, Spanish MEPs will start using Parliament to push debates and votes designed to score points back home. Weber has incentives to listen: Defeating Pedro Sánchez would topple one of Europe’s last major Socialist governments and deal a heavy blow to the S&D. As EPP secretary-general, Montserrat also coordinates the EPP’s member parties, and she is in line for a ministerial job if Partido Popular wins the election.
Advertisement
Behind-the-scenes movers
Anna Cavazzini
The multitasker
Greens, German
Cavazzini has placed herself at the heart of some of the EU’s biggest policy fights, including as the Greens’ top lawmaker on the International Trade Committee, where she pushed for stronger safeguards in the EU-U.S. trade deal. She also chairs the Internal Market Committee, where she is steering debates on Big Tech and digital markets, with key files on consumer protection and product standards to be presented by the European Commission in the coming months. Cavazzini has also landed the coveted job of leading negotiations on the Industrial Accelerator Act, the EU’s growth and competitiveness package. She will steer discussions on its politically sensitive provisions on Chinese investment in Europe.
Diego Solier
Tech stranger
ECR, Spain
A first-term independent MEP who quit a small Spanish anti-establishment party after its leader faced allegations of illegal campaign financing, Solier joined the European Conservatives and Reformists group and, despite not having a powerful national delegation behind him, landed roles dealing with a string of major tech files. He is Parliament’s lead negotiator on the Cloud and AI Development Act, a flagship of Europe’s tech-sovereignty push amid worsening transatlantic tensions, and leads the ECR’s position on the Cybersecurity Act.
Lukas Sieper
The influencer wild card
Renew, Germany
Everyone wants a piece of this 29-year-old German — or at least a cameo in his TikToks. One of Parliament’s youngest MEPs, the influencer-turned-politician made a name for himself through social-media savvy and late-night raves in the hallways. Despite leading a tiny party born over beers with university friends, Sieper was recruited by Renew in February and brought onto its leadership group to help shape communications strategy. Now he is organizing an influencer summit and cultivating allies across party lines by founding a football team. As the midterms loom, talk in the hallways is that he could try to leverage his popularity to snatch one of the precious jobs in Parliament.
Advertisement
Ilhan Kyuchuyk
Immunities chief
Renew, Bulgaria
This term, Parliament’s Legal Affairs Committee has already received more requests to waive MEPs’ immunity than during the entire previous mandate, including cases linked to corruption allegations and the Huawei and Qatargate influence scandals. That’s led to accusations of backroom deals between political groups to shield colleagues from prosecution. Senior lawmakers reject those claims, instead blaming poor-quality legal cases and flawed investigations. Now MEPs want to rewrite the rules on immunity. Leading the overhaul is committee chair Kyuchyuk, himself subject to a controversial immunity waiver request from the EU public prosecutor in Bulgaria that he was shielded from.
Adam Bielan
The MAGA connection
ECR, Poland
In mid-September 2026, Bielan was appointed president of the right-wing European Conservatives and Reformists, and, as leader of Poland’s Law and Justice delegation in the Parliament, maintains a direct line to party leader Jarosław Kaczyński. While ties between Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and the Trump administration have cooled, Bielan has emerged as a key bridge to Washington, and the ECR is the Republican Party’s official sister party in Europe. Bielan led ECR missions to meet senior U.S. officials and politicians, maintaining the strong bond between the U.S. and Poland.
Massimiliano Salini
Car crupier
EPP, Italy
The treasurer of the EPP group, Salini landed the role of lead negotiator on one of the Parliament’s most contentious files (and a top EPP priority): rolling back the de facto phase-out of a ban on the combustion engine. His job was initially to try to win over skeptical Social Democrats and liberals, but it’s become a struggle to unite his own group. Salini has to rally the EPP around a common position on emissions targets and alternative fuels, and in doing so he will need to decide whether to seek a centrist compromise or a deal with the far right.
Advertisement
Dynamic duos
Bálazs Orbán and Marieke Ehlers
Firewall breakers
PATRIOTS, HUNGARY AND PATRIOTS, THE NETHERLANDS
Viktor Orbán’s former political director Balázs Orbán (no relation) arrives in Parliament at the end of September, taking a seat from a colleague who returned to Hungary’s national parliament, giving the Patriots another seasoned political operator. The Hungarians are widely seen as experts at navigating the Parliament and bending its machinery to their advantage. Orbán will work alongside another powerful Hungarian Patriots MEP, Kinga Gál, ahead of the midterm reshuffle, as the group pushes the EPP to tear down the firewall and let it compete for top jobs.
Alongside him is Ehlers, the Patriots’ chief whip, who is tasked with finding common group positions and preparing plenary business. A former Parliament staffer with years of experience, she is also leading the Patriots’ push in the Constitutional Affairs Committee to rewrite Parliament’s rules, which the group argues are being weaponized to keep it on the sidelines.
Victor Negrescu and Christel Schaldemose
García’s headaches
S&D, ROMANIA AND S&D, DENMARK
These are two of Iratxe García’s most important lieutenants. They are also two of her biggest headaches. Negrescu is a seasoned strategist, with nearly a decade as an MEP and a stint as Romania’s Europe minister on his CV. He now leads an obscure working group tasked with shaping Parliament’s future, with reform proposals due by December. His trickier role is managing tensions between the S&D and Romania’s Social Democrats (PSD): Negrescu has tried to keep the PSD on a pro-EU course even as it flirts with the far-right at home, making him Brussels Socialists’ first port of call if that rapprochement deepens.
Schaldemose knows Parliament’s machinery inside out after 20 years as an MEP. Since 2024, she has served as a vice-president, overseeing the institution’s digital transformation and adaptation to AI, after previously leading negotiations on the Digital Services Act. She also leads the Danish Social Democrats, which are increasingly at odds with García’s Spanish delegation after Denmark joined in with the attacks on Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez over the Ceuta crisis. With Sánchez under electoral pressure and Nordic Social Democrats potentially gaining governing clout in Sweden and Finland, the Danes’ weight within the S&D could grow.
Advertisement
Niclas Herbst and René Repasi
Grand coalition nostalgics
EPP, GERMANY AND S&D, GERMANY
Herbst and Repasi — the European Parliament leaders of German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s center-right Christian Democrats and Vice Chancellor Lars Klingbeil’s center-left Social Democrats, respectively — are a key backchannel to the EPP-S&D coalition in the Parliament. The two MEPs are seeking to ease rising mistrust by pushing for a German-style grand coalition (or a Brussels-style package deal) with binding commitments and trade-offs to strengthen the alliance during the midterms, and therefore cut the far-right out of policymaking in Brussels.

Houthis say Saudi strike kills 6 in Yemen port city Mokha
SANAA – Saudi strikes on the strategic Red Sea port city of Mokha killed at least six people and wounded eight others, the Houthi-affiliated news agency Saba reported on Sept 22.
Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi movement has staged a lightning offensive in recent weeks to take over Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast, including Mokha, leaving the Saudi-backed government scrambling to respond.
“Six civilians, including two children and a woman, were killed and eight others, including a child and a woman, were injured in Saudi-led coalition airstrikes on Mokha,” Saba said.
The head of Yemen’s governing body Rashad al-Alimi held a call with US President Donald Trump to request American support against the pro-Iranian fighters, a source in Alimi’s office told AFP on Sept 21.
Trump did not promise military support, the source said, adding that the call took place on Sept 20 and was intended as a show of solidarity with Yemen’s embattled government.
US media has reported that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has also urged Trump to strike the Houthis.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham agreed to give military support to Saudi Arabia, media reports said on Sept 21.
Gains made by Yemen’s Houthis have cemented Iran and its allies hold over two key waterways, including the Strait of Hormuz, that the wider Gulf and top crude exporter Saudi Arabia rely on to ship out its oil.
The war in the Middle East began on Feb 28 with US-Israeli strikes on Iran, after which the Islamic republic responded with attacks around the region.
Iran-backed groups including the Houthis in Yemen and Hezbollah in Lebanon also later became involved.
The war in impoverished Yemen, which began in 2014 with the Houthi capture of the capital Sanaa, had been largely frozen since 2022 but resumed in July.
Saudi Arabia has led a coalition backing the internationally recognised government since 2015. Its intervention escalated the war, which has triggered one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. AFP

Stem cells reverse stroke damage and restore movement in mice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
01:49:32 UTC
10:49:32 KST

Stem cells reverse stroke damage and restore movement in mice
- Date:
- September 21, 2026
- Source:
- University of Zurich
- Summary:
- Stem cell transplants helped regenerate stroke-damaged brain tissue in mice, producing new neurons and restoring lost motor function. The treatment also improved blood vessels, inflammation, and the blood-brain barrier, raising hopes that a similar approach could eventually help repair the human brain after stroke.
- Share:
Stem cell transplants may be able to repair damage caused by stroke, according to researchers at the University of Zurich. In experiments with mice, the treatment helped generate new neurons, restore movement, and trigger several other forms of brain repair, offering a promising step toward regenerative treatments for neurological damage.
Stroke is extremely common, affecting about one in four adults over a lifetime. Roughly half of those who experience one are left with lasting problems such as paralysis or difficulty speaking.
These disabilities can occur because a stroke deprives parts of the brain of oxygen or causes bleeding that destroys brain cells. Once those cells are lost, the damage has traditionally been considered permanent because there are currently no treatments capable of rebuilding the affected brain tissue.
"That's why it is essential to pursue new therapeutic approaches to potential brain regeneration after diseases or accidents," says Christian Tackenberg, the Scientific Head of Division in the Neurodegeneration Group at the University of Zurich (UZH) Institute for Regenerative Medicine.
Stem Cells Could Help Rebuild Brain Tissue
One possible approach involves neural stem cells, which can develop into multiple types of cells found in the nervous system.
A research team led by Tackenberg and postdoctoral researcher Rebecca Weber tested that idea in two studies carried out in collaboration with a group headed by Ruslan Rust from the University of Southern California.
The results suggest that the transplanted cells do more than simply replace neurons lost after a stroke.
"Our findings show that neural stem cells not only form new neurons, but also induce other regeneration processes," Tackenberg says.
Human Stem Cells Become New Neurons
The researchers used human neural stem cells capable of producing different types of nervous system cells. These cells were created from induced pluripotent stem cells, which are made by reprogramming ordinary human somatic cells so that they regain the ability to develop into many different cell types.
The team then induced permanent strokes in mice. The resulting brain damage was designed to closely resemble important features of stroke in humans.
Because the transplanted cells came from humans, the mice were genetically modified so their immune systems would not reject them.
One week after the strokes were induced, the researchers transplanted the neural stem cells directly into damaged regions of the brain. They then tracked what happened using imaging techniques and biochemical analyses.
"We found that the stem cells survived for the full analysis period of five weeks and that most of them transformed into neurons, which actually even communicated with the already existing brain cells," Tackenberg says.
That ability to connect with the brain's existing cells is particularly important because simply producing new neurons would not necessarily restore function. The new cells must also become part of working neural networks.
The Brain Shows Multiple Signs of Repair
The researchers found evidence that the treatment triggered a much broader healing response.
New blood vessels formed in the damaged brain tissue, inflammatory processes became less intense, and the integrity of the blood-brain barrier improved.
The blood-brain barrier is a tightly controlled protective boundary that separates circulating blood from brain tissue. Damage to this barrier can contribute to inflammation and further injury following a stroke.
"Our analysis goes far beyond the scope of other studies, which focused on the immediate effects right after transplantation," Tackenberg explains.
Most importantly, the biological changes were accompanied by improvements in how the animals moved.
Stem cell transplantation reversed motor impairments caused by the strokes in the mice. Researchers measured those improvements in part using AI-assisted analysis of the animals' walking patterns.
Waiting a Week May Improve Stem Cell Therapy
The researchers designed the experiments with eventual human treatment in mind.
For example, the stem cells were produced without reagents derived from animals. Avoiding animal-derived materials can be important when developing therapies intended for human use because it may reduce potential safety and regulatory complications.
The University of Zurich team created a defined production protocol in collaboration with the Center for iPS Cell Research and Application (CiRA) at Kyoto University.
The second study also revealed an important insight about timing. The researchers found that stem cell transplantation worked better when it was performed one week after a stroke rather than immediately afterward.
That delay could make the approach considerably easier to use in a clinical setting. Doctors would have more time to prepare the treatment instead of needing to deliver it during the immediate emergency period following a stroke.
Researchers Work Toward Human Trials
Despite the encouraging findings, the researchers stress that several obstacles must still be addressed before the therapy could be tested widely in people.
"We need to minimize risks and simplify a potential application in humans," he says.
One concern is uncontrolled stem cell growth inside the brain. Tackenberg's group, again working with Ruslan Rust, is developing a type of safety switch intended to prevent that from happening.
The team is also exploring a less invasive way to deliver the cells.
Instead of transplanting stem cells directly into brain tissue, researchers are developing an endovascular injection approach. This would involve delivering the cells through blood vessels and could be much more practical than performing a brain graft.
There is already precedent for moving induced stem cell therapies into human testing. Initial clinical trials using induced stem cells to treat Parkinson's disease are underway in Japan, according to Tackenberg.
"Stroke could be one of the next diseases for which a clinical trial becomes possible."

Materials provided by University of Zurich. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Rebecca Z. Weber, Beatriz Achón Buil, Nora H. Rentsch, Patrick Perron, Stefanie Halliday, Allison Bosworth, Mingzi Zhang, Kassandra Kisler, Chantal Bodenmann, Kathrin J. Zürcher, Daniela Uhr, Debora Meier, Siri L. Peter, Melanie Generali, Shuo Lin, Markus A. Rüegg, Roger M. Nitsch, Christian Tackenberg, Ruslan Rust. Neural xenografts contribute to long-term recovery in stroke via molecular graft-host crosstalk. Nature Communications, 2025; 16 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41467-025-63725-3

Texas Governor Greg Abbott on Monday barred the state's environmental agency from issuing new permits for data centers until regulators complete a massive audit of the energy-hungry facilities seeking to connect to the Texas electrical grid.
The Republican governor's directive to the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality effectively freezes all state-issued permits to data center developers, which had flocked to the region for its abundant electricity, land and pro-business reputation.
Since the artificial intelligence boom began roughly three years ago, Texas has become one of the fastest-growing data hubs in the world. But intensifying public backlash over the facilities, and fears about AI more broadly, prompted Abbott last month to freeze the connection of new data centers to the state grid and order an audit of the facilities.
By the time of that directive, there were more than 470 gigawatts' worth of data center projects and other large energy users in line to connect to the grid - more than five times the state's peak demand.
The Electric Reliability Council of Texas, which operates the state grid, is in the early stages of auditing data center power use, tax incentives, and water consumption, among other factors.
'Data centers must... protect our grid and water' in Texas
“Simply put, Texans must come first,” Abbott said in a statement. “Data centers must pay their own way, protect our grid and water, and complete the (audits)."
Abbott is among a swelling number of governors who once raced to attract data center investments - and touted their public benefit - but are now tightening restrictions on the developments to ease their constituents' fears about rising power bills and environmental issues caused by the facilities.
Ed Hirs, an energy fellow at the University of Houston, said Abbott was walking back "his earlier pronouncements about data centers leading to lower electricity prices."

"The EU operation Aspides is making a crucial contribution to security in the region and global shipping, but the operation needs more naval assets and more air assets to address the increased level of threats in the region," she said.
Kallas sent a letter to the EU's 27 member states on September 19 asking them to up their contributions. The issue would be discussed at upcoming defense and foreign ministers' meetings, she said in the letter.
"This situation, which is still evolving as we speak, is already affecting European interests with repercussions on our supply chains and could have implications for our ability to support our economies, which were already hit by rising fuel prices," she said in the letter.
"For the moment, although the Houthis communicate that they would only target Saudi-linked interests, there is uncertainty over their course of action with respect to vessels that transit through the Strait. Regardless, they are now in a better position to potentially harm maritime shipping."
Houthis have made rapid advances in recent weeks along the Red Sea coast
The Houthis have made rapid advances in recent weeks along the Red Sea coast, further complicating routes in a region that also includes the Strait of Hormuz, where traffic had already dwindled because of the US-Iran war.
A lightning advance by the Iran-backed group this month has extended the wider Middle East conflict to a new theater and further threatened global energy supplies. The US has so far rebuffed repeated pleas from Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to join the fight in Yemen.

UN AI experts warn against ‘apocalyptic’ rhetoric on risks
- UN AI experts warn against using apocalyptic language about AI risks, emphasising the need for scientific understanding rather than fear-driven narratives.
- The International Scientific Panel on AI, formed in 2025, aims to clarify AI risks and inform UN decisions with nuanced, evidence-based discussions.
- Experts call for global, rational debate on AI risks, highlighting uncertainty and differing opinions over alarmist claims of existential threats.
AI generated
NEW YORK – Several experts on a United Nations artificial intelligence committee warned on Sept 21 against the apocalyptic rhetoric used by some professionals in the sector regarding AI risks.
“As scientists, it’s very important to invest in the science, to really understand what we know (from) what we don’t know, and investing in fear is not that helpful,” said Joelle Barral, an executive at Google DeepMind and a member of the International Scientific Panel on AI, an independent body.
She was responding to a question from AFP about recent public statements on AI’s potential dangers, particularly from Jacob Coxon.
The former Anthropic employee, who previously worked at OpenAI, said in early September that AI developers believed the technology “could kill us all by the end of the decade”.
A research engineer who left Google DeepMind in July made similar comments, saying it might already be “too late to avoid” humanity’s eradication by AI.
“We have to change the way we talk about AI risk because for a very long time, it’s either existential and everything is going to die and the killer robots are coming, or it doesn’t really matter,” Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa, an investigative reporter, said on Sept 21 at the same event, held in New York on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
“The truth, though, is far more nuanced and sophisticated,” she continued.
“You can’t turn that into ideology, which is, I think, where (the debate) has been heading.”
The International Scientific Panel on AI was created in 2025, with its members selected in February 2026.
Its mandate is to advance the scientific understanding of AI and inform UN deliberations.
Yoshua Bengio, a panel co-chair who is considered one of the fathers of AI, said it was important to distinguish between what scientists actually know about AI risks and what can only be “plausibly extrapolated” from that evidence – an area where experts still disagree.
“The problem with shouting very loudly is that someone else can also shout very loudly,” he said.
What is needed instead is “a global rational discussion about what is going on, including about the uncertainty, including about the severity of the risks”. AFP

How Hong Kong can keep the talking going when US-China officials don’t

How Hong Kong can keep the talking going when US-China officials don’t
Hong Kong can’t set the terms of the contest, but with Track 1.5 diplomacy, it can decide if it is the room in which competition is managed
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Neville Lai is the co-founder and CEO of Trigrams Research Group (TRG), an independent boutique research firm dedicated to helping organisations build future-proof capabilities and resilience through market research and strategic foresight to develop critical sectors in Asia. 
When Tung Chee-hwa died, the obituaries predictably described a Hong Kong shipping mogul who became the city’s first postcolonial chief executive. How his government navigated the Asian financial crisis and severe acute respiratory syndrome (Sars) epidemic and its retreat from Article 23 were highlighted. There was less attention paid to the political hybrid he embodied.
Tung sat as vice-chairman of China’s top political advisory body, the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference, until 2023 – state-leader rank, no diplomatic portfolio. His working instrument was the China-United States Exchange Foundation, which he established in Hong Kong in 2008, the year marking the 30th anniversary of Sino-US relations, to keep senior Americans and Chinese talking when their governments would not.
Standing without a mandate, exercised through a private vehicle: that is Track 1.5, and Tung was very good at it.
At the recent China-US Track 1.5 Dialogue in Beijing, Liu Haixing, head of the Communist Party’s International Department, said both countries should expand the “pie” of shared interests and reject zero-sum games to reach “normal stability with controllable disagreements”. This is not the stuff of summit headlines but of realistic ambition: neither a friendship nor a divorce, but a managed rivalry where shared interests can grow and the rest is fenced off.

Hunter mistook woman for deer in fatal US shooting, police say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
01:30:00 UTC
10:30:00 KST

Hunter mistook woman for deer in fatal US shooting, police say
Neil Vigdor
WASHINGTON – A hunter is facing a manslaughter charge in the US state of Delaware in the fatal shooting of a woman whom he mistook for a deer while she crossed an open field with three other people, the authorities said.
The man, Walter W. Moorhead, 74, fired his rifle from a ground blind, a tent, shed or other makeshift structure used by hunters to conceal themselves, when he struck Santos Maria Chilel Soto, 39, on a private property on the night of Sept 18 in Ellendale, Delaware, the Delaware State Police said.
Investigators said the shooting occurred around 7.40 pm local time, just over 30 minutes after sunset, in an area dotted with farms, about 120km south of Wilmington, Delaware, and west of Delaware’s well-known coastal resorts.
Soto, who a GoFundMe page said was a mother of five from Guatemala, was with her boyfriend and her boyfriend’s two children when she was shot, according to an arrest warrant. It was not clear why Soto, who lived in Georgetown, Delaware, was on the property.
The victim’s boyfriend told the police that the four of them had been walking together across the field when he heard an explosion and saw Soto fall to the ground with a gunshot wound to her torso, the warrant said.
An older white man, whom investigators identified as Moorhead, approached with a flashlight to search for the deer he thought he had shot, Detective M. Csapo of the Delaware State Police wrote in the warrant.
During an interview with police, the authorities said, Moorhead acknowledged that he had struck Soto.
Moorhead, of Salisbury, Maryland, was also charged with three counts of reckless endangering and possession of a firearm during the commission of a felony. He was released on a US$43,000 (S$54,900) cash bond.
Efforts to reach Moorhead were not immediately successful on Sept 21. It was not clear if he had a lawyer.
Moorhead had been hunting under what is known in Delaware as a crop damage permit, Corporal Raushan Rich of the Delaware State Police said in an email on Sept 21.
The programme allows commercial farms that experience crop damage to hunt antlerless deer, specifically mature does, more frequently than under normal deer hunting regulations.
The state, which expanded the programme in 2026, allows deer hunting from a half-hour before sunrise until a half-hour after sunset, which was about 7.06pm on Sept 18 in Ellendale.
In Delaware, the Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Control oversees hunting regulations. It did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Sept 21 or provide a copy of the hunting permit associated with the farm where the shooting occurred.
Details about who owns the property were also not immediately available.
In a Facebook post on Sept 19, Iglesia de Dios Fuente de Verdad Delaware in Georgetown – a Pentecostal church – announced Soto’s death. Organisers of the GoFundMe page were seeking donations to help return Soto’s body to Guatemala. NYTIMES

The New Zealand-India free trade agreement will make 57 percent of New Zealand's exports to India tariff-free from the first day, including sheep meat, wool and coal, McClay said in a statement on Tuesday.
More than 95 percent of forestry and wood exports will also be tariff-free on day one, while exporters will receive a second round of tariff cuts on Jan. 1, 2027, he said.
New Zealand exporters will also gain preferential quota access to India for albumins, apples and kiwifruit under the agreement.
McClay said the agreement would improve market access for New Zealand businesses in India, while providing greater certainty for services exporters, investors and companies seeking to expand in the Indian market.
The agreement is expected to help New Zealand exporters diversify markets and build resilience amid growing uncertainty in global markets, the minister noted. ■

4 European nations back India's bid for permanent UN seat, Jaishankar calls it 'historic'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
01:17:06 UTC
10:17:06 KST

Poland, Hungry, Slovakia and Czech Republic on Monday backed India's bid for a permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council, with Slovakia foreign minister Juraj Blanár saying India, as a leading country of the Global South and an emerging power in the Indo-Pacific, should have a place at the UN's top decision-making body.The remarks came after external affairs minister S Jaishankar participated in the first high-level Visegrád Group (V4) plus India meeting on the sidelines of the 81st UN General Assembly in New York."We all agree, as V4 countries, that India, as part of the Global South, an upcoming superpower in the Indo-Pacific region, must be at the table as a permanent member of the UN Security Council," Blanár said.The V4 comprises Poland, Hungary, Slovakia and Czechia. The four countries held their first ministerial-level meeting with India in the new V4+India format during the UNGA high-level week.Jaishankar described the meeting as a "new historic occasion" and said the discussions covered political, economic, defence, technology, space, connectivity and people-to-people ties."We had our first Visegrad Four and India meeting. It was, in a sense, a new historic occasion, and I would like to thank Minister Juraj (Foreign Minister of Slovakia) for convening us today. It was a very, very productive meeting.
What we agreed was that since India's relationship with the European Union itself is deepening, with the V4, we would take some special initiatives to create an annual business forum. As foreign ministers, we would meet annually. That was the consensus. We would also explore in technology and innovation whether we could be doing more. We have a very strong history with all the V4 countries in defense. We want to refresh and take forward that record and that cooperation. We discussed space issues, connectivity, and people-to-people mobility. We have students in each of the V4 countries. Overall, in terms of our cooperation, as well as a very good and useful exchange on the big global crisis, the Ukraine conflict, and what's happening in the Gulf. I think it was a very worthwhile and productive meeting. I'm very pleased about it."
Jaishankar on V4's role in global affairs
Asked about the political importance of the V4 for India on the global stage, Jaishankar said New Delhi viewed the four countries as partners with strong industrial, technological and innovation capabilities."We have very good relations with the V4 countries, and we know that these are countries with a very strong, very distinctive capability. They are industrial economies, economies with great innovation and technology talent. And I think how the V4 come together is for them to decide. But we certainly welcome the opportunity to work."India has been seeking reform of the UN Security Council and a permanent seat on the body. The Council currently has five permanent members, China, France, Russia, the UK and the US, alongside 10 non-permanent members elected for two-year terms.Jaishankar had formally launched India's campaign for a non-permanent UNSC term for 2028-29 in July, while New Delhi has continued to press for broader reform of the Council and permanent membership for India.
Jaishankar said the meeting also resulted in an agreement to strengthen cooperation through annual foreign ministerial meetings and an annual business forum.In a post on X, Jaishankar said: "Our first meeting in the V4+India format agreed to: Closer political cooperation including annual meetings of Foreign Ministers. Deeper economic cooperation, including the Annual Business Forum. Reinvigorating our defence cooperation. Further development of our cultural cooperation and people-to-people relations."The meeting included Poland's deputy prime minister and foreign minister Radosław Sikorski, Hungary's deputy prime minister and foreign minister Dr Anita Orbán, Slovakia's foreign minister Juraj Blanár and Czechia's foreign minister Petr Macinka.Jaishankar is leading the Indian delegation at the 81st UN General Assembly high-level week in New York and is scheduled to address the General Debate on September 26.

US set for major military expansion in Greenland – Reuters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22

US set for major military expansion in Greenland – Reuters
The US is set to establish a military presence at two additional sites in Greenland under a security agreement with Denmark and the self-governing Arctic territory, according to media reports, as Copenhagen insists the deal does not surrender Danish sovereignty.
US President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen are expected to sign the agreement at UN headquarters in New York on Tuesday, on the sidelines of the General Assembly. The full text has not yet been made public, but media reports suggest the US is seeking to expand its military footprint imminently.
Washington plans to reopen the former Cold War-era Bluie West One base at Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland and establish a presence at Mestersvig on the island’s east coast, Reuters reported on Monday, citing people familiar with the negotiations.
Mestersvig is currently used by Denmark’s Sirius Dog Sled Patrol, an elite military unit tasked with reconnaissance and enforcing Danish sovereignty in the remote Arctic region. Trump has repeatedly mocked Denmark’s reliance on dog-sled patrols as evidence that Copenhagen was failing to adequately protect Greenland.
Trump has portrayed the agreement in sweeping terms, saying last week that it gives the US “permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland.” He also claimed that no American adversary would be allowed to establish a base or military presence, or make sensitive investments on the island without Washington’s approval.
Denmark has stressed that the arrangement does not transfer sovereignty over Greenland to the United States.
Frederiksen said the agreement explicitly recognizes “the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark,” as well as the Greenlandic population’s right to self-determination. Copenhagen has presented the deal as a way of placing greater responsibility for Arctic security within NATO rather than handing control exclusively to Washington.
Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen has said Copenhagen remains willing to accommodate legitimate US security interests in the Arctic while maintaining its established “red lines.”
The agreement follows months of tensions triggered by Trump’s repeated demands for US control over Greenland, during which he at times declined to rule out military or economic pressure. Copenhagen and Nuuk firmly rejected any transfer of the territory.
Washington already enjoys extensive military access under a 1951 defense agreement, amended in 2004. During the Cold War, the US operated 17 installations and stationed more than 10,000 personnel in Greenland. Today, its presence is concentrated at Pituffik Space Base, with roughly 150 US military personnel stationed there.

US jury convicts man of attempted murder in shooting of Palestinian students
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
01:14:42 UTC
10:14:42 KST

A jury in the US state of Vermont has convicted 51-year-old Jason Eaton of attempted murder for shooting three Palestinian university students near the University of Vermont campus in Burlington in November 2023, The Guardian reported.
Eaton faces up to life in prison following the conviction.
The gun attack left Hisham Awartani paralysed from the waist down and wounded his close friends Tahseen Aliahmad and Kinnan Abdalhamid.
The jury returned its guilty verdict after several hours of deliberation following a week-long trial that heard direct testimony from all three victims alongside competing psychiatric experts.
Eaton, who did not dispute firing the shots, had pleaded not guilty, claiming he was not criminally responsible due to his mental state.
Defence lawyers highlighted his claims that US and Israeli intelligence agencies transmitted instructions to shoot via FM radio, alongside delusions that God commanded him to protect neighbours.
The jury dismissed the insanity defence.
Sentencing remand
Eaton was remanded in custody without bail pending sentencing, showing no emotion as the verdict was announced.
Awartani and Aliahmad, seated in the courtroom's front row, embraced supporters.
"Justice has been rendered for Hisham, Kinnan and Tahseen. After three years of sorrow, loss and struggle, our families finally feel relief," the families affirmed in a joint statement.
They stressed the outcome "affirms something fundamental: Jason Eaton is responsible for what he did", pointing out that Eaton's repeated use of "hateful" language during the trial confirmed his motives: "This was a hate crime. We have said so from the beginning."
The families also drew parallels to the broader plight of their people: "While our children fought to heal from being shot in Burlington, they watched Palestinian children lose their lives, their homes, their land, their families."
"Hisham, Kinnan and Tahseen have spent three years rebuilding their bodies and their lives after a hateful act almost killed them. We are profoundly relieved."
