In an unprecedented move, Netanyahu will spend only a few hours in New York, will not stay overnight and will depart for Israel that evening. Netanyahu will not take journalists with him on the plane.
Netanyahu is expected to land aboard the Wing of Zion at a military airfield in New Jersey or at Newark Liberty International Airport, rather than at JFK Airport. The decision is due to difficulties coordinating with U.S. authorities as well as concerns that New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani could order the Wing of Zion to leave the airport immediately rather than remain there until Netanyahu returns. It was therefore decided that the plane would land in New Jersey.
Officials familiar with the matter believe Netanyahu decided to dramatically shorten his visit to New York and not stay overnight because of concerns about protests.
Netanyahu has already canceled a planned stop in Texas, where he had intended to meet Elon Musk. An Israeli official, referring to the cancellation of the meeting with Musk, said: “There were coordination challenges, both because of the need for a refueling stop and because the Americans are less keen on last-minute arrangements.”
As previously reported, Netanyahu will not meet U.S. President Donald Trump during the visit and no other meetings in the city have yet been scheduled for him.
The U.S. president is expected to meet New York City Mayor Mamdani on Tuesday evening at Gracie Mansion, the mayor’s official residence. The meeting will be closed to the media. Trump, who has met the prime minister several times since returning to the White House, is scheduled to address the UN General Assembly on Tuesday. Immediately afterward, however, he is expected to return to Washington to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping.
As for Netanyahu, the prime minister is likely to meet U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Efforts are also underway to arrange meetings with foreign leaders who will be in the city, but his tight schedule has made coordinating such meetings particularly difficult. A U.S. administration official said Netanyahu’s presence in the United States would be limited because of the approaching elections in Israel.
Netanyahu’s speech will focus on the Iranian threat, and officials close to the prime minister say it is expected to include “surprises.”
Netanyahu’s speech is aimed first and foremost at the Israeli public, giving him valuable airtime to address Israelis during prime time. Israel’s delegation to the UN is preparing for possible disruptions, including heckling or a coordinated walkout by representatives of numerous countries, as occurred last year.

Wilson backs Türkiye’s return to F-35 program

“But the bottom line, let’s go back: Türkiye is a great ally of America, America is an ally of Türkiye, and we want mutual benefit,” he said.
The US suspended Türkiye from the F-35 fighter jet program in 2019 after objecting to its purchase of the Russian S-400 air defense system, claiming the system would endanger the fighter jets and is inoperable with NATO systems. Türkiye has said repeatedly that there is no conflict between the two and proposed a commission to study the issue.
Several Turkish defense entities were sanctioned under CAATSA.
During his meeting with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Türkiye in July on the sidelines of the NATO summit, Trump said he would “certainly” consider allowing Ankara to buy F-35 fighter jets and wants to remove the CAATSA sanctions on the country.

Details

Shackling prisoners giving birth should be a last resort – but it’s happening around Australia anyway
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
22:00:36 UTC
07:00:36 KST

“She was pregnant with twins,” Tahlia Isaac says. “She was meant to be released in 10 days, but she went into labour early.”
Isaac says officers handcuffed her fellow prisoner in the back of a van and took her away.
In her submission to a federal inquiry into shackling during childbirth, she says many woman who have experienced it “still think about the time they gave birth to their child cuffed to the bed, years later”.
“They weep when they describe wanting to cradle their newborn child but only had one available hand to do so,” says Isaac, the founder of Project:herSELF, a not-for-profit supporting formerly incarcerated women.
Lidia Thorpe, the Gunnai, Gunditjmara and Djab Wurrung woman and independent senator for Victoria, has introduced a private member’s bill to prohibit shackling during childbirth.
“No one giving birth is at risk of running away,” Thorpe said in her second reading of the bill. “Anyone who has given birth would agree that to be shackled whilst giving birth would be an incredibly violent and terrifying act.”
There is a patchwork of state and territory laws that state shackling should only be used as a “last resort” or only when “absolutely necessary”, but critics – and Thorpe – say it’s happening anyway.
“People are cuffed to their hospital bed by an arm and a leg in the delivery room, their legs shackled together by a chain,” Thorpe said.
As well as helping women who’ve gone through it, Isaac witnessed it herself when she was in prison. She says the woman who was taken away in the prison van was separated from her child and sent straight back.
“I just remember hearing her scream, just wailing and wailing. I think every woman in that centre was left horrified,” she says.
On Wednesday, Thorpe told the Senate about Heather Calgaret, a Yamatji, Noongar, Wongi and Pitjantjatjara woman, and mother of four children.
In 2019, she gave birth while shackled to a hospital bed in Victoria.
Days after the birth, Calgaret’s baby was removed, a decision her family said would have “crushed” her, and her health deteriorated after that.
“In November 2021, Heather died in custody after being administered a high dose of buprenorphine, a drug used to treat opioid addiction. She had no history of opiate use,” Thorpe told the Senate.
“Heather should still be here with us today.
“Her life was precious and her passing was preventable.”
In 2025, the coroner found the removal of her daughter was “pivotal” to Calgaret’s death.
According to an August report from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, about one in 10 of Australia’s prisoners are women.
According to the parliamentary library, between 5% and 10% of women in prison are pregnant, and at least half have a history of mental illness or childhood abuse.
Almost half the female prisoners identify as Indigenous.
The only data on giving birth while incarcerated was from 2017, when 25 women gave birth.
Fifteen years ago, the UN general assembly adopted the Bangkok Rules on the treatment of female prisoners, which state that prison should be a last resort for pregnant women and that “instruments of restraint shall never be used on women during labour, during birth and immediately after birth”.
The rules were adopted unanimously by the general assembly. But around the world, they are regularly flouted.
The National Justice Project told the inquiry into Thorpe’s bill that shackling someone during labour and childbirth was “not a grey area”.
“It is a clear breach of settled human rights standards and violates the rights of two people at once: the mother giving birth and the child being born,” the organisation said in its submission.
The Australian College of Midwives has said it was also against the Mandela rules for the treatment of prisoners and shackling was “an unsafe and unnecessary practice that may result in adverse outcomes for women and newborns, perinatal mental ill-health”.
The National Network of Incarcerated and Formerly Incarcerated Women and Girls tells the story of Yannetty*, who was six months pregnant when she was handcuffed and shackled and transported in 40C heat for a medical appointment in 2013 or 2014.
She said she was hot, swollen, frightened of fainting, and frightened for her baby.
“I was not treated like a pregnant woman going to receive medical care. I felt like I was being treated as though I was something dangerous that needed to be bound,” she said.
The chief executive of Sisters Inside, Debbie Kilroy, said shackling during childbirth was “state violence inflicted at the moment a person is most physically vulnerable and in need of care”.
“Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women will be disproportionately exposed to this violence because they are disproportionately targeted, criminalised and imprisoned. The practice sits within a much longer colonial history of controlling First Nations women, separating families and denying Aboriginal mothers’ authority over their own bodies and children,” she said.
The Guiding Principles for Corrections in Australia say “instruments of restraint are not used on prisoners … during and immediately following childbirth”.
The same is true for other significant medical conditions, the guidelines say, “unless an individualised assessment identifies a compelling safety risk that cannot be managed by other available means”.
In the ACT, restraints are a “last resort”, and only to be used on a pregnant detainee when “all other efforts have failed”, according to the parliamentary library. In NSW, pregnant prisoners “must not be restrained unless it is absolutely necessary”.
Other states and territories have similar caveats.
If passed, the bill would override those exemptions.
Amelia* only found out she was pregnant when she was strip-searched and put through a scanner once she got to prison. She was cuffed for all her ultrasound appointments, and struggled to roll into the right position because of the handcuffs.
Officials had drawn up her birthing plan, telling her she would be cuffed during labour. She was told she could have a support person with her – then they clarified it would be a prison officer, but she could nominate them.
In the end, she got out about 10 weeks before giving birth.
“The birth, anyway, was traumatic because I’m so scared of needles,” she said.
She was in labour for four days, had three failed epidurals, and got pre-eclampsia.
“Imagine that with cuffs. I do think about it. It’s ridiculous,” she said.
“I’m glad I got to do it the way I did.”
In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. International helplines can be found at befrienders.org
* Names have been changed

Negative religious coping is linked to a mind-body disconnect during acute stress
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
22:00:23 UTC
07:00:23 KST

A new study suggests that when facing a challenging situation, people who feel punished by or angry with God report feeling more stressed, yet their bodies show a smaller increase in blood pressure than expected. The findings provide evidence that psychological and physical responses to stress do not always match, especially when spiritual struggles are involved. The research was published in Psychology of Religion and Spirituality.
Religious coping refers to how people use their faith to understand and deal with difficult life events. While some individuals rely on positive strategies, such as seeking comfort from a higher power, others experience negative religious coping. This involves spiritual struggles, such as feeling abandoned by God, questioning divine intentions, or viewing hardships as a spiritual punishment. In daily life, this negative coping style is often linked to poorer mental health and a harder time managing emotions.
“Religion is often viewed as a source of comfort and support during stressful times, but not all forms of religious coping are beneficial,” lead author Ailbhe Dempsey, a researcher at the Study of Anxiety, Stress and Health Laboratory in the Department of Psychology at the University of Limerick, told PsyPost. “Negative religious coping, such as feeling punished or abandoned by God or questioning one’s faith, is consistently associated with poorer psychological well-being, yet we know relatively little about how it relates to the body’s response to acute stress.”
When a person faces a sudden psychological challenge, the body’s cardiovascular system naturally responds. Heart rate and blood pressure typically rise to supply the body with energy to meet the demands of the situation. This process is known as cardiovascular stress reactivity. Some research indicates that certain religious behaviors can influence this physical response. For instance, a study covered by PsyPost in 2026 found that frequent private religious practices are associated with smaller spikes in blood pressure during stressful tasks.
While extremely large spikes in blood pressure can increase the risk of heart disease over time, unusually low or blunted responses are not necessarily healthy. A 2011 study indicated that people who report high levels of stress in their daily lives tend to have blunted heart rate reactions to new stressful situations. Similarly, a 2020 study demonstrated that diminished physical stress responses are linked to higher levels of behavioral disengagement, meaning individuals are more likely to give up when faced with a challenge.
Scientists theorize that chronic emotional struggles might exhaust or downregulate the body’s stress systems, leading to these blunted physical reactions. To explore this complex relationship, Dempsey and her colleagues aimed to examine how negative religious coping affects both how stressed someone feels and how their heart and blood vessels physically react during a challenging moment.
“Most previous research has focused on general life stress rather than responses to a standardized stressor in a controlled setting,” Dempsey said. “We therefore wanted to examine both the psychological and cardiovascular responses associated with negative religious coping in young adults.”
To investigate this, the researchers recruited 81 healthy young adults with an average age of 19 from a Christian university in the southern United States. The participants completed questionnaires assessing their typical use of negative religious coping, rating how often they felt abandoned by God or questioned their faith during hard times. They also answered questions about their general religiosity, symptoms of depression, and personality traits.
During the laboratory session, participants sat quietly for a ten-minute resting period to establish a baseline for their heart rate and blood pressure. Then, they completed a stress-inducing task called the Paced Auditory Serial Addition Task. This involved listening to a fast-paced series of numbers and adding consecutive digits together out loud. To make the task more stressful, researchers included elements of social evaluation. Participants were told they were competing against peers on a fictional leaderboard, recorded on video, and asked to look at themselves in a mirror during the test. For every incorrect or missed answer, they were warned that points would be deducted.
Blood pressure and heart rate were continuously monitored while the participants completed the mental math challenge. Immediately after the task was over, the participants rated how stressed they felt on a scale from one to seven. The researchers then analyzed the data to see if typical religious coping styles were associated with the participants’ reactions in the lab.
The mental math task successfully triggered a stress response across the group, raising both average heart rates and blood pressures. However, the researchers found a divergence between the participants’ mental and physical reactions based on their religious coping styles. Individuals who reported higher levels of negative religious coping felt more stressed during the mental math task. Yet, these same individuals displayed a blunted physical response.
Specifically, they had a smaller increase in their diastolic blood pressure, which is the pressure in the arteries when the heart rests between beats. Negative religious coping accounted for an additional eight percent of the variance in this blunted blood pressure response and six percent of the variance in self-reported stress levels. These associations held true even after the researchers accounted for other factors that might influence stress, such as resting blood pressure, biological sex, overall religiosity, neuroticism, and symptoms of depression.
The researchers did not find a statistically significant association between negative religious coping and changes in heart rate or systolic blood pressure, which is the pressure in the arteries when the heart beats. While the physical measures were mixed, the psychological aspect of these results is consistent with research covered by PsyPost in 2022. That study, which examined self-reported mental health during the pandemic rather than immediate responses to a laboratory stress task, similarly found that negative religious coping was linked to heightened psychological distress.
“The main takeaway is that the way people engage with religion during difficult times may matter for how they experience stress,” Dempsey explained. “Importantly, psychological and physiological responses to stress did not necessarily move in the same direction, highlighting that feeling highly stressed does not always mean showing a larger cardiovascular response.”
“These findings add to evidence that struggles involving religion or faith can be an important aspect of how some people experience and cope with stress,” she added.
There are a few things to keep in mind regarding the current study. The research was observational and cross-sectional, meaning it can only highlight associations at a single point in time. “It is important not to interpret these findings as showing that negative religious coping causes blunted cardiovascular responses or greater stress, as the study was observational and cannot establish causation,” Dempsey cautioned. It is possible that individuals prone to heavy stress and emotion regulation difficulties naturally develop both a cynical view of their faith and a fatigued cardiovascular response.
The study also focused on a specific demographic. “In addition, our sample consisted of predominantly female undergraduate students at a private Christian university in the United States, which may limit how broadly the findings generalize,” Dempsey noted. Because religion might be more culturally embedded in this specific environment, struggles with faith could exert a stronger influence on stress than they would in other settings. The results might not perfectly translate to older adults or individuals in more secular or religiously diverse environments.
The researchers also noted that blood pressure was recorded semi-automatically. This required a researcher to push a button at specific times to take a reading, which introduces a slight possibility of human error, even when monitoring a stopwatch. Fully automated equipment might provide more precise measurements in future studies.
“Larger and more diverse studies are needed to better understand the relationship between negative religious coping, stress responses, and health,” Dempsey concluded. Including measures of how well people regulate their emotions could also help explain why spiritual struggles seem to disconnect the mind’s experience of stress from the body’s physical reaction.
The study, “Negative Religious Coping Is Associated With Blunted Cardiovascular Reactivity and Higher Self-Reported Stress in Response to Acute Psychological Stress,” was authored by Ailbhe Dempsey, Thomas A. Fergus, Siobhán Howard, Stephen Gallagher, and Annie T. Ginty.

UK: Man charged over suspected role in Rwanda genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
21:57:00 UTC
06:57:00 KST

UK: Man charged over suspected role in Rwanda genocide
September 21, 2026
UK authorities arrested and charged a man on Monday over alleged links to the Rwandan genocide, prosecutors and the London police said. It was the first arrest of its kind, although authorities have been pursuing the case for several years.
The 65-year-old man has been charged with one count of being an ancillary to genocide and six offenses of aiding crimes against humanity in Rwanda, officials said.
"This case demonstrates the UK is not a safe haven for individuals suspected of committing international crimes," said Commander Helen Flanagan, head of counterterror policing.
The Rwandan genocide took place in 1994, where over 800,000 ethnic Tutsis and moderate ethnic Hutus were killed in a 100-day rampage, orchestrated and led by the Hutu ruling majority. Local officials and ordinary citizens were involved in the mass killing.
UK law allows prosecutors to bring charges for some international offenses, including genocide and crimes against humanity, even if the crimes were committed abroad.
It is the latest case of an arrest in Europe of someone linked to Rwanda's genocide. In July, a German-Rwandan national was arrested for charges of taking part in the genocide and killing one person himself.
Meanwhile, in the Netherlands, a man was sentenced to life in prison for having taken part in attacks on homes, including launching a grenade on sheltering Tutsi civilians.
Suspect underwent name change
UK's Metropolitan Police war crimes investigators opened the case against the suspect in 2019, following a request by the Rwandan government.
The 65-year-old is originally from Kigali but lived in London at the time of the arrest.
He reportedly entered the UK as an asylum seeker in 1998, according to Rwandan Justice Minister Tharcisse Karugarama.
After being granted British citizenship in 2004, the man underwent a name change, and two years later, he was arrested over his connection to the genocide.
His extradition to Rwanda, along with four other men, was ultimately halted by a British UK court in 2017.
The failed extradition prompted the Rwandan government to urge UK authorities to investigate the matter themselves.
Frank Ferguson, head of the Crown Prosecution Service's counterterror division, said the man is "alleged to have directed and incited acts of murder and genocide carried out by others."
Authorities say investigations are ongoing for more suspects who are linked to the Rwandan genocide currently living in Britain.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The shutdown follows what Russian authorities described as the largest Ukrainian drone attack on Moscow since the start of the full-scale war.
As Kyiv Post previously reported, the strike hit the Gazprom Neft-owned refinery in Moscow’s southeastern Kapotnya district, roughly 15 kilometers (9 miles) from the Kremlin.
Ukraine’s General Staff confirmed hits on the AVT-6 primary crude-processing unit, an integrated oil refining unit and an isomerization unit, with fires reported across the facility.
The refinery processes around 11.6 million metric tons of crude annually and supplies roughly 35% to 40% of Moscow’s fuel needs and up to 70% of the gasoline and aviation kerosene consumed across the wider Moscow region.
President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed the strikes on Sunday, saying Ukrainian long-range weapons had targeted facilities directly supporting Russia’s war effort.
“In the Moscow region tonight, our long-range responses worked very noticeably,” Zelensky said.
“Key oil industry and logistics facilities supporting the aggressor’s war machine were hit. These represent billions of dollars sustaining the war effort.”
Russian Ballistic Strikes Hit Dnipro, Kryvyi Rih and Pavlohrad, 3 Wounded
Zelensky said Ukrainian forces used several domestically produced long-range systems during the operation, including FP-1, RZ-100, MICH-2000, Palianytsia, Vendetta, Liutyi, Bars, Flamingo, Sichnevyi and Pelican.
Long-range drones operated by the Security Service of Ukraine’s (SBU) Alpha Special Operations Center traveled more than 500 kilometers to penetrate air defenses around the Russian capital, Kyiv Post previously reported.
The attack also struck logistics facilities in the Moscow region, including a warehouse complex in Sofyino in the Ramensky district.

The refinery’s AVT-6 unit has a processing capacity of about 21,400 metric tons of crude per day, accounting for 53% of the plant’s total capacity, while the Euro+ complex accounts for the remaining 47%.
Fuel produced by the refinery was no longer being offered for sale on the St. Petersburg International Mercantile Exchange beginning Monday, Sept. 21.
The shutdown comes as Ukraine has intensified long-range strikes on Russian oil refining and logistics infrastructure critical to financing and supplying Moscow’s war against Ukraine.

Hundreds of flights from US East Coast airports have been cancelled or delayed due to a telecommunications line outage caused by a construction mistake, US officials said.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on X on Monday that around 1900 GMT, flights were resuming at LaGuardia Airport and Philadelphia, while flights into Newark and JFK Airports were paused.
"An Amtrak construction crew accidentally cut into a fibre line in New Jersey, which caused a telecom outage and forced the FAA to pause flights in the Northeast," Duffy said.
"This incident underscores the need for additional funding to modernise ageing infrastructure and prevent disruptions like this in the future."
Amtrak is the US passenger train company.
Massive rupture
Around 1900 GMT, Newark Airport, a key New York City-area hub, had 168 flights cancelled and 97 delayed, while Philadelphia had 63 cancelled flights and 189 delays, according to FlightAware.
Monday's airport disruption stemmed from two problems, according to Bryan Bedford, head of the Federal Aviation Administration.
After identifying an outage in the primary telecom line, "we discovered that the backup fibre had a break," Bedford said following a briefing to reporters on new air traffic technologies.
Bedford described the rupture on the backup line as "massive" due to the construction mistake.
He said he expected the primary system to be restored by early afternoon but estimated that repairing the backup line would need 13 hours.

Lithuania signs first 10-year gas supply deal with U.S.
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
05:52:50 CST
06:52:50 KST

VILNIUS, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Lithuania has secured natural gas supplies from the United States for 10 years, covering about 40 percent of the country's household gas demand, Lithuania's Ministry of Energy announced Monday.
Ignitis, the electricity and natural gas supply subsidiary of state-owned energy group Ignitis Group, signed on Monday the agreement with U.S. natural gas producer EQT.
According to a statement released by the Ministry of Energy, under the agreement, Ignitis will purchase 10 liquefied natural gas (LNG) cargoes from EQT between 2027 and 2036, with one cargo, equivalent to about 1 terawatt-hour (TWh) of gas, to be delivered each year.
The agreement marks the first long-term gas supply contract between Ignitis and a U.S. company and introduces U.S. Henry Hub-linked pricing into the pricing mechanism for the first time.
The contract's pricing is linked to two international natural gas price indices, the U.S. Henry Hub and the European TTF.
According to Ignitis, linking gas prices to two different markets will reduce reliance on the European TTF index and help mitigate the impact of sudden price increases in the European market on household gas prices.
"This long-term agreement is an important step toward strengthening the security and flexibility of natural gas supplies for Lithuanian household customers. It will diversify supply sources, enable more effective management of price fluctuation risks and ensure more stable supply conditions over the longer term," Ignitis CEO Andrius Kavaliauskas said.
The country's Energy Minister Lukas Savickas said the agreement would help reduce Lithuania's vulnerability to gas price fluctuations in the European market and mitigate their impact on household bills. ■

LUSAKA, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- The China-aid overseas training course on agricultural mechanization for Zambia opened in Lusaka, the country's capital, on Monday.
The program, running through Oct. 18, has brought together 40 officials and technicians from Zambia's Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock and Ministry of Agriculture. It is organized by Camco College, a subsidiary of the Chinese firm Camco Group, and the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Mechanization Sciences (CAAMS).
The training covers key areas including modern agricultural machinery, high-efficiency irrigation, conservation tillage, new energy applications, and post-harvest technologies.
Jin Jun, counselor of the Chinese Embassy in Zambia, said the course is a concrete step to implement the consensus reached by the two heads of state and the outcomes of the Beijing Summit of the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation (FOCAC).

Max Choombe, permanent secretary at the Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock, expressed gratitude to the Chinese embassy for supporting training programs for Zambians, saying the initiative will help consolidate bilateral relations as Zambia seeks to draw on China's experience in transforming its agricultural sector.
Choombe urged participants to apply the knowledge and skills gained from the course to boost productivity and advance Zambia's national agricultural development goals.
Wang Yubo, project manager at the CAAMS international cooperation center, said the course serves as a practical initiative to implement FOCAC outcomes and deepen China-Zambia agricultural cooperation.
Tailored to Zambia's local conditions and technical challenges, the program aims to strengthen mechanization capacity, foster talent, and enhance mutual understanding while CAAMS continues to support bilateral agricultural exchanges, Wang added.
Li Tie, chairman of Camco Group, noted that while agriculture is central to Zambia's economy, food security, and rural development, unlocking its full potential requires appropriate technologies, modern machinery, and skilled personnel.
Drawing on years of experience supplying equipment to Zambia, Li said providing machinery alone is insufficient; hence the course combines technical instruction, practical training, and international exchanges covering conservation tillage, post-harvest technologies, and renewable energy. ■

Sardine mortality subsides as South Africa maintains precautionary fishing measure
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
05:52:47 CST
06:52:47 KST

CAPE TOWN, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- South Africa's environment department said Monday that widespread sardine mortality is subsiding as the government maintains a precautionary fishing measure.
In a statement, the Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment said no renewed widespread mortality had been reported. "The only new report during the past week was an isolated fresh sardine stranding near Mbotyi on the northern Wild Coast on Sept. 11."
The department said the available evidence did not indicate that the mortality had reduced the sardine population sufficiently to warrant a complete closure of the fishery. The current measure is precautionary and time-limited and can be reviewed sooner if conditions deteriorate.
Industry reported that strong winds had prevented recent fishing west of Cape Agulhas, while fishing opportunities in Algoa Bay were also limited by weather. Only one sardine catch, amounting to 26 tonnes, has been taken since the beginning of September.
Pilchard herpesvirus (PHV) remains the strongest identified biological factor associated with the mortality and has been confirmed in affected sardines from the Western Cape and Algoa Bay, the department said.
"Monitoring, sampling and laboratory investigations are continuing," it said.
Earlier samples from KwaZulu-Natal (KZN) Province tested negative for PHV, but only a small number were tested. Additional samples are expected to help determine whether the result is consistent across a broader sample.
"If these also test negative, this will support, but not prove, that the event did not extend into KZN, consistent with the reported mortality front ending before it reached the province," the department said.
No effects on sardine-dependent seabirds or marine mammals have been confirmed.
The Small Pelagic Scientific Working Group will meet on Sept. 29 to review the available evidence and reconsider management of the fishery before the temporary measure ends.
A hydroacoustic survey planned for October and November will provide the first fisheries-independent estimate of sardine biomass and distribution following the event. ■

Roundup: Zimbabwean farmers adopt drought-tolerant crops for resilience
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
05:52:43 CST
06:52:43 KST

HARARE, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Faced with recurring droughts, Zimbabwean smallholder farmers who largely rely on rain-fed agriculture are turning to drought-tolerant traditional crops to safeguard food supplies and strengthen resilience.
The shift was reflected at the Good Seed and Food Festival in Harare, Zimbabwe's capital, on Saturday, where farmers showcased and exchanged seeds such as cowpeas, sorghum and millet.
Traditional crops have sustained communities for generations and are valued for their ability to perform under dry conditions, said Delmah Ndlovu, national chairperson of the Zimbabwe Smallholder Organic Farmers' Forum, an organization that seeks to improve smallholder livelihoods through sustainable ecological agriculture.
Crop diversification should be viewed as an integrated farming system that enables farmers to become more self-sufficient, he said, encouraging farmers to diversify their crops to build resilience.
"Having different crops gives the farmer protection. When one fails, the other does well," said Ndlovu, adding that growing a variety of beans and legumes helps farmers hedge against unpredictable weather conditions.
"We have traditional crops that provide farmers with leaves for relish, seeds for food and oil crops such as groundnuts and sunflowers for cooking oil and peanut butter. Some varieties mature quickly, while others take longer, giving farmers different options to meet their food and nutritional needs," he said.
Early-maturing seed varieties can help farmers cope with low rainfall, while late-maturing varieties are better suited to seasons with adequate rainfall, reducing the risk of total crop failure, Ndlovu added.
Zimbabwe's 2026/2027 rainfall season is forecast to be influenced by El Nino, which will increase the likelihood of a below-normal rainfall season.
"We learnt that if we grow traditional seeds and practice water harvesting, we can make the most of the little water available. We will continue doing the same so that we can still harvest enough grain even when we do not receive much rainfall," said Jenny Dube, a farmer from Chimanimani District, Manicaland Province.
Smallholder farmers account for 89 percent of agricultural producers, serving as the backbone of Zimbabwe's food security, according to a United Nations Development Program report.
As key drivers of food production, smallholder farmers play a crucial role in national development, said Melamiseli Ncube, a farmer from Nkayi District in Matabeleland North Province.
The farmer said adequate preparation, including the use of drought-resistant seed varieties, can help farmers mitigate the effects of drought, even in worst-case scenarios.
"Last season, we had a good harvest. After hearing about the El Nino, we set aside pest-resistant grain such as millet and sorghum. These reserves can sustain our household for two seasons without getting grain from other areas," he said. ■

MOSCOW, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Russia has zeroed out export duties on grain crops through the end of 2026, the Russian Agriculture Ministry announced Monday.
According to a new decree, the "floating" export tariff on wheat, barley, and corn has been scrapped until Dec. 31, 2026. Meanwhile, duties on sunflower oil and sunflower meal will be capped at the levels set for August 2026: 7,748 rubles (about 92.13 U.S. dollars) per metric tonne for sunflower oil and 312 rubles (about 3.71 dollars) per metric tonne for sunflower meal.
The decision aims to support domestic producers and exporters of grain and oilseed crops amid the ongoing restructuring of export logistics, the Agriculture Ministry said in a statement.
"These measures will reduce costs for market participants, make sales conditions more predictable, and support the industry's export potential," the ministry said.
"We expect the temporary adjustment of export duties to lower market players' costs, sustain production economics and ensure stable supplies of Russian agricultural goods," Maxim Borovoy, deputy minister of the Agriculture Ministry said earlier.
Russia introduced export duty mechanisms for grain, sunflower oil, and sunflower meal in 2021. The rates are calculated based on the difference between the base price and the indicative price. ■

Lawyers for Lindsay Clancy have asked a judge to investigate the conduct of the lone juror who wanted to convict the mother from Massachusetts of murder in the deaths of her three children.
In a motion filed Friday but made public Monday, Clancy’s lawyers asked the court to question the juror about his alleged use of a cellphone during deliberations, his truthfulness on a questionnaire that prospective jurors filled out before the trial began and his truthfulness when jurors were questioned by the judge a day before the trial ended.
The judge declared a mistrial on 4 September after the jury insisted it couldn’t reach a unanimous verdict, despite days of trying. Eleven of 12 jurors were ready to clear Clancy of criminal responsibility, with the majority feeling that she was in the grip of a rare condition called postpartum psychosis when she strangled her kids. But one juror, Michael Desronvil, sided with the prosecutors, who had argued that Clancy knew what she was doing.
Among other things, Clancy’s lawyer, Kevin Reddington, asked the court to obtain a record of any calls or texts Desronvil made between 8am and 4.30pm on each day the jury deliberated. Phone use during deliberations is prohibited in the state.
Prosecutors have yet to say whether they plan on putting Clancy on trial again. She remains charged with murder and is in a psychiatric hospital until her case is resolved.
In another motion on Monday, Clancy’s lawyers asked the judge to take the unusual step of dismissing the criminal case, rather than putting on a new trial, on the grounds that a mistrial shouldn’t have been declared in the first place.
They argued that the judge should have replaced the holdout juror with an alternate during the deliberations after a jury foreperson complained to the judge that one juror was refusing to listen to the law on reasonable doubt.
A spokesperson for Plymouth county district attorney Timothy Cruz would not comment on the motions.
Desronvil hasn’t been accused of any wrongdoing in connection with his service on the jury, though other jurors complained that he was inflexible in his opinion that Clancy was guilty.
In a statement released by his lawyer last week, Edward Paltzik, Desronvil said he “didn’t have any doubts” that Clancy knew what she was doing when she killed her three children.

The proclamation will mobilize state resources and accelerate preparations ahead of potential winter storms, coastal flooding and other impacts, according to a statement from the governor's office.
"The emerging El Nino event is already breaking records, and forecasters expect it to continue to strengthen, potentially becoming the strongest in recorded history," the statement said.
The proclamation directs state agencies to protect vulnerable communities, prepare roads and critical infrastructure, stockpile emergency supplies, and help local partners reduce the risk of flooding, landslide and coastal hazards.
El Nino is a natural climate pattern marked by warmer-than-average ocean temperatures in the tropical eastern Pacific. It can alter weather patterns and bring wetter, more intense winters to California, according to the governor's office.
The office urged Californians to sign up for emergency alerts and make evacuation plans. ■

UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Families displaced by hostilities in Yemen urgently need food and shelter support, while supplies are running thin as the violence and needs increase, UN humanitarians said Monday.
The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said that, with its partners, it scaled up support for displaced families and all those in need. But the response faces ongoing funding shortfalls and access constraints.
Over the weekend, OCHA said that 21,000 households were displaced across Yemen since Aug. 1, most of them in the governorates of Taiz and Lahj, a figure expected to rise as registration continues.
Since Aug. 1, the UN Human Rights Office verified 125 civilian casualties in 36 incidents, with 32 people killed and 93 others injured. This month, more than 80 percent of casualties were women and children. The actual toll is likely much higher.
OCHA said that ambulances were attacked in Lahj governorate on Friday, killing a driver and an emergency medical responder. Nine health facilities or locations in Taiz and Lahj governorates and in the city of Al Hodeidah were damaged, closed or directly attacked. Hospitals receiving the wounded are running short of blood, anesthetics and surgical supplies.
The office said that women and girls have historically faced high levels of risk in Yemen, particularly pregnant women, who have extremely limited access to health care. Three women die every day in Yemen due to pregnancy complications or during childbirth. The latest escalation in conflict has amplified these risks.
The UN Population Fund estimated that more than 2,700 pregnant women are among the displaced, including 300 expected to give birth in the next two weeks and at least 500 in need of emergency obstetric or newborn care. However, key emergency obstetric facilities have been closed in Taiz, forcing displaced women to give birth in the open without skilled medical care.
OCHA said that humanitarian partners have reached nearly 13,000 displaced households with rapid response kits and other urgently needed assistance. The World Health Organization has delivered surgical supplies and antibiotics to four hospitals in the cities of Aden and Marib.
OCHA called on the parties to protect civilians, including health workers, and ambulances and to facilitate the unhindered delivery of humanitarian aid. ■

China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
05:52:13 CST
06:52:13 KST

BRATISLAVA, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- The number of cars in Slovakia has doubled over the past two decades to 3.8 million, while the country is seeing a shift toward greener transport, according to data released by the Statistical Office of the Slovak Republic on Monday.
An average of about 105,000 cars have been added to Slovakia's roads each year, the office said in a statement marking European Mobility Week which was held from Sept. 16 to 22. This year's European Mobility Week will culminate in Car-Free Day on Tuesday, which promotes walking, cycling and public transport as alternatives to private cars.
Electric mobility is contributing to greener transport. More than 111,800 electric vehicles were produced in Slovakia last year. Slovak manufacturers accounted for about 5 percent of the 2.2 million electric vehicles sold by manufacturers in EU countries.
Public transport is also gaining importance, particularly in major cities. Slovaks made 502 million public transport journeys in 2025, nearly one-third more than that of 2019. On average, each resident made 93 public transport journeys, covering a total distance of 346 km.
Rail transport is one of the most environmentally friendly ways of travelling, enjoying growing interest. According to the Statistics Office data, Slovaks made 74 million rail journeys last year, meaning an average of 14 journeys and 701 km per resident.
In addition, cycling infrastructure has expanded significantly in recent years. The total length of cycling routes in Slovakia's regional capitals reached 624 km in 2025, an increase of two-thirds over the past six years. ■

3 U.S. media outlets file lawsuit after being barred from entering White House
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
05:52:09 CST
06:52:09 KST

WASHINGTON, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Three U.S. news organizations -- CNN, MSNOW and Politico -- said Monday that they are suing U.S. President Donald Trump and several White House officials after being barred from entering the White House.
"This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes," the three news organizations said in a joint statement.
"Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting. Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference," the statement continued.
The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, also listed Steven Cheung, assistant to the president for communications, Sean Curran, director of the Secret Service, and Susan Wiles, White House chief of staff, as defendants.
The latest lawsuit came after Trump said on social media Friday that CNN, MSNOW and Politico were banned from the White House "effective immediately," citing what he called constant "fake news."
On Saturday, reporters from the three media outlets were denied entry to the White House, and their press credentials were confiscated.
In a social media post, Trump reacted to the latest lawsuit on Monday. "As expected, Fake News CNN, Politico (Pay back the 8 Million Dollar contribution made by the U.S. Government to keep them afloat!), and MSNOW (formerly known as MSDNC!), have brought suit to gain access to the White House, and your President, ME!" Trump said in a post on his social media platform Truth Social.
"Almost without question and, as usual, we'll go for appeal," Trump continued, arguing that "Fake News people and publications that only write negatively, and who violate our National Security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown 'sources,' shouldn't be allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World."
Since the beginning of Trump's second term, his relationship with U.S. news organizations has remained tense, with the president frequently criticizing media outlets over what he calls "fake news" and taking legal action against some of them.
In February 2025, reporters from The Associated Press (AP) were barred from access to the White House Oval Office, Mar-a-Lago and Air Force One after the AP declined to adopt the Trump administration's renaming of the Gulf of Mexico as the "Gulf of America."
Trump has also filed lawsuits against media organizations including The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and CBS, accusing them of defamation or misleading reporting. ■

Libya's Sharara oil field output falls after pipeline valve closure
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
05:52:09 CST
06:52:09 KST

TRIPOLI, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Libya's National Oil Corporation (NOC) said Monday that crude oil production at the Sharara oil field in southwestern Libya had fallen significantly after an armed group shut a main valve on the pipeline transporting crude to the Zawiya terminal.
The NOC said in a statement that the group closed valve No. 7 on Monday morning on a pipeline operated by Akakus Oil Operations Company, causing increased pressure in the pipeline and a sharp decline in production.
The corporation said it had contacted the Petroleum Facilities Guard in the southwestern region to secure the pipeline, but its appeals yielded no results. Its technical teams were also unable to reach valves No. 6 and 7 to address the problem.
The NOC warned that continued closure could completely halt production at the field, disrupt oil transportation and exports, and threaten operations at the Zawiya refinery, potentially increasing fuel import costs.
The corporation urged the relevant authorities to secure oil facilities and reopen the pipeline, warning that it "may be forced to declare force majeure" if the closure continues.
The Sharara oil field, located in the Murzuq Basin, is one of Libya's largest oil fields, with a normal production capacity of about 300,000 barrels per day. ■

Uganda urges coffee farmers to remain resilient amid market, weather headwinds
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
05:52:08 CST
06:52:08 KST

KAMPALA, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- The Ugandan government has urged coffee farmers not to lose heart amid volatility in the global market and adverse weather conditions affecting production.
Frank Tumwebaze, minister of agriculture, animal industry and fisheries, said in a statement dated Sunday that the international coffee market had recently come under downward pressure amid increased supplies from major producing countries, particularly Brazil and Vietnam.
"Our price analysts attributed the immediate pressure partly to increased Brazilian exports as that country's harvest approached completion. This tells us that the current price movement is not unique to Uganda. It is part of a wider international market adjustment," Tumwebaze said.
Besides, Uganda is facing domestic supply challenges following a prolonged period of drought and unusually high temperatures in several coffee-growing areas, he said.
The resulting water stress has affected coffee flowering, cherry development, bean filling and, ultimately, processing yields and quality, according to the minister.
"The impact of this drought on coffee production at farm level has been felt at the national level," Tumwebaze said, noting that Uganda exported 846,376 60-kg bags of coffee in July 2026, down from 997,105 bags in the same month a year earlier.
Coffee export earnings also fell to 204.1 million U.S. dollars in July 2026 from 250.7 million dollars in July 2025, according to the minister.
Despite the challenges, farmers are not necessarily facing losses, Tumwebaze said, stressing that a decline in prices does not automatically mean farmers are operating at a loss.
He urged farmers and other players in the coffee value chain not to lose confidence, saying the resilience of Uganda's coffee industry continues to make coffee production and related activities profitable.
He added that the government was implementing measures to help farmers recover from the effects of adverse weather, mitigate future climate risks, and raise productivity and incomes.
Coffee remains a key commodity in Uganda's economic agenda, with about 1.7 million households depending on the crop, according to the ministry. ■

Denmark, Greenland, U.S. to sign Arctic security agreement
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
05:52:06 CST
06:52:06 KST

OSLO, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Denmark, its autonomous territory of Greenland and the United States will sign an agreement in New York on Tuesday to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic region, the Danish Prime Minister's Office said on Monday.
The agreement will be signed by Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and U.S. President Donald Trump, according to the office's statement.
The signing ceremony is expected to take place at United Nations headquarters at 10:30 a.m. local time (1430 GMT), on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, the statement said, but did not disclose the agreement's specific terms.
Trump announced on social media on Friday that the three sides had reached a deal, saying it would give the United States "permanent control" over Greenland's security.
In response, Frederiksen said on the same day that the agreement recognizes the Kingdom of Denmark's sovereignty and territorial integrity, as well as the Greenlandic people's right to self-determination.
Under a defense agreement signed by Denmark and the United States in 1951 and amended in 2004, the U.S. military already has broad authorization to maintain personnel and facilities in Greenland, including the Pituffik Space Base. ■

UN condemns continued Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
05:52:03 CST
06:52:03 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- The United Nations on Monday condemned the continued Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia while urging all parties to exercise restraint and prevent any further escalation.
"We reiterate our condemnation of the continued Houthi cross-border attacks against Saudi Arabia, including the attempt to target Riyadh, the capital. And this is in addition to attacks against civilians and energy infrastructure elsewhere in Saudi Arabia," Stephane Dujarric, the spokesman for the UN secretary-general said.
"We remain deeply concerned about the ongoing military escalation in and around Yemen, including Houthis offensives in Taiz, Lahj and Marib, with grave consequences for civilians in Yemen and across the region," Dujarric told reporters at a news briefing.
The United Nations urges the parties to uphold their obligations under international humanitarian law, which includes the prohibition against direct attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure, he said.
According to Dujarric, UN Special Envoy for Yemen Hans Grundberg is currently in Muscat, meeting with senior Omani officials and representatives of the Houthis. ■

Halt super-intelligent AI with non-proliferation treaty, Ed Davey to say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
21:30:26 UTC
06:30:26 KST

Ed Davey is to call for a global nuclear-style non-proliferation treaty to halt the development of super-intelligent AI when he makes his keynote speech at the Liberal Democrat conference, accusing Andy Burnham of relying on Donald Trump and “tech bros” to solve the problem.
When he addresses the faithful on the final day of the gathering in Brighton, the party leader will call for a global pause on super-intelligent AI, comparing it to a nuclear arms race that could result in technology that could “destroy us all”.
Davey is expected to lay out plans in his speech on Tuesday for a new international AI safety agency – modelled on the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and headquartered in the UK, after numerous warnings from AI researchers that artificial intelligence could wipe out humanity within the decade. “We didn’t leave the atom bomb to a few billionaires to police themselves,” he will say.
Davey is expected to call for a new global movement to work together to protect humanity from the risks of super-intelligent AI, saying that the IAEA was built by nations “working together to control a technology that could destroy us all”, but warning that the future of AI is being decided by “a tiny number of the richest and most powerful in California and in Beijing” with no guardrails to slow down development.
“As liberals – we know that something as existential as nuclear weapons or climate change cannot be left in the hands of a powerful few. And so it must be with AI. We can’t leave it to Mark Zuckerberg, to Sam Altman, or to Elon Musk to save us,” Davey will say.
On Monday, the prime minister announced a new AI partnership with the US ahead of Trump’s address to the UN general assembly on Tuesday.
But Davey will say the plan “doesn’t come close to meeting the scale of this threat” and “only risks making us more dependent on a Trump administration in the pocket of the tech bros”.
It comes after the Lib Dems’ home affairs spokesperson, Max Wilkinson, on Monday announced that the party proposed a big tech levy and promised to create a new online crime agency focused on offences including child sexual abuse material, trafficking in drugs and weapons, and deepfake AI-generated pornographic images.
Wilkinson said the Lib Dems would properly regulate use of Meta’s smart glasses, which he called “perv goggles”, telling the conference that the glasses “are more than a benign piece of tech that provides a bit of fun” and that people – especially women – were being recorded without consent or warning. “This is becoming the new norm, because this government won’t stand up to big tech to protect our civil liberties,” he said.
On Sunday Davey set out a proposal to cut fuel duty by 10p a litre for a fixed three-month period, as well as reducing the bus fare cap from £3 to £1 and other transport-related cost of living policies.
Davey defended himself in a series of interviews on Monday about complaints his party lacks vision, saying it was pointless to try to compete with the attention-grabbing ideas of the likes of Reform UK and the Greens.
“It’s a very noisy environment at the moment,” he told the BBC. “But let me tell you, some of the noise generated by the populists are things that divide our country, that are nasty, or that are just completely crazy. I don’t want to do that. I want to tell people that we have really well thought through policies that will cut their taxes.”
Asked if he would propose further tax cuts in the wake of the pledge to slash 10p from fuel duty for three months, Davey replied: “Absolutely.” These would, he said, be financed by higher economic growth due to the Lib Dem proposal to seek entry to the EU’s single market.
The Lib Dem leader did praise Burnham for wanting to reform adult social care, but told Sky News the “jury is out” on whether Burnham will deliver as prime minister. But Davey was positive about some of what Burnham has done.
“I think it’s good when other parties start talking about Liberal Democrat priorities,” he said. “We have led the debate on social care and carers because it’s so important for our health service. We’ve led the debate on political change because we need to change our political system, and Mr Burnham seems to be up for that.”

Why Trump-Xi summit must put Korean peninsula back on the agenda
US and Chinese indifference risks reinforcing North Korea’s calculation that the world will settle for merely managing its nuclear threat

 Listen
Kang Jun-young is a professor at the Graduate School of International and Area Studies, Hankuk University of Foreign Studies, and chairman of the Northeast Asia Future Cooperation Forum. 
The September 24 summit between President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump is no ordinary engagement. Their May summit took place in Beijing and largely centred on economic issues. This one will be on Trump’s home turf and is expected to put strategic questions on the table. Will the Korean peninsula and North Korea’s nuclear programme again be pushed to the margins?
In Beijing, both sides focused on their immediate national interests, such as trade, semiconductors, rare earths and Taiwan. The issue of the peninsula’s security threat never appeared on the agenda.
Trade, technology and artificial intelligence are again expected to dominate the agenda in Washington. Yet the North’s arsenal is no side issue – it is the most explosive variable capable of destabilising northeast Asia.

====================================================================================================

Britain-focused Andy Burnham starts racking up the air miles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
21:30:00 UTC
06:30:00 KST

British Prime Minister, Andy Burnham and his wife Marie-France van Heel board a plane for the United States, ahead of attending the 81st United Nations General Assembly. | Pool photo Toby Melville/WPA/Getty Images
NEW YORK — Even senior Whitehall officials believed Andy Burnham would not attend the U.N. General Assembly until the announcement came from the British prime minister’s own mouth.
Unlike his predecessor Keir Starmer, whose globetrotting earned him the nickname “never here Keir,” Britain’s new leader cast himself as a folksy man of the people, focused on domestic issues such as the cost of living and moving centers of state power outside London.
Two months in, Burnham is finding no premier can ignore the pull of diplomacy. He landed in New York late Monday night for a whirlwind schedule of meetings with world leaders, including his first face-to-face with U.S. President Donald Trump. His wife, the marketing executive Marie-France van Heel, will meet leaders’ spouses as part of a formal program.
Advertisement
Burnham traveled to Ukraine to meet President Volodymyr Zelenskyy last month. He has since met leaders including France’s Emmanuel Macron and Canada’s Mark Carney and plans to attend November’s COP31 climate summit in Turkey.
A decision looms over whether to attend two other major summits — the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda, attended by his foreign secretary and King Charles III, and the G20 summit in December at the Trump National Doral Miami resort.
Burnham will host G20 leaders next year in Manchester, the city where he spent nine years as mayor, at a cavernous former railway station turned conference center that previously hosted the Manchester bands Oasis and The Smiths.
Throughout his march to Downing Street, senior officials in the Whitehall machine quietly said they never doubted that Burnham would be dragged back to international affairs.
The question is how he explains this to a domestic audience.
Pinning it back to the domestic
So far, Burnham’s Downing Street is taking a similar tack to Starmer’s, especially in his last months: frame every foreign intervention through the lens of reducing the cost of living back home.
Advertisement
The intended message is not subtle. The prime minister’s official spokesperson said Burnham would use the meeting with Trump “to advance U.K. interests,” adding: “The British people at home are at the forefront of the Prime Minister’s mission in New York this week, because to deliver at home, we must ensure we’re leading international efforts to brighten a darkening global picture.”
Instead of jettisoning international summits, Burnham is largely attending them like Starmer did — albeit briefly (he will barely spend 24 hours in New York).
One difference is that rather than going abroad for bilateral meetings, Burnham is inviting foreign leaders for mini-breaks in the various corners of the U.K.
He attended an Everton football match with Carney in Liverpool, invited Ireland’s leader Micheál Martin to his “No. 10 North” in Manchester, took French President Emmanuel Macron to see an exhibition of the Bayeux Tapestry, welcomed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to the naval city of Portsmouth and met NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte in Oxford.
These inward visits mean Burnham can stick to “speed-dating” at multilateral summits, which take up less time and consume less political energy, explained one person with knowledge of the planning who was granted anonymity to speak frankly.
Yet he is still riding both horses — trying to take the lead on global affairs while facing a domestic audience.
Advertisement
No. 10 said ahead of the visit that Burnham is “determined that the U.K. will play a leading role” in tackling issues confronting the world. He has already taken a more muscular approach than Starmer to Israeli settlements on the West Bank, announcing sanctions alongside France, Canada and other countries earlier this month. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said at the time that “settler terrorists” were perpetrating “ethnic cleansing.”
Burnham will also spend Tuesday pushing for closer international co-operation on AI development to manage the technology’s risks. No. 10 said AI would form a “major part” of his visit and speech to UNGA and he would “raise it across the board” in meetings in New York. It was an unexpected pivot from a leader who has devoted little time to talking about the technology.
This will be a particular challenge when meeting Trump, who has described fears about AI’s safety as a “hoax” and said the only “guardrails” needed for AI would be a “strong and smart” president.
Burnham’s spokesperson said ahead of the visit: “The prime minister is determined that the U.K. will play a leadership role in a number of different areas. The U.K. is of course a G7 nation, and you would expect us to play a leadership role across a number of different challenges facing the world at the moment.”
Others around the ruling Labour Party still aren’t sure what that will look like.
Downing Street was straining ahead of the visit to avoid portraying Britain as a “middle power” standing up to the U.S., as Carney has encouraged fellow nations to do. The U.K. has too deep-rooted a security relationship with the U.S. to turn away from it in a meaningful way.
Advertisement
But unlike Carney, Burnham has arguably not set out a detailed vision of where he sees Britain’s place in the world — other than continuing the U.K.-U.S. special relationship, moving closer to the EU and individual interventions like on Israel.
“They’ve not done their intellectual thinking about what the alternative is,” complained one trade union general secretary recently. That person pointed to the U.K.’s approach to China, which remains in a zone of re-engagement that Starmer established on a visit to Beijing in January, and what it will mean for trade and industry. “They’ve not done any thinking on this stuff,” the person added.
In New York, Burnham will seek to prove he has given it all proper thought. He’ll just have to persuade voters he hasn’t dwelt on it for too long.

EU foreign policy chief calls for protection of ICC amid 'immense pressure'

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
22 September 2026•Update: 22 September 2026
EU Foreign Policy Chief Kaja Kallas called Monday for the International Criminal Court (ICC) to be protected, saying it is under “immense pressure” and warning that pressure on the court and its judges raises questions about commitment to the international legal order.
“First, we defend the mechanisms we already have to uphold International Humanitarian Law, domestic courts as well as international courts, the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court, the ICC,” she said at a UN General Assembly side event on humanitarian diplomacy and international humanitarian law.
Kallas said accountability was a key part of upholding international humanitarian law.
“Contrary to what should be happening, the ICC is now under immense pressure,” Kallas said.
She said pressure on the ICC and its judges was not only about the institution itself, but also raised questions about commitment to the international legal order established in the aftermath of World War II.
“And let us not forget, the ICC is the world's promise that victims of the gravest international crimes will not be forgotten because accountability has become politically inconvenient. We must protect it,” she said.
Kallas said international law was not the main problem, arguing that “impunity breeds impunity.”
She outlined three ways to strengthen accountability: defending existing judicial mechanisms, creating new ones where existing mechanisms fall short, and ensuring that legal cases can be properly built.
Kallas cited the Nuremberg and Tokyo trials, as well as tribunals for the former Yugoslavia and Rwanda, and the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression against Ukraine as examples of mechanisms established to pursue accountability.
She also highlighted EU-backed efforts to document alleged war crimes in Syria and a UN-led investigation into Afghanistan.
In Gaza, Kallas said it was essential to preserve evidence of potential war crimes as efforts to clear rubble begin.
“Be it in Syria, Afghanistan, Gaza, or anywhere in conflict, accountability cannot be selective or else the entire system is called into question,” she said.

The revenge of the East: The end of West Germany has finally come
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
21:25:28 UTC
06:25:28 KST

The revenge of the East: The end of West Germany has finally come
Occasionally, history does dish out poetic justice. It can also be exceedingly funny, if in a merciless way. Germany’s well-known tragedy – or let’s say, one of them – is that it suffers from a chronic deficiency of irony, so many Germans will fail to see the funny side of what has just happened. And yet, there is something very deserved as well as ironic about the recent catastrophe of the country’s establishment parties in three turning-point regional elections – in Saxony-Anhalt, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, and Berlin.
The stunning successes of the new-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in two of them (Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern) have attracted most attention. And rightly so: For one thing, any remaining establishment delusions about marginalizing the AfD out of German politics using a “firewall” are now where they have belonged for a very long time: on the trash heap of history. The last desperate firewalling efforts may continue for a little longer here and there, but it’s a Zombie now: not only ugly and brainless but dead to boot.
While German mainstream media can’t stop fretting and hyperventilating about “democracy-in-danger,” in reality, the end of the “firewall” – that is, a systematic discrimination cartel against a legal party – is, obviously, a very good thing for genuine democracy. Because the “firewall” policy was an insult to the latter, as it de facto partially disenfranchised the voters of Germany’s most popular party.
And while the “Die Linke” (The Left) party that has won in Berlin is really a semi-establishment party and has not been subject to a firewall but rather helped built it against the AfD, its victory in the capital still also amounts to a great setback for the older mainstream parties.
However, there are other important aspects of the three political earthquakes that have just shaken Germany’s establishment. Most importantly, both parties that make up Germany’s ruling coalition – the mainstream conservatives (CDU) and the centrist social democrats (SPD) have suffered humiliating, and in the case of the CDU even crushing, defeats.
In Berlin, the SPD was trounced so badly it ended up in fifth place. With the city is historically associated with SPD giants such as Ernst Reuter and Willy Brandt, everyone agrees that this is a disaster that may well end the political career of its local candidate.In Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, it is true, the regional SPD leader, Manuela Schwesig, ruthlessly distanced herself from her own party and was rewarded with second place. Not first place, because that went to the AfD. Schwesig’s defeat is now being sold as a success. That tells you much about how desperate the establishment is.
And then there is the CDU. What’s left to say, really? Historically, the CDU was the founding party of postwar (West) Germany, when it was led by a genius of political cunning and hardheaded realism, Konrad Adenauer. Since then, while it has, of course, not always been in charge in first Bonn and then Berlin, the CDU (with its Bavarian cousin CSU, strictly speaking) has been Germany’s default ruling party.
Now, for the first time in its history, the CDU has failed so abysmally that it is no longer represented in a regional parliament: In Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Adenauer’s once proud party which has morphed into Friedrich Merz’s unmerry band of stragglers has not cleared the five percent barrier and is out. The significance of this debacle cannot be overestimated, even if this is a regional result and not (yet) a national one.
There are plenty of rumors about the fate of Friedrich Merz, the obstinate chancellor of catastrophe and probably the greatest single loser in postwar German history (yes, beating even Erich Honecker). Yet those speculations are much less interesting than something generally overlooked. Which brings us back to why this is also a very funny moment of poetic justice in German history: The CDU has not been knocked out just anywhere, but in the former East Germany, which is also where the AfD has triumphed and shattered the “firewall.”
This is capital-H History in the making. Because it is about much more than just an irreversible fiasco for the CDU; it also goes beyond the wider decline and fall of Germany’s establishment parties and their political, media, and cultural ecosystem. What is really happening now, at long last, is the end of West Germany. Unlike the former East Germany, the GDR, West Germany did not really end with reunification in 1990. On the contrary, where the two Cold War Germanies could have come together fraternally to devise a new political home, that chance of national lifetime was missed with gusto, and instead West Germany simply took over East Germany: inside Germany as well, the Cold War ended not with a genuine new beginning but with the West seeking to impose its ways on the East.
The united Germany that emerged was, in many ways – and all ways that mattered – West Germany writ large. The fact that ex-chancellor Angela Merkel was from the East made as little difference to this extreme lopsidedness as US President Barak Obama’s blackness made to the persistence of racism in America. In the East, the resulting – and very plausible – resentment became a key ingredient in the AfD’s massive success. That success and the simultaneous regional collapse of the CDU, the party that embodied and, in effect, claimed to represent the essence of West German identity, now marks the beginning of the end of this period of German history.
Not much more than one generation after unification ended Cold War East Germany, West Germany’s time is finally up as well. For those in the former East Germany who were promised “flourishing landscapes” by yet another CDU icon, “Chancellor-of-Unity” Helmut Kohl, but got persisting national second-class status instead, this may well feel like richly deserved payback for a Western establishment that has cheated and used and, at best, looked down on them.
West Germany’s impending end is good news, in principle, even for the many Germans still anxiously stuck in their dated West German mindset who cannot understand this yet. At the same time, there also is great danger ahead: The process of finally shedding the old and ill-fitting skin of a West Germany designed as a Cold War client state has begun, but the political and psychological resistance will be great and perhaps even violent. West Germany’s ghost will leave history, but it may still do much harm on the way out.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

Typhoon Dujuan battered the Tokyo region with torrential rain early Tuesday, prompting evacuation advisories for more than 1 million people and hundreds of flight cancellations as flooding and landslides threatened parts of Japan.
Two people have been confirmed dead as heavy rainfall triggered landslides in Chiba and Kanagawa prefectures near Tokyo, local governments reported according to Japanese media including the Kyodo news agency.
Japan often sees strong typhoons in the late summer and early autumn, and other storms have already disrupted some events at the Asian Games being hosted in the country.
Dujuan was bringing winds of some 144 kilometres (89 miles) per hour Monday as it moved to around 130 kilometres south of Katsuura City near Tokyo.
By early Tuesday the storm had shifted away from the coast and was heading northeast out to sea, with slightly diminished winds, the Japanese Meteorological Agency (JMA) said.
Japan Airlines cancelled 135 flights and All Nippon Airways scrapped 140, while more than 9,000 households near Tokyo were without power.
More than 1.6 million residents in and around the capital were urged to evacuate Monday, according to the Fire and Disaster Management Agency. The evacuations are not mandatory.
Landslide warnings were issued for Tokyo as well as for Chiba, Kanagawa and Shizuoka prefectures. Railway operators in Tokyo and neighbouring regions suspended services on some lines.
In areas where warnings have been issued, "there's a risk the rain will continue as the typhoon moves north", the JMA's Takuya Hosomi told reporters.
The JMA warned on Sunday that rain and winds were expected to intensify even before the typhoon's arrival.
"The total rainfall through Tuesday could exceed the average monthly rainfall for September, resulting in record-breaking heavy rain," the agency said.
Dujuan forced the early closure of the Tokyo Game Show, one of the world's biggest video-game trade fairs, on Monday, its final day.
A major outdoor music festival and a baseball match both scheduled to be held in Chiba were also cancelled.
Social media posts showed images of roads in front of Kamakura station, a popular sightseeing spot, were flooded.
"There is flooding in various parts of the city, so travelling by car is dangerous," Kamakura City Mayor Takashi Matsuo said on X.
Flooding also inundated parts of Ichikawa city east of Tokyo.

Man convicted of attempted murder in shooting of three Palestinian students in Vermont
WASHINGTON – A man was convicted by a jury of attempted murder in the late 2023 shooting of three Palestinian American students in Vermont, two of whom were wounded and one was left paralysed from the waist down, prosecutors said on Sept 21.
Jason Eaton was found guilty on three counts of attempted second-degree murder for the shootings of Hisham Awartani, Tahseen Aliahmad and Kinnan Abdalhamid on Nov 25, 2023, in Burlington, Vermont, prosecutor Sarah George, the Chittenden County state’s attorney, said in a statement.
The conviction rejected Eaton's insanity defence and he will be sentenced at a later time, George said. A jury trial commenced in the Chittenden Superior Court a week ago and lasted till Sept 21.
Eaton faces a sentence of up to life without parole, with a presumptive minimum term of 20 years to serve on each count, George said.
The three Palestinian American students, who grew up in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, were walking in Burlington when Eaton approached and shot them, prosecutors and police said.
Awartani was paralysed from the chest down and now lives with paraplegia, his family said.
Aliahmad was struck in the chest and Abdalhamid was struck in the glute while running away, according to prosecutors. Aliahmad and Abdalhamid were visiting Awartani’s grandmother over a Thanksgiving break from school.
All three were 20 at the time and wore black-and-white Palestinian keffiyeh scarves while conversing in a mix of English and Arabic when the gunman confronted them, prosecutors said.
Their families said on Sept 21 justice “has been rendered” and that they feel relief.
Though Eaton pleaded not guilty, he did not dispute being the shooter. His legal team said he should not be found guilty due to insanity, referring to his claims that US and Israeli intelligence ordered him to carry out the shooting through radio and that God asked him to protect Jewish neighbours.
US rights advocates have noted rising anti-Arab, anti-Muslim and anti-Jewish bias since the start of US ally Israel’s devastating assault on Gaza following a deadly October 2023 Hamas attack on Israel.
Some fatal incidents that have sparked alarm include a 2023 deadly stabbing of a six-year-old Palestinian American child in Illinois whose killer was sentenced to 53 years in prison and died in custody, and a 2026 San Diego mosque shooting that left five dead, including two teenage suspects.
