Emine Erdogan calls for changes in consumption habits to tackle climate crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:52:30 UTC
04:52:30 KST

Turkish First Lady Emine Erdogan, who chairs the UN High-Level Advisory Board on Zero Waste, has called for changes in consumption habits and stronger international cooperation to address the climate crisis.
Speaking at the opening of New York Climate Week on Monday, Erdogan said the Zero Waste movement had turned individuals from “helpless observers” into actors in tackling climate change.
She said small behavioural changes could develop into broader social practices when widely adopted and supported by sound policies.
Erdogan attended the event in New York alongside Family and Social Services Minister Mahinur Ozdemir Goktas. The Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Ministry and the Zero Waste Foundation were among the main sponsors.
She said climate change was a consequence of the burden human activity had placed on the planet, pointing to fossil fuels, industrial processes, high emissions and excessive consumption.
‘Rebuild our relationship with nature’
Erdogan said humanity had created a system based on short product lifespans and growing waste, citing estimates that 9.2 billion tonnes of plastic have been produced since the 1950s, with 7 billion tonnes becoming waste.
She said the environmental costs of high consumption were often borne by vulnerable societies and future generations that contributed least to it.
“We must therefore begin by reducing excess in our habits alongside our waste, changing our mindset alongside our systems, and rebuilding our relationship with nature on the principles of balance and justice,” she said.
Erdogan described Zero Waste as a moral approach that promotes limits and responsibility as consumption and waste become increasingly normalised.
She said the programme launched at the Turkish presidential complex in 2017 had since spread to schools, hospitals, municipalities, public institutions and households.
“Our recovery rate, which stood at 13 percent at the time, has now surpassed 37 percent,” she said.
‘Shared responsibilities’
Erdogan said Zero Waste did not reduce the responsibilities of governments and companies, but instead expanded them.
She called for infrastructure that helps people make sustainable choices, more durable and reusable products, circular production technologies and stronger international cooperation.
She also recalled that Türkiye's Zero Waste resolution was adopted by the UN General Assembly in 2022, while March 30 was designated International Zero Waste Day and the UN High-Level Advisory Board on Zero Waste was established.
Erdogan said she hoped Zero Waste would be recognised as a tool for climate action at COP31, which Türkiye will host in November.
She warned that continuing habits that cause today's environmental problems would undermine future solutions.
“No target will be sufficient on its own, and no technology will be a solution on its own,” she said.
Erdogan said the success of New York Climate Week would ultimately depend on actions taken after the event, expressing hope it would lead to new habits and collective action.
Following her speech, Erdogan watched a live performance by contemporary marbling artist Garip Ay. Editors-in-chief of newspapers and television channels, along with other guests, attended the event.

Merkel, who led Germany from 2005 to 2021, did not mention the elections or Merz directly. Advertisement

Merkel then turned to the question of how politicians can reconnect with voters.
“We have to acknowledge that the question of how to maintain a connection with citizens and potential voters has changed dramatically,” she said. If politicians want to spread positive messages, she added, they must show the public “what guides my thinking, where I have doubts and what I have considered.”

What Russia’s Parliamentary Election Results Mean for Putin and the War
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:50:43 UTC
04:50:43 KST

Russia's electoral commission on Monday said that United Russia, the ruling party aligned with President Vladimir Putin, is projected to win the parliamentary election that has been widely criticized as a “sham.” The Central Election Commission (CEC) reported that 95% of the votes have been counted after a three-day election that began last Friday and ended Sunday.
While the final counts are not expected to be certified until later this week, preliminary figures show that the pro-Kremlin party is projected to win a record 355 seats in the country’s 450-seat Duma, the lower house of parliament, giving United Russia an even larger supermajority than its 2016 record high of 343 seats.
Voter turnout was high at just over 59%, according to a briefing from the CEC.
The election is the first parliamentary poll since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and the Kremlin has cast it as a referendum on support for what it calls a “special military operation” rather than a war. It was also, therefore, the first parliamentary election to include voters from four partly occupied regions of Ukraine—Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia—which Moscow claimed to annex illegally in 2022 but does not fully control. Voting also was held in Crimea, which was illegally annexed in 2014.
Despite the vote being framed as an opportunity for citizens to express sentiments about the war, it is widely considered an illusion of choice: Russia’s supreme court last month banned the federal candidate list of the one registered antiwar party, Yabloko, from participating in the State Duma.
“I would be very careful to kind of unpack the distribution of votes as something indicative of what people think of the war,” David Szakonyi, a professor at George Washington University whose research focuses on Putin-era Russia, tells TIME. “They were not given the choice to vote against it.”
“This playing field was tilted before the votes were even counted, and this was not by any means a free and fair election,” he adds.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told members of the press Monday that the election showed how Russians support the country’s leader and “point to the highest level of consolidation within Russian society around the head of state.”
Experts believe that the election will allow the Kremlin to continue justifying its war with Ukraine—and it could further consolidate Putin’s power.
How the results could shape Russia’s war against Ukraine
United Russia’s supermajority could embolden parliament to pass “drastic legislation” with regard to future war efforts, Szakonyi says. Although United Russia already held a constitutional supermajority in the outgoing Duma, the larger margin could embolden lawmakers to pursue more severe measures.
“They have every resource available to them to change the political system as Putin directs,” Szakonyi says, “and the propaganda in the next week or two is going to heavily emphasize the fact that United Russia improved its performance.”
Parliament could specifically use the election to request more sacrifices from citizens for the war effort, according to Szakonyi. He says, for example, that the party could support legislation expanding military recruitment or defending “greater investment in the war effort, at the expense of healthcare, education, and domestic spending in general.”
“It is highly possible that they will at least kind of build on these electoral results when they demand more from voters and citizens in the next couple months in order to win the war,” he continues.
Olena Lennon, a practitioner in residence of National Security at the University of New Haven, agrees that Putin did not necessarily need any more legislative power to exact his objectives. Instead, the election was “more about creating an image of national unity and demonstrating to various audiences that Putin has total political control," she says, adding that hosting an election offers the “optics of popular legitimacy, institutional strength, and political stability.”
“That potentially gives Putin greater political cover and legitimacy for unpopular measures in the future—such as putting the economy in wartime production mode and potentially full mobilization," Lennon says.
A new mobilization campaign could inject new momentum into Russia’s offensive campaign and replenish battlefield losses. Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said last month that he believes Russia is planning to draft an additional 300,000 troops for the war effort.
“We are confident that following the elections, they will carry out a mobilization. We believe this will not take place in the major cities,” Zelenskyy said on Aug. 23. “They’ll lose all 300,000 of these newly mobilized Russians there; we’ll wipe them out.”
Putin has denied that a new mobilization campaign is planned, calling the rumors “utter nonsense” on Sept. 1. Two days later, at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok, Putin emphasized that there “is no scenario today that would require mobilization.”
More than four years into the war, Russians are facing rising living costs amid inflation that some economists attribute partly to military spending, with the prices of several food staples in rising this year. The country is also experiencing fuel shortages as Ukraine continues to strategically target its oil refineries and depots.
U.S. President Donald Trump has criticized the tactic in recent weeks, arguing that it is impacting global fuel prices. Energy-market data over the past six months, however, shows that the ongoing conflict in the Middle East and subsequent constrictions of major oil passageways like the Strait of Hormuz is the much larger disruption to global oil and diesel supplies.
Trump’s latest comments on the matter came Monday.
“Russia has unfortunately lost control of its Diesel Oil Industry due to its War with Ukraine. A large number of their Diesel refineries have been blown up and are, at least temporarily, out of commission,” Trump said on Truth Social on Sept. 21. “This ridiculous and never ending War with Ukraine must be ended.”
Beginning Saturday, as Russia entered its last day of voting, the government said it intercepted more than 1,600 Ukrainian drones, including 450 directed toward Moscow. The figures, attributed to Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin and reported by state media TASS, have not been independently verified.
According to a statement by Sobyanin on Telegram, this was the largest ever drone attack on the Russian capital, damaging the city's oil refinery.
How the world reacted to the preliminary election results
European powers have largely condemned the results. That includes France's foreign ministry, which released a statement on Monday saying that the vote did not meet the conditions for “free, pluralistic, democratic elections.”
“Heightened repression against civil society and the opposition, the exclusion of several political parties, growing restrictions on freedom of expression and the banning of independent media have undermined the Russian people's ability to freely form and express their choice,” the statement said.
A joint statement from the United Kingdom, Canada, Norway, Australia, and New Zealand was also released Monday, calling the vote a “sham”—particularly as it pertained to the four occupied Ukrainian territories.
“Holding Russia’s State Duma elections in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine, as Russia did in Crimea and Donetsk, Kherson, Luhansk and Zaporizhzhia, is a gross violation of Ukraine’s sovereignty and independence, and the UN Charter,” the statement said. “We call on the international community to reject Russia’s attempts to normalise its occupation, condemn the holding of sham elections on Ukrainian territory.”
Kaja Kallas, the European Union’s foreign policy chief and a vice president of the European Commission, called the elections “another major setback for Russian democracy” in a post on X.
“The Kremlin silenced dissent, barred the only registered party that opposed its war in Ukraine, and shut out international election monitors,” she said. “The veneer of democracy is all that remains in Russia.”

Not the time to soften stance over Belarus, Lithuania says
UNITED NATIONS, Sept 21 - The European Union has no reason to ease sanctions on Belarus, Lithuania's foreign minister said on Monday, arguing that President Alexander Lukashenko's government continues to repress opponents, violate human rights and back Russia's war in Ukraine.
US President Donald Trump said earlier in the day that Washington was working on a deal to purchase potash from Belarus, a key sector sanctioned by the EU.
The comments came a week after his administration negotiated the release of political prisoners in Belarus in return for some sanctions lifting, the latest in a year of talks between the two sides.
The US diplomacy is sensitive because Lukashenko, in charge of the former Soviet state since 1994, has long been shunned by the West for repressing his opponents and supporting Russia's war in Ukraine.
"Of course we would prefer to coordinate on sanctions policy as it is the most effective way to do this, but EU sanctions policy is a bit different," Kęstutis Budrys told Reuters in an interview at the UN General Assembly. "We do not see any reasons why our position on Belarus should soften as Belarus is not changing its behaviour."
The comments underscore a growing transatlantic divergence in approach toward Belarus.
While Budrys welcomed the release of prisoners, of which he said there remained about 1,000, and Vilnius would continue to provide assistance when they were freed, he said the EU should continue applying pressure on both the Belarusian and Russian governments, arguing that sanctions remained effective.
"We see how Lukashenko tries to find ways to get rid of them, and it means that we have to continue," he said.
"On our side, we have to be very exact and continue what works, and that is the pressure on the regime," he said.
The minister, whose country borders Belarus, said Minsk continued to pose a security challenge to the bloc, accusing it of orchestrating hybrid attacks against EU member states.
He cited what he described as the weaponisation of migration flows, particularly affecting Lithuania, Poland and Latvia, as well as smuggling operations, balloon incursions and other activities aimed at undermining European security.
"They are one of the major sources of hybrid activities against the European Union," he said.
The EU's current sanctions framework on Belarus remains in force until February 2027. REUTERS

UK prosecutors charge first person for Rwanda genocide

UK prosecutors charge first person for Rwanda genocide
Vincent Brown is ‘alleged to have directed and incited acts of murder and genocide carried out by others’.
Prosecutors have brought the first-ever charges in the United Kingdom against a man for his alleged role in the 1994 Rwanda genocide.
After a seven-year investigation, Vincent Brown, a 65-year-old doctor who was formerly known as Vincent Bajinya, was arrested and charged on Monday with one count of conduct ancillary to genocide and six offences of aiding crimes against humanity in Rwanda, prosecutors and local authorities said.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items

- list 2 of 4Hutu and Tutsi: The history behind the divide
- list 3 of 4Geneva talks put Rwanda-DRC peace deal to the test

“The charges relate to allegations that Dr Brown took part in the genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda in 1994,” Frank Ferguson, head of the Crown Prosecution Service’s counterterror division, said in a statement. “He is alleged to have directed and incited acts of murder and genocide carried out by others.”
“This is the first time charges relating to the genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda have been brought in the United Kingdom,” the statement added.
Brown was first arrested in 2006. His extradition to Rwanda, along with four other men, was refused by a UK court in 2017. Metropolitan police war crimes investigators then began looking into the case in 2019 at the request of the Rwandan government. Several other countries have already prosecuted suspects in the Rwandan genocide.
Originally from Kigali, Brown lives in London, where he once worked for a charity assisting refugee nurses and midwives seeking work in Britain.
He is believed to have entered the UK as an asylum seeker in 1998, former Rwandan Justice Minister Tharcisse Karugarama told the Associated Press news agency in 2006.
The doctor changed his name when granted UK citizenship in 2004, attorney Philip Eldin-Taylor said at the time.
Brown is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates’ Court on Tuesday.
Police said they are continuing to investigate several other Rwandan genocide suspects living in Britain.
“This case demonstrates the UK is not a safe haven for individuals suspected of committing international crimes,” Commander Helen Flanagan, head of counterterror policing, said.
The Rwandan genocide saw an estimated 800,000 people, mostly Tutsis, killed in 100 days of slaughter.

Flights canceled, delayed at US East Coast after technical fault
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:47:00 UTC
04:47:00 KST

Flights at several major airports on the U.S. East Coast have been grounded or delayed on Monday following a technical malfunction, the top aviation body said, with reports of a primary circuit cable being cut as a source of the issue.
The technical problems occurred at a key regional air traffic control center, halting operations at every major airport in the New York City area for several hours on Monday, just as numerous foreign leaders were flying in for the U.N. General Assembly.
However, President Donald Trump's flight from Washington to New York was able to depart as scheduled.
The airports affected included JFK, Newark, LaGuardia and Westchester County in New York; Logan International Airport in Boston; Philadelphia International Airport; and Teterboro Airport in New Jersey.
The technical issues happened at the same Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) facility in Philadelphia – the Terminal Radar Approach Control center – that caused numerous disruptions at Newark Liberty International Airport in the spring of 2025.
The center controls approaches and departures, as well as the spacing between aircraft in the terminal's airspace.
Broadcaster NBC News reported that the travel plans of thousands of passengers have been affected.
The FAA has not yet provided any information on how long the disruption might last.
Monday's airport disruption stemmed from two problems, according to Bryan Bedford, head of the Federal Aviation Administration.
On Monday morning, the primary circuit that carries data into that air traffic control facility failed, affecting flights for Philadelphia, as well as Kennedy, LaGuardia and Newark airports, the Federal Aviation Administration said.
The FAA then discovered that the backup fiber optic line had been cut due to construction. Verizon said contractors had dug up and cut the cable that runs along the Amtrak rail line in New Jersey. The company said in a statement that its technicians were racing to get the cable fixed.
By early afternoon, some flights were starting to resume at LaGuardia and in Philadelphia, but significant delays are expected through the rest of the day. Some airlines were allowing their customers to change flights without charging them fees. The FAA advised travelers to check the status of their flights with their airline before heading to the airport.
Bedford told reporters that the agency is working to restore the key connection as soon as possible by installing a new circuit on the primary line, while also working to repair the backup fiber optic line. He said it's not clear how long that will take.
"That fiber break is probably 13 hours to repair. It's massive," Bedford said, according to a video posted online by a CBS transportation reporter.
The primary circuit that failed is due to be replaced as part of the overhaul of the nation's air traffic control system.
Also Monday, the FAA began testing a new computer system that uses AI to help predict schedule conflicts and weather issues to help air traffic controllers reroute traffic.
But that system is initially being tested only in the Washington, D.C., area, so it does not appear to be linked to the outages.
U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on X that around 7.00 p.m. GMT, flights were resuming at LaGuardia Airport and Philadelphia, while flights into Newark and JFK Airports were paused.
"An Amtrak construction crew accidentally cut into a fiber line in New Jersey, which caused a telecom outage and forced FAA to pause flights in the Northeast," Duffy said.
Around 7.00 p.m. GMT, Newark Airport, a key New York City-area hub, had 168 flights canceled and 97 delayed, while Philadelphia had 63 canceled flights and 189 delays, according to FlightAware.

Nestlé Russia stated that it would continue its commercial activities "in full." The Kremlin transferred its assets and those of Auchan under the temporary management of L.E.V. Management.
On Monday, the Swiss food giant said that its Russian subsidiary would continue operating in Russia, despite the Kremlin’s decision to transfer control of the assets to a little-known company, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
"The Nestle Group in Russia continues its commercial activities in full and declares its intention to unconditionally fulfill all obligations to customers, partners and employees," Russia’s TASS news agency quoted the company’s Russian press service as saying in an official statement.

The Kremlin said that hostile actions by "unfriendly" countries played a role in the decision to take control of Nestle’s and Auchan’s Russian assets.
In previous cases, the imposition of temporary management was often followed by state expropriation, with the assets subsequently transferred to individuals or companies linked to the Kremlin. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said that, for now, this was only temporary management.

Russia’s threat isn’t better missile, it’s 14,000 cheap ones. Its new deadly weapon was built in early 1990s, experts say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:42:39 UTC
04:42:39 KST

Russia wants to build 14,000 of a new cruise missile next year, enough to fire them at Ukrainian cities by the thousand. The weapon, the Dan-T, is a cheap air-launched jet missile that flies hundreds of kilometers on its own, RBC-Ukraine reported.
The danger is volume, not finesse. Russia aims to produce up to 2,000 Dan-T missiles by the end of this year and scale it drastically, RBC-Ukraine's sources say. Fired in large numbers, it would add a fresh layer to the Gerans and the cruise and ballistic missiles that already saturate Ukraine's skies on the worst nights.
Numbers make the threat
The experts are less worried about any single Dan-T than about the swarm. High speed, long range, and the ability to launch the missiles by the thousand would stretch Ukraine's air defense further with every strike, forcing crews to spend scarce interceptors on yet another cheap target.
The missile flies to its objective autonomously, and Russia claims a special flight profile designed to make it harder for air defense to spot and shoot down.
A target drone becomes a weapon
The Dan-T has an unusual pedigree. It began as the Dan-M, a jet-powered target drone Russia's Sokol bureau built in the early 1990s and imitated US Tomahawk cruise missiles for air-defense practice, now planned to be stripped of its recovery parachute, fitted with a warhead, and fired at Ukrainian cities. Like Russia's other new cruise weapons, it carries no operator link, steering itself by satellite and inertial navigation.
The Banderol joins the list
The Dan-T is not the only new weapon unsettling Ukraine's military. The experts named it alongside the S8000 Banderol, a separate cheap cruise missile that Russia already builds at up to 80 a month and has used in some of its heaviest strikes on Kyiv. The Dan-T closely resembles the Banderol and, being cheaper, may end up replacing it.

No median cuts, surface intersections on future high-speed NH corridors: NHAI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:42:30 UTC
04:42:30 KST

A view of the Barapullah Phase-3 elevated corridor that is scheduled to be inaugurated on September 29, 2026, in New Delhi on Saturday. (ANI Photo)
NEW DELHI: New access-controlled high-speed national highway corridors will have no median (divider) openings and no at-grade (surface level) intersections, a move that aims at eliminating conflict points and reducing crashes.It has also been mandated under new NHAI guidelines issued on Monday that these corridors won’t have raised concrete dividers but flush medians — painted centre lanes with thick wire ropes or crash barriers. These will also have advance exit signage at 5 km, 2 km, 1 km and 500 metres to help motorists prepare for lane changes well in advance.The design provisions are aimed at improving safety on access-controlled corridors where cars are allowed to travel at speeds of up to 100 kmph. Delhi-Dehradun Expressway, Ambala-Kotputli corridor and Trans-Haryana corridor are among such highways.NHAI said the guidelines seek to bring uniformity in the planning and design of access-controlled high-speed corridors and ensure consistency in technical standards across projects.“The guidelines will apply to all upcoming four-lane and six-lane greenfield and brownfield access-controlled high-speed national highways,” an NHAI spokesperson said.
Officials said eliminating median cuts and surface intersections will prevent dangerous cross movements and wrong-side driving, while standardised signage and geometric design will improve traffic flow and reduce the risk of high-speed crashes on the new generation of national highway corridors.
The move is significant as govt has set a target of developing 50,000 km of access-controlled high-speed corridors over the coming years.At present, there are no separate standards governing the planning and design of access-controlled high-speed national highways, except for expressways. The new document fills that gap by laying down dedicated norms for highways that are access-controlled but not classified as expressways.The guidelines also specify lane configuration based on detailed traffic assessment and future traffic projections. Depending on the expected traffic volume and the number of structures such as bridges, flyovers and interchanges, these corridors will have a right of way of 60 metres or 70 metres.

Former Prosecutor General Kravchenko resigns from prosecution service after failing to return to Ukraine
Former Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko was dismissed from Ukraine's prosecution service on Sept. 21 after submitting a resignation request, the Prosecutor General's Office said.
Although President Volodymyr Zelensky dismissed Kravchenko as prosecutor general on Sept. 15, he had formally remained a prosecutor within the Prosecutor General's Office under Ukrainian law.
Kravchenko submitted a request on Sept. 21 to leave the prosecution service entirely, Prosecutor General's Office spokesperson Mariana Haiovska told journalists. The acting prosecutor general signed an order approving his dismissal the same day.
Haiovska said Kravchenko had not returned to work after his official foreign business trip ended on Sept. 18.
"After the end of his business trip, Ruslan Kravchenko, as a prosecutor of the Prosecutor General's Office, did not begin performing his official duties," she said.
Earlier on Sept. 21, Haiovska said Kravchenko had not returned to work at the Prosecutor General’s Office as of 2 p.m. She added that she had no information on whether he had returned to Ukraine or where he was. Sources cited by Ukrainska Pravda later said Kravchenko had not crossed the Ukrainian border on his return as of Sept. 21.
Kravchenko left Ukraine in a government vehicle overnight on Sept. 14, according to Ukrainska Pravda sources in law enforcement. He subsequently said he was traveling on official business.
A directive signed by Kravchenko listed a five-day trip to Paris to attend a Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe event concerning Ukrainian children, although his name did not appear among the listed participants in the event agenda.
His departure came amid a confrontation involving the Prosecutor General's Office and Ukraine's anti-corruption agencies.
Kravchenko submitted his resignation as prosecutor general on Sept. 7 amid an investigation by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) into allegations that officials within the Prosecutor General's Office had protected fraudulent call centers. Kravchenko denied wrongdoing.
On Sept. 14, Kravchenko claimed that he had signed a notice of suspicion against NABU Director Semen Kryvonos and accused NABU and SAPO of taking materials related to investigations of their employees during searches connected to Operation Carthage.
The Prosecutor General's Office later said Kravchenko's claim that Kryvonos had been formally notified of suspicion was not true. Kryvonos also said he had not received such a document.
Zelensky suspended Kravchenko from the prosecutor general's post on Sept. 14. Parliament approved his dismissal the following day by 317 votes to none, after which Zelensky formally dismissed him.

04:37:01 KST

Eli Lilly CEO Dave Ricks told CNBC on Monday that 700,000 new seniors have started GLP-1 treatments since Medicare coverage of obesity drugs launched in July, and 70% of those patients are on Lilly medicines.
In an exclusive interview with CNBC, Ricks called the rollout of coverage "very encouraging" so far, saying its expansion of the broader GLP-1 market "is what we had hoped." His comments offer the latest metrics on how much the coverage is expanding access to the medicines, and who appears to be gaining more momentum among new patients between Lilly and its chief rival, Novo.
The coverage is through a temporary program called "Bridge," which allows eligible beneficiaries to obtain weight loss drugs for a $50 monthly co-pay. The federal Medicare program is for people age 65 and older or with disabilities and covers about 66 million people.
Lilly's blockbuster obesity injection Zepbound appears to be the biggest winner of Medicare coverage so far. Through the program, seniors can get access to Zepbound along with Lilly's newly launched obesity pill, Foundayo, Novo's competing Wegovy pill and blockbuster injection under the same name.
"We're capturing about seven out of 10 of those new patients, and a lot are still on Zepbound," he said. "I think we still see physicians focusing on those with the most body weight and the most complications. That's where Zepbound plays a big role."
Lilly's Foundayo plays a larger role for patients who are looking for a convenient treatment option and "maybe just need to lose 25 to 30 pounds," Ricks added. That pill launched in April a few months behind Novo's, but Ricks told CNBC that one-third of new patients on oral GLP-1s are taking Foundayo.
He said he hasn't heard of many logistical issues with the rollout, saying the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services "did a nice job rolling this out," educating physicians and working with both companies and the insurance system.

German auto workers protest historic job cuts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

19:34:39 UTC
04:34:39 KST

German auto workers protest historic job cuts
Tens of thousands of auto workers across Germany have staged protests demanding protection for employment and factories after Volkswagen announced plans to cut 100,000 jobs.
Employees at Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz, BMW, Audi, Porsche, and major suppliers are taking part in more than 280 actions nationwide on Monday. Germany’s largest industrial union, IG Metall, has warned that the country’s automotive industry “faces the risk of total collapse” as it grapples with high energy costs following reduced imports of Russian oil and gas, US tariffs, and growing competition from China.
”We expect corporate leaders and management teams to take responsibility for Germany as an automotive nation, for employees and for jobs,” IG Metall chief Christiane Benner told workers at Volkswagen’s headquarters in Wolfsburg.
Volkswagen’s planned reductions include some 50,000 previously announced cuts across its brands and another 50,000 under a new agreement. The company also slashed its 2026 operating-margin forecast on Friday to no more than 1%, citing weakness in China, restructuring costs, and problems at Porsche.
Other German carmakers are also scaling back. BMW is cutting about 8,000 jobs, while Mercedes-Benz is reducing production at home and expanding capacity in lower-cost Hungary.
The industrial contraction extends beyond layoffs. Volkswagen ended car production at its Dresden plant last December, marking the first closure of a German car factory in the company’s 90-year history.
The automaker has also dropped out of the Euro Stoxx 50 for the first time in 15 years, with its shares down more than 75% from their 2021 peak. By contrast, shares in German defense giant Rheinmetall have soared over 1,100% since the start of 2022 as Berlin boosts military spending.
Parts of the automotive sector are also turning to defense. Volkswagen’s Osnabrück plant, where car production is due to end next year, is set to shift toward military manufacturing, with Israeli arms maker Rafael lined up to produce air-defense systems and components. Mercedes-Benz has also explored opportunities in the sector.
Germany has budgeted €108.2 billion ($124 billion) for defense this year, with spending set to rise further under Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s drive to build what he has called Europe’s strongest conventional army.
Moscow has criticized the buildup. Russian President Vladimir Putin said in June that NATO had moved beyond supporting Ukraine and was now “openly” discussing preparations for war with Russia while increasing military budgets.

Australia will need to boost its population to support the elderly and the economy in the long term, experts warn, after the government's latest Intergenerational Report (IGR) found that people are expected to live longer and have fewer children.
The report landed as politicians float the idea of bringing back the Howard-era baby bonus and argue over the need to reduce migration.
Independent MP Bob Katter has recently suggested an up-front cash payment of $75,000 per child would reverse the declining birth rate, which is now expected to fall to just 1.34 children per woman by 2065.
The argument was dismissed by Treasurer Jim Chalmers and Nationals leader Matt Canavan, who said on Monday that family support policy should be more than just "here's some cash".
However, Australia does face challenging demographic questions, with experts saying the choice will come down to more migrants or more babies.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"We will have a large pool of elderly people that we have to support," Dr Pelin Akyol, research manager at the economic think tank The e61 Institute, told SBS News.
"If we have a smaller pool of people working, then it will be a big fiscal problem in this country — and in every country."
Global and domestic surveys show that most people want to have more children than they end up having, owing to cultural, social, and economic constraints which are difficult to address.
"With AI and everything else going on right now, it is hard to know what will happen," Akyol said. "But what we know at this point is that it's going to affect the economy in a bad way".
The fertility illusion
While the IGR highlights a collapsing birth rate, demographers caution that official metrics paint a distorted picture of Australian family choices.
Peter McDonald, emeritus professor of demography at the Australian National University, told SBS News that the country's reliance on international students and temporary visa holders skewed the headline Total Fertility Rate (TFR).
Temporary migrants are often young adults aged 20 to 35 who are in higher education or the early stages of their career. While they are counted as potential mothers, they "hardly have any births," McDonald said, which drives the TFR down.
"That's one of the central reasons why Australia's fertility rate has been falling because the temporary population's been rising," he said.
The birth rate for women born in Australia is around 1.64, higher than the Australian Bureau of Statistics headline fertility rate of 1.48. While this is still below the replacement rate of 2.1, Akyol said the immigration influence on TFR is different in Australia than in other comparable nations.
"In Germany, migrants have higher fertility rate than natives," she said. "But in Australia, it is the opposite".
McDonald also warns against placing too much faith in the long-term projections of the IGR — which assumes net overseas migration will remain flat at 235,000 annually for the next four decades — and that immigration and total births can't be viewed separately as they are "not independent of each other".
"If you can tell me what the birth rate is going to be in 10 years, you're a better man than me," he said. "But if you can tell me what it is in 40 years, then you're a miracle worker."
Is a baby bonus the answer?
Katter's proposed return to former treasurer Peter Costello's cash payment for each newborn child would cost upwards of an estimated $22.5 billion a year for the present 300,000 babies born each year in Australia.
Akyol's research into the 2004 policy indicates that cash incentives do increase the fertility rate, but the effect is "not huge" and, given how different the world is today, "it is not guaranteed we will see a similar effect".
While a $75,000 payment is "huge" compared to the $3,000 of the original policy and "might have an effect", Akyol doubted this was the best use of money when other factors like support benefits also play a key role in family decisions.
McDonald said Australia's tax system has become too narrowly focused on early childcare, making raising older children harder for working families.
"Today, about 58 per cent of families get no family allowance for their children," he said. "It's not just about very young children... supporting families with children is also about supporting older children, and we've gone a long, long way away from doing that."
A median worker claiming both employer and state parental leave would already receive around $48,700 before tax, something McDonald said disadvantages those without full-time employment. Instead of re-introducing lump-sum payments, he calls for a broader review of child equity.
"I think there's a need for an inquiry into the system of child support payments, to deal with two issues: one is the inequity of the system for very young children, and two, the lack of support for older children," he said.
"Children are a social good.... so I think there is justification for supporting families with children; it's called horizontal equity."
"Horizontal equity used to be quite a big thing back in the 1980s ... I think it needs to be revisited."
A national trade-off
To offset a declining taxpayer base, the IGR highlights increasing older workforce participation and leveraging artificial intelligence to automate labour gaps.
However, McDonald questioned the feasibility of expecting Australians to work deeper into their 60s and 70s.
"A lot of people, particularly those who work in physically demanding jobs, do not want to work beyond pension age. They've had enough," he said.
"AI is going to make a big difference to future labour force needs, but AI is not going to wipe the bottoms of people in aged care."
Akyol said current debates around migration could soon flip as birth rates drop across the globe, including in key migrant origin countries such as China and India. With a shrinking global talent pool, nations could shift from seeking to restrict migration to actively competing for skilled workers.
"In the long run, there might really be a competition for getting the best migrants," Akyol said. "Because in all developed countries, fertility rate has been decreasing... and it seems like there is no hope that it will just turn back and increase again."
"There is no easy solution here. There is a trade-off with every kind of policy."
Relying on immigration is the most direct mechanism to address workforce shortages in sectors like aged care, which are already under strain, McDonald said — something he said the government has failed to communicate in its messaging.
"The IGR shows the advantage of a higher level of migration for the federal government's bottom line," McDonald said. "Migrants make our prospects of dealing with a future aged population much better."

MOS creates basket-like aluminium pavilion at Art Omi in New York
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:30:38 UTC
04:30:38 KST

MOS creates basket-like aluminium pavilion at Art Omi in New York
US studio MOS Architects has used aluminium shingles to cover an egg-shaped pavilion at Art Omi in Upstate New York, creating a place to rest that draws stylistically on pre-modern basketry and mid-century futurism.
An experiment in form and material, A Dome with Four Oculi was installed on the expansive Art Omi campus as a place of shelter and rest.
The structure sits on stilts and consists of a shell that MOS compared to a crinoline dress.
It was then covered by aluminium shingles that overlap and are held in place by stainless steel bolts. Combined, the shell is around a quarter-inch thick. It has two portholes on the side that look out into the landscape and is open at the top.
MOS co-founder Michael Meredith told Dezeen that structurally it is like an "upside-down basket", connecting to both the studio's work in easy-to-assemble prefabricated aluminium structures and a focus on the potential for experimentation at small scales.
"We've been working for years with folded aluminium and basically using it like paper, almost like large-scale models," said Meredith.
It was designed to be put together with standard tools in just a few days.
Conceptually, the structure takes cues both from pre-modern basketry as well as from the Airstream trailer.
"There's something of woven architecture in it, almost pre-modern," said Meredith. "Woven structures have an economic use of material, lighter material in this case. There's something nomadic."
"But there's Airstream trailer quality too," he continued. "You can see a bunch of stuff in it."
Beyond the thematic elements, the structure also provides shelter and a place to sit in the fields of Art Omi, which hold dozens of rotating art and architecture installations.
The oculi on the sides of the structure also provide vistas across the field.
Triangular cutouts on the side provide access and give the structure as in a tent.
Viewed from elsewhere, the pavilion has a face-like quality. It almost looks like the top part of the head of the Iron Giant from the 1999 film.
"It's also, as everybody tells us, a little bit ridiculous," said Meredith, who said it was like a Buckminster Fuller dome reimagined by artist Philip Guston. He added that the woven nature of these structures makes it more practical than typical domes, as the sides could be modified and shaped as in basketry.
MOS is well known for its conceptual work and writings.
A Dome with Four Oculi relates to recent writings by the studio, such as its Smaller Architecture book, which calls for smaller architecture studios to experiment.
It was developed partly in response to what Meredith calls a "weird moment" for architecture. The prevalence and desire for bigness have left out an important space that architecture holds for expression.
"Architecture is in a weird moment in general. It used to be a more active part of cultural production," he said.
"At some point, though, it sort of shifted and just feels commercial. Everything just feels like a commodity," he continued.
"So that's what's nice about Art Omi. It's sort of outside the system, and it gives you a chance to reflect and think about something else."
The pavilion was part of Art Omi's fall architecture programming, which included TAELON7's Limbo Engawa pavilion.
Art Omi has been doubling down on its commitment to architecture and, in 2024, announced a series of 18 pavilions designed by established architecture studios such as SO-IL.
In London, Studio Saar created a shield-topped pavilion for London Design Festival, examining Britain's colonial history in India.
The photography is by Michael Vahrenwald.

The ‘stab in the back’ that wasn’t: Why Stalin sent the Red Army into Poland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:23:02 UTC
04:23:02 KST

The ‘stab in the back’ that wasn’t: Why Stalin sent the Red Army into Poland
On September 17, 1939, Soviet troops crossed into eastern Poland. By that time, the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth was about to collapse under the assault of Nazi forces. Soon, the Soviet military moved westward to meet the advancing Germans. Moscow and Berlin established a demarcation line according to which the USSR acquired parts of eastern Poland. Today, these territories belong to Belarus, Ukraine, and Lithuania.
This event still sparks debates both in Russia and Europe, and particularly in Poland. In Ukraine and Lithuania, political discourse has taken a surprising turn, suggesting that while the USSR was the aggressor state that invaded Poland on September 17, neither Ukraine nor Lithuania will yield any territory that they gained as a result of this aggression. For Lithuania, the situation is quite ironic, since it acquired its capital, Vilnius, precisely as a result of the Red Army’s Polish campaign.
Any commentary on this event provokes an intense and painful reaction from all sides that consider themselves victims of it. Nevertheless, it is essential to examine the circumstances surrounding the Soviet army’s invasion of Poland. For Russians, who lost countless lives during the Second World War, this topic is particularly sensitive; but the same holds true for Poles, who suffered comparable losses relative to their population size, and for Belarusians and Ukrainians, who found themselves in the middle of this significant territorial reallocation.
History can often be distorted by politics. From the late 1930s to the present day, interpretations of this event have evolved in various countries. It would be best to take a measured approach to assess what really happened, recognizing that each country has its own perspective shaped by its unique experience. We also need to remember that all parties had rational interests, yet none of them possessed enough information or the benefit of hindsight provided by post-war historians.
Buffer zone of discord
By 1939, both the Soviet Union and Poland were new states established on the basis of old nations. They had come into existence following the disintegration of the Russian Empire and the subsequent Russian Civil War. However, from the outset, there was a significant territorial dispute between Russia’s reincarnation in the form of the Soviet Union and Poland’s rebirth as the Second Polish Republic. The Poles laid claim not only to their own lands but also to all the lands Poland had once possessed, which included vast territories in Belarus and Ukraine. In Poland, this region is referred to as “Kresy Wschodnie,” which means “Eastern Borderlands.”
Overall, Poland’s ambitions extended even further. During the Russian Civil War, Polish forces advanced deep into Ukraine and captured Kiev before ultimately being defeated. The Red Army then launched its Polish campaign which also ended in failure a short way from Warsaw. Ultimately, the Poles acquired what they referred to as “Kresy” – the western regions of Ukraine and Belarus. For the most part, these territories weren’t populated by Poles, yet Poland had governed them before the territorial divisions of the 18th century and viewed them as its historical lands. During the interwar period, these regions underwent a process of polonization, with Ukrainian and Belarusian populations facing discrimination. One somewhat counterintuitive fact is that Ukrainian nationalist terrorism during that period was directed primarily not against the USSR, but against Poland.
Meanwhile, the Soviet Union regarded these lost territories as unjustly seized and was unwilling to relinquish its claims on them. In short, neither party was satisfied with such ‘peace’ and there was no warming of relations between the USSR and Poland.
The territorial dispute over the Vilnius region caused additional challenges. Poland seized Vilna (Vilnius), a city that Lithuania claimed as its historical capital and which was highly important to it both historically and culturally.
This atmosphere of ‘cold peace’ lasted throughout the 1920s. In the 1930s, the Nazis came to power in Germany. In 1938, Hitler annexed a significant part of Czechoslovakia (a few months later, he came to fully control the country). This crisis put the USSR and Poland at odds once again. The Soviet Union viewed the Nazis as a grave threat, and Moscow even considered intervening on behalf of Czechoslovakia. However, this required USSR troops to pass through Poland, which Warsaw resolutely rejected. It was opposed to any military cooperation with the USSR, even for transit purposes. Furthermore, during the German occupation of Czechoslovakia, Poland annexed the Teschen region (an area of 805 square kilometers with a population of 277,000) which was a small but notable territorial gain.
Throughout the negotiations regarding Czechoslovakia, the interests and positions of the USSR were overtly disregarded by Western allies – i.e. England, France, and Poland. The Soviet Union gained considerable political weight on the global stage only after WWII. Before that, its influence hardly rose to the level of a superpower. Consequently, Stalin had to swallow this bitter pill and prepare for the events to come.
Meanwhile, Hitler was determined to continue his aggressive expansion. The regime he constructed in Germany had a significant yet subtle flaw – its structure resembled a financial pyramid. The rapid growth of the country’s military industrial complex threatened to undermine its economy. The only salvation for the Third Reich lay in war or the unconditional submission of neighboring countries to its demands and threats. Poland was next on Hitler’s list of intended victims. He used the “Polish Corridor” – the strip of land separating mainland Germany from East Prussia – as leverage. The Germans maintained contact with this exclave solely by sea. Today, this area remains an exclave, but belongs to Russia: the current Russian city of Kaliningrad is the former German city of Königsberg. Additionally, Hitler demanded reconsideration of the status of Danzig, a city with a significant German population that had been designated a “free city” under the League of Nations’ protection.
Understandably, Poland wasn’t satisfied with these demands. The question was, how could it stand up to Germany, which was much more powerful. Clearly, the best option was to seek help from Western allies – Britain and France. They readily provided Poland with security guarantees and did indeed declare war on the Third Reich on September 3, just two days after it invaded Poland. However, what the Polish leaders didn’t realize was that their allies weren’t prepared to offer immediate assistance. Britain needed time to transport troops across the English Channel, while France had to mobilize and strategically deploy its troops. This couldn’t be done immediately, but it was uncertain whether Poland could hold out long enough.
Poland’s dialogue with Soviet diplomats was quite rude. Polish officials bluntly told People’s Commissar for Foreign Affairs Maxim Litvinov that they would ask for help “when it will be needed.” Throughout this time, the Polish government believed that “the dismemberment of Russia is at the heart of Poland’s eastern policy.”
It’s no secret that there were significant territorial disputes between the USSR and Poland, and that the two countries felt an aversion towards each other. In hindsight, Warsaw’s behavior appears reckless, but at the time, Poland believed that the guarantees from Western allies would suffice. They thought that by allowing even one Russian soldier into Poland, they could easily become hostages of such an ally. Strictly speaking, one can’t say that they were wrong. Nevertheless, the Soviet regime turned out to be a lot less strict than the German regime in Poland.
The USSR aimed to safeguard its interests in Eastern Europe. Moscow had no doubt that a large-scale war was imminent. And the USSR found itself in a vulnerable position. The key centers of Soviet power were located too close to the border. Leningrad (currently St. Petersburg) faced threats from both Finland and Estonia which it bordered, while Minsk and Kiev were dangerously close to the Polish border. The USSR wasn’t concerned about a threat coming directly from Estonia or Poland, but rather feared that a third party could use these regions as a launchpad for an attack on the USSR (by 1939, it was clear that this would be Germany). Stalin and his inner circle understood that the USSR would eventually confront Germany and were eager to secure the most advantageous position before the inevitable confrontation.
Mistrust and the fog of war
The USSR still had another option – direct negotiations with Western allies. Stalin was primarily interested in a coordinated plan of action against the Nazis. However, the Soviet Union had its own fears and biases. It’s important to note that, just like in the situation with Poland, neither British nor French leaders could foresee the future any better than their Soviet counterparts. And in 1939 they considered such an alliance no better than one with Hitler.
This might sound odd in 2026, but in the summer of 1939, Hitler wasn’t yet “the Hitler” that we’ve come to know. The Third Reich was still largely focused on repressing its own citizens. Anti-semitism with its discriminatory laws was abominable, yet not necessarily worse than the repressions in the US against African-Americans or the colonial practices of European powers. On the other hand, Stalin’s USSR, with its own repressions and ideology aimed at dismantling the capitalist world, certainly didn’t present itself as a beacon of virtue. This is why Moscow had its doubts about whether Britain and France were more reliable negotiating partners than Germany, and the same skepticism was shared by Paris and London in regard to Moscow. Additionally, Britain and France significantly underestimated the real weight of the USSR as an ally – and this was an error they would soon regret.
On August 11, an Anglo-French delegation arrived in Moscow. The problem was that the allies came with a very vague battle plan. The Soviet side insisted on including the term “indirect aggression” in the agreement, which implied using the territories of neighboring countries to wage war against the USSR. The allies believed that Stalin wanted free rein to act against the Baltic states, Finland, and wherever else he pleased. However, the Soviet Union needed this complicated wording to safeguard itself against a possible surprise alliance between Germany and Finland or the Baltic nations, leading to a potential invasion of the USSR from those territories.
Both sides distrusted each other and preferred to secure maximum guarantees with minimal commitments. Ultimately, the negotiations failed.
In response, the Soviet Union made a controversial move: it struck a deal with Hitler. On August 23, a non-aggression pact was signed between the USSR and Germany, outlining spheres of influence in Europe.
Under the famous Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, the USSR aimed to buy time and establish a buffer zone in Eastern Europe. Moscow secured a significant condition – the incorporation of Eastern Poland (currently Western Ukraine and Belarus) into the Soviet sphere of interest.
Even today, this pact is often regarded as a deal with the devil. However, it did not serve as an immediate trigger for war. For Hitler, war was inevitable. Stopping the war would lead to the collapse of his entire foreign policy, and Germany’s bloated military system could not come to a stop without causing economic disaster. Moreover, Hitler did not regard the Soviet Union as a formidable opponent; he even devised plans of a complete military defeat of the USSR in three months.
Looking back, we may say that the 1938-1939 negotiations represent one of the greatest failures in the history of diplomacy. Had the world powers united against the Nazis in 1939 – or better yet, in 1938 – there might have been no WWII, but only a major clean-up of issues left over from WWI. However, there’s no way to change history.
The barrier to Blitzkrieg
Poland’s pre-war planning was based on several questionable assumptions. Poland believed that its army was sufficiently large and was capable of holding off the Nazis long enough for Western allies to come to its aid. Ideas to form a defensive line along the Vistula River and use the river as a natural barrier were ultimately dismissed. Marshal Edward Rydz-Smigly, who led Poland’s defense, aimed to cover all fronts and surrender nothing. However, in reality, Poland had far fewer military resources than the enemy and couldn’t seize the initiative. Moreover, after the annexation of Czechoslovakia, the Third Reich bordered Poland on three sides. Even without additional complications, this combination spelled disaster for Poland. Yet another problem existed: between the wars, the Germans developed a range of operational, tactical, and technical solutions known as “Blitzkrieg,” which prioritized rapid, decisive maneuvers. And Poland became the testing ground for this strategy in real-life conditions.
On September 1, 1939, Hitler invaded Poland, marking the start of WWII. On September 3, the Allies declared war on Germany. The Wehrmacht charged at the Polish army like a gorilla breaking free from its cage. Within the first week, the Polish forces retreated chaotically on all fronts, and some units became encircled. By September 5, the Polish government fled toward the border. On September 16, before the USSR entered the conflict, the Polish leadership was already negotiating with Romania regarding evacuation. The high command moved to Brest and lost contact with the main body of troops.
After September 10, there was no longer any centralized control of the Polish army. By September 16, German forces reached Bialystok, Brest, and Lviv. Most organized Polish units remained to the west and were encircled. The Allies were unable to assist Poland; French troops were slowly deployed and managed to carry out only a limited offensive that pushed the front back a few kilometers into German territory. The Allies could have saved Poland by 1940, if only it could hold out until then – but this was clearly an insurmountable task for the country.
Soviet political leaders decided that further delay was pointless. On September 6, Moscow announced “large-scale military exercises” which in reality meant that the country mobilized its armed forces. However, it soon became apparent that the Soviet military was not as combat ready as was anticipated. The troops weren’t ready for combat, military equipment required repairs, and there was a great shortage of additional vehicles.
Regardless of this, the Polish forces were completely disorganized and could not offer fierce resistance. The notion that the Soviets “stabbed Poland in the back as it fought” the Nazis sounds quite dramatic, but by that time, all that remained of the Polish army were some isolated battalions. Poland had lost all its industrial regions, mobilization was impossible, the army was defeated, and the remaining troops tried to defend Warsaw. In essence, there was no one to “stab in the back.” Formally, the Polish army still numbered in the hundreds of thousands of soldiers and officers, but in reality they moved around chaotically in the rear. There was no one to lead them into battle.
On the night of September 17, Stalin personally informed German ambassador to the USSR Friedrich-Werner Graf von der Schulenburg that the Red Army was about to start its operation. A similar note was delivered to the Polish ambassador to the USSR. The next morning, Soviet mechanized columns crossed the border into Poland.
The Polish government promptly fled the country. Commander of the Polish armed forces Marshal Rydz-Smigly ordered, “I command an immediate retreat to Romania and Hungary by the shortest routes. Do not engage in combat with the Soviets.”
The entry of the Red Army into Poland was accompanied by considerable disorder. Polish resistance was sporadic and was largely initiated by local junior commanders. The advance of Soviet troops was marked by confusion and there were many non-combat losses. In areas where the Poles put up resistance, the Soviet army fought, but generally for the Poles, it looked more like disarmament than defeat in battle. For instance, during the assault on Grodno, 57 Red Army soldiers were killed, while about 1,500 Polish soldiers and officers surrendered. During the campaign, an estimated 737-1,475 Soviet soldiers and officers died – many of them for non-combat reasons; and about 240,000 soldiers were taken prisoner.
While Polish soldiers and officers offered some resistance, the Ukrainian, Belarusian, and Jewish people often sympathized with or even assisted the advancing Red Army units. Poland’s ideology was one of triumphant nationalism, so non-Polish cultures found themselves in a subordinate position and were often openly discriminated against.
The Wehrmacht immediately halted its advance into territories that were claimed by the USSR. A few days later, the demarcation line was finalized. Tensions arose only in Lviv, where Soviet forces encountered German troops. As a result, all three sides – the Red Army, the Polish garrison, and the German army – lost both soldiers and equipment.
A separate story unfolded in Brest. On September 22, a Red Army tank brigade entered the city, which had been occupied by German forces. Depending on the narrator, this event is often described as either the passage of troops or a joint parade. Soviet commander Semyon Krivoshein and German General Heinz Guderian watched as German soldiers withdrew from Brest and Soviet troops took their place. The situation was all the more awkward since Krivoshein was Jewish and felt as uncomfortable standing next to a Nazi commander as Guderian did standing next to him.
By September 29, the Red Army’s campaign in Poland was essentially over. The Soviet Union expanded its territory by 196,000 square km (half of the territory of Poland) with a population of up to 13 million people. The Vilna region, including the city of Vilnius, was handed over to Lithuania, while areas populated by Belarusians and Ukrainians were assigned to the respective Soviet republics.
The fate of prisoners of war and the people detained by Soviet security agencies raised further questions. Many Polish officers were later executed at Katyn. But most captives were either sent home or fled to the West through third counties where they formed the Anders’ Army, which became part of the Western coalition. In western Belarus and Ukraine, Soviet authority was established, which caused certain upheavals that always accompany such transitions. Many people suspected of disloyalty were deported further east. However, considering the war which would soon break out, such exile often saved their lives.
Liberation for some, occupation for others
Setting politics aside and focusing on the actual circumstances surrounding the Soviet campaign and its alternatives, we see that the situation didn’t look flattering from any side.
Firstly, we need to dismiss the idea that Hitler would not have started the war without the pact or that the war was started jointly by the Nazis and the USSR. The Soviet Union lacked the diplomatic weight to impose its will on partners in negotiations. Indeed, the Nazis didn’t want more problems in the East. However, from Hitler’s perspective, he struck a fantastic deal: he resolved a potentially contentious issue and rid himself of possible complications by ceding territories that he considered worthless – that didn’t have any significant resources or industrial centers – to the Soviet Union.
For the USSR, this meant gaining a buffer zone in case of a future confrontation with the Nazis and reuniting two important national republics. Did the decision regarding Poland align with strict moral standards? Not really. But Poland had little reason to complain – after all, its army had forcefully seized the disputed territories a few decades earlier, only to lose them in another military conflict. And while we may vehemently denounce USSR aggression, we must also ask: what were the alternatives? In fact, there were only two viable options. The first one was to fight against Hitler with a weak military force and with no solid guarantees from Western allies. Negotiations on a joint action plan with those allies had just failed, so why would Stalin trust them?
As for Poland, it was outright opposed to an alliance with Moscow. Indeed, there was another option: to do nothing. This meant handing over the Kresy to Hitler. On September 17, 1939, the choice was not “Poland or Hitler” or “totalitarians or democrats”; it was simply “Hitler or Stalin.” Given this reality, it’s worth asking the moralists whether they consider Hitler a more legitimate or humane ruler of Lviv and Grodno than Stalin.
In this grim world of ‘realpolitik’, Poland’s position proved to be extremely vulnerable. The leaders of the Second Polish Republic consistently rejected any ideas of jointly fighting against Hitler with the USSR. Of course, they reasonably feared being drawn into Moscow’s orbit and ultimately finding themselves living in a socialist Poland. Ironically, by the end of the war, this is indeed what happened, but by that time Poland had lost one-fifth of its population due to the war and the Nazi occupation, and Warsaw and the entire country were in ruins. Should Poland have considered making political concessions to the USSR earlier instead of waiting until Moscow controlled Poland’s territory, army, and political institutions? That’s a question only the Polish people can answer. Indeed, it’s hard to shake the feeling that in 1939, faced with two evils, Poland chose to do nothing and simply perish. The idea of doing nothing in such a situation might look good in a novel, but it’s hardly practical in politics.
For Western allies, 1939 clearly became the year of lost opportunities. One could argue that an allied operation against the Nazis involving Britain, France, the USSR, and what remained of Poland could have been a better option than what happened in reality: Germany’s swift occupation of France, followed by Britain and the USSR fighting Germany on their own – Britain at sea and in the air, and the USSR on land. However, at the time, deep mutual distrust and a poor understanding of the situation played a fatal role in forming an alliance between Western democracies and the Soviet Union.
The USSR ultimately benefited from the events of September 1939, but not as much as it had hoped. Its territorial gains included western Belarus and Ukraine, and this was soon followed by the annexation of the Baltic states. Since a larger war loomed on the horizon, this territory became valuable only as square kilometers. These buffer zones proved crucial in 1941 when the USSR entered the war against Germany. The issue of Finland’s status, which the USSR declared war on several months later, remained unresolved.
Most importantly, Stalin hoped that he would gain far more time than he actually did. The USSR had hoped that it would have several years to prepare for war, while France put up active resistance. In reality, the defense of France collapsed in the summer of 1940, and the USSR gained only one year and nine months of breathing room. And rather than becoming weaker, the Wehrmacht grew even stronger in the course of the conflict against Western allies.
In 1939, politicians gave more candid and sensible assessments of the situation. Winston Churchill observed:
“Russia has pursued a cold policy of self-interest. We could have wished that the Russian armies should be standing on their present lines as the friends of the allies in Poland, instead of as invaders. But that the Russian armies should stand on this line was clearly necessary for the safety of Russia against the Nazi menace. In any case, this line exists, and this means that an Eastern Front has been established that Nazi Germany would not dare attack.”
The Soviet Union operated within the framework of ‘realpolitik’, which didn’t look either nice or noble.
But in less than two years, the Russians found themselves engaged in the greatest war in history, which was a battle for their very survival. And undoubtedly, the Soviet Union used every means at its disposal to strengthen its position before that day arrived.

SDA Seeks to Expand Ground Architecture for Future Missile Tracking Satellites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:22:49 UTC
04:22:49 KST

The Space Development Agency is opening a competition to expand its ground architecture to support a growing fleet of missile warning, tracking, and defense satellites.
The agency issued a solicitation Sept. 18 requesting bids from companies to develop ground entry points for its missile defense satellites at locations around the world. By early next year, SDA plans to choose a single company to build, install, and maintain up to eight new ground entry points and to perform upgrades at current sites.
The ground segment expansion will support Tranche 3 of what SDA calls its Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture, a low-Earth orbit constellation envisioned to include hundreds of data transport and missile tracking satellites that will be refreshed every two years with new capability. So far, SDA has launched just eight missile tracking satellites as part of what it calls “Tranche 0” to demonstrate the viability of space-based missile tracking in LEO. The agency is in the midst of launching Tranche 1, which will feature 28 missile warning and tracking satellites. Tranche 2 will include 54, and Tranche 3 will have 108 spacecraft.
That proliferated space architecture requires a network of ground systems that can push data from satellites to military users who need it to inform decisions about how to respond to missile threats. SDA expects that distributing those ground systems across multiple locations will both improve the performance of the capability and make it more resilient.
For its first two operational tranches, SDA is requiring its satellite vendors to provide the ground stations needed to operate their spacecraft. General Dynamics Mission Systems is under contract to integrate those ground stations into ground operations centers, which serve as hubs for each tranche of satellites. SDA has awarded the company $816 million to date for that work.
For Tranche 3, the agency wants to transition to an enterprise model, according to a Government Accountability Office report issued in January. That approach would feature “new capabilities” and build on the earlier tranches. SDA has also selected SAIC to serve as a third-party integrator for Tranche 3, which GAO says should help address past challenges with ground system testing and operations.
SDA expects to start launching Tranche 3 satellites in late 2028 or 2029, but in the meantime it’s focused on populating Tranche 1. The agency has launched three batches of data transport satellites and has six missions left to complete the tranche. SDA Director Gurpartap Sandhoo told reporters Sept. 15 at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference that the first Tranche 1 tracking satellites should launch either late this year or early next.
The Space Force’s fiscal 2027 budget requests $3.5 billion for SDA’s LEO-based Resilient Missile Warning/Missile Tracking program. Budget documents indicate that fiscal ‘27 funding, if approved, will support early work on Tranche 3 ground entry points and other infrastructure to expand the “global footprint.”
