Canada’s Jews shouldn’t need a fundraising campaign to pray safely - comment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:22:42 UTC
04:22:42 KST

Const. Jeff Smith of the Belleville Police Service was waiting in an unmarked car outside Sons of Jacob Synagogue on Sunday evening when, according to Ontario’s police watchdog, a man with a shotgun opened fire on him.
About 25 people were inside for Kol Nidre, the service that opens Yom Kippur. The synagogue’s president, Norm Weddum, says the congregation had never received a threat.
Belleville is a city of about 55,000, roughly 110 miles east of Toronto, and Weddum describes its Jewish community as small. Somebody at the local police department decided that this synagogue, on this night, needed an armed officer outside anyway. Ontario Premier Doug Ford called Smith a hero who stopped a tragedy. I think Ford is right, and I’d like to know who put Smith there.
Here’s what happened inside, as Weddum tells it. He heard shots, some congregants went toward the doors, and then a second round came. He moved everyone back into the sanctuary, shut the wooden doors so no one could be seen from the entrance, and told people to get down on the floor. Bullets came through the windows. One stained-glass window has about 20 holes in it.
Doug Lobel, a congregant, told CP24 news station what they were thinking down there: “Was the gunman going to breach the doors and start targeting us?”
He didn’t get the chance. Smith returned fire; a second officer fired as well, and Smith and the man were both hit. Houses and cars on the street were damaged. Smith, a 13-year veteran, is in critical but stable condition. The suspect, 29-year-old Sean Ward from neighboring Quinte West, is in life-threatening condition. No one inside was hurt.
Read the statements slowly
The first statement from Belleville police said an officer had “encountered” an individual near an intersection. It didn’t say why an officer was there. Since then, the force has had nothing to add, because the Special Investigations Unit, the civilian agency that takes over in Ontario whenever police shoot at someone, has invoked its mandate.
Mayor Neil Ellis told CBC he hopes the SIU investigation gets to “the root cause.” I don’t doubt he was shaken; he said he cried when he heard the news. But the SIU’s job is to decide whether Smith and his colleague were justified in firing. Why a 29-year-old showed up on that corner with a gun isn’t its question. Someone else has to ask it, and nobody has said publicly who that is.
Police haven’t said what led to the shooting or whether the synagogue was the target. The SIU first described the weapon as a rifle and later as a shotgun. At least three people fired on a residential street, and nobody has said whose bullets went through the stained glass. I’m not going to guess at Ward’s motive. Whatever it was, Smith was there first.
'It pains me'
In June, Prime Minister Mark Carney stood in Holy Blossom Temple, Toronto’s oldest Reform synagogue, and said, “Canada’s civic compact is failing Jewish Canadians.” It was an unusually blunt thing for a prime minister to say. He noted that more than two-thirds of religion-motivated hate crimes the previous year had targeted Jews, who are about 1% of Canadians, and he announced another $75 million for security. Then he added, “It pains me that we had to commit $75 million to this.”
I believe him. I wish he’d stop saying it.
When a prime minister describes security money as a painful concession, the program that spends it tends to read the same way. The $75 million went to the Canada Community Security Program. The program describes itself as time-limited funding for communities at risk of hate-motivated crime. It covers up to 70% of eligible costs; under the program it replaced, the government paid half. Anything spent before a funding agreement is signed isn’t reimbursed. Guards qualify only as “time-limited third-party licensed security personnel.”
Read those rules as the treasurer of a synagogue the size of Sons of Jacob would. You raise the other 30% yourself, fill out the application, and wait for a signed agreement before spending a dollar. Then you hire guards on a “time-limited” basis, as if somebody at Public Safety Canada knows when the threat expires. The program is built for communities that can show they’re at risk. By its president’s account, this one had never been threatened.
Ford said out loud on Monday what those rules imply. He told reporters he was thankful such an experienced officer had been posted at the synagogue, and then added: “We never have enough security.” He’s the premier of Ontario. If anyone in the province can decide what counts as enough, it’s him.
On Sunday night, Toronto’s mayor, Olivia Chow, said Jews “should not need police presence to observe Yom Kippur.” Nobody disagrees with her. It’s no help to that treasurer deciding whether to apply for a guard this year.
Where I might be wrong
The best argument against everything above is Chow’s, taken seriously. A country that answers antisemitism by stationing police outside synagogues has accepted antisemitism as permanent. A dollar spent on a guard is a dollar that isn’t spent stopping someone before he picks up a gun. People who backed the new federal hate law would say the law is for slower work. They may be right. None of it would have helped the people lying on the floor of Sons of Jacob.
The harder objection, for me, is the guns. On Yom Kippur last year, at Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation in Manchester, England, worshipers were trying to keep an attacker from getting into the building. Armed police shot him about seven minutes after the first emergency call. One of the two men who died appears to have been hit by a police bullet.
In Belleville, at least three people fired on a residential street. If some of the rounds that came through that window turn out to be police rounds, this column gets harder to defend. I’d still defend it. Manchester’s police had to get there after the attack started, and Belleville’s officer was parked outside before it began. Nobody inside was hurt.
Reading this from afar
In August, I complained in this column that Israeli politicians had boiled their message to world Jewry down to three requests: “Educate your children. Come home. Speak well of us.” Expect to hear the second one a lot this week.
Some of the people who lay on that floor may one day make aliyah – the Hebrew word for immigrating to Israel – and Israel should be ready for them when they do. That’s a decision about where to raise your children and build a life. Nobody should be making it from a sanctuary floor.
What the Jews of Belleville need from us right now is support while they press their own governments for something those governments owe them. An Israeli minister who uses Sunday night to pitch aliyah would be making that job harder.
Queen’s Park should commit to a police presence at every synagogue in the province on the High Holidays (Queen’s Park is the Ontario legislature, roughly the province’s version of a state capitol). The province should pay for it, with no threat assessment required. The commitment should cover Purim as well. In March, gunfire hit Toronto’s Temple Emanu-El while the congregation was marking the holiday.
Ottawa should drop the 30% match and the “time-limited” condition for small congregations. A synagogue with two dozen people at Kol Nidre shouldn’t need a grant writer to get a guard.
Ontario’s prosecutors, known in Canada as the Crown, owe the public an explanation either way. The Combatting Hate Act took effect on July 18. It made hate-motivated crime a specific offense and created a crime of intimidating people to keep them from a place of worship, punishable by up to 10 years. When shots hit synagogues in Vaughan and Toronto in March, before the act was in force, the charges were reckless discharge of a firearm, mischief relating to religious property, and conspiracy. If the evidence shows Ward acted out of hatred, charge him under the new law. If it doesn’t, say so and explain why.
And Belleville police should tell us why Const. Smith was parked outside Sons of Jacob on Sunday night: who decided, based on what, and whether the synagogue got a bill. Whoever made that call got it right. Nobody else in Canada can copy it until they know what it was.

Foreign companies continuing to provide services to Iranian airlines will risk facing US secondary sanctions starting on Wednesday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced on Monday.
“On September 23, all Iranian airlines will be grounded globally,” Bessent told CNBC.
The move could effectively prevent Iranian carriers from operating at airports worldwide.
He noted that the US threat applies not only to the airlines themselves but also to airports, fuel suppliers, ticketing agencies, and other service providers.
“If they land, they cannot be supplied with fuel or landing services, nor can tickets be sold for them; otherwise, you will be cut off from the dollar system,” he said.
All Iranian airlines added to US sanctions list in September
Earlier this month, the US Treasury Department imposed sanctions on all active Iranian airlines not previously included on sanctions lists, warning that foreign companies assisting them could be barred from the global financial system.
The move is part of the Trump administration’s Operation Economic Outcast, designed to ramp up economic pressure on Tehran alongside the conflict with Iran.

Ukraine says foreign defense suppliers owe country about $10.58 billion, including $1.7 billion already paid for goods delivered late or never at all
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:21:50 UTC
04:21:50 KST

Foreign defense suppliers owe Ukraine approximately $10.58 billion, according to Ukraine’s Ministry of Finance. Of this amount, approximately $1.70 billion represents overdue receivables or funds that the Ministry of Defense has already paid to suppliers but for which the corresponding goods or services were either delivered late or not delivered at all.
Ukraine is seeking to recover these funds through the courts. However, in several cases, the statute of limitations is approaching or has already expired, potentially preventing the state from recovering the money.
A $22,400 legal bill could put $403 million in recoverable funds at risk
The government needs approximately $22,400 in legal fees to continue these proceedings. Without this funding, Ukraine could lose more than $403 million, roughly 18,000 times the amount required for legal services.
“The lack of funding for international disputes deprives Ukraine of the ability to forcibly recover these assets,” the Ministry of Finance said.
Funding shortfall could jeopardize legal cases and future financing
The ministry warned that a lack of funding could deprive the state budget of significant revenues, potentially force Ukraine to terminate contracts with foreign legal advisers already representing it, and delay the appointment of new advisers. It could also negatively affect Ukraine’s standing and make it more difficult to secure financing in the future, Ekonomichna Pravda reports.
Supplier debts to Ukraine’s Defense Ministry rise amid growing funding needs
The Ministry of Defense’s overdue receivables have been growing year after year. As of 1 January 2024, they amounted to approximately $886 million, rising to approximately $1.01 billion as of 1 January 2025.
In this context, receivables are amounts owed to the Ministry of Defense by suppliers for goods not delivered or services not provided on time, even though the ministry has already paid for them.
The Ministry of Finance raised these issues amid a funding shortfall for Ukraine’s Defense Forces in 2026, which the president has put at approximately $27 billion.

Turkish first lady urges global shift in consumption habits, calls for 'shared responsibilities' in climate action
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:21:25 UTC
04:21:25 KST

- 'We must rebuild our relationship with nature on the principles of balance and justice'
Turkish first lady Emine Erdogan, who chairs the UN High-Level Advisory Board on Zero Waste, called for a shift in consumption habits and stronger international cooperation to address the climate crisis.
“The Zero Waste movement has transformed individuals from helpless observers in the face of the climate crisis into leading actors in the solution,” Erdogan said at the opening event of New York Climate Week.
“It has demonstrated that seemingly small behavioral changes can evolve into a social culture when they become widespread, and into a lasting system when supported by sound policies,” she added.
Emine Erdogan attended the event in New York, alongside Turkish Family and Social Services Minister Mahinur Ozdemir Goktas. The Ministry of Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change and the Zero Waste Foundation were among the event's main sponsors.
She was welcomed at the venue by Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Minister Murat Kurum, Zero Waste Foundation Chairman Samed Agirbas, Climate Group CEO Helen Clarkson, senior board member Emma Cox and other officials.
Beginning her remarks by conveying the Turkish people's greetings and respect, she thanked the organizers for their hospitality.
“Climate change is one of the most visible consequences of the heavy burden that human activities have placed on the Earth,” she said.
“Of course, we know the role of fossil fuels, industrial processes and high emissions in this crisis. But we must also ask ourselves: Are fossil fuels alone responsible for bringing us face to face with such a massive crisis? Is it large-scale industries? Or is it an unlimited demand for consumption that forces all of these to continuously produce more?”
'We must rebuild our relationship with nature on the principles of balance and justice'
Emine Erdogan said climate change was, above all, a result of a transformation in humanity's moral outlook.
“We have established a system that accepts from the outset that everything we produce has a short lifespan and that every object will one day become waste,” she said.
She noted that approximately 9.2 billion tons of plastic had been produced worldwide since the 1950s, with 7 billion tons becoming waste, describing the figures as a clear indication of the costs of this approach.
“Moreover, this burden is not distributed fairly across the planet,” she said. “The environmental costs generated by high levels of consumption are often left on the shoulders of societies that contribute the least to that consumption, vulnerable regions and future generations.”
“We must therefore begin by reducing excess in our habits alongside our waste, changing our mindset alongside our systems, and rebuilding our relationship with nature on the principles of balance and justice,” she added.
Erdogan said the Zero Waste movement emerged from this understanding, describing it as a moral stance that reminds people of limits and responsibilities at a time when consumption and waste have become normalized aspects of daily life.
'Zero Waste is the translation of this sense of stewardship into everyday life'
Erdogan said there was a fundamental difference between viewing nature as an unlimited reservoir of resources and seeing it as something entrusted to humanity.
“Zero Waste is the translation of this sense of stewardship into everyday life,” she said.
She explained that the first steps toward turning this awareness into behavior and ultimately a lasting system were taken in the Turkish presidential complex.
“Zero Waste practices that we launched at the presidential complex in 2017 soon spread to schools, hospitals, municipalities, public institutions and households,” she said.
“Our recovery rate, which stood at 13% at the time, has now surpassed 37%,” she added.
She reiterated that the Zero Waste movement had empowered individuals to become leading actors in addressing the climate crisis.
Erdogan also stressed that the approach would not diminish the responsibilities of governments and companies, but would instead expand and clarify them.
“Building infrastructure that makes it easier for people to make the right choices, designing products to be more durable, repairable and reusable, developing technologies that enable circular production, and establishing international cooperation for these efforts are our shared responsibilities,” she said.
“That is why I consider the journey of the Zero Waste movement from local to global to be extremely valuable,” she added.
'No target will be sufficient on its own; no technology will be a solution on its own'
Erdogan recalled that the Zero Waste resolution Türkiye submitted to the UN General Assembly in 2022 was adopted with broad international support.
She also noted that March 30 had been designated as International Zero Waste Day and that the UN High-Level Advisory Board on Zero Waste, which she chairs, had been established.
“We attach great importance to ensuring that the Zero Waste approach is addressed as one of the powerful tools of climate action at COP31, which we will host in Türkiye in November,” she said.
Erdogan said the discussion of Zero Waste at the opening of New York Climate Week was a meaningful indication of growing global ownership of the movement and a shared search for solutions.
“While I am delivering this speech, dozens of tons of waste have been generated in New York. The situation is no different in Istanbul or in many cities around the world,” she said.
“One thing is certain: As long as we continue the habits that produce today's problems while discussing the solutions of the future, no target will be sufficient on its own, and no technology will be a solution on its own,” she added.
Erdogan said the true value of the gathering would be determined not by what was said at the event, but by what participants chose to do differently after leaving.
“I hope New York Climate Week will lead to new habits alongside new ideas, and collective action alongside shared responsibilities,” she said.
Following her speech, Erdogan watched a live performance by contemporary marbling artist Garip Ay.
Editors-in-chief of newspapers and television channels, along with numerous other guests, attended the event.

Macron asks EU to ease fuel rules as France prepares new support measures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:20:32 UTC
04:20:32 KST

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
21 September 2026•Update: 21 September 2026
French President Emmanuel Macron has asked the European Commission to temporarily ease some EU rules on fuel to increase supply and help contain prices, while the French government prepares new measures to support people affected by higher fuel costs, broadcaster BFM TV reported on Monday.
In a letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Sept. 18, Macron proposed temporarily easing European fuel quality specifications, allowing greater flexibility on biofuel blending in diesel and delaying some new obligations for fossil fuel importers.
Macron said the measures could “strengthen our short-term import and production capacity” and “increase the supply available on the domestic market,” according to the letter.
He said temporarily adjusting fuel quality requirements could increase refinery output by between 5% and 20%, depending on the refinery.
The specifications cover factors including fuel density, vaporization limits and desulfurization requirements.
Macron noted that diesel used on US roads can contain up to 15 parts per million of sulfur, compared with 10 ppm under EU rules.
He also proposed greater flexibility on diesel biofuel blending.
The current B7 standard allows up to 7% biodiesel, while B10 allows up to 10%.
Macron said greater use of B10 could support diesel supplies and provide additional flexibility for the market.
The European Commission has said B10 has slightly lower energy content and could result in a very small increase in consumption.
Macron also called for a one-year delay to a requirement due to take effect Jan. 1, 2027, under which crude oil, natural gas and coal importers would have to demonstrate that suppliers meet EU-equivalent requirements for measuring and controlling methane emissions.
He said the new rules could create additional litigation risks for importers.
The European Commission has recommended delaying financial sanctions under the rules until the end of 2029.
Macron said the proposed temporary measures were needed amid disruptions to global oil supplies following the near-total closure of the Strait of Hormuz since March, which he said had reduced global oil supply and changed hydrocarbon trade flows.
He said global oil stocks had fallen by more than 500 million barrels and warned that continued disruptions, including attacks targeting energy infrastructure in Russia and the Middle East and rising Asian demand, could further affect supplies.
Without the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and the restoration of Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline, global crude oil supply could fall by at least another 4 million barrels per day, Macron said, potentially putting further upward pressure on prices.
Macron said Europe was particularly exposed to disruptions in refined petroleum products, with the EU relying on the Middle East for 36% of its kerosene imports and 18% of its diesel imports.
He also backed “a clear acceleration at the European level on electrification efforts” and “moderation of natural gas consumption, particularly for heating needs.”
Meanwhile, the French government is due to announce new measures Tuesday to support people affected by higher fuel prices.
The measures will be presented at a news conference at the Economy Ministry in Paris at 5 p.m. local time (1500GMT) by government ministers.
The announcement follows meetings on fuel prices at the prime minister’s office Monday.
The Elysee Palace said France was also working to facilitate the peaceful reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and secure energy supplies.

Brownlow simply latest chapter as Daicos continues rewriting AFL history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:20:09 UTC
04:20:09 KST

Thu, 3 Sept, 8:10 pm, Final score, Dockers 40, Hawks 72
analysis
Brownlow a short stopover as Nick Daicos continues rewriting AFL history books
When Nathan Buckley's decade-long tenure as Collingwood coach came to an end midway through 2021, there was a silver lining for the club amid the painful exit of the club legend.
Buckley's tenure had seen the Pies flirt with winning a premiership in 2018 and 2019 before ultimately failing, but by the time he wrapped up, Collingwood seemed well out of the premiership window.
The silver lining came in the form of a player who was yet to set foot on an AFL field: Nick Daicos, then a teenager touted as a generational prospect years before he was eligible to be drafted.
The AFL world was no stranger to the Daicos surname due to the exploits of Nick's famous father, Peter, who was immortalised at Collingwood as a member of the club's 1990 premiership side.
You did not need to be a Collingwood fanatic to know about Nick Daicos. Everyone around the game knew the kid was on his way because of his prolific exploits at the junior levels.
The weight of expectation that comes with the level of hype Daicos had as a draft prospect can prove crippling. Unfortunately, years of evidence support this.
Sometimes even the most hyped prospects can take time to fit into the AFL system, and it makes sense. These are boys coming to a man's game.
The more rigorous training regimes, expanded playbooks, media commitments, dietary requirements, and everything else that comes with being an AFL player can be too much. That is even before we get to the pace of the game being completely different.
That hasn't been the case with Daicos, who, as an audacious Nike advert claimed on the morning of the Brownlow count, has proven it inevitable from day one.
From his first game, Daicos showed an ability to bend the game to his will in ways not seen in teenagers, and we have all been blessed to witness it.
Daicos's arrival helped catapult Collingwood from second-last in 2021 to fourth in his first season in the AFL.
Collingwood fell one point short of a grand final appearance in Daicos's debut season, but went all the way in his second.
After collecting boatloads of the football across halfback while occasionally dipping his toes in the midfield as a rookie, Daicos supercharged the Pies engine room in 2023, helping them claim the flag, and he has not looked back since.
From very early on in Daicos's career, the Brownlow win appeared to be a question of when rather than if, but it was the one accolade he was frustratingly made to wait on.
Daicos followed up his premiership by polling a ridiculous 38 votes in 2024, the most by any player in the league's history up until that point, only for that year's winner, Patrick Cripps, to poll 45.
Last year, he was again a seemingly unbackable favourite before being stunned by Gold Coast's Matt Rowell.
Missing out on a Brownlow after being among the favourites for a few years can be something that follows you.
Marcus Bontempelli, despite being widely considered the best player of his generation, has yet to win the prestigious medal.
Buckley was famously made to wait year after year before eventually breaking through in 2003, his 11th season, while Gary Ablett Jr was even denied by his own teammate before his maiden Brownlow triumph. It is almost a rite of passage if you're an all-timer.
Despite Bontempelli, Zak Butters and Bailey Smith all challenging him at various points during the count, Daicos would not be denied this year.
Almost in revenge for the previous two seasons, this year, Daicos turned in an individual season that would ultimately prove impossible to ignore for the umpires.
Daicos broke Cripps's record with 47 votes and set a few more records along the way.
He is now the only player in league history to poll over 30 votes in three consecutive seasons, the only player to put together six straight three-vote games, and the only player to put together 13 three-vote games in a single season.
Given the ease with which Daicos has played from his first contest in the AFL four seasons ago, it was surprising to talk about the weight of expectation actually weighing on him after winning his elusive first Brownlow.
You get the sense that the weight of expectation might be the only thing that is capable of slowing him down, because efforts from his AFL counterparts to do so have so far proven futile.
For a player so metronomic and seemingly superhuman on the field, it was refreshing to hear Daicos admit he too deals with nerves and struggles with criticism, just like the rest of us.
Daicos admitted to the Brownlow win being a relief after being denied for so many years as a favourite, even saying he had given up trusting in betting markets.
Now that the Brownlow box has been ticked off, it is frightening to think of what an unburdened Daicos could potentially achieve.
Still just 23 years of age, Daicos has gone from being the precocious youngster to one of Collingwood's veterans, and he will act as the bridge from one era of Collingwood premiership contention to the next, just as Scott Pendlebury did.
He seems good enough to single-handedly wrench Collingwood's premiership window open for as long as he wants.
Adding premierships to his 2023 triumph will be at the top of Daicos's to-do list, and the hope will be that in the process of achieving that goal, his resume ultimately becomes undeniable.
The chance to be Collingwood's greatest player is in play. The chance to be the greatest player in league history is as well, as premature as that shout may seem.
The records Daicos set with his maiden Brownlow win will eventually be just another footnote for a player who is poised to rewrite the game's history books.
Like the commercial said: inevitable.

Putin's party wins record Duma majority in Kremlin-controlled elections as EU vows sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:17:03 UTC
04:17:03 KST

Five Western nations and Kyiv condemned the voting in occupied Ukraine as illegal, while a Ukrainian drone strike on Moscow on the final day of polling killed two people.
Vladimir Putin's United Russia party has won a record supermajority in parliament, preliminary results showed Monday. The tightly controlled three-day vote excluded every party critical of the Kremlin or the war in Ukraine.
Central Election Commission chief Ella Pamfilova said United Russia had secured 355 of the State Duma's 450 seats. That beats its previous record of 343, set in 2016, and is well above the 301 needed to change the constitution. Final results are due later this week.
The Communist Party came second with 40 seats, followed by the nationalist LDPR on 25, New People on 20 and A Just Russia on four. Pamfilova put turnout at more than 59 percent.
It was Russia's first parliamentary election since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Criticism of the war is banned, and Yabloko, the only party calling for an end to the fighting, was barred from running for the national parliament, though it was allowed to stand in some regional votes.
"These indicators, of course, point to the highest level of consolidation within Russian society around the head of state," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.
United Russia told state media that 49 veterans who fought in Ukraine are expected to enter the Duma for the party.
Voting also took place in occupied parts of Ukraine, including Crimea and the Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia regions.
On Sunday, the final day of voting, Kyiv hit Moscow with its biggest drone attack of the war, killing two people and setting an oil refinery ablaze. Russia's defence ministry accused Ukraine of trying to disrupt the vote and vowed to intensify strikes on Kyiv.
Russia's 'veneer of democracy'
The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said the Kremlin had "silenced dissent" and shut out international election monitors.
"The veneer of democracy is all that remains in Russia," she said. "The State Duma elections held by Russia on 18–20 September underscored the continued and deepening erosion of democracy in Russia, taking place in an increasingly authoritarian political environment."
In a statement on behalf of the bloc, Kallas said the EU would impose sanctions on those who organised the vote or stood as candidates in occupied Ukrainian territory.
"The European Union reiterates that it does not and will never recognise either the holding of these so-called “elections” in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine or their results." the statement said.
Britain, Australia, Canada, New Zealand and Norway said in a joint statement that holding the election in occupied areas was a "gross violation" of Ukraine's sovereignty and the UN Charter. They said the vote could not change the status of those territories under international law.
"These sham elections are part of a wider system of occupation: the imposition of Russian administration, law, media, education, language and citizenship, backed by coercion and repression," the statement said.
Ukraine's foreign ministry had earlier called the voting in occupied regions a "farce" and said it would not recognise the results.
The election brought one surprise. In the Novgorod region, where it was allowed on the ballot for regional elections held at the same time, Yabloko won just over six percent of the vote, enough to enter the regional parliament.
Putin's political opponents are in exile, in prison or dead. His main rival, Alexei Navalny, died in an Arctic prison in 2024.

Polo strengthens into hurricane, threatening Mexico’s Pacific resort towns
Polo strengthened off Mexico’s Pacific coast into a hurricane on Sept 21 and is forecast to rapidly intensify into a major storm, threatening floods, dangerous surf and strong wind gusts in coastal states and near major beach resorts.
Around midday locally (2am on Sept 22, Singapore time), Polo was located some 435km south-south-east of port city Manzanillo and 305km south-south-west of tourist town Zihuatanejo, packing maximum sustained winds of 130kph, the US National Hurricane Center said.
Forecasters said the storm could become a major hurricane by Sept 22 and continue strengthening through midweek. While its core is expected to remain offshore, the storm is likely to lash parts of south-western Mexico with torrential rain and hazardous seas.
The NHC said coastal parts of Guerrero and Michoacan states could receive 10 to 20cm of rain through Sept 24, with isolated totals of up to 30cm, raising the risk of life-threatening flooding and mudslides, particularly in mountainous areas.
Private forecaster AccuWeather said the storm’s reach could extend out toward tourist hubs including Acapulco, Puerto Vallarta and Guadalajara, while southern Baja California Sur, including the Los Cabos area, could also see rough surf and strong gusts later this week.
Accuweather also warned that tropical moisture from Mexico is expected to push north through the rest of the week, threatening flash floods in the US South-west. REUTERS

Migrant child stows away to Spain under football bus
MADRID - A Moroccan boy travelled from Spain’s north African exclave of Ceuta to the mainland hidden under a visiting football team’s bus on Sept 21, sources at the club told AFP.
The Real Valladolid players found the child hidden by their coach’s wheel axle when it pulled over at a service station, the sources told AFP.

Under pressure to contain migration after a crisis in Ceuta on July 30 and 31, Spain’s government had insisted that no irregular migrants would be allowed to reach the mainland.

The boy under the coach had stayed hidden throughout the ferry crossing and for more than 100km by road before eventually calling for help, the Real Valladolid sources said.
Club members gave him food, water and clothing before police took charge of him.
The authorities say conditions in Ceuta have deteriorated since the migrant influx, sparking angry demonstrations by residents. AFP

Porsche Becomes a Burden for Volkswagen Group — Media
Kyiv • UNN
Porsche lost ground in China and suffered losses due to the transition to electric vehicles. Volkswagen wrote down €6 billion of the value of its stake in the brand.
Porsche, the carmaker, is becoming one of the Volkswagen Group’s biggest problems and is fading into the shadow of the Czech brand Škoda. Reuters writes, as reported by UNN.
Porsche, the manufacturer of luxury sports cars that was long Volkswagen’s most reliable source of profit, has become its biggest problem, creating an obstacle to CEO Oliver Blume’s restructuring plans at Europe’s largest automaker
Less than four years after its record-breaking stock market debut, Porsche has become a symbol of the problems facing the entire group: the company has lost its leading position in what was once a profitable Chinese market and suffered losses because of costly miscalculations during the transition to electric vehicles.
On Monday, thousands of workers protested against cuts at car plants across Germany, and this crisis extends beyond Porsche and the rest of Volkswagen’s sprawling empire, reflecting how Germany’s automotive sector is coming under pressure from Chinese competitors and U.S. tariffs.
On Friday, Volkswagen issued another profit warning, linking it to a €6 billion write-down on its 75% stake in Porsche - just weeks after approving extensive job cuts as part of the largest restructuring in the group’s 89-year history.
The write-down, which followed a €2.7 billion impairment a year earlier, points to a lack of proper oversight at Volkswagen, Jefferies analysts wrote, noting that, in their words, these were "endless surprises related to putting things in order."
Volkswagen attributed the write-down to poorer financial forecasts for Porsche, which made a high-profile stock market debut in 2022 in one of the largest IPOs on the continent in recent years.
In an internal memo seen by Reuters, Porsche CEO Michael Leiters stressed that the company remains committed to its medium-term profitability target of between 10% and 15%.
However, looking ahead, the company’s withdrawal from China, where it has reduced the number of dealerships, and pressure on its U.S. business from tariffs are raising questions about sales volumes.
Porsche has reportedly been going through difficult times for years, and Blume, who is leading the sports-car brand until the end of 2025, will oversee it during a crucial downturn while simultaneously serving as CEO of the group.

European children could face almost twice as much extreme fire weather: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:13:34 UTC
04:13:34 KST

Aysu Bicer
21 September 2026•Update: 21 September 2026
European children born in 2025 could face almost twice as much extreme fire weather during their lifetimes as those born in 1950, according to a new study published in the journal Environmental Research Letters on Monday.
Researchers found that, under current climate policies, a child born in Europe in 2025 could experience three more years of extreme fire-conducive weather than someone born 75 years earlier.
The increase is expected to be greatest in the Mediterranean, where children born in 2025 could face five additional years of extreme fire weather compared with people born during the post-war baby boom.
The study examined 21 climate scenarios, ranging from 1.5°C to 3.5°C (2.7°F to 6.3°F) of global warming by the end of the century. It defined extreme fire weather as days with conditions more severe than the worst 5% recorded during the 1985–2014 reference period.
Under current policies, which are projected to result in about 2.6°C (4.7°F) of warming, children born today are expected to experience 84% more exposure to extreme fire weather than those born in 1950.
The researchers estimated that 86% of this rise would be caused by climate change, with the remaining 14% linked to increased life expectancy.
Hot, dry, and windy conditions allow fires to spread rapidly and burn more intensely. The study notes these conditions have been exacerbated by more than a century of fossil fuel pollution, during which Europe has warmed at roughly twice the global average rate.
If global warming were limited to 1.5°C (2.7°F), children born in 2025 would experience 1.3 fewer years of extreme fire weather over their lifetimes compared with the current-policy scenario.
These findings come as Europe faces increasingly severe wildfire conditions, particularly across the Mediterranean region.

"And when it benefits the Nordic countries and security in the Arctic region, it also benefits NATO and Europe."
Since returning to the White House in January 2025, Trump has repeatedly insisted that the United States needs to control Greenland for strategic reasons, alarming NATO ally Denmark and sparking fierce pushback from the alliance.
According to Washington, the agreement ensures that China and Russia will not be able to establish military bases in Greenland or carry out sensitive investments there without its consent.
"This is something we have agreed on with the Americans for a very, very long time: the Arctic region, the North Atlantic, constitute an important defence zone for all members of the NATO alliance," Frederiksen said.

Thirteen-year-old surfer breaking records as first Indigenous world champ

Thirteen-year-old surfer Leihani Zoric breaks record as first Indigenous world champ
Leihani Zoric almost didn't compete in El Salvador, but now the 13-year-old is the youngest International Surfing Association (ISA) Under 18 World Junior Champion in history.
"When I went over there, I was extremely sick," Zoric told ABC Weekend Breakfast.
"I wasn't even going to go, my mum and dad were like, 'Leihani don't go, you're that sick'."
But the teenager was committed.
"I was like, 'no, I'm going to go. I believe that I can go all the way'," she told her parents.
And all the way she went, using visualisation to help her through.
"I wrote it down about 1,000 times [and] I said to myself, 'I'm going to become this year's Under 18 ISA gold medallist'," Zoric said.
"So, when it happened, I was like, oh my God, this is crazy."
Across more than a week of competition, Zoric was part of a 12-strong Australian team that went head-to-head with the world's best junior surfers.
She competed three age divisions above her own, to take out the title.
"It feels amazing," Zoric said.
"I'm really proud of myself for all my hard work and effort I've put in, and all the people that have helped me along the way."
It comes after a stand-out year so far, which includes winning the Junior Girls and Open Women's divisions at the 2026 Indigenous Surfing Titles.
She's now back home not only as a World Champion, but a history maker.
And she's taking it all in her stride, with a maturity that's beyond her years.
"I'm just so grateful to have been able to go to El Salvador and represent my culture and my country as best as I can," she said.
Creating a proud history
Zoric, from Byron Bay in northern New South Wales, is also the first Indigenous world champion surfer at any level.
"I'm really proud to have represented my Yued mob over in Western Australia," she said.
"We have such important history in our culture and I feel like [that] has really shaped me as a person."
Zoric first got a feel for surfing at two days old, when her dad put her on a surfboard in the shallows at Broken Head.
From then on, she just loved the water.
She takes inspiration from Soli Bailey, the first pro surfer to compete under the Aboriginal flag in the World Surfing League, and Cathy Freeman.
"Having those people inspire me has definitely made me want to be like them one day," she said.
Along with looking up to others, Zoric wants to be a positive role model herself.
When she's not in the water, she's busy creating connection, with things like Lei's Lu'au, a community day celebrating girls and women in surfing.
"I hope that I inspire, not just as an athlete, but being a good person and always caring about others, being encouraging and just having a positive attitude all the time," she said.
"Bringing people up and lifting their spirits and attitudes and just [making] them feel like they belong here in this world.
"Because everybody is important and special in their own unique ways."
Locana Cullen (Under 16 men's) and Lucy Darragh (Under 16 women's) also claimed individual golds at the World Junior Championships, with Australia winning three out of the four divisions.
The Australians also won their third consecutive team gold at the event.

Trump’s approval rating hits record low amid Iran war, economy fallout
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:10:52 UTC
04:10:52 KST

Trump approval rating hits career low of 32% amid Iran war, high costs
United States President Donald Trump’s approval rating has fallen to 32 percent – the lowest of his political career – as his fellow Republicans soured on his handling of the cost of living amid the unpopular Iran war, a new Reuters/Ipsos poll found.
The four-day poll, which closed on Sunday, showed 73 percent of Republicans approved of Trump’s job performance, down from 82 percent in a Reuters/Ipsos poll a week earlier. His overall approval was 35 percent then.
Trump returned to the White House in January 2025 on promises to tame inflation and end foreign wars. In a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted in the hours after he was first sworn in, he enjoyed a 47 percent approval rating.
Just 17 percent of respondents in the new poll approved of his handling of the cost of living – the top issue. Americans say it will determine how they vote in the November 3 midterm elections, when Trump’s Republicans are defending narrow congressional majorities.
Dissatisfaction among Republicans has been growing since Trump launched the war on Iran in February, which has pushed gasoline and diesel prices sharply higher. Now for the first time, Republicans who disapprove of Trump’s handling of the cost of living outnumber those who give him a thumbs up – 51 percent to 44 percent.
Trump said on Wednesday that the United States is “hopefully toward the end” of its war with Iran, raising the prospect of renewed diplomacy even as fighting continues in Yemen.
However, Tehran has not confirmed that direct negotiations with Washington have resumed.
The Reuters/Ipsos poll was conducted online and gathered 1,277 responses from US adults nationwide. It had a margin of error of three percentage points.

Why younger Australians are facing a tough economic future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:07:06 UTC
04:07:06 KST

analysis
Intergenerational Report shows younger Australians face tough economic future
Ask any soothsayer. Forecasting is a mug's game.
It is difficult enough to predict what will happen next month, let alone 40 years from now.
Regardless, for the past quarter of a century, Australian governments have sought to project where the nation is heading and predict the challenges and opportunities that may present themselves every five or so years.
They're rarely correct. But that's hardly the point. In many ways, it is just as instructive to figure out why previous forecasts missed the mark, delivering valuable insights into how best to approach the future.
This latest report, the seventh since 2002, has arrived at a seminal moment in history.
Loading...
There has been not been such disharmony and distrust between the superpowers for almost a century.
The first European war since 1945 has not only pitted Russia against the US and Europe; it has caused a growing schism in the NATO alliance, driven in large part by a capricious US president with little regard for the institutions that have underpinned Western democracy.
That's been exacerbated by a calamitous war in the Middle East that has reignited an energy crisis and acted as a catalyst for a looming global economic crisis.
The US dollar's longstanding position as the global reserve currency has been damaged by America's rapidly expanding debt and its use of financial sanctions, while its decision to punish trading partners has caused widespread discontent.
That, in turn, has ended a half-century-long decline in interest rates. Money is now likely to be more expensive as defence-oriented nations compete with industry — particularly the artificial intelligence giants — for funds.
Growing old not so gracefully
What will Australia look like in 40 years?
At an estimated 40 million, the population will be much bigger but much older, and the nation will be more indebted and have what increasingly appears to be a permanent budget deficit.
Demographics play a vital role in shaping an economy.
A country with an aging population has a smaller proportion of workers to shoulder the cost of looking after those in their advancing years. That squeezes national tax income, and there is a greater cost burden associated with higher health care and aged care.
And for those still working? More likely, higher tax bills.
Like many developed countries, Australia has low and declining fertility rates. According to the projections in the report, more Australians will die than be born in 2066.
As Treasurer Jim Chalmers pointed out at a speech yesterday at the Australian National University, many advanced economies have already surpassed that point, and most of the rest are expected to within the next few decades.
The population, however, will continue to grow as new arrivals make up for the downturn in Australian births, but at a more modest pace than in the past 20 years, as immigration has become a hot political issue.
As this graph from the 2026 Intergenerational Report shows, without immigration, the population would shrink, creating a whole new raft of problems.
Add to this volatile mix a new technology that looks set to revolutionise the workplace and perhaps even life as we now know it.
Exactly what artificial intelligence will deliver is anyone's guess. The more optimistic among us hope for higher living standards.
The government hopes it will help turn around Australia's chronic productivity growth problem, which has declined to zero. In the document, Treasury estimates a dramatic recovery in productivity as the technology weaves its way through Australian workplaces.
Many economists are not so sure.
How we created a productivity crisis
Population and productivity are closely intertwined.
Remember all those stories about Australia's "miracle economy" from just a few years ago? A quarter of a century without a recession.
But it was all a thimble-and-pea trick.
For more than 20 years, governments of both persuasions papered over the cracks in our economy by importing people.
It made it appear as though our economy was on a one-way trip to nirvana. But what the pollies didn't do was invest in infrastructure to cope with such a monumental and sudden burst in population.
And now we are paying the price, with cities that barely function, with inadequate public transport, health systems and schools.
In addition, our businesses held off on investment, preferring instead to dole out profits to shareholders and push stock prices higher.
Housing shortages, coupled with tax arrangements that diverted investment funds into suburban house-flipping ventures instead of productive activities, pushed up the cost of putting a roof over your head and drained household incomes.
The data was there all along. The GDP pie kept getting bigger, right through from the first Intergenerational Report in 2002. But divide it by the growing number of people, and you suddenly realise that everyone's share of the pie was shrinking.
Investment in technology and infrastructure per worker has declined. Little wonder we have a productivity problem.
But unless we fix it, our living standards are likely to stall and possibly fall.
Why younger generations are losing faith
During the past three decades, Australian households have grown richer.
On average, real net household wealth has grown from $500,000 in 1993 to more than $1.3 million in 2019/20.
But dig down into the data, and it becomes clear that those gains aren't evenly shared and that younger generations have missed out.
This graph from the report shows that those born in the 1950s did substantially better than those from the 1940s. Those born in the 1960s did even better.
But for those born from the 1970s on, the gains were smaller, if there were any at all.
That's because older households have ridden a property boom unlike any other in history in terms of longevity.
Those born in later decades were forced to buy in at prices that had grown twice as fast as earnings since the turn of the century.
Older generations also have seen their wealth buoyed by maturing superannuation balances and soaring stock markets.
"Gross housing wealth almost tripled in real terms between 1994 and 2020, while superannuation wealth grew five-fold," the report notes.
That disturbing trend was a key reason the government decided in the May budget to tighten the tax breaks around property investment.
It has also committed to strengthening the superannuation system to ensure an aging Australia will help pay for itself rather than rely solely on a publicly funded pension system.
The Australian superannuation scheme has become a focal point for other countries grappling with the same demographic issues and will help curtail spending pressure into the future.
We may be better placed than other nations to handle the upcoming challenges. But it won't be easy.

Dating app safety shouldn't be left to women, researchers say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:05:50 UTC
04:05:50 KST

Dating app harms fuel calls to extend digital duty of care to platforms
In short:
Almost all women surveyed in a new Australian study reported encountering harmful behaviour on dating apps, with many taking their own precautions to stay safe.
Researchers say platforms should do more to prevent systemic risks as the federal government considers a digital duty of care.
What's next?
Consultation on Labor's proposed digital duty of care closes on Tuesday, with advocates saying it has capacity to curb online abuse.
Women are being forced to act as their own safety system on dating apps where experiences of sexual harassment, manipulation and controlling behaviours are widespread, a study has found.
Australian researchers found 99 per cent of heterosexual women surveyed had encountered at least one harmful behaviour on a dating app in the previous three months.
Unsolicited explicit messages, attempts to monitor activity, love bombing, negging and gaslighting are common experiences on dating apps, according to the study released on Tuesday by the Minderoo Foundation-funded Behaviour Insights Team (BIT).
Women reported routinely screening profiles for warning signs, withholding identifying information and carefully managing interactions to protect themselves from potential harm.
These accounts have fuelled calls to ensure a proposed digital duty of care was implemented to require online services to tackle systemic risks.
Researchers have argued the scale of the problem showed women could not be expected to manage the risks alone, with dating platforms better placed to prevent harm before it occurred.
Women coaching each other to stay safe
Brisbane resident Rebecca Wilson, 33, said her harmful dating app experiences have included receiving "completely unsolicited" and "aggressively sexual" messages, photos and videos.
Ms Wilson said she was also once stalked by a man she had met via an app.
"We went on one date. I said to him, 'Look I'm just not interested anymore', and he didn't get the message," she said.
"Weeks later he kept popping up at the same places as me … following me around.
"He touched me at a bar right in front of my friends when it was clearly unsolicited."
With only minimal information on the man, Ms Wilson said she could not easily report him to authorities.
One issue was that using the "block" feature on the app meant she lost the ability to collect identifying material to progress a complaint.
"There's no way of being able to know the identity of who you were talking to," Ms WIlson said.
Ms Wilson said she and her friends have "coached" each other through how to navigate online dating safely.
"The current mechanisms are really just not enough on these apps," she said.
Harmful behaviour 'normalised'
The most common harmful behaviours on dating apps were psychological and emotional, which were encountered by 95 per cent of the 1,008 women across Australia surveyed for the BIT study.
About 89 per cent experienced monitoring and surveillance activity and 88 per cent reported being sent unsolicited sexual images and videos, and being pressured and manipulated into sending sexual content.
Almost six in 10 women reported fear-based controlling behaviour, including threats of physical harm. Of those, only about 22 per cent reported those threats to the platforms.
Among women who made reports to platforms generally, about 19 per cent felt their complaint was "barely" or "not at all" taken seriously, while 64 per cent said they were taken at least "somewhat" seriously.
Lead researcher Karen Tindall said the findings showed there was a need for greater efforts by the platforms to tackle "genuinely preventable risk".
"Right now, a lot of these behaviours are so normalised that women blame themselves or they think they are overreacting," she said.
"This data and research should validate women's experience and should shift the conversation toward fixing the system itself."
Dr Tindall said there were features built for safety that could lead to harm, such as preventing screenshots to prevent against image-based abuse.
"But that also removes a woman's ability to document what happened," she said.
"I'm not saying those safety features should be removed, but it means that safety features need to be tested for how they will be worked around, and whether they will work as intended."
Duty would shift responsibility onto platforms
The findings have been released as the federal government consults on its proposed digital duty of care, which is intended to require services to identify and mitigate foreseeable risks rather than relying on users to report harm after the fact.
The draft duty for adults could apply to dating platforms on which users have faced serious abuse, stalking, sexual violence or image-based abuse.
It would mean services were required to identify and mitigate systemic risks that could enable such conduct.
While the initial debate has focused on social media, the proposed duty would apply more broadly across digital services, including dating and messaging apps, online games, search engines and AI services.
Minderoo Foundation gender equality executive director Jacqueline Joudo Larsen said a digital duty of care could prevent harm and protect Australians.
"It is the single biggest lever to curb the reach, scale and speed at which abuse is occurring by shifting responsibility from individuals to companies that are designing and operating online platforms," she said.
"This is a standard that we hold other sectors to and it should be no different for the online space."
Ms Larsen said technology had "transformed" how people met, connected and built relationships.
"Those benefits are very meaningful," she said.
"But safety cannot be the price women pay for participation.
"This is a design problem that's entirely preventable."
Ms Larsen said Australia could be a leader in tech safety and, if it was serious about ending sexual and domestic violence, that was an "opportunity we can't squander".
Labor's proposal under scrutiny
Submissions on Labor's proposal close on Tuesday and draft legislation will likely be introduced next month.
The Coalition has criticised the draft, primarily due to concerns over discretionary powers allowing the minister to add additional "harms" for children and "serious harms" for adults.
In a social media post shared by Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, the Coalition dubbed the idea the "Albo-rithm" and suggested the government would seek to censor online spaces.
But Communications Minister Anika Wells has repeatedly said the intent of the rule making power was about acting with "urgency" if new threats, such as apps that allowed users to "nudify" photos, arose online.
"We think this is a sensible measure to try and deal with these emerging harms that are coming online every single day," she said earlier this month.
The discretion in the bill for adding additional harms would be disallowable by the Senate at any time, but Labor might have to make some changes to their plan in order to secure the Greens' support for the draft bill.
In another submission to the draft legislation, the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman has described the reforms as a "rare opportunity" to build trust and accountability into the digital economy from the outset.
Ombudsman Cynthia Gebert said trust would not be built by hoping companies did the right thing and urged the government to consider an independent external dispute mechanism for when system failures occurred.
"Everyday Australians need someone to turn to for support holding big tech companies accountable when they get things wrong and we stand ready to help," she said.
The submission said an external complaints system would provide a "practical avenue" for Australians to resolve issues such as restoration of account access, ensuring choices about algorithms are implemented and reconsidering incorrect decisions.

Hungary seeks US sanctions exemption over Russian energy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:04:52 UTC
04:04:52 KST

Hungary seeks US sanctions exemption over Russian energy
Hungary’s new government has asked for an exemption from US sanctions targeting Russian energy buyers, despite pledging to reduce the country’s dependence on supplies from Moscow.
The request comes after US President Donald Trump signed a sweeping expansion of sanctions against Russia into law on Friday. The legislation, criticized by the Kremlin as an “unfriendly move,” allows tariffs of up to 100% on goods from major buyers of Russian oil and gas, while providing for exemptions on US national security grounds.
The Hungarian Foreign Ministry approached the US State Department over the potential impact of the legislation before it was adopted, according to local media reports on Monday. The issue was also raised in Washington last week by Marton Hajdu, chairman of the Hungarian parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee and a member of the ruling Tisza party.
Hajdu said he told Republican lawmakers that Tisza was aware of the “risks and disadvantages of dependence on Russian energy,” while asking them to help exempt Hungary from the measures.
Washington reportedly said the legislation could apply to Hungary only after its existing US sanctions exemption expires on November 21 and if it is not renewed. The exemption was secured under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban.
Tisza pledged during its election campaign to end Hungary’s dependence on Russian energy by 2035, describing it as a “systemic risk.” The new pro-EU government under Prime Minister Peter Magyar has also described Moscow as a “threat.”
The policy marks a shift from Orban, who resisted EU efforts to curb Russian energy imports and secured exemptions for landlocked Hungary. He maintained that cutting Europe off from comparatively cheap Russian energy would damage the bloc’s economy.
Hungary remains heavily reliant on Russian supplies, which accounted for around 90% of its crude oil in 2025, according to S&P Global. Much of the oil has traditionally arrived through the Soviet-built Druzhba pipeline, where flows were halted for nearly three months earlier this year after Ukraine claimed its section had been damaged by a Russian strike, a claim disputed by Moscow. Hungary and Slovakia accused Kiev of deliberately delaying the restart for political reasons.
The EU has sharply reduced Russian energy purchases since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022. Russia’s share of the bloc’s gas imports fell from 45% in 2021 to 12% in 2025, while Russian crude dropped from 27% to around 2%. Brussels plans to phase out Russian LNG by the end of 2026 and pipeline gas by late 2027.
Moscow has rejected Western sanctions as “illegal,” saying that they have backfired on EU consumers. Russia has redirected much of its exports to other markets.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has acknowledged that the EU “cannot remain an industrial powerhouse” if energy prices remain structurally high.

Ukraine Sets New Hospital Rules Amid New Two-Level Air Raid Alert System
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:04:29 UTC
04:04:29 KST

Led by Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi, Ukraine’s government has ordered hospitals to continue life-saving procedures – such as surgery, resuscitation and intensive care – even during a red-level air threat, when patients and medical personnel must otherwise move to shelters immediately.
Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi announced the new rules on Monday, Sept. 10, building on the two-level air threat system unveiled earlier this month.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Emergency medical services will operate without interruption. Patients with urgent conditions will be admitted regardless of the threat level,” Koretskyi said.
Hospitals to operate under both yellow and red air alerts
The new system was imposed due to Russia’s increasingly changing attack tactics, designed to provide the public with more clarity over the level of danger while allowing parts of the economy to keep operating during less severe threats.
The yellow alert is primarily used for incoming drone strikes, while the red alert signals ballistic and other missile threats, alongside mass attacks.
The new measures announced by Koretskyi require hospitals to provide medical care, dispense medications and accommodate patients inside shelters or other designated safe areas.
Under a yellow-level alert, medical facilities will continue operating, but must provide employees, patients and visitors with unrestricted access to shelters.
Medical personnel and patients must immediately move to shelters under a red-level alert. However, procedures that cannot be safely interrupted will continue, and patients who cannot be relocated will be provided with treatment in the safest available areas of the facility.
EU Extends Russia Sanctions for 3 Years, Delists 2 Oligarchs
Emergency dispatch centers will continue to accept calls and ambulance crews will respond to patients regardless of the threat level, Koretskyi said.
The government also instructed authorities to strengthen protections around operating rooms, intensive care units, maternity wards and admissions departments.
The measure additionally covers rooms containing backup power supplies and critical medical equipment.
Metro running through drone alerts as well
Beyond the hospitals, the government recommended earlier in September that Kyiv keep its metro operating normally during yellow-level alerts.
The capital should also increase surface public transportation when necessary, allowing people to reach workplaces, metro stations and hospitals despite ongoing drone threats.
Kyiv shortens night curfew
Kyiv authorities have adopted a new curfew as well, shortening the restriction by one hour.
The curfew now runs from 1 a.m. to 5 a.m., instead of starting at midnight.
Since taking office amid a broader cabinet reshuffle on July 16, Koretskyi introduced measures aimed at reinforcing Ukraine’s resilience, including a winter preparedness plan centered on energy systems, fuel reserves and physical protection for critical infrastructure.
Ahead of the Sept. 1 school reopening, the government also introduced new security measures requiring local authorities to protect children by limiting large ceremonies in high-risk areas and ensuring rapid access to shelters.

Lib Dems reject ‘discriminatory and unworkable’ EHRC guidance on transgender people
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
18:58:51 UTC
03:58:51 KST

The Liberal Democrats have rejected official guidance by the equalities watchdog on how organisations should implement the supreme court ruling on transgender people, calling it “discriminatory and unworkable”.
The motion, passed overwhelmingly at the party’s annual conference in Brighton, makes the Lib Dems the first of the big three parties in parliament to call for a new approach to implementing last year’s ruling that the legal definition of a woman is based on biological sex only. The Greens have previously done so.
Formal guidance from the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC), put out in May, is intended to tell service providers and others how they must balance the rights of trans people with the requirement for some spaces to be single sex.
It has attracted criticism for being a de facto bar on trans people being in many public spaces by setting out that single-sex toilets and changing rooms must exclude transgender men and women when gender-neutral facilities are not always available.
The motion to the conference called the EHRC’s code “discriminatory and unworkable”, saying it “places an undue burden on service providers”. It calls for a revised code, plus a dedicated cross-party parliamentary committee “to review how the law should better protect trans people’s rights”.
Proposing the motion, the party member Lucas North condemned the EHRC guidance and noted a rise in anti-trans hate crimes. They added: “The rights of women and the rights of trans people do not have to be placed on opposite sides of a manufactured culture war.”
Another speaker for the motion, Rebecca Jones, said that as a trans woman she was “tired of being a culture war prop”.
She said: “You now fear using public spaces. You fear anyone that looks at you too much in case they hate trans people enough that they put you at risk. All whilst your government repeats the words ‘dignity’ and ‘respect’, whilst doing everything in their power to ensure trans people do not have them.”
But the councillor Mark Johnston, from Reigate in Surrey, said the motion would distract the party from the “realism” needed to ensure Nigel Farage did not become PM: “That realism means accepting the supreme court determination last year is unassailable.
“Are we going back to our constituencies to prepare for government, or are we going back to our bedrooms to prepare for irrelevance?”
Zoe Hollowood, a party activist, said the party should accept the supreme court ruling: “If we pass this motion, we are telling women we think they are second-class citizens … This policy is totally out of touch with both public sentiment and public priorities.”
The mood in the conference hall was strongly in favour of the motion, which was passed easily on a show of hands.
Earlier in the day the party leader, Ed Davey, told the BBC he broadly supported the motion, calling the EHRC guidance not “fit for purpose”.

18:58:41 UTC
03:58:41 KST

Escalating attacks on infrastructure by Russia and Ukraine are leaving civilians increasingly vulnerable as winter approaches, UN investigators have warned, raising concerns about a repeat of last winter’s suffering.
The UN’s Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine said on Monday both sides had intensified long-range strikes against civilian sites, including energy, industrial and port infrastructure, as well as ships in the Black Sea.
The commission said Russian attacks during the winter of 2025-2026 caused prolonged power and heating outages as temperatures fell to minus 20°C, leaving millions of civilians without adequate heating.
“Ukrainian authorities recorded cold-related deaths and injuries,” commission chair Erik Mose told the UN Human Rights Council.
The commission also voiced concern over reports of Ukrainian attacks on infrastructure inside Russia and Russian-controlled areas of Ukraine, saying they indicated rising civilian casualties and damage to civilian objects. It said it had been unable to investigate those reports because it lacked access.
“Continued attacks on energy infrastructure are making living conditions increasingly unbearable for civilians, and we are concerned that the coming winter will be more difficult to endure,” Mose said.
The findings came after US President Donald Trump called last week for an energy truce between Russia and Ukraine, although neither side has confirmed it will participate.
Children, foreign recruits
The commission also reported on Russia’s imposition of what it described as patriotic education in occupied areas, including military training for Ukrainian children from the age of 14.
It said children were taught to handle weapons and carry out military drills.
Investigators also examined the recruitment of foreign nationals to fight for Russia, saying some had been deceived or coerced into joining the Russian armed forces.
Mose said agents and intermediaries had recruited people from various countries with promises of civilian jobs before they were allegedly compelled to sign contracts with Russia’s defence ministry.
Many recruits did not understand Russian or the contracts they signed and were subsequently sent to the front lines in Ukraine, he said.
The commission said some were killed, wounded, captured or went missing, leaving families searching for relatives from abroad.

Eli Lilly CEO Dave Ricks told CNBC on Monday that one-third of new GLP-1 pill patients are taking the drugmaker's Foundayo, as the company tries to catch up to a lead in the space established by rival Novo.
In an exclusive interview, he said the company's share of the oral market is growing week over week.
"We're confident long term" about Lilly's place in the pill segment, Ricks said, especially as the company plans to launch Foundayo in more international markets in the coming months.
Ricks spoke with CNBC in front of the roughly 240 acres of land that will eventually host Lilly's $6.5 billion manufacturing facility at Generation Park in Houston, Texas. The company on Monday broke ground on the upcoming site nearly a year after first announcing it, and said it expects the plant to be operational by 2030.
The facility will most notably produce Lilly's closely watched GLP-1 pill for obesity, Foundayo, which entered the U.S. market in April.
But the plant will be responsible for manufacturing the active ingredients for Lilly's other small-molecule medicines across several disease areas, such as cardiometabolic health, oncology, immunology and neuroscience.
Ricks' comments and the groundbreaking came as Novo shares fell after the company's long-term strategy failed to assuage investor concerns about its ability to compete with Lilly in the obesity and diabetes market. While Novo beat Lilly to releasing a pill, Lilly said in August that it held about a 61% share in the overall market in the second quarter.
The production site is part of a string of new investments Lilly has funneled into reshoring manufacturing across the U.S. over the last year. In February 2025, Lilly committed to spending an additional $27 billion to build four new facilities, including the Houston site, in part to build goodwill with President Donald Trump.
But Lilly has also emphasized manufacturing capacity as a key competitive advantage against its main rival Novo alongside its drug portfolio. Since 2020, the company has committed more than $50 billion to expanding its manufacturing network, positioning itself to meet growing demand for obesity and diabetes treatments while supporting future product launches.
Demand for Foundayo is rising in the U.S. The company said in August that the pill booked $98 million in sales for the second quarter — its first three-month period on the market. Medicare's new landmark coverage of obesity drugs, which began in July, is expected to open up more access to the pill and Lilly's blockbuster weight loss drug Zepbound.

World Food Programme ramps up response in Yemen as hunger fears escalate, official says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
18:54:09 UTC
03:54:09 KST

World Food Programme ramps up response in Yemen as hunger fears escalate, official says
UNITED NATIONS, Sept 21 - The acting chief of the World Food Programme on Monday said the agency was ramping up its response to the escalating crisis in Yemen, where Houthi fighters seized the country's Red Sea coast, displacing tens of thousands of people.
Nearly 700 people have been killed and thousands injured, according to the UN, as the group made their advance. More than 120,000 Yemenis have fled their homes within Yemen, and thousands more by boat across the Red Sea to Africa.
"We are stepping up. We have supported around 60,000 people with hot meals and food commodities and we are building up our pipeline to respond to hundreds of thousands more," WFP Acting Executive Director Carl Skau told Reuters during the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
The escalation in Yemen comes as more than 18 million people, roughly half the population, face acute food insecurity and some 2.2 million children under age 5 are acutely malnourished, according to the WFP data.
Camps for the displaced are "already overstretched and our operations there are underfunded," Skau said. "People are not eating enough, there is no healthcare, and these are the places where you now see tens of thousands of newly arrived people with nothing, and having had their lives disrupted."
The surge by the Iran-backed group this month extended the wider Middle East conflict to a new theater and further threatened global energy supplies, resulting in a spike in oil prices, upending maritime trade in the region.
"Ninety percent of the food in Yemen is imported. So when ports are not working or when airports are not working, that's having an impact on food security in Yemen," said Skau, who recently visited the country.
Skau also warned that the agency was unable to operate in the Houthi-controlled areas as the group continues to occupy UN offices after it confiscated its assets and detained dozens of UN staff.
"Our offices in the north are occupied by the Houthi de facto authorities, and our assets are still confiscated, so under such circumstances it's very difficult for us to operate," said Skau.
The Swedish diplomat said the organization, the largest UN agency by budget, was severely underfunded and forced to cut back on life-saving aid. He said he would push for more funding at the diplomatic jamboree with nearly 130 heads of state visiting New York this week. REUTERS

UK brings first charges over the 1994 Rwanda genocide
Vincent Brown, 65, is accused of inciting and aiding murders of Tutsis after seven-year British investigation
Prosecutors said on Monday they had brought the first-ever charges in the UK against a man for his alleged role in the 1994 Rwanda genocide, after a complex seven-year investigation.
Vincent Brown, 65, was arrested and charged on Monday with one count of being an ancillary to genocide and six offences of aiding crimes against humanity in Rwanda, prosecutors and the London police said.
“He is alleged to have directed and incited acts of murder and genocide carried out by others” against the Tutsi, said Frank Ferguson, head of the Crown Prosecution Service’s special crime and counterterrorism division, in the first ever such charges in the UK.
Some 800,000 people, mostly Tutsis and moderate Hutus, were beaten, shot, or hacked to death with machetes in 100 days of slaughter.
