A bored-looking Farage unveils a new Welsh leader – he still seems fond of the old one | John Crace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
17:08:43 UTC
02:08:43 KST

Twenty-five or so Reform members of the Senedd were lined up against a wall. Almost as if they were in a police identification parade. Reform’s need to find a new leader in Wales is becoming habit-forming.
First, Nathan Gill was banged up for 10 and a half years on eight counts of taking £40K in bribes to make statements in support of Russia. Easily done. Who among us hasn’t been tempted by the Kremlin? And then last week, Dan Thomas chose to stand down after being arrested on suspicion of assault and coercive behaviour, leaving the Welsh leadership spot open once more. He denies the allegations.
It’s almost as if there’s a pattern emerging. That the job of Reform leader in Wales is somehow cursed. Otherwise law-abiding men and women suddenly find themselves accused of all sorts of things. So much so that it’s now the job that no one really wants.
Yet politics abhors a vacuum, and someone has to do the job. So it was a decidedly grumpy-looking Nigel Farage who turned up in Cardiff on Monday morning to pretend to be interested in announcing the next Reform Senedd leader. Perhaps he reckoned he had better things to do.
The event – if you can call a five-minute announcement that – was supposed to kick off at 11.45. Nige was booked on the 12.18 back to Paddington and had hoped to be in London for a late lunch. No champagne and oysters. There were no undercover reporters posing as Americans trying to make a potentially illegal donation this time. Instead, there was a 20-minute delay.
Nige really was going through the motions. He was thrilled by the results in Wales at the May elections, he began. He didn’t sound thrilled. Though that could be because Reform has been shedding support in Wales – as elsewhere – ever since. They have lost seven points in the opinion polls over the course of the summer and are looking less and less likely to challenge Plaid Cymru.
“Dan Thomas has been doing a brilliant job,” Nige continued. “I am sorry for his personal difficulties.” This was just weird. Almost as if he hadn’t even considered what Thomas had been alleged to have done. Yeah, Dan. Great bloke. Brilliant Reform leader. Always buys his round in the pub. It’s just unfortunate that he’s been arrested on suspicion of assault and coercive control. But it’s no big deal. He’ll soon be sorted.
Nige doubled down, calling the arrest a “bump in the road”. Not a word of sympathy or support for the person he is accused of having assaulted or subjected to coercive control. Besides, he was clear that Dan would come back soon. There would always be a welcome in the Reform valleys for Dan. We all need someone like Dan.
After the Song for Dan, Nige made the briefest of introductions to the new leader. Best to skip over the bit where almost half the Reform members of the Senedd had preferred a different candidate. The party in Wales is a hotbed of backstabbing. Not literally, mind. The job was going to Helen Jenner, the former deputy leader and Nige’s old-time Ukip mucker. “I’ve known her for years and I trust her,” he said.
Helen mumbled her thanks and said she would build on the good work done by others. It wasn’t clear if Dan would take over from her if he is cleared of the allegations, which he denies. It sounded like a possibility. In which case, I guess Dan might then only be keeping the seat warm for Nathan when he gets early release in 2031. You have to admire Reform’s loyalty.
And their amnesia. Because you also can’t help wondering if Nige is beginning to lose the plot somewhat. How else do you explain his recent Substack post in which he claimed that “British politics is awash with dirty money”? I mean, he’s obviously not entirely wrong. But why would he want to draw attention to it when questions remain over money received by Reform and figures associated with the party?
There’s the £40K that went to Gill from the Russians. There was the apparent eagerness on the part of Dan Jukes and James Orr to accept overseas donations. A meeting at which Nige was present. Though not listening, apparently. There’s the dosh from Ben Delo, a man convicted of failing to comply with anti-money-laundering legislation in the US.
There’s the cash from Posh George and his mum that is somewhat opaque to say the least. There are the police and parliamentary investigations. The £5m gift that went undeclared. With the best will in the world, none of this seems the model of transparency. But what do I know? And it’s good to know that Reform operates in a world where any transgressions are so readily forgiven.

Russia's election is over. Could mobilization be next?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
17:08:27 UTC
02:08:27 KST

Russia's election is over. Could mobilization be next?
The skyscrapers of the Moscow International Business Center are seen through barbed wire on the opposite bank of the Moscow River in Moscow, Russia, on April 25, 2026. (Contributor/Getty Images)
Nobody expected Russia's parliamentary election to wrest power from President Vladimir Putin, with preliminary results on Sept. 21 showing the Kremlin-backed United Russia party winning once again with nearly 58% of the vote.
Instead, the question after the election is whether, when, and in what form the Kremlin will launch a new mobilization wave that Kyiv has warned could follow the vote — and which Russia may ultimately need to pursue its war objectives.
Russia remains committed to capturing all of Donetsk Oblast, and the Kremlin wants this accomplished by the end of 2026, while Russia's military has sought to push the deadline to March 2027, according to Ukrainian officials.
Either way, to sustain the campaign, Russia will require more manpower. Ukrainian intelligence says Russia's General Staff is prepared to mobilize around 300,000 personnel in 2026 and 2027 each.
These forces are in addition to roughly 400,000 people a year that Russia needs to recruit just to replenish its forces, a senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent.
Contract recruitment, meanwhile, has been slowing: around 234,000 people signed contracts between January and August this year, compared with roughly 260,000 over the same period in 2025.
But Moscow is also burning through manpower at roughly the same pace it can replace it. President Volodymyr Zelensky said in July that Russia had suffered nearly 225,500 casualties since the start of 2026.
Russia's total military casualties over the course of the full-scale invasion are estimated by Ukrainian authorities at around 1.6 million, including about 700,000 killed. The figures are difficult to verify independently, as neither side publishes its casualty data.
read also
A fragmented mobilization
Putin's first partial mobilization announcement in 2022 triggered the biggest domestic backlash against Russia's war and prompted hundreds of thousands of Russians to leave the country.
This time, people familiar with the matter expect a more fragmented process that combines pressure on reservists, continued contract recruitment, and other measures without the need for a mobilization announcement.
"They will look for half-measures and give each step a separate justification," said Artem Klyga, a lawyer and head of the legal department at the Movement of Conscientious Objectors, an exiled independent Russian NGO that helps Russian citizens to legally avoid conscription.
The Kremlin has flatly denied such plans. On Sept. 1, Putin called reports of a looming mobilization "nonsense," after spokesperson Dmitry Peskov on Aug. 25 had called them "fabricated stories" spread by Ukraine to destabilize Russia internally.
"Everything the authorities are doing is aimed at distancing themselves as much as possible from the word 'mobilization' and from the fear associated with it," Klyga said.
How visible the mobilization process becomes depends on its scale.
The Kremlin still has to decide on how much of the General Staff's request it is willing to approve, as well as on the timing, a Ukrainian defense sector source familiar with the issue told the Kyiv Independent on condition of anonymity.
"If the number is manageable, it could remain hidden. If it is significant, they will not be able to hide it," they said.
Once called up, new recruits would need around two to four weeks of basic training before they could join combat units, according to the source.
read also
Reservists could be first
In Russia, active reservists are a relatively small group within the broader military reserve. They are civilians who have signed contracts committing them to remain available to the Defense Ministry while continuing their normal civilian lives.
Since 2025, the Kremlin has broadened the use of Russia's active reserve, including deployments to protect critical infrastructure and counter drone attacks in their home regions.
Now there are signs of growing pressure on the group.
Klyga said reservists accounted for around 60% of requests for help his organization received this summer, up from the usual 20% to 30% — the highest share it has ever recorded.
"We were genuinely surprised," he said. "A lot of them are receiving [summonses] for the first time in many years, and they panic."
Beyond that contracted reserve, the inactive military reserve is much larger. Any man that completes Russia's 12-month compulsory military service, which can begin from the age of 18, enters the inactive military reserve and becomes eligible for mobilization, even at age 19.
In Ukraine, the main mobilization framework generally applies to military-liable men ages 25 to 60.
Russia is also better equipped today to enforce summonses than in 2022. Electronic notices are legally considered delivered after seven days, even if the recipient does not open them. Failure to appear can trigger restrictions on loans, driving rights, and property and vehicle transactions.
read also
Beyond reservists
The ongoing voluntary contract recruitment is likely to remain one of the main ways Russia replenishes its army.
The system already reaches men across age groups and social backgrounds: students, conscripts, older men, those facing financial hardship, foreigners, and prisoners.
"When we talk about mobilization, we artificially exclude a large group of men who are already being recruited for the war," Klyga said. "In other words, they have already reached everyone they could reach."
What is likely to change is the level of pressure.
Ukrainian military intelligence says Russia is preparing tighter control over military registration, new mechanisms for recruiting prisoners, and additional coercive measures.
Klyga said his organization had already begun seeing more cases of deception and coercion by the end of 2025.
One of the more striking examples came in June, when police and military recruitment officers jointly carried out raids to identify and detain men who had supposedly failed to register for military service in several cities of Russia's Penza region.
Direct mass violence is not the norm, Klyga said, but such raids may signal a shift toward a more coercive recruitment model.
"Next, the pressure could expand to unemployed people and those looking for work," he said.
read also
What does this mean for Ukraine
President Volodymyr Zelensky said most newly mobilized Russian troops would likely be sent either to reinforce Russia’s offensive in eastern Ukraine, particularly in Donetsk Oblast, or to create pressure from the north, including toward Kyiv and Chernihiv from Belarus.
In both cases, the aim would be to stretch Ukrainian defenses and weaken its position in the east.
Meanwhile, Ukraine faces a manpower crisis of its own. Presidential Office head Kyrylo Budanov said in August that the country needs to mobilize at least 30,000 people every month simply to sustain its current force. For a country with a far smaller population base than Russia, maintaining that pace is a much heavier burden.
While Russia retains advantages in manpower, artillery stocks, and ballistic missiles, Syrskyi said in June that Ukraine had gained the upper hand in the drone war, including in FPV drones as well as medium- and long-range strikes.
Ukraine also seeks to level the advantage in other technology fields.
Two domestically produced ballistic missiles are expected to enter service in the coming months, while Kyiv is working with European partners on the Freyja anti-ballistic missile system.
Mykhailo Samus, a Ukrainian military expert and director of the New Geopolitics Research Network, said Ukraine’s response should be to expand the areas where it can offset Russia’s numerical advantage.
"If the Russians want to use the bodies of their citizens instead of technology, that is their choice," he told the Kyiv Independent. "We need to continue developing technology, improve the effectiveness of army corps, create troop groupings, increase the number of drones, and develop robotics and autonomous systems."
"This is not the First World War. This is a war of technology."

A 21-year-old candidate for Russia’s antiwar Yabloko party documented her campaign for the St. Petersburg legislature
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
17:08:10 UTC
02:08:10 KST

A 21-year-old candidate for Russia’s antiwar Yabloko party documented her campaign for the St. Petersburg legislature
Russia’s elections are over, and Yabloko faced unprecedented pressure throughout them. The party’s federal list was removed from the ballot back in the summer, and its regional lists followed. Only one survived, in the Novgorod region. Yabloko candidates running for regional legislatures in single-member districts complained of pressure, and several were removed from the ballot. The outlet Bereg has published the diary of Marina Peslyak, a 21-year-old antiwar candidate for St. Petersburg’s Legislative Assembly who managed to defend her place on the ballot. For more than a month, Peslyak recorded the election commission’s absurd demands, pressure from law enforcement, and the everyday work of running a campaign. Meduza is translating the diary here.
Bereg shortened and lightly edited Peslyak’s diary and added a timeline of the pressure on Yabloko to her entries.
August 11, thirty-eight days until the election
The day before, on August 10, the Supreme Court removed Yabloko from the State Duma election. Yabloko would have been the only party on the ballot calling for a ceasefire with Ukraine as soon as possible.
The district election commission (DEC) got in touch: one person’s donation doesn’t meet legal requirements, even though he filled in all his details correctly. I’m annoyed. One more formality I have to deal with.
Every message from the commission is insanely stressful. I’m afraid they’ve found another reason to kick me off the ballot.
Spent two hours sorting things out with Sberbank — even the staff don’t know how to return a payment like this. But I got it done. It seems like a small thing, but after two hours on one transaction, you just want to shut everything down and not do anything else today.
In the evening, The New York Times reached out. They asked me to comment on my campaign, my motivation, and Yabloko’s list being thrown out. It’s a really strange feeling: a few hours ago I was dealing with the bank, and now the NYT is writing to me.
August 12
I arranged to speak with the NYT journalist, but I’m worried about the possible consequences. Yabloko’s headquarters ignored my question about whether I should agree to the interview.
I wouldn’t want to be answering for the whole party when I’m a candidate for the city legislature. I’m anxious. I want to speak honestly, but I keep thinking about where my personal views end and where I start speaking on behalf of the party.
Lyudmila Vasilyeva wrote to me. She’s asking how she can help.
Gave the interview. It seems like it went fine, but I still have the feeling that now I’m going to replay every sentence [and worry].
August 13
Woke up in the night with a panic attack, thinking I might have said too much in the interview. I’m scared they’ll kick me off the ballot. Scared law enforcement officers will break into my home. Scared for my mom and my sister, who are staying with me right now. At night it all felt completely real, but by morning it was clear how badly I’d worked myself up.
Still, I just have to get up and keep going. I’m writing to everyone who signed up to volunteer.
Talking with the BBC about filming a documentary on my campaign. I don’t even know yet what there is to film: there are hardly any people involved, there’s no money either, and I can’t even get the campaigning off the ground. It’s awkward: it’s supposed to be a film about a campaign, but there’s practically no active campaign.
August 14
Yabloko appealed the Supreme Court’s decision to bar it from the election.
Met with Yabloko’s people in my district, and we talked about our next steps — what we can pull off with the resources I have. For the first time in several days, I felt a little calmer. It’s starting to feel like we at least have some kind of plan.
Messaging volunteers, setting up a meeting. Late at night, I’m writing a post asking for donations. It’s a little awkward to ask people for money again, but without it there’s nothing to run this campaign on.
August 15
Police issued warnings against taking part in unauthorized rallies to several people who had come out to support Yabloko outside the Supreme Court in Moscow on August 10.
Meeting with Lyudmila Vasilyeva and a BBC cameraman, taking photos, talking about the campaign’s problems. I’m filmed for an interview. Of course, she didn’t tell me anything new, but I was glad to see her two years after we last met. Back then I was collecting signatures for her myself, and now I’m the candidate.
It’s uncomfortable to sit in a café next to a metro station and film a conversation about what’s wrong in the country and what’s ahead for us. In a public place, on camera, we’re talking about things people don’t usually say out loud.
August 16
Yabloko found more than a billion rubles in donations to parliamentary parties from donors with foreign ties and demanded that those parties be removed from the election. One of the grounds for removing Yabloko itself was 16,900 rubles “from certain citizens who allegedly received funds from abroad.”
Taking part in a Yabloko photo shoot.
August 17
Russia’s Supreme Court rejected the appeal by Yabloko’s lawyers against the ruling that removed the party’s federal list. During the hearing, police outside the court detained more than 85 people who had come to support the party.
The same day, a court in Pskov sentenced Lev Shlosberg, Yabloko’s 63-year-old deputy chairman, to 11 years and one month in a penal colony in a case over repeatedly “discrediting” the Russian army and spreading “fake news” about the military.
The BBC film about my campaign isn’t happening: the cameraman suddenly left Russia, and the active phase of my campaign started pretty late.
Working on notifying the territorial election commission (TEC) about my printed campaign materials.
August 18, one month until the election
Three Muscovites who had come to the Supreme Court to support Yabloko on August 10 were detained a week later and accused of taking part in an unauthorized rally that obstructed traffic. They were jailed for 10–15 days for administrative offenses.
Yabloko was taken off the ballots. Central Election Commission head Ella Pamfilova said that Russians who “left and betrayed the country” should be stripped of the right to vote.
The ballot draw.
When I handed over my passport at the ID check at the entrance to the city election commission, a commission member said: “Oh, you’re the one we reinstated! Make sure she gets in, and everyone should know her face. Other complaints are citing her case now.” Funny.
August 19
Apple Savior Day. Went to a meeting at Yabloko’s city headquarters and handed over the results of the drawing so they could sign the contracts with media outlets.
August 20
Eight thousand people applied to join Yabloko after it was removed from the State Duma election, Kirill Goncharov, the head of its Moscow branch, told Bereg. At that point, the party had half that many members.
Going over legal issues with volunteers. Signing contracts with TV companies, writing the script for a video to air on TV. To get the video into the airtime slots the channels assigned me, I’ll have to hand it in in just a few days.
Yabloko can’t record videos for all its candidates: State Duma candidates get priority. We’ll try to do it on our own.
August 21
The Rodina party filed a lawsuit with the Pskov Regional Court demanding that Yabloko’s list be removed from the election for the regional legislature.
We’re trying to find a video editor. Not many responses so far. The price people are asking is sky-high [for the campaign’s budget] — 15,000 rubles.
August 22
Out of nowhere, they wrote to say Yabloko’s headquarters had found time to shoot the video. I need to be at headquarters at 5:00 p.m. and send the script by 3:00.
In the end, everything gets postponed because of bad weather: they were planning to shoot outside.
August 23
Drafting and signing a contract so I can use a special font developed by Yabloko [in my campaign materials]: the party is worried about copyright lawsuits.
August 24
Signing a contract to pay for the finished website, running to the St. Petersburg TV channel to hand over the video recorded at the Yabloko office, then to the TEC to hand in all the contracts and the video and audio materials.
By law, I only have to give the commission a cover letter and the campaign material itself, but they’re demanding every single contract for every transaction that went through my campaign account, the acceptance certificates, the payment orders…
A TEC staffer complained that I supposedly criticize them all the time in the media or on social media, even though they’re trying to help me “out of kindness”: “You seem like a smart girl, you should have known about requirements like this.” I’m not even angry. I’m tired of being surprised.
August 25
Yabloko was removed from the ballot for the Pskov regional legislature election.
Videos made for St. Petersburg’s State Duma candidates are being pulled en masse. Almost all the candidates got letters from TV channels saying their videos had been found to contain “extremism” and “discrediting the armed forces.” The St. Petersburg Election Commission sent them similar letters.
My video has different content, and the script is my own. So far, they’re leaving it alone.
August 26
The St. Petersburg TV channel calls and begs me to withdraw the video voluntarily. They say, “It’s not up to us.” Supposedly the St. Petersburg Election Commission sent them a notice to that effect. I didn’t get any letter from the St. Petersburg Election Commission.
VGTRK also sends a letter about pulling it from the air.
We’re shooting a second video. Since the first script was as toothless as possible (on purpose), the only things that could bother them are the party slogan and the call for peace. I’m sitting here crossing the words “peace,” “freedom,” and “life” out of my own script. I feel angry.
The worst part isn’t even that the video got pulled. What bugs me more is that I have no idea who’s making this decision. The TV people say one thing, the St. Petersburg Election Commission says another, and the TEC says nothing at all.
In the evening, the cameraman and I go to Nikolai Rybakov’s meeting with supporters. To be honest, I expected more. A routine speech in an intimate setting.
August 27
Filing a complaint with the Central Election Commission over the St. Petersburg Election Commission pulling my video.
I contact a print shop and realize I haven’t raised enough to print even 5,000 flyers. They cost 14,658 rubles. For a big campaign, that’s probably not a huge amount. But when you’re raising the money yourself, you feel every expense like that. I decide to put 30,000 rubles of my own into the campaign.
August 28, three weeks until the election
A court removed Yabloko from the elections for the Sverdlovsk and Kaliningrad regional legislatures. VKontakte cut off Yabloko’s broadcast “Mirny strim” (“Peace Stream”), during which the party was raising money for its election campaign.
Spend half the day writing the text for flyers and posters and send edits to the video editor. At first, I really didn’t like the video at all. It came out more creepy than hopeful, and hopeful is what I wanted despite the censorship. I really want to lift people’s spirits somehow, not make yet another unsettling video.
Heading to a meeting with supporters.
August 30
Finally sorted things out with the print shop (there wasn’t enough money, so in the end I paid for it myself). Going around to the TV companies again — this time to submit the censored video.
August 31
In a single day, Russian courts removed three Yabloko candidates running in single-member districts from the ballot — in the Tula region, Tatarstan, and Bashkortostan. In Moscow, Yabloko candidate Artyom Snegovsky was detained over alleged “discrediting” of the army.
Hi, I’m N.
I report for Meduza from inside Russia. I could go to prison for my work. To stay safe, I have to follow strict security protocols. I know my lawyer’s phone number by heart. And, of course, my articles are published anonymously.
Working for an independent news outlet while still living in Russia feels like something out of a spy film. My friends know me by one name. My colleagues and sources know me by another. But sometimes there’s a glitch. At a close friend’s birthday party, someone I don’t know reaches out to shake my hand. “Hi, I’m Lyosha.” It takes me a few seconds to decide how to introduce myself. Do I use my real name or my pseudonym? I’m trying to figure out whether this is someone I might one day end up writing about.
What I do is journalism in exile, even though I’m not in exile myself. I have the rare opportunity to do uncensored, on-the-ground reporting in Russia. Please support Meduza so I can continue this work.
September 1
Handing in the new video and an audio recording for radio to the TEC. Broadcasting starts tomorrow.
September 2
In the end, none of my video or audio materials were allowed on the air.
Going to the TEC again — they called me in to discuss the design of the campaign boards. The commission chair says three more donations were made in violation of the rules (I didn’t find any violations), so the money went to the state. And apparently I’m also supposed to reimburse the donors for those amounts. The law doesn’t say a word about this. I guess I’m supposed to do it out of my own pocket.
At the TEC, they say “the prosecutor’s office has taken an interest” in me. The best part is that all these transfers were made in accordance with the law.
I’m really nervous. I reread the law the TEC cited. It finally sinks in that they’re just trying to slow me down and keep me from running my campaign in peace. There’s very little time left as it is.
September 3
Get a reply from the St. Petersburg Election Commission saying they have nothing to do with my video and audio materials being kept off the air and that I need to go to the TEC (DEC). Then I don’t understand why the TV channels are telling me something else.
Get a letter from VGTRK saying my new video contains “extremism.” The channel’s management cites a demand to that effect from the St. Petersburg Election Commission.
It hurts that the new video won’t air either. So I’ll post it myself.
September 4, two weeks until the election
Two more Yabloko candidates were detained in Moscow: Anna Shatunovskaya-Byurno (Preobrazhensky single-member district) and Grigory Grishin (Leningradsky single-member district).
We’re setting up a group chat for volunteers. Going to the TEC again with booklets and all the contracts, which I spend a couple of hours filling out, copying, and signing every time before I submit them. Writing posts to explain the situation to my supporters.
September 5
Brought my flyers to Yabloko’s headquarters.
September 6
Brought flyers to supporters, and we’re also looking for volunteers. We don’t have enough people, though I’m grateful to every single one. The same day, we start canvassing neighborhoods.
September 7
In Yekaterinburg, six Yabloko candidates were detained. All of them were cited for displaying “extremist” symbols. A penalty for that administrative offense bars a person from running in elections for 12 months.
I’m officially invited to take part in a debate. I meet with my opponents, and we discuss safety: three of the participants, including me, have already faced attempts to get them removed from the ballot.
The conversation was surprisingly constructive, even though our main rival [United Russia candidate Alexei Kulkov] refused to take part in the debate. After all the trouble with commissions and paperwork, it’s nice to just have a normal conversation with other candidates.
Today’s my birthday. I’d like to keep at least the evening for myself.
September 8, ten days until the election
In the morning I get a bunch of calls. Turns out they’re from the prosecutor’s office. There’s a letter from them in my inbox too, dated September 7. Very ironic — thanks for the present. The letter came in the afternoon and went to spam, but I’m supposed to show up today at 5:00 p.m. I answered the call at four.
At the prosecutor’s office, they spoke to me politely and calmly. The staffer who took down my statement listened carefully and, as far as I could see, wrote down what I said without distorting it.
I came away feeling that even they didn’t fully understand why my video counted as a violation. The staffer saw it for the first time herself during our conversation and called the words in the video “prophetic.”
They gave me an official warning and told me to be more careful. They said several times that they were “forced” to issue the warning. Naturally, they didn’t open any case, because there’s nothing to open one over.
At first the whole situation scared me, but then the fear gave way to calm: I’m not the first person in Yabloko summoned to the prosecutor’s office over a video. After that, I mostly found the whole thing funny because it was so surreal.
It also turns out someone reported me for missing the deadline for submitting campaign materials. Supposedly I brought the video to the commission after it had already been distributed.
September 9
Media requests are coming in: Bumaga, SOTA Vision. Campaigning in my district.
In the evening, I go to Yabloko’s headquarters, sign papers related to election monitoring, and bring the flyers that were missing. Recruiting observers is hard: people whose official residence is outside a candidate’s district can’t serve as observers anymore.
By the way, nobody told me the flyers had run out until I asked. I don’t really get why people at Yabloko keep blowing me off. Is that normal for them, or am I just the lucky one?
Coming home, designing posters.
September 10
Handing out flyers in my district. There was a horrible downpour, and only one other person showed up besides me.
The Central Election Commission sent a brush-off reply saying it found no fault with the St. Petersburg Election Commission for pulling my video off the air. It took the Central Election Commission two weeks to answer.
September 11
Yabloko’s list was removed from the election in the Tomsk region. Only the Novgorod region is left.
Groundhog Day. I get up and head out to the district. Campaign, get home by 11:00 p.m. Almost every day looks the same now, and I can physically feel the exhaustion piling up.
In the afternoon, I was messaging with the print shop. There’s not much time left, and the posters still aren’t ready. I’m worried I’m some kind of “half-candidate.”
September 12
Picking up the posters and going straight to the TEC to submit the campaign materials. Then to the district to campaign.
September 13, five days until the election
Before, I felt like I was mostly carrying the campaign on my own. And then suddenly people showed up — on their own, too. It’s probably the first time in the whole campaign I felt like this matters to someone besides me. I’m really tired, but after that it got a little easier.
Actually, I got really lucky with my district — in terms of how people react. Everyone’s pretty positive about me as a candidate and about the party I’m running with. Although today, for the first time in the whole campaign, we met people who were “not going to” talk to Yabloko.
Writing a post about how we campaign. Asking people to help.
September 14, four days until the election
Still campaigning. The flyers ran out — turns out 5,000 isn’t that many. Urgently writing to the print shop. Panicking a little over how much there is to get done.
September 15, three days until the election
In St. Petersburg, Yabloko-appointed election commission members received summonses to report to the military enlistment office on the first day of voting.
Waiting for my flyers. Going to the district. Waiting for my flyers. Going to the TEC. Going to the district.
Going to Nikolai Rybakov’s meeting with supporters. Out of nowhere, they handed me the mic. They had introduced the candidates at the start, but I was late, so I decided to use the chance to introduce myself and ask people to help me. They handed me the mic so suddenly that I didn’t really know what I was saying. There were a thousand people in the room, and the stress was awful. Surprisingly, the appeal worked — quite a lot of people came up to me after the meeting.
Physically, I feel terrible. I haven’t eaten properly in more than a week. I can feel myself starting to get sick from the stress.
September 16, two days until the election
The debate is today. The first one of my life.
Honestly, it didn’t go very well for me. I was nervous. Sometimes I didn’t manage to say what I wanted; other times I could have answered better. But just taking part matters. At least now I know what a live debate is like and what I need to do differently next time.
The main topics were the environment, transportation, urban development, and how the campaign was going. It was more like a discussion than a debate. I got lost amid my opponents’ loud slogans. On top of that, I’d felt awful since morning, and the tension before the debate took its toll.
Yuri Kulikov, Yelena Belyaeva, Ivan Changli, and I attended the debate. Mikhail Amosov and Alexei Kulkov didn’t show up.
I think I got sick after the debate. Slept at home for an hour, and I’m back to campaigning. Stopped by Yabloko’s headquarters to drop off a batch of flyers, then brought campaign materials to Yabloko activists in the district. We’re going to hand out flyers and canvass apartment buildings.
The last few weeks of the campaign were almost identical: I get up at 10:00, leave the house at noon, and get back around midnight. I’m physically and emotionally drained, but I keep going anyway.
September 17, one day until the election
In the Rostov region, where early voting had started, police officers in balaclavas detained Yabloko observer Boris Miklyukov.
Last day of campaigning. I want to sleep for several days straight, but I have to keep going. We need as many people as possible to come out [to campaign] today — we’ll be handing out the last 2,000 flyers.
In the morning, voting members of one of the precinct commissions wrote to me asking for help if something goes wrong. I’m trying to set up a chat for observers, write a post, answer everyone who’s written to me, and get ready to go campaigning, all at the same time.
By now I’m so used to stress that it’s become my normal state. It’s scary, it’s hard, I’m tired, but I still get ready and go. Honestly, I have almost no strength left. But I feel it’s my duty to see the campaign through to the end myself.
Even if I don’t win, I’ve gained a tremendous amount of experience. I had the chance to speak out for peace legally, in times like these. I can do it, and I’m doing it.
September 18, first day of the election
Polling stations in Sochi suspended voting because of the threat of drones.
Yabloko chairman Nikolai Rybakov asked Central Election Commission head Ella Pamfilova to intervene over the pressure on Yabloko’s observers, who were being kept out of polling stations. In total, nearly 1,300 observers from the Communist Party and Yabloko were barred from polling stations.
My assistant and I bought water and snacks and went around to our observers and voting commission members so they wouldn’t go hungry. All day I went from one precinct commission to another, talked with commission chairs, and checked on how things were going at polling stations where we don’t have observers.
Something funny: one precinct commission complained that they didn’t have enough gifts for first-time voters. Usually the state provides commissions with those gifts. The chair asked me to “buy them gifts.” He said they’d be very grateful and would tell everyone who voted for me that the gifts were from me: “We’ll be able to see who voted for you, after all.” Is it stupidity or what? I don’t know. Surreal. Maybe United Russia people came by and did that…
Overall, the commission chairs were pretty polite with me. They all said turnout at their polling stations was about 30%.
September 19, second day of the election
Yabloko observers are still being kept out of polling stations. And at Precinct Election Commission No. 3104 in Perm, a Communist Party observer was turned away along with a Yabloko representative.
In St. Petersburg, police used force while detaining a Yabloko observer, and he lost consciousness. He was later cited for “disobeying” the police, and the commission chair accused him of “attempting to disrupt the election.” The observer’s name wasn’t released.
Still making the rounds of precinct commissions. The Communist Party got in touch — we’re trading news. Lots of their observers weren’t allowed in. Mine, thankfully, were.
September 20, last day of the election
A St. Petersburg precinct commission member named Darya (her surname wasn’t given) was detained over a complaint of “discrediting” the army filed by the precinct commission chair, according to Yabloko’s St. Petersburg branch. The complaint was prompted by her use of the word “war” in a private conversation. Darya believes the real reason may have been to remove her from the polling station. A Yabloko observer was taken to the same police station over filming that the commission considered illegal.
At one precinct commission, the chair (a participant in the “special military operation”) clashed with one of my observers. She was accused of talking to a voter — according to her, she said hi to her mom, who had come to vote. The observer was given a warning.
At another precinct commission, something strange happened. My observer stepped out during the vote count — as she said later, she felt unwell. One of the voting commission members later told me that the ballots were swapped at that moment. It’s hard to verify.
I ask commission chairs about turnout, and they give roughly the same figure: 50–60% over the three days.
Really tired. Late in the evening, I stopped by Yabloko’s headquarters on Shpalernaya Street and talked with other candidates.
Around 3:00 a.m., an acquaintance from one precinct commission sent me the tally sheet with the preliminary results for the precinct. The result was disappointing, of course. I was in second-to-last place, with just over 30 votes. The United Russia candidate [Alexei Kulkov], who didn’t campaign at all, had around 150. And [incumbent deputy] Amosov had around 300.
September 21, results
According to the Novgorod region election commission, with 96.86% of ballots counted, Yabloko is set to win representation in the regional duma with 6.2% of the vote. The Novgorod region is the only region where Yabloko was allowed to run in the regional legislative election.
According to preliminary data, I came in last. Considering that at almost every polling station I visited, another 400 votes appeared after voting ended, I’m not surprised. At one precinct commission, they told me I originally had 90-something votes, and then they falsified the count down to 40-something. According to preliminary data, the United Russia candidate came in second and Amosov first.
Above all, what mattered to me in this campaign was speaking up for peace — and showing people they’re not alone. This whole time, my team and I were able to talk with people about their real problems. Having the chance to speak out is very important to us.

Sybiha to raise humanitarian crisis in Oleshky at UN General Assembly
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
20:07:21 EEST
02:07:21 KST

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha plans to raise separately at the UN General Assembly in New York the humanitarian catastrophe in Oleshky, a city in the occupied part of Kherson region, he said upon arriving in New York for the General Assembly session.
"Oleshky is a city in Kherson region that has been under complete blockade for more than six months. More than 6,000 people remain there, including nearly 200 children. People are dying of hunger and cold. The occupiers are not allowing humanitarian aid in. We have been negotiating an evacuation for a long time, preparing lists and agreeing on a ceasefire regime. And Russia is not responding. We will talk about Oleshky here, at the highest level, and will put pressure on the world to hear this and force Russia to allow humanitarian access," Sybiha said in a video posted on his Facebook page on Monday.
He said Ukraine had also brought to New York the issue of the deportation and militarization of Ukrainian children, their return and accountability for those committing these crimes.
"We have a packed schedule. Dozens of meetings with partners from all continents. Six documents to sign. All of this is for one purpose – so that the world does not get used to this war, so that pressure on Russia grows and support for our army is strengthened," Sybiha said.
Sybiha also said there would be a separate UN Security Council meeting on Ukraine, the sixth Crimea Platform summit, and discussions on energy ahead of winter, the Black Sea and grain. The first lady will have a separate program of events promoting humanitarian initiatives.

Türkiye promoting COP31 presidency in New York
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
17:05:42 UTC
02:05:42 KST

Diyar Guldogan
21 September 2026•Update: 21 September 2026
Türkiye's preparations to host and chair the 31st UN Climate Change Conference, or COP31, are taking center stage in New York this week as world leaders gather for the 81st session of the UN General Assembly.
Posters promoting Türkiye's COP31 presidency and featuring President Recep Tayyip Erdogan have been displayed on the Turkish House, or Turkevi, Türkiye's diplomatic complex in Manhattan, under the theme "The Future of the World is in Türkiye."
Promotional vehicles carrying COP31-themed digital displays have also been circulating through New York, including Times Square and routes connecting the area with the UN headquarters.
Türkiye is using the UN General Assembly week to showcase its preparations for the conference and promote its climate agenda ahead of the Antalya gathering in November.
Erdogan is scheduled to take part in a high-level climate meeting organized by UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Wednesday, where he will provide information about Türkiye's preparations to host COP31.
First lady Emine Erdogan, who chairs the UN Zero Waste Advisory Board, is also scheduled to participate in programs related to Türkiye's climate and sustainability initiatives during the UN General Assembly week.
COP31 exhibition at Turkevi
Türkiye has prepared a series of exhibitions and interactive installations at Turkevi to introduce its COP31 preparations to international visitors.
The exhibition, titled "Seeing the Unseen, Hearing the Unheard: SCOPE as a Vision of the Future," will combine artificial intelligence, sound, mapping technologies, immersive displays, and art installations.
Visitors will encounter an interactive installation featuring Caretta, Türkiye's COP31 mascot, as well as a photography experience drawing on the traditional Turkish art of ebru.
Another section will feature a three-dimensional model of the COP31 venue in Antalya. A mapping presentation will be used to illustrate the layout and visitor experience planned for the conference site.
The exhibition will also present Türkiye's COP31 Action Agenda through digital displays.
Other installations will focus on the effects of climate change on oceans, agriculture, soil, and the global climate system. A final section, titled "LET'S COP – Türkiye's Climate Journey," will showcase Türkiye's climate-related work through a large LED wall.
A separate COP31 exhibition will be held at Glasshouse in New York, featuring four presentations focused on climate and nature.
The exhibition will present Türkiye's climate vision and Action Agenda before highlighting works by artists Ilhami Atalay and Ekrem Sahin.
Atalay's "Return of the Birds – Tawaf" will explore the collective movement of birds and the concept of gathering around a common center. Sahin's "Sound of Water" photography exhibition will examine climate change through water.
The program will conclude with a live paper marbling (ebru) performance by artist Garip Ay.
Turkish Minister of Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change and COP31 President Murat Kurum is also holding a series of meetings in New York as Türkiye steps up preparations for the Antalya conference.

What will happen to gasoline and diesel prices in the fall, and will the surge in fuel demand lead to higher prices?
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
20:02:54 EEST
02:02:54 KST

What will happen to gasoline and diesel prices in the fall, and will the surge in fuel demand lead to higher prices?
Kyiv • UNN
A-95 gasoline costs UAH 93.33, while diesel costs UAH 98.55 per liter. An expert predicts high, volatile prices and a risk of diesel becoming more expensive.
The Ukrainian fuel market entered autumn with a sharp rise in prices. As of September 18, the average price of A-95 gasoline reached UAH 93.33 per liter, while diesel fuel cost UAH 98.55 per liter. In some networks, diesel has already crossed the psychological threshold of UAH 100. An additional risk factor could be panic-driven demand if drivers and businesses simultaneously begin building up stocks amid fears of new Russian strikes on fuel infrastructure.
What is happening in the domestic fuel market, and what prices should drivers prepare for in the coming month? UNN asked fuel market expert Leonid Kosianchuk.
The energy expert acknowledges that there are currently no grounds for optimistic forecasts regarding the situation on the Ukrainian fuel market, and that the difficulties are indeed real. They are related to the fact that our country currently receives almost 90% of its petroleum products from Europe.
"The situation there (on the European market — editor's note) is very complicated. Especially considering that Saudi Aramco — a state-owned oil company — announced that, as far as supplies to the European market for October are concerned, they will either suspend them or limit them," the expert clarified.
According to Kosianchuk, ORLEN Lietuva could serve as an alternative to Saudi Aramco. It operates the only oil refinery in the Baltic countries, the Mažeikiai Refinery, as well as oil pipelines and the terminal in Būtingė. The company is one of the main suppliers of gasoline and diesel fuel in Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia. Its capacity could help cover certain shortages and prevent the crisis from deepening.
Diesel is becoming more expensive faster than gasoline: what is behind this
The most tense situation has emerged precisely with diesel fuel. In mid-September, its European quotations rose to a record $1,644 per ton. In just five days, the increase amounted to about $172 per ton, or approximately UAH 7.7 per liter when converted. The price later fell back to $1,553 per ton, but this level remains high nonetheless.
Fuel market expert Leonid Kosianchuk, in an exclusive comment to UNN, drew attention specifically to this unusual gap between gasoline and diesel.
"For the first time in all my many years of work in this market, we are seeing diesel fuel cost almost UAH 10 more than gasoline," he said.
Actual prices at Ukrainian gas stations confirm this: on September 21, the difference between the average price of A-95 gasoline and diesel fuel was more than UAH 5 per liter. Moreover, last week some major networks kept diesel at UAH 99.8–99.9, while one network had already set the price at UAH 100 per liter.
Leonid Kosianchuk explains that the reason for this trend is not a shortage of fuel directly at Ukrainian gas stations.
"Ukraine is heavily dependent on imports of finished petroleum products, so the domestic price responds to European quotations, resource availability, logistics costs, and risks to supply routes," the expert explained.
Why prices may rise even after quotations decline
To answer this question, which confounds many Ukrainians trying to understand the issue, it is worth noting that retail prices respond to the external market with a delay. The fuel being sold to drivers at gas stations today may have been purchased when European quotations were at their peak. Therefore, even after they decline, operators continue for some time to receive more expensive batches and pass these costs on to the price displayed on the signs. The Ukrainian market observed such a situation in the second half of September: external quotations had already moved away from their highs, but Ukrainian storage tanks continued to be filled with more expensive supplies.
That is why a quick return to summer prices should not be expected, although as of September 21 there were already signs of some "cooling" in the wholesale market. Demand is currently weak, and some traders are selling supplies below the calculated replacement cost. However, new batches of diesel fuel remain expensive at current European prices.
Commenting on the situation, Leonid Kosyanchuk emphasizes that the issue of resource availability and the issue of its cost now need to be considered separately.
"There is no reason today to say that there will be no diesel fuel or gasoline. However, there is a problem with pricing. The main issue is not whether fuel will be available. The main issue is the price at which it will be offered," the expert explained.
He particularly emphasized that logistics costs, as well as insurance and security risks, are currently added to the external price of fuel. Due to problems along certain routes, traders are forced to change their supply routes. For example, using an alternative route through Moldova can add approximately $25–30 per tonne to the cost of the resource. Additional costs also arise because of delays at the borders or the need to reload the fuel.
Could panic buying push prices even higher?
Several days earlier, society reacted sharply to a call by Serhii Kuiun, director of the A-95 Consulting Group, to build up fuel reserves. One of the reasons was a possible shortage amid the situation on the global oil market and the intensification of russian armed forces’ attacks on gas stations. However, the expert later clarified that he was primarily referring to possible local disruptions caused by Russian strikes on fuel infrastructure. In his assessment, a total shortage like the one in spring 2022 is not expected at present. However, if a large number of consumers simultaneously go to gas stations and begin filling their tanks and additional containers to capacity, this could temporarily alter the balance. Stocks at individual stations would run out faster, forcing operators to urgently transfer resources between regions or purchase additional batches. If external quotations and logistics develop unfavorably, this could accelerate increases in retail prices.
Moreover, Kuiun describes preventing such a scenario as one of the purposes of building up reserves: the reserve should help weather a possible short-term disruption in supply without a simultaneous influx of consumers at gas stations. He stresses that there is currently enough fuel on the market, but does not rule out local disruptions.
However, expert Leonid Kosyanchuk категорically disagrees with him on this point. He explains that even before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the supply of fuel on the domestic market significantly exceeded demand for drivers. Unlike Finland, where gas stations are located at fairly considerable distances from one another and the number of fuel operators is limited, in our country dozens of networks offered and continue to offer their services through an extensive system of gas stations both in cities and outside them.
Therefore, the main near-term risk for truck and passenger-car drivers lies not in a physical shortage of gasoline or diesel fuel caused by the enemy destroying several dozen more gas stations. Difficulties may arise in other areas.
The first is an increase in the price of fuel for retail consumers because the cost of storing fuel in depots located outside Ukraine will be factored into it. Against the backdrop of intensified Russian attacks on infrastructure, operators are increasingly inclined to store significant reserves of gasoline and diesel in depots located in countries bordering Ukraine. Several months of renting such a hub cannot fail to affect the final cost of fuel at gas stations.
Secondly, according to Leonid Kosyanchuk, difficulties may arise with the timely delivery of gasoline and diesel fuel to Ukraine. Mobilization into the army has created a labor shortage in the field of drivers as well. It is currently quite difficult to find a man with a driver's license of the appropriate category and practical experience who could be entrusted with driving a fuel tanker. Involving men aged 60+ in this work could be dangerous for them themselves. After all, many people at this age already have chronic illnesses and may not be physically able to endure days of waiting in a fuel tanker's cab at the border, followed by a long journey carrying a high-risk cargo. Therefore, if the leading players in the fuel market fail to resolve the "staffing issue" in the near future, Ukrainians may soon face a fuel shortage due to delays in supplies.
What to expect from fuel prices in the fall
As Leonid Kosyanchuk explained in an exclusive comment to UNN, the baseline scenario for the coming weeks is the continuation of high and highly volatile prices. Diesel fuel remains at the greatest risk of further increases. If European quotations rise again, the UAH 100-per-liter mark may appear not just at individual gas stations, but at a significantly larger number of them. Market participants recorded potential for a further increase in retail diesel prices even after European prices retreated from their peak levels. If, however, the "retreat" in the external market continues and supply routes operate steadily, the increase in Ukraine may slow down or stop once networks sell through their more expensive stocks. However, an immediate price reduction should not be expected: retail prices respond to changes in cost with a time lag.
The situation with gasoline is somewhat calmer, although there is still little room for a sharp decline here either. Diesel remains more vulnerable because of the more expensive European supply and its greater sensitivity to disruptions in deliveries.
At the same time, according to the expert, fuel businesses and ordinary drivers should not place too much hope in assistance from the state, which will most likely not intervene in pricing policy in any way. This differs from European countries, which are reducing the tax burden on fuel in the face of the threat of an energy crisis.
Recall
On September 17, Ukrnafta and SOCAR raised fuel prices twice.

Government targets later Parliament for readiness bill
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
18:00:07 BST
02:00:07 KST

The Government is aiming to bring forward proposals for new defence readiness legislation later in this Parliament, but has not set a specific date for introducing the measures.
Defence Minister Luke Pollard provided the update in response to a written parliamentary question from Conservative MP Stuart Anderson, who asked when the Defence Readiness Bill would be presented to Parliament. Pollard said the Government is examining what additional legal powers may be required to prepare the country for a major crisis or conflict, following a recommendation in the Strategic Defence Review.
He said: “Defence Readiness legislation is being considered to ensure the Government has the powers it needs to keep the UK safe in crisis or war, as recommended in the Strategic Defence Review.”
The legislation has yet to reach the stage where ministers can provide a firm timetable. Instead, the MOD says detailed policy work is continuing to determine precisely what powers are required and what their wider implications would be.
Pollard said: “We are aiming to deliver legislative proposals later this Parliament. It will take time to develop the detailed policy requirements, understand their implications and establish what new legislation is required.”
That wording leaves both the detailed contents and timing of the proposed legislation under development. It also indicates that the Government has not yet concluded exactly which elements of its defence readiness plans will require new primary legislation.
Any eventual legislation will also have to compete for Parliamentary time.
Pollard added: “As is standard with the legislative process, any future legislation will be brought forward when Parliamentary time allows.”
The proposed measures stem from the Strategic Defence Review’s focus on improving the ability of the state, Armed Forces, industry and wider society to respond to a serious security crisis or war. The precise powers to be included have not yet been published. The MOD says officials are working across government on potential measures, with further engagement expected once that work is sufficiently developed.

01:59:05 KST

The U.S. is working on a major agreement to purchase potash from Belarus, U.S. President Donald Trump said on Sept. 21, calling it more advantageous than buying the fertilizer from Canada.
"The United States is working on a massive Deal with respect to the purchase of Potash from Belarus," Trump announced on his Truth Social media platform, calling it "very good news for our Farmers and Ranchers."
The news comes amid an apparent thaw in U.S.-Belarusian relations, accompanied by Washington easing sanctions and the Lukashenko regime releasing some of its political prisoners.
The Trump administration lifted economic restrictions on Belarusian potash exports in December 2025, leading to more than 100 political prisoners being released from Belarus, including prominent opposition figures Maria Kalesnikava and Viktor Babaryka.
In March 2026, U.S. envoy John Coale said a broader deal with Minsk could include sanctions relief and the restoration of diplomatic relations. Belarusian dictator Alexander Lukashenko had said the U.S. had proposed a "big deal" with Belarus.
Potash is one of Belarus's key exports and its most significant mineral resource, with the state-owned producer Belaruskali ranking among the world's largest suppliers.
Reports emerged in the spring of 2026 that the U.S. was also asking Lithuania, Poland, and Ukraine to allow Belarusian fertilizers to transit through their territories.
Belarus, a landlocked country lodged between Ukraine, Russia, and NATO's eastern members, has been a key ally of Moscow during the all-out war, allowing Russian forces to use its territory as a staging ground for attacks on Ukraine in 2022.
Canada is the world's leading exporter of potash, accounting for over 39% of global exports as of 2024. More than half of this trade is destined for U.S. markets.
Trump's return to office led to a sharp deterioration in U.S.-Canadian economic relations, with the U.S. president imposing 50% tariffs on certain Canadian imports and Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney responding with matching tariffs on U.S. goods.

Sarah Bseiso: A Gaza survivor’s story of burns, loss and healing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:58:08 UTC
01:58:08 KST

Breadcrumb
Sarah Bseiso: A Gaza survivor’s account of the burns, loss and healing endured during Israel’s genocide
Sarah Bseiso was 17 when she was severely burned during Israel's genocide in Gaza in 2023.
She arrived in the United States (US) for treatment about a year and a half ago and, with support from Heal Palestine, now lives in New Jersey with her mother and sister, having since undergone a large number of operations.
Before the genocide, she was in her final year of secondary school and remembers the moment Israeli violence reached her family home as unlike anything she had experienced before.
"It was not like any other war we had known before," she recalled.
Sarah was inside her grandfather's house when she heard drones and Israeli aircraft around them. Her brothers Ahmad and Hamoud were outside, and when Ahmad called to say that Hamoud was scared, she went outside to calm him down and hugged him. On their way back to the house, she felt something hit her.
"I felt something very hot hit me and push me several steps forward. Then the kitchen caught fire completely, and the flames began burning everything," she explained.
She continued, "While I was trying to understand what was happening, I noticed that my leather shoe had burnt, as had my feet and my medical glasses. I don't know why I forgot that Hamoud was with me and that we were inside the flames."
In sharing this, Sarah noted that she initially thought Ahmad had pulled Hamoud away, before realising that the fire had come from Ahmad’s side and the missile had left his whole body “riddled with holes.”
As she screamed, her father pulled her from the fire, but both of her brothers, Ahmad, 16, and Hamoud, eight, died in the attack, with Ahmad dying immediately and Hamoud succumbing days later to his injuries, fourth-degree burns and smoke inhalation.
Sarah recalls hearing Hamoud's voice and moans from a nearby room while she was suffering from her own burns. No one was able to help him because of the extent of his injuries, the siege and the bombardment.
Her father risked his life under bombardment to take her to a nearby hospital, where doctors gave her fluids to replace some of what she had lost, but they were unable to provide the treatment she needed.
As Sarah explained, “Treatment and medication were unavailable, and the hospital was under siege.”
Sarah eventually travelled to the US as part of a medical evacuation via Egypt, where she stayed briefly. She spent her first three and a half months in intensive care and underwent numerous operations.
"I don't know how many operations there were. Work is still being done to restore my skin, and the movement of my fingers is limited. Some of the operations are to improve the skin," she told The New Arab.
The pain of healing
After a year and a half of treatment, Sarah's recovery remains ongoing. Alongside the physical effects of her injuries, she has had to deal with the deaths of her brothers, the loss of her home and the separation of her family.
She recalls how the Israeli army took over their home for a period, in addition to targeting it. Family members were also dispersed outside Gaza, while the uncertainty of not knowing whether she could reach relatives in the territory remained difficult.
"It is a difficult matter, especially when the internet goes down in Gaza, and we are unable to communicate with them. Every report about a bombing in an area causes a lot of terror, because the media does not specify the details exactly, leaving a lot of speculation and fear about the fate of loved ones," she explained.
Despite those difficulties, Sarah says her physical condition has improved since she arrived in the US. When she first arrived, she was unable to move parts of her face and body and spent her first weeks in intensive care.
"When I arrived, the condition of my face was critical, and I could not move my mouth, neck or joints, but now I am better able to move them," she explained. "In the first weeks, I was in intensive care, and the situation was very difficult. I felt lonely even though I do not have a problem communicating in English."
The adjustment was difficult because she felt separated from the people and surroundings she knew. The nurses who cared for her, however, helped her through those first days.
"I felt that the people around me were not like me, that I did not belong to them and that I did not know them. I felt suffocated in the first days, but I received the affection of the nurses," she recalled.
Physical therapy brought its own challenges, with Sarah describing some sessions as extremely painful. Her therapists and medical staff sometimes used music and dance during treatment, which she remembers fondly.
"I sometimes feel severe pain during physical therapy, as if my whole body is going to tear apart. Sometimes the therapist would stop, and treatment would begin through dance and music, and the staff would join us. I loved them very much," she explained.
The repeated operations also left Sarah afraid that she might die during treatment.
"At first, I was overcome by a strong feeling of fear, in addition to the operations, and I was afraid of dying under the weight of these operations," she recalled.
On one occasion, the pain became so overwhelming that Sarah told a therapist she would not have escaped the fire if she had known what the treatment would be like.
"I once swore in front of one of the therapists, essentially saying that if I had known the pain during the treatment period would be like this, I would not have left the fire," she explained.
The comment frightened the therapist, who requested a psychologist, believing that Sarah might harm herself. Heal Palestine did the same.
Gaza beyond the genocide
For Sarah, however, the difficulties of adjusting to life in the US have also been tied to how she feels Gaza and Palestinians are viewed. She says Gaza was not defined by the genocide, but by the community she experienced there.
"We are not beggars or a charity project. We are not hungry either. Our circumstances were imposed on us," she said.
When Sarah remembers Gaza, she focuses on the sense of safety she felt there and the people who would help her when she got lost.
"Gaza was a beautiful city. I did not feel afraid in Gaza. For example, I have a problem with directions, and I would always get lost and find my way because someone was always there to help," she explained.
That sense of connection extended beyond the people she knew personally.
"I felt that everyone in the street belonged to me, and that no matter how lost I became, there was no reason to be afraid in Gaza," she continued.
That being said, living in the US has not given her the same sense of belonging, despite having lived there for around a year and a half.
"Here, I have been walking down the same street for a year, but I don't feel there is anything there that I belong to," she reflected.
"Gaza was a city that spread its goodness and blessings to everyone, although the circumstances we went through were difficult, and anyone could go through them," she added.
A glimpse of life before
Sarah is now also thinking about what she might do after her treatment. She does not know what she had planned to study, but, coming from a family with many doctors, she would probably have pursued medicine, although she expects her treatment to continue for another year or a year and a half before she can prepare for the required exams and decide on her specialisation based on her grades.
Outside the hospital, moments such as a Heal Palestine camp last summer have helped her reconnect with parts of her life before the injury. She remembers the camp as wonderful because she was surrounded by Palestinians who understood what she had been through.
"We were surrounded by nature and under the shade of trees, alongside Palestinians from Gaza and from different areas who understood what I had been through. During that period, I was able to sleep without any problems," she recalled.
One of the activities at the camp was particularly meaningful because it reminded Sarah of her childhood in Gaza: horse riding. Her father had trained her and her brothers to ride Arab horses from a young age and would challenge them to discover their skills.
"The summer camp was the first opportunity to ride a horse since the incident, and my feelings were indescribable," she said.
She was initially afraid because she had to hold the reins with both hands, knowing that she could not fully move her left hand. She worried that she would lose control of the horse, but she succeeded.
Gaza's patients left waiting
Sarah's story comes as thousands of other Palestinians in Gaza continue to need medical treatment outside the territory.
The latest data from the World Health Organisation indicates that more than 18,000 Palestinian patients and wounded people in Gaza still need medical evacuation, while Israel refuses to grant entry visas to many foreign doctors or doctors of Palestinian origin who want to enter to assist.
One of them is US doctor of Palestinian origin Thaer Ahmad, who has entered Gaza several times before and after the genocide, while on other occasions he was prevented from entering. Ahmad has also spoken about the decision by US President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio in August to halt medical evacuation visas from Gaza to the US.
In an exclusive interview with The New Arab, Ahmad described the decision as one that would have serious consequences for children who need specialist treatment.
"The decision to halt humanitarian visas for children from Gaza will follow the secretary of state throughout his professional career," he said.
Ahmad has met children who were previously evacuated to the US, including some who were taken to Dallas and Chicago. He pointed to the number of children received by the US compared with other countries in the region.
"Some had previously been evacuated to Dallas and Chicago, and I met many of them. What is striking is that the US received fewer than 80 children, while we hear about other countries in the region receiving more than 2,000 cases, even though the US has specialist doctors capable of helping these children with their injuries, while most of these specialisations are not available around the world," he explained.
Ahmad added that the decision had closed a route for Palestinian families seeking treatment in the US, many of whom, he argued, did not intend to remain in the country.
"The US government decided to close these doors. It is a catastrophic decision in every sense of the word, especially since Palestinian families who come to the US for treatment do not intend to stay," he said.
He also referred to one case he had worked on in which a patient had already returned.
“One of the cases I worked on has already returned, while the family members are living in Egypt, waiting for the borders to open so they can reunite with their families,” Ahmad noted, adding that medical evacuations did not place an unreasonable burden on the US healthcare system.
"Taxpayers' money is not being spent on the children. We did not receive thousands of children, so we could say this puts pressure on our healthcare system, especially since our hospital systems are capable of accommodating them," he explained.
For Ahmad, the issue remains what happens to Palestinians who have travelled abroad for treatment and want to return to their families.
"These people want to return. It is strange. The decision was taken for political reasons, but it is also a very inhumane and tragic decision," he concluded.

Trump Pressures Ukraine over Rising Diesel Prices Ahead of UN General Assembly Meeting
US President Donald Trump pressed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy during a September 20 phone call to stop targeting Russian oil refineries, the Financial Times reported on September 21.
Trump expressed concern that Ukrainian strikes are worsening a global diesel shortage and driving domestic energy prices higher.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
While Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries hit an already fragile market, restricted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz is the primary driver of the current diesel crisis, according to the International Energy Agency’s September oil market report.
Following the Middle Eastern chokepoint’s closure, Persian Gulf diesel and gasoil exports dropped by roughly 1 million barrels per day—accounting for the majority of the combined Middle East and Russian supply decline.
According to a senior Ukrainian official who was on the call, Trump’s messaging focused heavily on “diesel, diesel… diesel,” urging Zelenskyy to order the Ukrainian military to halt its deep-strike drone and missile campaign against Russian fuel processing infrastructure.
Another official familiar with the exchange noted that Trump emphasized his growing concern over rising diesel costs and stressed the need for Russian fuel supplies to reach global markets to ease inflationary pressures, according to the Financial Times.
The conversation came shortly after Ukrainian forces launched a major drone strike on the Russian capital, setting a key oil refinery ablaze in the Moscow region.
In a post on Truth Social following the call, Trump asserted that Russia had “lost control of its Diesel Oil Industry” and reiterated calls to end the war. US diesel prices reached a record $6.51 per gallon on September 21, representing a more than 70 percent increase since the outbreak of broader Middle East hostilities earlier this year, the Financial Times wrote.
Following the conversation, Zelenskyy stated that the discussion was “important” and noted that an upcoming in-person meeting with Trump on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York “could change a lot,” the Financial Times reported.
“There is diplomatic momentum,” Zelenskyy stated, while reiterating in separate comments that Russia continues to escalate its aggression and target Ukrainian civilian infrastructure.
Zelenskyy emphasized that Ukraine’s long-range drone campaign forms “part of the pressure that is actually working and the world can feel it,” maintaining that diplomatic efforts must proceed in parallel.
Ukrainian officials told the Financial Times that while Trump previously suggested both sides had agreed to refrain from striking energy facilities, no reciprocal ceasefire has been implemented as Russia continues its aerial bombardment of Ukrainian power grids and civilian infrastructure.
Despite a relentless campaign of Ukrainian strikes that has knocked out roughly a fifth of Russia’s oil refining capacity, Russian refineries earned unprecedented profits of 938 billion rubles ($11.13 billion) in the first half of the year.
Driven by soaring exchange prices and massive state “damper” subsidies, these windfalls have offset reduced refining volumes, even as direct and indirect damages to Russia’s oil sector mounted and Ukraine expanded its campaign to target shadow-fleet tankers at sea.
