Germany was built for stability, so what happens when it disappears?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:36:59 UTC
01:36:59 KST

Germany’s age of political stability is ending
The latest state elections in Germany have confirmed a trend that is becoming increasingly difficult to dismiss. The issue is no longer the occasional success of one party or failure of another, but the gradual dismantling of a political system that for decades appeared almost permanent.
The postwar German model rested on competition between two “people’s parties,” the Christian Democrats and Social Democrats and this conservative-social democratic axis provided stability after the upheavals of the first half of the 20th century, allowing governments to alternate while remaining within broadly accepted political boundaries.
Germany adhered to this model particularly closely, so the political landscape expanded significantly only twice, first with the rise of the Greens in the 1980s, which brought the rebellious generation of 1968 into the establishment, and then after reunification with the emergence of the Left from the former East German political tradition, but that orderly system is now breaking down.
The results in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin, following Saxony-Anhalt two weeks earlier, leap off the page, as the AfD won 38.2% in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, while the CDU fell below the 5% threshold for the first time in a German state election. In Berlin, meanwhile, the Left finished first, with the CDU second and the SPD falling to fifth place.
For the leaderships of the CDU and SPD, it’s tempting to reduce the problem to the rise of the AfD and concentrate on how it should be contained, but the deeper problem is the fragmentation of the entire electoral landscape and the disappearance of the political manageability that Germany once took for granted.
Whether the AfD itself is capable of governing effectively remains another question, given the party has never governed a German state, while the established parties continue to reject coalitions with it.
Germany is therefore moving towards something resembling the politics of smaller European countries such as Belgium, the Netherlands, or Austria, with fragmented parliaments and increasingly complicated multiparty coalitions.
There’s nothing inherently unworkable about such a system and plenty of European countries function this way, but Germany is different. Its political culture has traditionally valued predictability and institutional continuity, but if fragmentation now spreads inside the CDU and SPD themselves, the consequences will extend beyond election arithmetic.
Germany isn’t particularly comfortable with political upheaval and when Germany becomes politically nervous, its neighbors have historically had reason to pay attention.

Stop relying on chatbots for customer care, UK service providers urged
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:35:31 UTC
01:35:31 KST

Stop relying on AI chatbots for customer care and guarantee the “right to talk to a human”, Citizens Advice has urged essential service providers, as research found they wasted time, caused stress and delayed problem solving for more than half of users.
The spread of the AI-powered systems to provide help about the provision of vital services such as energy, banking, phones and internet, is making it harder for millions of already digitally excluded people to handle snags, according to the frontline charity that last year provided more than 2.7 million people with one-on-one help in England and Wales.
The charity concluded that chatbots caused harm, saying too often they trapped humans in an “endless loop” in which nothing got resolved, and almost half of people who had to use a chatbot found them unhelpful, with some concluding the chatbot seemed rigged to “make me give up”.
It called for service providers to respect a new right for customers to speak to a human after it investigated the wider impact of digital exclusion, estimated to affect at least 14 million UK citizens. It uncovered slower and less reliable support for people who struggle with or have limited access to online systems and found the erosion of phone, face-to-face and paper communication had created a two-tier support system.
“Going round in circles with a chatbot isn’t just annoying, it can be a blockade to essential services,” said Tom MacInnes, policy director at Citizens Advice. “We’ve seen organisations’ overreliance on chatbots and online forms leaving people unable to fix billing problems, sort out their debt or even access homelessness prevention services. There’s a role for chatbots, but the quiet erosion of face-to-face and telephone services is letting too many people fall through the cracks.”
That erosion of traditional ways of communicating means that people without good digital access can face serious difficulties getting simple problems fixed. For example, the charity found that submitting energy meter readings to correct a wrong bill can take less than an hour online if systems are working properly. Without good digital access it takes as long as six weeks offline, putting people “at risk of further harm”. In some locations applying for low-cost social tariff broadband – itself intended to reduce digital exclusion – is being made harder by being digital only, Citizens Advice found after it took evidence from its frontline advisers and hundreds of case summaries.
One adviser reported that when people struggled with digital-only applications for homelessness support they ended up “homeless for longer … they’re in danger … they’re losing money … they get into debt” and said: “It can ruin a lot of people’s lives.”
The warnings come amid growing frustration with the proliferation of AI customer services. Online message boards with titles like: “I’m so sick of AI Customer ‘Support” Chat Bots” and “Has anyone ever actually had their problem solved by a company’s chatbot?” are filled with tales of woe. Several chronicle frustrated customers’ attempts to circumvent phone-based chatbots by repeatedly yelling “human!”.
Only 20% of UK adults polled on behalf of Citizens Advice in July said chatbots were their preferred way to communicate, with phone calls, email and instant messaging all preferred.
Gripes about other forms of digital exclusion include multifactor authentication, which requires rapid and dextrous manipulation of more than one device just to log in and time-limits to complete transactions.
Of the people who found it difficult or not possible to talk to a human to resolve an issue with their essential services, 49% felt stress or frustration, 27% felt powerless, 44% experienced delays to resolution and 14% gave up trying to resolve the issue altogether.
The UK government has previously said it is investing £11.9m in a digital inclusion innovation fund, supporting local projects to help people get online. About 1.7m households in the UK do not have a laptop, tablet or desktop computer.
A government spokesperson said: “Businesses have a legal obligation to provide contact information in a manner which is clear and easily accessible.”

The 22nd Malaysia International Halal Showcase (MIHAS 2026) is set to begin Wednesday in the capital Kuala Lumpur under the theme “Shaping Trust, Driving Resilience,” bringing together companies, buyers and industry representatives from across the global halal economy.
The four-day event, hosted by Malaysia’s Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry (MITI) and organized by the Malaysia External Trade Development Corporation (MATRADE), will take place at the Malaysia International Trade and Exhibition Centre (MITEC) from Sept. 23 to 26.
Around 50,000 visitors from 45 countries are expected to attend, while 1,700 companies will showcase their products and services across some 2,000 booths.
Organizers are targeting 5 billion Malaysian ringgit ($1.23 billion) in total sales through the exhibition and its business-matching program.

“We believe this approach will enhance the MIHAS experience and support our efforts to achieve RM5 billion in sales value this year,” he added.
MIHAS 2026 will cover 14 sectors across the halal economy, ranging from food and beverages to pharmaceuticals, cosmetics and personal care, modest fashion, halal logistics, Islamic finance, technology, services and Muslim-friendly tourism.
The AI system will offer business matching, multilingual support, exhibition navigation, meeting management and post-event engagement.
MIHAS’ International Sourcing Programme, its flagship business-matching initiative, is expected to facilitate around 4,000 meetings between 450 international buyers, including 50 premium buyers, and approximately 600 Malaysian exporters.
The event will also feature its Knowledge Hub, Women in Export pavilion, MIHAS Awards and Hosted Buyer Programme.
The Women in Export initiative has been expanded from a standalone forum into a dedicated pavilion this year, bringing together 80 exhibitors, including 60 from Malaysia and 20 from other countries.
The Knowledge Hub, established in 2021, will provide exporters, particularly micro, small and medium-sized enterprises, with trade intelligence and information on global market opportunities.
Its Power Talk 2026, themed “The Next Wave of the Halal Trade,” will bring together industry representatives to discuss supply-chain resilience and international competitiveness amid global trade uncertainties.
MIHAS 2026 will also feature daily modest-fashion runway presentations and live culinary demonstrations.
The MIHAS Kitchen has expanded to two floors this year and will host live cooking sessions by 32 chefs during the four-day event, up from 15 last year.
First launched in 2004, MIHAS has developed into a major international platform connecting businesses across the halal economy.

'Germany's Mamdani': Who is Berlin mayor hopeful Elif Eralp?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:32:19 UTC
01:32:19 KST

Breadcrumb
Who is Elif Eralp, the leftist leader with Turkish roots dubbed 'Germany's Mamdani'
Born into a Turkish family that fled the 1980 military coup, Elif Eralp is now within reach of governing Berlin after leading the left-wing Die Linke party to a historic election victory in the German capital.
The 45-year-old lawyer emerged as one of the biggest winners of Sunday's Berlin state election, with Die Linke finishing first and putting her in contention to become the city's next governing mayor.
Eralp has presented herself as a politician from a migrant background who puts housing, social justice and combating racism at the heart of local politics.
She has also spoken out against Germany's crackdown on pro-Palestinian activism, saying that "Germany must end its repression of those who stand in solidarity with Palestine and hold the Israeli government accountable".
Eralp's parents were socialists and trade unionists who were forced to leave Turkey after the 1980 coup for fear of persecution.
Her mother was pregnant with her when the family arrived in Germany, where Eralp was born in Munich in 1981. The family later moved to Dortmund and then Hamburg, where she grew up and studied law. She is married and has two children.
Early political activism
Eralp became politically active at an early age. As a child, she founded an environmental club before becoming involved in the anti-nuclear movement in Hamburg and Gorleben.
After studying law, she moved to Berlin in 2010 and worked as a legal adviser to Die Linke's federal parliamentary group alongside her trade union activities.
She officially joined the party in 2017 after years of working within its parliamentary groups.
She has linked her decision to join to the need for a political force that would offer an alternative to liberal economic policies and confront the rise of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD).
In 2018, she joined Die Linke's Berlin leadership and entered the state parliament in 2021. She later became deputy parliamentary group leader and has served as a deputy party leader in Berlin since last year.
Housing fuels Eralp's political rise
Eralp has built much of her political profile around Berlin's housing crisis, advocating rent controls, more public housing and bringing some properties owned by major housing companies into public ownership.
She has also called for curbs on the influence of major property companies and stronger protections against tenants being forced out by rising rents, advocating for Berlin to become a "city of solidarity".
Her focus on housing has allowed her to campaign heavily on everyday concerns such as rents, living costs and public services.
She has reportedly drawn inspiration from progressive US politician Zohran Mamdani in New York, particularly his focus on affordability as an issue capable of mobilising voters.
Palestine and Israel
Eralp's victory took on added significance as the far-right AfD won a separate state election in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern on the same day.
Confronting the far right and combating racism have been central to Eralp's political message, alongside calls for greater political and social participation among people from migrant backgrounds.
But her rise has also brought renewed attention to one of the most sensitive issues within Germany's left: Israel and Palestine.
During the campaign, Eralp stressed that antisemitism must be confronted and that she takes the concerns of Berlin's Jewish community seriously.
At the same time, she has expressed solidarity with Palestinians and stressed her desire to protect Jewish, Muslim and Palestinian communities in Berlin.
The position reflects a broader challenge for Die Linke as it seeks to maintain its focus on migration, anti-racism and Palestinian rights while addressing concerns over antisemitism and appealing to Berlin's diverse electorate.
Elif Eralp's path to governing Berlin
Eralp's rise was far from assured at the start of the campaign, but she put the housing crisis, cost of living, social justice and confronting the far right at the centre of her message.
Sunday's result transformed her political standing.
Die Linke won 25.7% of the vote, the party’s best result in Berlin since reunification, and more than double its 12.2% share in 2023.
Meanwhile, the governing coalition of the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and Social Democratic Party (SPD) lost its majority.
Eralp has said she wants to negotiate with the Greens and SPD over forming a new state government.
But finishing first does not automatically make her governing mayor. Taking the post will depend on coalition negotiations and whether the parties can agree on a governing programme.
Housing is likely to be among the most difficult issues in those talks, given Eralp's support for bringing major housing companies into public ownership and implementing the result of Berlin's 2021 housing referendum.
Any new government will also face significant financial constraints, potentially putting ambitious campaign promises up against competing spending priorities.
Die Linke's positions on Israel and Gaza could prove another point of contention as Eralp attempts to move the party from opposition into government in one of Europe's most diverse capitals.
Her rise is therefore no longer simply the story of the daughter of Turkish refugees who reached parliament. It now raises the question of whether she can turn a campaign built around housing, social justice and combating racism into a governing programme while navigating the demands of potential coalition partners.

How Washington left Saudi Arabia’s plea for help unanswered
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:31:34 UTC
01:31:34 KST

Breadcrumb
How Trump failed to answer Saudi plea for help against Houthis when Riyadh needed it most
Saudi Arabia has spent decades building its security partnership with Washington, buying billions of dollars in US weapons and cultivating close ties with successive American administrations.
But when Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman made a direct plea to US President Donald Trump for military help against Yemen's Houthis, Washington ultimately stepped away.
For two weeks, Trump had wrestled with whether to order US strikes on Houthi targets as the Iran-backed group intensified attacks on Saudi Arabia and made territorial gains in Yemen.
The issue came to a head on Thursday when Mohammed bin Salman called Trump and urged him to intervene against the rapidly advancing Iran-backed group, according to the New York Times.
Trump had told advisers a day earlier that he opposed strikes. After the call, however, he changed course and ordered the Pentagon to prepare for an attack.
By Sunday, US commanders had reportedly approved target lists and troops were loading bombs onto warplanes. Then Trump reversed course again, calling off the strikes, at least for now.
So why did Trump stop short when one of Washington's closest Middle Eastern partners was asking for help?
Why is Saudi Arabia asking for US help?
Riyadh's plea comes at one of its most vulnerable moments in years, as the Houthis renewed attacks on Saudi cities, oil infrastructure and shipping while making significant advances in western Yemen, taking the whole of Yemen's Red Sea coast including the area around the strategically important Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
The threat has been compounded by the wider war with Iran, which has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and increased Saudi Arabia's reliance on alternative export routes through the Red Sea.
Saudi Arabia's East-West oil pipeline, a crucial route for bypassing Hormuz, has also been largely shut following an attack Riyadh blamed on Iran-backed Iraqi militias.
That has left the kingdom facing pressure on its oil export routes from multiple directions.
Former US ambassador to Saudi Arabia Michael Ratney said Riyadh had spent decades investing in its US security partnership precisely for such a crisis.
"The reason a country like Saudi Arabia invests so heavily in developing a security partnership with the United States is for just this sort of eventuality," Ratney told the NYT.
Saudi officials have also made clear that they do not want to confront the Houthis alone after the kingdom's previous military campaign in Yemen became a costly, years-long conflict.
Why did Trump hesitate?
For Trump, intervening would mean opening another front while the US is already at war with Iran.
Most of his inner circle were either deeply sceptical of or opposed to joining Saudi Arabia's fight, amid concerns over pressure on the US military and its weapons stockpiles.
There were also doubts that another bombing campaign would work. The US struck more than 1,000 Houthi targets during a campaign lasting more than 50 days in 2025, but the group survived and has since rebuilt much of its military capability.
Trump has also stressed that the Houthis are currently targeting Saudi Arabia rather than the United States.
He said on Sunday that Washington had remained in communication with the group and that the Houthis had so far agreed not to fight the US. Houthi officials have disputed Trump's claim that they contacted Washington.
That gives Trump little incentive to restart a direct confrontation that could bring American ships back into the Houthis' sights and further threaten shipping through Bab al-Mandeb.
What does this mean for the US-Saudi relationship?
The Trump administration last week asked Congress to approve the sale of 48 F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia in a deal estimated at $24.3 billion, saying it would strengthen the security of a "major non-NATO ally", can be an indication that Washington has not abandoned Riyadh altogether.
But advanced weapons sales are different from direct US military intervention, and the latest crisis has exposed the limits of what Riyadh can expect from Washington when their immediate interests diverge.
Saudi Arabia has already been looking to broaden its security partnerships. Last month, it signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement (MJDA) with Turkey and Pakistan, under which an armed attack on one of the three countries is considered an attack on all.
Turkey has since said it is prepared to help meet Saudi military needs as Houthi attacks intensify.
For Riyadh, it is a reminder that even close ties with Washington offer no guarantee of US support when American interests lie elsewhere.

Ground-based beam could keep British solar drone flying
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
17:30:56 BST
01:30:56 KST

PHASA-35, the solar-powered stratospheric aircraft developed by BAE Systems’ Prismatic, has been selected as the flight demonstration platform for a power beaming technology intended to keep high-altitude aircraft flying through the night and the winter, under a £15.7 million contract linked to the Advanced Research and Invention Agency, the company stated.
The work forms part of ARIA’s Enduring Atmospheric Platforms programme, which aims to develop low-cost, long-endurance platforms for high-altitude communications. It runs in three stages over three and a half years and concludes with an integrated flight demonstration aboard PHASA-35.
The problem it addresses is the one every solar-powered high-altitude aircraft faces. Flight depends on the sun, and the company describes that as a significant challenge in places like Britain, where winter daylight is limited and the nights are long. According to BAE Systems, power beaming removes that dependency by supplying constant power regardless of season, making it easier to fly continuously for up to several months at a time.
The system uses what the company describes as a highly controlled ground-based energy beam directed at a dedicated receiver built into the aircraft’s wing, which converts it back into electricity to power the aircraft and charge its batteries. The release notes that similar microwave frequencies are already widely used in aviation, satellite communications and radar.
Bob Davidson, chief executive of Prismatic, said: “PHASA-35 has already proven its worth in the stratosphere as a low-cost alternative to satellites and now this exciting project will explore whether we can make it even more capable. This is a strong example of British organisations working together to advance an emerging technology.”
Rico Chandra, programme director for Enduring Atmospheric Platforms at ARIA, said: “This research expands the UK’s leadership in high-altitude platforms to become the place where this industry is designed, built and scaled. Getting there means backing bold ideas, from fixed-wing solar aircraft to designs nobody predicted, including aircraft that fly on spinning wings instead of propellers.”
PHASA-35 has a 35-metre wingspan and weighs 150kg, and according to the company has the potential to operate above 66,000ft for months at a time, delivering persistent communications, Earth observation and surveillance at a fraction of the cost of traditional satellites and with greater flexibility to deploy and upgrade.
According to the company the benefit may extend beyond endurance, since reducing the weight of onboard battery arrays could free capacity on an aircraft that already carries a payload of up to 15kg, which the company says can be used for sensors across intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, communications, Earth observation and defence applications.
Batteries are a large share of the weight on any solar aircraft of this kind, since they have to carry the aircraft through every hour of darkness, and the longer the night the more of them are needed. An aircraft able to draw power from the ground overnight could, in principle, carry fewer batteries and more equipment.
ARIA was established in 2023 as an independent body funding high-risk research, modelled in part on the American Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, with the freedom to back programmes that conventional funding routes would not.
Prismatic became part of BAE Systems in 2019, and PHASA-35 has flown a series of stratospheric trials in recent years.

A Government programme intended to raise public awareness of threats to the UK and strengthen national resilience is already under way and will continue through 2027, according to a parliamentary answer.
The timetable was set out in response to a written question from Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who asked when the national conversation on defence and security promised in the Defence Investment Plan would be delivered. Armed Forces Minister Louise Sandher-Jones said the work is being led by the Cabinet Office through the Home Defence Programme.
She said: “The National Conversation is a programme of public engagement led by the Cabinet Office as part of the Home Defence Programme. Delivery is already underway and will continue through 2027.”
Defence will support the programme through public engagement and communications intended to explain the threats facing the UK, the role played by the Armed Forces in deterrence and resilience, and how individuals, communities and employers can contribute.
Sandher-Jones said: “Defence is supporting this work through planned public engagement activities and a coherent programme of communications. These have been designed to improve understanding of the threats facing the UK, explain the role of Defence in deterrence and national resilience, and encourage practical participation by individuals, communities and employers.”
The work also links into the National Risk Register, which was updated in July 2026, and the internal National Security Risk Assessment used by government to assess the likelihood and potential impact of risks affecting the UK and its interests. According to Sandher-Jones, the public-facing register is intended to show how the Government is preparing for those risks while improving public awareness and supporting a broader approach to national resilience.
Defence is also contributing to a separate Cabinet Office-led national resilience public awareness campaign announced in the Annual Statement on National Resilience on 14 July. The Government intends to judge the wider programme against levels of public preparedness, participation and resilience.
Sandher-Jones said: “Success will be measured by increased public preparedness, participation and resilience.”
Government communications on defence and security are expected to increase ahead of ALBISTON SHADOW, described in the answer as a major UK Home Defence exercise, and NATO’s Crisis Management Exercise in spring 2027.

Continued Russian attacks on Ukraine's critical energy infrastructure are increasing civilian vulnerability and could make the coming winter even harder to endure, a UN-mandated commission warned Monday.
The Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine said Russian forces continued "systematic waves of attacks" on energy infrastructure during the severe winter of 2025-26, when temperatures fell to minus 20C (-4 F).
Power installations, transmission lines, heating facilities and gas infrastructure were damaged or destroyed, leaving millions of civilians facing prolonged power outages and heating shortages. Previous UN monitoring has also documented "systematic" Russian attacks causing extensive disruptions to electricity, heating and water.
"Continued attacks on energy infrastructure are making living conditions increasingly unbearable for civilians, and we are concerned that the coming winter will be more difficult to endure," commission Chair Erik Mose said.
The commission said Ukrainian authorities recorded cold-related deaths and injuries, while some civilians relocated during the coldest months.
It also cited reports of Ukrainian attacks on infrastructure in Russia and Russian-controlled areas of Ukraine that caused civilian casualties and damage to civilian objects, but said it had been unable to investigate the incidents due to a lack of access and information.

Kremlin claims Russia is 'no threat' in response to warning from France's Le Pen and Bardella

16:29:50 UTC

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Monday that Russia posed “no threat” to France or any other European country, responding to a statement criticising Moscow issued by Marine Le Pen and Jordan Bardella on Saturday.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Monday that Russia posed "no threat" to France or any other European country, local media reported. His comments came after the far-right National Rally party's Marine Le Pen and Jordan Bardella issued a warning to Moscow on the weekend.
"We will never tolerate a foreign power, specifically Russia, attempting to dictate our country's policies through intimidation, threats, destabilisation, or psychological pressure, either directly or indirectly," the pair said in a joint statement.
In response, Peskov told reporters that Russia was "not threatening France or any other country in Europe," adding that "President Putin has stated this on numerous occasions. We have no disputes with any European states that could give rise to any serious disagreements."
He added that "Russia poses no threat. Russia does not threaten anyone, nor does it blackmail anyone."
It comes as the pro-Putin United Russia party won a record supermajority in the State Duma, the lower house of Russia's parliament, authorities announced on Monday. Voting wrapped up on Sunday after a tightly controlled election that excluded parties critical of the Kremlin and the war in Ukraine.
Macron's crisis meeting
Last week, Russian authorities moved to seize the businesses and assets of companies including Nestlé and France's Auchan.
The French Ministry of Foreign Affairs reacted by condemning what it called the companies' "unjustified placement under temporary administration of Russian subsidiaries."
Meanwhile, Le Pen and Bardella's statement, which denounced the move as an "act hostile to the interests of France and Europe," followed a crisis meeting convened by French President Emmanuel Macron with party leaders from across the political spectrum on Friday, including Bardella.
During the meeting, Macron briefed attendees on several issues, including potential security threats posed by Russia.
He later told reporters that Moscow's expanding shadow operations across Europe represented a growing threat, adding that he had ordered measures to protect France's critical infrastructure from Russian "hybrid attacks."
In their statement, Le Pen and Bardella pointed to the recent drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in Germany, which German authorities have blamed on Russia.
"France is also affected by these actions, which specifically target our economic interests and companies in our defence industry," they said, while warning that Moscow could escalate tensions with countries supporting Ukraine, citing intelligence reports.
However, their condemnation of Russia is at odds with the National Rally's past leniency towards the Kremlin.
In 2011, Le Pen said she admired Russian President Vladimir Putin "to a certain extent," while arguing that France should work on building closer ties with Moscow.
She also "disagreed" with the idea that Moscow's annexation of Crimea in 2014 was illegal, citing a referendum held under Russian occupation.
The National Front — which subsequently became the National Rally party in 2018 — also contracted a controversial €9.4 million loan from a Russian bank in 2014 after French banks refused to finance their operations. The money was used to fund its 2015 departmental and regional elections campaign.
In September 2023, the party declared it had repaid the loan in full.
Funding for Ukraine
Despite the strong criticism of Moscow and "foreign pressure" in their statement, Le Pen and Bardella stressed that questions around financial support for Ukraine remained "legitimate."
In a recent interview with Bloomberg, Bardella sought to appease the controversy sparked by comments from Louis Aliot, the National Rally party's vice-president and mayor of Perpignan.
Speaking to BFM-TV in early September, Aliot said he would "turn off the tap" when asked about aid to Ukraine.
"The health system, the education system, the whole economy, everything has been cut to the bone, and yet we still find money to fund more weapons (...) I’m willing to accept that, but who pays for all this? You also have to know how to stop a war," he said.
Bardella responded by arguing that the plan was not to abandon Ukraine but that unconditional financial and military aid were not viable solutions.
French authorities react to Russian election
The United Russia party retained its majority in Russia’s parliament, election officials said Monday, after three days of voting that saw Putin tighten his grip on power.
Preliminary results indicated that United Russia would get 355 out of 450 seats in the State Duma, the Central Election Commission said, which would be a record high for the party if confirmed.
France's Ministry of Foreign Affairs has issued a statement acknowledging "the expected outcome" of the elections but said it regretted "that the conditions for a free, pluralistic, and democratic election" had not been met.
The ministry also declared that it was "disappointed" that Russia did not invite the observation mission of the OSCE's Representative Office for Human Rights and Democracy (OHR) to monitor the voting process.

‘Half my day’s pay goes to filling up my car now’: diesel crisis ripples across Britain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:29:25 UTC
01:29:25 KST

The smoke rising from the Kapotnya oil refinery to the south-east of Moscow marks one of Ukraine’s biggest air raids on the Russian capital since the start of the war, and the latest salvo in an energy crisis that threatens to affect households and businesses across the globe.
More than 1,500 miles away, British motorists are braced for the ripple effect from that conflict, and the US-Israel war on Iran. Average UK diesel prices are expected to reach record highs within days – while across Europe and the US, pump prices have already surpassed all-time highs.
In a call on Sunday, Donald Trump pressed Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russian refineries over concerns that the attacks were pushing up global fuel prices, the Financial Times reported. On Truth Social, Trump said Russia has “unfortunately lost control of its Diesel Oil Industry” and called for an end to “this ridiculous and never ending war”.
While the price of Brent crude oil – which briefly fell below $100 a barel on Monday – remains in flux, already hard-pressed households and small firms face a far greater cost threat at forecourt pumps as the combined impact of Russia’s war-damaged refineries and the Middle East crisis has erased about a fifth of the world’s diesel supplies.
“Around half my day’s pay goes to filling up my car now,” says Jon Barden, a former humanitarian adviser turned handyman, who says his fuel costs have doubled. His diesel Ford estate, once used for camping trips, is now used to carry heavy tools to jobs around Tottenham in north London.
Across Britain’s forecourts, the average price of diesel has climbed by 54% to 196.28p a litre since the Middle East crisis began in late February. It is expected to reach a record £2 a litre within days, with some forecourts already charging above the psychologically important mark.
In Europe, pump prices have already hit record highs in recent weeks, leading to unrest and growing calls for government leaders to protect consumers from the surge in cost.
While the popularity of fully electric and hybrid petrol vehicles may be on the rise in the UK and Europe amid attempts to move away from polluting fossil fuels, diesel remains the overwhelmingly dominant fuel. It is the single biggest cost for many independent traders and small business owners, powering transport, tools and services. It is also the economic lifeblood for farmers, and logistics and haulage businesses, layering costs on to grocery bills and consumer purchases.
“I’ve had to put my prices up,” says Barden. “I don’t want to because the people around here don’t have a lot of money. But when fuel prices go up everything else follows. The things I need to buy from Wickes to do a job will cost more before I even fill up,” he says.
In part, the surge in fuel prices is due to the rise in global oil prices following Iran’s effective blockade on the Strait of Hormuz, a vital trade route for Gulf oil. The price of Brent crude has climbed to a four-year high, raising the cost of refined oil products such as diesel and gas oil.
Yet the most pressing energy crisis is not a shortage of crude, but a shortage of the refining capacity to turn crude into the fuels consumers need. The Middle East crisis has severely damaged many of the region’s refineries, which once supplied 10% of the world’s fuels. What little can be produced has struggled to circumvent the blocked trade artery.
Output from Russia’s war-damaged refineries has fallen by almost a third over the past year to reach a 20-year low following sustained drone attacks by Ukraine, according to the International Energy Agency. The latest strike on Kapotnya came after a similar attack by Ukraine in June.
Although Russian oil exports have been subject to toughened EU sanctions since 2022, a reduction in exports to other parts of the world, including Asia, is likely to push up global prices.
In China, which hosts the world’s largest refining capacity, and had been the largest importer of Iranian crude, exports of refined oil products have been capped since March to safeguard the country’s domestic supply.
The global refining slump has helped to keep oil market prices down by dampening the demand for crude. But this is cold comfort for economists who warn that the ‘crack spread’ – or the price difference between crude oil and its refined products – has climbed above $100 a barrel on the continent for the first time and is likely to rip through the economy by raising the cost of all transported goods, as well as household bills.
Diesel in particular is “the workhorse fuel that powers business, haulage, deliveries and rural communities”, according to Luke Bosdet, the AA spokesperson on fuel prices. “Increased fuel costs are passed on to customers, and then on to consumers, which adds to inflation.”
While sales of new diesel passenger cars have plummeted over recent years as motorists increasingly opt for petrol, hybrids, and electric vehicles, the UK’s consumption of diesel has continued to climb because of its role as a crucial industrial fuel.
“Almost everything on supermarket shelves got there on a lorry,” Richard Smith, the managing director of the Road Haulage Association said. “When diesel goes up that cost has nowhere to go but on to the price of goods.”
The AA’s chief concern is for “small businesses, such as taxis and vehicle-based services, and rural communities who already do higher mileages even before diesel costs went through the roof”, Bosdet adds. “They don’t get to add diesel surcharges to invoices, like many of the big companies, for fear of losing customers.”
Mehmet, from Clacton, began driving black cabs in central London 35 years ago. “When I first started, diesel cost 10 bob a gallon,” he laughs. In modern terms this would be 11p a litre, or a fraction of the looming £2 a litre average expected nationwide within days, while cab fares remain capped.
Diesel taxis are easily outnumbered by EVs in London, but they still make up about a third of the black cabs. Drivers were told in February that they would be allowed to raise their fares by 4% this year. At the time, the rise was above inflation – amid concerns over an exodus of black cab drivers. However, the US-Israeli bombardment of Iran ignited a war that has caused fuel costs to surge and inflation to remain well above the Bank of England’s 2% target, at 3.1% last month.
“We’re stuck with it,” says Mehmet. “We don’t want the meter price to go up, because then we lose custom. But we can see oil companies making billions in profit while we take home less. How can that be right?”
The UK may be acutely exposed to the global squeeze on road fuel supplies. The number of refineries in the UK has dwindled since the start of the century from nine to four, causing the UK’s reliance on diesel imports to climb from 14% of the UK’s diesel consumption in the early 2000s to 54% last year, according to Fuels Industry UK.
Elizabeth de Jong, chief executive of Fuel Industry UK, said: “Our latest annual statistics, published earlier this week, show that UK demand for petroleum products increased by 1% in 2025 to almost 61m tonnes, while the closure of the Grangemouth and Lindsey refineries reduced UK refining capacity by almost a quarter.
“We are currently having to import about 55% of our road diesel, meaning a growing dependence on overseas supply. Global events such as the conflict in the Middle East demonstrate the vital role that UK refineries play and why they are crucial to our economy,” she said.

“Brazil is one of the most significant contexts worldwide for the Italian presence abroad. Nearly one million Italian citizens live here, along with a community of approximately 32 million people of Italian descent: an extraordinary presence that, over the generations, has contributed profoundly to Brazil’s growth and development and that today serves as a natural bridge between our two countries.”
    This was stated by Massimo Dell’Utri, Undersecretary of State for Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, who was on a mission to Brazil from September 17 to 22, with stops in São Paulo and Porto Alegre, as part of activities related to his portfolio for Italians abroad.
                                    
                                       
				    “Being here,” Dell’Utri emphasized, “means first and foremost encountering a community that has managed to maintain a strong bond with Italy, while fully integrating into Brazilian society and contributing to its economic, social, and cultural growth. Italian identity in Brazil is not merely a remembrance of our roots: it is a living, dynamic reality capable of shaping the future.”
    The Italian presence in Brazil has taken on a particularly significant dimension over time. As of July 31, 2026, there were 979,650 Italian citizens registered in consular records, with São Paulo alone exceeding 400,000 and Porto Alegre exceeding 140,000. “A community of this size,” added the Undersecretary, “requires a diplomatic-consular network capable of meeting the needs of our citizens. For this reason, I would like to thank the staff of the Embassy, the Consulates, and the honorary network for the daily work they carry out in the service of Italians.”
    Particular attention is being paid to consular services, digitization, and the network’s ability to respond to ever-increasing demand. “We know that the growth of the community places ever-increasing pressure on our offices. Our task is to continue improving services, simplifying procedures, and investing in innovation. Digitization is not an end in itself, but a tool to bring the public administration closer to citizens.”
   In 2025, the Italian consular network in Brazil issued over 93,000 passports, while the use of digital services and the issuance of electronic ID cards also grew significantly.
                                    
                                       
				   Another central theme of the mission is the representation of Italians abroad, particularly in light of the upcoming elections to renew the Com.It.Es. “The Com.It.Es. serve as an important link between Italian communities, the diplomatic-consular network, and institutions. Their role is invaluable, and for this reason, it is essential that citizens be informed and able to participate with full knowledge of the facts.” The elections to renew the Com.It.Es. were formally called on September 3. In Brazil, seven committees will be involved. To vote, one must apply for registration on the voter roll by November 4, 2026, while candidate slates may be submitted from September 23 to October 3. Ballots must be received by consular offices by December 4. 
   “Our goal,” concluded Dell’Utri, “is to strengthen the relationship between Italy and its communities abroad. Italians around the world are not simply citizens living outside the national borders: they are an integral part of our country and an extraordinary network of relationships, skills, culture, and opportunities. Brazil is one of the most important examples of this.”

69% of Russian soldiers on Zaporizhzhia front line have criminal records, Ukrainian military says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

69% of Russian soldiers on Zaporizhzhia front line have criminal records, Ukrainian military says
Of the Russian force fighting near the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, 69% of servicemen have criminal records, Anastasiia Shevchenko, a spokesperson for Operational Task Force South, said on Sept. 21.
The figure likely reflects both the overrepresentation of those from poor and disadvantaged parts of Russian society among voluntary recruits, and the widely reported practice of offering men contracts to avoid prison time, often under coercive circumstances.
According to internal analysis conducted by the Ukrainian military, 31% of the overall Russian force had signed up to avoid criminal charges, and 24% were in the military to improve their financial situation, Shevchenko said in comments to Ukrinform.
Since holding an unpopular "partial mobilization" in fall 2022 — conducted in response to a successfull Ukrainian offensive — Moscow has deliberately avoided a forced draft and has instead mostly relied on luring in volunteer recruits with substantial sign-up bonuses.
These voluntary incentives work best in the most economically and socially depressed regions of Russia, where military service is often perceived as a quick pathway to financial stability for entire families, or as a way out of crippling debt.
This recruitment is complemented by foreign fighters from countries primarily in the Global South, as well as by prisoners, who were first recruited en masse by the Wagner mercenary group in 2022.
While Russia still fields special units in its regiments and brigades made up of those taken straight from the penal system with promises of amnesty, many of the regular recruits have also had some form of criminal past.
Although Kyiv has said recruitment rates remain stable, the current inflow of new Russian soldiers — often used in one-way infiltration assaults across the front line — has not been enough to produce major Russian battlefield gains in 2026.
Having concluded a three-day parliamentary election choreographed to reaffirm the wartime legitimacy of Russian President Vladimir Putin and his "party of power," the Kremlin is preparing to conduct a new round of forced mobilization to boost the military's stagnant offensive efforts, Kyiv has warned.
According to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, Russia plans to mobilize 300,000 troops to complement existing inflows of recruits into the Russian army, and to either boost Moscow's main offensive effort on the "fortress belt" cities of Donetsk Oblast, or to create new threats in other areas, including Ukraine's northern border.

Sirens sound as drones approach the border

Airports in Lublin and Rzeszów temporarily suspended operations to give military aircraft freedom of movement. Polish authorities said the measures were preventive and intended to protect Polish airspace.
More strikes on the border zone
On 13 September, Russian strikes near the Yahodyn-Dorohusk border crossing damaged a gas station and hit the locomotive of a Kyiv-Warsaw passenger train about two kilometers from the Polish border. No deaths were reported, and the border crossing temporarily halted operations.
On 19 September, Poland again activated ground-based air-defense systems and increased radar reconnaissance in response to another wave of Russian strikes on Ukraine. The operation ended the same day with no violation of Polish airspace recorded.
Shelters, sirens, and a 1939 echo
Beyond sirens, authorities have marked nearly 3,500 official shelter locations in Lublin Voivodeship. More than 500 State Fire Service stations and volunteer fire units took part in special exercises on 19 September to practice responses to warning signals and emergency alerts.
"We are building a civil-protection system virtually from scratch," Kierwiński said at a briefing in Lublin. "We have very, very little time."
The 17 September strikes fell on the anniversary of the Soviet Union's 1939 invasion of Poland. Prime Minister Donald Tusk described the Russian attack as "massive, extremely brutal."
The 13 September strikes near the border also drew a response from Kyiv. Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha described them as Putin's terror "knocking" directly on the doors of the EU and NATO and called for a "full trade embargo, a total entry ban, and complete sanctions against Russia's military-industrial complex."

The source said al-Zaidi intends to provide fresh assurances over his government's commitment to the disarmament process and ensuring that the Iraqi state retains a monopoly over the use of force.

UK charges man over alleged Rwanda genocide offences

UK charges man over alleged Rwanda genocide offences
LONDON, Sept 21 - A 65-year-old Rwandan man has been charged with genocide-related offences allegedly committed during the 1994 Rwanda Tutsi killings, British prosecutors said on Monday.
Vincent Brown, formerly known as Vincent Bajinya, was charged with one offence of conduct ancillary to genocide and six offences of conduct ancillary to murder as a crime against humanity.
Britain's Counter Terrorism Policing War Crimes Team said Brown was accused of encouraging others to kill Tutsis in Kigali in April 1994. The investigation began in 2019 following a request from the Rwandan government and involved years of international cooperation, it added.
Brown was accused of having "directed and incited acts of murder and genocide carried out by others", the Crown Prosecution Service said.
The charges against Brown were the first brought in the United Kingdom relating to the Rwandan genocide, the CPS added.
Brown, who is remanded in custody, is due to appear at London's Westminster Magistrates' Court on Tuesday.
Police said investigations into six other individuals remain ongoing, including two men arrested in 2024 and 2026 on suspicion of genocide and crimes against humanity who remain on bail.
More than 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus were killed in 100 days in the 1994 genocide, orchestrated by the Hutu ruling majority and meticulously executed by local officials and ordinary citizens. REUTERS

As Fears of Post-Election Mobilization Swirl, Russian Activists Prepare for the Worst
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:17:13 UTC
01:17:13 KST

Rumors that the Kremlin could order another mobilization to sustain its invasion of Ukraine after this month’s parliamentary elections have circulated in Russian media for months.
Now that the ruling, pro-Kremlin United Russia party has secured a record majority, anti-war activists and lawyers told The Moscow Times that anxiety is rising, even though helping Russians avoid military service has long been a routine part of their work.
When the Kremlin called up 300,000 reservists in September 2022 in Russia’s first mobilization since World War II, the announcement sparked an exodus of tens of thousands of Russians and protests in dozens of cities. At least 20,468 of the men who were mobilized in 2022 were confirmed killed as of this month, according to an independent tally.
Activists told The Moscow Times that the renewed speculation about another mobilization “echoes with pain” — and that a new call-up could be faster and harder to evade than the one in 2022.
“Almost everyone here has friends or relatives who have already been affected by [the draft],” said an activist for New Tuva, an exiled anti-war and Indigenous rights movement from Tyva, a southern Siberian republic bordering Mongolia. The activist spoke on condition of anonymity for safety reasons.
A region the size of Tunisia with a predominantly Indigenous population of less than 350,000 people, Tyva has suffered the highest per capita losses of any Russian region in the war. More than 2,100 men and women from the republic have been killed, according to figures compiled by activists.
During the 2022 mobilization, men in the region were taken from their workplaces, detained on the street or collected from their homes at night to be sent to the front, said Sholbaana Kuular of New Tuva.
“We have been living with anxiety and fear since June because we have not yet recovered from the so-called ‘first wave’,” she said.
President Vladimir Putin directly linked the Sept. 18-20 elections to public support for the war, urging Russians to vote and “demonstrate that millions of people stand behind our soldiers.”
Yet Russian officials, including Putin himself, have repeatedly sought to dispel speculation over a new draft. Over the past three months, they have denied planning a new mobilization 18 times.
After the 2022 mobilization triggered widespread discontent, the Kremlin has relied on contract soldiers lured to sign up through payments of up to 5.5 million rubles ($70,000) for a year of service — or simply forced to sign military contracts.
Because military contracts cannot be annulled while the 2022 mobilization decree remains in force, lawyers say that contract soldiers and mobilized servicemen remain bound to serve until the war ends or the authorities release them.
Activists have documented cases in at least 17 regions in which security forces and military enlistment officers detained men and pressured them to sign contracts following coordinated street raids. Some were reportedly threatened with having drugs planted on them.
Idite Lesom (“Get Lost”), a group that helps Russian men avoid military service, said pressure on potential recruits and conscripts performing their mandatory military service has risen sharply in recent months.
“The authorities are making extremely effective use of the fear of mobilization,” Idite Lesom spokesman Ivan Chuviliayev told The Moscow Times.
Recruiters tell men that they can still choose some of the terms of their service if they sign a contract voluntarily while warning that they would have no such choice during a mobilization, he said.
“They are building this very effective narrative: ‘Sign a contract now, before mobilization begins. Once mobilization starts, it will be too late’,” Chuviliayev said.
In 2024, Russia introduced an electronic military register containing records on citizens liable for military service, which could make a new mobilization easier to carry out.
The register allows authorities to use electronic summonses to prevent conscripts from leaving the country. Russians subject to mandatory military service are barred from leaving Russia from the date a summons is deemed served. An electronic summons is considered served seven days after it appears in the register, regardless of whether the recipient has seen it.
New Tuva volunteers help fellow Tyvans by connecting them with military lawyers or translating guidance on avoiding military service into Tyvan, the republic’s widely spoken Indigenous Turkic language.
“Covert mobilization in Tyva has not stopped for a single day, and so our work has continued uninterrupted,” Kuular said.
Tyva is one of many regions and ethnic republics where fears of a second mobilization are particularly acute, as these places are still grappling with the effects of the first wave.
Maria Vyushkova, a leading expert on regional and ethnic disparities in Russia’s war casualties, has attributed this disparity to the disproportionate mobilization of ethnic minorities and Indigenous peoples in 2022.
“It cannot be ruled out that the same will happen in the event of a second mobilization,” Vyushkova warned in an interview with The Moscow Times in January.
The election results could also help indicate which regions might face the heaviest recruitment pressure in the event of another mobilization, exiled political commentator Ekaterina Schulmann said.
“Every Russian citizen has a vital interest in ensuring that, in their own region, United Russia gets as small a number of votes as possible,” Schulmann said.
“Because if United Russia performs particularly well, that will be seen as evidence that the local administration is working well and effectively and that the population is disciplined and compliant,” she added, suggesting that the authorities see such regions as easier places to draft men.
Sargylana Kondakova, co-founder of the Free Yakutia Foundation, an anti-war and Indigenous rights group from the republic of Sakha (Yakutia), likewise said that if a second mobilization happens, it would be “nothing like the first,” especially because of the introduction of digital summonses.
“We are seeing a large wave of emigration from the republic. People often ask us what documents to prepare before leaving the country,” said Kondakova. “And those people who can’t leave are preparing to hide locally.”
In Tyva, men who could afford to leave the country did so over the summer, while those who lacked the financial means to go abroad relocated to nearby regions in hopes of evading a call-up, according to the anonymous New Tuva volunteer based in the republic.
Estimates of the number of people who have left Russia since February 2022 range from 500,000 to 1.3 million. Yet it is hard to measure how many more are considering leaving this year.
Despite widespread fatigue with the war, activist Kondakova ruled out a return of the street protests seen in 2022 — even in Sakha, where Russia’s largest women-led anti-mobilization protest took place.
“Most of those who were willing to protest left and the remaining people are apathetic and depressed. It would be wrong to say that they came to terms with their fate,” said Kondakova. “They will resist, but in their own quiet way.”
For now, experts say the Kremlin is still recruiting enough soldiers to cover its battlefield losses.
Military analyst Dmitry Kuznets told The Moscow Times that Russia is recruiting around 30,000 people a month, allowing it to offset the number of troops killed, seriously wounded, captured or missing. He said the recruitment rate had remained unchanged since July.
“There is no need for an urgent mobilization” in Russia, he said. “Whether [Putin] is assessing the situation rationally remains an open question.”

After 9 women murdered, police link 1 death to possible love triangle

Police investigating murders of 9 women in South Africa neighborhood link 1 death to possible love triangle
South African police said Monday they had arrested three people over the killing of one of nine women found dead in a neighborhood east of Johannesburg in a series of murders that have alarmed the nation.
The discovery of the nine bodies in Kempton Park over two months has fueled fear and anger, as authorities investigate whether a serial killer or killers were responsible.
A man and two women were arrested over the weekend over the killing of Jabulile Ntimba, whose body was found on Sept. 17 and was the ninth victim, police said.
As in most of the cases, her body was found on the side of the road, partly clothed.
"There does appear to be an indication that her murder may have stemmed from a relationship-related matter, including what has been described as a possible love triangle," deputy police chief Tebello Mosikili said.
Gender-based violence is endemic in South Africa, despite years of government pledges to tackle the problem and even declaring it a national disaster.
The South African Police Service has issued a public warning for women to be cautious when doing activities like jogging in the area.
President Cyril Ramaphosa on Monday echoed the police pledge that those responsible for the killings would be held accountable.
"We will be pulling out all stops to find these perpetrators," he told journalists, vowing additional measures to tackle violence against women.
"We are going to be deploying more money, more resources, more technology, to ensure that we deal with the fear that women are now subjected to," he said.
The latest arrests bring to four the number of people held by police in connection with the Kempton Park killings.
"While the investigation must establish whether these cases are linked, the possibility that a perpetrator or perpetrators may be targeting women demands our urgent and determined attention," acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia said in a statement. "A multidisciplinary investigation has been established to examine possible links between the cases, identify those responsible and bring them to justice."
A man arrested over the murder of a woman whose body was found in July remains in custody and is due back in court on Oct. 28, police said.
"We are not going to rush these investigations simply to make arrests. We owe it to the victims, we owe it to their families, and we owe it to justice to get this right," Mosikili said.
Separately, police said another woman was found dead on Sunday in Soweto, south of Johannesburg, her body wrapped in a duvet and dumped near a dam.
Police also said two alleged serial rapists were due in court in the eastern province of KwaZulu-Natal. A 46-year-old man has been linked by DNA to 16 rape cases in the province's largest city, Durban, while a 36-year-old man has been linked to at least 14 cases across two provinces.
Violence continues to plague South Africa
South Africa suffers from a murder rate of more than 60 a day on average, one of the highest globally.
The country recorded 5,427 murders between April and July — an average of 45 a day — according to the latest crime statistics.
Femicide rates in South Africa are among the highest in the world, according to the U.N.'s agency for gender equality. Last year, the government declared gender-based violence and femicide a national disaster, according to the U.N.
A 2024 study in South Africa revealed that three women were killed every day by an intimate partner from 2020 to 2021. A study in 2022 found that more than 35% of South African adult women had experienced physical or sexual violence at some point.
Amnesty International South Africa previously said the recent discovery of the bodies was "just another horrific reminder that women in South Africa are not safe."
The Commission for Gender Equality has called for urgent preventive action, including a safety audit of the affected areas involving police, municipal officials, transport authorities and community safety structures.
It said the audit should assess lighting, surveillance, pedestrian and public transport routes, neglected spaces, police visibility and access to emergency assistance.
"Women should not have to be killed before an area receives heightened attention," commission spokesperson Javu Baloyi said.

The US president says fertilizer from Lukashenko's Russia-allied regime will cost far less than Canadian supplies, the latest sign of Washington's warming relationship with Minsk.
US President Donald Trump said Washington was working on a "massive" deal to buy fertilizer from Belarus, despite Minsk's repression of dissidents and support for Russia's war in Ukraine.
Trump said on social media that the cost of the potash from Belarus would be "substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada," the US neighbour against which he has stepped up a trade war.
Potash is a potassium-rich salt mined mainly for fertilizer, helping crops grow and improving yields. Canada supplies most of the potash used by American farmers.
Belarus is one of the world's largest producers, but the European Union bans imports of Belarusian potash and has frozen the assets of state producer Belaruskali.
The announcement is the latest in a series of deals between Washington and Minsk. Talks led by US envoy John Coale have seen Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko pardon hundreds of political prisoners in exchange for the easing of US sanctions on Belarusian firms, including its potash industry.
Belarus remains a close ally of Russia and allowed Moscow to use its territory as a staging ground for the 2022 invasion of Ukraine and more recently authorised joint nuclear drills.

Houthis move to seize strategic terrain after Trump calls off airstrikes at last minute
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:14:38 UTC
01:14:38 KST

Houthi fighters are moving to seize strategic heights in Yemen that would cut the Red Sea coast off from areas held by Saudi-backed forces after Donald Trump called off US strikes on the group at the last minute, reportedly as bombs were being loaded on to aircraft.
Amid increasingly heavy fighting in Yemen, which has displaced tens of thousands of people in recent weeks, the New York Times reported on Monday that the US president had flip-flopped wildly in recent days after a call from Saudi Arabia for US strikes on the Houthis.
It comes amid the Houthis’ rapid advance on the ground with the group gaining control over much of Yemen’s Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and advancing to areas adjacent to the crucial Bab al-Mandab strait, which Saudi Arabia has used as an alternative route for oil exports bypassing disruption in the strait of Hormuz.
In the call reported by the New York Times, Saudi Arabia’s crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, implored Trump to step in to help halt the Houthi advance after weeks of such appeals. Trump, who had been resisting joining the Saudi war in Yemen, after the call then told the Pentagon to prepare for airstrikes against the Houthis before reversing course once again, the report said.
Trump has frequently given mixed signals to Riyadh, telling reporters during a visit to Ireland earlier this month that the Houthis “called us, and they don’t want to fight us”, adding that the group was “allowing ships to pass” the Bab al-Mandab strait and that the situation would “work out very well”.
He added that the Houthi problem was limited to “one country” an apparent reference to Saudi Arabia promising to “take care of fixing that”.
The UN says hostilities in Yemen have displaced at least 125,000 people since the start of September. Taiz city has received the largest number of displaced persons, taking in up to 86,000 Yemenis since the recent escalation began.
The rapid advance by the Iran-aligned group this month has extended the wider Middle East conflict to a new theatre and further threatened global energy supplies.
Washington has so far rebuffed repeated pleas from Prince Mohammed to join the fight in Yemen with the Houthis claiming on Saturday they had fired on Riyadh, where columns of smoke were visible near the main airport.
The Yemeni president, Rashad al-Alimi, spoke to Trump on Sunday, requesting support for his UN-recognised government in its fight against the Houthis. Trump made no direct pledge of military support during the call, sources said.
Saudi Arabia has launched hundreds of strikes in recent days on Houthi positions in the strategic Kahboub mountains, according to the group, but making little impact on the advance of its fighters.
Fighting has centred on the outskirts of the remote Al-Wazi’iyah district in Taiz province and Ras al-Ara along the Indian Ocean coast, which separate the Red Sea coast from the city of Aden, where the government is based. The Houthis aim to secure the rear of their forces around the Bab al-Mandab strait by taking control of the mountains, which would also allow them to open new fronts, according to sources who spoke to Reuters.
The surge in fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis has created a new dilemma for Trump, under pressure to help defend Washington’s close Saudi allies but anxious not to further expand the deeply unpopular war he launched in February against Iran.
The US bombed the Houthis for two months in early 2025, but Trump called off those strikes after reaching a ceasefire with the group and has kept out of the conflict since.
Amid the broad failure of the US-Israeli war against Iran, and with the US midterm elections looming, the Trump administration’s priorities appear to be to secure at least some oil supplies through the strait of Hormuz, while avoiding a wider entanglement in Yemen.
That, however, invites longer-term risks, not least the growing alienation of key US allies in the Gulf, including Saudi Arabia, where Washington is increasingly seen as an unreliable ally, that could also undermine the so-called “security for oil” understanding where the US provides a defence umbrella for Gulf states in exchange for energy supplies.
Reuters contributed to this report

01:13:07 KST

A send-off for mobilised men in Kazan, Tatarstan. Photo: Yegor Aleyev / TASS
Today marks the fourth anniversary of the “partial” mobilisation. Announced by Vladimir Putin in September 2022 following a series of military setbacks on the battlefield, the decree triggered the sudden conscription of hundreds of thousands of civilian men into the armed forces. The chaotic drive sparked a massive exodus, with hundreds of thousands of Russians fleeing across the borders to neighbouring countries to avoid being sent to the front. Over the past four years, the demographic makeup of the Russian military has shifted continuously, but the fate of those drafted in the autumn of 2022 remains one of the most opaque aspects of the war in Ukraine.
In our count of Russian army’s losses, we attempt to establish exactly how a person ended up in the war: whether they signed a contract before February 2022, enlisted as a volunteer after the invasion began, were recruited as an inmate from a penal colony, or were mobilised. Over time, information regarding mobilised soldiers has grown increasingly scarce: obituaries from the past two years most often omit any mention of how the deceased ended up at the front. Therefore, we consider our figure of 20,500 mobilised personnel killed to be our most conservative estimate and a significant undercount.
Assigning the “mobilised” status is further complicated by the fact that other types of recruitment can be identified through indirect signs. For example, a “volunteer” can be identified by their age, by social media profiles pointing to a civilian life prior to 2022, or by holding the rank of private at the time of death (if someone served in the army before the war, it is highly unlikely they would remain a private by 2026). The “inmate” status can be assigned if we locate an active prison sentence matching the deceased’s full name. For the “mobilised” status, however, there are no indirect indicators—only explicit mentions of mobilisation in an obituary.
Because of this lack of data, we cannot provide a full assessment of what has happened to mobilised men over these years. However, we have gained access to two major data leaks, which we have used to track developments over the past two years.
Mediazona and other media outlets obtained the first leak from a Russian military medic, Alexey Zhilyaev: the bulk of the dataset concerns patients in Defence Ministry hospitals, but it also includes the rosters of several military units and formations. These lists contain the names of around 40,000 mobilised men, predominantly covering the period of 2023–2024.
The second leak consists of the staffing rosters of several hundred military units, with records current as of July 2025. This leak contains data on more than 200,000 Russian servicemen, 16,000 of whom are designated as “mobilised”.
As usual, before working with the leaks, we verified their data against state registries and other open sources, and concluded that they are reliable.
From the first leak, we selected 2,515 mobilised soldiers—focusing exclusively on those who served in units mentioned in the second leak—and examined how their status had changed over the course of a year.
The discrepancy amounted to 1,152 men. The fate of 912 of them remains unknown: they could have been transferred to other military units for which we lack data, or discharged on medical grounds. The latter is more likely, as the core of our first list is based on records of the wounded.
Of the 1,152 men missing from the later rosters, 240 were killed.
In the July 2025 leak, 1,363 men remained. Of these, 972 entries on the staffing roster retained the “mobilised” designation. However, 355 men had changed their status, becoming contract soldiers (marked “fixed term”), with contract signing dates in 2024 and 2025.
Another 36 men were in the process of being discharged on medical grounds.
Out of the 1,363 men, only 21 became officers—specifically, junior lieutenants.
At the time of this summary’s publication, we have managed to confirm the deaths of 187 soldiers from the second list via state registries.
In total, out of the initial 2,515 mobilised men, we have confirmed the deaths of 427. Meanwhile, only 173 of these have been recorded via obituaries and added to our RUSSIA 200 database.
Based on these figures, we can assume that our data on killed mobilised soldiers underestimates the true losses in this category by at least half (and likely even more, given our classification errors). We are unable to estimate the number of wounded. Furthermore, even among those who remain on military unit rosters, at least a quarter have signed a contract and lost their “mobilised” status.

Russian losses in the war with Ukraine.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:12:51 UTC
