9 ‘boundaries’ keep Earth livable. We’ve breached 7 of them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
15:52:18 UTC
00:52:18 KST

Humans are continuing to push Earth beyond livable levels of heat, pollution and other conditions—both for us and for millions of species.
That’s the upshot of the annual Planetary Health Check, released on Monday by the Planetary Boundaries Science Lab at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK) in Germany.
The report shows that seven of the nine chemical and physical “boundaries” we need to stay within to keep the planet habitable are at their worst recorded values since scientists first conceived of them in 2009.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
“The diagnosis is unambiguous. Pressure is rising across every Planetary Boundary already outside the safe operating space,” said lead author of the report and PIK scientist Boris Sakschewski in a statement. “It means that the risk of large-scale, persistent and potentially irreversible change is increasing, while our margin for error in tackling these problems is shrinking.”
Sakschewski and other PIK researchers came up with these measures as a key to a sort of planetary life-support system—keeping within the boundaries they laid out is crucial to maintaining the environment we and other species have adapted to it over eons.
When they published the first Planetary Health Check in 2023, they found that human actions, from fossil fuel burning to excess fertilizer use, had pushed Earth past six of the nine boundaries. Last year we breached a seventh—ocean acidification.
Surpassing one of these limits isn’t a recipe for automatic doom, like flipping a switch. Rather “it’s like blood pressure,” said Katherine Richardson, an Earth systems scientist at the University of Copenhagen and lead author of the 2023 report, to Scientific American at the time of that report’s release. A high value is “not a guarantee that you’re going to have a heart attack,” but it raises the risks of one, she said.
Each measure is compared against a preindustrial baseline, or the period before humans began burning fossil fuels in earnest—roughly the mid-19th century. Beyond each boundary is a “zone of increasing risk,” in which the odds of moving away from those preindustrial conditions rise.
Among the boundaries that have been breached, according to the new report, are carbon dioxide concentrations, which reached a record 426 parts per million (ppm) because fossil fuel burning had not decreased at nearly the needed pace. That is compared with 280 ppm, which was the concentration prior to the industrial revolution, and 350 ppm, which many scientists consider a “safe” limit (and was surpassed in 1987).
Those rising CO2 levels are rapidly changing the planet’s climate, leading to weather extremes such as the unprecedented heat waves in Europe and other areas of the world this summer. Research has shown that many of these would not have happened without the influence of climate change. Earlier this month the United Nations acknowledged that global temperatures would blow past the goal of Paris Agreement’s target of no more than 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) of warming.
Fossil fuels and the CO2 they release are also what pushed the planet past the ocean acidification boundary last year because the ocean absorbs some of the excess gas from the atmosphere, lowering the water’s pH. That increasing acidity can make it hard for shell-building organisms to develop their protective dwellings and could even causes shells and corals to dissolve. This would be a blow not only to biodiversity but also to economically valuable ecosystems; a 2020 report by the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration found that ocean acidification would cost the country’s economy billions of dollars.
Humans are putting pressure on other aspects of the environment as well. Excess phosphorus and nitrogen from widespread fertilizer use flows into rivers and seas where they can spark toxic algal blooms. Artificial chemicals, such as plastics, dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (DDT) and “forever chemical,” or perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) , disruptively accumulate in food chains.
Just two of the nine limits remain intact: ozone depletion and aerosol pollution in the atmosphere. Only ozone shows clear progress away from the planetary boundary as a result of the success of the Montreal Protocol, which set up the phasing out of the chemicals that erode Earth’s protective ozone layer. Aerosol emissions have declined globally—partly from efforts to reduce pollution from global shipping—but are still high in some regions.
The new report’s authors underscored the urgency of maintaining momentum to keep below the boundaries where we are seeing progress and to reverse course where we are not.
“We do not have the luxury of time, but we do have the knowledge, capacity and solutions to change course,” said Johan Rockström, PIK’s director and a co-author of the report, in a statement. “Accelerating action to return to the safe operating space across all Planetary Boundaries is essential to protect lives and livelihoods, and to deliver on the promise of shared future prosperity.”

What F-16 Gun Kills Tell Us About the Future of Ukraine’s Air Force
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
15:50:26 UTC
00:50:26 KST

A remarkable cockpit photograph released by Ukraine last week captures far more than the destruction of a Russian Geran jet-powered attack drone. It illustrates both how far the Ukrainian Air Force has come—and the gap between the force it has today and the one it would need to become a major European air power in the future.
This is important because the future of Ukraine’s ability to defend itself does not depend on getting a few more F-16s, but rather on its ability to build an air force capable of the challenge.
The photograph is extraordinary. Taken from the cockpit of a Ukrainian F-16 during a Russian mass air attack on Sept. 10 and released a week later, the image shows a Geran drone falling from the sky, trailing smoke. According to my sources in Ukraine, it was the pilot’s third gun kill of the sortie.
Think about that for a moment.
An aircraft designed during the Cold War and transferred to Ukraine after decades of service in Western Europe, is being flown by a pilot with the Ukrainian Air Force against Russian cruise missiles in an air war unlike anything NATO has previously experienced. And the pilot is shooting them down with the F-16’s 20mm cannon.
On the night of Sept. 9-10, Russia launched 149 Shahed-type cruise missiles, along with decoys and other unmanned aircraft, against Ukraine. According to the Ukrainian Air Force, 128 were destroyed or suppressed. Roughly half of these were Gerans, which are jet-powered variants of the Shahed.
The photograph is not only a terrific advertisement for the ingenuity and skill of airmen in Ukraine, but also a warning to those drawing the wrong conclusions about airpower from this conflict.
Ukraine’s success with the F-16 does not mean these aircraft are sufficient for its long-term needs.
The F-16 Ukraine Has Is Not the F-16 of Today
The European aircraft originally provided to Ukraine are principally F-16AM/BM Mid-Life Update aircraft. They began life as older Block 15 F-16 fighters and subsequently received substantial avionics and weapons upgrades. They remain capable airplanes, and they have been modernized with capabilities comparable to later F-16C/D models. But there is an important distinction between an upgraded aircraft conceived more than 40 years ago and what the F-16 has become today.
The newest F-16 Block 70/72 aircraft are equipped with the APG-83 active electronically scanned array radar, enhanced mission computers and electronic warfare capabilities, advanced datalinks, updated cockpit displays, infrared search-and-track integration, and compatibility with a wide range of modern weapons. Its upgraded airframe is rated for a 12,000-hour structural service life.
The APG-83 is derived from the AESA radars used in the F-22 and F-35, providing pilots greater situational awareness, electronic protection, and the ability to search and track targets more effectively in a complex electromagnetic environment. That matters enormously over Ukraine.
The Ukrainian Air Force is not confronting a single threat. Its pilots face an extraordinarily complicated mixture of slow propeller-driven drones, faster jet-powered Gerans, cruise missiles, Russian fighters, long-range surface-to-air missile systems, electronic warfare, and dense ground-based air defenses.
A modern fighter must therefore do much more than fly fast and carry missiles. It needs to find, identify, prioritize, share, and engage multiple threats while surviving in a heavily contested electromagnetic environment. That is fundamentally an information problem—and modern sensors, electronic warfare and networking are what increasingly determine success.
Shooting Gerans Is Only One Mission
A second lesson from this photograph is the means the pilot used to dispatch the threat. Using the F-16’s gun preserves scarce air-to-air missiles. Ukrainian Air Force officials have acknowledged the pace of Russian air attacks imposes significant pressure on Ukraine’s missile inventories
Ukraine’s air force must perform several missions simultaneously: defend cities and critical infrastructure against cruise missiles; deter or engage Russian air forces; suppress enemy air defenses; conduct precision attacks into Russia; protect Ukrainian ground forces; and contribute to the broader intelligence and command-and-control picture. That requires both highly capable aircraft and scale.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in 2024 that Ukraine needed 120 to 130 F-16s to challenge the number of Russian aircraft committed to the war—many more than they currently possess. That was Ukraine’s stated requirement, not an independent assessment, but it illustrates the difference between possessing F-16s and operating a combat air force of meaningful size. Aircraft numbers by themselves, however, can also be misleading.
A force of 100 fighters is inherently smaller than it seems. At any given moment, some are undergoing maintenance while several must be earmarked for training. The aircraft left must be dispersed, protected, and repaired. Pilots must get enough flying hours to remain proficient. Weapons, engines, spare parts, and ground support equipment must be continuously available.
Airpower depends on a system—not simply an inventory of airplanes.
Building an Air Force, Not Donating Aircraft
One of the more consequential developments in Western assistance to Ukraine is largely unseen, but vitally important. The Air Force Capability Coalition has gradually moved beyond simply transferring F-16s to Ukraine toward creating a Western-style aviation ecosystem encompassing combat aircraft, pilot and maintainer training, weapons, logistics, protected infrastructure, command and control, and airborne early warning.
Ukraine’s future force architecture also includes French-built Mirage 2000s and Swedish Gripens alongside U.S.-made F-16s.
This is the correct way to think about airpower: A modern fighter becomes dramatically more effective when it is properly supported. Airborne early-warning aircraft that can see hundreds of miles, ground-based sensors, secure datalinks for sharing targeting info, and commanders able to assemble those inputs into a common operational picture all enhance operational performance.
There are legitimate questions about cost, training capacity, sustainment, competing aircraft types, and the rate at which any fighter force can realistically be expanded. Discussion about offering newer F-16s miss the point that doing so would not eliminate the need for ground-based air defense, inexpensive drone interceptors, or other cost-effective ways of defeating mass attacks. No country can economically afford to use its most sophisticated weapon against every inexpensive threat.
But the strategic distinction is important. The F-16s flying over Ukraine today began as an emergency wartime capability. Ukraine’s Defense Ministry now describes the broader effort as a transition from its Soviet aviation inheritance toward a modern, networked Western model. That transition will ultimately be far more consequential than any individual aircraft transfer.
The image released this week captures the beginning of that story: A pilot in the Ukrainian Air Force maneuvering an F-16 over Ukraine while the wreckage of a Russian cruise missile falls toward the earth. The next chapter is about whether Ukraine’s wartime collection of fighters evolves into the sustainable, technologically modern, and fully integrated air force it needs, with the capacity to defend its airspace for decades—and carry the fight to the aggressor if required.
That is the difference between providing Ukraine airplanes and helping Ukraine build a credible air force.

EU moves to curb energy and water for data centres
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
15:49:57 UTC
00:49:57 KST

The European Commission has unveiled new sustainability rules aimed at monitoring water and energy consumption of energy-hungry data centres - although minimum performance rules will only be introduced in 2027.
The European Union is writing the sustainability rulebook for AI's power-hungry future, but tech giants like Microsoft are already weighing in on how the bloc's new rules should work.
EU data centres with more than 500 kW of installed capacity that report under the bloc's energy efficiency rules will receive an electronic sustainability label as of 21 September, according to new rules unveiled by the European Commission on Monday.
"The aim of the rating scheme is to increase transparency about the energy use of data centres and to become a resource that will inform better policymaking and procurement of more sustainable digital assets and services across Europe," the Commission said in its new rules on rating schemes for data centres.
The move comes as Brussels aims to triple data centre capacity across the bloc by 2035, as part of a push to reduce reliance on Big Tech and develop Europe's own AI capabilities. EU lawmakers have, however, recently raised concerns about Microsoft's efforts to influence the new rules.
At the same time, the EU is grappling with a growing energy crisis and data centres are already seen as a growing source of electricity demand and have faced opposition from some local communities.
The Commission argues that the bloc needs data centres to underpin cloud computing, AI and digital services, but their rapid expansion is putting pressure on electricity networks, water resources and local communities.
In 2024, data centres in Europe used 68 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity and the EU expects that number to hit 114 TWh by 2030, gobbling up 3.2% of all the electricity in the bloc, up from the current 2.5%, according to EU data.
The new sustainability label is intended to make facilities comparable on power and water efficiency as well as the sourcing of their electricity. However, despite mandatory reporting requirements for data centres above 500 kW being in place since 2023, the Commission acknowledged that compliance remains incomplete.
"In the first year (…) we had something like one third of the data centres reported. In the second year, it improved, and in the third year, the preliminary results improved further. We are, I think, hitting the 50% mark easily,” a Commission official speaking on condition of anonymity told reporters on Monday.
The Commission official noted, however, that enforcement largely rests with EU countries. The real pressure will come early next year.
Ceilings on energy and water only in 2027
For now, the Commission is stopping short of imposing a hard ceiling on energy or water consumption.
The real regulatory teeth — minimum performance standards — will be announced in 2027 to establish a floor and to prevent new facilities from being built below certain efficiency standards, according to the Commission official.
However, the "probation time” creates an important opening for the industry, which has been lobbying the Commission on these key sustainability parameters.
In a July 2026 submission to Germany's federal government, Microsoft said it supported using clean power, energy and water efficiency as sustainability indicators, while specifically seeking changes to the proposed water-efficiency bands in the label, according to the German lobby register.
Bram Vranken, a researcher and campaigner at the watchdog Corporate Europe Observatory (CEO), criticised Big Tech's influence over the new EU rules on data centres.
"The Microsoft confidentiality clause is kept in – though rewritten – so that's hugely problematic. It will also mean that much of the information in the label will be impossible to check," Vranken told Euronews.
He added that with the current rules, if a Google data centre scores high on the label in terms of energy efficiency, it might consume an undisclosed gigawatt of power without being properly disclosed.
Because the bloc needs to rely on Big Tech companies to build its infrastructure, it gives them considerable importance in the regulatory debate. While the Commission's new rules reflect its ambition to make Europe a "leading AI continent", they also highlight the tension between rapidly expanding the infrastructure needed for AI and regulating the US technology companies expected to provide much of it.
Commission officials say the new sustainability label can recognise low-emission energy, including nuclear, while the future minimum-performance standards could eventually become mandatory.
Brussels is also examining whether data centres could become more active participants in the electricity system by providing flexibility and potentially supplying waste heat to as many as four million European homes.

The top American television networks suspended on Monday their involvement in a rotation of broadcasters covering President Donald Trump, as three leading outlets filed a lawsuit after being banned from the White House last week.

"This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles," the organizations said in a court filing.
Shortly afterward, the five major U.S. broadcasters said they were halting "pool" coverage of the White House in solidarity with CNN.
CNN had been scheduled to serve Monday as the White House TV pool, a rotating assignment in which a broadcaster films on behalf of all television outlets for the day.
"The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting," ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox and NBC said in a statement.
The boycott means there will be no pooled coverage of Trump's travel to the U.N. General Assembly in New York on Monday, where he is due to meet a series of world leaders.
Trump was unrepentant, with the 80-year-old Republican branding the media a "cancer" and a threat to national security.
"The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish," Trump said on his Truth Social network.
"It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America."
Trump announced the ban on Friday in a major escalation of his years-long assault on the U.S. media, especially on outlets that report critically on him and his administration.
Journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were denied access to the White House grounds on Saturday and had their passes confiscated.
The outlets said the White House revoked their journalists' credentials "without notice or process" because it "objected to our reporting."
"Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference," they said in their joint statement.
Their lawsuit calls for the immediate overturning of the ban and a ruling that it violates the First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution, which upholds the right to free speech.
Trump has not detailed what prompted the ban, but said in response to a question from an Agence France-Presse (AFP) reporter in the Oval Office on Friday that it was "really just cumulative stories over the last two years."
"They want to try and diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration," Trump added.
Trump warned Friday that other outlets could face a similar fate, without saying which.
The billionaire former reality TV star has long attacked media outlets that have aired critical coverage of his campaigns and administrations, repeatedly blasting the press as the "enemy of the people."
Through both terms in the office, he has claimed journalists have failed to show sufficient appreciation for his accomplishments. Trump has also stood out in presidential history for routinely insulting journalists he doesn't like, both in person and on social media.

ECHR to hear case concerning fate of 10 Ukrainian children after Russia's annexation of Crimea
The European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) will hold a public hearing on 22 September in a case concerning 10 Ukrainian children who were living in childcare institutions when Russia seized Crimea in 2014.
Source: ECHR on 21 September, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The case was brought by the Ukrainian Helsinki Human Rights Union (UHHRU), which says the children were forcibly given Russian citizenship before being put up for adoption, and that some may have since been adopted.
Ahead of the hearing, Thórdís Kolbrún Reykfjord Gylfadóttir, Special Envoy of the Council of Europe Secretary General on the situation of children of Ukraine, said the case is a reminder of the need to keep Ukrainian children at the heart of the political agenda.
Quote: "Behind every case is a child whose fate matters, whose identity must be protected, and whose whereabouts must be known. We must not stop asking questions and demanding answers."
More details: The applicants state that after Russia established de facto control over Crimea, it kept the children in institutions, withheld information about their whereabouts, and placed them within Russian adoption or foster care systems.
They argue that this breached the children's right to liberty and security under the European Convention on Human Rights.
The UHHRU also argues that the arbitrary change of the children's citizenship and the publication of their details on adoption websites failed to respect and protect their social identity as Ukrainian citizens and violated their right to privacy and family life under the European Convention on Human Rights.
The court will rule on the admissibility and merits of the case at a later date.
Background:
- In September, the European Court of Human Rights threw out an application brought against Ukraine by a Donetsk woman who complained that attacks by the Armed Forces of Ukraine had destroyed her flat.
- In July, the ECHR ruled that Russia had violated property rights and the right to a fair trial in a case concerning the seizure of land from owners in occupied Sevastopol.

Turkish foreign minister urges US to use influence on Israel to end destabilizing actions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
15:46:19 UTC
00:46:19 KST

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said Monday that Türkiye expects the United States to use its influence to urge Israel to end policies that undermine regional and global peace and stability.
Speaking at a panel titled “Türkiye-US Relations on the Eve of the Centennial,” organized by the Turkish Communications Directorate in New York, Fidan said Türkiye and the US share an interest in sovereign and stable states capable of providing security and welfare in the region, particularly Syria and Iraq.
Fidan also called for greater regional ownership of security, saying: “Local solutions have a better chance to live.”
This is why we believe that countries of the region should take greater responsibility for the security and stability of their own geography. This is why we need to embrace and advance regional ownership,” he said, citing the Mecca alliance between Türkiye, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia as an example.
Fidan said three key challenges were the Iran war, the risk of the Yemen conflict spreading to neighboring countries and Israel’s destabilizing policies across the region.
"These threats reinforce one another and obstruct diplomacy. Addressing them requires effective regional responsibility and close cooperation with the United States," he said.
"In particular, we expect the United States to further use its influence to urge Israel to end its policies that undermine both regional and global peace and stability," he added.
Fidan said the Mecca alliance between Türkiye, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia “provides regional ownership and institutional foundation, while strengthening cooperation and supporting regional peace and security.”
Fidan described Gaza as a central test of efforts to establish regional security and said a lasting resolution to the Palestinian issue remains essential.
"A lasting resolution of the Palestinian question remains essential for stability in the Middle East and beyond," he said, adding that Türkiye supports US President Donald Trump's efforts to bring the Gaza crisis to an end.
"Commitments put forth through the peace plan must now be fully implemented,” he said.
Fidan said Türkiye also supports dialogue and diplomacy for achieving lasting peace in Ukraine and maintaining channels of communication with both Kyiv and Moscow.
‘Regional ownership’
Asked by Kilic Bugra Kanat, research director at the SETA Foundation in Washington, D.C., whether the initiative was primarily a deterrence mechanism or the beginning of a more institutionalized regional security architecture, Fidan said regional ownership aligns with the new approach the US is adopting not only in the Middle East but also in Europe and the Asia-Pacific.
He said Türkiye's regional vision rests on "no domination, no submission, but cooperation," describing the defense arrangement as a starting point for building regional ownership.
Fidan said a longstanding lack of trust among regional countries has fueled counterterrorism campaigns, wars and the invitation of outside forces into regional conflicts.
“We come together around a defense club, not to deter somebody, to make sure that we commit to each other's security, territorial integrity, and sovereignty,” he added.
“There are other countries that would like to be part of this regional platform, and our idea is once we institutionalize our partnership in a proper way, I think that the invitation will be open to other countries to join,” he added.
Asked whether the defense agreement had passed its first test following recent Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, Fidan pushed back on the comparison, noting that NATO's Article 5 has been invoked only once in decades and arguing it was unfair to judge a "newborn" defense alliance against a decade-old Yemen crisis when "we've just started."
Turkish-US relationship demonstrated 'time-tested enduring value'
Fidan said the bilateral relationship between Türkiye and the US had “time-tested enduring value” and had evolved from ties between two geographically distant nations into a partnership and alliance with an impact beyond their borders.
He noted that Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and US President Trump had a “central role” in the current momentum in bilateral ties, adding that the task was to translate it into concrete benefits and institutionalize cooperation.
"Our task is to turn this momentum into concrete benefits and institutionalize our cooperation not only for our countries but also for maintaining peace and stability in our region," he said.
"As we enter our second century of diplomatic relations, we are determined to realize the full potential of our cooperation and resolve the issues holding it back," he added.
Responding to questions from participants, Fidan said Türkiye maintains “great coordination” with US mediators including Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner on issues ranging from the Russia-Ukraine war to Gaza, Libya, the Horn of Africa and the South Caucasus, describing bilateral cooperation as at an “unprecedented level.”
On the CAATSA sanctions and the sale of F-35 fighter jets, Fidan said Erdogan and Trump agreed during their White House meeting that the issue should be resolved “as soon as possible”, and that both sides have since been working to remove the obstacle, though it is "taking a little bit more time than we expected."

Government identifies 50 sites for accelerated housing programme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
15:46:14 UTC
00:46:14 KST

Government identifies 50 sites for accelerated housing programme
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Housing minister Elanor Boekholt-O’Sullivan has drawn up a list of 50 locations where the Dutch government wants to speed up housebuilding to meet the target of 100,000 new homes a year.
The plan includes 26 sites near railway stations that are already well served by transport links and utilities, making them relatively easy to develop.
The first five locations have already been identified in Maastricht, Haarlem, Leeuwarden, Deventer and Weert, with another five due to be announced later this year. All 10 developments are supposed to be finished by 2040.
The cabinet is investing €7 billion over the next eight years in affordable homes and wants to scrap planning rules and building requirements that slow down the process.
Affordable homes are supposed to account for two-thirds of all new projects, with at least 30% going on social housing.
Around €3 billion of the funding will take the form of subsidies, while investors who build houses for the mid-rental sector will receive a payment for each unit they construct from 2029.
The government is anxious to retain private investors who have been selling rental flats in response to the Affordable Rent Act, which has tightened the rules used to calculate rent levels, and lingering uncertainty over the “box 3” tax on income from assets.
Local and regional subsidies
Local councils will be encouraged to buy land for housing, with the national government providing financial support to share the risk. The municipalities and provinces will also be able to hire 200 equivalent full-time staff to work on issuing permits, while a team of experts will tour the country using their specialist knowledge to revive projects that have become stuck in the system.
Analysts noted that some of the regulations would have the effect of pumping more money into existing plans. “That means that some building projects probably won’t go ahead because they’re not profitable,” Stefan Groot, housing market economist for Rabobank, told NRC.
Boekholt-O’Sullivan said: “I will continue with what works and reform what doesn’t. It is clear what has to happen, money is avaiable and there are enough building projects.
“What matters now is moving from the drawing board to the foundations. The government can’t do it alone: we need builders, investors, local authorities and provinces to work with us.”

nearly 1,000 wooden chimes turn le bruit du bois into an alpine instrument
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
15:45:26 UTC
00:45:26 KST

High above Faverges-Seythenex in the French Alps, a long timber structure cuts across the grassy slope. It is a pavilion, but its architecture comes with a second use. Visitors can pick up a wooden stick and play it. Rows of suspended timber pieces produce a sequence of tones that travels along the structure and out into the valley. Those who have been there recall how its sounds have joined the wind and distant cowbells which already move through the landscape.
Called Le Bruit du Bois, or The Sound of Wood, the fifteen-square-meter installation was designed by Antoine Aunave, Flora Peyrot, Mathilde Steenhaut, and Luc Loviton for the 2026 Festival des Cabanes. The four ENSA Montpellier students won this year’s competition with the proposal, which was selected from close to 200 entries. The festival placed fourteen temporary structures around the Sources du Lac d’Annecy for its eleventh edition.
The idea becomes clearest once someone starts moving along The Sound of Wood pavilion. The timber elements change in length across the structure to give each section a different sound. Running a stick through them sends a progression of tones down the wall. A single gesture turns the whole elevation into something closer to an oversized xylophone, with the surrounding valley acting as its acoustic room.
There are close to 1,000 of these wooden chimes. Fabricating and installing them became a substantial part of the build for the young team, who worked with a group of fellow architecture students to construct the project on site. Their repetition gives the pavilion its visual character too. Seen from a distance, the pieces gather into a thin horizontal band against the steep terrain. Up close, the gaps between them let the landscape remain visible through the wall.
the timber pavilion stretches horizontally across the steep alpine landscape
a slender batten becomes structure and sound
At the center of the design is a timber batten measuring just four centimeters across. The same slender profile is repeated through the pavilion, bending slightly as it rises and responding to the wind with small movements. The architects use this single dimension to build the structure and generate its sound, allowing a straightforward piece of milled timber to do much of the work.
The pavilion sits above the uneven ground on an elevated walkway, with a handrail following one edge. Its asymmetrical frame stretches farther on the north side, guiding the approach before visitors move into the denser field of hanging pieces. Inside, the experience becomes more enclosed. Timber surrounds the body while openings between the chimes keep views toward the mountains and fields in reach.
visitors can play Le Bruit du Bois by moving a wooden stick across its chimes
architecture joins the existing sounds of the alps
Sound gives the cabin a relationship with its setting that a framed view alone could hardly achieve. A visitor can set off a run of wooden tones, then let them fade back into the valley. At other moments, the breeze moves through the slender pieces on its own. The pavilion shifts between something people actively play and something that responds to the weather around it.
It’s especially fitting for Le Festival des Cabanes, an architecture festival built around temporary interventions in the landscape around Lake Annecy. Here, the project asks visitors to listen as much as look. The satisfying part is how little machinery the effect requires. Timber, movement, and the acoustics of an open valley are enough to turn a small cabin into an instrument that can be heard well beyond its footprint.

a four centimeter timber profile repeats throughout the slender structure
different lengths of timber produce different tones as visitors move along the pavilion
wind can set the timber elements in motion between visits
the elevated walkway follows the uneven ground of Les Combes de Seythenex

British Museum bans photos of Bayeux Tapestry as crowds linger
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Bayeux Tapestry craze prompts photo ban at British Museum
The British Museum said on Monday that it has banned people from taking photos of the Bayeux Tapestry to prevent crowds from backing up at the new exhibit. The 1,000-year-old artwork is on display in the UK after an unprecedented loan from France, and tickets are sold out until December 31.
The British Museum has banned visitors from taking pictures of the Bayeux Tapestry in order to keep the crowds flowing through an unprecedented London exhibition, a spokesperson confirmed Monday.
Excited visitors have been flocking to see the nearly 1,000-year-old artwork since the start of the sold-out exhibition earlier this month.
Read moreBayeux Tapestry 'mania' sweeps UK as first exhibition outside France opens
"There has been enormous interest in viewing the tapestry, and our priority is to ensure that all visitors have the best experience possible," a spokesperson said in a statement.
"In order to do this, we have made the decision to restrict photography while people are moving along the length of the tapestry."
The 11th-century wonder of the medieval world offers an insight into life in England both before and after the invasion by William the Conqueror's Norman army.
The unprecedented loan from France, the result of years of diplomacy and set to last until next July, has been hailed as a symbol of renewed cross-Channel ties following the rancour of Brexit.
Watch moreThe Bayeux Tapestry's risky journey across the Channel
Depicting the 1066 Battle of Hastings, the 70-metre-long tapestry has shadowy origins.
It is widely thought to have been made in England almost 1,000 years ago before being transferred to Bayeux in France.
Under the visitors' guidance section on the British Museum's website it states that the sightseers move through the exhibition in a one-way system for a visit that lasts "approximately 40 minutes".
"Drawing or sketching are not permitted. Photography is not permitted," it adds.
Photography had initially been allowed, but that decision was reversed when queues began to build up as visitors dawdled. It was not immediately clear when the ban went into effect.
In what is believed to be its first time travelling outside France, the tapestry depicting 627 figures and more than 700 animals has been laid flat in a raised glass cabinet.
In its home in Bayeux, northwestern France, it is displayed hanging vertically.
Animations projected on the wall in London accompany the tapestry, zooming in on details and key events in the artwork, which is replete with gore and drama.
Tickets to the exhibition are sold out until December 31, with a second tranche for viewings until July 11 due to go on sale on October 21.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Vance defends White House media restrictions as news outlets sue Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21

00:43:52 KST

Vance defends White House media restrictions as news outlets sue Trump
'They can still report. They still have the access to free speech. They're just not going to get an office in the White House anymore,' vice president says
Diyar Guldogan
21 September 2026•Update: 21 September 2026
WASHINGTON
US Vice President JD Vance on Monday defended the Trump administration's decision to restrict CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, arguing that the outlets are not being prevented from reporting on the administration but are instead losing special access to the White House.
Vance's comments came after CNN, MS NOW and Politico filed a lawsuit against President Donald Trump and his administration, arguing that the restrictions violate their rights under the First Amendment.
Asked by reporters whether it was appropriate for the president to ban media outlets because he dislikes what they report, Vance challenged the premise of the question.
"He's not banning media outlets," Vance said. "What he's doing is saying, 'We're not going to give you special access to the White House if you engage in what is effectively propaganda'."
Vance claimed that roughly 92% of the stories published by the three outlets about Trump and his administration are "negative." He argued that such coverage does not represent the views of the American public.
"So, if you're going to engage in what is effectively far-left propaganda, why would a Republican White House give you special access?" he said.
The vice president was then asked about his past statements supporting free speech and whether the administration's actions amounted to an attack on press freedom.
Vance rejected that characterization, saying the outlets remain free to report on the administration and communicate with government officials outside the White House.
"They can still report on the Trump White House," Vance said. "They can still get the public reports. They can still, of course, talk to people in the administration and outside the administration."
Vance said the administration's decision was specifically about access to the White House rather than the ability of the organizations to publish news.
"What the president has said is, 'We're not going to give you special access inside the White House'," he said.
"They can still report. They still have the access to free speech. They're just not going to get an office in the White House anymore."
Trump barred reporters from the three organizations from entering the White House compound last week. Security personnel turned away journalists from all three companies on Saturday morning following the directive.

Why Bangladesh Skipped the Delhi BRICS Summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
15:41:00 UTC
00:41:00 KST

After the significant mass uprising of 2024, Bangladesh has had two governments, yet there has still been no bilateral visit between the heads of government of Bangladesh and India. A possible India visit by Bangladesh’s Prime Minister Tarique Rahman came under discussion ahead of the recently held BRICS summit. In the end, neither the Bangladeshi prime minister nor any representative from Dhaka attended the summit in New Delhi.
It could be said that Bangladesh’s absence from the BRICS summit came amid a broader recalibration of Dhaka-Delhi relations following the 2024 political transition. After the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP)-led government assumed office in February this year, diplomatic engagement between Dhaka and New Delhi has increased. Both sides have expressed their willingness to improve relations. However, political trust and some unresolved issues continue to remain as challenges to further advancing ties.
The formal position of the Bangladesh government is that the invitation to the BRICS summit was extended to Bangladesh as the chair of BIMSTEC, not to Rahman as prime minister. State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir clarified that Rahman’s first visit to India should not take place through a multilateral conference but rather be a full-fledged bilateral visit. Kobir also said that Dhaka would consider such a visit only when a “conducive environment” is created.
New Delhi responded that Rahman received two separate invitations: one for a bilateral visit and another to participate in the BRICS outreach session as the chair of BIMSTEC. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi first invited his Bangladeshi counterpart, along with his family, in February immediately after the BNP-led government took office.
In August, New Delhi reportedly made preparations for a possible visit by Rahman, but it ultimately did not take place. Media reports now suggest that discussions are underway to facilitate his visit in November this year.
Bangladesh is not a member of BRICS, but because this year’s BRICS summit was held in South Asia, Bangladesh’s invitation as the chair of BIMSTEC and its participation in the outreach session were relevant. The main benefit to Dhaka would have been the opportunity to meet global leaders and expand diplomatic engagement.
Many countries sent their foreign ministers to the BRICS summit. Why did Bangladesh decline to send any representative?
The explanation provided by Kobir regarding the expectation of a “conducive environment” and ensuring “mutual respect” is relevant here. Bangladesh’s High Commissioner to New Delhi, Riyaz Hamidullah, also said that Rahman could not attend the BRICS summit in India due to “certain circumstances” in the overall bilateral relationship.
Rahman’s government has made a commitment to move away from the previous framework of diplomacy and pursue a “Bangladesh First” policy. Thus, while the prime minister has not set foot in India since taking office, Rahman has already visited Malaysia and China and is visiting the United States for the U.N. General Assembly meeting this week.
The bilateral relationship with India became asymmetric during the previous Awami League regime. Issues such as border killings and alleged interference in domestic politics have also triggered public resentment toward India. The new government has to consider not only improving relations with New Delhi but also ensuring dignity and domestic political acceptance.
Many Awami League leaders convicted by Dhaka’s courts are currently in India and have been involved in various forms of political campaigning. Sheikh Hasina, the ousted prime minister of Bangladesh, delivered a virtual address from Delhi on August 5, which further deepened the trust deficit between the two countries. Bangladesh has demanded the extradition of Hasina, as well as the return of those allegedly involved in the killing of Sharif Osman Hadi, the murdered spokesperson of a platform called Inqilab Mancha.
Recent developments suggest that Hasina’s presence in India and her political statements from there remain at the center of the current difficulties in Bangladesh-India relations. New Delhi believes that political engagement can create a pathway to resolve existing disputes. Dhaka, on the other hand, wants a conducive political environment and mutual respect to be established before a visit.
India has its own concerns about the future trajectory of relations. Bangladesh’s growing engagement with China, including discussions over infrastructure cooperation, has drawn attention in New Delhi due to the strategic importance of the region. For India, the challenge is not only rebuilding ties with the new government in Dhaka but also navigating a changing geopolitical environment in South Asia.
Creating a favorable political and trustworthy environment requires not only diplomatic efforts from both sides but also a more supportive surrounding atmosphere. For instance, some Indian media outlets and political figures continue to spread disinformation and misleading narratives about Bangladesh, particularly regarding the treatment of religious minorities. Such trends have increased in Indian media since the fall of the Awami League government.
Bangladesh’s law and order situation has also been subject to comments by Indian political figures that Dhaka considers inaccurate, while some Indian media present an exaggerated picture of developments on the ground. It is worth noting that Bangladesh ranks better than India in both the Reporters Without Borders (RSF) World Press Freedom Index and the Global Terrorism Index of the Institute for Economics & Peace (IEP).
In the long run, distance between Bangladesh and India is unlikely, meaning Rahman may visit India sooner or later. The two countries need to continue working together. Resolving issues of mutual interest remains essential.
Bangladesh’s overall relationship with India should not be viewed solely through the lens of recent political circumstances. The relationship between the two countries is deeply rooted in economic, social, and cultural connections between their peoples.
Bangladesh’s absence from the BRICS Summit will not determine the future of Dhaka-Delhi relations. The key question now is how both governments create a pathway for improving ties – one that accommodates mutual interests, political sensitivities, and strategic realities.

====================================================================================================

Europe is under attack from three sides – but the EU and Nato are unfit to defend us | Nathalie Tocci
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
15:37:32 UTC
00:37:32 KST

Europe’s strategic predicament is ever clearer, and ever darker. The continent is at war, which is being fought militarily in Ukraine, but is escalating rapidly across Europe through hybrid attacks. Germany’s disclosure that it blames Russia for the drone attack at Leipzig airport; a Russian drone strike on a train near the Ukraine-Poland border; an Italian jet shooting down a Russian drone over Lithuania; flares fired from a Russian warship at a Danish helicopter – all within the space of a couple of weeks – tell a coherent story. Whether because Russia is bogged down and unable to advance in Ukraine, or because it believes the US will not come to Europe’s rescue, Vladimir Putin’s regime is ever more bent on escalating its aggression in Europe.
Putin’s calculus is not irrational. Trump never misses a chance to lash out at Europe – the latest example being his threats of further tariffs on the EU if Brussels proceeds to offer Canada “associate membership”. Europeans have grown numb to Trump’s insults and threats, but these threats do underline his deep antipathy, suggesting that if a Russian attack warranted a response, Trump might look the other way. The US certainly can’t be relied on to have Europe’s back.
This is the context in which Ursula von der Leyen caused surprise last week by proposing associate membership of the EU for Canada. To bolster Europe’s defences, the European Commission president also wants a “European security council”, and a mutual solidarity mechanism to respond to hybrid attacks.
While they have distinct rationales, these ideas fit into the same strategic logic: in a world of predatory powers, the “rest of the west” must huddle together.
The threats are not only external. Along with Putin’s Russia and Maga America, the rise of the far right in Europe completes a triangle of threats. The far right is a threat to liberal democracy. But by instigating internal division and pushing for disintegration, it also supports the divide-and-rule designs of predatory external powers, representing a challenge to Europe’s independence and sovereignty. It has taken the earthquake of the AfD’s successes in German regional elections for von der Leyen to acknowledge openly that Europe’s threats are also homegrown. Better late than never.
Faced with this unprecedented convergence of threats from three sides, leaders are scrambling for a response. Nato has what it takes to defend Europe against Russia. But if its majority shareholder – the US – is unwilling to step in, the question of its plans, structures and capacities is moot. If a hybrid attack on a European country caused civilian casualties, would Nato be bypassed if Washington signalled its unwillingness to act? Collective defence would not even be invoked if the anticipated result were the US’s betrayal of its European allies.
This is where von der Leyen’s emergency protocol comes in, filling the gap between the high-water mark of mutual assistance – article 42.7 of the EU’s founding treaty, which covers armed aggression – and nothing at all. The attacked state would activate the protocol, an emergency European Council would convene, and the commission and EU high representative would propose responses, including evacuation and medical support, stockpiling and energy security, economic coercion, military mobility and more. The mechanism could extend to like-minded non-EU partners, starting with Canada, Norway, the UK and Ukraine. The proposal to offer Canada associate membership, while still undefined, can be read in this light as well.
On paper, it all makes sense. In practice, it is hard to see such a mechanism operating seamlessly, let alone rapidly, given the EU’s organisational complexities, its slowness to act and its internal divisions.
Hence the proposal for a European security council, consisting of those countries willing and able to contribute to the defence of Europe, without the US if need be. Some of these countries would be EU members, but not all – again, Canada, the UK, Ukraine and possibly Turkey.
Both the problem and the solution are clear. To protect itself against predatory powers, what remains of the west must cooperate ever more closely. But the existing multilateral organisations – Nato and the EU – are unfit for purpose. Nato will remain anchored to the US, while the EU is slow and cumbersome, built for peacetime. Its membership, while large, is not wide enough, excluding key players in the wider European space.
Developing alternative forms of EU membership could be of interest not just to Canada, but to the UK, too. The idea was first raised by Berlin for Ukraine, in fact, but Kyiv turned down the offer, seeing it as second-class. Ukraine deserves full EU membership, but if a substantial associate membership is on the table in the short term, it should take that, while continuing to press for more.
The rise of far-right nationalism means that reaching consensus within the EU will become harder, not easier – which is precisely where the proposal for a smaller, more agile European security council comes in, provided far-right governments do not simultaneously come to power across major European countries.
Von der Leyen’s security proposals are sensible and urgently needed. The potential pitfall lies not in the message, but in the messenger. In her years at the helm of the commission she has grown a reputation for centralising power and overstepping boundaries, irking other EU officials in Brussels as well as European capitals. When it comes to security and defence especially, sovereignty is jealously guarded by the EU’s nation state governments. It would be tragic if European governments ended up killing off a set of good ideas because of Europe’s institutional turf wars. Rearranging the deck chairs on the Titanic is the last thing Europe and its partners need right now.
- 
  Nathalie Tocci is a Guardian Europe columnist

PrivatBank puts Dnipro-Arena, training base up for sale at UAH 140.7 mln
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
18:37:14 EEST
00:37:14 KST

PrivatBank has put Dnipro-Arena stadium and a training base in Dnipro up for an open auction through the Prozorro.Sale system at a starting price of UAH 140.7 million excluding VAT, the bank's press service said.
The auction will be held on October 6 in a three-round English auction format. The guarantee deposit is UAH 7.04 million.
The lot includes the stadium, with a total area of 15,950 square meters, a training base complex covering 13,060 square meters, and a separate covered football field of 7,470 square meters.
Dnipro-Arena has a capacity of approximately 31,000 spectators, a VIP box with 296 seats, a 550-seat restaurant, a 105-by-68-meter football pitch with heating and automatic irrigation, and parking for buses and cars.
The training base includes four natural-grass pitches, three open artificial-turf pitches, a covered pitch with stands for 506 spectators, a cottage settlement, a dormitory building, a medical and rehabilitation center, a swimming pool, a gym and other infrastructure.
The land plots under the facilities are owned by the municipality. PrivatBank uses some of them under lease agreements, while the right to use one plot is still being formalized.
The property will be transferred to the buyer after the bank receives permission from the Antimonopoly Committee of Ukraine (AMCU) for the concentration or a conclusion that such permission is not required, and after full payment for the property.
Persons subject to sanctions, associated with unacceptably high-risk jurisdictions, involved in corruption offenses, terrorist financing or money laundering will not be allowed to participate in the auction.
The restrictions also apply to companies with opaque ownership structures in offshore jurisdictions, as well as persons affiliated with oligarchs and former managers or owners of PrivatBank.
As reported, PrivatBank last attempted to sell the complex in autumn 2025, but the auction scheduled for October 30 did not take place due to a lack of bids. The starting price was UAH 150 million.
The bank subsequently attempted to lease Dnipro-Arena and the training base, but the January 2026 auction also failed due to a lack of participants. The starting rent was UAH 2.7 million per month including VAT.
PrivatBank is Ukraine's largest bank. According to the National Bank of Ukraine, the bank's total assets amounted to UAH 979.31 billion as of August 1, 2026, or 22.7% of the total.

WATCH protesters smash politician’s car during Ceuta migrant unrest
Furious anti-immigration protesters attacked a car carrying a local politician in the troubled Spanish enclave of Ceuta on Sunday. Locals, whose communities have been overrun by thousands of illegal migrants invading from Morocco, believed the vehicle carried a member of a pro-migrant activist group.
Footage shows protesters surrounding the vehicle, kicking and striking it, pelting it with eggs, and smashing its windows as police tried to hold them back. Riot police opened fire to disperse the crowd, multiple media outlets have reported.

Putin's United Russia secures record Duma supermajority
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
15:34:00 UTC
00:34:00 KST

President Vladimir Putin's United Russia party secured a record supermajority in the State Duma, officials said Monday, following a three-day election held without parties opposed to the Kremlin or Russia's war in Ukraine.
Electoral chief Ella Pamfilova said preliminary results showed United Russia – which has dominated Russian politics for 25 years – won 355 of the Duma's 450 seats.
The result handed Putin's party an increased supermajority and beat its previous record of 343 seats – giving it a free hand for constitutional changes.
The Kremlin said the first parliamentary election since Moscow sent troops to Ukraine in 2022 showed Russians were united around Putin, who has been in power since New Year's Eve 1999.
The conflict has killed hundreds of thousands, displaced millions in Ukraine and hit ordinary lives in Russia more than ever this year.
Moscow has banned criticism of its military campaign and the only party that called for an end to the war – Yabloko – was barred for running for the federal parliament. It was, however, approved in some regions for local voting.
"These indicators, of course, point to the highest level of consolidation within Russian society around the head of state," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told a briefing with journalists.
Putin had encouraged Russians to vote in support of troops in Ukraine and Moscow also organised voting in occupied Ukraine.
Pamfilova said turnout was over 59%, thanking Russians for voting despite what she called "psychological pressure on Russia."
Russia's Ukraine campaign broke its ties with the West. Kyiv hit Moscow with its biggest drone attack of the war Sunday, the last day of voting, killing two people and setting an oil refinery ablaze.
"Despite the extreme situation, we were successful in ensuring the maximum security of these elections," Pamfilova told a Moscow press conference.
Forty-nine veterans who fought for Moscow in Ukraine are expected to enter parliament to represent United Russia, the party told Russian state media.
The Kremlin has sought to promote soldiers who fought in Ukraine into positions of authority when they return, with Moscow glorifying its troops.
While nobody in Russia doubted United Russia would win, the election did bring one unexpected result: in the Novgorod region, in western Russia, war-critical Yabloko entered the regional parliament.
On social media, Yabloko's Novgorod branch said it received some 12,000 votes – just over 6% of votes in the region – enough to enter the regional legislature.
"Peace, freedom and life without fear – these are the values that have struck a chord in people's hearts and souls," it said.
Russia's Communist Party came second in the vote, winning 40 Duma seats. The nationalist LDPR party took 25 seats and the New People party won 20.
The election result is expected to further tighten Putin's grip on power.
Some fear a new military mobilization in Russia. Putin has denied this while Kyiv accuses Moscow of planning a call-up in the coming weeks.
The election took place amid the escalation of the Ukraine war with no diplomatic solution in sight.
In some regions, voting also took place for the local heads.
In Chechnya, Ramzan Kadyrov – known for ruling the Muslim-majority republic – won 99.85% of the vote, the electoral commission said.
Opposing Kadyrov is hugely dangerous in Chechnya, which is known for extra-judicial killings.
Putin's political opponents are in exile, prison or dead – such as his main opponents Alexei Navalny who died in an Arctic prison in 2024.
The EU's top diplomat Kaja Kallas dismissed Russia's "so-called" election.
"The Kremlin silenced dissent, barred the only registered party that opposed its war in Ukraine, and shut out international election monitors. The veneer of democracy is all that remains in Russia," Kallas said.
In a joint statement, five countries including the U.K., Australia and Canada, condemned Russia's "sham" parliamentary elections in swathes of occupied Ukraine, branding the move "part of a wider system of occupation."

2nd Gaza hospital cuts services over fuel shortage in past 2 days

Lina Altawell
21 September 2026•Update: 21 September 2026
Al-Wafa Hospital for Medical Rehabilitation and Specialized Surgery in the Gaza Strip said Monday it had reduced services because of an operational crisis caused by shortages of fuel and maintenance supplies amid the Israeli blockade.
It is the second hospital in Gaza to announce service reductions within two days because of fuel shortages, following a similar announcement Sunday by the nongovernmental Kuwait Specialized Hospital.
The crisis comes amid the repercussions of Israel’s genocidal war since Oct. 8, 2023, accompanied by a tightened blockade and extensive damage to Gaza’s infrastructure and health system.
Al-Wafa Hospital, a nongovernmental facility, said in a statement that it had temporarily suspended several essential services, including outpatient clinics, surgical operations, outpatient physical and occupational therapy, speech therapy, and treatment for swallowing disorders.
“The suspension of these services comes amid an operational and humanitarian crisis that has reached an extremely dangerous stage,” the hospital said.
The facility is facing severe shortages of diesel and other fuel needed to operate electricity generators and vehicles, along with difficulties obtaining oils, tires, spare parts, and maintenance supplies required to keep vehicles, equipment, and essential services running, it said.
Electric generators are the main source of power for Gaza hospitals to operate critical departments and medical equipment amid a complete electricity outage across the enclave for a third year.
The hospital said its administration was forced to suspend services to preserve available resources and direct them toward inpatients and essential medical services that cannot be discontinued.
Al-Wafa Hospital provides services to thousands of Palestinians, including wounded people and persons with disabilities, and receives large numbers of patients every month who depend on continued treatment and rehabilitation services.
The hospital warned that if the fuel and operational supply crisis continues without urgent intervention, further services could be reduced, threatening its ability to continue providing medical and rehabilitation care.
The administration issued an urgent appeal to the World Health Organization, the UN, health and humanitarian organizations, and donors to provide fuel, oil, spare parts, and other urgent operational needs.
On Monday, Gaza Health Ministry Director General Munir al-Bursh said the WHO had decided to stop diesel supplies to more than 20 hospitals and health centers starting Sept. 19 because of a funding shortage.
The WHO has not commented on the decision cited by the Health Ministry, though it has announced reductions in funding for its activities and programs in recent months.
Al-Bursh said the limited quantities of fuel entering Gaza “barely keep health facilities operating.”
His announcement coincided with shortages of oils and spare parts for hospital generators, which have caused several generators to stop operating.
Gaza’s government media office has repeatedly said Israel is failing to meet its obligations under the ceasefire agreement in force since Oct. 10, 2025, including allowing the agreed quantities of aid and fuel to enter the enclave.
Since the start of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, more than 73,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 174,000 injured, while around 90% of the enclave’s infrastructure has been destroyed.

Feature: Esports opens window on Chinese culture for Kenyan Gen Z
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
23:33:38 CST
00:33:38 KST

Game enthusiasts in costumes reenact game characters at a cosplay session during the first Kenya "Elephant Cup" Honor of Kings Esports Invitational Tournament and the 2026 Nairobi Youth Digital Entertainment Festival in Nairobi, Kenya, Sept. 20, 2026. Held from Saturday to Sunday in Nairobi, the event centered on the theme "Esports Connects the World, Youth Creates the Future." It served as a dynamic platform for China-Africa youth engagement, deepening cultural understanding through competitive esports, digital art, and gaming. (Xinhua/Yang Guang)
by Ronald Njoroge
NAIROBI, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Dressed as Wukong, the legendary Monkey King from Chinese mythology, Asgar Mukadam captivated an energetic Nairobi crowd and took home the overall cosplay victory.
The 30-year-old lawyer from Kenya's coastal city of Mombasa spent two weeks crafting his winning costume using fabrics and cardboard weaponry inspired by the popular mobile game Honor of Kings.
"I'm very excited and very happy that the Chinese people have given me a good opportunity to showcase my skills because I have always been inspired by Chinese culture and their martial arts," Mukadam told Xinhua on Sunday.
Mukadam was among the young Kenyans who brought iconic Chinese legends to life during the first Kenya "Elephant Cup" Honor of Kings Esports Invitational Tournament and the 2026 Nairobi Youth Digital Entertainment Festival.
Held from Saturday to Sunday in Nairobi, the event centered on the theme "Esports Connects the World, Youth Creates the Future." It served as a dynamic platform for China-Africa youth engagement, deepening cultural understanding through competitive esports, digital art, and gaming.
Organized by the Kenya Chinese Youth Association and the Kenya Overseas Chinese Association, the tournament brought together nearly 200 players across almost 40 registered teams. Competitors faced off in Honor of Kings, the hit mobile multiplayer online battle arena game developed by Chinese internet giant Tencent.
The event also featured a friendly showdown between Kenyan and Chinese esports teams, highlighting deepening international camaraderie on the digital stage.
Fellow cosplay competitor Henry Wasonga, a 27-year-old finance officer at a Chinese-owned firm in Kenya, transformed into Li Bai, the legendary Tang Dynasty poet depicted in the game as an agile swordsman.
Wasonga, who faced hardship growing up, shared that he felt a deep personal connection to the character's journey of resilience and independence.
Completing the trio of vibrant transformations was Mercy Njihia, a 26-year-old sales and marketing executive, who embodied Mulan, the legendary Chinese woman warrior celebrated for her courage and depicted in the game wielding twin blades.
Local gaming leaders praised the growing popularity of Chinese digital entertainment across the region.
Dickson Ouya, 28, captain of the finalist esports team Kenyan Avengers, noted the surging popularity of Chinese mobile games among local youth, citing their high production quality and engaging mechanics.
Jefferson Amimo, captain of the Iron Stallion esports team, explained that African youth are drawn to Chinese games because they weave rich mythology directly into the gameplay, offering players an immersive cultural experience.
Anne Emurudu, captain of the all-female esports team Shadow Reign, expressed her enthusiasm for Chinese mobile games, praising their inclusive design and rich storytelling.
Canice Musa, leader of the Kenyan esports team Bot Nation, similarly underscored the widespread adoption and growing presence of Chinese titles within the country's vibrant gaming ecosystem.
Diplomats, sports administrators, and youth leaders emphasized that esports and digital entertainment represent a rapidly expanding frontier for cultural exchange and economic collaboration between China and Africa.
Zhang Zhizhong, minister counselor at the Chinese Embassy in Kenya, noted that high-performing games serve as a powerful medium for sharing deep cultural heritage across borders.
"A game needs advanced creative design and a rich cultural foundation to resonate globally," Zhang said, encouraging Kenyan participants to use the game's historical characters as a portal to explore Chinese history and language further.
Ronny Lusigi, president of the Esports Kenya Federation, underscored the economic and developmental potential of gaming for the nation's vast youth population.
"Esports is no longer just about gaming; it is a global industry creating careers, businesses, and new opportunities," Lusigi said, noting that over 11 million young Kenyans engage in gaming.
Lusigi called for deeper partnerships between Kenyan game developers and China's digital industry to help bring African stories to global audiences, noting that some publishers of Chinese esports games are already incorporating elements of African culture and blending them with Asian traditions, a fusion that fosters meaningful international, people-to-people exchanges.
Henry Rotich, director in charge of metrology and testing at the Kenya Bureau of Standards, praised the discipline, strategy, and teamwork displayed by the young competitors.
Rotich observed that while traditional bilateral relations are built through diplomacy and trade, long-lasting ties are equally rooted in sports, technology, and digital interaction among the youth.
Yang Min, president of the Kenya Chinese Youth Association, said that esports has become a common language shared by young people around the world.
"Through Honor of Kings, Chinese and Kenyan youth have come together out of shared interest. Through the Chinese mythological and historical figures featured in the game, young people can discover and experience Chinese culture in a natural and engaging way." ■

"We handled almost 626,000 passengers in a single month, averaging more than 20,000 passengers a day," said Dusan Novota, chief executive officer of Bratislava Airport.

The growth was driven by strong demand for holiday and regular routes. Antalya, a famed Turkish holiday destination, was the most popular destination from Bratislava in August, followed by Barcelona, Rome, London and Kosice.
The airport surpassed the 3-million-passenger mark in a calendar year for the first time in its 75-year history in August. Passenger traffic is expected to exceed 4 million by the end of 2026, according to the airport. ■

China Focus: China moves to strengthen food security across grain supply chain in 2026-2030
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
23:32:59 CST
00:32:59 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- China is moving to strengthen food security over the next five years by enhancing its capacity to coordinate grain production, purchasing, storage, processing and sales, as it seeks to build a more efficient and modern grain circulation system.
The country will focus on facilitating grain purchases and sales and maintaining market stability, strengthening grain reserves, and improving the quality and resilience of the grain industry, Liu Huanxin, head of the National Food and Strategic Reserves Administration, said at a media conference Monday.
Liu said China's grain industry is expected to see its annual industrial output value exceed 4.5 trillion yuan (about 666.8 billion U.S. dollars) during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), as the country seeks to better meet growing demand for higher-quality, more nutritious and healthier food.
On grain purchasing and sales, China will encourage more grain businesses to enter the market, organize policy-based grain purchases and storage, improve grain trading platforms, strengthen links between grain production and consumption and maintain order in the grain market.
The country will continue to optimize the structure and regional distribution of grain reserves to better meet market regulation and emergency supply needs, and will steadily expand high-standard grain storage capacity and upgrade eligible older warehouses.
Efforts will also be made to extend the grain industry chain, support major grain-producing counties in expanding processing capacity, promote grain conservation and reduce losses across the entire post-harvest chain, and support the grain industry's transition toward innovation-driven, higher-quality development, said Liu.
China's grain industry has maintained steady growth in recent years, with the total industrial output value of grain enterprises rising from 3 trillion yuan at the end of the 13th Five-Year Plan period (2016-2020) to over 4 trillion yuan at the end of the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-2025).
A national crop farming development plan for the 15th Five-Year Plan period released last week calls for steadily enhancing comprehensive grain production capacity, holding the bottom line of basic self-sufficiency in grains and ensuring absolute security in staple foods.
The crop farming plan is aligned with a broader agricultural and rural modernization plan for the same period, which sets a target of increasing China's comprehensive grain production capacity to 1.45 trillion jin (about 725 million tonnes) by 2030.
The crop farming plan also calls for breeding and promoting breakthrough varieties, applying intelligent machinery, conserving water in agriculture and using fertilizers and pesticides more precisely.
China's grain market has remained generally stable despite fluctuations in international markets, underpinned by stable production, a well-established reserves system and strong processing capacity, Liu said.
The country's annual grain output has stayed above 650 million tonnes since 2015, exceeding 700 million tonnes for the first time in 2024 and reaching 715 million tonnes in 2025. Per capita grain availability has surpassed 500 kg, higher than the global average, providing a solid foundation for the country's food security.
The country's grain stock-to-use ratio remains well above the international grain security threshold of 17 to 18 percent, Liu said. If abnormal market fluctuations occur, reserves can be used to regulate supply and demand and help stabilize the grain market.
The country has about 24,000 grain processing enterprises engaged in grain and edible oil processing, food and condiment production, feed processing and deep processing, among other businesses. Processing capacity for flour, rice and edible oil is sufficient to meet domestic demand, Liu said. ■

MOSCOW, September 21. /TASS/. The world’s leading media outlets should cooperate in combating cross-border disinformation, Timofey V, an expert at the Global Fact-Checking Network (GFCN), told a media forum dedicated to the 65th anniversary of the Organization of Asia-Pacific News Agencies (OANA).
The event is organized by TASS news agency as the chair of OANA.
According to him, the key vulnerability of the modern media environment lies in the isolation of national response mechanisms.
"Fakes have become fully cross-border: the material is created in one jurisdiction, instantly adapted to another, and affects the audience of several countries at once," V noted.
The expert emphasized the importance of ensuring global information transparency, under which specialists from different countries have access to data on any cross-border disinformation campaigns.
V believes that OANA news agencies need educational formats of interaction, including closed practical webinars for press services and media, as well as joint educational products taking into account national specifics. According to him, GFCN is already actively cooperating with the BRICS and CIS platforms, but the partnership with OANA brings this work to the level of systematic cooperation with national agencies.
"The practical result of our joint work is the development of fact-checking standards, access to deep analytics and analysis of large-scale disinformation campaigns," the expert said. "This is how international cooperation turns from a common idea into a daily working tool."
The discussion of countering disinformation will continue on September 22 at the International Forum Dialogue on Fakes 4.0, where a specialized discussion in the OANA-GFCN format is planned.
The OANA Media Forum in Moscow is taking place in the year marking the 65th anniversary of the organization, which brings together 41 news agencies from 33 countries. The forum is organized by TASS, which will chair OANA until 2028. TASS General Director Andrey Kondrashov heads the organization, while TASS Deputy Director General Marat Abulkhatin is OANA’s secretary general.
