Inside Israel’s ‘soft’ ethnic cleansing plan for Gaza through the eyes of its victims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
13:01:52 UTC
22:01:52 KST

On November 25, 2025, Wissam Yassin, 50, left the Gaza Strip with her two daughters through the Kerem Shalom crossing, as part of an evacuation organized by the French Embassy. It came after several attempts by Yassin, who works for the U.S.-funded Alhurra television channel, and her ex-husband, who works for Radio France, to secure a way out for their two daughters.
Yassin and her family were instructed to go to a UNICEF facility, after which the French Embassy took responsibility for their departure. They left via the Rafah Crossing, traveled through Kerem Shalom, reached Jordan, and were flown directly to France.
“I felt as though I had been uprooted from my place and taken somewhere else,” Yassin, who cared for her children on her own throughout at least five displacements, said. “I wished I could stay in Gaza, but at the same time, I wanted a future and a dignified life for my children.”
Yassin’s family is one of thousands of families forced to leave Gaza since October 2023 – through embassy evacuations, academic fellowships, and World Health Organization (WHO) medical corridors. These are the only channels through which departure is currently possible, and they move slowly and selectively. The people who leave do so while fully aware that they may not be able to return, but they’re also aware that Israeli officials have openly stated, at the highest levels of government, that emptying Gaza of its Palestinian population is an explicit policy and ultimate goal.
The displacement plan
Israeli statements calling for the removal of Gaza’s population have not been hidden. Since the beginning of the war, Israeli officials have repeatedly and publicly made them.
The first major step toward displacement came in October 2023, when more than 1.1 million Palestinians were pushed from northern Gaza toward the south, a move widely described as a possible prelude to forcibly removing the population through the Rafah crossing. Egyptian opposition to Israeli and U.S. pressures to take in the displaced population prevented it and kept the population inside Gaza.
On September 2, 2026, Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said there was “no real solution for Gaza” without such forced migration, and that “Israel would facilitate Palestinian migration from Gaza to other places by sea, air, and every possible means.”
The following day, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir revealed a national action plan for what he called the “voluntary migration” of Palestinians of Gaza, targeting 1.8 million residents over seven years, with around 250,000 people to be removed in the first year.
On September 16, Katz said it’s only a matter of time before Israel resumes war on Gaza and encourages its people to evacuate the Strip.
In March 2025, Israeli media reported the establishment of the Voluntary Emigration Administration, within its Ministry of Defense, dedicated to working out destinations to send the people of Gaza to, in collaboration with its allies.
It is against this backdrop that Palestinians weighing whether to leave must make their decisions.
‘They kill the idea of steadfastness itself’
Palestinian writer and academic Yousri Al-Ghoul, 46, spent the entire duration of the war in northern Gaza – a region that has been deliberately cut off from the rest of the Strip, subjected to prolonged siege and starvation, and endured some of the most relentless bombardment of the entire genocide, with entire neighborhoods razed and its population reduced to a fraction of what it was before October 2023. Through it all, the father of six was active on social media, calling on people to remain steadfast and stay in the Strip.
On December 15, 2025, he and his family were evacuated to Switzerland through an academic fellowship with a university in Lausanne. While in northern Gaza, Al-Ghoul had lived with the fear of being assassinated, as Israeli forces have persistently targeted writers, intellectuals, and prominent figures in Gaza throughout the war.
After avenues for survival in Gaza had been exhausted, Al-Ghoul contacted friends in European countries and asked for help evacuating his family of six to ensure their safety.
According to Al-Ghoul, there are three main channels through which people can currently leave Gaza: family reunification for Palestinians with European citizenship or residency who can apply to bring family members stranded in the Strip; WHO medical evacuations for patients and their families; and academic fellowships for students or academics.
Beyond these options, al-Ghoul says, there are no other ways to leave Gaza.
Al-Ghoul is candid about what his own departure, as an influencer with significant followship, means in the context of Israel’s broader objectives. “Israel was also interested in removing people it considered wanted; its objective was not limited to killing people but was part of a deeper strategic goal of emptying Gaza of its Palestinian population.”
He frames his own case with particular clarity. “When Yousri Al-Ghoul leaves Gaza — the man who had called for steadfastness since the beginning of the war and urged the people of northern Gaza to remain in the north and not leave — the objective achieved by the occupation through his departure is greater than killing him,” he explained. “By forcing me to leave, they kill the idea of steadfastness itself.”
In announcing the Voluntary Emigration Administration, Katz reportedly said the directorate will operate in coordination with international organizations and other governing bodies, in accordance with government instructions, and will coordinate the activities of relevant ministries.
Al-Ghoul doesn’t assume that European organizations and institutions evacuating Palestinians are necessarily acting to help Israel implement its displacement plans. “They are motivated by humanitarian concerns and believe they are helping Palestinians by removing them from Gaza instead of leaving them to face death and killing alone,” he noted.
That does not, however, change the reality that it is proceeding according to Israel’s plan: create the conditions that make it impossible for people to subsist, and they will “voluntarily” seek an escape from the intolerable.
‘Soft migration’
Ahmad Mahmoud — a pseudonym used to protect his identity — left Gaza in May 2026 through the World Health Organization. One of his children required treatment abroad. He applied to the WHO, and after months of pursuing it, he was told the entire family could be evacuated to a European country.
The WHO instructed him to go to a camp operated by the organization in Mawasi, Khan Younis, where the family spent the night. The following morning, they boarded a bus to the Kerem Shalom crossing, then to Jordan, and from there to Spain.
Mahmoud says that if any organization were capable of helping Israel empty the Strip, it would be the WHO, because it holds the most comprehensive data and records on Gaza’s population and families.
While stressing that he does not accuse the WHO of complicity, he describes what happened after his family left as evidence of something more than medical evacuation.
“As soon as we reached Jordan, the WHO’s role ended completely,” Mahmoud said. “We were taken over by delegations from the Spanish Foreign Ministry, which began talking to us about asylum and about providing accommodation and a safe place in Spain.”
He described the dynamic as a form of “soft migration,” whereby families leaving through humanitarian channels with the intention of returning once the option becomes available are being steered immediately toward asylum applications and permanent settlement abroad.
‘Here, nobody knows me’
For Wissam Yassin, the physical distance from Gaza has not resolved the international conflict her departure created.
“Although leaving was an opportunity to survive,” she said, “I did not want to leave Gaza. I never wanted to leave the Strip this way. I always loved traveling and then coming back, but I never imagined that I would leave in a way that meant I could not return.”
“It was a shock to be in a tent, a woman alone without a family, without anyone to support me or help me through the difficult life of displacement, and then, overnight, find myself in Paris. It was a shock by every measure.”
Although friends and colleagues in Gaza envied her for being able to leave Gaza, she says she felt like “a plant that had been uprooted and thrown away.” Despite being in a safe place with the long-lost possibility of planning and enjoying normalcy, she still feels like a stranger.
“Here, nobody knows me,” Yassin said. “Nobody knows who I am or what I am. I left all my history in Gaza, among my family and loved ones who know who I am, what I have done in my life. Here in France, I am completely a stranger.”
Yassin says it sometimes occurs to her that European countries working to evacuate Palestinians from Gaza may be helping Israel implement its displacement plans. “But at the same time, people in Gaza deserve a real chance at life,” she said. “I am grateful to France for receiving me and giving me enough safety and stability – a home, a safe environment, and a school for her children.”

China prepares for Trump-Xi summit in Washington
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
13:01:35 UTC
22:01:35 KST

Breadcrumb
From a position of strength, China prepares for Trump-Xi summit in Washington
Chinese President Xi Jinping is due to meet his US counterpart Donald Trump in Washington within a few days, as global attention turns to whether the two countries can fulfil their agreement to work towards constructive steps towards international stability.
Beijing is preparing to begin this week's summit with Washington from a position of strength, backed by a series of recent diplomatic efforts.
The two sides have held intensive preparatory talks in New York to negotiate possible outcomes on trade, artificial intelligence and rare earth minerals.
Beijing announced on Monday, 21 September, that it was ready to work with Washington to build "strategic stability" and "manage differences".
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said China "will work with the United States to enrich the substance of constructive strategic stability in China-US relations, strengthen dialogue and cooperation, and properly manage differences".
The South China Morning Post reported on Sunday, 20 September, citing Chinese experts, that Beijing's confidence "could be strengthened by US efforts to make progress in its war with Iran and the Russia-Ukraine conflict, given that Washington may need Beijing's cooperation to help resolve them, even if reaching a truce in the near term remains unlikely."
"In recent months, the Trump administration has explicitly asked Beijing for greater diplomatic cooperation to manage ongoing conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, particularly those involving Iran," the paper added.
Moreover, China maintains a structural advantage through its dominance of rare earth elements and critical minerals, creating deep dependencies for US defence and technology manufacturers.
There is a belief in Chinese circles that US President Donald Trump's claim of permanent security control over Greenland just days before his Chinese counterpart's state visit is an attempt to strengthen US influence.
Based on this, warnings have emerged about a potentially negative impact on high-stakes talks, which could affect trust between major powers and peaceful development projects in the Arctic, according to the Chinese assessment.
Despite the cordial rhetoric between the two leaders, with Trump planning to personally welcome Xi at Andrews military base, many issues threaten to disrupt the positive atmosphere for the summit.
Rumours are abound regarding a potential US arms package for Taiwan have led to threats in the media to cancel the meeting altogether.
Trump also recently signed the Lindsey Graham Russia and Iran Sanctions Act of 2026, which directly penalises China's energy imports from Russia just days before Xi's arrival.
The White House also recently classified China as the main source of essential chemicals for synthetic drugs.
Trump's public complaints about Chinese interference in elections ahead of the 2026 midterm elections have further exacerbated bilateral tensions.
A few weeks before his trip to Washington, Chinese President Xi Jinping embarked on one of his most intensive foreign tours.
He made a state visit to Egypt after concluding the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, and then attended the BRICS summit in New Delhi.
The BRICS summit formed a united front against US tariffs and sanctions, which Beijing describes as unilateral.
Chinese President Xi Jinping is scheduled to meet his US counterpart Donald Trump at the White House on 24 September, four months after Trump's official visit to Beijing in May.
The latest summit produced a series of economic agreements, the establishment of a new US-China Trade and Investment Council, an agreement to open a dialogue between the two governments on artificial intelligence, and a commitment by the two leaders to build what the two governments described as a "constructive relationship of strategic stability".

Asian Games | China's Zhang defends men's all-around gymnastics title
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
21:01:33 CST
22:01:33 KST

Zhang Boheng prepares for the horizontal bar of the men's artistic gymnastics all-around final at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, Sept. 21, 2026. (Xinhua/Jia Yuchen)
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- China's Zhang Boheng retained the men's all-around gymnastics title at the 2026 Asian Games on Monday.
Fresh from winning the event at the Asian Championships, the 26-year-old collected 85.065 points to take gold, while Japan's Shinnosuke Oka and Daiki Hashimoto finished second and third, respectively.
Hashimoto, the Tokyo Olympic all-around champion, made a strong start with 14.500 points on pommel horse, while Zhang opened with 13.800 on floor exercise.
Oka's consistent performance kept the battle for gold close. The reigning Olympic all-around champion moved ahead of Zhang and Hashimoto after scoring 14.633 on parallel bars in the fourth rotation.
Zhang in action during the floor exercise of the men's artistic gymnastics all-around final. (Xinhua/Jia Yuchen)
Zhang responded with 14.700 on the same apparatus in the fifth rotation, taking a narrow 0.167-point lead over Oka into the final round.
With Zhang competing on horizontal bar and Oka and Hashimoto on floor exercise, the title remained up for grabs. Zhang scored 14.033 to secure his second consecutive Asian Games all-around title, while Oka finished with 13.833 on floor to take silver and Hashimoto's 13.433 left him with bronze.
Zhang said competing last on horizontal bar allowed him to adjust his routine based on his rivals' scores. After watching Oka and Hashimoto complete their floor routines, he opted to reduce the difficulty of his routine and lower the risk of errors.
"Gymnastics keeps progressing, and both Japanese all-around gymnasts have high levels in difficulty and execution," Zhang said.
Looking ahead to the 2028 Olympics, Zhang said he needed to develop a broader range of difficult skills and improve his competitive mindset as he aims to deliver a stronger overall performance.
The all-around competition also served as qualification for the team and apparatus finals. China topped the team standings with 255.361 points, ahead of Japan on 254.460, setting up another close contest between the two traditional powers. South Korea qualified third with 238.327.
The women's all-around competition will take place Tuesday, followed by the men's and women's team finals Wednesday. ■

China Focus: China nurtures emerging professions to fuel industrial upgrading
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
21:01:32 CST
22:01:32 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- At an AI-focused training camp recently held by the Huawei ICT Academy at Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications (BUPT), over 70 students underwent three days of integrated training and hands-on practice on AI fundamentals, AI operator development and open-source large models.
This training camp was just one link in a joint talent-cultivation chain involving BUPT and Chinese tech giant Huawei, which has been deepening industry-education integration. Such initiatives provide students with opportunities to engage with cutting-edge technologies and gain hands-on experience via real-world projects, according to Gao Peng, deputy dean of the Ye Peida School of Innovation and Entrepreneurship at BUPT.
"Through such training camps, BUPT and Huawei aim to cultivate engineering-oriented AI talents equipped with a solid theoretical foundation, practical skills and an innovative spirit, thereby injecting fresh momentum into the development of China's fast-growing AI industry," Gao said.
Such AI-talent cultivation efforts echo China's recent announcement of 11 new occupations and 23 new work types, reflecting how AI-driven economic and industrial development is increasingly steering education and employment in new directions.
NEW JOB HIGHLIGHTS
The latest new professions, released by the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security and other government departments, reflect fresh trends and market demands driven by China's industrial transformation, and open up more career avenues for high-quality employment, industry insiders noted.
Among these new work opportunities, five jobs related to digital economy are highlights, including digital twin engineering technician, embodied intelligent robot application technician and industrial product digital modeler. They cover frontier areas such as AI applications, industrial digitalization and simulation modeling.
Three of them are "green occupations," namely microgrid administrator, hydrogen fuel cell manufacturing technician and water electrolysis hydrogen production operator. Notably, microgrid administrator is classified as both a green and a digital occupation.
These new jobs in the green-transformation sector are a reflection of the country's talent-demand on its quest for comprehensive green transformation in both the economy and social development.
Against the backdrop of China's evolving service industries, modern service occupations are also emerging as bright spots. There are positions serving enterprise development and industrial upgrading, like sports data analysts, airport airspace clearance inspectors, low-altitude logistics operators and AI agent developers. New jobs also respond to people's aspirations for a better life, including incense-making artisans and age-friendly renovation designers.
ECHOING INDUSTRIAL TRANSFORMATION
The emergence of new occupations mirrors the accelerated iteration of the country's industrial structures and expanding gaps for talents equipped with new skills in the job market, especially in sectors such as AI, embodied intelligent robots and modern services.
The added value of core digital economy industries accounted for more than 10.5 percent of China's GDP, with the core AI industry exceeding 1.2 trillion yuan (about 177.8 billion U.S. dollars) in scale, the Digital China Development Report (2025) released by the National Data Administration in April showed.
However, talent gaps continue to expand. An official from the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security said China is expected to face a sizable shortage of workers with digital skills for some time. McKinsey & Company also forecasts that China will require 6 million AI professionals by 2030, but could face a shortfall of 4 million.
Data from online recruitment platform Zhaopin revealed that in the second quarter of 2026, industries related to new quality productive forces, including robotics, new materials and AI, continued to serve as the main drivers of talent demand growth, sustaining positive momentum in China's job market.
Taking the AI sector as an example, job market competition for AI talents is shifting toward those with compound capabilities, which is driving the transformation of universities and companies in terms of talent cultivation models.
EXPLORING NEW CULTIVATION MODELS
The Ministry of Education recently released the 2026 undergraduate major catalog, which is aimed at better adaptation to the development of emerging interdisciplinary fields, thereby better meeting demand for cultivating versatile talents. Eleven existing majors, like future robots, and four new majors, including embodied intelligent robots, have been included in the category of interdisciplines in the catalog.
In April 2026, the Ministry of Education and four other departments issued an "AI + Education" action plan, proposing to "make AI a public fundamental course in colleges and universities, compile course textbooks by disciplines and majors, and ensure that all students acquire AI knowledge."
The action plan also promotes colleges and universities to optimize the talent-training programs of traditional disciplines and majors, while guiding them to offer interdisciplinary AI courses.
Universities, additionally, are partnering with enterprises to cultivate talent adapted to new business forms and industrial upgrading. The AI training camp co-hosted by BUPT and Huawei is a good case in point.
Via an integrated training model consisting of "courses, training, competitions and selection," Huawei will continue to support college students in mastering core skills like operator development, model tuning and performance testing, working hand in hand with universities to cultivate more talents with core AI technologies, said Wang Xin, deputy director of the China Industry Development and Ecosystem Department at Huawei.
KEEPING PACE WITH DEVELOPMENT
China has been dynamically updating its occupational classification catalog. Since 2019, the country has issued eight batches of 121 new occupations. Also, China has so far recognized 113 digital occupations and 142 green occupations.
Such moves are anticipated to help promote employment and entrepreneurship, offer workers more diverse career paths, and better match talent supply with job demand.
Li Chang'an, a researcher at the Academy of China Open Economy Studies under the University of International Business and Economics, said that it precisely aligns with ongoing industrial transformation and new trends in the labor market, holding important practical significance for optimizing the country's employment structures and improving the training system for occupational skills.
During the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) period, China aims to explore new employment space in the digital economy, green economy and silver economy.
The Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security said that, looking ahead, it will formulate national standards for the new occupations to guide vocational education, skills training and talent assessment.
The ministry is also committed to smoothing the pathways for talent growth and development, and speed up the cultivation of a workforce that is sufficient in number and optimally structured, providing strong talent support for high-quality economic and social development. ■

China Focus: China rolls out AI "classrooms" to fuel humanoid robot boom
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
21:01:32 CST
22:01:32 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Rows of humanoid robots repeat the same motions over and over -- picking up water bottles, sliding trays into microwaves and scanning parcel labels. Nearby, human operators in motion-capture suits fold laundry and smooth out bedsheets, their movements captured by sensors and fed into AI training systems.
Scenes like these are unfolding in many places in China. Industry insiders call these facilities "embodied AI training grounds".
China is now home to more than 140 humanoid robot manufacturers. In 2025, the country shipped 14,400 humanoid robots, accounting for roughly eight in every 10 units shipped globally.
Yet impressive as these numbers are, the industry still faces a fundamental challenge: turning robots that can run, jump and dance in controlled settings into machines capable of reliably handling the countless, unpredictable tasks of everyday life.
A critical part of enabling them to handle everyday tasks is access to vast amounts of data.
Just as large language models learned from vast amounts of text to reshape the digital world, robots need vast amounts of real-world interaction data to master the physical one. They need to learn, through repeated encounters, how to grasp objects of different shapes, navigate unfamiliar spaces, respond to changes in their surroundings and complete everyday tasks.
But while the internet is overflowing with text, physical-world interaction data for robots has never been collected systematically. That is the gap these new training grounds, where robots learn to navigate and perform tasks in real-world environments through repetitive, data-intensive training, are being built to fill.
A recent research report shows that, as of the end of June 2026, China had opened more than 70 embodied AI training grounds. In addition, over 40 embodied AI training grounds are under construction or in the planning stage. Most are located in the Yangtze River Delta, the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region and the Pearl River Delta.
In south China's Guangdong Province, the provincial training ground has taken on a role that goes beyond teaching robots. Dubbed a "robot school" by its operator, it regularly brings robot makers together with potential users, helping manufacturers, healthcare providers and energy companies find suitable embodied AI solutions while giving robot developers access to real-world environments in which their robots can learn and be tested.
A similar model is taking shape in Hangzhou, capital of east China's Zhejiang Province. There, the National Pilot Base for Embodied AI Applications acts as a "super connector," bringing together state-owned enterprises, leading technology firms and application companies through an open cooperation mechanism.
"Previously, developing a single application scenario could cost a company tens of millions of yuan just in training data. Now, by moving into the base, you can access everything you need in just one place," said Zhang Haiwei, founder of a Hangzhou-based robot firm.
As these training grounds evolve from isolated facilities into a broader ecosystem, policy support is also moving in to accelerate their development.
In June 2026, Chinese authorities jointly launched a special action plan for real-scene training of humanoid robots and embodied AI, requiring each provincial region to identify at least 20 priority scenarios and create trainable, testable and verifiable real-scene training spaces.
At the same time, efforts are underway to improve not only the amount of training data, but also its quality. An industry standard on embodied AI dataset quality, drafted by a consortium of more than 40 organizations, is scheduled to take effect on Nov. 1. The standard is expected to help shift dataset development from a focus on scale toward greater quality, while addressing a long-standing gap in the field.
The business model is evolving, too. Wang Maolin, co-founder of an embodied AI ecosystem platform based in Shenzhen in southern China, said the next step is to move beyond simply supplying data and develop "training-as-a-service," creating diversified revenue streams that can help turn training grounds from heavy-asset investments into sustainable operations.
With policy support and growing momentum behind their development, embodied AI training grounds are no longer confined to China's major economic hubs. According to industry insiders, training grounds are now reaching into China's third- and fourth-tier cities, creating a multi-tiered network shaped not only by talent and capital, but increasingly by the availability of real-world scenarios and the data they can generate. ■

TOKYO, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- China continued its strong start in swimming at the 2026 Asian Games on Monday, winning five gold medals and setting two Asian records on the second day of competition.
One of the day's standout performances came from 13-year-old Yu Zidi, who won her second gold of the Games in the women's 200-meter individual medley in an Asian record of 2 minutes, 6.10 seconds.
It was the first Asian swimming record of the Games before China lowered another in the men's 4x200 freestyle relay later in the evening.
Yu described the record as "an unexpected surprise" and said following the technical details laid out by her coach had been key.
"I didn't know beforehand what time I would swim," she said. "The most important thing was the technical details my coach gave me."
Xu Jiayu successfully defended his men's 50 backstroke title in a Games-record 24.04 seconds, claiming his second gold after winning the 100 backstroke on Sunday. Teammate Wang Zicheng took silver in 24.49.
"I hope my performance can inspire the younger athletes," said Xu, who completed a backstroke double for the third consecutive Asian Games.
The 30-year-old said the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics remained a goal but acknowledged the challenges of continuing to compete as an older athlete. He credited the national team with giving veteran swimmers greater flexibility and more personalized training plans.
"I can train more freely and relax more in Hangzhou. I have time to go out, enjoy nature, rather than being immersed in training every day," Xu said. "I think it can improve our efficiency and also put us in a better mood when facing our work."
China also took the top two places in the women's 50 backstroke, with Wan Letian winning gold in 27.47 and Wang Xue'er taking silver in 27.66.
For Wan, the victory carried added significance because she raced without her coach by her side for the first time.
"Before, my coach was always there to help me relieve the pressure. This time I had to rely completely on myself," Wan said. "I think the result is very good for me."
South Korea's Kim Yeong-beom also made his mark in the men's 50 freestyle, breaking the Asian Games record twice on Monday and winning the final in 21.66.
China's Dong Zhihao shared the men's 100m breaststroke gold with Japan's Ohashi Shin after both clocked 58.64. World champion Qin Haiyang took bronze in 59.01.
Siobhan Haughey of Hong Kong, China won the women's 200 freestyle in 1:54.96. Returning to the pool where she set the Asian record in the event five years ago, Haughey said she had "so many great memories" there and recalled the sense of calm and confidence she felt before the Olympic final.
"I remember my coach told me to enjoy the moment because it's not often that you get to be at the finals of the Olympics," Haughey said.
Haughey also praised Yu's performance.
"It's so amazing to see young swimmers swim that fast, and she's only 13, so I'm sure she still has a long way to go," she said.
The night ended with China winning the men's 4x200 freestyle relay in an Asian record of 7:00.17, with Zhang Zhanshuo producing a dramatic comeback on the anchor leg to overtake Japan in the final 50 meters. Japan finished second in 7:01.05 and South Korea third in 7:06.76.
For Xu Haibo, it was his first time teaming up with the three more experienced swimmers in international competition.
"Seeing Zhang Zhanshuo gradually catch up, my heart was almost jumping out of my chest," Xu said. "I was so excited that I shouted my throat out."
Pan Zhanle said the relay had helped him rediscover the form he showed at the national championships, while acknowledging he still has room for improvement.
Zhang, who clocked 1:42.9 on the anchor leg to erase a deficit of nearly two seconds, said he never stopped believing a comeback was possible.
"I have three very strong teammates, including a world-record holder. Why should I be afraid of the opponents?" Zhang said.
"This is a very good start. My Asian Games have just begun," he added. ■

====================================================================================================

China Focus: From deadlines to rest stops -- China expands protections for delivery riders
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
21:00:51 CST
22:00:51 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- When a heavy rain flooded streets in north China's Tianjin Municipality in early August, food-delivery rider Zhai Zhongguo found his electric scooter struggling to get through the water. Some residential compounds ended up so waterlogged that he even had to get off and walk to take orders inside.
"In this kind of weather, I just hope customers won't place an order unless they really need to," he said.
In China, the clock starts ticking the moment a food delivery order is placed. Riders are given a set amount of time to deliver each order, a system designed by food delivery platforms to ensure prompt service. Under pressure from the countdown, some riders may resort to speeding or running red lights to save time, putting their own safety and that of pedestrians at risk. When bad weather strikes, however, making the deadline can become even more difficult.
To ease pressure on delivery riders, especially during bad weather, food delivery platforms and local authorities have rolled out human-centered measures, such as more flexible delivery deadlines and "red-light pauses."
When Typhoon Dolphin hit Suzhou in east China's Jiangsu Province early last month, local authorities urged major delivery platforms to waive penalties and deductions for weather-related delays, while delivery services were temporarily suspended in some areas.
In Beijing in north China, Meituan, Taobao Flash Shopping and JD Food Delivery said on Aug. 13 that they would introduce a "red-light pause" system in the city. Time spent waiting at traffic lights would be added back to riders' delivery windows instead of counting against them. These companies also said riders would get more time to complete deliveries in severe weather or when faced with difficult road conditions.
Zhai said he has noticed delivery rules being adjusted when bad weather hits. During a spell of heavy rain, for example, orders that normally came with a 30-minute delivery window were given about 50 minutes instead.
"You just have to ride more slowly when it rains. Safety comes first," said Liu Xingwei, a Taobao Flash Shopping delivery rider in Tianjin's Binhai New Area. "If you explain the delay to customers beforehand, most of them understand."
Platforms are also giving riders a broader safety net, from weather allowances and insurance to protective gear. Meituan said it has covered riders' heat-related medical expenses at its own expense since June 1, while providing per-order subsidies during high temperatures. Taobao Flash Shopping has offered active riders free heatstroke insurance and additional payments based on temperature and rainfall. JD Food Delivery has introduced a monthly high-temperature allowance of 300 yuan (about 44.5 U.S. dollars) for some riders, while offering others additional payments for orders delivered during heavy rain.
In Nanchang, capital of east China's Jiangxi Province, Meituan rider Zhou Zhenbo said he does not receive a high-temperature allowance, but can earn extra pay during peak delivery periods and receive shopping coupons for heat-relief items such as cooling sleeves. At Zhai's station in Tianjin, there is no cash allowance for hot or rainy days, he said, but riders are provided with heat-relief supplies.
Beyond easing the pressure of delivery deadlines, Chinese authorities are also paying greater attention to the health and well-being of delivery workers. Rules issued in 2024 require platforms to prompt riders to take breaks when they reach limits on continuous order-taking or daily working hours, and to stop sending them orders for a set period.
But for riders on the road, finding time and place to rest can still be a challenge.
For Zhai, who typically logs on at 8 a.m., takes a lunch break around 1 p.m., returns at 3:30 p.m. and finishes around 8 p.m., his working hours and order volume remain largely unchanged, even in extreme weather. At times, back-to-back orders leave him with little opportunity to find a rest station.
To enable delivery riders and other outdoor workers can get drinking water, charge their phones or escape the heat and rain, more Chinese cities are expanding rest stations for them. Tianjin, where Zhai works, now has more than 5,700 union-run stations, with the municipal trade union moving more of them closer to logistics hubs and delivery sites to make them easier for riders to reach. In Nanchang, 80 standardized rider rest stations had been built by June, while community service centers across the city have also opened their doors to workers.
At a rider rest station in Nanchang's Xihu District, the midday heat sent delivery workers through the door for a brief break. They filled large bottles with ice water before heading back out to their next orders. A few minutes in the shade and a bottle of cold water could not ease the physical demands of the job, but they offered riders a much-needed pause from the heat and the road. ■

China has attached great importance to the booming tourism performance industry in both national and industrial development blueprints. The 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) for cultural and tourism development released earlier this month urged cultivating high-quality tourism performance projects by "creating and staging a number of high-quality tourism performances that reflect the characteristics of the times and meet market demand, enhancing their cultural content, and supporting the upgrading of tourism performance equipment." ■

Brain structure, function, and behavior show independent patterns of sex differences
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
13:00:25 UTC
22:00:25 KST

Men and women show distinct biological differences in how their brains activate during various tasks, the physical size of specific brain regions, and their behavioral traits. A new study published in Nature Communications reveals that while each of these factors can accurately predict a person’s sex, an individual’s degree of sex typicality in one domain is entirely unrelated to the others. These results suggest that sex differences in the human brain are highly context-dependent and operate independently across structure, function, and behavior.
Biological sex differences appear in the prevalence of various neuropsychiatric conditions, such as autism and mood disorders. They also manifest in specific aspects of cognition and physical behavior. Past neuroimaging research has attempted to map out how male and female brains differ in their physical structure and functional activity.
Functional magnetic resonance imaging, or fMRI, allows researchers to observe which brain regions activate when a person performs specific mental tasks. Structural MRI measures the physical volume and shape of brain tissue. Many previous fMRI studies on sex differences have relied on small numbers of participants completing single tasks. This reliance on limited data has led to intense debate about the true extent and relevance of sex differences in human brain function.
To address this gap, researchers Siyuan Liu and Armin Raznahan at the National Institute of Mental Health led a comprehensive analysis of brain activity, anatomy, and behavior. The research team aimed to determine if sex differences in brain function are tied to specific tasks, if they align with physical brain volume, and how they relate to behavior.
The researchers analyzed data from nearly 1,000 healthy young adults. The participants underwent fMRI scans while completing seven different tasks. These tasks were designed to measure emotion processing, gambling, relational reasoning, social cognition, language processing, working memory, and motor skills. By scanning participants during this wide array of activities, the team could observe both task-specific brain activation and general activation patterns.
The analysis revealed widespread sex differences in brain activation across 85 percent of the outer layer of the brain, known as the cerebral cortex. These differences were highly reproducible but mostly specific to individual tasks. For instance, certain brain regions showed more activation in females during a language task but more activation in males during a gambling task.
A small number of regions, particularly those involved in motor control and physical sensation, showed a general tendency for higher activation in females across all seven tasks. Across the board, the effect sizes for these functional differences were small to moderate.
Next, the researchers examined whether these functional differences matched up with anatomical differences. They used structural MRI scans from the same participants to measure the volume of gray matter, which is the tissue containing the main bodies of nerve cells. The team found reproducible sex differences in gray matter volume across various regions of the cerebral cortex.
They then mapped the areas with functional activation differences over the areas with physical volume differences. The spatial patterns did not overlap in a coordinated way. Brain regions that exhibited sex differences in volume were generally not the same regions that showed sex differences in task activation. This lack of alignment suggests that sex differences in brain structure and brain function represent distinct biological phenomena.
The team then incorporated behavioral data, analyzing participant scores across 86 different behavioral traits. These traits ranged from physical grip strength and visual judgment to tendencies toward anxiety and psychological distress. Using a machine learning framework, the researchers tested whether an individual’s combined profile of brain activity, brain volume, or behavior could predict their biological sex.
The machine learning models accurately predicted a participant’s sex based on any of the three categories alone. Task-specific brain activation predicted sex with 88 percent accuracy, regional brain volume with 86 percent accuracy, and behavior with 91 percent accuracy. The models also generated a sex typicality score for each person within each category, rating how closely their data matched the average male or female profile.
Despite the high predictive accuracy of all three categories, a participant’s sex typicality score in one domain did not correlate with their score in another. An individual might have a highly male-typical brain volume, but a strongly female-typical pattern of brain activation during a language task. Only a tiny fraction of individuals exhibited consistently male-typical or female-typical profiles across all measurements of brain and behavior.
In their final analysis, the researchers looked for interactions between sex, brain activation, and behavior. They conducted a brain-wide association study to see if variations in brain activation between individuals correlated with variations in behavior. They first confirmed that measurable links exist between task-induced brain activation and specific behavioral traits within each sex group.
When the team compared these brain-behavior associations between men and women, they found striking similarities. The overall topography of how brain activity relates to behavior is broadly consistent across both sexes. The researchers detected a few isolated instances where the relationship between brain activity and behavior diverged between males and females. However, these rare differences did not preferentially involve behaviors that were themselves heavily sex-biased.
The study relies on observational data, meaning it can only identify associations rather than establish direct biological causes. Finding a sex difference in brain activation or structure does not mean that sex directly dictates how the brain operates, nor does it guarantee that the physical difference has a functional consequence. The research is focused exclusively on the biological construct of sex based on self-identification as male or female, rather than the psychosocial concept of gender.
The findings are also limited to specific types of neuroimaging. Functional MRI during tasks and structural gray matter measurements capture only a portion of the brain’s complex organization. Other techniques, such as resting-state fMRI or imaging that tracks the brain’s white matter connections, could reveal different patterns of sex-based variation. Future research will need to explore how these independent traits develop over a person’s lifespan and whether they fluctuate during different stages of brain development and aging.
The study, “Robust but independent sex differences in human brain function, structure, and behavior,” was authored by Siyuan Liu, Bridget W. Mahony, Ethan T. Whitman, Stephen J. Gotts, Dustin Moraczewski, Adam Thomas, Alex Martin, and Armin Raznahan.

Foreign diplomats visit historic, natural sites in Urmia
TEHRAN - Ambassadors and diplomats from nine countries, along with representatives of two international organizations, visited Lake Urmia and several historic sites in Urmia during a visit to the northwestern Iranian city.
The diplomats from Sri Lanka, the Philippines, Thailand, Nicaragua, Indonesia, Kazakhstan, Romania, Malaysia and South Korea, as well as the deputy secretary-general of the Economic Cooperation Organization (ECO) and the secretary-general of the Asian Mayors Forum, were among the visitors invited by Mayor Aidin Rahmani-Rezaeieh to attend the 9th Urmia Grape Festival.
The visit was organized as part of efforts to showcase Urmia’s cultural, historical, tourism and economic potential and use the grape festival as a platform for expanding international exchanges.
The delegation first visited Urmia’s historic bazaar and Jameh Mosque before traveling to Lake Urmia, one of Iran’s best-known natural landmarks.
The visitors were accompanied by Morteza Safari, director-general of West Azarbaijan’s Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts Department; Hossein Panahi, head of the Urmia City Council; Rahmani-Rezaeieh; and a number of municipal officials.
The diplomatic visit followed the 9th Urmia Grape Festival, which was held from September 10 to 20 at Chi Chest Coastal Village near Lake Urmia.
Speaking to the Tehran Times, Rahmani-Rezaeieh said the festival was rooted in an old local tradition of giving thanks for the grape harvest.
“People used to celebrate it at the end of Shahrivar (mid-September) and thank God for the harvest,” he said.
The mayor said this year’s festival was larger in scope, with the municipality seeking not only to preserve the tradition but also to introduce it to younger generations.
The event featured sections dedicated to innovation, industry and investment, history and identity, sports, mothers and children, food and rural products.
The innovation section presented agricultural technologies and projects related to grapes, along with specialist discussion panels. Another section focused on agricultural industry and investment, while the history and identity section displayed photographs that organizers said were more than 300 years old.
A market at the festival also allowed villagers and farmers to sell their products directly to visitors.
The diplomatic tour provided an opportunity to introduce foreign guests to West Azarbaijan’s cultural heritage and tourism attractions, while the participation of international guests in the grape festival highlighted the potential of cultural events to facilitate people-to-people and international exchanges.
During the visit, the guests were presented with a book on West Azarbaijan’s history and nature.

Got an Android Phone? Google Thinks You’ll Probably Want a Googlebook Laptop
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

iPhones and Macs are like two peas in a pod. Apple’s hardware synergy means you can launch iPhone apps right from the macOS desktop, respond to texts without picking up your iPhone, and even copy text on one platform and paste it on the other. That kind of seamless connectivity does not natively exist for Android phone owners at the operating system level.
Google’s trying to change that with Googlebooks, a new class of laptop. First teased in May, the company finally shared more details about the new OS at a media-only event in New York City last week. Like with Android, hardware manufacturers can make their own Googlebooks, provided they hit specific standards set by Google.
Today marks the launch of five new computers that comply with the Googlebooks standard, one each from HP, Dell, Lenovo, Acer, and Asus. These machines are powered by either Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X Elite chip or Intel’s Core Ultra 3 (MediaTek also supports the Googlebook platform with its new Dimensity CX C10 Max chip, but none of the new laptops use the chip yet).
Preorders open today, and the machines hit store shelves on October 4, starting at $899. Every purchase includes a full year of Google AI Pro service with 5 terabytes of storage.
Here are the new laptops, all of which are clamshells except the Acer, which is a 2-in-1 machine:
Some of the standards Google has set include using “premium materials,” like aluminum, magnesium, or carbon fiber, to make them lightweight. They need at least 16 GB of RAM, deliver more than 45 tera operations per second (TOPS), a touchscreen (LCD or OLED), a backlit keyboard, a haptic trackpad, Dolby Atmos speakers, studio-quality microphones with noise cancellation, and at least 14 hours of battery life. Googlebooks will receive 10 years of software updates.
They must feature the Glowbar—the signature LED strip on the laptop’s exterior that identifies the machine as a Googlebook. It’s a callback to the glowbar Google used on its original Chromebook Pixel. (Speaking of which, Google hasn’t shared whether it’s making its own Googlebook under its Made by Google Pixel hardware division.) Developers can access the Glowbar to customize the lights to specific actions in their apps, and there’s also an Easter egg app consumers can unlock to customize the light color and animation themselves. Like HiLight introduced on the latest Pixel phones, the Glowbar will illuminate when you talk to Gemini.
“There’s a lot the laptop gets right, but much of it was designed decades ago, before mobile devices were invented,” Sameer Samat, president of the Android ecosystem, said at the event. “Reinventing laptops is a multi-year endeavor. Our first step is to focus on the Android community because today there isn’t a laptop that is designed to seamlessly work with your Android phone.”
Googlebook merges Android’s mobile-first operating system with ChromeOS, the OS powering Chromebooks. Google says Chromebooks aren’t going anywhere and will continue to serve schools and act as the budget-friendly option for consumers. While the Googlebook interface feels like a blown-up version of Android, it’s not just an Android-powered desktop. Rather, it’s a distinct OS optimized for x86 and ARM chip architectures.
What’s particularly interesting is how Android apps work on the device. They’re categorized in three ways. When you set up your Googlebook with your Android phone, important data flows seamlessly to the laptop, including Wi-Fi networks, passwords, settings, messages, contacts, and photos. Not all of your phone apps will automatically be installed, though, as Google deems some apps as “better on the web," like Facebook. (You can still install the Facebook app if you want and get the mobile-shaped experience.)
The next tier of Android app is “Optimized for Desktop.” These apps take advantage of the bigger screens with better layouts and a little more functionality. The final tier is “Made for Desktop,” like the desktop versions of Chrome. Google says around 20 or so apps are either optimized for desktop or made for the desktop so far, including CapCut, Adobe Photoshop, Notability, and Fantastical. As the platform grows, Google expects more developers will target Android’s “Made for Desktop” tier and bring their desktop-grade apps from Windows and macOS to Googlebook.
People want to play games on their laptops, and so Google says you’ll be able to access more than 20,000 titles on the Play Store, many of which support cross-device play between mobile, tablets, and laptops. Google says around 50 of the 100 top titles are optimized for keyboard, trackpad, and touchscreen. But since you can’t download AAA games for Googlebooks (yet), especially without a discrete GPU, Google is offering 1 year of Nvidia’s GeForce Now game streaming service, which is optimized for the platform.
New Frontiers
Googlebook is an opportunity for Google to bring artificial intelligence to the forefront of the laptop computing experience, which is why many of the core new features are AI-powered. For example, similar to Android 17, you can generate your own desktop widgets with simple prompts to Gemini.
Magic Pointer is the marquee Gemini feature. Wiggle the mouse pointer over anything, and a Gemini overlay will suggest contextual actions. For example, if you wiggle over an event someone invited you to, you’ll get a prompt to automatically “Create an event” and have it added to your Google Calendar with one tap. Or if you’re wondering what breed of dog you’re looking at (whether it’s a video or photo), wiggle and ask Gemini, “What’s the breed?” If you’re wondering whether an email is a phishing attempt, wiggle over it and ask Gemini.
AI companies are also heavily focused on voice-to-text as the future of computing, which is why Google is injecting its Rambler feature natively into Googlebook. It debuted on the latest Google Pixel 11 smartphones and is a potent AI-powered voice dictation engine that transcribes whatever you say. It intelligently cuts your “ums” and “uhs,” and even knows when you make a mistake and restate something, keeping the parts it believes you want to convey. You can ask it to format sentences in a particular tone, include bullets or emoji, and even mix in different languages. You can call up Rambler with Google’s Quick Insert key, a key found on Googlebook keyboards and newer Chromebook keyboards. Rambler works in any text field.
The rest of the platform leans heavily into Android smartphone continuity. In the Files app, context-aware search lets you find photos by simply typing “dog” instead of the file name—and it searches files on your phone just as easily as local storage. Meanwhile, “Continue on” hands off ongoing tasks so apps open on your laptop right where you left off on mobile, and an app-casting feature lets you stream phone-only apps like DoorDash directly to the desktop.
What if you have an iPhone? Google offers a new “Link to iOS” app that lets users access messages and some notifications on the desktop, but cross-platform limitations mean you can’t enjoy the same breadth of features. Then again, iPhone owners will probably stick to Macs. At least Android now has something comparable.

Apple Mac Mini (M6) Review: For the AI Curious
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Ports remain the same. Two forward-facing USB-C 3 ports (up to 10 gigabytes per second), as well as a headphone jack and a power indicator light. On the back, there are three Thunderbolt 4 ports, HDMI 2.1, an Ethernet jack, and the power adapter port. Using the available USB-C ports and HDMI on the back, you can connect up to two 5K 120-Hz external displays (such as the Studio Display XDR or BenQ 5K MA270S) or three 4K displays.
One controversial design is that the power button is still hidden underneath the back left corner of the computer. If you know where it is, just tilt the Mac Mini to the side and reach your finger back—easy. If you don't know (or keep forgetting, as I do), it means having to flip the thing over entirely, with all your cables attached. It remains a silly design decision in my view, but it's nowhere near as egregious as the Magic Mouse it pairs with (sold separately), which still infamously charges from the bottom. But I digress.
I still wish it had an SD card slot (forward-facing, like the Mac Studio) though. Plenty of photographers and videographers would be well suited for the Mac Mini, and yet they'll need to buy an additional dock or adapter. And yes, some color options, like the iMac, would be nice. But from the outside, it's the same well-built, compact mini PC it's always been. It's the performance under the hood where you'll need to dig in to see the extra value in this latest generation.
AI Gains
Right off the bat, I was eager to test a couple of new components in the M6 Mac Mini. First, there are the advances in the M6 chip itself. This is our first glimpse of the next generation of Apple Silicon, and the first built on a 2-nm process node. It represents a significant step up in transistor count on the die—46 billion in this case. That's around a 35 percent increase in transistor density, which translates to higher efficiency and more performance. In theory.
The M6 Mac Mini also adds two more CPU cores than the M4 model, for a total of 12. That's a 21 percent increase in single-thread performance and a 36 percent improvement in a multi-threaded run. Those numbers sound impressive, but compared to the M5 in the MacBook Air, they're not as substantial. It's only around 10 percent faster than the M5 Pro chip in the MacBook Pro in single-threaded performance (and unsurprisingly, much further behind in multi-threaded). Those two extra CPU cores, though, do prop up the multi-threaded performance, even compared to the base M5 chip. It's hard to do apples-to-apples comparisons to only a laptop.
Like previous Mac Minis, it has a fan inside. And when you get to work on something heavy, you'll definitely hear it start to make some noise. It's not terrible, but if you're coming from a MacBook, you'll definitely notice. That active cooling ensures you get stronger performance from that M6 chip than you would in a MacBook Air (though I won't be able to do a side-by-side comparison until the M6 MacBook Air comes out, presumably in 2027).

The Anatomy of a Biliteracy Learning Walk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

José Medina, Elena Izquierdo, and Vanessa Espitia Mendoza talk us through the need for administrators to learn how to lead Dual Language Bilingual Education programs
Dual language bilingual education (DLBE) programs succeed or struggle in large part because of leadership. Leaders, including principals, assistant principals, instructional coaches, teacher leaders, and district administrators, are often asked to do the impossible—lead DLBE programs with little preparation or support (Izquierdo, 2021).
In the article “Learning to Lead Dual Language Bilingual Education” in Language Magazine (March 2026), we emphasized the importance of leader-readiness and identified the Biliteracy Learning Walk (BLW) as a key response to this leadership challenge. This follow-up article explores the critical aspect of BLWs to ensure that DLBE leaders are better prepared to support the complex needs of DLBE programming.
Despite the substantial leadership demands placed on DLBE leaders, most school districts continue to align with instructional leadership and coaching frameworks that support a monolingual educational context. This mismatch matters. A school or district leader conducting a traditional classroom walkthrough may recognize student engagement, classroom management, and lesson structure. But will they notice whether the language allocation plan is being followed or if teachers are intentionally leveraging cross-linguistic connections to support transfer of content and language learning?
Rather than functioning as a compliance-oriented walkthrough tool, the BLW creates a structured opportunity for school and district leaders to observe biliteracy instruction within authentic dual language classroom contexts (Izquierdo et al., 2026). Through collaborative inquiry and in-the-moment coaching, leaders deepen their understanding of biliteracy pedagogy while developing their capacity as instructional coaches. Their learning around biliteracy pedagogy is no longer grounded in theory but rather becomes a part of their practice because it is taking place in DLBE classroom settings in their own school and/or district.
By centering a bilingual/biliteracy perspective of teaching and learning, the BLW challenges a status quo that has never fully embraced a student’s full linguistic repertoire. In the sections that follow, we examine the anatomy of a BLW, proposing a framework for helping leaders to recognize, support, and sustain biliteracy instruction across all content areas.
What Is a Biliteracy Learning Walk?
A biliteracy learning walk is a collaborative, nonevaluative instructional observation process specifically designed to examine the conditions that support bilingualism and biliteracy development within a DLBE context.
Unlike traditional walkthrough and coaching frameworks, BLWs focus explicitly on:
- language allocation and fidelity;
- content, language, and culture integration as part of the lesson planning process;
- listening, speaking, reading, writing, and metalinguistic awareness as keys to access grade-level standards;
- authentic biliteracy instructional practices aligned with the needs of each of the two program languages;
- cross-linguistic connections and transfer;
- holistic assessment practices that support biliteracy trajectories;
- culturally and linguistically sustaining practices;
- and sociocultural competence and critical consciousness as foundational to dual language programming.
BLWs create leadership learning structures that help principals, assistant principals, instructional coaches, teacher leaders, and district administrators deepen their understanding of effective biliteracy learning environments. DeMatthews and Izquierdo (2018) argue that school and district leaders play a critical role in sustaining equitable DLBE program implementation and that leadership preparation must intentionally address bilingual education competencies rather than relying solely on generalized leadership frameworks. Similarly, Izquierdo (2012) emphasizes that leadership matters significantly for emergent bilingual students because leaders shape the instructional environment in which biliteracy development occurs. BLWs operationalize this important component of DLBE leadership work.
The Six Phases of a Biliteracy Learning Walk
BLWs can be structured in different ways to meet school and district needs; after working with multiple leadership teams, our findings recommend a minimum of 180 minutes for authentic biliteracy learning and coaching. School and district leaders serve in demanding roles that often leave little time for professional growth opportunities. The suggested time frame becomes manageable while also ensuring that leaders are provided with the support that is essential to lead DLBE. During the designated time frame, the BLW facilitator guides participants through all six phases of the process.
Before the Biliteracy Learning Walk
(Includes Phases 1 and 2)
Phase 1: Establishing the Biliteracy Instructional Focus
Purpose: Clarify the purpose of the learning walk and identify biliteracy priorities.
Estimated time: Ten minutes
Participants: Four to six school and/or district leaders meet at a designated school to engage in the BLW
Effective BLWs begin long before classroom observations occur. Prior to the BLW, school leaders and district administrators participate in targeted professional learning focused on the C6 Biliteracy Instructional Framework (C6BIF). The C6BIF (Medina, 2020) was conceptualized to support leaders, many of whom have little or no experience in biliteracy instruction, by providing a system that names important elements of instruction in a DLBE classroom setting.
During the allotted ten minutes, the BLW facilitator establishes purpose for the BLW by empowering the school leadership team to share campus instructional goals with the BLW participants. Additionally, the BLW facilitator reviews the C6BIF and the 3Ws Observation Protocol. Both tools become central components of Phase 2 and Phase 3, during which participants learn how to identify, document, and analyze evidence of biliteracy instruction across diverse classroom settings.
Phase 2: Preparing Observers to See Biliteracy in Action
Purpose: Build shared understanding of biliteracy practices through observations.
Estimated time: 20 minutes
The C6BIF is a tool that helps leaders make sense of their learning around biliteracy in the classroom setting. Moreover, Izquierdo et al. (2026) note that the “C6BIF transforms leadership preparation from a delayed prerequisite into an integral part of implementation itself, enabling school and district leaders to respond to immediate expectations, while also developing the expertise needed to lead high-quality, equitable DLBE programs over time.”
During the allotted time, the BLW facilitator reminds participants of the instructional practices they will be seeking as they visit DLBE classrooms. Because the C6BIF puts the research into actionable and observable practices, leaders begin developing the instructional language needed to name and analyze biliteracy pedagogy. This is foundational to instructional coaching, collaborative reflection, and systems-level implementation. For many participants, this phase represents the first time they intentionally observe evidence of biliteracy instructional systems that support DLBE programming.
Sample Observable Biliteracy Practices Aligned to the C6BIF
The BLW facilitator also reminds participants that the 3Ws Observation Protocol will be used to capture their observations. Unlike observation and coaching frameworks grounded in monolingual contexts, the 3Ws Observation Protocol positions participants to identify and disrupt linguistically oppressive instructional practices. The Wows represent the biliteracy instructional practices that should be replicated; the Wonders are questions that may arise during the classroom visit; and the What Ifs are recommended actions for biliteracy implementation. The 3Ws Observation Protocol will be fully described in the following phase of the BLW.
During the Biliteracy Learning Walk
(Includes Phases 3 and 4)
Phase 3: The Dual Language Bilingual Education Classroom Observation
Purpose: Observe biliteracy instruction in action using a focused, nonevaluative lens.
Estimated time: 90 minutes
The BLW is a critical component in DLBE leadership professional growth. Whether the school or district administrator is multilingual or not, has served in dual language programs or not, or chose to serve in their current position or not, they are responsible for guiding and sustaining a DLBE program that seeks to provide linguistic and educational reparation to student communities historically marginalized by US schooling systems (Medina, 2025).
During the 90-minute observation, the four to six BLW participants visit as many DLBE classrooms as possible. Each visit is eight to ten minutes. Although leadership growth remains the primary goal of the observations, the process also strengthens multiple systems that support DLBE sustainability.
- There is a shift from viewing classroom observations as evaluative to as an opportunity for growth for all involved.
- Participants are expected to use the C6BIF descriptors to observe, name, and code what they see during the dual language classroom visit.
- The BLW facilitator must provide in-the-moment coaching to the participants, to include consideration of the following questions:
  - What are the students doing and does it support the goals of DLBE?
  - What is the teacher doing and does it support the goals of DLBE?
  - Does the environmental print reflect authentic work in both program languages and support cross-linguistic work transfer?
- There is an opportunity for the BLW facilitator to engage students in conversations about their participation in DLBE and their understanding of the biliteracy instructional practices.
The 3 Ws Observation Protocol
If the C6 Biliteracy Instructional Framework establishes biliteracy pedagogical systems that can be named, replicated, and scaled, the 3Ws Observation Protocol provides a tool for collecting qualitative and quantitative data to support the BLW as a process for sustaining DLBE programs. It becomes the vehicle that is leveraged by leaders during any classroom observation.
What leaders observe, name, and document becomes the qualitative data that is collected. Using the six descriptors in the C6BIF, they can document implementation trends through quantitative coding. DLBE leaders become action researchers through their participation in the BLW. Over time, these observation patterns help schools and districts identify implementation strengths, instructional trends, and opportunities for systems-level support.
Sample Wows, Wonders, and What Ifs Captured During a Biliteracy Learning Walk
The C6BIF and 3Ws Observation Protocol operationalize the foundational understanding that is needed by school leaders and district administrators to fully support dual language bilingual education programming. Both tools, through the BLW, make it possible for leaders to engage in meaningful and contextualized professional learning as they collaboratively guide biliteracy instruction.
Phase 4: Identifying School and/or District Biliteracy Systems Implementation
Purpose: Examine systems, structures, and policies that support (or hinder) biliteracy instruction.
Estimated time: 40 minutes
Izquierdo and Spies (2014) emphasize that sustaining dual language bilingual education requires intentional leadership systems capable of monitoring implementation fidelity and instructional coherence across classrooms. As school districts scale DLBE programming, much of the focus is on preparing teachers, but often, school and district leaders are an afterthought (Izquierdo et al., 2026). This is a critical mistake because when programs do not yield the promised student achievement outcomes, leadership is rarely considered a reason for that failure. In fact, school leaders and district leaders play a central role in shaping the long-term success of DLBE programs.
After the completion of the BLW, participants review the 3Ws Observation Protocol that was completed for each of the classrooms visited. Although individual teacher and student actions are not the focus of the BLW, they provide important contextual information that informs job-embedded leadership coaching. The BLW facilitator provides any additional support needed to the participants to appropriately code the observation statements using the C6BIF.
Reviewing the Wows
Participants are asked to first review all the data collected as part of the Wows section of the 3Ws Observation Protocol. Depending on how many dual language classrooms are visited, leaders identify biliteracy instructional practices that were observed in many of those settings. On a piece of anchor chart paper, the BLW facilitator documents the patterns that the participants observed. They record the qualitative statements alongside the corresponding quantitative coding. The goal is to capture five to seven Wows that reflect a strong overall school implementation of that instructional practice.
Reviewing the Wonders
Following the sharing of the Wows captured via the BLW, participating leaders review the Wonders. Although the group may have many unanswered questions that arise during the learning walk, the goal is to calibrate among the participants and select the three or four most important questions they would like to pose to the leadership team serving that school. The BLW facilitator records the Wonders on a second piece of anchor chart paper.
Reviewing the What Ifs
Finally, school and district leaders are asked to review their recommendations for action, as generated in the What Ifs section of the protocol. Calibration among participants takes place once again until participants identify the three or four action items that will become a part of the data report that is shared with school leaders. These recommendations are captured on a third piece of chart paper.
Throughout the process, the facilitator reminds the participants that via the BLW, they are embracing their role as biliteracy advocates and coaches. The final triangulated report synthesizing participant observations, coded patterns, and action recommendations is then completed. For example, leaders may identify strong evidence of oral language production across classrooms while simultaneously noticing inconsistent implementation of cross-linguistic transfer practices.
The BLW deepens leadership understanding of the pedagogy needed for DLBE success while strengthening opportunities for sustained and systemic implementation of practices across classrooms, schools, and districts. The images below illustrate the qualitative and quantitative data collected by leaders during a BLW. Notice that the observation of a biliteracy practice (qualitative data) is identified and then coded (quantitative data) using the C6BIF. Finally, the last image reflects the biliteracy instructional patterns that were captured by the BLW participants.
After the Biliteracy Learning Walk
(Includes Phases 5 and 6)
Phase 5: The Reflective Debrief
Purpose: Engage in collaborative reflection to analyze evidence, celebrate strengths, and identify opportunities.
Estimated time: 20 minutes 
The reflective debrief is a powerful tool for leadership development because it is a result of in-the-moment, job-embedded coaching. It moves learning around biliteracy from the abstract to the concrete. By empowering school and district leaders, whether seasoned or new to dual language education, to embrace linguistically sustaining practices that are foundational to effective DLBE implementation, the BLW provides a safe space to grow as leaders.
DeMatthews and Izquierdo (2019) propose that effective dual language leadership requires a social justice orientation capable of challenging subtractive schooling structures while sustaining culturally and linguistically affirming environments. Reflective debriefing helps leaders surface these broader equity questions.
During the last 20 minutes of the BLW process, the facilitator invites the school leaders on the campus where the observations took place to co-facilitate. Leaders first address the Wows identified as evidence of strong instructional systems, making connections to specific focal areas of opportunity they have addressed. They can also make connections between the Wows and items that are part of their campus improvement plans. For some participants, this reflection process surfaces the realization that biliteracy instructional systems are not something apart from what happens in nondual language classrooms; instead, they are integral to all that happens instructionally in a school and district.
School leaders then have an opportunity to answer any questions that were posed as part of the Wonders section of the report. Finally, they share initial reactions to the recommended items in the What Ifs portion of the data report. Participants, at this point in the BLW, understand that reflection is an integral part of the implementation of biliteracy instructional systems.
For participating leaders, this part of the BLW creates an opportunity for reflection about the systems currently in place, or absent, across the campuses they serve. As a closing activity for the BLW, the facilitator asks the school and district leaders to view themselves as the lead biliteracy coach in their schools and identify the following:
- Their greatest learning moment during the BLW
- One immediate action item
- One long-term action item
Phase 6: Coaching for Biliteracy and Action Planning
Purpose: Co-create next steps, provide coaching, and plan for implementation to sustain and grow biliteracy instruction.
Estimated time: After the Biliteracy Learning Walk
Medina and Izquierdo (2021) emphasize that serving in DLBE requires specific competencies of the teachers, campus administrators, district leaders, superintendents, and school boards. The BLW is an important component in supporting leaders engaged in this work, especially when considering that administrator certification programs rarely prepare leaders for service in biliteracy educational contexts. The BLW, however, cannot function as an isolated event; rather, it must be a part of an ongoing leadership learning cycle.
After the Biliteracy Learning Walk
BLWs become transformative when observation evidence informs professional learning and systemic action planning. What happens after the BLW is essential if participants are to integrate their learning into everyday actions that support the students, teachers, families, and communities in which they serve. The following are commitments made by all participants in the BLW process:
- As a school or district leader, I commit to embracing and modeling:
  - the importance of the goals of dual language bilingual education;
  - content, language, and culture learning targets in all meetings I facilitate;
  - the use of the 4+1 language domains in all settings;
  - the importance of cross-linguistic connections for transfer;
  - and the idea that at the core, DLBE is grounded in equity and social justice above all else.
Research on effective professional development consistently demonstrates that job-embedded coaching and collaborative inquiry produce stronger instructional outcomes than isolated workshops alone (Darling-Hammond et al., 2017). One of the most powerful ways for leaders to grow is to model the biliteracy instructional practices that are expected to be implemented in every dual language classroom. After all, large-scale dual language implementation must remain grounded in the explicit commitments capable of resisting English-dominant pressures and accountability structures (Medina and Izquierdo, 2021).
Reimagining Biliteracy Instructional Leadership
BLWs are not neutral technical exercises. They are equity-centered leadership practices that communicate what schools and districts value, protect, and prioritize. Generic walkthrough and coaching frameworks alone are insufficient for supporting the linguistic, pedagogical, and social justice complexities of biliteracy development. BLWs offer an essential pathway toward more responsive and equity-centered leadership practices. Most important, BLWs help leaders learn to see dual language classrooms differently—not as monolingual classrooms translated into another language but as sophisticated biliteracy learning spaces requiring specialized instructional expertise. 
As dual language bilingual education continues to grow nationally, leadership development systems must evolve accordingly. The future of DLBE depends not only on strong classroom instruction but also on leadership systems capable of sustaining equitable biliteracy practices over time. If schools and districts hope to sustain high-quality biliteracy instruction, leaders must learn how to recognize, support, and protect it.
