CNN, MS NOW, and Politico Sue Trump Administration Over White House Ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
12:43:09 UTC
21:43:09 KST

CNN, MS NOW, and Politico sued the Trump Administration on Monday following President Donald Trump's decision to ban the three media outlets from the White House.
"This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes,” the companies said in a joint statement.
Trump took to Truth Social shortly afterwards and insisted the White House "is not instituting an assault on the free press" but is instead targeting "fake news"—something he argued is "totally out of control" and "a threat to our national security."
Vice President J.D. Vance, when asked about the lawsuit, argued that Trump is not "banning" media outlets. "What he's doing is saying we're not gonna give you special access to the White House if you engage in what is effectively propaganda," he said.
The White House later doubled down on its stance, issuing a press release titled "White House access is a privilege—not a right," during which they argued "the First Amendment protects their right to publish; it does not entitle them to a hard pass, briefing room seat, or place in the press pool."
CNN, MS NOW, and Politico said their reporters were denied access to the White House over the weekend and had their badges seized following Trump's ban issued Friday.
MS NOW reporter Akayla Gardner on Saturday described arriving at the White House campus to discover her badge no longer worked. "The officer asked me to hand over my badge. He said that it was disabled. I asked why I was not able to get inside. He said it was above him," she recounted. Reporters from CNN and Politico shared similar experiences.
“Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists’ credentials because it objected to our reporting. Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference," the joint statement from the outlets continued.
Trump announced his decision to ban the three media outlets Friday afternoon in a Truth Social post that warned other news outlets could face similar restrictions.
“Effective immediately, I am banning Fake News CNN, MSNOW... and Politico... from the White House as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ fake news!” Trump said. “Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report fiction and lies when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America.”
When asked in the Oval Office later that day if the media ban is likely to be struck down in court, Trump responded: “I think it's good to point it out whether it survives or doesn't. I don't think that a court should allow fake news to be written day after day after day.”
The ban has presented a new test of the First Amendment’s protection of a free press as his Administration moves to punish news organizations whose coverage he dislikes.
The First Amendment forbids the government from "abridging" the freedom of the press—a principle intended to allow news organizations to scrutinize those in power without fear of government retaliation over their reporting.
TV networks unite in solidarity against Trump's White House media ban
CNN is one of five U.S. news outlets in the White House press pool that rotates responsibility for pooled live video coverage. The network was originally due to cover Trump's trip to the U.N. General Assembly in New York on Monday.
In light of the ban, the other major television networks are standing with CNN by declining to replace its White House pool crew. The decision means the shared TV pool will not cover Trump’s events that have been designated for pool coverage.
In a rare joint statement, ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News, and NBC said: “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No Administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.”
Bryan Boughton, current chair of the TV pool and Fox News Washington bureau chief, had earlier issued a memo to the White House press corps detailing the decision. "This is to advise that, effective today, the TV pool will not be covering events designated as pool coverage of the President,” read the memo, according to CNN. “This follows the White House’s position preventing CNN from fulfilling its assigned pool duties. There will be no replacement pool put in place. All other pool coverage will continue as normal, including Congress, VIPs, and selected events in Washington and around the country.”
The Associated Press also sent a note to media late Monday morning, informing them of the changed plans. "Please be advised that no network travel pool is expected to be with U.S. President Donald Trump today as he heads to New York for the United Nations General Assembly," read the notice.
In a show of support, some media publications—including the New York Times and Washington Post—announced they would hold off on publishing or distributing still photographs taken as part of the White House pool coverage on Monday until midnight E.T.
TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.
The Trump Administration's battle with the press
Trump has made several previous attempts to bar or restrict reporters from government spaces.
During his first term, he revoked the White House press credentials of Jim Acosta, who was then a CNN correspondent, after a tense exchange during a news conference. CNN challenged the decision in court and a judge ordered the White House to reinstate his press pass.
In early 2025, shortly after returning to office, Trump tried to bar Associated Press journalists from spaces where access is limited, such as the Oval Office and Air Force One, when the news organization declined to update their stylebook after Trump signed an Executive Order renaming the "Gulf of Mexico" as the “Gulf of America.” The Associated Press sued, and the case remains ongoing.
The Department of Defense has also imposed various restrictions limiting journalists’ access in the Pentagon.
In an unprecedented move in June, the department designated its press office a classified area.
“The Pentagon Press Office has been redesignated as a Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility due to speechwriters from the Office of the Secretary of War sharing the facility,” said deputy Pentagon press secretary Joel Valdez. “As a result, journalists will no longer be permitted to enter the office space. There’s nothing controversial about that.”
Trump has also verbally lashed out at several female reporters.
Last month, CNN issued a statement in defense of its reporter Kristen Holmes, after Trump told her to "be quiet" and called her a "loud, boisterous person" during a tense exchange in the Oval Office.
The White House's Rapid Response social media account later shared a clip of the exchange, referring to Holmes as “a disgraceful, humiliating embarrassment to her alleged profession.”
In its response to the rhetoric, CNN said: “Public officials are free to challenge reporting they disagree with, but personal attacks on journalists for asking questions are beneath the office and inconsistent with the principles of a free press."

Russia Muted Air Sirens During Moscow Strike for Parliamentary Elections Turnout
Russian authorities in the Moscow region withheld air-raid sirens and SMS warnings during a major Ukrainian strike as officials appeared to prioritize State Duma election turnout over public safety, according to the Institute for the Study of War.
In its September 20 assessment, ISW noted that authorities had issued sirens and SMS notifications during significantly smaller previous attacks, making the absence of warnings during the September 19–20 strike particularly notable.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
ISW described the overnight barrage as the largest combined missile and drone strike package Ukraine has launched against strategic targets in the Moscow region.
Moscow City Mayor Sergei Sobyanin claimed that air defenses had downed more than 1,600 Ukrainian drones since September 19, including 450 on the approaches to the capital.
According to ISW, authorities did restrict mobile service, a routine countermeasure during Ukrainian strikes, but did so without major public announcements.
They did not, however, activate air-alert sirens or send the SMS notifications that residents had received during far smaller attacks.
Moscow region residents voiced anger over the silence, ISW reported, with some posting complaints on the Telegram channel of Moscow region Governor Andrey Vorobyov before the channel disabled comments.
A prominent Kremlin-affiliated milblogger criticized the official response, ISW noted, warning that it eroded public trust in Russian authorities and that the mobile restrictions do "not really help."
The strike extended Ukraine's long-range campaign against Russian oil infrastructure, which has continued in the absence of a Russian agreement to the energy ceasefire that US President Donald Trump proposed on September 14.
Zelenskyy has repeatedly reaffirmed Ukraine's willingness to accept a mutual moratorium on energy strikes, while the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, has rejected each proposal.
Ukraine's General Staff reported that the barrage struck the Gazpromneft-Moscow Oil Refinery in Moscow City, roughly 450 kilometers from the Ukrainian border, sparking a large fire and damaging its primary oil-processing unit.
The refinery ranks among Russia's largest, with an annual capacity of about 12 million tons. Ukrainian manufacturer FirePoint reported that its FP-1 drones forced the plant to pause refining and lifted the share of offline Russian refining capacity from 10 to 14 percent.
Russian officials acknowledged strikes across 17 Moscow municipalities as voting in the State Duma elections concluded on September 20.
ISW assessed that Ukrainian forces did not deliberately target polling stations or other electoral infrastructure, and that authorities appeared to place a high turnout above civilian protection.
The Moscow refinery strike extended a rapid series of Ukrainian long-range attacks on Russia's oil-processing network.
On September 13, drones hit the TANECO refinery in Nizhnekamsk, Tatarstan, roughly 1,200 kilometers from Ukraine, setting a storage tank ablaze.
The same night, in response to the Russian military aggression, Ukraine strikes damaged a processing unit and a tank farm at the Sloviansk-EKO refinery in the Krasnodar region, one of Russia's largest independent plants, which produces more than 4 million tons of crude a year. A separate strike hit the nearby Slavyansky refinery, which processes about 5.2 million tons annually.

Türkiye identifies 1,000 more foreigners in citizenship fraud probe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
12:39:20 UTC
21:39:20 KST

Turkish authorities have identified 1,070 foreigners who allegedly acquired Turkish citizenship through fraudulent real estate transactions, as a second operation targeting companies involved in the scheme was launched in Istanbul.
The operation was conducted early on Sept. 21 in Istanbul, Justice Minister Akın Gürlek announced in a social media post.
As part of the investigation, authorities examined property transactions involving several construction companies, including Gül İnşaat, Beyaz İnşaat and LIV İnşaat.
Investigators reviewed real estate sales involving 734 foreign nationals and determined that 274 of the transactions were fictitious.
The investigation found that 1,070 people, including the applicants’ family members, had obtained citizenship through unlawful means, while 11 others were still undergoing the citizenship process.
Authorities have also initiated procedures to revoke the citizenships.
The investigation uncovered more than 3.5 billion Turkish Liras ($71.7 million) worth of fictitious property transactions. Legal proceedings were launched against 88 suspects, 72 of whom were detained.
Police seized digital materials from addresses linked to the suspects and the companies under investigation. Authorities also imposed measures on 2,011 properties, one hotel, 86 vehicles, two yachts and 42 bank accounts.
Thirty companies were also seized and placed under trusteeship.
Türkiye introduced its citizenship-by-investment program in 2017, initially requiring a minimum real estate investment of $1 million. The threshold was reduced to $250,000 in 2018 and later raised to $400,000 in June 2022, where it remains.
However, properties valued below the required investment threshold had been sold using inflated appraisals by construction and real estate companies to enable applicants to qualify for Turkish citizenship.
The latest operation followed an investigation launched in August, when authorities began proceedings to revoke the citizenship of 687 foreign nationals.
Following that operation, the Interior Ministry said it had revoked or canceled the citizenship of 6,134 foreign nationals to date.

Russia has intensified repression of critics overseas, UN expert says
Unknown

2026-09-21

Russia has intensified repression of critics overseas, UN expert says
GENEVA – Russia has intensified surveillance, intimidation and reprisals against critics overseas since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, a UN expert said on Sept 21.
The Special Rapporteur on human rights in Russia told the Human Rights Council in Geneva that Russia had become one of the most prolific perpetrators of “transnational repression”, through attempted assassinations, assaults and poisonings.
“It is the continuation, beyond Russia’s borders, of the same structural, state-sponsored system of repression I have documented at home,” Mariana Katzarova said in a statement, citing her new report based on 400 documented cases.
“Leaving Russia does not mean leaving Russian repression behind,” she added.
Some 650,000 to 900,000 people have left Russia since 2022, her report said.
Russia’s diplomatic mission in Geneva did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment, though Moscow has in the past denied allegations of hostile actions on foreign soil and alleged a Western smear campaign.
Incidents of “transnational repression” tripled from 29 during 2014-2021 to 89 between 2022-2024, the report found, citing civil society data.
While Russia has a long history of assassinations and intimidation beyond borders – including the murder of former KGB agent Alexander Litvinenko in London in 2006 – the method and scale of targeting has changed from overt violence towards covert, administrative and digital tools, Katzarova found.
“Repression now travels through arrest warrants, databases, banks, digital systems and proxies – cheaper, scalable, and built to evade attribution,” Katzarova said.
Blocked bank accounts
The report explained how Russia places individuals on the Federal Financial Monitoring Service (Rosfinmonitoring) list of “terrorists and extremists”, sparking red flags and blocked accounts in European and American banking institutions.
The Russian authorities have also restricted services and travel documents to citizens abroad, the report said.
It cited the case of Elena Pushkareva whom the Russian Embassy in Canada refused consular services to, citing a “security threat”, after she protested over the release of Alexei Navalny and other political prisoners.
Russia is the most frequent user of Interpol arrest requests, though roughly half of Russia-related cases reviewed by Interpol's oversight body in 2024 were non-compliant, Katzarova said.
Targets include anti-war emigrants, journalists and non-governmental organisations.
While targeting occurs mainly in South Caucasus and Central Asian States, documented incidents have dramatically increased in Europe and beyond, the report said. REUTERS

ECB launches 'Pontes' to settle tokenised assets in central bank money
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
12:38:50 UTC
21:38:50 KST

The Eurosystem has launched Pontes, a system allowing banks to settle trades in tokenised assets using central bank money, and the ECB said it will invest some of its own funds in tokenised securities through it, the first concrete steps towards making the euro fit for the digital age.
Europe's central banks now have a working bridge into tokenised markets.
Launched on Monday, Pontes lets wholesale transactions in tokenised assets, meaning stocks, bonds and other instruments recorded as digital tokens on distributed ledgers, to settle in the safest form of money available — reserves held at the central bank itself.
It matters because the absence of a risk-free settlement asset has been one of the main barriers holding blockchain technology back. Without it, tokenised trades have typically settled in commercial bank money or stablecoins, carrying credit risk that large institutions are reluctant to accept.
"The Eurosystem is working to enable a more integrated, innovative and resilient European financial market in the digital age," said ECB President Christine Lagarde.
Thirteen institutions have completed onboarding and are ready to use the system immediately, including Deutsche Bank, Santander, Société Générale, KfW and the European Investment Bank, alongside four ledger operators including Clearstream.
The ECB also intends to become a user itself.
In a separate announcement, it said it has begun preparatory work to invest a small portion of its own funds in tokenised securities, with purchases settled through Pontes.
The initial focus will be euro-denominated debt issued by euro area governments, regional authorities, agencies and European supranational institutions.
The own-funds portfolio sits outside monetary policy and generates income to cover the bank's running costs. No amount was specified, and the Executive Board will decide on timing once the groundwork is done.
"Pontes brings tokenised markets another step closer to the core of the euro area's financial infrastructure," said Richard Baker, founder and CEO of Tokenovate, which builds technology to help financial institutions automate post-trade processing, collateral management and tokenised settlement.
Baker noted the service will initially run within existing market hours, but that "the longer-term opportunity is to support more continuous, potentially 24/7, settlement."
That gap is where Europe is playing catch-up.
American markets have moved faster as the New York Stock Exchange is building a blockchain-based venue for trading tokenised shares and funds around the clock, and BlackRock has run a tokenised money market fund since 2024.
Pontes itself will only reach full capability, with longer operating hours and enhanced features, by 2028.
The two sides are also taking different routes.
Washington, under US President Donald Trump, abandoned plans for a Federal Reserve digital currency and backed privately issued stablecoins instead. On the other hand, Frankfurt is betting that public central bank money should sit at the centre.
Where the digital euro stands
Pontes is aimed at banks and markets, not consumers. The retail equivalent, the digital euro, would let the public make everyday payments directly in central bank money.
That project is further from reality.
The European Parliament's economic committee approved its position in June, opening negotiations with member states, and final legislation is targeted for the end of this year.
If that holds, a pilot involving 36 payment providers will begin in September 2027, with first issuance possible in 2029.

From an exclusive Venetian island retreat to a 17th-century convent turned wellness resort, these hotels in Europe are guaranteed to blow you away.
If you’re looking for a truly exceptional hotel stay, a five-star rating isn’t enough. You need to look to the big guns: The Michelin Guide.
The tyre company is well known for its reviews of restaurants and associated Michelin stars, but in 2024, it began awarding “keys” to properties around the globe.
One Key means a “very special” stay, while Two Keys means it will be "exceptional".
But Three Keys? A Three Key hotel offers something next level. According to Michelin: “It is one of the world's most remarkable and extraordinary stays and a destination for the trip of a lifetime.”
Sounds good to us.
According to the 2026 Michelin Key selection, which was unveiled last week, there are just 155 Three Key hotels around the globe – including eight new additions in Europe for this year.

All of the new Michelin Three Key hotels in Europe

Russia 'lost control' of its oil refining industry due to Ukraine's attacks, Trump says
Russia has effectively "lost control" of its diesel production sector as a result of the war with Ukraine, U.S. President Donald Trump said on Sept. 21, urging an end to the fighting.
The comments come as President Volodymyr Zelensky travels to New York to meet Trump and discuss a potential mutual Ukrainian-Russian pause in strikes against energy infrastructure and targets on the Black Sea.
The two leaders are scheduled to meet on Sept. 22, a Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent.
"Russia has unfortunately lost control of its Diesel Oil Industry due to its War with Ukraine," Trump said on his Truth Social platform.
The U.S. president added that a large number of Russian "refineries have been blown up and are, at least temporarily, out of commission," noting that the "whole world suffers" as a result of the war.
Responding to Trump on social media, Zelensky echoed his sentiment that the war must end, saying, "From the very first minute, Ukraine has sought peace."
"There are also ideas on the table for bringing peace closer, starting with strong de-escalation steps. Ukraine's energy sector, critical infrastructure, and our food exports must stop being targets for Russia, and this will lead to matching de-escalation steps on our part," Zelensky said on X.
"It will no longer be the case that only the country under attack suffers. The nature of war is now such that the aggressor will suffer as well."
Kyiv has been consistently targeting Russian oil depots and refineries throughout the war to increase pressure on Moscow's economy and undermine its ability to wage war.
In turn, Russian forces have been seeking to destroy Ukraine's energy grid through mass drone and missile strikes, causing regular blackouts across the country.
Trump previously blamed Ukrainian strikes against Russian refineries for the rising costs of diesel fuel. Experts who spoke to the Kyiv Independent disputed this claim, noting that there is little evidence to support it and that rising fuel prices have been driven mainly by the U.S.-Iran war.
Kyiv has already signaled it is ready for an energy truce, provided that Russia abides by it. The Kremlin called Trump's proposal for a pause in energy strikes a "very good idea" but tied it to additional conditions, namely the lifting of sanctions against Russia.

'Be realistic, demand the impossible': Portugal's MUZEU wants visitors to think and reflect
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
12:33:51 UTC
21:33:51 KST

Braga is the third biggest city in Portugal, but it was missing a museum of contemporary art until April this year. MUZEU has a mission to help people experience the moment through the art and to encourage them to think and reflect.
A rally for revolution is the inspiration behind MUZEU, the new contemporary art museum in the Portuguese city of Braga.
Its motto “Be realistic, demand the impossible“ is taken directly from the famous photograph shot by Gérard-Aimé during the civil unrest of May 1968 in Paris, capturing graffiti on the Pont de Neuilly bearing the phrase “Soyez réalistes, demandez l’impossible”.
“May of 1968 was a time of liberation within a country that sought a freedom of movement, not really political, but a freedom to break the social and moral walls of the time that existed“ - founder of MUZEU, José Teixeira, told Euronews Culture.
“Nowadays we are living a new version of May 1968 - morally, socially and ethically. A liberation that opens ourselves and opens the community to the communities and to a communal life. Because today, in the moment we live, especially in Portugal, we value meritocracy, individualism. There is a need for a new debate about the communities and how comprehension and compassion should be brought to the table as a means to solve that as well".
100 artworks by 84 artists on 5 floors
José Teixeira, the founder of MUZEU is the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of dstgroup, one of Portugal's leading industrial companies. He's also the 35th richest person in Portugal according to Forbes.
Spanning five floors and an exhibition area of approximately 3,000 square meters, his collection brings together more than a hundred artworks by 84 artists - 45 from Portugal and 39 from abroad. A total of 16 countries are represented - comprising 57 men and 27 women.
Among many others Teixiera's collection features the work of Pablo Picasso, Alex Katz, Artur Lescher, Candida Höfer, Nan Goldin, and Eduardo Batarda.
A dedicated gallery has been set aside for the work of Anselm Kiefer.
Photography holds a uniquely important place in the collection, reflecting one of the Teixeira's great passions as he believes: "photography captures the moment without taking it away".
To read, to think and to live in a community
A keen collector over four decades, Teixeira's company's campus in Braga is full of large scale works of art, libraries, and sporting equipment for his staff to take advantage of.
Despite his immense wealth and the privilege it provides, Teixeira describes himself as a working man who wants to lead by example.
“Simone Weil is a French philosopher that lived in France during the Nazi occupation of France. She wanted to write about work, so she stopped lecturing classes and sent an application to Renault and worked there as a press operator and milling machine operator," says Teixeira.
"Later, after working, she wrote a book about it. So if you want to speak about work, you need to know how to do it and do it like Simone Weil - ask the real questions. This is the true importance of literature, poetry, arts, and everything that I spoke about. Poets speak through metaphors, I speak through art works I collect.“
Teixeira likes to think about himself as the signal man, pointing the direction for people working with him and for him - to read, to go to museums, to reflect and think about how to live in a community.
As fragile as people killed by it
A significant element in the new exhibition at MUZEU which opened last Thursday is Handle with care by Lebanese-Canadian artist Elias Nafaa. It comprises of 300 hand-cast glass replicas of weapons used in contemporary conflicts, presented for the first time this year at The Québec City Biennial.
For Nafaa, Handle with care transforms instruments of destruction into delicate objects of contemplation: “I want to make them [weapons] out of a very fragile material so that they are as fragile as what they're destroying," he tells Euronews Culture.
"I wanted to reverse the power dynamics, so instead of them looking down on me, I would look down on them, and I wanted to scale them down so they don't feel as strong or powerful as they are or destructive as they are. This became the start of the work that you see here,“ adds Nafaa.
“18,000 weapons were used by the end of 2025 and I think now it's over 20,000 that were used on Lebanon by the Israeli army. And what you see here is 300 pieces. I have six models that I researched and identified that were used more commonly.
"The frequency of its use in this space is proportional to its use like in real life so for example the smaller ones which are used mostly you will see more of them in the place the bigger ones which I use a bit less you'll see less of in this space."
Visitors should be aware of the difficulties Nafaa had in getting his work exhibited as it was kept in custody for more than two weeks until the eve of the exhibition opening.
Ironically, Nafaa says that while real weapon travel the world mostly fast and freely - legally and illegally - his artwork was being held for a much longer time.
“Handle with Care“ is part of MUZEU’s inaugural programme titled Abrir Abril and is open until 31 October 2026.

Tunisia arrests 15 protesters backing jailed Sumud Flotilla activists
Tunisian authorities have detained 15 people who took part in a protest calling for the release of four activists from the Global Sumud Flotilla to Gaza, the Tunisian Sumud (Steadfastness) Committee said on Monday.
The committee said authorities launched a campaign of arrests immediately after the protest in Tunis on Saturday, detaining participants on the street and at their homes.
Among those detained was Rachid Othman, a member of the National Committee for the Defence of Flotilla Activists, who spoke extensively to the media on Saturday about the condition of the four detained activists, who are on hunger strike.
Amid Israel's genocidal war and siege of Gaza in 2024 and 2025, the Global Sumud Flotilla organised a number of land and sea convoys seeking to reach the devastated enclave.
The convoys were stopped either by the Israeli military at sea or by local authorities in Egypt and Libya.
In March 2026, Tunisian authorities arrested seven flotilla activists on charges related to the misuse of funds, which fellow activists said were politically motivated.
Three were released shortly afterwards, but four, Wael Nouar, Nabil Chennoufi, Ghassan Boughediri and Ghassan Hanchiri, remain in detention.
In September, the Tunisian judiciary extended their pre-trial detention by four months.
Nouar has been on hunger strike for 36 days and has reportedly lost 26 kilograms. There are serious concerns over his health, with Othman warning on Saturday that his life was at risk.
The other three activists have reportedly been on hunger strike for 11 days.
In its statement on the arrests of protesters, the Tunisian Sumud Committee said: "At a time when the heroes of the Sumud Flotilla continue their hunger strike and are entering a critical stage between life and death - with Wael Nouar's hunger strike having reached its 36th day, and those of Nabil Chennoufi, Ghassan Boughediri, and Ghassan Hanchiri having reached their 11th day, as they demand their freedom - the regime is now targeting those who support them."
Lawyer and human rights activist Dalila Msaddek linked the latest arrests to the repressive policies adopted by President Kais Saied since his 2021 power grab, when he suspended parliament and later expanded presidential powers. His government has since overseen the arrest of hundreds of opposition politicians and activists.
"It is the same policy since the coup: arrest someone, then target their lawyer, then arrest the journalist who will speak about them, and then the protester who supports them. With every detention, a new wave of arrests is unleashed," she wrote on Facebook.

FM Wadephul: We must make Russia realize need to end war
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul made this statement before departing for New York to participate in the general debate of the 81st UN General Assembly, according to Ukrinform.
The diplomat noted that during such important meetings, the discussion cannot be limited to merely taking stock of all crises, conflicts, and wars. All politically responsible figures must be prepared to seriously pursue every step—no matter how small—toward resolving the problem.
“We will not give up, especially where our interests are most at stake: Putin’s war, with its increasingly deadly attacks on civilian infrastructure, is forcing Ukrainians to look forward to the coming winter with anxiety, while also leading his country toward economic ruin and countless deaths. Russia must be made to realize that the time has come to embark on a path of serious negotiations. Along this path, we want to strengthen Ukraine so that, with international support, it remains resilient and strong in the long term,” Wadephul stated.
He pointed out that, at the same time, Russia is increasingly openly threatening EU and NATO member states by violating airspace, destroying undersea cables, and carrying out hybrid attacks. Therefore, Germany will coordinate with its partners on how best to protect critical undersea infrastructure and how to take more effective measures against Russia’s old shadow fleet tankers off its coast.
According to the German minister, the international community must also consider how it can collectively assume greater responsibility for maritime security. For months, Iran and its militants have been blocking vital trade routes in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Supplies of energy resources, fertilizers, and aid are becoming inaccessible or are barely reaching those who urgently need them. Germany and Europe are suffering the consequences, while many countries in the Global South are facing even more dramatic hardships, where rising prices and crop failures threaten their very existence, Wadephul said.
He noted that today the prospect of sustainable, conflict-free coexistence has given way to constant escalation and urged people not to grow accustomed to this. Germany, its representative assured, “will do its part and work to overcome the oppressive silence between the conflicting parties—both in Europe and in the Middle East.”
On the sidelines of the UN General Assembly debates, Wadephul plans to meet with key G7 partners and will use this opportunity to further strengthen partnerships around the world.
As previously reported, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz was forced to cancel his visit and speech at the UN General Assembly due to domestic political issues. Germany will be represented by its foreign minister.

Morocco arrests election boycott campaigners days before vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
12:32:08 UTC
21:32:08 KST

Breadcrumb
Morocco arrests campaigners behind election boycott movement days before vote
Moroccan authorities have detained members of a left-wing political party campaigning for a boycott of the country's upcoming parliamentary elections, days before voters head to the polls on 23 September.
At least six members of the Democratic Labour Way Party, known in Arabic as Annahj Addimocrati Al-Oummali, were detained in the city of Kenitra while distributing leaflets urging people not to vote, according to Moroccan media reports.
The activists were taken to a police station for questioning before being released, while the leaflets in their possession were confiscated, reports said.
Four other party members were detained in Beni Mellal on 12 September in connection with leaflets calling for an election boycott. They were reportedly questioned by the Royal Gendarmerie as part of an investigation overseen by prosecutors before being released.
The party has also reported authorities intervening against its boycott activities in other cities, including Casablanca, Tangier and Al Hoceima.
The Moroccan Association for Human Rights (AMDH) said on Saturday that arrests had taken place in Beni Mellal and Kenitra, while party activists had faced restrictions in Casablanca, Salé, Tangier and Al Hoceima. The rights group described the measures as arbitrary and said peaceful advocacy for an election boycott was protected by freedom of expression.
The party's youth wing separately said that 16 activists had been detained in connection with boycott campaigning by Friday, with another four members in Tangier receiving summonses. Those figures could not be independently verified.
The Democratic Labour Way Party has condemned the campaign of arrests and restrictions against its members and vowed to continue urging Moroccans to boycott the election.
The party formally announced in June that it would boycott the 23 September parliamentary elections, arguing that the vote lacked the minimum conditions for a democratic process.
The arrests occurs amid questions in Morocco over the legal limits of campaigning for voters to stay away from the polls.
Morocco recently strengthened electoral legislation covering attempts to influence voters through false information and other deceptive methods.
Under Article 51, using fake news, false rumours or other deceptive tactics to sway voters or convince them to stay home can carry a prison sentence of two to five years and a fine of 50,000 to 100,000 Moroccan dirhams (around $5,000-$10,000). The rules extend to content spread through social media, online platforms and AI tools.
The government has presented the measures as safeguards against disinformation and manipulation during the election period.
However, the law does not make simply advocating an election boycott a criminal offence.
Moroccan constitutional law researcher Maryam Belil told local outlet Sawt Al Maghrib that abstaining from voting or expressing a political position in favour of an election boycott did not in itself constitute a crime.
She said criminal liability under Article 51 required the use of methods specified by the legislation, such as false information or deceptive practices intended to influence voters.
The detentions come amid wider concern over political disengagement ahead of Wednesday's vote, particularly among young Moroccans.
Only around 3% of Moroccans aged 18 to 24 are registered to vote, according to Reuters, amid widespread frustration over unemployment and distrust of political institutions.

====================================================================================================

EXPLAINER – Who gets access to advanced AI? US curbs fuel debate over technology and power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
12:28:38 UTC
21:28:38 KST

The US is tightening controls on who can access its most advanced artificial intelligence systems, extending its technology restrictions beyond chips and hardware as competition with China intensifies.
As increasingly powerful AI systems raise security concerns, government intervention and selective releases by developers are reshaping who can use the technology – and on whose terms.
"The idea of a completely borderless internet was always somewhat idealized," Antonio Calcara, head of the Geopolitics and Technology Programme at the Centre for Security, Diplomacy and Strategy in Brussels, told Anadolu.
Governments and corporations have long shaped digital infrastructure, he said, but national security concerns increasingly influence how technology is developed, shared and controlled.
That tension surfaced in June when the US government ordered Anthropic to block foreign nationals from accessing its Claude Fable 5 and Claude Mythos 5 models.
The company took both models offline worldwide, saying it could not reliably distinguish users by nationality. The restrictions were subsequently lifted, but the episode demonstrated Washington’s ability to interrupt access far beyond US borders.
Separately, US President Donald Trump in June ordered federal agencies to develop a voluntary framework under which developers could give the US government access to certain advanced AI models for up to 30 days before releasing them to other trusted partners.
Companies have also limited distribution themselves. Anthropic initially offered Claude Mythos to selected partners, while OpenAI released GPT-5.6 to a small group in June at the US government’s request before widening access the following month.
These arrangements differ from export controls, but together reflect growing scrutiny of who gains access to the most powerful systems.
Milton Mueller, a professor at the Georgia Institute of Technology and co-founder of the Internet Governance Project, said barriers are growing even as the internet’s basic infrastructure remains global.
"We have already created certain forms of fragmentation and barriers," Mueller told Anadolu, explaining that the restrictions largely affect the services people can access rather than the underlying internet itself.
Washington has imposed export controls on advanced semiconductors and other technologies to China. Beijing blocks many major US platforms through its so-called Great Firewall and restricts cross-border data transfers.
Economic incentives favor access to global markets, Mueller said, but national security concerns increasingly drive governments to impose restrictions.
Applying traditional export controls to AI models, however, is particularly difficult.
Weapons, advanced chips and other physical goods can be stopped from crossing borders. AI models delivered through online services can be accessed from almost anywhere, making it much harder to control who uses them.
Mueller compared the challenge to earlier US efforts to restrict encryption exports, which became harder to enforce as the technology moved from specialized hardware into widely available software.
Similar restrictions on AI could require extensive monitoring of who is accessing online services and from where, he said. That would be technically possible, according to Mueller, but difficult and costly to enforce on a global scale.
Control over advanced technology can also give countries leverage over their rivals.
The US, home to many of the world's leading technology companies, can use its legal and regulatory power to restrict who has access to their products and services.
Political scientists Henry Farrell and Abraham Newman call the use of control over critical global networks “weaponized interdependence.”
Their research argues that globalization has concentrated important services and technologies in a small number of countries and companies, giving governments power to restrict rivals’ access.
Closer ties between Silicon Valley and Washington also have advocates within the industry. In their book The Technological Republic, Palantir CEO Alexander Karp and executive Nicholas Zamiska argue that such cooperation is essential to US technological and military strength.
But restrictions can carry diplomatic costs.
Calcara said major powers cannot simply keep technological advantages to themselves while expecting to build strong alliances.
Washington needs partners as well as technological superiority in its long-term competition with China, he said. Restricting access too broadly could undermine the strategic advantages it seeks to protect.
The competition also complicates a debate over how quickly AI should advance.
Some technology leaders want developers and governments to slow work on the most advanced systems, warning that capabilities are outpacing safeguards.
In his essay We Must Pace the Frontier, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for greater coordination among AI companies and governments to slow the pace of cutting-edge development.
He also linked safety to competition with China, arguing that restrictions on advanced semiconductor exports could slow Beijing’s progress and give governments more time to introduce safeguards.
Trump has rejected calls to slow development, saying they risk benefiting China.
“There is a sick conspiracy going on against AI and data centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China,” he posted on his social media platform Truth Social earlier this month. “Whoever wins AI, wins!"
Mueller questioned the premise.
"If this is a race, what is the finish line?” Mueller asked.
AI advances do not automatically increase the power of the country where they originate, he argued. Benefits often flow primarily to the companies and people using the technology, although military applications could provide more direct strategic advantages.
He also questioned whether a slowdown could succeed without agreement among competing powers, seeing little prospect of the US, China and Russia simultaneously limiting development.
Mueller remains deeply skeptical of claims that AI could threaten humanity’s survival and questioned whether proposed safeguards could prevent such an outcome even if the risk were real.
The disagreement leaves policymakers facing the competing demands to preserve a technological lead, prevent misuse and decide how much international cooperation either goal requires.
Although Washington largely justifies technology restrictions on security grounds, Mueller said commercial interests also shape policy.
US companies can benefit when foreign competitors face restrictions, creating incentives to frame business concerns as national security imperatives, he said.
Mueller also questioned whether policymakers sometimes overstate the risks of relying on foreign countries for important technologies and other economic inputs.
Companies seeking market protection also find it easy to convince politicians by framing their interests as national security imperatives, he added.
China has repeatedly criticized US technology restrictions as protectionist, accusing Washington of stretching national security arguments to contain its development.
Yet rivalry has not ruled out cooperation.
Senior US and Chinese officials discussed a proposed notification mechanism for AI incidents affecting national security during talks ahead of a meeting between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping later this week.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told reporters Sunday that greater transparency between the two countries was increasingly important as their AI capabilities advanced.
"We think that, just like with any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the number one and the number two AI powers in the world is very important," Bessent told reporters Sunday.
Whether that concern can produce broader cooperation remains uncertain.
Mueller expressed doubt that the leaders’ meeting would significantly alter the technology rivalry, expecting any agreements to focus on narrower trade issues.
Restrictions could also shape technology choices far beyond the US and China.
Developing the most advanced models requires vast computing resources, infrastructure and investment, concentrating capabilities among relatively few companies and wealthy countries.
Calcara said that concentration risks deepening smaller countries’ dependence on foreign providers.
European allies remain closely tied to American technology and transatlantic security structures. Elsewhere, access and affordability could matter more.
Countries in Africa, Southeast Asia and other parts of the Global South could increasingly turn to Chinese technology if it is cheaper, more accessible or subject to fewer political restrictions than US alternatives, Calcara said.
Chinese developers have released increasingly capable open-weight models, allowing users to download and adapt them under the applicable licenses.
That flexibility could increase their appeal where customers want greater control over the technology they use.
Calcara warned that broader restrictions on American systems could therefore strengthen Chinese alternatives in markets where governments and companies can choose between providers.
The divide could also affect scientific research.
Tighter controls could gradually produce more separate US- and China-centered technology systems, with different standards and fewer opportunities for researchers and talent to move between them, he said.
Mueller said restrictions are already affecting academic exchanges, pointing to tighter US policies toward foreign researchers and international students.
Such barriers could make the technology rivalry harder to reverse, even if the two countries reach agreements in other areas.
For Washington, the challenge is therefore not only whether it can restrict access to advanced AI, but what influence it might lose by doing so.
Mueller, however, expects restrictions to persist as long as Washington views China as a strategic threat, with Beijing responding through measures of its own.

Details
The strikes near the countries’ shared border marked a new escalation of tensions, raising the risk of further cross-border fighting. They also threatened to complicate mediation efforts by regional states, including China.

Scientists create a needle-thin brain implant that can do three jobs at once
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
12:25:22 UTC
21:25:22 KST

Scientists create a needle-thin brain implant that can do three jobs at once
Scientists have created a flexible, needle-thin brain implant that can record signals, deliver drugs, and stimulate multiple brain regions at once.
- Date:
- September 21, 2026
- Source:
- Technical University of Denmark
- Summary:
- A new needle-thin brain implant can record neural activity, deliver drugs, and stimulate multiple brain regions using a single flexible fiber. Successful tests in mice suggest it could give scientists a more precise, less invasive way to study the brain and may eventually help treat neurological disorders such as epilepsy.
- Share:
A new type of brain implant could give scientists a more precise way to study the brain and may eventually contribute to treatments for neurological conditions such as epilepsy.
Researchers from DTU, the University of Copenhagen, University College London, and other institutions have developed a long, needle-thin brain electrode equipped with microscopic channels. Known as the microfluidic Axialtrode (mAxialtrode), the device is designed to provide multiple functional points along the length of the implant. This allows researchers to record neural activity and deliver medication to specific locations across different parts of the brain.
The findings were published in the journal Advanced Science.
A Multifunction Tool for Brain Research
For now, the technology is primarily intended as a research tool. Scientists could use it to investigate how signals travel through different layers of the brain during processes involving epilepsy, memory, and decision-making.
Over the longer term, the researchers say the mAxialtrode could also have therapeutic applications. One possibility would be using the device to deliver drugs to precise locations while simultaneously applying electrical stimulation or light stimulation to selected areas of the brain.
Postdoc Kunyang Sui, who developed the mAxialtrode concept together with Associate Professor Christos Markos, says one of the main advantages is that several capabilities can be combined within a single implant. That could allow researchers to perform more precise experiments while reducing the need for multiple devices inserted into the brain.
"Most current brain implants are based on hard materials such as silicon, which can irritate the brain and trigger inflammatory reactions in the tissue. The new implant differs in that it is made of soft, plastic-like optical fibers and has a specially angled tip that makes it smaller and reduces the damage caused when it is placed in the brain," says Kunyang Sui.
Sui cautions that the technology is still far from routine clinical use. Extensive testing, additional development, and regulatory approvals would be required before it could be used to treat patients.
Moving Beyond Conventional Optical Fibers
Brain researchers currently use flat-ended optical fibers in many experiments. These thin fibers, made from glass or plastic, can carry light into deep regions of the brain. They are frequently used in optogenetics, a technique in which specific nerve cells are activated using light.
Conventional fibers, however, have an important limitation. They typically interact with brain tissue only at the end of the fiber, meaning researchers can stimulate or monitor just one location at a time.
The outermost end is called the distal tip, or the "nose" of the fiber. Light is emitted and contact with brain tissue occurs only at this point. As a result, scientists may be limited to measuring or stimulating one brain layer at a time, even though many brain functions depend on communication among several layers and deeper structures.
How the New Brain Implant Works
The needle-thin mAxialtrode begins as a much larger polymer rod. Researchers heat the material and draw it into an extremely thin fiber, somewhat like producing a very fine strand of sugar, but with far greater precision.
A light-conducting core runs through the center of the fiber. Surrounding it are eight microscopic channels that can transport liquids. Those channels can also hold extremely thin metal wires used to measure electrical activity in the brain.
The finished fiber measures less than half a millimeter across. It is also highly flexible, allowing it to move along with brain tissue rather than pressing rigidly through it. This difference in stiffness could be important because harder implants can trigger inflammatory responses when they remain in the brain for long periods.
Tested in Living Mice
The researchers tested the system not only in the laboratory but also "in vivo," meaning in living mice. The electrode was implanted in the animals' brains and connected to light sources, recording equipment, and small pumps used to deliver fluids.
The experiments showed that the device could stimulate nerve cells using both blue and red light. At the same time, researchers were able to record electrical activity from shallow and deeper brain regions, including the cerebral cortex and hippocampus.
They were also able to inject different substances at separate depths, with delivery points spaced almost three millimeters apart. All of these measurements and forms of stimulation were carried out using a single lightweight fiber, which the mice were able to carry without any obvious signs of discomfort.
Potential Applications in Epilepsy and Neuroscience
The in vivo experiments and neurophysiological validation were performed in close collaboration with Associate Professor Rune W. Berg of the University of Copenhagen and Associate Professor Rob C. Wykes from University College London. Their contributions included expertise in analyzing neural circuits and models relevant to epilepsy.
The research team is now working to patent the technology behind the brain electrode. The scientists are also exploring what would be required to begin testing the device in patients within a clinical setting.
Journal Reference:
- Kunyang Sui, Neela K. Codadu, Daman Rathore, Guanghui Li, Marcello Meneghetti, Anders L. Bøcker, Rune W. Berg, Rob C. Wykes, Christos Markos. Multimodal Layer‐Crossing Interrogation of Brain Circuits Enabled by Microfluidic Axialtrodes. Advanced Science, 2026; 13 (18) DOI: 10.1002/advs.202519744

EU may extend Russia sanctions for three years if oligarchs Usmanov and Fridman are delisted
EU diplomats in Brussels are considering a compromise that would extend individual sanctions against Russia for 36 months in exchange for the removal of Russian oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the list at the insistence of Slovakia and France.
Source: European Pravda's Brussels correspondent, citing several European diplomats who spoke on condition of anonymity
Details: The Committee of Permanent Representatives of EU member states (Coreper) is currently considering a proposal from the Irish presidency to extend sanctions against Russia over violations of Ukraine's territorial integrity and sovereignty for 36 months.
Meanwhile, Slovakia continues to insist that Russian oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman be removed from the sanctions list. France also supports Usmanov's removal, citing national interests.
European Pravda sources said a compromise could be approved under which Usmanov and Fridman would be removed from the list in exchange for the extension of the sanctions regime for 36 months.
Two other individuals could also be removed from the list following a relevant court ruling, although details are yet unclear.
The Coreper meeting which is expected to finalise the decision on extending the sanctions began at 15:00 Kyiv time. Such meetings are usually held behind closed doors.
The current sanctions regime, the list for which the EU began compiling in 2014, covers individuals and legal entities responsible for actions that undermine or threaten Ukraine's territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence. Since 2022, the list has included Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin, senior members of Russia's political elite, prominent oligarchs and former Ukrainian president Viktor Yanukovych.
Background:
- On 14 September, Coreper extended the sanctions regime over violations of Ukraine's territorial integrity and sovereignty for seven days, as Slovakia and France continue to insist that two Russian oligarchs be removed from the list.
- European Pravda sources in French diplomatic circles explained why Paris wants to lift sanctions on Usmanov. It later emerged that France plans to "exchange" the removal of Usmanov from sanctions lists for the release of several of its citizens who are currently in prisons in Azerbaijan.
- The last extension of personal sanctions took place on 14 March. Then too, Slovakia pushed until the final hours on that occasion for Russian oligarchs Mikhail Fridman and Alisher Usmanov to be removed from the list.

Dubai declares 10 days of mourning for ruler's brother Sheikh Ahmed bin Rashid Al Maktoum

Dubai has declared ten days of official mourning after the death of Sheikh Ahmed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, the emirate's ruler's youngest brother.
Sheikh Ahmed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, the youngest brother of UAE Vice President and Prime Minister and Ruler of Dubai Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum has died at the age of 76, the Dubai Media Office announced on Monday.
The Ruler's Court declared 10 days of official mourning across the emirate, with flags to be flown at half-mast from Monday.
Sheikh Mohammed paid tribute to his brother in a post on X. "You are absent from our eyes but not from our prayers and hearts," he wrote.
Crown Prince of Dubai and Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defence Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed Al Maktoum also paid tribute, saying Sheikh Ahmed would remain in the family's hearts, memory and prayers.
UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan sent his condolences to Sheikh Mohammed, describing Sheikh Ahmed's contribution to the UAE's development since its founding as a lasting source of inspiration.
Sheikh Ahmed served as Deputy Chairman of Dubai Police and Public Security. He was Group Chairman of ARM Holding, one of Dubai's largest private investment firms, with interests in real estate, hospitality, health tech, telecoms and banking.
He founded the Dubai Real Estate Centre in 1991, which grew to manage more than 3,200 residential, commercial and industrial units.
Al Wasl Sports Club, which he founded in 1960, described him as one of the UAE's most prominent sports pioneers. He remained its president for decades, during which the club became one of the most decorated in UAE football.
He also established the Dubai International Marine Club in 1988, serving as its first president, and helped launch the Victory Team offshore powerboat racing operation.
In the early 1990s, he founded Jebel Ali Racecourse and helped launch the Dubai Racing Club, strengthening the UAE's standing in international equestrian sport.
He was also known for his philanthropic work and support for community and charitable initiatives across the UAE.
The 10-day mourning period will run until 1 October, with flags flown at half-mast across the emirate throughout.

Flying with your cat or dog? These are Europe’s best pet-friendly airlines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
12:20:21 UTC
21:20:21 KST

From cabin rules and weight allowances to dedicated airport lounges, a new ranking reveals which carriers make travelling with pets the easiest.
For pet owners, planning a holiday can involve a lot more than booking flights and hotels. There’s the quandary of whether their furry friend can board a plane with them, and exactly where they’d be allowed to travel to.
Fortunately across Europe, it’s common for airlines to allow pets in the cabin. Things get trickier though when a cat or dog is on the larger side. How willing are European airlines to put pets in the hold or ship them separately in cargo?
AirAdvisor, a global flight and baggage compensation service, reviewed the pet policies of 22 European airlines, investigating whether pets are allowed in the cabin, can be flown as baggage or in the aircraft’s hold and if four-legged travellers can accompany their owners into branded lounges.
The company found that certain dog breeds, such as bulldogs and pugs, may face additional restrictions, while pets younger than 12 weeks old are usually not permitted to board.
Premium and business class cabins are typically not favourable to pet owners. Codeshare journeys, where a carrier's partner airline operates the flight and crew in its place, aren't great for pets either. Connections involving different airlines can also be a challenge.
According to AirAdvisor, pet owners should be mindful of destinations, including the UK, USA, Australia and Hong Kong, where some airlines only allow pets to travel separately as freight.
So, which carriers in Europe get the tail-wagging seal of approval?
How Europe’s best pet-friendly airlines compare
Aegean Airlines
Passengers on Aegean Airlines' flights are permitted to travel with a dog or cat in the cabin, with the pet and carrier weighing no more than 8kg combined. This will cost passengers between €35 on domestic flights within Greece to €65 for long-distance intercontinental flights.
Heavier four-legged travellers can travel in the hold, with costs ranging from €50 to €90 for direct domestic flights to €110 to €180 for direct international flights. The additional cost depends on the pet's weight and there is a small additional charge if travelling on a connection.
The Greek carrier also allows pets in its branded lounges, so long as they are kept in their carriers.
Air France-KLM Group
On board Air France, passengers are allowed one dog or cat to accompany them in the cabin, so long as they weigh no more than 8kg. Pets weighing between 8kg and 75kg must travel in the hold, while any that weigh over this limit are not allowed at all.
Whether travelling in-cabin or in-hold internationally, pets must be at least 15 weeks old, although pets eight weeks and above are allowed to travel within France and Corsica or from France to Guadeloupe, Martinique or Réunion in the cabin.
The cost for in-cabin travel ranges from €70 to €250 and from €100 to €750 in the hold. Air France only accepts soft-sided carriers and welcomes pets to its lounge, so long as they are kept in their carrier.
KLM follows many of the same policies as Air France, however, the Dutch carrier's additional costs range from €70 to €500 each way.
Austrian Airlines
Passengers flying with Austrian Airlines are allowed two cats or dogs in the cabin, so long as the weight doesn't exceed 8kg. It costs between €65 for domestic flights within Austria to €125 for long-distance intercontinental flights.
Pets must be kept in a soft, bite-proof carrier in the cabin as well as when visiting Austrian Airlines lounges.
Brussels Airlines
Passengers are allowed to travel with up to two small cats or dogs in Brussels Airlines' cabins, where the weight limit is 8kg, including the pet's carriers. This can cost between €80 to €115, depending on the flight route.
However, passengers travelling with rabbit, fish, rodent or bird companions must have them travel as cargo in the hold. Here, additional costs vary depending on the pet's carrier size, with medium carriers ranging between €100 and €190 and larger ones fetching fees from €200 and €380.
Finnair
With Finnair, cats and dogs can travel either in the cabin or in the hold across all the carrier's routes. Also, pet hedgehogs, tortoises and rabbits can be transported from any EU country, either in cabin or the hold. Ferrets, however, can travel in the hold from any country. Passengers can bring two pets of the same species in one carrier, so long as the weight does not go beyond 8kg.
In-cabin fees are €60 within Europe and €120 for intercontinental flights, and hold fees are €140 within Europe and €650 for intercontinental flights. It does work out more cost-effective to book pets on board at least seven days before departure. Pets are also welcome in Finnair lounges, so long as they are kept in their carrier.
LOT Polish Airlines
Cats, dogs and ferrets can travel in LOT's cabins, or in the hold. In-cabin travel is limited to two pets of the same species, with a weight limit of 8kg. Additional in-cabin costs are €44 for domestic flights within Poland, €70 for short-haul flights and €100 for long-haul.
LOT welcomes passengers and their furry friends to its lounges and allows them to roam around under their human's constant supervision.
Lufthansa
Lufthansa flights allow passengers to travel with up to two pets, either in the cabin, the hold or separately as cargo. In-cabin pet fares will vary due to route and the animal's size, ranging from €50 to €110 one-way. Cargo hold fees range from €80 to €380.
The Cologne-based carrier allows pets in its branded lounges, but they must be kept in their carriers at all times.
SAS Scandinavian Airlines
SAS allows up to two pets per traveller, with a weight no more than 8kg if in-cabin. Pets must be at least eight weeks old to travel and will require a vet's certificate if under 14 weeks. Additional in-cabin fees start at €55 for domestic flights within its inter-Scandinavian network, rising to €149 on routes to China. Hold fees range from €90 for domestic flights to €725 on China routes.
The airline also allows pets in its lounges, but they have to be kept in their carriers.
TAP Air Portugal
TAP only allows cats and dogs to travel onboard. A passenger is allowed up to two pets that are at least 10 weeks old to fly in the cabin. The in-cabin weight limit is 8kg, while it's 32kg in the hold.
On TAP, passengers can expect to pay an additional €40 on domestic flights across Portugal booked online during the low season, all the way up to €170 on intercontinental flights booked online during the high season. Hold prices range from €78 to €247.

African athlete sets new half marathon world record
Kenyan runner Agnes Ngetich has broken the women-only half marathon world record by one second, clocking 1:05:15 to win gold at the World Athletics Road Running Championships in Copenhagen.
The 25-year-old eclipsed the 1:05:16 mark set by compatriot Peres Jepchirchir in Gdynia, Poland, in 2020.
Race data published by World Athletics on Sunday showed that Ngetich led from the start and opened a ten-second advantage by the five-kilometer mark. She finished 50 seconds ahead of fellow Kenyan Veronica Loleo, who took silver in 1:06:05, while Rwanda’s Florence Niyonkuru claimed bronze with a national record of 1:06:08.
The women-only record applies to races contested without male athletes or pacemakers. Ethiopia’s Letesenbet Gidey holds the overall women’s half marathon record of 1:02:52, achieved in a mixed race in 2021. Ngetich herself ran 1:03:04 in a mixed race in Valencia in 2024, the second-fastest women’s half marathon time recorded at the time.
The Copenhagen victory gave her a second global title this year following her triumph at the World Cross Country Championships in Tallahassee, Florida, in January. She also holds the mixed-race and women-only 10 km world records of 28:46 and 29:27 respectively.
“I am very happy and very grateful to now hold the world half marathon record, too,” Ngetich said, according to World Athletics.
Ngetich said she would consult her coach about her next steps but planned to return to track racing for the 2027 World Championships in Beijing. “It is my dream to win a gold medal on the track,” she said, describing it as “the only one I am missing.”

Houthis eye highlands amid report Trump halted strikes last minute
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
12:18:03 UTC
21:18:03 KST

Yemen's Houthi rebels pushed to seize strategic heights Monday to sever the Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed forces, following reports that President Donald Trump aborted U.S. strikes against the group at the last minute.
A lightning advance by the Iran-backed group this month has extended the wider Middle East conflict to a new theater and further threatened global energy supplies.
Washington has so far rebuffed repeated pleas from Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to join the fight in Yemen. The Houthis said Saturday they had fired on Riyadh, where loud booms were followed by columns of smoke visible near the airport.
Saudi Arabia has not commented on the first apparent strikes on the capital since the escalation began.
The New York Times reported that the Trump administration had prepared on Sunday to launch airstrikes against the Houthis after fresh calls from the Saudi crown prince. But the newspaper said Trump called off the airstrikes at the last minute, even as troops were loading bombs onto aircraft.
Reuters could not immediately verify the report. The U.S. military's Central Command referred questions to the White House. The White House did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment.
Trump spoke Sunday to Rashid al-Alimi, president of Yemen's Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government, who asked him for U.S. military help, four sources told Reuters. Two of the sources, one Yemeni and one Western, said Trump made no direct pledge of military support during the call.
The Houthis, who have controlled Yemen's capital since 2014, seized the country's Red Sea coast this month in an advance that routed forces of the Saudi-backed government.
Saudi Arabia has launched hundreds of strikes in recent days on the fighters' positions in the highlands, the Houthis say.
According to the United Nations, nearly 700 people have been killed and thousands injured in the flare-up in fighting. Nearly 130,000 Yemenis have fled homes within Yemen, and more than 3,000 have fled by boat across the Red Sea to Africa.
Five Yemeni military sources told Reuters the Houthis were now seeking to seize strategic heights, known as the Kahboub Mountains, in two provinces, Taiz and Lahij, which separate the Red Sea coast from the government-held south.
Fighting has centered on the outskirts of the remote mountain al-Wazi'iyah district in Taiz province, and Ras al-Ara along the Indian Ocean coast between the mouth of the Red Sea that the fighters captured last week and the government's base in Aden.
The Houthis aim to secure the rear of their forces around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait leading into the Red Sea by taking control of the heights, according to the sources. That would let them open new fronts and help protect their new positions.
The surge in fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis creates a dilemma for Trump, under pressure to help defend Washington's Saudi allies but anxious not to further expand the deeply unpopular war he launched in February against Iran.
The United States bombed the Houthis for two months in early 2025, but Trump called off those strikes after reaching a ceasefire with the group and has kept out of the conflict since.
The Houthis' newfound control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait risks cutting off the main alternative route that Saudi Arabia has used for oil exports that bypass disruption in the Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi Arabia has responded by increasing shipments through Hormuz, where a small number of tankers are increasingly shuttling back and forth to bring out oil, charging record fees of as much as a quarter of the value of the cargo to brave the wartime risk. They then transfer the oil to other ships in the Indian Ocean, bound for customers in Asia or elsewhere.
Satellite data shows Saudi exports through Hormuz reaching 2.9 million barrels per day in recent days, up from just 700,000 in August, making up for a halt to Saudi loadings on the Red Sea.
That has helped put a cap on the global price of crude oil, which has retreated closer to $100 a barrel after approaching $110 last week. But consumers and industry are still paying record prices for refined fuels.
The U.S. retail price of diesel, politically sensitive for Trump, hit another all-time high Monday above $6.51 a gallon, from around $3.75 before the war began in February.
In the latest reported attack in Hormuz, Britain's UKMTO maritime security agency said a ship sailing into the strait had been hit with a projectile, causing minor injuries to crew.
Diplomacy in the wider conflict has largely been stalled since a June interim agreement between the United States and Iran collapsed within weeks.
Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian is due to fly Tuesday to New York to attend the U.N. General Assembly, the first such visit since Trump launched "Operation Epic Fury" against his country alongside Israel in February.

Guidance: Design Approved Organization Scheme (DAOS)
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
13:17:33 BST
21:17:33 KST

Design Approved Organization Scheme (DAOS)
DAOS is the means by which the MOD can assess the competency of design organisations.
Documents
Details
Design Approved Organization Scheme (DAOS) provides an independent assessment of the competence of defence contractors and service organisations involved in the design of aircraft systems, associated equipment and airborne explosive ordnance and armament equipment.
MOD policy is to only procure from contractors who have been assessed as competent as stated in Regulatory Article (RA) 1005. A design organization must have a MOD sponsor (typically a DE&S DT) who will apply on their behalf to DAOS Branch Head using DAOS form 80.
Details of the approval scheme are published in MAA Regulatory Article 5000 series.
DAOS organisations will be subject to periodic on site review, based on risk, by the DAOS branch or the CAAi (CAA International).
The CAAi has been contracted by the MOD to undertake on site surveillance audits, for which they will levy a charge. Details of CAA (Civil Aviation Authority) charges can be provided by DSA-MAA-OA-DAOSGroup@mod.gov.uk
Organisations where the scope of the approval covers ITAR, complex weapons, mission software, UK Eyes only design/PDS, will be assessed by the MAA.
The MAA is to be notified of proposed changes which could affect continued possession of the approval submitted to the DAOS Branch Head using the DAOS form 82.
Depending on the nature and magnitude of any change, the MAA may need to carry out an on site assessment before issuing a revised DAOS Certificate.
A list of Approved Organisations within the scheme can be found here.
For further information please contact the DAOS team:
MAA IE&R

Ukraine has ‘lost its steel industry’ – Metinvest exec
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
12:14:49 UTC
21:14:49 KST

Ukraine has ‘lost its steel industry’ – Metinvest exec
Ukraine has effectively lost its steel industry after Russian strikes brought production at the country’s three largest plants to a halt, a senior Metinvest executive has told the Financial Times.
Ballistic missiles have disabled major steelworks in Kiev-controlled parts of Russia’s Zaporozhye Region and Ukraine’s Dnepropetrovsk Region, repeatedly striking Metinvest’s Zaporozhstal and Kamet Steel plants and ArcelorMittal’s facility in Krivoy Rog. The latest attack on Thursday damaged production equipment, workshops and railway infrastructure, the outlet reported on Sunday.
The three plants, which together accounted for about 90% of Ukraine’s steel output, are now idle, Aleksandr Vodoviz, head of the CEO’s office at Metinvest – owned by Ukrainian oligarch Rinat Akhmetov – told the FT. “As of today, [Ukraine] doesn’t have a steel industry any more,” he said.
The Russian Defense Ministry said the strikes targeted Zaporozhstal, describing the facility as a key producer of pig iron and rolled steel used by Ukrainian and European military enterprises.
Vodoviz said it was unclear when production could resume, with repairs potentially taking “days, weeks, months, or years.” The plants employ more than 15,000 people, and their shutdown could have a major impact on tax revenues for the Ukrainian budget, he added.
Zaporozhstal has been struck several times over the past month, with Vodoviz claiming the attacks had targeted its blast furnaces. “They knew everything about the plant, they knew exactly where to hit,” he said.
Moscow has also reported strikes on industrial and logistics facilities related to Kiev’s military. Russian forces last week hit the Radionix electronics plant and a data center in Kiev, which were involved in missile production and data processing for the Ukrainian Army, according to the Defense Ministry.
Other recent targets cited by the ministry include drone production and storage sites, power infrastructure, bridges, ports, warehouses, and logistics hubs. It also reported hitting a Fire Point warehouse in Kiev Region that it said stored drone components.
The attacks come as Kiev has ramped up long-range strikes on Russian energy, industrial, and civilian infrastructure, including residential buildings, warehouses, and oil refineries.
Kiev claims it considers Russian oil facilities legitimate military targets because they allegedly help finance and supply Moscow’s military campaign. Russia has condemned strikes on civilians as acts of terrorism, while maintaining that its forces only target military and defense-related facilities.
“There is a war of attrition, and now an economic war of attrition – Russia is trying to hurt Ukraine’s economy as much as possible and so does Ukraine,” Alyona Bilan, chief economist at investment bank Dragon Capital, told the FT, adding that Ukraine is unlikely to record any economic growth this year.
The damage extends beyond steelmaking. Some 2.1 million square meters of Ukraine’s roughly 5 million square meters of modern warehouse space has been destroyed, including 900,000 square meters in recent months, retailer Ruslan Shostak told the FT. The attacks could also cost Kiev around $1.5 billion in tax revenue, according to Ukrainian officials.
Ukraine’s steel industry was already shrinking before the latest strikes. The country produced around 7.4 million tons of crude steel in 2025, down from 7.6 million tons a year earlier and far below pre-conflict levels, according to the World Steel Association.
Producers have also faced growing pressure from cheaper Turkish steel made with Russian raw materials and tighter EU import restrictions. Metinvest COO Aleksandr Mironenko said last week that Kiev had been too slow to protect domestic producers with anti-dumping measures, adding to pressure on an industry now left without its three biggest plants.
