How Europe’s energy shock is fuelling the far right ahead of elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
12:12:51 UTC
21:12:51 KST

Far-right parties in Europe are exploiting the fuel crisis, blaming the mainstream for soaring energy bills. With key elections upcoming, governments are recognsing that a prolonged energy crisis could have political costs.
The far right’s victory in a German regional election this weekend has offered an early warning of how Europe’s energy crisis could reshape politics ahead of major elections in France and Italy next year.
The Alternative for Germany (AfD) emerged as the strongest party in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on Sunday, extending a run of electoral gains that has shaken Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s governing coalition. Its success comes as nationalist and far-right parties across Europe seek to turn soaring fuel and energy costs into an electoral weapon.
The immediate political threat is now spreading beyond Germany. France, Italy, Spain and Poland all face key elections next year, raising the stakes for governments struggling to shield voters from rising gas, diesel and petrol prices while avoiding another expensive round of energy subsidies.
Despite relief measures announced by Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron, the renewed energy squeeze is giving populist parties an unusually potent combination of grievances: household hardship, anger over climate-related taxes and regulations, and opposition to Europe’s efforts to sever its dependence on Russian energy.
Germany has provided the clearest early test. The AfD has campaigned heavily against high living costs and fuel-price increases, portraying them not simply as the result of the latest geopolitical disruption but as the consequence of choices made in Berlin and Brussels.
Energy is particularly useful territory for the AfD because it links an immediate household grievance with one of the party’s central geopolitical arguments. It has called for restoring cheap Russian gas and lifting sanctions on Russian energy, arguing that Europe’s current policy has inflicted severe economic costs on Germany.
Alice Weidel, the AfD's leader, has described cheap Russian energy as crucial to the success of German industry.
"The established parties want to take the money out of your pocket - fuel is being deliberately made so expensive. We want to lower fuel prices: scrap the CO2 levy, reduce VAT and the EU energy tax to a minimum," Weidel wrote on X one day before the local elections.
Two days before the elections, Merz announced fuel discounts and fuel price caps in a bid to cut soaring energy prices following damage to a Saudi pipeline that had provided an alternative route to the besieged Strait of Hormuz.
"Whether commuters, businesses, or regular car drivers – the high fuel prices are burdening our country. Together with the states, we are ensuring a tax cut of around 17 cents per litre of gasoline and diesel. This is to apply from 1 October until the end of 2026," Merz said.
But the German result suggests that emergency relief may not be enough to prevent the energy crisis becoming a wider political liability. That prospect is particularly troubling for mainstream parties in France and Italy, where the cost of fuel has long proved capable of mobilising voter anger and where next year’s elections could give energy policy a much larger national – and European – significance.
France fears fuel shortages
Macron earlier responded to the pressure by convening an emergency security meeting with the party leaders in the Elysée Palace on 18 September. He also announced an upcoming G7 energy meeting to discuss releasing a second batch of oil reserves, pushing the energy crisis from a pricing issue to a potential shortage concern.
"We have to be extremely vigilant, and we do not want to run short. We have rebuilt our gas stocks, and we are securing our supplies," Macron told reporters after the Elysée meeting.
France consumes around 600,000 barrels of diesel per day and imports half of it, Macron said, pointing to 300,000 barrels potentially at risk of shortages due to damage to a Saudi pipeline.
"We should not frighten people. We have to tell the truth about geopolitical instability and what it creates in our country, and we have to prepare for it. That is exactly what France is doing and what it has accelerated in recent weeks," Macron added.
French far-right leader Marine Le Pen said tax cuts were the only way to bring down fuel prices at the pump. "The VAT must be lowered from 20% to 5.5% on fuel. The French need it to go to work, to do their shopping, and to pick up their children from school".
Meanwhile, in Italy, Giorgia Meloni's right-wing government has moved to scrap road tax for 14.5 million cars and motorcycles from next year, at a cost of more than €2 billion, on top of a diesel excise duty cut already costing about €2.8 billion.
Rome had previously asked the European Commission to relax fiscal rules for households and industries struggling with soaring energy costs, arguing that energy security should be treated with the same urgency as defence spending.
The measures are designed to relieve immediate pressure on consumers, but they also show how energy prices are forcing governments to spend heavily to neutralise a potential political issue.
Slovakia takes aim at 'liberal west' failed policies
In Slovakia, populist Prime Minister Roberto Fico blamed Europe's war rhetoric against Russia for distracting from its own failures in tackling rising energy prices and fuel shortages, bluntly opposing military escalation.
"The West’s military rhetoric and the search for a pretext for a military conflict with Russia are intended to distract from the liberal world’s inability to address basic challenges such as the price and availability of energy and fuel, as well as illegal migration," he wrote in a post on X on Sunday evening.

Serhiy Kutsy, driver of Serhiy Kropyva, deputy head of the International Cooperation Department at the Prosecutor General's Office and a suspect in the Carthage case, posted UAH 3 million bail and was released from custody, the Anti-Corruption Action Center (AnTAC) said.
“The driver of Carthage suspect Serhiy Kropyva, Serhiy ‘Kamrad’ Kutsy, managed to post UAH 3 million bail and was released from custody,” AnTAC said in a Telegram post on Monday.
Kutsy is now required to appear whenever summoned by a detective, prosecutor or court; report any change of residence or employment; surrender his passports for travel abroad; refrain from communicating with certain people, including Kropyva and Kropyva's partner Yelyzaveta Ivakhnenko, who are defendants in the case and remain in custody; and wear an electronic monitoring bracelet.
AnTAC said that after posting bail through his lawyer, Kutsy withdrew his appeal. The Appeals Chamber accepted the withdrawal.
Kropyva remains in custody with the option of posting UAH 120 million bail.
According to investigators, Kutsy was a member of a criminal organization headed by Kropyva. In particular, he provided security during Kropyva's trips in an official vehicle and his meetings with other people, used unregistered license plates, received money from people linked to call centers and passed it on to Kropyva. He also helped Kropyva communicate with other members of the organization, participated in money laundering and carried out other instructions from him.
As reported, the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) exposed five members of a criminal organization headed by an official at the Prosecutor General's Office who systematically received illegal payments for protecting a network of fraudulent call centers and laundered more than UAH 42 million through property purchases, including apartments in the Carpathians, jewelry and deposits in relatives' accounts. The Prosecutor General's Office also said it intended to assist the investigation and announced the official's suspension from his duties.
Amid the scandal over Kropyva's possible involvement in the Carthage case, Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko submitted his resignation. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy suspended him from office, and on September 15 the Verkhovna Rada approved Kravchenko's dismissal. Kropyva is identified in covert investigative materials as Kravchenko's confidant. According to investigators, he coordinated household matters and repairs at Kravchenko's house. Kravchenko has not been notified of suspicion.
At the same time, after submitting his resignation, Kravchenko signed a notice of suspicion against NABU Director Semen Kryvonos on September 14. NABU and SAPO said in response that they viewed the move as a continuation of a systematic attack on the independence of anti-corruption bodies.
The Prosecutor General's Office said late on September 14 that no such notice of suspicion had been issued.
Kravchenko, in turn, said he had left Ukraine on a business trip. According to Ukrainska Pravda journalist Mykhailo Tkach, Kravchenko's wife left Ukraine for Moldova on September 12.
Kravchenko said he had traveled to France to attend a hearing of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) parliamentary network, but PACE said he and his representatives would not participate in the meeting.

CHP-8 is a combined heat and power plant in Moscow’s southeastern Nizhny Novgorod district. It supplies electricity and heating to residential areas and major industrial facilities across several parts of the Russian capital.
The facility is part of Mosenergo, a subsidiary of the Russian state-controlled energy giant Gazprom.
Unlike a conventional power station, a combined heat and power plant simultaneously produces electricity and heat for residential and industrial consumers. Damage to such a facility could therefore affect both the power supply and district heating.
The measures around CHP-8 follow similar attempts to shield strategic Russian facilities with nets, barriers and improvised structures as Ukraine expands its long-range drone campaign.
Book Genocide: How Russia Has Waged War on Ukrainian Books for Centuries
However, ASTRA did not report that CHP-8 itself was struck during the latest attack.
Record attack hits Moscow refinery
The fortification work began after a massive Ukrainian aerial attack on Moscow and the surrounding region overnight into Sunday, Sept. 20.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin claimed Russian forces had intercepted more than 1,600 drones since Saturday, including around 450 approaching Moscow.
“The unprecedented attack was clearly planned with the aim of disrupting the elections,” Sobyanin said on his Telegram channel.
Russian authorities reported that three people were killed and around 20 others injured during the attacks. Kyiv has not independently confirmed the Russian casualty figures.
Several drones reached the Moscow Oil Refinery in the Kapotnya district, where explosions and a large fire were reported. Reuters witnesses saw smoke rising from the refinery, while Sobyanin acknowledged that part of the facility had been damaged.
The refinery processed approximately 11.6 million metric tons of oil in 2024, producing 2.9 million tons of gasoline and 3.2 million tons of diesel, according to Reuters.
ASTRA also reported strikes on a warehouse complex in Sofyino and a power facility in Dzerzhinsky, east of Moscow. The full extent of the damage has not been independently established.
The construction follows an unconfirmed proposal for Russia and Ukraine to stop targeting energy facilities. Kyiv has said it would consider halting such strikes only if Moscow does the same and international partners can verify that both sides comply.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Culture Minister Li Yuan (李遠) on Sunday outlined six priorities for cultural development as the ministry prepares to expand programs with a smaller budget than last year.
CNA reported that the priorities cover young people, cultural talent, technology, original intellectual property, investment, and international cooperation. Li said the proposals would guide cultural policy through 2030.
For young people, the ministry plans to expand beyond its Culture Points program by supporting more Taiwan-made stories, videos, and other original content. It also wants to encourage young people to participate in community projects and become more involved in cultural and civic life.

Li said the ministry wants companies to move beyond one-time sponsorships and develop longer-term partnerships with cultural organizations. It will also seek international investment and cooperation to help Taiwan’s cultural industries reach overseas markets.
International outreach is the sixth priority. The ministry plans to promote more Taiwanese cultural content abroad while attracting international cultural professionals to Taiwan and strengthening the country’s role in global cultural networks.
The plans come as the ministry faces tighter funding after the legislature cut about NT$1 billion (US$31.4 million) from its proposed NT$29.6 billion 2026 budget and froze another NT$386 million. The cuts and freezes include funding for Public Television Service and the Taiwan Creative Content Agency.

NASA just powered up Roman’s massive 300-megapixel camera
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
12:10:58 UTC
21:10:58 KST

NASA just powered up Roman’s massive 300-megapixel camera
- Date:
- September 21, 2026
- Source:
- NASA
- Summary:
- NASA’s Roman Space Telescope has successfully activated its 300-megapixel infrared camera, which will capture enormous stretches of the cosmos with Hubble-like sharpness. Its planet-hunting coronagraph is also working as expected, putting Roman another major step closer to beginning science operations in 2027.
- Share:
NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope has reached another major milestone in space. Mission teams have successfully powered up the Wide Field Instrument, a 300-megapixel infrared camera designed to survey enormous areas of the universe rapidly while still capturing extremely fine detail.
Roman's planet-imaging system, the Coronagraph Instrument, has also completed an early checkout of its digital, electronic, and mechanical systems after waking up earlier this month.
The tests are part of a months-long commissioning process that will continue as Roman travels roughly one million miles toward its destination at the second Lagrange point, L2.
Roman's 300-Megapixel Camera Comes Online
The Wide Field Instrument, or WFI, is designed to combine an unusually broad view of the sky with the kind of sharp detail associated with space telescopes such as NASA's Hubble. A single WFI image will cover an area of sky larger than the apparent size of a full moon.
That combination of wide coverage and high resolution will allow Roman to carry out enormous surveys of the cosmos. Scientists plan to use those observations to learn more about planets beyond our solar system, investigate mysteries such as dark energy, and study how matter is arranged throughout the universe. Roman's expansive and detailed observations are also expected to create a valuable dataset for many additional scientific studies.
"After years of effort to build and test the instrument on the ground, we now have confirmation that it is operational in space. This is a huge milestone for the team at Goddard, our industry teams at BAE Systems, Inc. and Teledyne, and our science centers," said Josh Schlieder, the Wide Field Instrument scientist at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. "There is much to do, but we are on our way to groundbreaking science."
Cooling Roman's Infrared Detectors
Before engineers could switch on the WFI, the instrument spent 10 days drying out and undergoing decontamination. During that period, its detectors were kept at a relatively warm (compared to their final operating temperature) minus 85 degrees Fahrenheit, or minus 65 Celsius.
On the morning of Sep. 11, the team shut off the instrument heater and allowed the WFI to cool to minus 225 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 143 degrees Celsius). At that temperature, engineers were able to activate Roman's 18 infrared detectors. Together, those detectors have a light-sensitive area approximately the size of a laptop screen.
Later that evening, the team turned on the instrument's calibration system. The following morning, engineers began sending test data through the WFI and transmitting it back to teams on Earth.
Testing Roman's Filters and Focus
On Saturday evening, engineers turned their attention to the element wheel, which contains filters, prisms, and other optical components. The system controls which wavelengths of light reach the detectors and can separate light from cosmic objects into individual colors. This marked the first time the mechanism had been tested without gravity.
By Sunday morning, the team was testing the WFI's focusing mechanism. That system will be critical for keeping the hundreds of thousands of images Roman is expected to capture properly focused.
Throughout these tests, the detectors continued cooling toward their final operating temperature of about minus 300 Fahrenheit (minus 183 Celsius).
The results showed that the Wide Field Instrument is functioning as expected. Roman remains on schedule to release its first science images by early 2027.
Roman's Coronagraph Passes Early Checks
Roman's Coronagraph Instrument is built to demonstrate some of the most advanced technology ever sent into space for directly imaging planets orbiting other stars.
The instrument combines optics, masks, self-flexing mirrors, and sensors that are designed to suppress the overwhelming glare of a star. By blocking that light, the coronagraph could allow scientists to detect the much fainter light reflected by planets orbiting nearby.
Scientists and engineers working at the Coronagraph Commanding Center at Caltech/IPAC in Pasadena, California, verified that they can communicate with every major part of the instrument. Those systems include its software, thermal controls, mechanisms, cameras, and the avionics that operate them.
In practical terms, the test confirmed that ground teams can remotely control the instrument's various systems, including movable mechanisms that position its masks, color filters, lenses, and prisms.
Preparing the Coronagraph for Science
Engineers also verified that the coronagraph's thermal system is functioning properly and can warm the hardware to its operating temperature, a relatively comfortable 72 degrees Fahrenheit (22 Celsius).
With the exception of its detectors, the coronagraph is intended to operate near room temperature. That design makes the system easier to test while also helping preserve the material properties required by its deformable mirrors.
"Now that this test is complete, we've been decontaminating: sitting idle with our detectors warm so anything that's stuck to the surface, such as water or trace chemicals, will tend to leave it," said Eric Cady, an optical engineer leading commissioning efforts for the Roman Coronagraph at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. "This will continue for 30 days, with occasional stops to do other early calibration activities."

Ukrainian company unveils interceptor for jet-powered Shahed drones: top speed of 416 km/h
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

Ukrainian company unveils interceptor for jet-powered Shahed drones: top speed of 416 km/h
Ukrainian company Vluchnyk has completed internal testing of the Zorelit v5 (Starship), an anti-aircraft interceptor drone designed specifically to counter jet-powered attack UAVs.
Source: Vluchnyk, speaking to Militarnyi, a Ukrainian military news outlet; the company's website
Quote from Stepan Radiboh, Vluchnyk's CEO: "Zorelit v5 has completed all testing and is ready for military use. We are open to direct contracts with military units, and once the product is codified, we will also make it available through the e-Points system E-points are earned by Ukrainian units for confirmed strikes on Russian soldiers and equipment ."
Details: The drone has a stated top speed of 416 km/h and a range of up to 47 km on a single charge. At a cruising speed of around 200 km/h, it can remain airborne for approximately 17 minutes. The UAV is designed to carry a warhead weighing between 300 and 600 g.
The manufacturer says Zorelit v5 is designed to intercept Russian reconnaissance UAVs, Gerbera-type and Geran-2 drones and high-speed jet-powered Geran-3 and Geran-4 drones.
The interceptor can also be equipped with an AI-based system that automatically detects and tracks targets and provides terminal guidance during the final stage of flight. Separately, it can be integrated with the SkyMap system to enable automatic guidance to the target area.
Zorelit v5 was developed from the earlier Zorelit v4 interceptor, which the company says has been used in combat, entered service and received a NATO Stock Number (NSN). Some technical solutions proved in combat were carried over to the new version.
Vluchnyk's website lists the price of one Zorelit v5 at UAH 89,500 (US$2,000).
Background: Ukrainska Pravda previously reported that an interceptor drone developed by the Security Service of Ukraine's military counterintelligence division to counter jet-powered Shahed-type drones had successfully completed testing.

Study finds environmental awareness alone fails to change fast fashion buying
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
20:09:27 CST
21:09:27 KST

MELBOURNE, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Awareness of the environmental impact of ultra-fast fashion may not be enough to stop consumers from buying, with price and convenience often taking priority, new research finds.
The study found that shoppers often weighed sustainability concerns against affordability and convenience, using budgets and careful planning to make their choices feel more acceptable, according to a statement released Monday by Australia's RMIT University.
RMIT study co-author Associate Professor Carol Tan said despite this trend, it was important to understand that ultra-fast-fashion shopping was not simply thoughtless or impulsive.
Researchers identified two patterns they called "strategic spontaneity" and "cognitive buffering." The former involved preparing purchases by building wish-lists, parking items in carts, monitoring discounts, and waiting for payday, while the latter involved using budgets, spending limits and other rationalizations to reduce concerns about the environmental impact.
"I know it's bad for the planet, but when I'm on a budget and need an outfit for Saturday, I just block that out," one participant said.
Social media also influenced purchases by exposing shoppers to trends and making it easier to move quickly from discovering an item to buying it, according to the findings published in the Journal of Global Fashion Marketing.
What participants clicked, searched for and saved influenced later recommendations and promotions, keeping them engaged, the researchers noted.
The findings suggest sustainability messages could be more effective if they address affordability and value for money, such as comparing the cost per wear of durable and cheaper clothing. ■

China Focus: From clean plates to clean cities, Shaoxing's green push inspires global action
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
20:09:21 CST
21:09:21 KST

The main forum of the Global Observance of World Cleanup Day 2026 is held in Shaoxing, east China's Zhejiang Province, Sept. 20, 2026. (Xinhua)
HANGZHOU, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- In a restaurant in the eastern Chinese city of Shaoxing, a waiter gently reminds diners to order just enough, pointing to a small sign on the wall that reads, "Clean your plate."
This is no isolated gesture. In Shaoxing's Fushan subdistrict, similar scenes play out almost every day in more than 600 restaurants. Small-portion ordering and free takeout services are now standard at local eateries.
For residents of this historic water town in east China's Zhejiang Province, such small acts have long become part of daily life. The message is simple, but its impact reaches far beyond the dining table.
These grassroots efforts drew international attention to Shaoxing, which hosted the Global Observance of World Cleanup Day 2026 from Saturday to Monday. Themed "From Clean Plates to Clean Cities," it marked the first time China has been chosen to host the event.
The gathering brought together around 800 participants from UN agencies, international organizations, industries and businesses. They called for coordinated action across the entire chain, from reducing waste in homes to building circular, resource-efficient cities.
"From the moment I arrived, I was truly impressed by its water-town charm and clean, well-kept urban landscape -- a beautiful city that combines a rich historical heritage with vibrant modern governance," said Cecilia Andersson, Programme Management Officer and Waste Management Lead at UN-Habitat.
"Reducing food waste can conserve resources, strengthen food security and reduce pressure on waste collection and treatment systems," she added, noting that this year's theme highlights how preventing waste at source can contribute to cleaner, healthier and more resource-efficient cities.
In Shaoxing, such efforts are already yielding results. Some areas have introduced wedding banquet guidelines -- optimizing menus and cutting waste -- which have lowered food loss at rural banquets by an average of 25 percent.
These initiatives are part of a citywide campaign. Since 2023, Shaoxing has completed 514 clean city construction projects, raising public satisfaction from 91.08 percent to 95.02 percent.
Beyond the dining table, Shaoxing's green efforts extend to waste management and various industries.
The city has built nearly 4,500 waste sorting collection points and upgraded its waste management platform. By exploring new incineration technology, Shaoxing is turning household waste, once an "urban burden," into recyclable resources.
Its green efforts are also evident in its industrial sectors. Shaoxing's Keqiao, the world's largest textile distribution hub, has long been renowned for materials used in products ranging from curtains to apparel.
Inside a new materials company in Keqiao, discarded polyester textiles are depolymerized and respun into fabric that rivals virgin fiber. During the 2026 FIFA World Cup, jerseys for several national teams were made from these green fibers.
The green circular economy extends beyond cities and factories into the countryside. Shaoxing is developing green, circular modern agriculture, turning ecological advantages into industrial and income-generating benefits.
The Kuaijishan Ancient Chinese Torreya Community, one of the Globally Important Agricultural Heritage Systems, exemplifies this approach. Local authorities have integrated protection with circular utilization, promoting intercropping under torreya trees with plants such as winter melon and peony.
"This year's theme reminds us that the journey to sustainable cities starts at home," said Anacláudia Rossbach, Under-Secretary-General and Executive Director of UN-Habitat. "The choices we make in our kitchens and communities shape the way our cities function."
Experts noted that the event's debut in China reflects international recognition of the country's green urban-rural development, while also promoting global cooperation in human settlements.
"We will work with all countries to stay true to the original aspiration of thrift, promote sound practices, and build clean homes," said Ni Hong, minister of housing and urban-rural development, calling for systematic policies and collaborative exploration of new urban governance models to keep cities vibrant and sustainable.
Liu Jie, governor of Zhejiang, said the province will continuously improve living standards and contribute more to building a Beautiful China and promoting global sustainable development.
The global event comes as China works to improve nationwide efforts in waste management and environmental cleanup. In January, China released an action plan to significantly expand its solid waste treatment capacity over the next five years, as part of broader efforts to advance a comprehensive green transition across the economy and society.
Meanwhile, China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) outlines initiatives for comprehensive solid waste treatment, stronger environmental risk controls, and significant progress in addressing emerging pollutants.
Established by the United Nations General Assembly in 2023, World Cleanup Day is observed annually on Sept. 20 to raise public awareness of the role cleanup efforts play in sustainable development.
Previous editions have addressed a wide range of global environmental issues, from the challenges of waste pollution in polar regions to efforts targeting textile and fashion waste.
"Every clean place leads to a cleaner neighbourhood. Every cleaner neighbourhood builds a resilient city," said Nga Kor Ming, President of the UN-Habitat Assembly and Minister of Housing and Local Government of Malaysia, in a video address.
"Let the flowing waters of Shaoxing remind us that when resources flow circularly, communities thrive," he added. "Let's turn today's awareness into tomorrow's lasting policy." ■

Their daily duties include monitoring the surrounding waters, patrolling the island, maintaining navigation aids and recording observations, with any unusual activity reported promptly.

A smart microgrid combining wind, solar and energy storage, along with a seawater desalination system, began operating in 2019, ending the island's reliance on weather-dependent power and rainwater. In 2021, an all-electric kitchen and other facilities were put into operation, further improving conditions for those stationed there.

Asian Games | China's Zhang defends men's all-around gymnastics title (updated)
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
20:09:13 CST
21:09:13 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- China's Zhang Boheng retained the men's all-around gymnastics title at the 2026 Asian Games on Monday.
Fresh from winning the event at the Asian Championships, the 26-year-old collected 85.065 points to take gold, while Japan's Shinnosuke Oka and Daiki Hashimoto finished second and third, respectively.
Hashimoto, the Tokyo Olympic all-around champion, made a strong start with 14.500 points on pommel horse, while Zhang opened with 13.800 on floor exercise.
Oka's consistent performance kept the battle for gold close. The reigning Olympic all-around champion moved ahead of Zhang and Hashimoto after scoring 14.633 on parallel bars in the fourth rotation.
Zhang responded with 14.700 on the same apparatus in the fifth rotation, taking a narrow 0.167-point lead over Oka into the final round.
With Zhang competing on horizontal bar and Oka and Hashimoto on floor exercise, the title remained up for grabs. Zhang scored 14.033 to secure his second consecutive Asian Games all-around title, while Oka finished with 13.833 on floor to take silver and Hashimoto's 13.433 left him with bronze.
Zhang said competing last on horizontal bar allowed him to adjust his routine based on his rivals' scores. After watching Oka and Hashimoto complete their floor routines, he opted to reduce the difficulty of his routine and lower the risk of errors.
"Gymnastics keeps progressing, and both Japanese all-around gymnasts have high levels in difficulty and execution," Zhang said.
Looking ahead to the 2028 Olympics, Zhang said he needed to develop a broader range of difficult skills and improve his competitive mindset as he aims to deliver a stronger overall performance.
The all-around competition also served as qualification for the team and apparatus finals. China topped the team standings with 255.361 points, ahead of Japan on 254.460, setting up another close contest between the two traditional powers. South Korea qualified third with 238.327.
The women's all-around competition will take place Tuesday, followed by the men's and women's team finals Wednesday. ■

ANKARA, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Authorities have destroyed 217,608 cannabis and skunk plants in southeastern Türkiye, the Interior Ministry said on Monday.

Wu Mengjie (L) of China spikes the ball during the women's volleyball semifinal match between China and Thailand at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Komaki, Japan, Sept. 21, 2026. (Xinhua/Cen Yunpeng)
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- China edged Thailand 3-2 in the women's volleyball semifinals at the 2026 Asian Games on Monday, avenging its defeat in last month's Asian Championship final and advancing to the gold-medal match.
China started strongly and built a four-point lead in the opening set, but Thailand responded with improved attacking and blocking. The teams remained level from 12-12 through 18-18 before Thailand pulled away to take the set 25-23.
China regained its composure in the second set, using quick attacks to establish a lead of about four points and holding on to win 25-21 to level the match.
China took control in the third, opening a lead of more than 10 points before cruising to a 25-11 victory and a 2-1 advantage.
The fourth set was much tighter, with neither side able to pull clear. The teams were tied at 26-26 before Thailand produced strong serving at crucial moments to take the set 28-26 and forced a decider.
China dominated the fifth set, using aggressive attacks to steadily extend its lead before closing out the match 15-6.
China head coach Zhao Yong said his players maintained their determination throughout the match.
"Both sides played a fantastic match, but our players showed a slightly greater hunger for victory on the court," Zhao said.
China reached the semifinals with a 3-0 victory over Vietnam in Sunday's quarterfinals, while newly crowned Asian champion Thailand advanced after sweeping Indonesia.
Monday's semifinal was a rematch of last month's Asian Championship final in Tianjin, China, where Thailand overtook China 3-2 to secure its first ever Olympic berth in women's volleyball. ■

Another Chinese water museum joins global network, boosting water heritage protection
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
20:08:57 CST
21:08:57 KST

YINCHUAN, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- The Ningxia water conservancy museum in Wuzhong, northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, was recently admitted to the Global Network of Water Museums (WAMU-NET), becoming the 11th water conservancy and water culture institution in China to join this network.
Previously, 10 such institutions in the country, including the National Water Museum of China, the Yellow River Museum and the Changjiang (Yangtze River) Civilization Museum, had already joined the network.
The latest admission will help raise the profile of Yellow River water culture and Ningxia's irrigation heritage, while giving local institutions access to global expertise in protecting water cultural heritage and managing water resources, according to the Ningxia Water Conservancy.
Headquartered in Italy's Venice, WAMU-NET is a flagship initiative of UNESCO's Intergovernmental Hydrological Programme. It aims to advance the protection, research and promotion of water cultural heritage through global collaboration among water museums, and to raise public awareness of the sustainable use of water resources.
The network now covers more than 40 countries, bringing together over 120 water museums, water culture institutions and individual members.
The ancient Yellow River irrigation district in Ningxia is one of China's four major ancient irrigation districts and an important vehicle for promoting Yellow River culture. In October 2017, it was inscribed on the World Heritage Irrigation Structures (WHIS) list. As of September 2025, it was one of 42 WHIS sites across China.
A WHIS exhibition center officially opened in Yinchuan, capital of Ningxia, in May 2025. The first venue in the Yellow River basin to present 2,000 years of irrigation heritage in a systematic way, it filled a gap in the region's cultural offerings by bringing its water and Yellow River culture together under one roof.
In recent years, Ningxia has stepped up its protection and use of water cultural heritage, enacting China's first local legislation specifically focused on the protection of the WHIS and adding a dedicated chapter on water culture to its conservation plan (2018-2035) for the ancient Yellow River irrigation district.
These local initiatives are part of a broader national push. The Ministry of Water Resources has, notably, been building an institutional framework for protecting water heritage.
In July 2026, it issued guidelines on advancing water culture, calling for a three-pronged framework for protecting, passing on and promoting water culture. These guidelines also set out measures including drawing up technical standards for protecting and managing representative water heritage sites, promoting the digital preservation of water heritage, and encouraging local governments across the country to explore dedicated legislation. ■

China, Madagascar launch first joint operation against telecom fraud
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
20:08:48 CST
21:08:48 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Chinese and Malagasy police have carried out their first joint operation targeting telecom and online fraud, dismantling multiple criminal dens in the Malagasy capital Antananarivo and other areas, China's Ministry of Public Security (MPS) announced Monday.
The operation comes as telecom fraud syndicates, squeezed out of Southeast Asia by intensified crackdowns, have increasingly relocated to regions that include the Middle East, Africa and Central America.
Madagascar has emerged as one such destination, with its own authorities acknowledging a significant influx of fraud operators from Southeast Asia.
At the invitation of Malagasy authorities, Chinese police sent a working group to assist with the anti-fraud crackdown. Malagasy officials helped repatriate the first batch of 50 suspects to China on Sept. 8. Investigations into the cases are underway.
China has in recent years strengthened law enforcement cooperation with over 30 countries, including Spain, the United Arab Emirates and Myanmar, to tackle cross-border telecom and cyber fraud, developing cooperation mechanisms and achieving results in joint efforts against these crimes.
Since 2023, China and Myanmar have carried out joint operations that led to the dismantling of four major criminal gangs in Myanmar's Kokang region. Earlier this year, police authorities from China, the United States and the United Arab Emirates conducted their first joint law enforcement operation, resulting in the arrest of 276 suspects.
Cooperation with Cambodia, Laos, Thailand, Vietnam, Malaysia, Indonesia, Sri Lanka and other countries has also led to the arrest and repatriation of more than 20,000 telecom and online fraud suspects this year.
Earlier this month, China initiated the International Alliance Combating Telecom and Cyber Fraud, with 46 founding member countries. The alliance is an intergovernmental organization designed to promote cooperation among law enforcement agencies in tackling transnational telecom and cyber fraud and related crimes.
Through this new alliance, China will work with law enforcement partners worldwide to root out illegal fraud hideouts, track down suspects and protect the legitimate rights and interests of people, an official with the MPS said. ■

WATCH Ukrainian press gang snatch TV crew member outside Kiev studio
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21

WATCH Ukrainian press gang snatch TV crew member outside Kiev studio
A Ukrainian TV employee has been forcibly detained by a press gang outside his workplace in Kiev, with footage showing police and draft enforcers in military fatigues shoving the resisting man into a vehicle.
The incident occurred outside the main studio of Inter, one of Ukraine’s major national television channels. The detained man was identified by local media as an editing director working for the broadcaster’s news operation.
The clip, posted on Telegram on Sunday, captures a chaotic scene outside the studio as several officers surround the employee while other people attempt to intervene.
Scuffles can also be seen nearby, with a man in military fatigues pushing a civilian to the ground.
The footage appears to have been recorded by the detained man’s colleagues, who can be heard warning the officers that their conduct will be shown on television.
Российское "ипсо" в виде бусификации нагрянуло к сотрудникам телеканала Интер.
Вот тут поддерживаю, пропагандонов войны нужно отправлять на передовую в первую очередь pic.twitter.com/3APXt7qi1e
The Kiev branch of the Territorial Center of Recruitment and Social Support (TCC), the body overseeing mobilization, later defended the detention, insisting that the officers had done nothing unlawful.
According to the TCC, the editing director had no registered deferment from military service and was wanted for violating Ukraine’s mobilization rules. The agency added that neither the employee nor his employer had taken steps to secure his exemption.
Ukraine barred most military-age men from leaving the country after the conflict with Russia escalated in February 2022 and later lowered the minimum mobilization age from 27 to 25.
The country’s conscription drive has become increasingly contentious amid Kiev’s battlefield setbacks and a shortage of willing recruits.
Ukraine does not provide regular updates on its battlefield losses, but Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said last week that Ukrainian forces had recently been suffering around 27,000 killed and wounded per month, citing information from Ukrainian partners.
Russian Defense Minister Andrey Belousov, meanwhile, said in December that Ukraine had lost nearly 500,000 troops killed or wounded in 2025 alone.
Numerous videos of so-called “busification” – a term Ukrainians use for the forcible detention and transportation of military-age men to recruitment centers – have circulated online. Such incidents have repeatedly triggered confrontations between TCC personnel and civilians.
Moscow has long accused Kiev of seeking to fight “to the last Ukrainian” at the behest of Western powers that are waging a proxy war against Russia.

CNN, MS NOW and Politico will sue the Trump administration after being denied access to the White House, the news outlets said in a joint statement on Monday.
President Donald Trump said on Friday he was banning the outlets from the presidential residence as punishment for distributing what he calls "fake news."
"This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes," CNN, MS NOW and Politico said in a joint statement.
The outlets said the White House revoked their journalists' credentials "without notice or process" because it "objected to our reporting."
"Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference," they said.
Trump did not detail what prompted the ban but said "media Outlets shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they're covering the President of the United States."
The 80-year-old Republican, who has long had a fiery relationship with the mainstream media, warned on Friday that other outlets could face a similar fate but did not say which ones.
In his second term, Trump and his Republican administration have upped the ante and punished certain media outlets, both in the courtroom and through regulatory action.
Trump has also lashed out at individual reporters in person or over social media, sometimes in strikingly personal terms, insulting them in briefings or in his recent speech at the White House Corresondents’ Association dinner.
CNN had been scheduled to serve as the White House TV pool on Monday, a rotating assignment in which a broadcaster films on behalf of all television outlets for the day.
Updated guidance from the White House late Sunday simply listed a back-up crew.

PROFILE - Elif Eralp, Germany’s Mamdani, clinches historic win in Berlin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
12:02:57 UTC
21:02:57 KST

- Eralp’s Left Party wins Berlin state vote and eyes becoming the city-state’s first governing mayor with a migrant background
- Supporters compare her rise to New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s 2025 victory; she calls him a role model
-  She campaigned to cap soaring rents and condemned war crimes by Netanyahu’s government in Gaza
Berlin voters handed a historic win on Sunday to Elif Eralp, a human rights advocate of Turkish origin who now stands to become the city-state’s first governing mayor with a migrant background.
Her socialist Left Party took 25.7% of the vote—more than doubling its share from three years ago. In the spring, the party was still polling in the mid-teens. The surge was widely interpreted as evidence that Eralp had won Berliners’ trust and captured the city’s mood.
“Berliners, thank you — thank you for your trust,” Eralp told jubilant supporters on Sunday night. “Together, we made history today. Starting now, we will change Berlin — together.” She said “love and justice” had prevailed over “hatred.”
In recent months, supporters and many commentators in international media have compared her rise to New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s 2025 victory. Eralp also embraced that parallel during the campaign.
“I hope what in Manhattan, in New York was possible will be possible here in Berlin as well,” she told Anadolu only days before the vote. “Mamdani focused on social demands and that’s what we also do. And he brought different communities together, that was a big success, and that's what we also try to do.”
Like Mamdani, she put everyday economic pressures at the center of her campaign: soaring rents, higher transport costs, and problems in street waste collection. Her team ran a door-to-door campaign across neighborhoods and did not skip districts that backed the anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD).
She proposed a rent cap on city-owned apartments, a state office to fight illegal rent hikes, and a revival of plans to bring large housing companies into public ownership. She pledged that a Left Party-led government would make Berlin more affordable for all. 
From migrant family to Berlin politics
Eralp’s parents came to Germany from Türkiye after the 1980 military coup. Born in Munich in 1981, she grew up in Dortmund and Hamburg and has lived in Berlin for 16 years.
She has said she decided to study law after witnessing injustice and discrimination as a child, and has repeatedly recalled how, in primary school, she was affected by the wave of right-wing extremist violence targeting migrants in Germany in the 1990s.
That path took her into human rights work. She became a legal policy adviser to the Left Party’s group in the Bundestag, joined the party in 2017 and entered the Berlin state parliament in 2021. She has long worked against discrimination and argued for voting rights for people with a migrant background.
She still lives in a rented apartment and has looked for a new one for years without success. Asked whether landlords rejected her because of her Turkish surname, she said she did not know, because landlords do not have to give a reason.
 A fightback against the AfD surge
Eralp cast herself as an answer to the far-right AfD after that party’s strong showing in Saxony-Anhalt two weeks earlier. A Left Party win in Berlin, she argued, would mark a turning point against the AfD’s momentum.
“I am the answer to Saxony-Anhalt election,” she said after that vote. It would be a strong signal, she argued, if someone with a migrant background became governing mayor in Berlin and offered answers to social injustice instead of blaming refugees.
She also sharply criticised Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservative CDU for adopting far-right positions associated with the AfD and for failing, in her view, to address people’s main concerns. Many voters, she said, feel that “those at the top just do what they want” and no longer hear them.
Protest voters fear social decline and accept scapegoat theories, she said, “although refugees are not to blame for the mess we are in, but a neoliberal policy that cuts funds for social spending and does not support the poorest.”
The Left Party, she said, is the alternative: new measures against rent increases, action against large real-estate firms that squeeze tenants, and more affordable cities regardless of social background or origin.  
Protests, Gaza and free speech
Eralp also made the debate over pro-Palestinian protests part of her profile. She accused the outgoing CDU-led coalition under Governing Mayor Kai Wegner of canceling events and using disproportionate police force against peaceful demonstrators.
“The mayor of Berlin never listened to the issues of the Palestinian people here in Berlin, which is a big mistake,” she said. “We saw a lot of violence and repression against the people. And I want that this stops.”
She has been an outspoken critic of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government and its far-right ministers, and she has condemned war crimes in Gaza. Asked about the International Criminal Court arrest warrant against Netanyahu, she said she would push to have him arrested if he came to Berlin.
“Netanyahu must be arrested and answer before international courts for the crimes he has committed,” she said in a recent interview.
She strongly rejects accusations of antisemitism against her party, saying it supports the protection of Jewish life as well as Palestinian and Muslim life, and that both Israel and Palestine have a right to exist. Criticism of war crimes by Netanyahu’s government in Gaza, she argues, is not antisemitism. She has also said that throughout her career, she has taken part in campaigns against antisemitism. 
Coalition talks will test the comparison
Eralp’s election-night triumph does not yet give her the mayor’s office. The next challenge is turning a campaign built on cheaper rents and a change of course into a coalition that can govern Berlin.
Despite its clear lead, the Left Party fell far short of an absolute majority and would need at least two partners. After a race fought against CDU policy, the most viable path is a three-party alliance with the center-left SPD and the environmentalist Greens.
That is where the Mamdani parallel will be tested. Attention in the coming days will turn to whether Eralp can hold her core promises while bargaining with parties that do not share all of the Left Party’s positions.
Eralp has said her party’s program won the election and that cheaper rents and social justice must be written into any coalition deal. Potential partners will press her on what she is willing to drop. How far she bends — and how much of that agenda survives — will determine whether the Mamdani comparison fades as campaign rhetoric or becomes something she can actually deliver in office.

Congress nominee Milan Pradhan sent to judicial custody till October 5

With planet's future on the line world leaders convene at UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
12:02:00 UTC
21:02:00 KST

World leaders convene at the United Nations this week amid global conflict and division, facing warnings that artificial intelligence could threaten humanity while climate shocks and inflation further strain hundreds of millions of lives.
The annual high-level gathering at the U.N. General Assembly will also be consumed with major wars in Iran, Gaza, Ukraine, Sudan, Congo and Myanmar and a persisting question: Can the leaders do anything to end them?
And what can they do about the relentless rise of global warming threatening the future of the planet, the growing inequalities within and among nations and shocks to the global economy as blocked shipping routes and supply chains increase the cost of living and slow growth?
The future of the United Nations will also definitely be on the agenda. At 81, its powers are still the victorious nations from World War II, not the 21st century's major global players. The U.N.'s 193 member nations have agreed to a wide-ranging reform package that includes updating key institutions such as the powerful U.N. Security Council, where the U.S., Russia, China, Britain and France hold inordinate sway because of their veto power. Reform, however, is easier said than implemented.
Behind the scenes, there will be speculation about who will lead the United Nations next. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres' second five-year term ends Dec. 31 and no clear successor has emerged.
There is still no question that the U.N. remains THE gathering place for its 193 member nations and their leaders. Some 130 heads of state and government are expected to speak at the General Assembly starting Tuesday along with dozens of ministers.
Among the headliners will be U.S. President Donald Trump and French President Emanuel Macron. Both will speak Tuesday after Guterres' opening "state of the world" address.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan is also set to address the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) Tuesday.
He is expected to reiterate Türkiye's call for ending inaction in the face of Israel's oppression of Palestinians in Gaza and voice concerns and expectations on other international issues.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian will speak Wednesday.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu – whom New York Mayor Zoran Mamdani wanted arrested for his treatment of Palestinians in Gaza until he learned he has no such authority – will address the assembly on Thursday. For a second year, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas won't be coming to the U.N. because the U.S. has refused to give him a visa. He will nonetheless address the assembly by video the same day.
The United States, under its agreement with the U.N. to host the organization, is required to allow diplomats from all member nations to attend meetings.
Equally telling is who else isn't coming. China's President Xi Jinping is meeting Trump in Washington Wednesday, yet he is skipping – some diplomats say snubbing – the U.N. gathering and sending a vice president instead. Russian President Vladimir Putin isn't coming either and Indian President Narendra Modi has backed out.
France's U.N. ambassador, Jerome Bonnafont, said it is "extremely critical" for world leaders this week to support the U.N. as the place where the world's nations meet – especially at a time of such polarization.
"We believe in multilateralism," he said, "and we believe that the high-level week is the occasion for countries in the world to reaffirm that they prefer cooperation and dialogue to confrontation."
There is no doubt it's been a tough year for the world body. It has been pushed to the sidelines when it comes to its key responsibility of ensuring international peace and security and trying to end major conflicts in the Mideast and Ukraine. The U.S. failure to pay billions of dollars in outstanding arrears has left the organization's finances in rocky shape.
But veteran U.N. watcher Richard Gowan, the International Crisis Group's global issues and institutions program director, says 2025 was even worse.
A year ago, he said, people were contemplating that Trump would use his U.N. speech to announce that the United States would leave the world organization. Trump didn't announce a pullout last September and the U.N. muddled through the past 12 months with financial troubles that forced cutbacks to its peacekeeping operations and humanitarian aid.
In recent days, the U.S. paid $725 million of its dues to the U.N.'s regular operating budget for this year, enough to keep the Trump administration from losing its vote in the General Assembly. The payment was a strong indication Trump will keep the U.S. in the United Nations.
The U.N. is no longer "in freefall," Gowan said, but it "is stuck in an open-ended or permanent crisis." Put more graphically, he said, "The U.N. may not be in emergency care like it was last year, but it does seem to be trapped in a trauma center for the foreseeable future."
Former U.N. deputy secretary-general Mark Malloch-Brown, a United Nations Foundation board member, said, "While the world still trusts the U.N., the global public is eager for change."
The future of artificial intelligence has pushed to the forefront of global concerns, with its speeding advances and the dawning recognition that there are no industry controls, let alone any global guardrails for a technology that has many advantages but also many disadvantages and unknowns.
Days before the global gathering, leaders of three major AI companies warned about the technology getting out of human control and called for a pause, but Trump dismissed their concerns as "a hoax," and urged continued advances to keep the U.S. ahead of China.
The U.N. Security Council added a high-level meeting on AI to its agenda on Wednesday afternoon, a sign of the growing apprehension and need to address the issue. It was already slated to hold a high-level meeting on Ukraine with Zelenskyy on Wednesday morning.
For the U.N. chief, this will be his last assembly meeting with global leaders. He previewed his speech last week, telling U.N. reporters that power is shifting in "an era of deep uncertainty."
"At a time when the world faces three existential threats," he said, "international cooperation is more necessary than ever."
Others will be vying for the spotlight on issues from rising sea levels and funding education to the fight for gender equality. Hundreds of private meetings will also convene in U.N. cubicles, hotels, diplomatic missions and restaurants.
Esther Brimmer, a senior fellow in global governance at the Council on Foreign Relations and former U.S. assistant secretary of state for international organization affairs in the Obama administration, said in-person meetings can help countries hash out ideas that get implemented months later.
She called the situation in 2026 "much more serious and complex than in decades past."
"With that said, I'm also not without hope as well," Brimmer said. "Over the past decades we've learned a lot about international cooperation."

In state elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the CDU has once again suffered major losses. Der Standard explains why Merz appeared before the cameras as soon as the first exit poll results were in (Austria) :
“For days, rumours had been circulating about who might succeed him as chancellor: Hendrik Wüst, the CDU state premier of North Rhine-Westphalia; Markus Söder, the CSU state premier of Bavaria; or Federal Minister of the Interior Alexander Dobrindt (CSU). CDU must rid itself of this liability
For the Fidesz-affiliated paper Magyar Nemzet, both the chancellor and the firewall against the AfD are on the verge of collapse (Hungary) :
German State Elections Test Merz as Far Right Surges in East
“Merz could first be removed as party leader in the hope that he will then step down as Chancellor of his own accord. ... Should this lame duck remain in his politically defunct office, the CDU/CSU, which is currently polling at 20 percent, could plunge even further into the political abyss. Not the time for a prolonged cliffhanger

In the current global situation, Germany, as the EU’s most important country, must remain stable and reliable.”

“With the collapse of the political centre, the most radical alternatives on both left and right have gained massive support, making the country even harder to govern and increasing the risk of polarisation in one of the EU’s key powerhouses. ... They must reaffirm their commitment to a firm, reformist programme focused on the needs of the many citizens who feel neglected. “Why is the political situation in Germany important to us? It is the EU’s largest economy, with a GDP of over 4 trillion euros. … And since last year it has been Ukraine’s largest military donor. A defeat for Merz’s party in these elections could lead to a snap election in the Bundestag. ... And such snap elections are particularly dangerous. This is because the Alternative for Germany – a party that wants to resume importing Russian gas and opposes financial aid for Ukraine – is currently leading in the polls. The next Bundestag elections are due to take place in 2029. It would be better if things stayed that way.”
At least no AfD governments for now
The Economist (UK) seeks out the silver lining:
“There were some bright spots for centrists. Not long ago the AfD was hoping for a far bigger win in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, and perhaps even a small one in Berlin, given its fractured electorate. Instead the AfD was given a serious scare by the surging SPD in ‘Meck-Pom’, and in Berlin it underperformed its polling. Alice Weidel, the AfD’s co-leader, insisted that voters had given her party a mandate to rule in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. But the fact is that it will not govern either there or in the capital ... However you cut it, German politics is fragmenting, fraying and radicalising.”

Zelenskyy was ready to hold elections but backed off because Zaluzhnyi might run, says ex-defence minister Fedorov

Zelenskyy was ready to hold elections but backed off because Zaluzhnyi might run, says ex-defence minister Fedorov
Former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov has said President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had been prepared to hold elections before the end of the war but abandoned the idea because former commander-in-chief Valerii Zaluzhnyi might have run.
Source: Fedorov quoted in the Ukrainska Pravda article "Mykhailo Fedorov's election bid: How the ex-defence minister outplayed Yermak, became a problem for Zelenskyy and beat a deadly disease" (English translation coming soon)
Details: Fedorov said he had proposed as early as June that elections be held. He believes they could be organised before the war ends, with a presidential election first and parliamentary elections to follow.
According to Fedorov, Zelenskyy was initially prepared to go ahead with the plan but changed his mind when he realised Zaluzhnyi might run.
Quote from Fedorov: "I told the president straight out: 'We need to hold elections because then you will stop thinking about them and start thinking about your legacy.' He asked: 'What's in it for you?' I replied: 'Victory in the war.'"
More details: Fedorov also said that after he began publicly advocating for elections, he received no offers of funding for a possible political venture, even though, according to him, "plenty of people were interested".
One senior member of Zelenskyy's team told Ukrainska Pravda that Fedorov is now viewed as a political opponent, partly because of his position towards the president.
Some members of the opposition also see Fedorov as a rival to Zaluzhnyi, the source added.
The member of Zelenskyy's team said: "He's seen as a political opponent by everyone except Zhelezniak and a few other MPs. The opposition sees Misha that way because he is effectively competing with Zaluzhnyi, whom Poroshenko planned to support.
Batkivshchyna [the parliamentary faction led by Yuliia Tymoshenko] is against elections right now because for some reason they believe Yuliia's ratings will improve after the war. Servant of the People sees Misha as an opponent because he is against the president and all of us. So now he is a non-system opposition politician – he is against everyone."
Background:
- In an address on 18 August, Fedorov called for measures to ensure that Russia does not get to decide when Ukrainians can once again elect their government.
- A source from the President's Office told the BBC that Fedorov's idea of holding elections demonstrates a "complete lack of realism".
- Fedorov's team told Ukrainska Pravda that his call for elections did not mean he wanted them held "tomorrow", but was intended to highlight the need to make thorough preparations and resolve all the issues related to the process in detail.
- In an interview with CBS on 16 September, Zelenskyy reiterated that elections cannot be held while active hostilities continue due to a number of factors: legislation, the logistics of organising voting abroad and in temporarily occupied territories, and safety concerns.

Epstein survivors struggle financially as they continue to heal their wounds: ‘It doesn’t just go away’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
12:00:24 UTC
21:00:24 KST

Danielle Bensky wants a typical life.
“I would just love to own a house one day and have a dog,” said Bensky, who is among the Jeffrey Epstein survivors advocating for accountability. “I think that’s the dream – literally just to have a normal existence where we’re not trying to fight the government and constantly be facing our own abuse.”
For Bensky and many other survivors of the convicted sex trafficker, the simple dreams enjoyed by so many Americans remain out of reach. In addition to the psychological and physical toll of sexual trauma, some Epstein victims face extreme financial pressures related to their pursuit of justice for the well-connected predator.
“Right now, I am uninsured,” Bensky said.
Bensky has received coverage for mental health treatment because of a settlement between an investment bank and US Virgin Island authorities that led to the creation of a mental health fund. But there are many other costs associated with healing, she said.
Physical therapy for a post-traumatic injury costs approximately $200 per visit, she said. Bensky knows she should go more than twice per month, “but I can’t afford it,” she said. The yoga that helps keep Bensky centered comes to about $250 monthly.
“I’ve been doing all this advocacy for the year, and I’ve had to take time off from work,” Bensky said, explaining she has now hit roadblocks in securing work due to her advocacy. “There are certain places that won’t even hire some of us now because they’re saying that we’re ‘too political’.”
“I’m paying for everything out of pocket,” Bensky said about healthcare.
Congressional Democrats Ayanna Pressley, Teresa Leger Fernández and Deborah Ross this week introduced legislation to address survivors’ financial burdens. This proposed legislation seeks to launch a restitution fund in the judicial branch “for survivors of sexual violence whose rights were violated by the federal government, including all survivors of abuse by Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell”.
“Though it often goes overlooked or ignored, the deep financial burden that survivors of sexual violence carry – coupled with mental and physical trauma – can be debilitating. Navigating such harm can lead to time away from work or the need to leave a job entirely, resulting in a loss in income while rent is due, daily needs have to be met, and medical expenses to address physical injury and mental health support pile up,” Pressley said in a statement. “The Survivors’ Rights Restitution Act shines a light on this critical gap in support for survivors and would force our government to bring the meaningful accountability and compensation that survivors are owed.”
Many survivors support this initiative, but the likelihood of it passing both chambers of Congress and securing Donald Trump’s signature seems unlikely in the near future given heightened partisanship and geopolitical distractions. As a result, an initiative for steadier financial footing is poised more to be a long-term prospect rather than immediate relief.
Jess Michaels said that her financial future was derailed after Epstein assaulted her. She had flourished as a professional dancer but the attack left her unable to pursue work.
“I would go into auditions and I would lose my nerve,” Michaels said. “I would be unable to finish an audition. I would be unable to go to auditions because I would be stuck in bed, frozen or crying, and that lasted throughout my 20s.”
“The career that I had worked for collapsed … What does that end up costing someone?” Michaels said. She noted that for much of the time, “it meant I didn’t even have insurance”.
“Sexual harm is an injury that demands first aid care, just like any other injury, before it is a crime demanding an interrogation,” Michaels said. She said she has for years been dealing with physical ailments related to nervous system harm.
“That’s why I am someone that deals with gastrointestinal issues, cardiovascular issues, immune system issues, endocrine issues, endocrine system issues,” she said. “There’s something that happens when you have PTSD for a long period of time. It doesn’t just go away.”
If the bill passes, Michaels wants to spend money on her health which, she said, had deteriorated over the past year amid the stresses of advocacy. Even though Michaels has health insurance, “a functional medicine doctor that actually understands what I’m going through is expensive, and it’s often not covered by insurance”.
“Right now I can’t afford to get the exact type of doctor that I really need,” she said. “I have to wing it with AI, my [primary care provider], my insurance company, and I’m navigating all of those things, which is exhausting all on its own.”
Annie Farmer, an outspoken Epstein survivor who testified against his accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell at the British socialite’s 2021 trial, is now able to receive money for therapy from the Virgin Islands mental health fund. But from 2019 until the near-present, Farmer spent “many thousands” of dollars on therapy.
Farmer said that her she has not been working this year because her advocacy “has taken over my life”.
“That’s obviously a choice I made. I could have kept working and not really been so involved in all the advocacy, but I think it would have been hard to do both in the way at the level I’ve been involved,” Farmer said. “I couldn’t work full-time, certainly, so there’s a cost to that.”
Farmer felt as if she had the flexibility to make that choice because she received funds from the Epstein compensation and mental health funds, but said some others are not in that position. “I’ve been able to do this and still be OK and be comfortable, but I think for people that either haven’t received those funds or received significantly less, it is that much more stressful.”
Survivors praised World Without Exploitation, an organization dedicated to ending commercial sexual exploitation, for financial assistance with advocacy. But, they said, the cost of participating in advocacy remains steep even with assistance.
“I’ve paid a lot of money to be able to be an advocate this year,” Bensky said. “I paid to get myself to the State of the Union [address]. I paid yesterday to go and speak at Ayana Pressley’s press conference.”
“The advocacy component of this is so important, and it feels very crucial to many of us,” Bensky said. “So we will always pay to get ourselves there in the name of trying to make it safer and make change.”
Michaels said there are costs associated with advocacy even when her travel expenses are covered in full; outside costs, such as dog sitting, could add up to $175 to $200 per day.
“People go, ‘Oh, you chose to do it,’ but who’s going to do it for us?” Michaels said. “Nobody’s going to do it for us, and nobody can really do it for us.”
“Some victims received very little, while others received a lot. The amount of money received depended on the severity of the abuse and how the abuse affected the survivor,” Spencer Kuvin, chief legal officer of Goldlaw, who has represented multiple Epstein survivors. “Some survivors received tens of thousands while others received millions.”
Michaels disabused any potential skeptics who might think that participation in the fund automatically meant a lifelong windfall. Similar sexual assault cases that didn’t relate to Epstein, Michaels’ attorney said, might result in settlements up to $2.5m. “I got a fraction of a fraction of a fraction of that.”
Julie Roginsky, who pursued a sexual harassment claim against the former Fox News CEO Roger Ailes and co-launched the non-profit Lift Our Voices, said that many do not understand the long-term ramifications for survivors – even those who have been lauded for their bravery.
“After that applause dies down, you’re lying in bed at night at 2 o’clock in the morning, looking at the ceiling and wondering: what the hell just happened to my life? It’s been completely turned upside down,” Roginsky said. In a high-profile case such as with Epstein, barriers to work are not atypical.
“That is incredibly debilitating to know that you did the right thing, you spoke up for yourself and for other women, and it’s following you for the rest of your life – not just because of what happened to you, but also because people now refuse to give you a chance professionally,” she added.
When survivors come to Roginsky or her colleagues with questions about coming forward, she always tells them that it’s a personal decision because there are ramifications that can be “brutal”.
“I absolutely encourage people to come forward for themselves and to hold their perpetrators accountable and to help others, but at the same time, there is a huge cost to that,” Roginsky said.

Jamie Oliver’s recipes for fish pie pasta bake and tomato and feta lentils
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
12:00:24 UTC
21:00:24 KST

Of course, the act of cooking can be many things – joy, ritual, nourishment, comfort, celebration, indulgence – but this fish pie pasta bake and tomato and feta lentils are strictly about speed. Because, in reality, these are exactly the kind of recipes we all need in our repertoire, ready to whip out on a Wednesday night.
Fish pie pasta bake (pictured top)
Prep 5 min
 Cook 20 min
 Serves 4
320g frozen spinach
  1 onion (160g)
  Olive oil
  300g dried macaroni
  50g plain flour
  2 heaped tsp English mustard
  500ml semi-skimmed milk
  Salt and black pepper
  400g frozen fish pie mix, from sustainable sources
100g cheddar
2 red chicory
  60g rocket
  Red-wine vinegar
  Extra-virgin olive oil
Turn on the grill to high. Boil the kettle. Defrost the spinach in a bowl in the microwave. Peel and finely chop the onion, and place in a large ovenproof frying pan on a high heat with one tablespoon of olive oil. Cook, stirring regularly, for five minutes, or until soft. Cook the pasta in a pan of boiling salted water for eight minutes, until al dente, then drain, reserving a mugful of the starchy cooking water.
Stir the flour and mustard into the onions, then gradually stir in the milk. Add the spinach to the pan, water and all, then season. Stir in the fish chunks and simmer for five minutes on a medium heat, then stir in the drained pasta, along with a splash of the reserved water, if needed. Coarsely grate and mix in half the cheese, grating the rest over the top. Carefully transfer to the highest shelf of the grill for a few minutes, until golden and bubbling.
Meanwhile, finely slice the chicory bases and separate the leaves, toss with the rocket and a tablespoon each of red-wine vinegar and extra-virgin olive oil, then season. Serve with the fish pie pasta bake.
Tomato and feta lentils
Prep 5 min
 Cook 20 min
 Serves 4
4 garlic cloves
  1 fresh red chilli
  Olive oil
  500g ripe tomatoes
  1 460g jar roast red peppers
  ½ pomegranate
  30g shelled unsalted pistachios
1 bunch dill (20g)
  4 flatbreads
  2 400g tins lentils
  Red-wine vinegar
  Salt and black pepper
  100g feta
Peel the garlic and finely slice with the chilli, then put in a shallow casserole pan on a medium-high heat with two tablespoons of olive oil. Cook, stirring regularly, until soft but not coloured. Chop and add the tomatoes. Tip the peppers, juice and all, into a blender, blitz smooth, then pour into the pan. Cook, stirring occasionally, for eight minutes, or until thickened.
Meanwhile, hold the pomegranate half cut side down in your palm and bash the back of it so the seeds tumble out into a bowl. Finely chop the pistachios. Pick and chop the dill. Warm the flatbreads.
Drain the lentils and add to the pan with a half-tablespoon of red-wine vinegar. Simmer for a final five minutes, then stir through half the pomegranate seeds and half the chopped dill, and season.
Scatter over the pistachios and the remaining pomegranate seeds, crumble over the feta, and sprinkle over the remaining dill. Serve with warm flatbreads.

- 
  The Guardian aims to publish recipes for sustainable seafood. Check ratings in your region: UK; Australia; US.
