Guidance: Land Open Systems Architecture (LOSA)
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
11:05:00 BST
19:05:00 KST

Land Open Systems Architecture (LOSA)
Land Open Systems Architecture (LOSA) is the Ministry of Defence’s approachs to support land capability integration.
Documents
Details
Land Open Systems Architecture (LOSA) is the Ministry of Defence’s approach to using open standards, common data models and defined interfaces to support land capability integration. It helps systems exchange information more consistently, reduces bespoke integration effort, and makes it easier to upgrade or replace digital capabilities throughout their service life.
LOSA is supported by a set of core products: the Land Data Model (LDM), Generic Vehicle Architecture (GVA), Generic Soldier Architecture (GSA) and Generic Base Architecture (GBA). The LDM acts as the parent data model from which the GVA and GSA data models are derived. The Generic Architectures provide more specific approaches for vehicles, soldier systems and base infrastructure.
What LOSA does
Although LOSA is rooted in the land environment, its principles may support wider defence integration where common data models, open standards and defined interfaces are needed. It gives programmes, suppliers and integrators a consistent way to design digital and data elements so that systems can exchange information with shared meaning, rather than relying on bespoke project-by-project integration.
By promoting common architecture and reusable integration patterns, LOSA helps defence platforms work together more effectively and makes future upgrades easier. It supports interoperability across platforms, soldier systems and base infrastructure, while also helping UK land capabilities align more easily with NATO, allies and industry partners.
Who should use LOSA
You should use LOSA if you are working on systems, services or equipment that need to exchange data or integrate with other MOD, allied or industry systems.
LOSA is intended for MOD delivery teams, suppliers and systems integrators involved in the design, procurement, development or integration of defence capability. Although LOSA has strong roots in the land environment, its principles can also support wider defence integration where systems need to share information, use common data models or apply open standards.
This may include vehicles, soldier systems, sensors, communications equipment, command-and-control applications, software services and deployable or fixed infrastructure. LOSA is most relevant where systems need to work together, share information with common meaning, or remain adaptable as technology changes.
Why LOSA is relevant
Modern land capabilities are increasingly data-centric: sensors, communications, platforms, soldier systems, software services and command-and-control applications all need to share information quickly and consistently. Without a common approach, each programme can end up creating bespoke interfaces and data mappings, making systems harder to integrate, upgrade and reuse across the land environment.
LOSA is relevant because it provides the open architecture principles, common data models and defined interfaces needed to manage this complexity. By separating data and integration approaches from individual proprietary solutions, LOSA helps reduce vendor lock-in, gives MOD greater freedom to upgrade or replace components over time, and enables a wider range of suppliers to deliver compatible capability. In doing so, it supports the Land Industrial Strategy’s focus on innovation, competition and interoperability, while helping enable the Defence Investment Plan’s ambition for a more integrated, digitally enabled and adaptable force.
International collaboration
The LOSA approach and the LDM are actively used to enable interoperability between NATO members by providing a common way to describe, structure and exchange data. This helps different nations’ platforms, sensors, soldier systems and command applications share information with consistent meaning, reducing the need for bespoke integration work between individual systems.
This is particularly important for coalition operations, joint experimentation and multinational capability development, where UK systems must be able to work alongside allied systems. By promoting open standards, shared data models and reusable integration approaches, LOSA helps the UK collaborate more effectively with NATO partners and supports a more coherent approach to future capability integration.
Benefits
The LOSA products
LOSA is supported by four key products. These provide the foundations for common architecture, interfaces and data exchange in the land environment.
LOSA booklet
The LOSA booklet provides a short, accessible introduction for users who need to understand LOSA before accessing more detailed material. The booklet can be found at the top of this page.
Contact
Contact the LOSA team if you need access to LOSA guidance, standards or supporting material.

Italy moves to cap foreign students with limited Italian skills in classrooms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:03:20 UTC
19:03:20 KST

Giada Zampano
21 September 2026•Update: 21 September 2026
Italy’s conservative government led by Premier Giorgia Meloni plans to introduce a decree limiting the number of foreign students with poor Italian-language skills in classrooms, sparking criticism from educators and migrant advocates who say the measure risks creating new barriers to integration.
The proposal would give legal force to a guideline introduced in 2010 that recommended foreign students account for no more than 30% of a class but was rarely enforced, particularly in neighborhoods with large immigrant populations.
Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara has said the cap would apply only to non-EU students with little or no knowledge of Italian, rather than to all foreign pupils. Schools would assess language proficiency and educational preparedness, with the limits aimed at students requiring significant language support.
The decree is also expected to require some foreign parents to attend Italian-language courses and to ban the wearing of burqas and niqabs in schools.
Supporters say the measures are needed to improve educational outcomes and integration, but critics argue they focus on restrictions rather than investment in schools serving large immigrant populations.
Italy has about 930,000 foreign students, equal to 11.6% of the national school population, according the latest data available. Nearly two-thirds, about 607,000, were born in Italy, while roughly 323,000 were born abroad.
Although the national figure is well below the proposed threshold, immigrant populations are concentrated in some urban neighborhoods and northern regions, raising questions about how the policy can be implemented in practice.
School leaders have warned that some schools, particularly in migrant-heavy districts, have few alternatives for placing students. Antonello Giannelli, head of Italy's National Association of School Principals, has said schools cannot simply refuse admission to children.
Education unions have called instead for increased funding for language instruction, specialized teachers and cultural mediators. According to official data, students without Italian citizenship are significantly more likely to leave school early than their Italian peers.
Legal experts have also warned that strict enforcement could raise constitutional concerns if children are required to attend schools far from their communities in order to comply with classroom limits.
Speaking on Sunday at a youth festival organized by her nationalist conservative Brothers of Italy party in Rome, Meloni defended the package as a way to strengthen integration.
"For us, anyone who comes to Italy and wants to build their future here must learn our language, understand our culture, and respect our rules," she said. "It is the only serious way to welcome them."
Meloni said the decree would also prohibit the burqa, the full-body veil worn by some Muslim women, and the niqab, which covers the face except for the eyes. She did not refer to the hijab, the headscarf worn by many Muslim women.
The measures are the latest in a series of initiatives by Meloni's right-wing coalition aimed at tying immigration more closely to integration requirements, an issue that remains at the center of political debate in Italy.

A simple guide to the Yemen conflict
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:01:30 UTC
19:01:30 KST

A simple guide to the Yemen conflict
Here’s a brief history of Yemen’s war – from the Houthi takeover in 2014 to the latest escalation.
Yemen is back in the global spotlight after the Iran-aligned Houthi group earlier this month made military gains against the forces loyal to the internationally recognised government, tightening its grip over the Red Sea coast.
The latest escalation in the Arab region’s most impoverished nation follows a period of relative calm that had largely held since the United Nations-brokered ceasefire in 2022 between the Iran-aligned group and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.
The Houthi takeover of northwestern Yemen, including the capital Sanaa, in 2014 had drawn Saudi military intervention. The fighting left tens of thousands dead and millions displaced, creating a humanitarian crisis.
In 2023, Saudi Arabia and the Houthis agreed to a UN roadmap towards a permanent ceasefire after direct talks, but the roadmap was never formalised.
Here’s a simple guide to Yemen’s war, from the Houthi takeover in 2014 to the latest escalation.
From the 2014 Houthi takeover to the expansion of the Saudi-backed government
- The Houthis took over vast swaths of northwestern Yemen, including the capital, Sanaa, in September 2014, and months later assumed control of the government, forcing President Abd-Rabbu Mansour Hadi to flee to Aden and then to Saudi Arabia.
- Alarmed by the rise of the Iran-aligned Houthis on its border, Saudi Arabia intervened in support of the internationally recognised government of Hadi in March 2015, carrying out thousands of attacks. Saudi Arabia sees Iran as a regional threat due to the latter’s financial and military power, as well as support for armed groups like Hezbollah.
- In this period, Houthi rebels targeted strategic infrastructure across Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), including airports, gas fields and oil tankers in the Red Sea. According to data analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies, Saudi Arabia’s military intercepted more than 4,000 Houthi missiles, drones and other standoff weapons between 2017 and 2022.
- In 2019, the UN reported that about 24 million people (80 percent of the population) needed some form of assistance, making Yemen “the world’s worst humanitarian crisis” after nearly five years of war. The country also experienced the world’s worst cholera outbreak, amid the war‑damaged health and water systems. Millions of people were exposed, and hundreds of thousands of suspected cases were recorded.
- After seven years of conflict, the UN-mediated truce took effect in April 2022, bringing a marked de-escalation in fighting, even while a low-intensity conflict had remained since.
- In January of this year, Yemen’s internationally recognised government expanded its control of the southern and eastern parts of the country after the UAE-backed Southern Transitional Council (STC) announced its dissolution.
- The UAE’s backing of the STC, which called for the secession and independence of southern Yemen, strained Saudi-UAE ties, with Riyadh asking the Emirati forces to leave the country.
Who are the main players?
The Houthis
The Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah (supporters of God), are an armed group in control of mainly northwestern Yemen and several areas close to Saudi Arabia. Since September 10, they have tightened control over the country’s Red Sea coast, a vital shipping lane.
The Houthis from Yemen’s Zaidi Shia minority emerged in the northern mountainous region of Saada in the 1990s, demanding a greater share of power.
They capitalised on the widespread public anger against the weak transitional government that came to power after longtime President Ali Abdullah Saleh was forced to step down following the 2011 Arab Spring protests.
The Houthis initially allied with military units loyal to former President Saleh as they captured the Red Sea port of Hodeidah in October 2014. In January 2015, they seized the presidential palace in Sanaa, forcing President Abd-Rabbu Mansour Hadi to flee to the southern port city of Aden. Hadi later moved to Saudi Arabia, from where he ran his government-in-exile until his resignation in 2022.
The Houthi group then spent years, with Iran’s backing, fighting a military coalition led by Saudi Arabia.
Seen as part of a regional alliance known as the “axis of resistance” and backed by Iran, the Houthi group nevertheless has its own base, its own interests, and its own ambitions.
The group has gained international prominence for its attacks on Israel and shipping in the Red Sea since the start of Israel’s genocide in Gaza in October 2023.
Saudi Arabia
Riyadh entered the Yemen war when it led a military coalition against the Houthis in March 2015, seeking to restore the government of then-President Hadi.
Houthis have accused Riyadh of carrying out hundreds of attacks in support of the internationally recognised government battling the Houthis in the latest fighting.
Presidential Leadership Council
The PLC was established in 2022 when former President Hadi formally transferred his powers to the new eight-member body.
It represents the internationally recognised government of Yemen, with a mandate to manage the country’s political, security and military affairs, and to steer negotiations towards a permanent ceasefire. It is chaired by Rashad al-Alimi, an adviser to Hadi and former interior minister with the government of the late President Saleh.
Its membership is drawn from a mix of northern and southern politicians and military-linked leaders in a bid to unite major anti-Houthi forces under one roof.
The PLC is backed by Saudi Arabia and the alliance that Riyadh leads. Since taking over complete control of southern Yemen after the dissolution of the STC, the PLC aims to unite Yemen, including the areas controlled by the Houthis.
Islah party
The Yemeni Congregation for Reform, better known as Islah, is a Sunni Islamist movement with historical ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. It is a faction within the recognised PLC-led government but has long had an independent identity. Its major stronghold has long been Marib, the country’s sole gas-producing region with one of its largest oilfields.
National Resistance Forces
The National Resistance Forces is a government-aligned military faction led by Tareq Saleh, nephew of the late former President Saleh.
The force has maintained ties to Saudi Arabia and, like the Islah party, is part of the PLC. It aims for a unified Yemen, positioning itself as a counterweight to both the Houthis and southern secessionists.
Who controls what in Yemen?
The Houthi movement controls Sanaa, the capital, and most of northwestern and northern Yemen, including the entire Red Sea coastline and the Bab al-Mandeb strait, one of the busiest global maritime routes. The control over Bab al-Mandeb by the Iran-aligned Houthis has raised concerns about navigation amid the closure of the Strait of Hormuz by Iran in response to the US-Israel war on Tehran.
The internationally recognised government, meanwhile, controls much of the rest of the country.
What is the humanitarian situation?
More than 112,000 people have been displaced in Yemen and close to 3,000 have fled the conflict to Djibouti, according to the UN.
The International Organization for Migration estimated that 22 million Yemenis, nearly half the population, are in urgent need of humanitarian aid.
The UN Security Council, meanwhile, has condemned the Houthis’ continuing attacks on Saudi Arabia, saying they have caused civilian casualties, including women and children, and damaged energy infrastructure.
What do we know about the latest fighting?
Tensions escalated in July after Yemen’s government forces claimed an attack on an airport in Sanaa, preventing an aircraft from Iran from landing. More attacks followed, and it further escalated in late August when the Houthis launched a major offensive, saying the 2022 truce had been violated by government forces.
The Saudi Arabia-led coalition on Saturday evening said on X that it “successfully intercepted and destroyed” a missile attack attempting to target Riyadh – the first attack on the capital since the Yemen conflict erupted in July.
The coalition added that the Houthis had tried to target “civilians and civilian infrastructure” in several cities in the west of the kingdom, including the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea, an important export hub for Saudi oil, which were additionally thwarted.
The Houthis confirmed they had targeted “sensitive sites” in Riyadh, as well as Aramco facilities in Yanbu.
“The message from the Yemeni group is that despite the Saudi bombardment campaign across Yemen, it will continue to step up its attacks and meet escalation with escalation,” said Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from Sanaa.
The incident comes days after Riyadh accused the Houthis of targeting Mecca on Wednesday, denouncing it as a “cowardly terrorist attack” on Islam’s holy city. The Houthis strongly denied the accusation, calling it a “worn-out lie”.
Meanwhile, on the ground in Yemen, the armed forces of the Saudi-backed internationally recognised government and the Houthis are engaged in fierce fighting in southern Marib as well as Taiz, Lahj, al-Jawf and al-Bayda.
The Yemeni army also said 13 soldiers were killed in two days of clashes with Houthi forces in the southwestern provinces of Taiz and Lahj.
On September 10, the Houthis made their most crucial gain in this bout of fighting by seizing the crucial Red Sea city of Mocha, expanding control over the strategic Bab al-Mandeb strait.
Despite appeals from Riyadh for United States President Donald Trump to strike the Houthis directly, Washington has so far held back, wary of opening a new front while still fighting a costly war with Iran.
Meanwhile, US officials have met Houthi representatives in Oman over the weekend. The Houthis reportedly assured Washington that vessels not linked to Saudi Arabia would not be targeted.
The Houthis have banned the passage of Saudi ships, adding pressure on Riyadh, which has used the Red Sea as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz. Last week, the Houthis also attacked the East-West pipeline, disrupting the export of Saudi oil and causing global oil prices to cross $100 per barrel.

Sound guardians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:01:00 UTC
19:01:00 KST

For Abidin, a Balik elder who lives in East Kalimantan in Borneo, Indonesia, the sounds of nature aren’t merely a backdrop but a vital part of how he navigates the world. But as the rainforest around him has become more developed, the calls of creatures once heard everywhere have grown scarce. And that process is speeding up. To relieve Indonesia’s capital city of Jakarta, which is sinking due to overdevelopment and vulnerable to climate change, the government is building a new one, Nusantara, close to Abidin’s home. The noise of construction and city life is beginning to overpower the soundscape he relies on, and researchers suspect they may already be pushing wildlife away.
In this short documentary, the US director Leah Varjacques traces an effort to record the sounds of the rainforest before they’re altered forever. The film follows Abidin working with a research team that includes Wendy Erb, a bioacoustic scientist from the Cornell Lab of Ornithology in New York, to collect audio from caves, treetops and everywhere in between. In doing so, they hope to create a record for posterity so that the rainforest’s soundscapes – and the culture and ancestral knowledge embedded within them – are never fully erased.

Neuroscientists uncover a previously unknown brain benefit of very slow running
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:00:16 UTC
19:00:16 KST

A recent study published in Imaging Neuroscience indicates that engaging in a very slow jog for just ten minutes can improve a person’s mood and enhance their ability to focus. The research suggests that the gentle, rhythmic bouncing of running at a low intensity provides a measurable boost to brain regions involved in mental control and emotional regulation.
Human beings have a long evolutionary history of running, a form of movement that provides widespread physical and mental health benefits. The prefrontal cortex, a brain area located behind the forehead that is responsible for complex thinking and emotional control, appears particularly responsive to aerobic exercise.
Earlier work has shown that different forms of activity can stimulate this brain region. For example, a 2014 study revealed that even very mild, low-effort pedaling on a stationary bike is enough to activate the prefrontal cortex and improve mental focus. Building on that concept, researchers later found that a 2021 study of a ten-minute session of moderate-intensity running boosts mood and strongly activates the same brain areas.
But moderate running can be physically taxing, elevating the heart rate to a level that might feel uncomfortable or stressful for older adults or people who are not regularly active. This research progression led scientists to wonder if the gentlest possible jog could still deliver these same brain and mood benefits without the physical strain.
The research was led by Hideaki Soya, a professor emeritus at the Institute of Health and Sport Sciences at the University of Tsukuba, and Ryuta Kuwamizu, an assistant professor at the university, alongside Chorphaka Damrongthai and colleagues at the Soya Laboratory. “Running is widely believed to benefit the brain, but studies combining rigorous brain imaging with tightly controlled running protocols have been relatively limited, partly because exercise intensity is much easier to control on a bike,” Soya and Kuwamizu told PsyPost.
The researchers wanted to test running under controlled laboratory conditions at the very bottom of the intensity range, using speeds that could also be used for walking. “If the benefits were still present at such a low intensity, running could become accessible to people who cannot, or simply do not want to, run hard,” they explained.
To measure mental performance, the researchers focused on executive function, a term for the mental skills that help people pay attention, manage time, and switch focus. They were especially interested in whether the physical characteristics unique to running, such as the vertical bouncing of the head with each step, might play a role in how the exercise affects the brain.
To explore this question, the researchers recruited 24 healthy young adults. Each participant completed two separate sessions on different days. One session involved sitting quietly on a treadmill for ten minutes to serve as a resting control condition, while the other session involved running on the treadmill at a very slow pace for ten minutes.
The researchers tailored the running speed to each person’s fitness level, ensuring it remained at a very light intensity. For the men in the study, this averaged about 3.4 miles per hour, and for the women, it averaged about 2.4 miles per hour. These are speeds that most people could comfortably walk, but the participants were instructed to maintain a running form with small steps.
Before and after each session, participants completed a brief survey assessing their mood on two dimensions: arousal and pleasure. They also completed a computer-based task called the Stroop test to measure their executive function. The Stroop test asks participants to look at color words, such as the word “RED,” printed in an unmatched color like blue ink, and then quickly identify the ink color rather than the written word. This creates a mental conflict, and the extra time it takes to answer correctly is a measure of cognitive interference.
To observe brain activity, the researchers used functional near-infrared spectroscopy. This non-invasive imaging technique uses light sensors placed on the scalp to measure changes in blood oxygen levels in the brain. Because exercise can cause changes in skin blood flow and heart rate that might interfere with these readings, the researchers waited five minutes after the running session before measuring brain activity.
During a separate two-minute run, the team also attached a small sensor to the participants’ heads to measure vertical head acceleration. This allowed them to capture the rhythmic bouncing motion of the participants’ steps.
The researchers found that the ten-minute slow run provided noticeable benefits compared to the resting session. Participants reported feeling more energetic and experiencing a more pleasant mood after the very light run.
“Notably, the increase in pleasant mood was particularly strong, suggesting that slow running may be especially effective at improving how people feel,” the researchers noted. They were surprised to see that the increase in pleasant mood appeared particularly pronounced compared with what they had observed with very-light-intensity pedaling in their previous studies.
Performance on the Stroop test also improved. Following the slow run, participants reacted faster to the conflicting color words, which suggests a temporary sharpening of their executive function and focus.
The brain imaging data supported these behavioral changes. After the slow run, the researchers saw increased blood oxygen levels in specific left-sided areas of the prefrontal cortex while participants completed the Stroop test. These specific regions, known as the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and the frontopolar area, are heavily involved in overriding impulses and managing complex tasks.
When the researchers analyzed the head acceleration data, they noticed an interesting pattern. The amount of vertical bouncing a participant experienced during their run positively correlated with how much their pleasant mood increased. This provides evidence that the physical sensation of rhythmic up-and-down motion might be one of the mechanical factors that make running feel enjoyable.
“Intriguingly, this increase in pleasant mood was correlated with the magnitude of each runner’s head acceleration, raising the possibility that the gentle bouncing rhythm characteristic of running may itself contribute to why running feels good,” the researchers said. “Importantly, this head acceleration reflects the rhythmic vertical motion of the whole body, rather than simply movement of the head.”
The practical significance of the study lies in its cost-benefit balance, demonstrating that a very easy, walking-compatible pace with very low physiological strain is sufficient to produce measurable improvements. “If you have avoided running because it seems too demanding, slow running may offer a very accessible way to begin,” Soya and Kuwamizu added.
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2023, which found that a ten-minute bout of very light-intensity exercise dilated the pupils and was associated with increased left prefrontal cortex activation and better executive function. The current results also align with a study covered by PsyPost in 2024, which found that short bursts of light-intensity physical activity increased blood flow to the prefrontal cortex, though that earlier study tested brief desk movements in children without directly measuring cognitive performance.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind regarding this study. The experiment involved a small group of healthy young adults, meaning the results might look different in older populations or those with specific health conditions.
“Please do not read this as ‘slow running is better than harder running’ or as a claim that everyone should switch to slow running,” the researchers cautioned. “For those who enjoy brisk or vigorous running, it remains an excellent form of exercise for body and brain.”
They emphasized that their point is about the floor, not the ceiling, showing that measurable brain benefits of running can already appear at its very lowest intensity.
The study also relied on brain imaging equipment that lacked short-separation channels, which are specialized sensors used to filter out superficial blood flow in the scalp. While the researchers used specific timing and analytical techniques to reduce this noise, future studies using more advanced sensors could help confirm that the observed signals originate entirely from within the brain.
Additionally, the researchers compared running only to a resting state. Because they did not include a walking condition at the same speed, it is difficult to completely separate the effects of the running motion from the general effects of being upright and moving.
The team noted that the relationship between head acceleration and pleasant mood is currently exploratory and correlational, meaning causality is not yet established. “By directly comparing running with walking, we aim to determine whether the rhythmic vertical acceleration characteristic of running contributes to changes in mood and brain function,” they said.
Looking ahead, the researchers plan to test slow running in populations who may benefit from it most, including older adults, people with low fitness, and those with depressive symptoms. They also hope to better understand the neural mechanisms through which slow running influences the brain, such as how it might engage arousal-related catecholaminergic systems—neural pathways involving dopamine and noradrenaline.
“Our long-term goal is to establish slow running as an evidence-based, easily accessible daily habit for maintaining mental and cognitive health across the lifespan,” they explained.
“Running is one of the most fundamental human movements, yet many people feel that it is not for them,” Soya and Kuwamizu concluded. “We are beginning to think that slow running may be more than simply running slowly. It may be a form of locomotion in which we move slowly while preserving the gentle, rhythmic vertical oscillation characteristic of running—and enjoy the pleasant ‘vertical groove’ created by that rhythm.”
The study, “Slow running benefits: Boosts in mood and facilitation of prefrontal cortex function even at very light intensity,” was authored by Chorphaka Damrongthai, Ryuta Kuwamizu, Yudai Yamazaki, Naoki Aoike, Dongmin Lee, Kyeongho Byun, Ferenc Torma, Kazuki Hyodo, Worachat Churdchomjan, Michael A. Yassa, Kazutaka Adachi, and Hideaki Soya.

Expect ‘high tide’ of Chinese biotech deals as threat of US curbs fades: analysts
Stocks jump on reports Washington will allow most licensing deals under ‘substantially softer stance’ than had been feared, analysts say
US-China biotech deals are expected to thrive because Washington is reportedly leaning away from sweeping restrictions, according to analysts, giving Chinese healthcare firms a major boost following Beijing’s ambitious five-year plan for the sector.
Out-licensing deals between China and the US would “ride on a high tide” in the favourable environment, said Nomura’s head of China healthcare research Jialin Zhang, in a research note on Sunday.
The US Treasury Department was drafting investment rules for American pharmaceutical firms that would preserve their ability to license most Chinese drugs, barring links to pathogens or weaponisable biotechnology, Reuters reported on Friday, citing unnamed sources.
That stance would represent a “substantially softer stance” than had been feared based on restrictions outlined in two US bills earlier this year, said Tony Ren, head of Asia Healthcare Research at Macquarie, in a note on Monday.

We Have a Climate Imagination Problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

Earlier this year I stood in a draughty sports hall, facing rows of 10-year-olds sitting cross-legged on the scuffed floor. I asked them a question: “What does climate change mean?”
Small hands shot up: “The sea rises and floods everything,” one child said. “Fires are gonna burn all the forests,” another added. “We all die.”
The litany of apocalypse continued until I interrupted with a second question. “And what can we do about it?”
Silence.
After some shuffling, one girl tentatively offered: “Solar panels?” Then a louder boy called out, “Recycle!” His classmates nodded.
And that was pretty much it.
I've worked in climate communication for nearly 30 years, interspersing sessions with CEOs, activists, and politicians with talks to school kids. Over those decades, I’ve watched the average 10-year-old acquire an increasingly sophisticated picture of the climate crisis they will inherit. They can imagine burning forests, flooded cities, dying species, and an uninhabitable planet. Many of them seem to understand climate science better than some CEOs.
But ask these children to picture what we do about it, and suddenly their extraordinary imaginations contract to a recycling bin.
To be clear, I am enthusiastically in favour of recycling—just not as our answer to a planetary emergency. But I understand why I’m still hearing that inadequate response. Since the greenhouse effect and global warming first entered mainstream public consciousness in the 1980s, we’ve offered people ever more detailed maps of the apocalypse with barely a sketch of the way out.
The climate movement, of which I’m a proud member, has been complicit in this communications crisis. Most messages shared by progressive forces are merely an ad nauseam echo of: climate change is real, humans are to blame, and the consequences are catastrophic. I call this framing the earned dystopia, and it’s so ubiquitous most pre-teens can parrot it.
After so many years, can we not imagine a different story?
One reason for this imagination deficit is that storytelling has been treated as merely the spoonful of sugar to help the scientific medicine go down. Storytellers are asked to act as the marketing department for climate science.
But if that subservient role for storytellers was ever needed, it’s increasingly futile now that climate change has started communicating itself. Our growing count of horrifying floods, fires, storms, and droughts capture headlines without my help.
We have clear science and brutal direct experience of climate change, so why haven’t politicians and populations sprung into action?
The logic of the climate crisis is clear. What we’re missing is the magic.
Long before humans measured atmospheric carbon, we whispered tales of flood and fire. Stories have always helped us understand who we are and what we might become. Increasingly, researchers are proving this singular power of stories to spark ideas, possibilities, and acts of imagination.
I believe part of this magic comes from stories’ purpose in curating emotions rather than evidence.
Today, we don’t particularly lack information about heat pumps, electric vehicles, or regenerative agriculture. More details than you could ever want are just a click away. What we’re missing is an emotional architecture for change; how it feels to want a different future and to believe we can reach it.
That’s where great storytelling could change everything. Our ability to enter a story and temporarily experience the character's world as our own is called narrative transportation. Studies prove that this experience of emoting along with fictional people can directly influence real people’s attitudes, intentions, and even our behaviors. Few other mechanisms can achieve the same effect.
Climate politics has sensed this power, but translated it into the narrower language of “public narrative.” Politicians now plot narratives for electrification and renewables. Campaigners construct counter-narratives to fossil fuels. Brand teams test sustainability narratives against each other. In climate circles, everyone is searching for the breakthrough narrative that will finally unlock action. But too often the term is simply a cypher for messaging. And messaging is not the same thing as mythology.
A political narrative tells us how to understand an issue while mythology helps us understand ourselves. And climate change is mythological in scale. It contains terrifying monsters, underdog heroes, unexpected allies, destruction and rebirth. Or at least it should. My problem is with the enormous cultural library of apocalyptic narratives compared to a surprisingly small shelf of fables that foreshadow a better ending.
We need a plot twist in climate storytelling, moving beyond the threat and into the thrilling adventure of solving it. Tales of the messy decades in which billions of people change how they power homes, grow food, travel, build cities, and protect one another from a climate that has already changed
That’s a job for storytellers.
Culture makers are beginning to catch on. I’ve been invited by television and film writers, social-media creators, and brands to help climate solutions appear in comedy, drama, adventure, and everyday life. Ever more box-office hits, like The Wild Robot, Avatar, and the upcoming Digger, reflect our fight against climate and nature crises. Sesame Street is helping kids cope with extreme weather. New climate fiction novels weave answers into stirring worldbuilding. These all work because they are compelling and moving stories above all, not climate science lectures dressed in a thin veil of narrative. Many other scriptwriters, novelists, social media creators, musicians and artists must add to this list.
I passionately believe that climate solutions are the most important story of this century.
When I return to that classroom over the coming years and ask the same two questions, the first answers will remain frightening. But when I ask what we can do about it, I hope every hand will shoot up, because we’ll have filled kids' imaginations with enough possibilities that they can start inventing answers we haven’t thought of yet. That will be a good day.

We Need to Stop Talking Like Climate Change Is Partisan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:00:03 UTC
19:00:03 KST

This summer of disasters has shown us that climate impacts are not political, and it is past time we stopped talking about them as if they were. A flood doesn’t knock on your door and ask who you voted for in the last election before it sweeps your house away, nor does wildfire smoke distinguish between Republicans and Democrats before it chokes the air.
People who raise awareness about climate change know that how you communicate your message matters, and there’s much to learn from them. We surveyed the top organizations and individuals who regularly communicate about climate change across the U.S. and Canada. Almost none said that advocating for candidates or policies was the goal of their work. Their top priority was helping people understand what’s happening and why it matters: we’ve always had heatwaves and droughts, storms, and floods—but the faster the planet warms, the worse these events get.
Climate change is loading the weather dice against us, and its effects are growing. A recent study estimated that deaths caused by extreme heat are vastly under-reported. Air pollution, whether from burning fossil fuels or wildfire smoke, is responsible for a growing list of health impacts, from increased risk of asthma and dementia to premature death. The financial toll of climate change is also on the rise as climate-related expenses, including rising utility bills and insurance premiums, are already adding at least $400 to $900 to yearly household budgets. And as we have seen over the past few years, there are no climate havens: we are all at risk.
Here’s the thing, though: when people connect what’s happening to why it’s happening, their support for all sorts of climate action grows. This fact is true in the U.S., in Canada, and in dozens of other countries too. Why? Because we need solutions at scale that make the easiest, most affordable choice the best choice for the planet and our future. This requires action at every level: individual, community, and corporate action, but also government policy that enables and accelerates the rest.
Even as the impacts from climate change grow, data show that we still aren’t hearing or talking about it enough. Just under half of Canadians and 41% of Americans read or hear about climate change once a week. Only 20% of Americans discuss global warming with family and friends a few times a month or more. And nearly half, 44%, say they never discuss it at all.
Why aren’t we hearing about it more? Why do so many articles about the devastation of the Nepal floods, the soaring costs of home insurance, or the escalating health risks of wildfire smoke fail to make the connection between these issues and climate change?
There are many reasons, but one is the fact that polarized public discourse has made climate conversations more difficult, and even well-meaning efforts to “move climate change up” people’s priority list often fundamentally misrepresent the risks. The reality is that climate change doesn’t need to move up any list; it is already impacting any homeowner’s, farmer’s, teacher’s, or parent’s top concerns. But that connection isn’t always obvious: it needs to be made, again and again.
Given this contraction in public climate conversations, we wanted to learn from those who are still doing climate communication. What’s working, and how can we amplify it? Here’s what we found.
The first and most important lesson is that talking about climate change means talking about everyday life. When we asked climate newsletter writers, podcast hosts, people who regularly post on social media, and those building climate content for non-profits, their response was clear. Their first priority is to connect the climate crisis to other concerns people face: our jobs, our health, the places we love. They don’t set up climate change as a rival to those worries. Instead, they understand that climate change is already shaping the things people worry about. When we connect the dots between what we love and how climate change threatens it, it becomes obvious that nearly all of us have our own reasons to care and act.
The second priority climate communicators identified was shifting public perceptions and norms. And this issue is equally vital. Three years ago, 71% of Canadians and 63% of Americans reported they were worried about climate change. But most people keep their worries to themselves and underestimate how many others share their concerns. When people don't hear their neighbors, coworkers, and friends talking about climate change, they’re less willing to bring it up themselves. Conversely, of everything people can learn about climate change, knowing that others care best predicts whether people speak up. And here's why it matters: if we don't talk about climate change, how will we know who else cares about it—and if we think we're alone in our concern, why would we act?
Climate communicators are not pushing to make this a partisan issue—in fact, only 4% prioritized advocating for elected officials or candidates. Instead, they’re working to inform and educate their audiences about climate action, climate science, risks, and impacts, in hopes of equipping others to talk about climate change themselves.
Climate communication that isn’t polarizing and connects directly to what we already care about is exactly what we need; we just need more of it. Yet only 41% of the communicators surveyed report having received any financial support for their climate communication in the past five years. A third work entirely alone, and two-thirds work either alone or with a small team of ten or fewer colleagues. Even with these limitations, they are producing content and getting the word out: nearly eight-in-ten say they’re publishing content about climate change at least once a week.
We know that climate shocks, like the ones we’ve experienced this summer, open windows of opportunity: people who live through climate change-exacerbated extreme events are more supportive of climate science and climate action and are more civically and politically engaged. On this warming planet, we all need to learn from what the few who are talking about climate change are already doing. Research has shown that friends and family are trusted messengers who can initiate a pro-climate conversation loop. We all need to become climate communicators and stop letting those who want to delay climate action as long as possible polarize it and silence us.
To care about climate change today, one doesn’t need to be anything other than a human being living on planet Earth. And when we stop talking about climate change like it’s a political issue and start talking about it as a shared challenge that we all need to work together to solve, that’s when we’ll finally be able to start talking about saving ourselves.

Press review: State Duma set to keep five parties while Europe faces record fuel prices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:00:01 UTC
19:00:01 KST

MOSCOW, September 21. /TASS/. The single voting day to elect lawmakers to the 9th Russian State Duma has ended, with the lower chamber of the Russian parliament set to include the same five parties and United Russia retaining the majority of seats; Europe is grappling with record-high diesel and gasoline prices, seeking a way out; and the US and Denmark seem to have found a way out of the crisis over Greenland. These stories topped Monday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.
Media: Russian State Duma to include same five parties following election, with United Russia retaining its leadership
The Single Voting Day 2026 has ended in Russia. The results of the elections held September 18-20 will determine the 450 members of parliament, as well as new governors and regional lawmakers. Preliminary results indicate that United Russia maintains a solid lead in the party-list vote. It is followed by the Communist Party of the Russian Federation (CPRF), the Liberal Democratic Party of the Russian Federation (LDPR), New People, and the A Just Russia - For Truth, according to the Russian Central Election Commission’s report as of the end of September 20. Meanwhile, unprecedented cyberattacks from abroad and drone raids sought to actively disrupt the voting.
At the time all polling stations in Russia closed, voter turnout for the federal parliamentary elections stood at 56.66%, the CEC reported. This figure has already surpassed the turnout rates from the 2021, 2016, 2003, and 1993 elections. Meanwhile, the final turnout on the electronic voting platform exceeded 90%. The final election results will not be announced until September 25 at the earliest. In addition to the parliamentary elections, Russians elected regional lawmakers and municipal authority representatives in 39 regions, as well as regional heads in eight regions through direct voting.
The political system successfully passed a stress test by ensuring that the elections were held under wartime conditions, including drone attacks, new sanctions, and problems in the fuel market, Konstantin Kostin, head of the Civil Society Development Foundation and former head of the presidential administration’s Domestic Policy Department, told Vedomosti. "This fact, along with United Russia’s lead, is an important argument in support of Russia’s position in international relations and at the negotiating table," he emphasized.
Most Russians support the current course, while a minority believes their vote can make a difference. "Two factors - the desire for stability and the demand for change - overlap, resulting in a very high voter turnout," Kalachev noted. Boycotting the election as a form of protest does not seem to have been very popular, he said.
The Donetsk and Lugansk People’s Republics, as well as the Kherson and Zaporozhye Regions, participated in parliamentary elections for the first time in history as Russia’s full-fledged subjects. According to Central Election Commission (CEC) Deputy Chairman Nikolay Bulayev, these regions are already fully integrated into the country’s overall electoral system. The same technologies are used there as throughout the country.
However, as AI and the digital ecosystem of elections become more complex, cybersecurity issues are also the rise, Dmitry Orlov, CEO of the Agency for Political and Economic Communications, told Izvestia.
Nevertheless, the political system’s ability to respond to these challenges remains paramount, a task that the 2026 campaign successfully met, the expert pointed out.
Vedomosti: How record-high diesel and gasoline prices affecting Europe
French President Emmanuel Macron called French fuel prices "unbearable" on this X page. On September 18, he met with representatives of major political parties to discuss the situation in the fuel market. As of September 17, gasoline averaged 2.6 euros per liter in the EU and 2.12 euros per liter in the eurozone.
EU governments have three main tools at their disposal: a temporary reduction in the tax component of prices, targeted assistance to vulnerable households and transportation companies, and measures to ensure greater supplies to the European market, Vladislav Belov, deputy director of the Institute of Europe, told Vedomosti. Abnormally high prices for diesel and gasoline are becoming an additional factor holding back economic growth in the EU, the expert noted. According to him, high diesel fuel prices increase costs in freight transportation, agriculture, construction, and parts of the manufacturing sector, and are then passed on to consumer prices through supply chains. Therefore, if current price levels persist in the medium term, one can expect additional inflationary pressure, a decline in real incomes and consumer demand, as well as a deterioration in the competitiveness of European manufacturers, Belov emphasized.
European countries lead the world in motor fuel prices primarily due to taxes, Alexander Frolov, deputy director of the MGIMO International Energy Policy and Security Institute, pointed out. The situation in the Middle East has worsened the disruption of Russian fuel supplies to the global market caused by attacks on Ukraine, which has driven up prices and exacerbated the chronic energy crisis that Europe has been facing since the late 2010s, the expert stressed. With the severing of business ties with Russia and the strategy to phase out its hydrocarbons by the end of 2027, the safety net has vanished, and the search for replacements in alternative markets only drives up prices, Frolov said. "Europe is affected by any upheaval on the periphery, which could previously be offset by Russian supplies combined with conservation measures," he stressed.
The causes of the fuel price crisis are the same across all regions of the world, but for the US, a key factor is the exceptionally high profitability of oil and petroleum product exports, which diverts fuel from the domestic market, Alexey Belogoriyev, research director at the Institute for Energy and Finance Foundation, emphasized. Europe, on the other hand, is a net importer: these are fundamentally different starting points, he said. The expert also stressed that EU countries are indeed experiencing the consequences of decades of "dieselization" of passenger vehicles and the severing of energy ties with Russia. Public perception of the crisis is similar in the US and Europe, but the economic consequences for European consumers are more severe, Belogoriyev noted.
Kommersant: What US should expect from new Greenland deal
The US and Denmark appear to have reached an agreement to resolve the crisis around Greenland. President Donald Trump announced that the parties will soon conclude a deal under which the Americans will, on the one hand, be able to significantly and indefinitely expand their military presence on the island and, on the other hand, prevent any attempts by their opponents to gain a foothold in this strategically important region. And although the US already had extensive rights and capabilities in Greenland, Trump considers this a diplomatic breakthrough.
The conflict between Washington and Copenhagen over the status of Greenland, which is officially part of Denmark with autonomous status, has lasted more than a year and a half and is approaching a resolution. Washington will apparently no longer attempt to buy the island, threaten to seize it by force, or persuade its residents to revolt against the central government. The US president did not disclose the text of the draft agreement but revealed its three key components. First, he said, it will be open-ended. Second, it will allow the US to significantly expand its military presence on the island, something the Americans, according to him, intend to do "immediately." And third, no US opponents will be able to establish military bases or make significant investments on the island without written approval from the Americans.
Meanwhile, it remains unclear whether this truly constitutes a diplomatic breakthrough, as Trump is eager to portray it, until the text of the new agreement is made public. Both American and European media outlets have pointed out that the US already held extensive rights and capabilities on the island under the 1951 US-Danish agreement on the defense of Greenland. They argue that the White House has achieved nothing new and that the deal merely allows the US administration to "save face."
According to international security expert Konstantin Bogdanov, American interest in Greenland is longstanding and predominantly military in nature. "Greenland’s primary significance lies in its convenient location as a forward early-warning outpost. There is a radar station there that is part of the US missile and nuclear strike warning system, oriented toward the north and northwest - that is, toward the potential trajectories of ballistic missiles launched from Russian territory, as well as cruise missiles launched over the Arctic," he told Kommersant.
Over the past 10 to 15 years, he noted, the US has reacted nervously to China’s attempts to initiate investment and infrastructure projects in Greenland. "In its current form, the agreement preserves and strengthens US priority in Greenland, eases concerns about the emergence of Chinese influence there (including the possibility of deploying technical intelligence assets), and, most importantly, resolves the diplomatic crisis in relations with Copenhagen that arose due to President Trump’s clumsy remarks," the expert concluded.
Media: Results of German local elections become 'disastrous' for Chancellor Friedrich Merz
The latest state elections in Germany have dealt a blow to the ruling party and Chancellor Friedrich Merz. The chancellor himself described the results in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania as a "catastrophe." In Berlin, meanwhile, the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) is losing its grip on the city government. Strong gains by the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) are making it increasingly difficult for mainstream parties to form coalitions, leaving their governments increasingly unstable. As Germany slides deeper into deindustrialization, the protest vote is gaining momentum.
According to Fyodor Basov, a senior researcher at the World Economy and International Relations Institute under the Russian Academy of Sciences, the popularity of the Alternative for Germany in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania is growing for economic reasons, such as a decline in the population’s purchasing power and a lack of economic growth. Unemployment in this already economically weak region has reached 8%, which is higher than the national average. The far-right’s ratings are also boosted by ongoing debates over the possibility of resuming operations of the Nord Stream 2 pipeline as the region is located on the Baltic Sea coast, through which the gas pipeline runs. Following the 2022 sabotage, electricity and energy prices skyrocketed by 30-40%, placing the greatest burden on ordinary citizens, the expert told Izvestia.
If the CDU fails to win seats in the state parliament of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, it will be not just a slap in the face, but a serious blow to the reputation of Merz and the party, Alexander Kamkin, an associate professor at the Russian Financial University, told Vedomosti. Given the current state of German politics, Merz has few allies, Artyom Sokolov, a senior research fellow at the MGIMO International Studies Institute, agreed. Despite all his stubbornness, the chancellor risks going down in history as a failed head of government who did not complete his full term. Merz’s government is currently paralyzed, and the CDU could lose its seats in the state parliament of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and be defeated by the Left Party in Berlin. All of this means significant setbacks for the ruling party, the expert noted. Immediately after the elections, Merz will put his leadership to a vote of confidence at an emergency meeting of CDU executives and state party leaders.
The elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin are a test of the effectiveness of Merz’s government, for which success at the regional level is of the utmost importance, Maria Khorolskaya, a researcher at the World Economy and International Relations Institute under the Russian Academy of Sciences, pointed out. The main loser in these elections will be the CDU; the party has seen its support decline in both Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin. As for Merz himself, the expert stressed that the chancellor may weather the storm and preserve the federal coalition. The head of government intends to hold on to his post, and finding a replacement who satisfies everyone will not happen quickly. The second most likely scenario is a change in the chancellorship while keeping the current government intact, Khorolskaya concluded.
Izvestia: NATO practicing blockade of Baltic Sea's access to Atlantic
NATO has deployed a major naval task force in the North Sea and the Atlantic, including a UK aircraft carrier strike group. As part of the Strike Warrior 26-2 exercises, the alliance’s member states intend to systematically test, for the first time, the joint use of all three types of drone systems: surface, underwater, and aerial UAVs. London cites the protection of deep-sea internet cables and seabed infrastructure as the official reason for the maneuvers. However, experts say that the stated goal of defending communications is a cover for more aggressive scenarios: the task force is training to intercept Russian Northern Fleet submarines at the boundary between Iceland and the Faroe Islands, as well as block exits from the Baltic Sea to the Atlantic.
The North Sea is of vital importance to Russian shipping: it is traversed by ships and vessels traveling from the Baltic Sea to the Atlantic. Therefore, extensive NATO maneuvers in the region affect the interests of both Russia’s civilian and military fleets, military expert Dmitry Boltenkov told Izvestia. According to him, due to the alliance’s increased activity in the Northeast Atlantic, Russian ships regularly set sail to monitor the situation and escort vessels. The Russian Navy will closely track the actions of NATO forces, the expert added.
Since its inception, NATO’s primary task has been preparing for confrontation, first with the Soviet Union and now with Russia. All of the alliance’s tactics, scenarios, and maneuver plans have historically been based on an assessment of our forces, weapons, and resources, Vice Admiral Alexander Brazhnik, former chief of staff and first deputy commander of the Baltic Fleet, stressed. "The main goal of these exercises, shrouded in a veil of formal secrecy, is to practice specific methods of conducting combat operations at sea, such as anti-submarine warfare, coordinating with aviation, and repelling attacks. At the same time, these maneuvers are traditionally accompanied by attempts to seal off the area in order to conceal Russia’s true capabilities and tactical maneuvers from outsiders," he explained.
According to the vice admiral, although the North Sea does not directly border Russia, it is an area of international waters where freedom of navigation applies to all. Such combat training exercises have always been monitored. The Russian Navy, air force, and satellite constellation will undoubtedly track the actions of a potential adversary and study NATO’s tactics and forces deployed. In this regard, the West’s strategy has remained unchanged for decades, Brazhnik emphasized.

Despite court wins, California election war with Trump rages on

Despite court wins, California election war with Trump rages on
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Los Angeles County has received multiple subpoenas seeking voter information, which appear to be part of a nationwide effort by Homeland Security officials to identify noncitizens who have illegally voted.
- Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has claimed without evidence that there may be more than 190,000 noncitizens on California voter rolls, which state officials have called baseless.
With the deadline for mailing out millions of California ballots nearing, Los Angeles County’s top election official welcomed the U.S. Postal Service’s recent assurance that it will process those ballots as normal — not under the untested new vetting system backed by President Trump and rejected as unworkable by the U.S. Supreme Court.
“That certainly serves as a stabilizing force, as we’re literally weeks away from mailing the ballots,” said Dean Logan, head of the L.A. County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk’s office.
Still, there are other Trump administration challenges to deal with, he said — including unsubstantiated public claims of widespread voter fraud, refusals by top-ranking officials to rule out deployments of armed federal agents to polling places, and behind-the-scenes criminal probes into local voter lists.
Since March, Logan’s office has received a series of federal grand jury subpoenas demanding voter registration and other information on dozens of individuals who the Trump administration says may not be U.S. citizens, Logan confirmed to The Times.
Logan said his office is now in the “interesting place” of having to comply with the subpoenas despite suspecting that the Department of Homeland Security relied on inaccurate or outdated voter information to compile the names to investigate.
“We’re responding appropriately as directed through a subpoena, but that doesn’t afford the dialogue for us to get the background on what they’re looking for and how they came up with the names that they did,” Logan said. “There’s really no information being provided to us on that.”
The subpoenas appear to mirror others received by elections officials elsewhere in the country as part of a new Homeland Security effort to identify noncitizen voting, which Trump has long alleged without evidence is widespread.
In July, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin publicly claimed, again without evidence, that there may be more than 190,000 such voters on California rolls. On Friday, the Justice Department announced it had charged 16 noncitizens in six states with illegal voting and other election-related crimes following investigations alongside its Homeland Security partners.
Gov. Gavin Newsom signed legislation to boost security for California elections, an effort to guard against potential Trump administration interference in the Nov. 3 midterm election.
California Secretary of State Shirley Weber dismissed Mullin’s claims. Independent elections experts and Democratic officials say voter fraud should be taken seriously, but is exceedingly rare. California has more than 23 million registered voters.
Mullin’s remarks and the subpoenas appear part of a much larger and unprecedented federal effort to bolster allegations from Trump that the upcoming Nov. 3 elections are unsafe and corrupted by noncitizen voters.
Trump issued two executive orders, one requiring voters to provide additional identification and proof of citizenship, and one ordering the Postal Service to refuse mail ballots it deems illegitimate. The Justice Department has sued California and other states for their voter rolls, and Homeland Security has threatened state elections officials with criminal sanctions if they don’t purge noncitizens from their rolls.
Trump gave a speech in July alleging that the American election system is “so vulnerable that no one can possibly defend it.” Earlier this month, he encouraged his supporters to “cheat like hell” to keep Republicans in power, and told them they would receive $5,000 each if they succeed — which many experts derided as a “bribe.”
Last week, FBI Director Kash Patel refused to rule out sending federal agents to polls.
Despite all that, California officials and independent elections experts have maintained the election will be safe — in part because Trump’s executive orders and the Justice Department’s many lawsuits seeking state voter rolls have all been blocked by the courts.
“The bottom line for voters in California right now is nothing has changed. We’ve had safe and secure elections, and we will continue to do so,” said Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.).
Logan said it “is clear that the administration is aggressively pursuing their narrative” about voter fraud being widespread as part of Trump’s old “playbook” of questioning votes he expects to lose — but that the election in California will nonetheless “be fair and secure and transparent.”
The fight over fraud
At least three subpoenas have been issued to Logan’s office — one in March, one in July and one this month — including from the U.S. attorney’s office for the Southern District of California, The Times confirmed.
U.S. Atty. Adam Gordon, who leads the federal prosecutor’s office in San Diego, did not respond to a request for comment. First Assistant U.S. Atty. Bill Essayli, who leads the federal prosecutor’s office in Los Angeles and has announced two voter fraud cases in recent weeks, also did not respond to questions about his office’s election work.
Essayli did say Saturday, in response to Gov. Gavin Newsom touting new state laws aimed at safeguarding California elections from Trump administration interference, that no state law can prevent the Justice Department from investigating voter fraud and that his office “will continue to investigate, arrest, and prosecute all violations of federal election laws.”
Additional information, including how the subpoenas may relate to Mullin’s claims, wasn’t immediately available.
Mullin in July alleged in a letter to Weber that a federal review of unspecified data found “as many as 190,832 non-citizens registered to vote in California.”
Weber responded in writing that she had “serious doubts about the reliability” of that analysis, as California election officials “work every day to maintain accurate voter rolls” and have never shared their rolls with the Trump administration — despite the administration’s failed lawsuit demanding them.
Weber criticized Mullin for having made such claims with “no detail whatsoever that my office can use to evaluate the veracity of your allegations,” and asked that he provide a “detailed description” of the data and methodology used to reach such conclusions.
Weber’s office said Mullin’s letter was “part of a broader effort to intimidate Californians and make it burdensome to participate in our democracy.”
In a statement to The Times, a Homeland Security spokesperson said the department offered to meet with Weber and her staff “to engage in a collaborative good faith discussion” about identifying noncitizens on state rolls, which she declined.
The spokesperson said Mullin’s count of potential noncitizens on California rolls was based on “publicly available data from states’ voter rolls” that was cross-referenced with its own lists of “known” noncitizens. “It’s not rocket science; it’s an easy step to secure our elections.”
Independent experts also have questioned Mullin’s claims, pointing to investigations elsewhere — including in Texas — that found Homeland Security data on alleged noncitizen voters were substantially inaccurate. A federal judge recently blocked the use of a Trump administration database known as the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements program based on the likelihood that it could lead to legitimate voters being purged from rolls.
Last week, Padilla and Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) released a Homeland Security whistleblower report alleging that department leaders, under a new “Unlawful Voter Initiative,” were requiring poorly trained employees to identify at least five potentially illegal voters per hour — one every 12 minutes — using questionable data the department said it compiled using “magic.”
In a letter to Mullin, the senators demanded the initiative be halted, arguing that work at such a “breakneck pace” is bound to produce errors and that agency officials appeared to be circumventing court orders blocking their access to state vote rolls by gathering such information “by any means, regardless of state laws.”
Padilla on Friday asked California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta’s office to investigate the whistleblower’s claims. A spokesperson for Bonta’s office said the allegations “describe yet another fishing expedition by the Trump Administration to uncover evidence of widespread voter fraud despite repeated findings that there is none,” but otherwise declined to comment.
The Homeland Security spokesperson rejected the whistleblower claims, saying its work has been “conducted diligently and professionally” as part of a “commonplace law enforcement” effort. The spokesperson said that the agency cannot comment on active investigations, but that its investigative branch — Homeland Security Investigations, or HSI — is “actively rooting out and investigating election fraud wherever it can be found.”
“There is no quota on criminality. DHS will pursue each and every illegal voter to the fullest extent of the law,” the spokesperson said.
Fears and reassurances
Recent polling has shown that fewer than half of Americans expect the midterms to be “free and fair,” and that Californians are more concerned about Trump administration interference than voter fraud.
Election experts said some of the worst threats have already been blocked, but acknowledged remaining worries.
Rick Hasen, director of the Safeguarding Democracy Project at UCLA Law, said he is concerned the Trump administration will try to deny the outcome or seize ballots in close congressional races — but only if control of the House or Senate rests on them.
The justices turned down an emergency appeal from Trump’s lawyers, who argued the government needed a new and untested system of unique bar codes to track millions of mailed ballots.
Brendan Nyhan, a political scientist at Dartmouth College and co-director of Bright Line Watch, said he worries that isolated incidents of federal agents intimidating voters or seizing ballots in key races will throw the legitimacy of the entire election into question — and that the Trump administration will capitalize on that to serve its own agenda.
Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), part of a Democratic task force preparing for such issues, said that Trump and other administration officials are trying to interfere in the election because they know they have “failed to deliver for the American people” and the Republican Party stands to lose power as a result.
Schiff said that Democratic leaders are fighting back “and largely succeeding,” but that “the best way to uphold the integrity of our elections” remains voters making their voices heard.
Padilla said the attempt by Homeland Security to push its way into elections has been “shoddy” in part because “they don’t have the expertise [and] it’s not their charge,” but also because Trump has put Mullin and other election “conspiracy theorists” in charge.
“If you install a conspiracy theorist into these roles, then they’re gonna come out with these claims that are not based on facts, not based on evidence, not based on any data,” he said.
Padilla said Trump and his supporters are “absolutely laying the groundwork” to question November election results they don’t like, but voters should know that “there’s even more of us standing up and fighting back and protecting their right to vote.”
