'Rules need to be upheld': Australia's push to change a contentious UN power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
08:33:32 UTC
17:33:32 KST

Australia would push to reform the United Nations if given a seat on its Security Council, Foreign Minister Penny Wong has said, as she joined Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in New York for the United Nations General Assembly.
Speaking with SBS News, Wong said Russia's use of veto powers to exempt itself from repercussions during its invasion of Ukraine was an example of where Australia would seek reform.
"We've had a longstanding position as a country of reform of the veto, and we know it's been misused previously," Wong told SBS News on Monday.
"What happened in relation to Russia's invasion of Ukraine was that a permanent member of the Security Council used its veto to prevent any action being taken for its own breach of the charter. That was an example where we would like reform."
Fifteen countries sit on the Security Council, and its five permanent members — China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States — have the right to veto any resolution or decision.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
In 2022, Russia vetoed a Security Council resolution that described its attempts to unlawfully annex four regions of Ukraine as “a threat to international peace and security”, demanding Russia “immediately, completely and unconditionally withdraw all of its military forces” from Ukrainian territory. Ten of fifteen members had voted in favour of the resolution, while four abstained.
Wong said that Australia was "for reform", but that Australians were "very practical people".
"We recognise rules need to be upheld; the UN needs to be reformed.
"We want to make sure, where it really matters, that we continue to be part of setting the direction about that reform."
Wong has backed Albanese's bid for a seat on the council, which Australia has not held since 2014. Asked whether the veto powers in their current state rendered the campaign redundant, Wong stood by the pursuit.
"We might be distant from New York, but we are not distant from the rest of the world, and the world does have an effect on what happens in our economy, in our lives.
"So what I would say is we want to be able to advocate for Australia's interests in every forum that matters, and the UN Security Council matters."
International law under 'pressure'
International law is under a "great deal of pressure", Wong said, but the best response would be for countries to "come together" and advocate for the observance of international law.
"You've got two options, don't you? You can throw your hands up and say, 'I give up'. Or you can say, 'This actually matters to many countries.'
"We're not a superpower, but we're a country with substance and power to work with others to try and ensure that we hold onto the rules that matter."
Asked whether Australia could hold the United States to account over accusations around the war in Iran, as well as its actions in Venezuela, Wong said it was a task for the international community to work out the rules that "we really want to hold on to, that matter to us".
"I think trading arrangements matter to us. They certainly matter to Australia, and we've been very clear about our difference with the Trump administration."
But Australia does not intend to join its like-minded international partners in broader sanctions on Israeli settlements on the West Bank, Wong said, referring to "targeted sanctions" announced earlier this month as the UK banned trade in the occupied territories, and nine European countries said they were considering the same.
"I've announced already that we would engage in targeted sanctions," Wong said, noting that no country that had announced it would engage in the sanctions on a blanket basis had yet implemented them.
"And we certainly will be working with them as they do that to understand how they intend to deal with that," she said, and added that she has a "very clear intention" of engaging in more action against settlements, "which are an obstacle to peace", and "engaging in behaviour which makes two states less likely" in the case of the E-1 settlement, a contentious development plan for a 12-square-kilometre corridor in the West Bank.
"We'll continue to work closely with our like-minded countries just as we did a year ago, when, with others, we recognised the state of Palestine, which was part of the precursor to the peace plan, which we want to see implemented."

Ukrainian climbers Hryhorii Ilchyshyn and Yaroslav Tkach won gold medals in the speed relay at the World Climbing Series stage in Chongqing, China. During the tournament, the Ukrainian duo broke the European record twice, defeating the United States team in the final. The National Olympic Committee of Ukraine reports this, UNN writes.
A World Climbing Series stage in speed climbing took place in Chongqing, China. One hundred athletes from five continents took part in the competition — 57 men and 43 women
On their way to victory, the Ukrainian duo broke the European record twice. First, in the quarterfinal against China's first team, the Ukrainians improved the continental record to 10.26 seconds. The speed relay is a new discipline that made its debut at the World Climbing Series level only this year and is currently being considered as one of the future main disciplines on the competition calendar

Ukraine Urges Global Shutdown of Russian House Centers, Citing Security Threat
Germany closed the Russian House cultural center in Berlin on September 18, ending years of what Ukraine describes as malign Russian influence. Despite the shutdown, similar centers still operate in at least seven European countries, Ukraine's foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, warned on September 19.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Sybiha set out the assessment in a post on X on September 19, framing the network as a front for hostile operations. He identified Rossotrudnichestvo and the so-called Russkiy Dom, or "Russian House," centers as instruments of disinformation, destabilization, and espionage.
"Our shared European home is not the place for 'Russian houses' promoting war propaganda," Sybiha wrote. He commended the measures European authorities have taken to block the network across the continent.
The network's reach extends well beyond Europe, the minister noted. Its scale is even greater in Africa, Central and Eastern Asia, the Asia-Pacific, and South America, he added.
In several countries, the official infrastructure remains intact, Sybiha stated, and in some it is woven directly into Russia's diplomatic presence. He characterized the centers as part of a comprehensive Russian effort to wage a global battle for public opinion.
Ukraine has formally appealed to governments worldwide to recognize the network as a national security threat, the minister explained. Kyiv has presented arguments for restricting the centers' operations and closing them entirely.
The Berlin shutdown extends a steady contraction of Russia's overseas cultural network. At least 13 Russian Houses have closed worldwide since Moscow's full-scale invasion began in 2022, down from roughly 15 centers operating across the European Union before the war.
Slovenia became the first EU state to expel its branch in April 2022, followed by Romania's closure of the Bucharest center in February 2023 and the shuttering of houses in Slovakia, Croatia, North Macedonia, and Montenegro that same year.
Moldova's center ceased operations entirely on July 4, 2026, with officials citing subversive activity conducted under the guise of culture.

Moldova Reports Suspicious Drone-Like Objects and Explosion. Here's What We Know
Residents in central Moldova reported unidentified airborne objects and an apparent explosion early on September 20.
However, according to Moldovan emergency services reports cited by RBC the same day, police found no debris or evidence of impact to confirm that anything had fallen or detonated on the ground.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Moldovan police, the first alert came at around 01:50 a.m., when a resident of the village of Berezloji contacted officers in the city of Orhei. The man stated that he had seen a flying object resembling a drone.
A second call reached police in the city of Călărași at around 02:00 a.m. A resident of the village of Dereneu described a bright light in the sky, followed by an explosion.
Officers began checks across both areas, examining terrain inside and beyond the villages, police noted. The preliminary inspection uncovered no debris, no traces of an impact, and no fires that would confirm an explosion on the ground or the fall of any object.
Authorities have not confirmed the nature or origin of the reported objects. Police indicated that checks in the affected districts were continuing.
The reports add to a series of airspace incidents along Moldova's border with Ukraine in recent weeks. On September 17, an unidentified drone crossed into Moldovan airspace from the Odesa region during a mass Russian attack, leaving Ukrainian territory minutes later.
Earlier, on August 27, five drones entered the country's airspace during an overnight assault, tracking toward the Ștefan Vodă district before turning back.
On August 17, a Russian "Banderol" loitering munition crashed near the village of Tălmaza, following a drone explosion on August 9 near Krokmaz that damaged farm structures.

Türkiye begins serial production of first domestically developed high-speed train
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
08:30:45 UTC
17:30:45 KST

(AA Photo)
Türkiye has begun serial production of its first domestically developed high-speed train, Transport and Infrastructure Minister Abdulkadir Uraloğlu said, as the country moves to expand its indigenous rail manufacturing capabilities.
The train, developed by Turkish Rail System Vehicles Industry (TÜRASAŞ), is designed to operate at speeds of up to 225 kilometers per hour. The first train set is currently undergoing testing, reaching 250 kilometers per hour during dynamic running safety tests, Uraloğlu said.
Production of the second train set has now begun, marking the transition to serial production, according to the minister.
Türkiye aims to manufacture 14 electric high-speed train sets over the next two years, with seven planned for 2027 and another seven in 2028. Each eight-car train will have a capacity of 577 passengers and will be developed using domestic engineering capabilities.
Critical components, including the Train Control and Management System and traction system, are also being designed and manufactured domestically in cooperation with Turkish defense and technology company ASELSAN.
Uraloğlu said serial production will eventually be carried out at Türkiye’s first dedicated high-speed train factory, which is currently 90 percent complete. The 18,000-square-meter facility will bring production, assembly and testing operations under one roof once completed.
The factory is designed to have a production capacity of one high-speed train set per month, allowing Türkiye to scale up manufacturing as it seeks to strengthen domestic capabilities in railway technology and reduce reliance on imported systems.
The project is part of Türkiye’s broader efforts to expand its high-speed rail network.

Iran shuts down French cultural center over security concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
08:25:45 UTC
17:25:45 KST

Iran shuts down French cultural center over security concerns
Iran has shut down a French-language center in Tehran, accusing the embassy-affiliated institution of operating illegally and engaging in activities which threaten the country’s national security.
Relations between Paris and Tehran have deteriorated despite France staying out of the war which the US and Israel launched against Iran in late February and denouncing the initial strikes as a breach of international law.
In July, two French diplomats were detained by Iranian security services, which accused them of interfering in the country’s internal affairs. They were subsequently expelled from the country. France retaliated in August by expelling two of Iran’s diplomats.
“Based on the Tehran prosecutor’s office’s order, the illegal center affiliated with the French Embassy in Tehran, which has operated for years under the guise of language instruction, has been closed,” the Iranian judiciary’s Mizan news agency said on Sunday.
Iranian authorities claimed that the institution had repeatedly ignored warnings to obtain the licenses required under the country’s laws and had conducted activities that “violated diplomatic conventions.” They also accused it of using language instruction as cover to promote projects opposed to Iranian-Islamic culture, identify and build networks, and facilitate the departure of skilled Iranians from the country.
France has condemned the closure as an attack on its cultural presence in Iran and said it would take “appropriate measures” in response. Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot has ordered the Iranian ambassador to be summoned.
The French Language Centre (CLF) offered French language courses in Tehran, with thousands of Iranians attending its classes each year, according to the French Foreign Ministry.
In January 2023, Tehran closed the French Institute for Research in Iran after the satirical magazine Charlie Hebdo published dozens of cartoons mocking then-Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and Iran’s religious establishment. The images, some of which were graphic or sexually explicit, were selected through an international contest called “Mullahs Get Out” and were intended to support anti-government protests in Iran.

Kalin, Libya’s acting defence chief discuss deepening Türkiye-Libya ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
08:24:02 UTC
17:24:02 KST

The head of Türkiye’s National Intelligence Organization (MIT), Ibrahim Kalin, met with Libya’s acting defence minister, Abdussalam Zubi, in Istanbul, as Ankara and Tripoli seek to deepen cooperation and support efforts to unify Libya’s divided institutions.
The Saturday meeting came as negotiations aimed at bringing Libya’s military and political institutions together have gained momentum, according to Turkish security sources.
Kalin and Zubi discussed developments in Libya and the wider region, steps to maintain Türkiye-Libya cooperation, and ongoing efforts to achieve political and military unity and preserve stability in the North African country.
Zubi thanked Türkiye for its efforts to advance unity in Libya, while Kalin reiterated Ankara’s determination to continue supporting Libya’s security and stability.
A relationship built around security, trade and the Mediterranean
Türkiye’s engagement with Libya has expanded considerably over the past several years, encompassing security, energy, trade and maritime cooperation.
A landmark step came in November 2019, when Türkiye and Libya’s then Government of National Accord signed a memorandum on the delimitation of maritime jurisdiction areas in the Mediterranean.
The agreement, registered with the United Nations, defines a maritime boundary between the two countries’ continental shelf and exclusive economic zone areas.
The accord has remained a central element of Türkiye-Libya relations and the wider geopolitical debate over maritime boundaries in the Eastern Mediterranean.
Ankara maintains that the agreement protects the maritime rights of both Türkiye and Libya and was concluded in accordance with international law.
The maritime understanding was followed in October 2022 by a separate memorandum on cooperation in hydrocarbons, covering scientific, technical, technological, legal, administrative and commercial cooperation on land and at sea.
The agreements have helped broaden the relationship beyond security cooperation, placing energy and the Mediterranean at the heart of Ankara-Tripoli ties.
Ankara backs efforts to consolidate Libya’s institutions
Türkiye has also increasingly framed its engagement around Libya’s territorial integrity, political unity and institutional consolidation.
In August, Kalin said Türkiye would continue supporting efforts to bring Libya’s eastern and western administrations together under a single Libyan framework, while Turkish and Libyan officials discussed measures to strengthen security and stability.
International and regional efforts have sought to establish unified institutions and pave the way for lasting political stability.
Against that backdrop, Ankara’s contacts with figures from different Libyan institutions have become an important component of its engagement with the country.
The latest Kalin-Zubi meeting underscores the breadth of that engagement, linking security cooperation with the broader effort to help Libya achieve political and military unity.

The NRL is reportedly set to axe top referee Ashley Klein for the preliminary finals after admitting the Warriors were wrongly denied a crucial late penalty in their 12-10 semifinal loss to Newcastle.
NRL officials today confirmed the Warriors should have been awarded a penalty for an escort infringement by the Knights' Tyson Frizell with a minute left in yesterday's Eden Park thriller.
Had the penalty been awarded, the Warriors would have had the chance to level at 12-12 via a penalty goal from just to the side of the posts and send the match to extra time.
But the call was instead missed on the field, with the bunker unable to review the play, despite a stoppage for an injury soon afterwards.

The Newcastle veteran appeared to get in the way of Leka Halasima as he chased through on a kick in the Warriors' last attacking raid.
Given the seconds that would have come off the clock while the Warriors lined up the shot, there would probably not have been time for a restart.
"I thought they were trying to find ways to take it off us," Warriors coach Andrew Webster said after the game.
"The last one, two points would have drawn the game, he is going across Leka, pretending to try and catch the ball which they've told us you can't do."
AAP understands Klein will pay for the error by losing his spot in the preliminary finals, with Grant Atkins or Gerard Sutton likely to be called up.
Klein has overseen every game of the past five State of Origin series and two of the last four grand finals.

Meanwhile, the NRL have threatened bans for fans who threw projectiles at Klein as he walked off Eden Park on Sunday night.

zuckoff uses bluetooth to let you know when smart glasses are nearby
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
08:15:18 UTC
17:15:18 KST

ZUCKOFF RECOGNIZES CAMERA GLASSES THROUGH BLUETOOTH
Created by Polish developer Paweł Szydłowski, ZuckOff is an independent app that makes the otherwise invisible presence of camera-equipped glasses more legible through Bluetooth. The app listens for signals emitted by devices including Ray-Ban Meta, Oakley Meta, and Snap Spectacles, alerting users when compatible hardware is nearby while showing the evidence behind each detection.
As cameras and other sensors appear disguised as objects that resemble ordinary eyewear, their technological capabilities can become difficult for people nearby to recognize. ZuckOff approaches that problem at the level of the device’s wireless communication, turning Bluetooth advertisements into information that can be inspected on a phone, watch, or computer.
image by Sadjad Frogh
Paweł Szydłowski’s APP SHOWS USERS WHY A DEVICE is FLAGGED
ZuckOff exposes the wireless signals that can indicate the presence of a potentially recording device, responding to a particular ambiguity created by camera glasses. Paweł Szydłowski’s app currently identifies Ray-Ban Meta and Oakley Meta through their manufacturer signature, as well as Snap Spectacles. It can also record other Bluetooth devices it encounters, including display glasses and headsets such as Quest and Vision Pro, but does not flag those devices as camera glasses.
The app assigns confidence levels, including possible, likely, and strong. A Ray-Ban Meta detection, for example, can show its manufacturer ID, the advertised service, signal strength, approximate distance, and other identifying information. Users can therefore inspect the reasoning rather than receiving an unexplained notification, making ZuckOff an interface for interpreting an increasingly dense wireless environment.
image courtesy of Meta
seeing why a device was flagged
The app’s Sightings interface keeps a record of every Bluetooth device heard nearby, whether or not it is identified as camera glasses. Individual devices can be followed through a signal timeline, creating a record of when they appeared and how their signal changed. Users who own compatible glasses can also mark their own devices, preventing them from repeatedly generating alerts.
The interface deliberately communicates uncertainty. Signal strength can suggest proximity but cannot establish direction, while Bluetooth advertising cannot reveal whether a camera is actively being used.
ZuckOff also has limitations. Camera glasses are easiest to detect when they power on, pair, or leave their case, and most continue broadcasting while they are being worn. Some standalone models can remain silent, however. This means that not detecting a pair does not necessarily mean there are no camera glasses nearby, while detecting one does not mean that its camera is being used.
The app does not require an account, and users can export the full Bluetooth log as a CSV. Its detection rules are based on real device captures. ZuckOff is asking people to share short scans from camera glasses that are not yet supported, or to lend hardware for testing. The team is also open to working with privacy groups. This means the list of detectable devices can grow as new camera glasses appear. Each new device adds another Bluetooth signature that the app can learn to recognize.

The US deported more than 25,000 migrants to third countries under secret agreements - investigation
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
11:14:22 EEST

The US deported more than 25,000 migrants to third countries under secret agreements - investigation
Kyiv • UNN
An investigation by Forbidden Stories uncovered secret US agreements with 35 countries on the deportation of more than 25,000 migrants. $410 million was allocated for the program.
The United States deported more than 25,000 people under secret agreements with 35 countries that agreed to accept migrants who have no ties whatsoever to those states, according to an investigation by Forbidden Stories. Agence France-Presse (AFP) reports this, writes UNN.
Details
As the publication notes, after U.S. President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, Washington began concluding agreements with developing countries to accept migrants who cannot legally be sent back to their countries of origin.
The Forbidden Stories investigation found that the U.S. administration had allocated $410 million to be paid directly to countries accepting deportees or to UN agencies to facilitate their relocation.
According to data collected by Forbidden Stories together with a consortium of international journalists, as of August 31, 2026, at least 25,447 people had already been deported to third countries.
The vast majority—about 20,000 people—were sent to Mexico. The rest were distributed among 27 other countries in Latin America, Africa, and the Pacific region, while agreements had already been finalized with seven more countries.
The terms of these agreements vary, including regarding citizens of which countries may be deported and whether people with criminal convictions may be accepted.
An AFP investigation conducted earlier this year found that Washington was using visa bans and restrictions against African countries to pressure them into agreeing to accept deportees.
Lawyers told the publication that deportees end up in a "legal black hole": they are held without being charged in countries with which they have no ties whatsoever and where they have very few or no rights at all.
Forbidden Stories reported that as many as 49 of the 54 African countries had been approached with an offer to accept deportees from third countries.
According to Forbidden Stories, most of the negotiations and payments were handled by a little-known unit of the U.S. Department of State—the Office of Remigration, established in May 2025.

31 years ago, Ganesha ‘drank’ milk and India went viral: How a September 21, 1995 claim spread from temple to temple, crossed borders within hours and became a global story without social media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
08:12:19 UTC
17:12:19 KST

31 years ago, Ganesha ‘drank’ milk and India went viral: How a September 21, 1995 claim spread from temple to temple, crossed borders within hours and became a global story without social media
31 years ago, Ganesha ‘drank’ milk and India went viral: How a September 21, 1995 claim spread from temple to temple, crossed borders within hours and became a global story without social media
Smita Mishra / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Sep 21, 2026, 13:42 IST
Thirty-one years ago, on September 21, 1995, I came home from school to find that something was strangely different. My aunt, who would diligently wait for me every day and was always the one to serve me lunch, was missing. She was more than just the person who fed me; she would sit with me, tell me interesting stories and make the afternoon feel special.I looked for her everywhere. Finally, the housemaid arrived with my plate of dal and rice and casually told me, “Didi has gone to feed milk to Lord Ganesha.”I was puzzled. What did she mean? After lunch, I called a friend from the landline. She had the same story. Her mother, too, was not at home. By evening, my aunt returned, visibly excited, and told my mother, who had just come back from work, what she had seen.“I took a spoon of milk to feed Ganesha, and the milk disappeared,” she said. My mother looked at her in disbelief. “Really?” she asked. “Really. I saw it with my own eyes,” she insisted, quite overwhelmed with emotions.The news spread fast, Ganesha idols were apparently drinking milk. There were no smartphones, social media platforms, WhatsApp groups or instant notifications to amplify the news.
India’s internet had only just arrived, television was still dominated by Doordarshan, and newspapers remained the primary source of next-day news. Yet, within hours, temples were overflowing, milk was disappearing from shops and the story had travelled beyond India.
The incident got global coverage
The morning India heard an extraordinary claimIt was not the age of viral news. In fact viral was the world synonymous with just one thing-the infectious disease of influenza. There was no way to immediately search the internet, watch a viral video or check social media posts from another city. Then what caused the spread of this frenzy? According to a contemporary Times of India report preserved in the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research's Bombay archive, Mumbai and several other parts of India were swept by reports that Ganesha idols were accepting milk offerings. The report described the news as spreading “like wildfire” as thousands of devotees rushed to temples. Astrologer Jayant Salgaonkar was quoted saying, “I myself witnessed it.” Times of India report preserved by TIFRThe crucial point was that people did not merely hear the claim. They went to temples and tried it for themselves. Devotees carried spoons filled with milk towards the trunks or mouths of Ganesha idols, and many reported seeing the milk disappear.India was still largely offlineThe episode becomes even more extraordinary when viewed against India's technological landscape in 1995. Public internet access had only just been launched by VSNL in August that year. According to historical International Telecommunication Union data, internet use in India in 1995 stood at just 0.026% of the population.Telephones were also far from universal. India had approximately 11.98 million fixed telephone connections in 1995, equivalent to around 1.24 fixed lines per 100 people.This meant that the mechanisms of mass communication were fundamentally different from those available today. A person could call a relative, but there was no instant group messaging system through which hundreds of people could receive the same information simultaneously. News moved through conversations, local networks, religious communities, radio, television and newspapers. And yet the Ganesha story moved extraordinarily quickly.Not an age of 24-hour newsIt would be inaccurate to suggest that India had only Doordarshan in 1995. The country's television landscape had already begun changing. Zee TV had launched in 1992, Star TV had entered the Indian market in 1991 and Sony Entertainment Television launched in 1995. But the explosion of private, round-the-clock news channels that would later transform India's news culture was still years away.Doordarshan nevertheless remained hugely influential. An academic study citing Ministry of Information & Broadcasting figures puts India's television universe in 1995 at approximately 40 million television households and 250 million viewers.There was therefore a very different relationship between an event and the news cycle. Newspapers generally reported what had happened the previous day, television had scheduled programming rather than today's constant breaking-news stream, and there was no digital ecosystem continuously refreshing itself. The Ganesha phenomenon had to travel through people before it could become a mass media story.When the milk became part of the storyThe reports quickly produced visible consequences. A contemporaryLos Angeles Times report published on September 23, 1995, said millions of Indians had rushed to test the phenomenon and reported that milk had “virtually disappeared” from shops in New Delhi by noon.
There was a milk shortage nationwide
That detail captures the extraordinary feedback loop created by the phenomenon. People heard that Ganesha was drinking milk, went out to buy milk, took it to temples and offered it to idols. The resulting rush itself became evidence of how seriously the story was being taken.Contemporary reports described crowds gathering at temples, with devotees carrying spoons, bowls and containers of milk.From one temple to the worldThe most remarkable part of the episode was perhaps how quickly it crossed India's borders. Reports soon emerged from Hindu communities in Britain, the United States, Canada, Nepal and elsewhere. A contemporary Los Angeles Times reportnoted that the reports had spread beyond India to Hindu communities in other countries, including Britain and Los Angeles.Hinduism Today later recalled receiving telephone calls and fax messages from different parts of the world reporting similar experiences. Its contemporary account provides a fascinating glimpse into how an international religious community communicated before email, social media and messaging apps became commonplace.The technology may appear primitive by today's standards, but the human network was remarkably effective. Someone in India could telephone a relative abroad, that person could contact a local temple, and within hours another community could be trying the same experiment.The story did not need an algorithm to travel. It travelled through relationships.The science behind the phenomenonAs the reports spread, scientists and sceptics began examining what devotees were observing. One of the principal scientific explanations involved capillary action and surface tension. Rather than the idol literally consuming the milk, the liquid could move along the surface of the material, creating the appearance that it was being absorbed by the idol.For devotees, however, the scientific explanation did not necessarily invalidate what they had experienced. The same physical observation could be interpreted through very different frameworks: as a religious sign by believers, as a scientific phenomenon by researchers, and as an extraordinary mass social event by journalists.
People queuing up in temples for offering milk to Lord Ganesha
What made the episode so unusualLooking back from the age of smartphones, the 1995 episode is remarkable not simply because of what people believed they were seeing, but because of how quickly the information travelled.India's public internet had only just begun. Fixed telephone connections were limited, television was expanding but had not yet become the 24-hour news environment of today, and newspapers operated on a fundamentally different news cycle. Yet within hours, a local report had become a national phenomenon and then an international story.A telephone call led to another telephone call. A conversation at one temple led to another. Newspapers carried the story forward, television added another layer of coverage and international media transformed what had begun as a local religious phenomenon into a global news story.The first great pre-social-media viral phenomenon?Calling the Ganesha milk episode the world's first viral phenomenon would be too absolute. Stories travelled internationally long before 1995, through newspapers, radio, television and word of mouth.But the episode offers a remarkable case study of mass communication before the social-media era. Millions of people participated in the same rapidly spreading story without having access to the tools that today make such mass participation almost instantaneous.
That is what makes September 21, 1995, worth remembering 31 years later. The question is no longer simply whether Ganesha idols were actually drinking milk. The episode has another story to tell, about technology, faith, communication and human networks.In 2026, information can travel around the world in seconds. In 1995, it travelled from person to person, from telephone to telephone, from temple to temple and eventually from newspaper to newspaper.And somehow, by the end of that extraordinary day, a spoonful of milk had become a global story.(All images are AI Generated)
"Smita Mishra is the Editor of Times of India Lifestyle, Times Food, and Times Travel. She is known for crafting in-depth and compelling features that blend storytelling with analysis. Her passion lies in exploring culinary arts, travel, style, relationships, health and literature through her writing. She leads TOI Books and oversees the editorial aspects of Times of India's literary initiatives, such as Times Literature Festivals and AutHer Awards. Smita brings a wealth of expertise in the digital realm, stemming from her previous roles at Zee News, Dainik Jagran, and India Today. Her contributions have been pivotal in launching numerous online properties and making meaningful editorial enhancements.

"Military police have deployed in the area surrounding the site of the explosion to secure it in cooperation with the relevant authorities, while military engineering units have begun securing the site and surrounding areas," the ministry said, according to SANA.

Aleppo's local security forces placed personnel on alert and closed the Aleppo-Damascus highway and roads leading to the site as a precaution. Authorities also established a security cordon around the area and barred traffic and civilians from approaching.
Aleppo Gov. Azzam al-Gharib urged residents to remain in their homes and avoid approaching or gathering near the site. He said hospitals, ambulances and emergency services were on standby and called on residents to rely on official information and avoid circulating unconfirmed reports.
The Emergency and Disaster Management Ministry warned residents in al-Eis and surrounding areas against approaching the site because of the risk of shrapnel, unexploded ordnance and other hazardous objects.
"Due to explosions occurring in the al-Eis area and its surroundings south of Aleppo, we urge everyone not to leave their homes and not to approach the sites of the explosions," al-Gharib said in a statement.
He added that "hospitals and ambulance and emergency teams are on standby, while the relevant authorities are monitoring the situation on the ground and responding to any emergency."
The ministry's Early Warning and Preparedness Department advised residents to move to a safe area when possible without putting themselves at risk, keep roads clear for emergency teams and shelter inside buildings if they could not leave safely. It also urged residents to stay away from windows, doors, glass, rooftops and other exposed areas.
Authorities were investigating the cause of the explosions.
The explosion came amid a series of blasts at military weapons and ammunition sites in Syria in recent weeks, including incidents in Idlib and Deir el-Zour.
At least 14 people were killed and 11 wounded on Sept. 9, when an explosion ripped through a temporary storage for weapons and war remnants in the northwestern province of Idlib.

U.S. Air Force tests drones for runway damage checks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
08:08:16 UTC
17:08:16 KST

- U.S. Air Force officers at the Air Force Institute of Technology are testing small drones to scout damaged airfields before engineers enter.
- AFIT is studying a multirotor drone for confined areas and a fixed-wing aircraft for wide-area sweeps of runways, taxiways and aprons.
U.S. Air Force officers studying at the Air Force Institute of Technology (AFIT) are testing whether small drones can scout a damaged airfield before engineers walk onto it.
The research targets a job that still depends mostly on people. After an attack, U.S. Air Force civil engineers have to reopen runways while dealing with unexploded ordnance, possible chemical or biological contamination, cratered pavement and debris. AFIT says they often start without a clear picture of those hazards, which raises the risk to the engineers and slows the Air Force’s ability to get combat power back.
Today, airfield hazards are mostly spotted by eye. An engineer on the ground describes what they see over the radio, and command and control assembles the picture from those spoken reports. AFIT says the method works but is often slow or incomplete.
The drone project is led by Capt. Ross C. Jurek, a graduate engineering management student. His team of Civil Engineer graduate students, backed by faculty in developmental and digital systems engineering, builds on more than a decade of Air Force Civil Engineer work on airfield reconnaissance with small unmanned aircraft. This group adds a fixed-wing aircraft alongside multirotor systems. Jurek says drones can help airmen quickly map unfamiliar locations, assess runways and routes, identify hazards and build situational awareness before committing people and equipment.
The research is tied to two existing Air Force capabilities, Integrated Base Response and Recovery and Rapid Airfield Damage Repair, which underpin how the service recovers after an attack.
“The goal is to put the sensor into the uncertain environment first and get the best possible information to the decision-maker as quickly as possible,” said Capt. Ross C. Jurek.
The two aircraft types do different jobs. The multirotor, the focus of Jurek’s graduate research, can launch from almost anywhere, hover and change viewing angle. It can work through confined, unpredictable routes that Damage Assessment and Response Teams (DARTs) would otherwise have to enter physically first.
The fixed-wing aircraft is the subject of a separate developmental engineering project that Jurek runs with Capts. Peter Stobinski, Nicholas Rife and Spencer Peters. It gives up maneuverability for endurance and reach, and sweeps runways, taxiways and parking aprons for craters, spalls (broken chunks of pavement) and debris over much larger areas. AFIT says the two could work as layers, with one covering a wide area while the other inspects confined or hazardous spots.
“Speed, precision, and usability are key to this effort,” said Capt. Nicholas Rife, a systems engineering student on the fixed-wing team.
Jurek’s thesis, advised by Lt. Col. Daniel Weeks, sets drone reconnaissance against conventional DART routes on three measures: speed, accuracy and safety. It also evaluates the whole process, from mission planning and flight execution to camera coverage, imagery collection and the time an analyst needs to turn footage into a usable picture of hazards. AFIT says the case for fielding the drones ends if an aerial first look cannot get accurate information to Civil Engineer leaders faster than current DART methods.
The students are also asked to look past the aircraft. Their coursework follows an operational problem from concept through requirements, design and testing toward fielding, and it accounts for the sensor, the communications link, software, the training pipeline, approvals and the operator.
“The biggest impact is safer Airmen and faster, higher-quality information,” said Jurek.
AFIT did not say when Jurek’s thesis will be finished, what the tests have shown so far, which drones the team is using or whether the Air Force plans to field them. The research is ongoing.

The capacity utilization rate across the Turkish manufacturing industry rose by 0.7 percenrage points in September to reach 74.2%.
The Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye (CBRT) announced that among the main industrial groups, the highest utilization rate in September was 74.5% in intermediate goods, down 0.2 percentage points from the previous month.
At the other end, durable consumer goods recorded the lowest rate at 66.4%, a decline of 1.8 percentage points month-on-month.
By sector, the manufacture of wood products posted the highest capacity usage at 83.7%, while the lowest rate, 59.8%, was recorded in the leather industry.
The figures are based on responses to a business tendency survey of domestic manufacturing units.
The Turkish Central Bank said 1,982 companies participated in the survey this month, adding that the data does not reflect the bank’s views or forecasts.

Denmark says NATO shares responsibility for Arctic security under Greenland deal
- Denmark, Greenland and the US will sign a security deal on Sept 22, placing Arctic security under NATO's responsibility instead of solely US or Danish control.
- The agreement aims to promote security, stability and cooperation in the Arctic, with Denmark acknowledging the need to strengthen its military presence on Greenland.
- President Trump claims the deal grants the US "permanent control" over Greenland's security, but Denmark and Greenland emphasise respect for sovereignty and have not confirmed this claim.
AI generated
COPENHAGEN – Denmark, Greenland and the United States are set to sign a deal on Greenland's security on Sept 22, an agreement Denmark says will put Arctic security under NATO’s watch rather than leaving it solely to Washington and Copenhagen.
The agreement, expected to be signed at the UN General Assembly in New York on Sept 22, has not been made public, though US President Donald Trump says it grants the US “permanent control”.
Denmark and Greenland have not commented on Trump’s claim but said the deal will benefit the Arctic island and respect its sovereignty.
The deal follows months of pressure from Trump, who has said the United States should control Greenland and at times refused to rule out using military or economic force to acquire the semi-autonomous Danish territory.
His threats, which peaked in January, triggered a diplomatic crisis within NATO and pushed Denmark and Greenland into negotiations with Washington aimed at defusing the pressure.
“It (the agreement) will be in a form where responsibility for security in the Arctic is not only Danish or American,” Danish Foreign Minister Lars Rasmussen told national broadcaster TV2 on Sept 20.
He added that to a large extent “it would be NATO that looks after the Arctic”.
Promoting ‘security, stability and cooperation’
A NATO spokesperson said on Sept 19 that the alliance welcomed the agreement, which would “help advance security, stability and cooperation in this vital region”.
Rasmussen, who travelled to New York overnight, declined to discuss the contents of the agreement.
“But we have said from the start that we are open to accommodating the United States’ legitimate security interests,” Rasmussen told Danish news agency Ritzau on Sept 20.
Trump said in a post on Truth Social on Sept 18 the agreement gives the United States “permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland,” and that no US adversary could have a base or military presence there without Washington's written approval.
Denmark has not responded to Trump’s claim, though Copenhagen has earlier acknowledged it underinvested in Greenland’s defence for decades and has pledged to expand its military presence on the island, including more NATO troops.
Key details have not been made public, including whether the deal amends the 1951 defence agreement that is the legal basis for the US presence in Greenland.
Greenland’s government has sought to reassure the public about the deal.
Erik Jensen, an opposition lawmaker in Greenland, wrote on Facebook that he had read the draft agreement.
“I feel reassured and am not worried,” he said, adding that the island's foreign minister was handling the work well. REUTERS

U.S. Air Force F-16s head to Greenland from Alaska
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
08:02:59 UTC
17:02:59 KST

- The Alaskan NORAD Region deployed U.S. Air Force F-16s from Eielson Air Force Base to Goose Bay, Canada, for an operation running Sept. 13-26.
- NORAD says aircraft and personnel will move forward into Greenland to operate alongside partners from Denmark and NATO in austere Arctic conditions.
NORAD has sent U.S. Air Force F-16 fighters from Alaska to the Atlantic side of Canada, and plans to take aircraft and personnel on into Greenland, in an Arctic operation running Sept. 13-26.
The Alaskan NORAD Region moved the F-16s from Eielson Air Force Base to Goose Bay, in Canada’s Newfoundland and Labrador province, for Operation ARCTIC VANGUARD 26-4.2. NORAD, the North American Aerospace Defense Command, is the joint U.S.-Canadian command that guards the continent’s airspace. During this operation the Alaskan region is working directly with its Canadian counterpart, the Canadian NORAD Region.
Royal Canadian Air Force strategic airlift supported the move. A U.S. Air Force photo dated Sept. 10 shows airmen from the 354th Fighter Wing loading cargo onto an RCAF CC-177 Globemaster III at Eielson.
Eielson sits in interior Alaska, Goose Bay is on Canada’s Atlantic side, and Greenland lies beyond it. NORAD says the deployment tests whether it can move multirole combat aircraft from Alaska to forward Arctic locations, stage them through northeastern Canada, and keep them flying in sub-zero weather with little support infrastructure. The command has not released results.
In Greenland, NORAD personnel and aircraft will work in what the command calls austere conditions, meaning remote sites with limited facilities, alongside partners from the Kingdom of Denmark and NATO. A U.S. Air Force photo released with the announcement shows F-16s taking fuel from a KC-135 Stratotanker over Greenland on Sept. 16. NORAD did not say how many F-16s or personnel are involved, or where in Greenland they will operate.
“Operation ARCTIC VANGUARD demonstrates that austere conditions and vast distances present no barrier to NORAD’s collective defense,” said U.S. Air Force Lt. Gen. Robert D. Davis, commander of the Alaskan NORAD Region. “Deploying combat airpower from Alaska across Canada and forward into Greenland validates our agile combat capabilities and demonstrates our seamless integration with the Canadian NORAD Region, the Kingdom of Denmark, and our NATO allies. Together, we maintain continuous vigilance and credible deterrence across North America’s northern approaches.”
The F-16s are not the only U.S. fighters working in Greenland under the same operation name. U.S. Northern Command announced on Sept. 16 that F-35A fighters from the Wisconsin Air National Guard’s 115th Fighter Wing had flown missions from Pituffik Space Base under ARCTIC VANGUARD. Pituffik, formerly Thule Air Base, is in northwestern Greenland and is the northernmost U.S. military installation in the world.
In February 2025, F-16s and KC-135 tankers deployed to Pituffik for Operation NOBLE DEFENDER, working in temperatures as low as minus 34 C (minus 29 F). In October 2025, NORAD sent two F-35s, two F-16s and three KC-135s for an exercise meant to test how quickly it could deploy forces to the Arctic.
ARCTIC VANGUARD operates under what NORAD and U.S. Northern Command call the Nordic Bridge concept. The commands describe it as a way to line up their Arctic operations, exercises, training and investments with other U.S. combatant commands, NATO, individual countries and regional partners. NORAD says the approach allows more consistent presence of multinational forces in the region, across multiple domains and locations.
The operation belongs to a recurring series of NORAD and U.S. Northern Command deployments across the North American Arctic. The current iteration is scheduled to end Sept. 26. NORAD has not said how long the F-16s will stay in Greenland or when they will return to Alaska.

Five stand-out projects at the Oslo Architecture Triennale
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
08:00:35 UTC
17:00:35 KST

Five stand-out projects at the Oslo Architecture Triennale
Projects using reclaimed natural materials and local resources proved popular at this year's Oslo Architecture Triennale. From innovative wool tiles to monolithic stone walls, we round up key highlights from the event.
In its ninth edition, this year's Oslo Architecture Triennale includes exhibitions, seminars and workshops centred around the theme What If Nature Comes First?
Taking place from 17 September to 1 October at Oslo's Sofienberg Church, many of the projects on display in the main exhibition championed the reuse of various natural materials and sourcing materials locally.
"This triennale shows what architecture looks like when nature comes first"
"Construction is one of the biggest single drivers of nature loss and emissions, and we keep building and demolishing the way we always have," said Oslo Architecture Triennale director Line Ramstad.
"What we talk about too little is how much is already available to us in materials, in buildings that still stand, and in knowledge we already have," she continued.
"This triennale shows what architecture looks like when nature comes first, and what it would take to scale solutions that already exist."
Read on for five stand-out projects at the Oslo Architecture Triennale:
Upcycling Wool Ecologies by Grinham Research Group
An installation cloaked in multicoloured fluted tiles made from waste sheep wool was presented at the triennale by the Grinham Research Group at Harvard University.
To make the tiles, wool is treated with an alkaline solution that partially breaks down its keratin proteins into a gel, which is then crosslinked and combined with residual wool fibres to form a petrochemical-free plastic material.
Conceptualised for retrofitting the outside of buildings, the tiles have a multi-layer design made up of a low-density back panel that acts as an insulative board and a denser outer panel with a fluted surface that is more durable and weatherised.
"We're looking at this application because external retrofits are less cost-prohibitive – replacing interior insulation is more cost-prohibitive because you need to dig into the wall," said Harvard University researcher Leonard Palmer.
"There is an abundance of waste wool in the world," he continued. "Sheep wool is like nature's plastic; it has really good properties – it's insulative, fire-resistant and anti-bacterial."
Lasting Larvikite by Martin Hopland and Studio Wideroe
Oslo-based architecture firms Arkitekt Martin Hopland and architecture firm Studio Wideroe collaborated on a trio of stone wall prototypes, which they assembled using Larvikite stone from Norway's Larvik quarry.
One wall has a mismatched mosaic appearance made entirely from excess stone, another features a profile pattern of horizontal bands atop a plinth, and the third wall has stone elements rotated 90 degrees to create an ornamental design.
"We feel like it's time we get back to where we were a couple of hundred years ago," Arkitekt Martin Hopland founder Martin Hopland told Dezeen.
"This has the huge potential to solve three things at once," added Studio Wideroe founder Magnus Widerøe. "Reducing the waste the stone quarry produces, replacing high-intensity processed materials like concrete, and using a material that actually lasts."
Materiet Former by Ask Holmen
Norwegian architect Ask Holmen created four sculptural benches placed around the exterior of Sofienberg Church, reusing stone sourced from a local stone mason.
Holmen stacked circular, curved and rectangular slabs to form the seating, which he hopes will become places of conversation during the triennale.
"The bench is like a sunken portal – when you sit down, you are in between worlds," he told Dezeen. "It's an invitation for dialogue, and when you enter into a dialogue with someone, you never leave the same as you came in."
"I didn't know what stone elements I would get, so the elements themselves led me to the aesthetics," Holmen continued. "It's an open process and an interesting way that we can also approach architecture; maybe we can have a way of thinking that balances between rigidity and flexibility."
Open Sauna Experimental Construction by Oslo Badstuforening, Oslo School of Architecture and Design and UCLouvain-Loci
Non-profit sauna association Oslo Badstuforening worked with students and professors at the Oslo School of Architecture and Design (AHO) and Belgium's UCLouvain-Loci to build a sauna next to the Sofienberg Church.
Over two five-day sessions, master's students built the sauna from recycled building materials, including timber structure and cladding, small glass brick windows and colourful polycarbonate panels lining the split roof.
"The light coming from the top is inspired by the stained glass windows in the church," said AHO assistant professor Matthew Dylan Anderson.
"Through interviews with the target group of kids who will be using the sauna, we found out they didn't like the idea of people seeing into the sauna so that they can play with their mates, hence the small glass brick windows."
Initiating Common Ground by Studio Dreist
In the lead-up to the triennale, Vienna-based collective Studio Dreist hosted workshops where participants learned to work with cocciopesto, an ancient Roman building technique that uses lime and crushed brick.
The outcome of the workshops was a collection of air-dried panels, which were laid on a reused-timber frame to form a large communal table at the triennale exhibition.
"We were asked to make a table for the church, so we looked for materials that were local," said Studio Dreist cofounder Sophie Coqui. "Oslo has a long brick history, similar to Vienna, so we thought about how to repurpose brick into a table."
"We are curious in materials, we are not super specialised in one," added fellow cofounder Luisa Zwetkow. "We are trying to figure out how materials and processes work – it's different planning to use a material if you've already worked with it."
Oslo Architecture Triennale takes place from 17 September to 1 October at Sofienberg Church in Oslo, Norway. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

Some of China’s 11,000 mega bridges could be at risk from small drones: study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
08:00:05 UTC
17:00:05 KST

Advertisement
Some of China’s 11,000 mega bridges could be at risk from small drones: study
Chinese researchers simulate attacks on a typical suspension bridge and find a precisely targeted small strike could trigger collapse
3-MIN READ3-MIN
7
 Listen
Scientists in China have simulated a drone attack on one of the country’s major suspension bridges to determine the vulnerability of key transport hubs to modern warfare tactics.
The researchers found that a drone carrying just 30kg (66lbs) of TNT could trigger a bridge collapse if it detonated within inches of the main suspension cable at the point where it meets a support tower.
The targeted bridge strikes that have featured in Russia’s war on Ukraine show that warfare has shifted from mass firepower to precision strikes, turning once hard-to-reach structures into prime targets, they said.
“These events starkly reveal the extreme vulnerability of modern bridges to unconventional explosive attacks,” the team wrote in a paper published in the September issue of the Chinese-language Journal of Railway Science and Engineering.

US deported over 25,000 migrants to countries they had no ties to: Investigation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
07:58:45 UTC
16:58:45 KST

Seyit Kurt
21 September 2026•Update: 21 September 2026
The US deported more than 25,000 people to countries they had no ties to under agreements struck by the Trump administration, according to an investigation by Forbidden Stories.
Since President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, his administration has reached agreements with 35 countries to accept so-called “third-country nationals” – migrants deported from the US to countries other than their countries of origin. Details of the agreements have largely remained undisclosed.
As of Aug. 31, at least 25,447 people had been sent to 28 countries under the policy, according to the investigation, which analyzed information from multiple sources, including migrant rights organizations. The US government has not publicly disclosed the figures.
The investigation, conducted by a consortium of 72 journalists from 26 media organizations in 15 countries, included more than 100 interviews with deportees, government officials, lawyers and experts.
Internal State Department records obtained by The Washington Post, one of the consortium members, showed that the US planned to spend at least $410 million as part of efforts to secure agreements with third countries.
Of that amount, $81 million was earmarked for governments that signed the agreements, while more than $178 million was allocated to the International Organization for Migration and over $123 million to the UN refugee agency.
The agreements are largely negotiated by the State Department's Office of Remigration, a division established in 2025 as part of an overhaul of the department.
The White House, responding to the investigation, said the migrants sent to third countries are people whose home countries refuse to accept them, including those with removal orders who have asked not to be returned to their countries of origin.
A US federal appeals court on Sept. 18 ordered the third-country removals halted, ruling that migrants had not been given sufficient notice or an opportunity to challenge their deportation.

- Turkish defense officials inspected aircraft maintenance facilities at Royal Air Force Coningsby in England on Sept. 15-17 as part of Türkiye's Eurofighter Typhoon purchase.
- Türkiye ordered 20 Typhoons in a £5.4 billion deal signed in October 2025, with deliveries scheduled from 2030 to 2032.
Turkish defense specialists inspected aircraft maintenance facilities at Royal Air Force Coningsby in England on Sept. 15-17 as work continues on Türkiye’s purchase of Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jets from the United Kingdom.
The Turkish Ministry of National Defense announced the visit in a post on X. The delegation included personnel from the ministry, the Turkish Air Force Command’s aircraft maintenance working group and the General Directorate of Military Factories. The ministry called the trip a step toward planning maintenance and sustainment, checking technical infrastructure compatibility and strengthening cooperation with the UK.
The post did not say how many people traveled, which facilities they toured or what they found. It also did not say whether any maintenance work on Turkish Typhoons will be done at Coningsby, in Lincolnshire.
Türkiye ordered 20 Typhoons under a £5.4 billion ($7.2 billion) agreement signed in Ankara in October 2025. The jets will be delivered in three batches: six in 2030, eight in 2031 and six in 2032. Final assembly will take place at BAE Systems’ Warton site in Lancashire. The Defence Blog reported on Aug. 1 that BAE Systems had confirmed production of the aircraft was underway.
Support for the fleet is being arranged separately. In March 2026, BAE Systems won a UK government contract covering training, support equipment and services for Türkiye’s Typhoons. It includes simulators, electronic warfare systems, spare parts and technical assistance for an initial three years after the aircraft enter service. Türkiye and the UK also signed a separate agreement on March 25, 2026, covering technical and logistics support for the fleet.
Under the training package, the Royal Air Force will train 10 Turkish instructor pilots and nearly 100 Turkish maintenance personnel.

Germany's Merz struggles to stay on track after regional losses

Breadcrumb
Germany's Merz struggles to stay on track after far left wins Berlin state election, far-right AfD in northeast
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz faced a struggle to stabilise his position and keep his agenda on track Monday after voters inflicted two more defeats on his party, ejecting it from a state legislature for the first time in its eight-decade history.
The unpopular Merz vowed to stay on and push through reforms to Germany, Europe's biggest economy, minutes after polls closed Sunday in regional elections in Berlin and in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, a largely rural eastern region on the Baltic Sea coast.
Still, final results underlined the extent of what Merz conceded was a "disaster" in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. His center-right Christian Democratic Union fell just below the 5% of the vote needed to keep seats in the regional parliament, the first time that has happened in 77 years of modern Germany's federal republic, after losing more than half its support.
The CDU also dropped to second place in Berlin behind the hard-left Left Party, which is in pole position to lead the next city government—though Merz's party could, depending on how coalition talks go, still retain city hall.
Neo-Nazi party gains again 
Neither state is one of Germany's political heavyweights. The CDU's 2023 win in Berlin was its only one in the past 25 years in the capital, which has tended to lean left, and the party was already weak in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
But the manner of its defeat in the latter in particular adds to the headwinds Merz faces after a stinging defeat by the far-right, neo-Nazi Alternative for Germany two weeks ago in Saxony-Anhalt, another region in the formerly communist east, damaged his authority and set off speculation that he might be replaced.
Alternative for Germany, or AfD, emerged as the strongest party in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, but the center-left Social Democrats—the junior party in Merz's national governing coalition—were fairly close behind after a campaign focused squarely on the state governor, Manuela Schwesig, as a bulwark against the far-right party. That polarization helped squeeze other mainstream parties, including the CDU.
A left-leaning three-party coalition under Schwesig would have a majority in the new regional legislature.
How Germany should be reformed 
Schwesig and others in the governing parties have cast doubt on aspects of the federal government's reform agenda, which is meant to bolster a chronically sluggish economy. The reform plans include a potentially painful overhaul of the creaking pension system, a reduction of Germany’s stifling bureaucracy and cuts to income tax for low- and middle-income families.
The head of the Social Democrats' group in the national parliament, Matthias Miersch, said it was clear that "we need reforms." But he told ARD television that "we must also take people's concerns seriously."
Merz faces more meetings Monday with his party's leadership. Much will depend on the CDU's influential regional leaders; the party's eight state governors last week backed the chancellor, though questions remained about how wholehearted their support was.
There are at least no more electoral tests this year. However, five state elections are scheduled next year, three of them in April.
They include one in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany's most populous state, currently led by a prominent CDU figure often cited as a possible successor to Merz, Hendrik Wüst. None of the five elections is in the east, where AfD is strongest.
"I don't see that swapping out a leadership figure would really bring a change," Education Minister Karin Prien, who is also a deputy CDU leader, told Phoenix television, adding that she doesn't see "another personnel offer" coming.
"So we must now discuss with one another—together with the chancellor as a government, and on the other hand as a party—how we win more acceptance and more credibility among the population," Prien said.

US has deported 25,000 to third countries under secretive deals: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
07:50:00 UTC
16:50:00 KST

US has deported 25,000 to third countries under secretive deals: Report
- The US has deported over 25,000 migrants to third countries under secret agreements with 35 nations, mostly to Mexico, since President Trump took office in January 2025.
- The US allocated US$410 million to fund these deals, paying governments and UN agencies to accept migrants with no ties to those countries.
- Critics say deportees face legal limbo and rights abuses; the US uses visa restrictions to pressure countries, while UN agencies defend their involvement as helping migrants.
AI generated
NAIROBI – The US has deported more than 25,000 people under secretive agreements with 35 countries to take migrants with no ties to those nations, according to an investigation published on Sept 21.
Since US President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, Washington has been signing deals with developing countries for them to take in migrants who cannot legally be sent home.
The investigation by non-profit organisation Forbidden Stories found the administration has earmarked US$410 million (S$523 million) to be paid directly to the receiving countries, or to UN agencies to facilitate the returns.
At least 25,447 people had already been deported to third countries by Aug 31, 2026, according to data compiled by Forbidden Stories with a consortium of international journalists.
The vast majority – around 20,000 – were sent to Mexico, but the rest were dispersed to 27 other countries across Latin America, Africa and the Pacific, and agreements have been finalised with seven more.
The deals vary, including over which nationalities can be deported and whether people with criminal records can be accepted.
An AFP investigation earlier in 2026 found Washington is using visa bans and restrictions on African countries to strong-arm them into accepting deportees.
Lawyers told AFP that deportees were being thrown into a “legal black hole”, held without charge in countries where they have no ties and few if any rights.
Forbidden Stories said 49 of Africa’s 54 countries had been approached about accepting third-country deportees.
A little-known State Department division called the Office of Remigration, created in May 2025, has handled most of the negotiations and payments, according to Forbidden Stories.
The office is headed by Christian Jove Ehrhardt, a 41-year-old diplomat who previously worked as a security officer.
The report details his visits to Cameroon, which signed a memorandum of understanding with the US in December on accepting deportees. A week later, it also signed a five-year health assistance programme worth nearly US$400 million.
The following month, the State Department said it would provide a further US$30 million to the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) in Cameroon to “facilitate the voluntary return of refugees and combat illegal immigration”.
The first plane carrying deportees arrived in Cameroon on Jan 14.
Payments
Other agreements have involved direct payments to governments.
Palau, a small Pacific island nation with a population of under 18,000, signed an agreement in December 2025 to accept up to 75 third-country nationals in return for US$7.5 million.
However, only three people have so far been sent under the agreement.
In Eswatini, 32 people have arrived since July 2025 out of a possible 160 under an agreement worth more than US$5 million. It has accepted deportees with criminal records, the investigation found.
Of the US$410 million planned for the agreements, internal State Department records showed that US$81 million was earmarked for signatory governments.
The rest was intended for aid organisations, including more than US$178 million for the UN’s International Organization for Migration (IOM), and US$123 million for UNHCR.
The agencies have faced criticism over their involvement, although UNHCR told Forbidden Stories that it was not party to the bilateral agreements and that US funding was being used in line with its mandate to strengthen asylum systems.
An IOM spokesperson told Forbidden Stories that the agency’s decisions to accept funding rested “on a single question: whether our engagement will improve the lives of the migrants affected. In these instances, we believe strongly it does”. AFP

Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps Recaptures 125 Sq Km in "Operation Vivaldi" in Donetsk Region
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
07:45:43 UTC
16:45:43 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps Recaptures 125 Sq Km in "Operation Vivaldi" in Donetsk Region
Ukraine's Third Army Corps has taken full control of Drobysheve and liberated the settlements of Shandryholove and Derylove as part of its ongoing Operation Vivaldi offensive, according to a statement posted online.
The advance was announced by Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi, commander of the Third Army Corps, in a post on the unit's Telegram channel on September 20.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"During assault operations, drones and unmanned ground vehicles always move ahead of the infantry," Biletskyi noted. He claimed the corps had set a global precedent in robotic warfare:
"The Third Army Corps was the first in the world to begin air-deploying ground robotic systems. Our heavy bomber drones deliver suicide ground drones more than 10 kilometers into the enemy's rear."
Across the first two seasons of Vivaldi, the corps and attached units have returned 125 square kilometers to Ukrainian control, 50 of which were de-occupied, according to the statement.
The post reported another 800 Russian troops killed in the latest phase, putting total losses across both seasons above 3,000 personnel. Biletskyi added that the corps continues to grind down the offensive potential of three Russian armies at once — the 20th, 25th, and 1st Tank.
Artillery and unmanned systems struck a range of Russian targets, the corps stated:
- command posts;
- communication nodes;
- logistics and supply lines;
- river crossings;
- enemy reserves.
Air defense and electronic warfare units formed a protective dome over the combat zone, according to the post. Blinded, Russian forces failed to detect the operation's design as Ukrainian units consolidated on liberated ground.
Unmanned ground vehicles have become a central instrument in Ukraine's assault tactics, taking on roles once assigned to infantry.
The platforms range from logistics carriers to remotely operated weapons systems and one-way suicide machines. By air-dropping them deep behind Russian lines, Ukrainian forces can strike rear-area positions while keeping soldiers out of the most exposed ground.
The corps credited the second season's success to formations including the 60th Separate Mechanized Brigade, the 21st KRAKEN regiment, the Main Directorate of Intelligence of Ukraine (HUR) special unit Artan, and the DOZOR mobile border detachment, among others.
Biletskyi signaled more gains ahead. "The music of Vivaldi continues," he wrote, adding that further news would come soon.
The latest advances extend Operation Vivaldi's opening phase. In its first season, the corps cleared 75 square kilometers of Russian infiltration positions in the northern Donetsk region and retook Novoselivka, Oleksandrivka, Yarova, and the outskirts of Korovyi Yar.
That phase also liberated Serednie and dealt a heavy blow to Russia's 20th and 25th Combined Arms Armies, which lost around 1,500 personnel, more than 12,000 drones, and hundreds of armored vehicles and artillery systems.

Three South Korean military officers wounded in explosion near border
South Korean officers injured in DMZ explosion, possibly caused by a landmine, according to local media reports.
Three South Korean military officers have been wounded in an explosion in the western sector of the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) that separates North and South Korea, Seoul’s Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) said.
The cause of Monday’s explosion was not immediately clear, the Ministry of Defence said.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3South Korea says US-North Korea talks possible, rules out Hormuz deployment
- list 2 of 3Seoul court orders North Korea to pay $32.5m for blowing up office
- list 3 of 3North Korea fires ballistic missiles off eastern coast, Seoul says
Two of the officers were evacuated from the site by helicopter, while the third was transported by land before being airlifted, according to the ministry. The officers are being treated at a military hospital near the capital Seoul, it said.
Mine explosions and other blasts are a recurring hazard in and around the DMZ, where legacy devices and suspected stray mines have periodically wounded military personnel on both sides.
The DMZ, which is 248km (154 miles) long and 4km (2.5 miles) wide, is one of the world’s most heavily armed borders. An estimated 2 million mines are peppered inside and near the border, which is also guarded by barbed wire fences, tank traps and combat troops on both sides. The zone is a legacy of the Korean War from 1950 to 1953, which ended with an armistice but not a peace treaty.
There have been growing concerns in South Korea about increased activity by North Korean soldiers near the military demarcation line as the North strengthens its border defences during prolonged tensions.

U.S. Air Force inactivates four A-10 units in Arizona
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
07:45:02 UTC
16:45:02 KST

- The U.S. Air Force inactivated four A-10 units at Davis-Monthan Air Force Base, Arizona, on Sept. 18, marking the end of the A-10 legacy there.
- The 355th Operations Group, activated in 1992, oversaw all formal A-10 pilot initial qualification and requalification training for the base.
The U.S. Air Force inactivated four A-10 units at Davis-Monthan Air Force Base, Arizona, on Sept. 18, in a ceremony it described as the official end of the A-10 legacy at the base.
The units were the 355th Operations Group, 357th Fighter Squadron, 357th Fighter Generation Squadron and 355th Training Squadron. Col. Jose Cabrera, commander of the 355th Wing, presided. Airmen, families, retired A-10 pilots, local civic leaders and community members attended.
The 355th Operations Group was activated on May 1, 1992, and controlled the flying units of the 355th Wing. From 1992 to 2026 it supplied A-10 Thunderbolt II aircraft for close air support, forward air control and combat search and rescue. The group deployed personnel around the world and oversaw all formal A-10 initial qualification and requalification training for pilots.
Fairchild Republic built the A-10 to attack enemy forces near friendly ground troops. The aircraft is designed around a 30 mm (1.2-inch) GAU-8/A cannon.
“For decades, every single active-duty pilot, who flew into harm’s way, was built right there on this flightline. For nearly 50 years, the A-10 Thunderbolt has occupied a sacred place in American air power. It was never just an airplane. It was a promise. Davis-Monthan was part of that promise,” said Col. Jose Cabrera, 355th Wing commander.
Each unit’s last commander and Cabrera rolled and cased the unit’s guidon to mark its inactivation. The audience answered with a loud shout of “attack” as each outgoing commander gave up command.
“We say the word ‘attack.’ We have a great amount of pride when we say that word because it’s not just the challenge or response,” said Lt. Col. Rodney Dwyer, final commander of the 355th Operations Group and 355th Training Squadron.
Retired Lt. Gen. Glen “Wally” Moorhead, the pilot who flew the first A-10 into Davis-Monthan, also spoke.
“Nov. 7, 1975 was when I first flew the A-10 at DM,” said retired Lt. Gen. Glen “Wally” Moorhead.
Moorhead said he was selected in 1974 as the last and youngest member of the A-10 testing at Edwards Air Force Base, California. He said he knew a follow-on assignment would make him the first A-10 pilot at Davis-Monthan.
“This has been an incredible job and opportunity, but it’s also been heavy. I think about my time as a wingman, my job was to learn. As an instructor pilot, it was to teach. And now my charge [as a commander] is to leave,” said Lt. Col. Ryan Rutter, final commander of the 357th Fighter Squadron.
The ceremony ended with a group photo of former 355th Operations Group members and a flyover by two A-10s.
The announcement did not say whether any A-10s remain at Davis-Monthan, what will happen to the base’s aircraft, or what mission the 355th Wing will take on next.
Historical documents and memorabilia from the four units are being packed into containers for shipment to the National Museum of the U.S. Air Force at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio.
