On the International Day of Peace: Architecture Between Conflict and Coexistence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

Every year on September 21, the United Nations marks the International Day of Peace, an observance that invites global reflection on the conditions necessary to cultivate non-violence, social stability, and human dignity. Under the 2026 theme, "Invest in Peace – For Everyone, Everywhere, Every Day," the international body emphasizes that peace is neither static nor self-sustaining. Rather than an abstract condition defined solely by diplomatic agreements, peace operates as an ongoing social process, shaped by economic equity, institutional integrity, and the quality of civic life across communities.
Conflict is also experienced through space. War and political instability can transform homes, public infrastructure, cultural heritage, and landscapes, while displacement can reshape neighborhoods and entire urban regions. Beyond areas directly affected by conflict, questions of segregation, unequal access to resources, exclusion, and the militarization of public space reveal how social and political tensions can become embedded in the built environment.
These relationships between space, conflict, and social life have been explored through a range of architectural and urban projects, from post-conflict reconstruction and emergency housing to the preservation of cultural heritage and the transformation of contested public spaces. Rather than positioning architecture as a solution to complex political conflicts, these examples offer ways to examine how the built environment is affected by conflict and, in turn, how spatial decisions can influence processes of recovery, memory, displacement, and coexistence. Below is a selection of ArchDaily articles that examine these intersections.

Egypt says Suez Canal ‘safe’ as shipping traffic returns to normal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
06:20:57 UTC
15:20:57 KST

(AA Photo)
Egypt has said the Suez Canal remains “safe,” with maritime traffic operating normally along one of the world’s most important shipping routes.
According to a statement from the Suez Canal Authority, Chairman Osama Rabie spoke at a ceremony in Alexandria marking World Maritime Day 2026 organized by the Maritime Transport Sector of the Ministry of Transport.
Rabie said vessel traffic through the canal was proceeding regularly and that revenue reached $567.1 million in August, up 56.7 percent from the same month of 2025.
He stressed that navigation traffic remained stable and services were being provided with high efficiency.
According to navigation reports, 1,358 vessels carrying 68.3 million metric tons of net cargo transited the canal in August, compared with 1,070 vessels carrying 45.2 million metric tons during the same month last year.
Rabie said this represented increases of 27 percent in vessel numbers, 51.1 percent in net cargo and 56.7 percent in revenue.
Referring to global and regional geopolitical changes in recent years, he said international crises had directly affected global supply chains but stressed that the Suez Canal had once again demonstrated its critical and irreplaceable role in securing those supply chains.
Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty recently said that tensions in the Red Sea had cost Egypt around $11 billion in lost Suez Canal revenues.

Does Australia's favourite travel destination hold the secret to a longer life?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
06:20:08 UTC
15:20:08 KST

In brief
- Ageing populations are increasing worldwide, including in Australia.
- Japan has had a dwindling birth rate and ageing population for decades.
This article contains a reference to suicide.
Long famous for the longevity of its citizens, Japan surpassed a record 100,000 people aged 100 or older this year.
According to the country's health, labour and welfare ministry, Japan's number of centenarians increased for the 56th consecutive year to 107,677 — 88 per cent of whom were women.
Ageing populations are increasing worldwide, including in Australia, where life expectancy, already the third-highest in the world behind Monaco and Japan, is expected to climb over the next 40 years.
According to the Australian government's latest Intergenerational Report, released on Monday, Australia's ageing population is expected to transform the economy.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
As we look to a future with an older population and a longer life expectancy, what lessons can Australia take from Japan?
Henry Brodaty, Scientia professor of ageing and mental health at the University of New South Wales, said there were some obvious differences between Japan and Australia, notably the former's healthier lifestyle: Japanese people largely eat fewer high-fat and ultra-processed foods.
"They eat a lot of fish, which has been associated with a better diet and a lower risk of dementia," Brodaty told SBS News.
He said that social isolation and alcohol intake, both risk factors for dementia, were lower in Japan than in Australia, though Japan had high rates of high blood pressure and vascular disease. Stress levels were also much higher than Australia's.
"In fact, our suicide rate is about 12 to 100,000," Brodaty said. "And theirs is about 16 to 100,000."
Urban supports for longevity
Professor Marco Amati from RMIT University's Centre for Urban Research said Japan has elderly care baked into its urban planning.
"One of the biggest challenges for Australia is to do with aged care facilities, which have many issues; notably, there was a royal commission into that," he told SBS News.
Amati said Japan was good at providing end-of-life care for the elderly, with a clear commitment to providing social housing, public transport, and amenities to a high enough standard as to allow people to "age in place". Amati described this as the "Holy Grail", the "most dignified way to age".
"Everybody would prefer to remain at home, surrounded by your community, age in place, and pass away in a familiar environment," he said.
"If you have a situation where people own their own home, and they have to sell their house to go into aged care, that can be very traumatic."
By contrast, in Japan, housing communities are set up to allow ageing in place, including in rental accommodation or in public housing, and for people with early-onset dementia.
In such places, technological advancements have enabled the monitoring of elderly residents in non-obtrusive ways, ensuring that any end-of-life incidents do not go unnoticed — a common issue for elderly people with few surviving relatives.
Amati said that while similar housing approaches may not be achievable in Australia, they were still useful to know about.
"In Australia it's a whole different mix," he said. "But having that kind of a commitment or even knowing that it exists is useful to know."
Australia's biggest threat to long life
The biggest threat to long life in Australia is dementia, which in 2024 overtook cancer and heart disease to become Australia's biggest killer nationally.
Brodaty quoted recent figures from a US study published in the journal Nature: for people aged 55, the lifetime risk of dementia was 42 per cent.
"It's a scary statistic," Brodaty said.
The earlier people embrace brain health, the higher their chances of living longer. Importantly, Brodaty says, their chances of maintaining good lifetime cognition were higher, too.
"Eating a diet that's rich in vegetables, legumes, extra virgin olive oil, fish, lesser amounts of red meat and sweets, lesser amounts of processed food, watching their blood pressure and getting it checked and treated if it's high," were the best practices, Brodaty said.
Keeping socially connected and having purpose in life were also important. People who live longer "have something that drives them to live and feel valued".
Importantly, Brodaty said there were many simple ways to reduce your chances of getting dementia by almost half.
"We cannot smoke; we can avoid head injury if we can, avoid or treat diabetes. We know that people who have more exposure to green spaces and blue spaces also have a lower rate of dementia," Brodaty said.
"Eating well, remaining socially connected, keeping our brains active, using our brains, being physically active. Exercise is one of the best things we can do for our health in multiple ways."
Living longer, but at what cost?
But the comparison between Australia and Japan can only go so far, Brodaty said.
"We have to consider the demography of the two countries. Australia has 26,270,000 people. Japan has over 100,000,000 people."
Japan's long-lived, ageing population underscores a severe demographic crisis. It's part of the reason the number of centenarians seems "distorted", Brodaty said.
Japan has had a dwindling birth rate and ageing population for decades.
"This is really quite a crisis for Japan economically, because the number of people of working age, proportionately, is decreasing, and the number of people of working age who can look after older people is shrinking."
In Japan, there are roughly two working-age people for every elderly person aged 65 or older.
"Imagine that if we have only one person of working age to help support every older person," Brodaty asked. "How could we possibly arrange our society to deal with that?"
Brodaty said that while this would be an increasing crisis, there was a way to avert it.
"That is to try to help people live their lifespan healthily," he said. "So we talk about healthspan and lifespan, and that gap is what we're trying to narrow."
Readers seeking crisis support can ring Lifeline on 13 11 14 or text 0477 13 11 14, the Suicide Call Back Service on 1300 659 467 and Kids Helpline on 1800 55 1800 (for young people aged up to 25). More information and support with mental health is available at beyondblue.org.au and on 1300 22 4636.
Embrace Multicultural Mental Health supports people from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds.

US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz said on Sunday that the “door is open” for Iran to return to negotiations to end the conflict in the Middle East.
Speaking at an Al-Monitor Live event in New York on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, Waltz said the Trump administration believes time is on its side in the conflict with Iran, which began Feb. 28.
“I do believe that to be the case,” Waltz said when asked by Al-Monitor senior adviser Andrew Parasiliti whether Washington believes time is on its side.
He added that the “door is open for Iran to come back to the negotiating table,” while dismissing as “fantastical” reports that Tehran has demanded an end to US sanctions and reparations as conditions for renewed talks.

Peace in Gaza
On Gaza, Waltz described the administration’s approach as a “new type of multilateralism” and said talks with Israel on implementing President Donald Trump’s 20-point Gaza plan could “move forward after the elections are settled,” referring to Israel’s Oct. 27 parliamentary election.
The plan includes a Palestinian technocratic administration, reconstruction and an International Stabilization Force, while negotiations over Hamas’ disarmament and an Israeli withdrawal have stalled.
Waltz claimed there were “prospective members” interested in joining the Abraham Accords, to normalize relations with Israel, but did not name them.
He also welcomed Israel and Morocco’s decision earlier this month to exchange ambassadors.
On Iraq, Waltz praised Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s efforts to bring Iran-backed militias under state control, saying Iran’s “weakened state” could create an opening to curb their influence.

overlapping concrete walls and columns blur inside and outside in okinawa house
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
06:15:51 UTC
15:15:51 KST

a large roof unifies a house of overlapping concrete spaces
Overlapping Spaces is a house in Okinawa, Japan, designed by IGArchitects as a composition of reinforced-concrete walls, columns, and a large roof. Rather than dividing the house into conventional rooms, the project creates a continuous spatial field by overlapping structural elements. Walls and columns define different degrees of enclosure, while the large roof unifies the spaces beneath it. The resulting architecture is composed of a series of spaces that are neither completely inside nor outside. Boundaries become ambiguous as views, light, air, and movement pass between the structural elements.
Overlapping spaces define a flexible framework for living
The walls and columns are not treated simply as structural necessities. Their positions establish the rhythm, scale, and sequence of the house, while the roof creates a generous sheltered environment for everyday life. The project reduces the architecture to a small number of strong elements and allows their relationships to generate spatial richness. Instead of prescribing a fixed use for each room, the overlapping spaces provide a flexible framework for different activities and ways of living. Through this project, design studio IGArchitects explores how a strong structural order can coexist with openness and ambiguity, creating architecture that is both defined and adaptable.

Trump welcomes Xi this week amid persistent tensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
06:15:13 UTC
15:15:13 KST

This file photo shows China's President Xi Jinping (R) and U.S. President Donald Trump visit the Temple of Heaven in Beijing, May 14, 2026. (AP File Photo)
When President Donald Trump first ran for office, he called out China as a menace to the U.S. economy, saying it had gutted America’s factories and eroded the middle class.
That tough talk helped Trump get to the White House a decade ago, but since then, he increasingly speaks in glowing terms about Chinese President Xi Jinping, the geopolitical rival Trump will fete on Sept. 24 with a state dinner.
“He’s a great gentleman; we get along great,” Trump said this month. “We have a very good trading relationship and, you know, they’re a competitor and all of that, but we have a very good relationship with President Xi.”
On issue after issue, the Republican president has given Xi a pass.
Trump shrugged off reports that China had provided Iran with satellite imagery, saying, “I think he’s behaved reasonably well.” After accusing Beijing of accessing U.S. voter files back in 2020, Trump indicated he was hesitant to retaliate: “I think China is maybe a little bit different today than it was then.”
Trump’s magnanimity comes as China and the United States are in a contest for global leadership, with some of America’s traditional allies rethinking their strategies. China has expanded its dominance in manufacturing and pushed into new technologies such as artificial intelligence and electric vehicles that create risks for the economies of the U.S., Germany, Italy, France, South Korea and Japan, among others.
Unable to change Chinese behavior, Trump has resorted to hospitality.
He traveled to Beijing in May, and the two leaders could meet again two more times this year at international summits.
Trump has insisted that the U.S. is comfortably ahead of China, but his efforts last year to confront China with a mounting set of tariffs backfired. China holds a relative monopoly on the rare earths used in electronics and deployed that to help force a trade armistice with Trump.
“Trump has dramatically shifted his approach to China because his initial attempt to use super-high tariffs and export restrictions was unsuccessful,” said Michael Kovrig, a senior adviser at the International Crisis Group. “Xi and Trump got into a contest of leverage, and Xi came out on top.”
Meanwhile, Trump has largely undermined the economic and national security alliances that could previously apply pressure on China, said Kovrig.
Trump has mocked French President Emmanuel Macron in speeches. He has run hot and cold on NATO after several of its members did not fully support his choice to start a war with Iran. Trump has launched a potentially brutal trade fight with Canada, a longtime ally he has trolled as becoming the 51st American state.
“He’s executing Xi’s wedge tactics for him, and along the way, helping Xi to tell a story about China as the more stable and responsible power,” Kovrig said. “It’s led to a wave of Western leaders visiting Beijing and seeking to stabilize and improve their relations with Xi so they can focus more on dealing with problems Trump is causing them.”
While Xi met three times on the sidelines of international summits with Democratic President Joe Biden, Trump will have achieved a pair of reciprocal state visits in a sign that the leaders of the world’s two largest economies feel comfortable speaking to each other.
The trade imbalance with China in goods has declined relative to the same period in 2025, according to Census Bureau figures, though the administration has noted that China appears to be routing more goods through other nations such as Vietnam to minimize the tariffs.
Trump’s continued tariffs on China have not curbed its manufacturing sector. China has found new markets and boxed out competition from other industrialized countries. China is exporting more of its goods to the rest of the world with a $1.2 trillion global trade surplus last year as its low-priced EVs undercut the auto sectors in Germany, Japan and South Korea.
Both China and the U.S. are using their trade truce to retrench. China is building up its military and AI capabilities despite limited access to advanced computer chips. The Trump administration has pursued partnerships to develop rare earths.

Grand Ayatollah Shobeiri Zanjani passes away at age of 98
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
06:14:12 UTC
15:14:12 KST

His office announced in the early hours of Monday that “the pure soul of the jurist of the Ahl al-Bayt (peace be upon them) and the exalted authority of the global Shia community, Grand Ayatollah Shobeiri Zanjani, has joined God.”
The announcement quoted the Quranic verse: “Those whom the angels take in death while they are good, they say, ‘Peace be upon you; enter Paradise for what you used to do.’”
The late marja had been admitted to a hospital in the holy city of Qom on Friday evening after a pulmonary complication and remained under intensive care for two days before his passing. Funeral and burial arrangements will be announced later, his office said.
The office offered condolences to the Islamic seminaries, the noble people of Iran, and followers of the marja’iyya across the world. It described his blessed life as one of “deep reflection, continuous scholarly struggle, sincere effort to preserve and elevate authentic jurisprudence, the spread of Islamic teachings, the safeguarding of Shia Islam and goodwill toward the people.”
Grand Ayatollah Shobeiri Zanjani was born on March 2, 1928, in Qom, three months after his father, the late Ayatollah Sayyid Ahmad Shobeiri Zanjani, settled beside the shrine of Hazrat Fatima Masoumeh (peace be upon her). He was named Musa in honor of that sacred proximity. His father was a prominent jurist, a close associate of the founder of the Qom seminary, Sheikh Abdul-Karim Haeri Yazdi, and a companion of Imam Khomeini in the scholarly circles of the city.
He began seminary studies as a child. He later attended the advanced lessons of leading masters in Qom and Najaf, including Grand Ayatollahs Sayyid Hossein Borujerdi, Sayyid Mohammad Mohaqeq Damad, Sayyid Abolqasem Khoei, Sayyid Mohsen Hakim, Sayyid Abd al-Hadi Shirazi, and Imam Khomeini.
He became one of the foremost authorities in ilm al-rijal, the science of evaluating hadith narrators, and taught advanced fiqh in Qom for more than four decades, according to Press TV.
After the passing of Grand Ayatollah Mohammad Ali Araki in 1994, the Society of Seminary Teachers of Qom named him among the seven jurists qualified for marja’iyya.

Iran economy contracts during US war: Official statistics

(FILES) Shopkeepers arrange dried fruits and nuts in front of their shop at a market in Tehran on August 24, 2026. Iran's economy contracted by more than 10 percent during the Middle East war, which began with US-Israeli attacks in late February that unleashed turmoil and battered the Islamic republic's economy. (AFP Photo)
Iran's economy contracted by more than 10 percent during the Middle East war, which began with U.S.-Israeli attacks in late February.
The country's gross domestic product (GDP) shrank by 10.1 percent year-on-year from late March to late June, a period known in Iran as the first quarter of the Persian calendar, according to the Statistical Center of Iran on Sept. 20.
Iran has been at war with the United States since late February, when U.S.-Israeli strikes killed the Islamic republic's supreme leader and senior military officials at the start of a vast offensive.
The strikes sparked Tehran's retaliation in blocking the Strait of Hormuz — causing global oil prices to surge — as the conflict spread in the Middle East.
Aside from this, Iran's economy has long struggled with hyperinflation and devaluation of its currency, caused in large part by economic sanctions.

Singapore retrenchment rates hit highest level since pandemic
The number of job vacancies declined in the second quarter, especially in the financial services and information and communications sectors
There were 4,620 retrenchments in the second quarter of this year, up from the 3,830 retrenchments posted in the first quarter of the year, the ministry said in its labour market report for the period.
It is the highest since the 5,640 retrenchments recorded in the fourth quarter of 2020 during the Covid pandemic. Retrenchments fell after 2020, when Singapore’s population declined as travel curbs and job losses encouraged foreign workers to leave the business hub, creating a tighter labour market.
The manpower ministry said that the quarter-on-quarter increase was “concentrated in outward-oriented sectors, including manufacturing, information and communications and financial services”.

Bedri Rahmi Eyüboğlu’s art lives beyond the canvas in public spaces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
06:02:17 UTC
15:02:17 KST

AA Photo
The works of Turkish modern art pioneer Bedri Rahmi Eyüboğlu extended far beyond the canvas, becoming part of buildings, markets, hospitals, hotels and public spaces in Türkiye and abroad.
From Istanbul to the Mediterranean and from Paris to Brussels, his murals, mosaics, reliefs and stained-glass works brought traditional Anatolian motifs into architecture and continue to preserve his artistic legacy in the urban landscape.
Eyüboğlu, who died on Sept. 21, 1975, at the age of 64, believed that art should be “at eye level with the public,” an approach that led him from the canvas to architectural surfaces and public spaces.
Born in 1911, Eyüboğlu developed an interest in painting at high school and entered Istanbul’s State Academy of Fine Arts in 1929.
He went to France in 1931 and worked at André Lhote’s studio in Paris from 1932 to 1933. After returning to Türkiye, he joined the D Group and became an assistant to French painter Léopold Lévy at the Academy in 1937.
Over time, he moved away from the Cubist and Constructivist approaches of his early career and turned increasingly toward local sources, combining miniature art, kilim weaving, tilework, traditional textile printing and Hittite reliefs with a modern visual language.
His journeys across Anatolia also shaped his work. He observed local people, daily life and folk culture, incorporating village landscapes, traditional clothing, women, roads and other elements of Anatolian life into his art.
Eyüboğlu’s efforts to integrate art with architecture emerged strongly in the 1940s.
For the Lido Swimming Pool in Istanbul’s Ortaköy district, he produced mosaic panels in 1943 featuring women carrying food, parachutes and sailing boats. He described the works as embroidery rather than painting. The panels were later lost following changes to the building.
He also designed a three-part wall panel for the Ankara Opera House featuring two lovers on a flying horse. Together with his wife, painter Eren Eyüboğlu, he created two large mosaic panels for the Etibank General Directorate in Ankara, featuring Hittite-inspired figures.
In Istanbul, his works became part of commercial, residential and public architecture. A 1957, 60-square-meter panel at Doğubank Business Center in Sirkeci incorporated stylized versions of the letters “D” and “B.”
At the Istanbul Manifaturacılar Çarşısı (İMÇ) in Fatih, Eyüboğlu created two panels in 1965. His 35-square-meter “İstanbul Abstract Composition” brought together the city’s silhouette, minarets, seagulls, waves and fish in an abstract composition. A second panel drew on Anatolian women’s lace and weaving traditions.
His work at Aksu Business Center near Karaköy included the exterior “Confectioners Relief,” combining fish, nets and boats with kilim motifs, and the 1965 “Ox Cart” mosaic depicting oxen pulling a traditional cart through an Anatolian landscape.
His collaboration with Vakko began in the 1950s with textile printing and later expanded into large-scale works. Four monumental works originally created for the company’s Merter factory were preserved after the building was demolished and are now displayed at the Vakko Moda Merkezi in Nakkaştepe.
Eyüboğlu also created a 100-square-meter mosaic for the former Samatya SSK Istanbul Hospital, now Istanbul Training and Research Hospital, in 1959.
His architectural legacy extended to hotels. A 1968 relief at the Divan Hotel in Harbiye was preserved during restoration, while the “Pigeons” mosaic at The Marmara Pera in Tepebaşı was completed in 1975.
From Dalaman to Brussels
Eyüboğlu’s art was not confined to cities.
In 1974, during a blue cruise, he painted a fish figure on a flat rock at Taşyaka Cove in Dalaman, Muğla. The site later became known as Bedri Rahmi Cove and remains a popular stop for daily boat tours from Göcek, where visitors take photographs in front of the work.
His international architectural legacy includes a monumental mosaic created for NATO headquarters. Completed in 1959, the approximately 50-square-meter, 10-ton mosaic was presented by the Turkish government to NATO in 1960. It was first installed at the alliance’s headquarters in Paris and later moved to Brussels following the relocation of NATO headquarters. It was transferred again to the alliance’s new headquarters complex in 2016 and remains there.
Eyüboğlu also created stained-glass works for the Turkish Embassy in Bonn, the former capital of West Germany. Following German reunification and the relocation of the capital to Berlin, the works were transferred to the new Turkish Embassy and incorporated into its architecture.
He died in Istanbul on Sept. 21, 1975, at the age of 64.
More than five decades after his death, his works remain embedded in places where people live, work, travel and gather, from apartment blocks and hospitals in Istanbul to a Mediterranean cove and diplomatic buildings in Europe.

Historic Vefa High School raises modern Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
06:01:59 UTC
15:01:59 KST

AA Photo
The corridors of Vefa High School in the historic Fatih district of Istanbul carry the footsteps of an empire’s twilight and a modern republic’s dawn.
Founded in 1872 as the “Dersaadet İdadi-i Mülkiye-i Şahane (The Imperial Civil High School of Istanbul)” under Ottoman rule, this historic institution stands as one of Türkiye’s oldest schools, seamlessly bridging 19th-century traditions with the digital age.
Vefa’s history reflects Türkiye’s own resilience, having endured wars, political shifts and the birth of a modern republic. Over the generations, the iconic school has educated the nation’s intellectual and cultural elite, including literary giants Reşat Nuri Gültekin and Peyami Safa, as well as legendary actors Kemal Sunal and Şener Şen.
Vefa High School looks vastly different today than it did in its Ottoman beginnings. Restored with alumni support and public funds following the 1999 Düzce earthquake, the campus features a historic 112-bed dormitory designed by renowned architect Mimar Kemalettin — a standing architectural landmark that now houses top-tier students.
Part of the Şehzade Mosque on campus, along with the Şehit Ali Paşa Library, is used for educational purposes. Of these spaces, the library located in the guesthouse is named after Prof. Dr. İlber Ortaylı, one of modern Türkiye’s most distinguished scholars.
Now operating under a five-year model with a preparatory year, the school has fully stepped into the 21st century by outfitting its classrooms with modern multimedia technology.
With 730 current students, Vefa proves that true heritage is about evolving while remembering your roots. It remains a timeless symbol of Turkish education, proving that history is not just a subject to study, but a tradition to be lived.

Türkiye targets 2.1 million more jobs by 2029
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
06:01:44 UTC
15:01:44 KST

Türkiye aims to increase employment by about 2.13 million people over three years under its new Medium-Term Program, which includes measures to expand childcare, support young jobseekers and prepare workers for changes in the economy.
The program projects employment rising from an estimated 32.58 million in 2026 to 34.71 million in 2029.
Economic growth is targeted at 4.2 percent in 2027, 4.6 percent in 2028 and 5 percent in 2029.
Per capita income is projected to rise from $20,523 in 2026 to $24,842 by the end of the program.
To increase women’s participation in the workforce, the government plans to expand affordable, accessible childcare alongside services for older people and people with disabilities.
After-school culture, arts and sports programs will also be expanded to provide safe settings for children and help women enter or remain in employment.
The program calls for an assessment of how slowing population growth affects the social security system and preparations for long-term care insurance.
For young people who are neither in education nor employment, it envisages wider access to the Labor Force Adaptation Program, with vocational training and skills development tailored to their needs.
Employment support programs will be assessed regularly, with resources directed toward those that perform better in helping participants move into lasting jobs.
The plan also addresses the effects of the green and digital transitions on the labor market.
A proposed map of occupations and employment will identify green jobs, professions affected by the green transition, areas at risk of job losses and new skills requirements.
Under the National Just Transition Strategy for 2027–2029, implementation and monitoring arrangements will be established, alongside targeted social protection and employment measures for workers most affected by the changes.
Worker and employer representatives will have a greater role in designing and monitoring these policies.

It said the professor reported the incident to the authorities for further action.The institute said Doolla and the Head of Department had counselled the student and assured him that the incident would not adversely affect his academic career. The student subsequently returned to his hostel room, where he was later found dead.The incident has since triggered student protests on campus, with students demanding accountability and transparency from the administration.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) said Sunday that Taiwan’s economic growth must be matched by greater cultural vitality, arguing that economic strength makes a country powerful while culture makes it great.

The government will pursue cross-government initiatives, including the Ministry of Culture and Ministry of Sports’ “Ocean Voyage Project.” The “Taiwan Cultural Year in Europe” and “Great Voyage Project” will expand Taiwan’s international cultural connections.
Lai also highlighted cultural credits for people aged 13 to 22, performances for young audiences, and cultural activities in schools.
AI will play a role in the government’s strategy, Lai said. The government plans to strengthen protections for original works, provide adaptation and professional development training, and establish mentorship programs to help creators navigate the AI era.
The government will also encourage original content and expand international investment and co-productions. Lai said the goal is to help global audiences understand Taiwan through its creative works while enabling Taiwanese creators to enter international markets.

Prosecutors said the action followed a Sept. 17 Capital Markets Board (SPK) report on suspected market manipulation.
Gürlek said money and asset transactions had been frozen for executives and officials connected to Pusula Finans Holding, Pusula Yatırım, Tera Yatırım, Tera Portföy, Hedef Holding, Hedef Portföy, Bulls Yatırım, Bulls Portföy and Ufuk Yatırım Yönetim ve Gayrimenkul.
Institutions were also instructed not to process transactions reducing the assets of board members, authorized signatories, their spouses and first-degree blood relatives without informing and consulting prosecutors.
The measures aim to prevent assets from being concealed, transferred to third parties or depleted, Gürlek said.
In a Sept. 17 request, prosecutors asked the Financial Crimes Investigation Board (MASAK) to examine financial records of executives at Pusula, Tera, Hedef and Bulls group companies and their first-degree relatives.
The review covers overseas money and cryptocurrency transfers since 2024, as well as account inflows and outflows.
Earlier detainees included Tera Yatırım Holding Chairman Emre Tezmen, executives Alper Öztürk, Emre Alkin and Kerem Alkin, Pusula executive Serdar Turhan and Doğa Sigorta Chairman Nihat Kırmızı.
Four suspects had previously been remanded in custody, while 51 people were placed under foreign travel bans and asset restrictions.
Media reports said that transfers of $15 million from Turhan’s account and 25 million euros from Pusula Portföy Chairman Muhammed Yarız’s account to accounts in Switzerland.
The SPK halted trading in funds run by seven asset managers on TEFAS, Türkiye’s electronic fund trading platform, on Sept. 17 following defaults on payments to investors seeking to redeem their holdings.
It ordered 131 funds into liquidation.
The regulator authorized private lender İşbank and state-owned Ziraat Bankası to oversee the liquidation processes
In a Sept. 20 decision, the board extended the liquidation period from three months to six, citing the funds’ portfolio structures and market conditions.
The SPK clarified on Sept. 21 that liquidation could be completed before the six-month deadline and that the other liquidation and payment rules remained unchanged.

US, South Korea and Japan discuss response after North Korea missile launches
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
05:59:29 UTC
14:59:29 KST

The United States, South Korea and Japan held phone consultations on Monday to share information and discuss their response after North Korea launched two short-range ballistic missiles, Seoul’s foreign ministry said.
The launches on Sunday marked North Korea’s 14th ballistic missile launch of the year and its first in eight days, according to South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff. The missiles were fired from the Wonsan area toward the Sea of Japan, also known as the East Sea.
Baek Yong-jin, director general for Korean Peninsula policy at South Korea’s Foreign Ministry, spoke with David Wilezol, deputy assistant secretary of state for Northeast Asia, and Takashi Ariyoshi, a senior Japanese foreign ministry official.
“The three officials shared relevant information and discussed future responses,” the South Korean ministry said.
Allies maintain missile-response channel
The ministry said the three countries maintain a channel for rapidly sharing information and assessments whenever North Korea conducts a ballistic missile launch.
South Korea’s military said the first missile flew about 450 kilometres, while the second travelled more than 600 kilometres. The launches were tracked jointly by South Korean and US intelligence authorities, with information also shared with Japan.
The latest launches came after North Korean leader Kim Jong-un’s sister, Kim Yo-jong, criticised the US-led Pacific Vanguard multinational maritime exercise near Guam and warned that Pyongyang could take a stronger response.
South Korean and Japanese officials have also linked the timing of the launches to recent regional military activities, although North Korea has not explicitly said the missiles were fired in response to Pacific Vanguard.
The launches come ahead of a planned meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping later this week and as world leaders gather in New York for the UN General Assembly.

Turkish-origin Eralp leads left to victory in Berlin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
05:58:24 UTC
14:58:24 KST

AA photo.
Elif Eralp, a politician of Turkish origin, led Germany’s Left Party to victory in Berlin’s Sept. 20 state election, while Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservatives suffered setbacks in both states that voted.
Provisional results gave Die Linke 25.7 percent in Berlin, more than doubling its share from 2023.
Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) finished second with 18.8 percent.
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) took 16.3 percent, followed by the Greens with 14.3 percent and the Social Democrats (SPD) with 12.1 percent.
The Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance fell below the 5 percent parliamentary threshold with 4.7 percent.
“We made history, friends,” Eralp told supporters in Turkish during her victory speech.
The 45-year-old lawyer campaigned on affordable housing and rising rents.
She will need coalition partners and the support of the state parliament to become Berlin’s governing mayor.
An alliance with the Greens and SPD would give her party a majority.
The outgoing CDU-SPD coalition lost its parliamentary majority.
Eralp worked as a legal policy adviser to the Left Party’s Bundestag group from 2010 to 2021 before entering Berlin’s state parliament.
She is also deputy leader of the party’s Berlin branch.
Eralp’s parents, who were active in socialist politics and trade unions in Türkiye, fled to Germany in 1980 following a military coup when the mother was eight months pregnant.
Eralp was born in Munich and went on to study law in Hamburg, going on to defend migrants’ rights.
She was hired as a staffer for Die Linke’s faction in the German parliament in 2010 and moved to Berlin permanently not long after.
She lives in the trendy Kreuzberg district with her husband and two children, and is often quick to emphasize that, like most Berliners, they rent their flat and are not homeowners.
Merz labels results ‘a disaster’
In Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the AfD won 38.2 percent, ahead of the SPD’s 35.5 percent.
The CDU received 4.9 percent, failing to enter a state parliament for the first time.
The AfD fell short of an outright majority, and the other parties ruled out governing with it.
The incumbent SPD-Left coalition also lost its majority, but could retain power by bringing in the Greens.
“We cannot gloss over the result in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. It is a disaster,” Merz said after the first projections were released.
He nevertheless pledged to remain in office and pursue his reform agenda.
He described the CDU’s Berlin performance as a “decent result,” citing the difficult circumstances of its campaign.
The losses followed the AfD’s Sept. 6 victory in Saxony-Anhalt, which had already prompted calls from within the CDU for Merz to step down.
The chancellor has also canceled a planned trip to New York for the U.N. General Assembly.

Image: U.S. Department of State
World leaders are gathering in New York for the 81st U.N. General Assembly, with wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, climate change and the risks of artificial intelligence expected to dominate discussions.
About 130 heads of state and government are expected to speak alongside dozens of ministers during the general debate, which runs from Sept. 22 to 28.
Secretary-General Antonio Guterres will deliver his final annual opening address before his second term ends on Dec. 31.
“International cooperation is more necessary than ever,” he said ahead of the gathering, identifying uncontrolled AI development, climate change and widening inequality as existential threats.
U.S. President Donald Trump, French President Emmanuel Macron and President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan are among the opening-day speakers.
Erdoğan is scheduled to speak fourth among national leaders, after the representatives of Brazil, the United States and Jordan.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian are scheduled to address the assembly on Sept. 23. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will speak the following day.
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas will also address the assembly on Sept. 24, appearing by video after Washington denied him a visa for a second consecutive year.
Chinese President Xi Jinping will not attend, although he is expected to meet Trump in Washington during the week.
Russian President Vladimir Putin is also staying away, with Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov due to address the assembly on Sept. 26.
The wars in Gaza, Iran, Ukraine and Sudan will feature prominently in diplomatic meetings, alongside shipping security in the Strait of Hormuz and crises in Yemen, Myanmar and Haiti.
The Security Council is scheduled to hold separate high-level meetings on Ukraine and AI on Sept. 23, with Zelensky attending the Ukraine session.
AI safety has gained attention following calls by industry leaders to slow development.
Guterres has urged governments to coordinate their response, warning that national measures alone cannot address risks that cross borders.
Climate targets, development financing, pandemic preparedness, nuclear disarmament and rising sea levels are also on the week’s agenda.
The gathering will address the U.N.’s own financial difficulties and efforts to reform its institutions, including the Security Council, where the United States, Russia, China, Britain and France hold veto power.
Washington recently paid $725 million toward the U.N.’s regular budget, removing the risk of losing its General Assembly vote in 2027.
It still owed $1.312 billion to that budget, U.N. spokesman Farhan Haq said on Sept. 16.
New York authorities have increased security and restricted traffic around U.N. headquarters.
Temporary flight restrictions, including a ban on unauthorized drones, are in place around the complex through Sept. 26.

====================================================================================================

World Insights: Mecca defense pact faces 1st test as Houthi-Saudi confrontation escalates
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
13:53:31 CST
14:53:31 KST

SANAA, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Six weeks after Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan agreed in Mecca to treat an armed attack against one as an attack against all, the rapidly escalating Houthi-Saudi confrontation is putting that pledge to its first serious test.
Houthi forces have advanced along Yemen's western coast toward the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait while stepping up missile and drone attacks deep inside Saudi Arabia. Riyadh, meanwhile, has intensified airstrikes against Houthi targets in Yemen.
The confrontation took a particularly sensitive turn after Saudi Arabia said it intercepted a Houthi drone south of Mecca before it could enter the holy city's airspace. The Houthis denied targeting Mecca.
Then, on Saturday, the threat reached Riyadh. As explosions were heard in the Saudi capital and authorities issued an aerial alert, the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted a Houthi ballistic missile targeting the city. The Houthis said they had attacked targets in Riyadh and the Red Sea energy hub of Yanbu.
The escalating exchange of fire is transforming renewed fighting in Yemen into a broader test of regional deterrence. Türkiye and Pakistan have pledged support for Saudi Arabia, but neither has announced direct combat involvement against the Houthis.
That leaves the Mecca agreement facing a question: Can its members make collective defense credible enough to deter further attacks without drawing themselves into a wider war?
PRESSURE SPREADS BEYOND YEMEN
Saudi Arabia is facing mounting pressure across an expanding geographic arc, stretching from the battlefields in Yemen and the Bab al-Mandab Strait to its cities and energy infrastructure.
The Houthis said Saturday they launched ballistic and cruise missiles and drones against "sensitive targets" in Riyadh and a facility of the Saudi oil giant, Aramco, in the western Saudi city of Yanbu.
The Saudi side said air defenses intercepted the missile targeting Riyadh and thwarted attacks on Baish, Taif, Farasan and Yanbu.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Sarea said the group's strategy is "escalation for escalation," linking its attacks to intensified Saudi air operations in Yemen.
Meanwhile, the battlefield inside Yemen has shifted sharply.
On Sept. 10, Houthi forces captured Mocha, a strategic Red Sea port in southwestern Taiz province. A day later, they seized Dhubab and Mayyun Island in the Bab al-Mandab Strait after government forces withdrew farther south into neighboring Lahj province.
Fighting has since raged around the Kahbub mountain area and nearby heights overlooking approaches to the strait, with both sides rushing reinforcements to the front.
The Bab al-Mandab Strait links the Gulf of Aden with the Red Sea and, farther north, the Suez Canal, placing it astride one of the world's most important trade and energy corridors.
With shipping through the Strait of Hormuz already disrupted by wider regional tensions, instability around the strait adds pressure around another critical maritime chokepoint.
FROM PLEDGE TO PRACTICE
On Aug. 7, Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Muhammad Shehbaz Sharif signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement.
Its central principle is collective defense: any armed attack against any of the three countries will be considered an attack against them all.
The three countries began building the pact's institutional structure later that month, agreeing in Istanbul to strengthen military coordination and defense-industrial cooperation and establish a permanent secretariat in Saudi Arabia.
The Houthi attacks have abruptly moved the discussion from planning to practice.
Türkiye has offered the clearest indication of what its support could involve. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said Saturday that Ankara would honor its commitments and could provide technical assistance to meet Saudi military needs.
Pakistan has delivered an even stronger political message. Islamabad has repeatedly condemned attacks on Saudi Arabia and reaffirmed support for the kingdom's sovereignty and territorial integrity. Pakistan's military has said the country would go "to any extent" to defend Saudi sovereignty.
Yet neither Islamabad nor Ankara has announced direct combat operations against the Houthis.
For Ankara and Islamabad, collective defense need not immediately translate into direct intervention in Yemen. Support could instead involve air-defense coordination, intelligence, technical assistance, logistics and other measures designed to strengthen Saudi defenses without opening another front, said analysts.
DETERRENCE WITHOUT ENTANGLEMENT?
The current escalation is testing whether the new alliance can turn its collective-defense pledge into a credible deterrent without being drawn directly into the conflict, Aden-based political analyst Muqbil Naji told Xinhua.
"The challenge is not simply to show solidarity with Saudi Arabia, but to make that solidarity credible enough to influence the calculations of those attacking it," said Naji.
Turkish and Pakistani support could strengthen Saudi Arabia's ability to detect and intercept incoming threats, but could not guarantee protection from every missile or drone, he noted.
"More defenses can reduce the risk, but they cannot remove it," he said. "The bigger challenge is preventing the attacks from continuing."
Yet analysts argued that efforts to reinforce Saudi defenses could introduce another risk: the deeper Türkiye and Pakistan become involved, the harder the confrontation may become to contain.
"The more actors enter the equation, the harder it becomes to keep the conflict contained," said Ali bin Hadi, a military observer based in Aden.
That risk could grow significantly if Turkish or Pakistani personnel or assets were directly hit, bin Hadi said. "Once their own forces come under attack, staying purely defensive becomes much harder."
For now, analysts see room for deterrence without direct intervention. Türkiye and Pakistan could reinforce Saudi defenses while preserving diplomatic space and limiting their exposure to the fighting.
But that balance remains fragile. A high-casualty attack inside Saudi Arabia, serious damage to critical energy infrastructure, or another incident around the holy sites could sharply alter calculations.
The Mecca pact's first test, therefore, may not be whether Turkish or Pakistani forces enter the Yemen conflict, but whether their commitment can make further escalation costly enough to deter it, said analysts. ■

Türkiye renews effort to ease Afghanistan-Pakistan tensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
05:44:00 UTC
14:44:00 KST

Türkiye has renewed efforts to ease tensions between Afghanistan and Pakistan, with National Intelligence Organization (MİT) chief İbrahim Kalın visiting both countries as a senior Qatari security official held separate talks with Taliban leaders.
Kalın visited Kabul and Kandahar on Sept. 16, meeting senior Taliban officials to discuss security cooperation, counterterrorism, drug trafficking and regional developments, according to Turkish security sources.
He then traveled to Islamabad, where he met Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir and Inter-Services Intelligence Director-General Asim Malik.
Türkiye reiterated its commitment to resolving Afghan-Pakistani tensions through dialogue during the meetings, the sources said.
Hamad bin Khamis al-Kaabi, deputy head of Qatar’s National Security Council, also visited Kabul, where he met Taliban Defense Minister Mohammad Yaqoob Mujahid.
Taliban statements described the discussions as focused on bilateral relations and cooperation.
Türkiye and Qatar brokered a ceasefire between Afghanistan and Pakistan in Doha on Oct. 19, 2025.
Subsequent negotiations and mediation efforts, including those involving China, have failed to secure a lasting settlement.
Islamabad accuses the Taliban administration of sheltering Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and Baloch separatist militants responsible for attacks in Pakistan.
Kabul denies the allegations.
Pakistan has tied the reopening of trade routes to action against militants operating from Afghan territory.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Sajjad Haider Khan said on Sept. 17 that Islamabad was prepared to restore trade and transit links if its security concerns were addressed.
The visits also followed an August defense agreement between Türkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia.
The Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, signed Aug. 7 by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Pakistani Prime Minister Shahbaz Sharif, stipulates that an armed attack against any one of the three countries will be regarded as an attack against all three.
At an Aug. 31 meeting in Istanbul, the three countries pledged to support de-escalation and peaceful solutions to regional disputes.
A day after Kalın’s Pakistan visit was announced, a bombing and gun attack struck a police compound in Kohat, in the northwestern province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
The Sept. 18 attack killed 22 people, including 16 police officers, and wounded 103, Pakistan’s state news agency reported, citing police and hospital officials.

Portuguese singer-songwriter Jorge Palma dies aged 76
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
05:37:37 UTC
14:37:37 KST

Singer of "Deixa-me Rir" and "A Gente Vai Continuar" died aged 76 from cardiorespiratory arrest, after over 50 years devoted to Portuguese music.
Portuguese singer-songwriter Jorge Palma died this Monday at the age of 76, his family announced in a message on social media.
"It is with deep sorrow and consternation that Jorge Palma's family and agency announce his death, which occurred on Monday night, at the age of 76, following a cardiorespiratory arrest," the musician's family said.
In what they describe as a moment of "immeasurable pain", his wife, Rita Tomé, his sons, Vicente and Francisco Palma, and his agents, André Sebastião and Tiago Branco, asked that Jorge Palma be remembered through what best defined him: his songs and his words. The family also thanked all the expressions of friendship they have received over the years.
The family also recalled that Jorge Palma, whose career spanned 54 years, "leaves behind a remarkable body of work that forms part of the history" of Portuguese music, as well as "many friends around the world, people he won over with his generosity and brilliance".
Born in Lisbon in 1950, Jorge Palma entered the world of music at an early age, becoming one of the most influential singers and songwriters in contemporary Portuguese music. He began taking classes at the age of six and, four years later, enrolled at the Lisbon Music Conservatory.
At 14 he decided to abandon classical music to devote himself to pop-rock, embarking on a path that would cut across several generations.
Before performing under his own name, he played in the band Sindicato, which took part in the first edition of the Vilar de Mouros Festival in 1971, and in Black Boys. At the same time, he began working in areas such as composition, orchestration and recording.
In 1972, when he was just 22, he released his first solo single, "The Nine Billion Names of God". Shortly afterwards he was called up for military service, but chose to leave Portugal and settle in Denmark.
It was only in 1974, after the 25 April revolution, that he returned to Portugal, began working as an orchestrator and, the following year, released his first album, "Como uma viagem na palma da mão".
Over the course of his career, he released a further 13 albums of original material. For Jorge Palma, each record worked as a snapshot of a particular phase of his life. In an interview with Lusa in 2022, he explained that the people he related to, the places he lived, his daily life, and what he listened to and read ended up leaving different marks on each album.
In the 1980s, he resumed his piano studies at the conservatory, which he completed in 1990. The following year came "Só", a project in which he revisited, on solo piano, songs from his albums of the previous two decades, becoming the first compilation of his career.
The 1990s opened up new horizons. Jorge Palma formed Palma's Gang alongside Zé Pedro and Kalu of Xutos & Pontapés, and Flak and Alex Cortez of Rádio Macau. He composed for theatre and for other artists and joined the project Rio Grande. After a decade of multiple experiences, he returned to original studio albums with "É proibido fumar" in 2001.
"Norte" (2004), "Voo nocturno" (2007) and "Com todo o respeito" (2011) followed. His most recent – and final – album, "Vida", was released in 2023.
Over the years, his work received several awards. In 2002, he was awarded the José Afonso Prize for the album "Jorge Palma". Ten years later, he won the first edition of the Pedro Osório Prize, awarded by the Portuguese Society of Authors, with "Com todo o respeito".
In 2020, at the end of a concert marking his 70th birthday, he was honoured by Lisbon City Council with the cultural merit medal. That same year, he was decorated by the then President of the Republic, Marcelo Rebelo de Sousa, as a Commander of the Order of Infante D. Henrique.
In April this year, Jorge Palma received the Career Award at the 8th PLAY – Portuguese Music Awards, granted by decision of the board of Audiogest, the body that represents and manages the rights of multinational, national and independent record labels.

US Army Acquires Long-Range Ukrainian Surveillance Drones in $10.6m Deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
05:22:28 UTC
14:22:28 KST

The US Army is set to acquire Ukrainian-developed Raybird reconnaissance drones under a $10.64 million contract, in a further sign of Kyiv’s growing prominence in drone warfare.
The contract was awarded to Skyeton Inc., the North Las Vegas-based US subsidiary of Ukrainian drone manufacturer Skyeton, according to a Pentagon announcement.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Under the deal, the company will deliver Raybird drones and supporting equipment to Redstone Arsenal, the US Army’s weapons development and testing center in Alabama, by December 15, 2026. The number of aircraft ordered was not disclosed.
Also known as the ACS-3, the Raybird is a medium-sized reconnaissance drone that has been operated by the Ukrainian military since 2018. Skyeton says Raybird systems have accumulated more than 350,000 combat flight hours.
The aircraft is launched using a catapult and recovered by parachute. It can remain airborne for up to 24 hours, travel as far as 2,500 kilometers and transmit live data over distances exceeding 200 kilometers.
Surveillance behind enemy lines
The Raybird can carry up to 6 kilograms of equipment, including surveillance cameras, radar and sensors designed to locate enemy radio signals.
Ukraine has used Raybirds to conduct surveillance deep behind Russian lines, including locating air-defense systems and long-range weapons. Information gathered by the drones can then be passed to artillery units or attack-drone operators.

Skyeton says the Raybird’s protected communications systems allow it to operate amid heavy electronic jamming.
Ukraine has emerged as a major force in drone development and warfare, building a fast-growing industry shaped by direct battlefield experience. The country now has around 450 drone producers, while its broader defense sector comprises more than 1,000 companies.

China breaks ground on the world’s first supercritical CO2 and molten salt energy plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
05:41:58 UTC
14:41:58 KST

China breaks ground on the world’s first supercritical CO2 and molten salt energy plant
Ruitan demonstration project in Shandong aims to reduce energy waste and stabilise grid electricity supply
China has broken ground on the world’s first utility-scale combined supercritical carbon dioxide power generation and molten salt energy storage project, which could help reduce energy waste and improve grid stability.
On September 16, construction began on the Ruitan demonstration project at China Huaneng’s Bajiao power station in Yantai. The project in Shandong province, eastern China, is expected to go into operation next year.
During periods when energy demand is low, surplus electricity generated by the plant’s existing coal power units will be used to heat up molten salt, according to a report by state news agency Xinhua on September 16.
During hours of peak energy demand, the stored heat will power a supercritical unit that uses carbon dioxide rather than steam to produce electricity.
The first phase of the project will feature a 50-megawatt supercritical unit and a 100-megawatt, or 400-megawatt-hour, molten salt energy storage system.
